full: ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd II ibn ʿAbd al-Majīd
primaryTitle: Last Powerful Ottoman Sultan — Pan-Islamic Caliph
bio: Abdülhamid II or Abdul Hamid II was the 34th sultan of the Ottoman Empire, from 1876 to 1909, and the last sultan to exert effective control over the fracturing state. He oversaw a period of decline with rebellions, and presided over an unsuccessful war with the Russian Empire (1877–78), the loss of Egypt, Cyprus, Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro, Tunisia, and Thessaly from Ottoman control (1877–1882), followed by a successful war against Greece in 1897, though Ottoman gains were tempered by subsequent Western European intervention.
bio_full:
Abdülhamid II or Abdul Hamid II (Ottoman Turkish: عبد الحميد ثانی, romanized: Abd ul-Hamid-i s̱ānī; Turkish: II. Abdülhamid; 21 September 1842 – 10 February 1918) was the 34th sultan of the Ottoman Empire, from 1876 to 1909, and the last sultan to exert effective control over the fracturing state. He oversaw a period of decline with rebellions (particularly in the Balkans), and presided over an unsuccessful war with the Russian Empire (1877–78), the loss of Egypt, Cyprus, Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro, Tunisia, and Thessaly from Ottoman control (1877–1882), followed by a successful war against Greece in 1897, though Ottoman gains were tempered by subsequent Western European intervention.
Elevated to power in the wake of Young Ottoman coups, he promulgated the Ottoman Empire's first constitution, a sign of the progressive thinking that marked his early rule. But his enthronement came in the context of the Great Eastern Crisis, which began with the Empire's default on its loans, uprisings by Christian Balkan minorities, and a war with the Russian Empire. At the end of the crisis, Ottoman rule in the Balkans and its international prestige were severely diminished, and the Empire lost its economic sovereignty as its finances came under the control of the Great Powers through the Ottoman Public Debt Administration.
In 1878, Abdul Hamid consolidated his rule by suspending both the constitution and the parliament, purging the Young Ottomans, and curtailing the power of the Sublime Porte. He ruled as an autocrat for three decades. Ideologically an Islamist, the sultan asserted his title of Caliph to Muslims around the world. His paranoia about being overthrown, like his uncle and half-brother, led to the creation of secret police organizations, such as the Yıldız Intelligence Agency and the Umur-u Hafiye, and a censorship regime. The Ottoman Empire's modernization and centralization continued during his reign, including reform of the bureaucracy, extension of the Rumelia Railway and the Anatolia Railway, and construction of the Baghdad Railway and the Hejaz Railway with German assistance. Systems for population registration, sedentarization of tribal groups, and control over the press were part of a unique imperialist system in fringe provinces known as borrowed colonialism. The farthest-reaching reforms were in education through the establishment of many professional schools and a network of primary, secondary, and military schools throughout the Empire.
Ironically, the same educational institutions that the Sultan sponsored proved to be his downfall. Large sections of the Ottoman intelligentsia were discontent with his repressive policies, which coalesced into the Young Turks movement. Ethnic minorities started organizing their own national liberation movements, resulting in insurgencies in Macedonia and Eastern Anatolia. Armenians especially suffered from massacres and pogroms at the hands of the Hamidiye regiments. Of the many assassination attempts during Abdul Hamid's reign, one of the most famous is the Armenian Revolutionary Federation's Yıldız assassination attempt of 1905. In 1908, the Committee of Union and Progress forced him to recall parliament and reinstate the constitution in the Young Turk Revolution. Abdul Hamid II attempted to reassert his absolutism a year later, resulting in his deposition by pro-constitutionalist forces in the 31 March incident, though the role he played in these events is disputed.
Abdul Hamid has been long vilified as a reactionary "Red Sultan" for his tyrannical leadership and condoning of atrocities. It was initial consensus that his personal rule created an era of stagnation which held the Ottoman Empire back from the otherwise dynamic Belle Époque. Recent assessments have highlighted his promotion of education and public works projects, his reign a culmination and advancement of the Tanzimat reforms. Since the AKP's rise to power, scholars have attributed a resurgence in his personality cult an attempt to check Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's established image as the founder of modern Turkey.

Early life

Hamid Efendi was born on 21 September 1842 either in Çırağan Palace, Ortaköy, or at Topkapı Palace, both in Constantinople. He was the son of Sultan Abdulmejid I and Tirimüjgan Kadın (Circassia, 20 August 1819 – Constantinople, Feriye Palace, 2 November 1853), originally named Virjinia. Following his mother's death, he became the adoptive son of his father's legal wife, Perestu Kadın. Perestu was also the adoptive mother of Abdul Hamid's half-sister Cemile Sultan, whose mother Düzdidil Kadın had died in 1845, leaving her motherless at the age of two. The two were brought up in the same household, where they spent their childhood together.
Unlike many other Ottoman sultans, Abdul Hamid II visited distant countries. In the summer of 1867, nine years before he ascended the throne, he accompanied his uncle Sultan Abdul Aziz on a visit to Paris (30 June – 10 July 1867), London (12–23 July 1867), Vienna (28–30 July 1867), and capitals or cities of a number of other European countries.

Accession to the Ottoman throne
Abdul Hamid ascended the throne after his brother Murad was deposed on 31 August 1876. At his accession, some commentators were impressed that he rode practically unattended to the Eyüp Sultan Mosque, where he was presented with the Sword of Osman. Most people expected Abdul Hamid II to support liberal movements, but he acceded to the throne at a critical time. Economic and political turmoil, local wars in the Balkans, and the Russo-Turkish War threatened the Empire's very existence.

First Constitutional Era, 1876–1878
Abdul Hamid worked with the Young Ottomans to realize some form of constitutional arrangement. This new form could help bring about a liberal transition with an Islamic provenance. The Young Ottomans believed that the modern parliamentary system was a restatement of the practice of consultation, or shura, that had existed in early Islam.
In December 1876, due to the 1875 insurrection in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ongoing war with Serbia and Montenegro, and the feeling aroused throughout Europe by the cruelty used in stamping out the 1876 Bulgarian rebellion, Abdul Hamid promulgated a constitution and a parliament. Midhat Pasha headed the commission to establish a new constitution, and the cabinet passed the constitution on 6 December 1876, allowing for a bicameral legislature with senatorial appointments made by the sultan. The first ever election in the Ottoman Empire was held in 1877. Crucially, the constitution gave Abdul Hamid the right to exile anyone he deemed a threat to the state.
The delegates to the Constantinople Conference were surprised by the promulgation of a constitution, but European powers at the conference rejected the constitution as a too-radical change; they preferred the 1856 constitution (Islâhat Hatt-ı Hümâyûnu) or the 1839 Gülhane edict (Hatt-ı Şerif), and questioned whether a parliament was necessary to act as an official voice of the people.
In any event, like many other would-be reforms of the Ottoman Empire, it proved nearly impossible. Russia continued to mobilize for war, and early in 1877 the Ottoman Empire went to war with the Russian Empire.

War with Russia

Abdul Hamid's biggest fear, near dissolution, was realized with the Russian declaration of war on 24 April 1877. In that conflict, the Ottoman Empire fought without help from European allies. Russian chancellor Prince Gorchakov had by that time effectively purchased Austrian neutrality with the Reichstadt Agreement. The British Empire, though still fearing the Russian threat to the British presence in India, did not involve itself in the conflict because of public opinion against the Ottomans, following reports of Ottoman brutality in putting down the Bulgarian uprising. Russia's victory was quick; the conflict ended in February 1878.

bio: Abdullah bin 'Abd Manaf bin al-Nu'man (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Abd Manaf ibn al-Nu'man ibn Sinan al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Abu Nu'aym's Ma'rifat al-Sahaba records that he was present at the Battle of Badr. It cites the lists of Badr participants handed down from Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Lahi'a, which differ on his clan: Musa ibn Uqba's list places him in the Khazraj, Ibn Ishaq's in the Banu al-Nu'man ibn Sinan, and Ibn Lahi'a's, from Urwa, in the Banu Khansa'. Ibn Abd al-Barr also includes him in al-Isti'ab, his dictionary of the Companions. The sources consulted give no other details of his life and no date or place of death.

bio_sources.title: Abu Nu'aym, Ma'rifat al-Sahaba — Abd Allah ibn Abd Manaf ibn al-Nu'man ibn Sinan al-Ansari (Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia)
Index of entries (Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Abd al-Barr) — Abd Allah ibn Abd Manaf ibn al-Nu'man ibn Sinan

bio: Abdullah bin 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayy was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. His original name was al-Hubab, and the Prophet renamed him Abd Allah. His father, Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, is regarded in Muslim tradition as a hypocrite (munafiq), but the son was well regarded. Ibn Hibban describes him as a good Muslim who opposed his father openly for God's sake. He fought at Badr. Abu Nu'aym records that he was wounded at Uhud. In one report, from A'isha, a front tooth was broken and the Prophet told him to take a tooth of gold; another report speaks of an injury to his nose. In 627 he and his father both took part in the campaign against the Banu al-Mustaliq. When his father's hostile words about the Muhajirun reached the Prophet, Abd Allah offered to kill his father himself. The Prophet refused and, in a report from Abu Hurayra, told him to treat his father well. When his father died in 631, Abd Allah asked the Prophet to lead the funeral prayer, and the Prophet agreed. Little else is known of his personal life. He was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Yamama in 633, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr.

bio_sources.title: Wikipedia — Abd-Allah ibn Abd-Allah ibn Ubayy
Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Malik — Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym (Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia)

bio: Abdullah bin 'Abs (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin 'Abs was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formation of the Islamic community in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who joined the nascent Islamic movement during its crucial formative period.

Abdullah bin 'Abs is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the outnumbered Muslim forces led by Prophet Muhammad. Those who participated in this battle, known as the "Companions of Badr" or "Badriyun," hold a special status in Islamic historical accounts due to their role in this pivotal moment.

Based in Medina, Abdullah bin 'Abs was part of the community that formed around the Prophet following the migration from Mecca in 622 CE. This period, known as the Medinan phase of early Islam, was characterized by the establishment of the first Muslim polity and the gradual expansion of Islamic influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

The companions of the Prophet, known collectively as the Sahaba, are regarded in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad. Their testimonies and accounts became foundational sources for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and historical understanding of the early Islamic period.

Abdullah bin 'Abs died in 634 CE, which places his death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the rule of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. This was a period of rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula, though the specific circumstances of Abdullah bin 'Abs's death are not detailed in the available historical sources.

His legacy, like that of other Companions of Badr, rests primarily on his participation in the foundational events of early Islamic history. The Battle of Badr and its participants became subjects of reverence in Islamic historical memory, representing the early struggles and eventual success of the Muslim community in establishing itself as a significant force in Arabian society.

bio: Abdullah bin 'Amir bin Rabi'a (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.

Born around 595 CE in Mecca, he lived during the formative period of the Islamic community and witnessed the religion's emergence and early development.

As a Sahabi (companion of the Prophet), Abdullah bin 'Amir was part of the small but growing Muslim community in Mecca during Islam's earliest years. His family's early conversion to Islam meant that he grew up within the faith rather than converting later in life, making him representative of the second generation of Muslims who were raised in Islamic households from childhood.

Living in Mecca during the early 7th century, Abdullah bin 'Amir experienced firsthand the challenges faced by the early Muslim community, including social pressure and persecution from the established Meccan tribes who opposed the new religious movement. His presence among the companions during this crucial period meant he was a direct witness to the Prophet's teachings and practices.

Abdullah bin 'Amir's significance in Islamic history lies primarily in his role as a transmitter of Islamic knowledge and traditions. As part of the generation that directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad, he served as a link between the Prophet's teachings and subsequent generations of Muslims. His contributions to hadith sciences, the systematic study and preservation of the Prophet's sayings and actions, helped establish the foundation for Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

His relatively short life, ending around 635 CE, coincided with the rapid expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Although he died during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, his role as one of the early-born Muslims provided continuity and authenticity to the transmission of Islamic teachings.

The historical record of Abdullah bin 'Amir bin Rabi'a, while not extensively detailed in terms of specific achievements or major events, represents the broader group of early Muslim companions whose collective efforts in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge proved essential for the religion's development. His status as a companion and his involvement in hadith sciences underscore the importance of the early Muslim community in maintaining the integrity of Islamic teachings for future generations.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Abdullah bin 'Amr (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin 'Amr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he became one of the Sahaba, the term used to describe those who personally knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime.

Abdullah bin 'Amr was based in Medina, the city that became the political and spiritual center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE. As a resident of Medina during this crucial period, he would have witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic state and participated in the community's efforts to defend itself against various threats.

He is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, which took place in 625 CE near Medina. This battle was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community and the Meccan forces, occurring roughly a year after the Muslim victory at the Battle of Badr. The Battle of Uhud proved to be a significant test for the early Muslim community, as it resulted in considerable casualties and strategic challenges.

Abdullah bin 'Amr died in 625 CE as a martyr during the Battle of Uhud, making him one of the companions who gave his life in defense of the nascent Muslim community. His death at approximately 28 years of age reflects the youth of many early Muslims who played important roles in the religion's foundational period.

In Islamic tradition, those who die as martyrs in defense of their faith hold special significance, and Abdullah bin 'Amr's sacrifice at Uhud places him among the revered figures of early Islamic history. The Battle of Uhud itself remains an important event in Islamic historical memory, representing both the challenges faced by the early community and the dedication of companions like Abdullah bin 'Amr who were willing to sacrifice their lives for their beliefs.

His life, though brief, exemplifies the commitment and sacrifice of the early Muslim community during the Prophet Muhammad's lifetime, a period that established the foundations of Islamic civilization and religious practice.

bio: Abdullah bin 'Ayyash bin Abi Rabi'a (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a al-Makhzumi, known as Abu al-Harith, was from the Makhzum clan of Quraysh. He was born in Abyssinia during the Prophet's lifetime, after his father Ayyash had emigrated there. It is said that he saw the Prophet as a child, but this is reported with uncertainty. Al-Bukhari judged a report of him hearing the Prophet directly to be weaker than the version without it, and al-'Ijli describes him as a trustworthy Medinan Successor (tabi'i). He narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas and his father. Those who narrated from him include his son al-Harith, Nafi' the client of Ibn Umar, and Sulayman ibn Yasar. He recited the Qur'an to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and one later dictionary calls him the best reciter of Medina in his time. His Qur'an students included his client Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', Shayba ibn Nisah and Abd al-Rahman ibn Hurmuz. He lived in Mecca and then Medina, and came to Damascus on campaign. Ibn Manzur's abridgement of the History of Damascus states that he was killed in Sistan in 78 AH (c. 697 CE); another source says only that he died after 70 AH.

bio: Abdullah bin 'Umair (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Umayr al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj of Medina who fought at the Battle of Badr. Ibn Sa'd's Tabaqat gives his lineage as Abd Allah ibn Umayr ibn Haritha ibn Tha'laba ibn Khilas ibn Umayya ibn Jidara, and lists him among the Banu al-Abjar, that is Khudra ibn Awf of the Khazraj. Ibn Abd al-Barr's al-Isti'ab gives a different form: Abd Allah ibn Umayr ibn Adi ibn Umayya ibn Khudara ibn Awf ibn al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj. He says all authorities agree that he was at Badr, although the genealogist Ibn Umara did not know of him. Ibn al-Athir's Usd al-Ghaba discusses whether his clan was Khudara or Khudra. Abu Nu'aym notes that Ibn Shihab called him Abd Allah ibn Rabi'. The sources consulted give no date or place of his death.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Abdullah bin 'Unays al-Juhani (c. 591 CE–674 CE, Syria) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin 'Unays al-Juhani was a companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived from approximately 591 to 674 CE. Born in the Arabian Peninsula during the pre-Islamic period, he later settled in Medina and became one of the early converts to Islam.

Abdullah is most notably remembered as one of the participants in the Second Pledge of Aqabah, a pivotal event in early Islamic history that took place around 622 CE. This pledge involved representatives from the tribes of Medina who secretly met with Prophet Muhammad to invite him and his followers to migrate to their city, promising protection and support. The Second Pledge of Aqabah was crucial in establishing the foundation for the Muslim community's move from Mecca to Medina, known as the Hijra, which marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

As a companion of the Prophet, Abdullah bin 'Unays was among those who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community in Medina. The companions, known as Sahaba in Arabic, hold special significance in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who learned directly from the Prophet and helped establish the religious and social foundations of Islam.

Following the Prophet's death in 632 CE, Abdullah continued to live in the expanding Islamic state. He eventually moved to Syria, which had become part of the rapidly growing Islamic empire under the Rashidun Caliphate. Syria served as an important administrative and military center during this period, and many companions settled there as the Islamic community spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Abdullah's association with hadith sciences indicates that he was among those who transmitted reports about the Prophet's sayings, actions, and teachings. This transmission of prophetic traditions was crucial for preserving Islamic religious guidance for future generations, as the companions' accounts formed the basis for much of Islamic law and practice.

He lived through the reigns of all four Rashidun caliphs and witnessed the transformation of Islam from a small community in Medina to a major empire spanning from Spain to Central Asia. Abdullah bin 'Unays died in 674 CE in Syria, having lived for over eight decades and witnessed the most formative period of Islamic civilization. His participation in the Second Pledge of Aqabah ensures his place in Islamic historical memory as one of those who helped facilitate the crucial early development of the Muslim community.

bio: Abdullah bin 'Urfuta bin 'Adi (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Urfuta ibn Adi ibn Umayya ibn Khudara ibn Awf al-Ansari is listed among the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad who fought at the Battle of Badr. He was an ally (halif) of the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj in Medina. Ibn Ishaq and Musa ibn Uqba both name him among those present at Badr. It is also reported that he had emigrated to Abyssinia with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. Ibn al-Athir holds that he is a different man from Abd Allah ibn Umayr, though Ibn Mandah had treated the two as one. The sources consulted give no date or place of his death.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdullah bin Abi Awfa (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Arabia. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa al-Aslami was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and a narrator of hadith, from the tribe of Aslam. His father, known as Abu Awfa, was named Alqama ibn Khalid. Biographers give his kunya variously as Abu Mu'awiya, Abu Ibrahim or Abu Muhammad. Al-Dhahabi counts him among those who took the Pledge of Ridwan, the "Companions of the Tree". He reported that he went on seven campaigns with the Prophet, during which they ate locusts, and that he was wounded in the forearm at the Battle of Hunayn. He was associated with Kufa, where he spent his last years; in old age he lost his sight, and Ibn Hibban notes that he dyed his hair with henna. Among the hadith he transmitted is a supplication of the Prophet asking God to purify him with snow, hail and cold water, recorded in Sunan al-Nasa'i. He reported that Qur'an 3:77 was revealed about a trader who swore falsely in the market that he had been offered more for his goods, and he called such a person a treacherous consumer of usury. Ibn Hibban and al-Dhahabi both state that he was the last of the Prophet's Companions to die in Kufa. Ibn Hibban dates his death to 87 AH; al-Dhahabi gives 86 AH, with 88 AH also reported, and says he was nearly a hundred years old.

full: Abdullah bin Abi Habiba bin al-'Az'ar
primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdullah bin Abi Habiba bin al-'Az'ar (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Abi Habiba bin al-'Az'ar was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early 7th century CE. Born around 600 CE, he was among the Muslims based in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community.

Abdullah bin Abi Habiba is most notably recognized for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree (Bay'at al-Ridwan). This significant event took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah, a location between Mecca and Medina, when the Prophet Muhammad and approximately 1,400 Muslim followers were prevented from completing their pilgrimage to Mecca. Under a tree at this site, the companions pledged their loyalty to the Prophet, demonstrating their willingness to fight if necessary, though the situation was ultimately resolved through negotiation rather than conflict.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds special significance in Islamic history and is referenced in the Quran (48:18), where those who participated are praised for their loyalty and faith. The verse states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree, and that God knew what was in their hearts. This divine approval has given particular honor to all those who took part in this pledge.

As one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, Abdullah bin Abi Habiba was part of a distinguished group within the broader community of Sahaba. The companions who participated in this pledge are considered to have demonstrated exceptional commitment to the Prophet and the early Muslim community during a moment of potential crisis.

Abdullah bin Abi Habiba lived through the crucial early decades of Islam, witnessing the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina and the various challenges it faced. He died around 640 CE, during the period of the early Rashidun Caliphate, having lived through the Prophet's lifetime and into the era of the first caliphs.

While specific details of his individual contributions beyond his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan are not extensively documented, his inclusion among the Companions of the Prophet places him within the foundational generation of Muslims whose presence and support were instrumental in the early development of the Islamic community.

bio: Abdullah bin Abi Talha (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Abi Talha was the son of the Ansari Companion Abu Talha Zayd ibn Sahl, of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj, and of Umm Sulaym bint Milhan, which made him a half-brother of Anas ibn Malik through their mother. His kunya was Abu Yahya. He was born during the Prophet's lifetime; Ibn Sa'd, quoted by Ibn Hajar, places his birth after the Battle of Hunayn. According to the reports, Umm Sulaym conceived him on the night that an earlier son of hers died, and the Prophet prayed for blessing on the couple. When he was born, Anas carried him to the Prophet with some dates sent by Umm Sulaym; the Prophet chewed a date, placed it in the infant's mouth and named him Abd Allah. Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Hajar include him in their dictionaries of Companions. He lived in Medina and narrated few hadith, transmitting from his father and from Anas. He is listed among the narrators of Sahih Muslim. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir state that he fought alongside Ali at Siffin. He had ten sons who had all learned the Qur'an, most of whom transmitted knowledge; the best known were Ishaq, a teacher of Malik ibn Anas, and Abd Allah. Reports of his death differ. Al-Dhahabi and Ibn al-Athir say he died in Medina during the caliphate of al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik, while Ibn Hajar cites a report giving 84 AH in Medina; Abu Nu'aym says he was martyred in Fars.

bio: Abdullah bin al-Arqam (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Katib al-Wahy — Scribe of the Revelation.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn al-Arqam ibn Abd Yaghuth was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Zuhra of Quraysh. Ibn al-Athir notes that the Prophet's mother, Amina bint Wahb, was the aunt of his father al-Arqam. He accepted Islam in the year of the Conquest of Mecca. He served as a scribe for the Prophet, answering letters on his behalf, including letters to kings; according to a report of Ibn Ishaq, the Prophet trusted him so fully that he had him seal such letters without reading them. After the Prophet's death he wrote for Abu Bakr, and later for Umar. Umar put him in charge of the treasury (bayt al-mal), and according to Ibn Abd al-Barr he held the post for the whole of Umar's caliphate and two years of Uthman's, until he asked Uthman to relieve him and Uthman agreed. When Uthman offered him a large sum for his service (thirty thousand in Malik's report, and other amounts in other versions), he refused, saying that he had worked only for God. Umar is reported to have said that he had not seen anyone who feared God more than Abd Allah ibn al-Arqam. He went blind before his death, and he died during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan.

bio: Abdullah bin al-Harith (c. 569–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi was an early Muslim of the Banu Sahm clan of Quraysh; genealogists differ slightly on the names in his lineage. His mother was Umm al-Hajjaj, of the Banu Shanuq of Kinana. He accepted Islam early and was among the Muslims who made the second emigration to Abyssinia, together with several of his brothers, among them al-Sa'ib and Abu Qays. He was a poet and was known as al-Mubriq, a name linked to a line of his verse beginning "idha ana lam abriq". Ibn Ishaq preserves verses he composed in Abyssinia after the Muslims had found security under the Negus and could worship God without fear. In other verses he reproached Quraysh for rejecting faith, comparing them to the peoples of Ad, Madyan and Thamud. Accounts of his death differ: one report says he and his brother al-Sa'ib were killed as martyrs at al-Ta'if; another says he and his brother Abu Qays were killed at al-Yamama; and Ibn Ishaq states that he died in Abyssinia.

bio: Abdullah bin al-Humayyir (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin al-Humayyir was a companion (sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the foundational period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he witnessed and participated in the early development of the Muslim community during the late 6th and early 7th centuries.

As one of the companions of the Prophet, Abdullah bin al-Humayyir was part of the close-knit group of early Muslims who accepted Islam during Muhammad's prophetic mission. He was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Islamic state after the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the political and spiritual capital of the growing Muslim community, and companions like Abdullah bin al-Humayyir played crucial roles in supporting the Prophet's mission and helping establish Islamic practices and governance.

Abdullah bin al-Humayyir is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE. This battle holds immense significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. The Battle of Badr is considered a turning point that demonstrated the strength and divine support of the early Muslim state. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr, known as the "Companions of Badr," hold a special status in Islamic tradition due to their participation in this pivotal event.

The companions who participated in Badr are regarded as having made exceptional sacrifices for the early Muslim community during a critical period when the survival of Islam was uncertain. Their willingness to risk their lives in defense of their faith and community contributed directly to Islam's ability to establish itself as a lasting religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula.

Abdullah bin al-Humayyir died in 634 CE, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. His death occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, when the Muslim community was beginning its expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the leadership of the first caliph, Abu Bakr. As one of the surviving companions from the Prophet's era, his passing marked the gradual transition from the generation that had direct contact with Muhammad to the subsequent generations who would carry forward the Islamic tradition based on the teachings and examples preserved by the companions.

Abdullah bin al-Jadd bin Qays bin Sakhr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the Prophet's time there.

Abdullah is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, meaning he participated in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the town of Badr, located between Mecca and Medina, and marked a turning point in the establishment of the Islamic state.

The designation "Companion of Badr" carries special honor in Islamic historical tradition, as those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad in this pivotal battle are remembered for their early commitment to the faith and their role in securing the survival of the nascent Muslim community. The battle involved approximately 300 Muslim fighters facing a much larger Meccan army, making their victory particularly significant for the morale and future of the Islamic movement.

As a Sahaba, or Companion of the Prophet, Abdullah belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the revelation and early implementation of Islamic teachings. The Sahaba are considered important figures in Islamic history as they served as the primary transmitters of Islamic knowledge, practices, and traditions to subsequent generations.

Abdullah's tribal lineage traces back through the bin al-Jadd bin Qays bin Sakhr family line, indicating his integration into the established social structures of Arabian society during the pre-Islamic and early Islamic periods. His presence in Medina suggests he was part of the community that welcomed the Prophet during the Hijra or joined the Muslim community after Muhammad's arrival in the city.

He died in 634 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate following the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This places his death during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph, as the Islamic community was expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula and establishing its administrative and military structures across the region.

bio: Abdullah bin al-Nu'man bin Baldama (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin al-Nu'man bin Baldama was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he became one of the Sahaba, the Arabic term for the companions who lived during the time of Prophet Muhammad and embraced Islam.

Abdullah is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as a "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the town of Badr, located between Mecca and Medina, and is considered a pivotal moment that helped establish the nascent Islamic state.

The designation "Companion of Badr" carries special weight in Islamic historical records, as those who participated in this battle are regarded with particular reverence within the Muslim community. The Battle of Badr involved approximately 300 Muslims facing a much larger Meccan army, and their unexpected victory was seen as divine validation of their cause.

Based in Medina, Abdullah would have witnessed the crucial early years of the Islamic community's development following the Hijra, the Prophet's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. This period saw the establishment of the first Islamic state and the implementation of foundational Islamic principles in governance and society.

As a Sahabi, Abdullah belonged to the generation that received Islamic teachings directly from Prophet Muhammad and participated in the religious and social transformation of Arabian society. The companions played essential roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, practices, and historical accounts to subsequent generations.

Abdullah bin al-Nu'man bin Baldama died in 634 CE, which coincided with the period immediately following Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This places his death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph, as the Islamic community began its expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

His life span encompassed the entire prophetic period of Muhammad's mission and the initial phase of Islamic expansion, making him a witness to the foundational era of Islamic civilization.

Genealogists disagree about his lineage; he is placed in the clan of Banu Sa'ida of the Khazraj. He fought alongside the Prophet at the Battle of Badr. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir include him in their dictionaries of Companions.
