bio: Abdullah bin Jahsh (c. 593–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Jahsh was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and his brother-in-law. His father, Jahsh ibn Riyab, had come to Mecca from the tribe of Asad, and his mother, Umayma bint Abd al-Muttalib, was of the Hashim clan of Quraysh. His sister Zaynab bint Jahsh became one of the Prophet's wives. He was born in Mecca c. 586 and accepted Islam through the influence of Abu Bakr. He joined the second emigration to Abyssinia in 616, returned to Mecca in late 619, and was among the first to emigrate to Medina in 622. In Rajab of 2 AH (October 623) the Prophet sent him with seven other Emigrants to Nakhla, where they attacked a Qurayshi caravan during the sacred month, killing one man and capturing two. The Prophet at first disapproved, saying, "I did not instruct you to fight in the sacred month," and a revelation later addressed the matter. He fought at Badr and then at Uhud, where he was killed in 625 at about the age of forty; his family reported that his body was mutilated. He is buried in Medina. He married Fatima bint Abi Hubaysh, and they had a son, Muhammad. He was described as neither tall nor short, with a lot of hair.

bio_sources.title: Wikipedia — Abd Allah ibn Jahsh

bio: Abdullah bin Jubayr (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Jubayr ibn al-Nu'man was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Tha'laba ibn Amr ibn Awf, a branch of the Aws. His brother Khawwat ibn Jubayr was also a Companion. He was present at the Pledge of Aqaba among the seventy Ansar who pledged allegiance to the Prophet, and he fought at Badr, where, according to WikiShia, he captured Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi, husband of the Prophet's daughter Zaynab. At the Battle of Uhud in 3 AH (625) the Prophet appointed him commander of the archers, fifty in number, posted on the hill of Aynayn, ordering them to hold their position and protect the Muslims' rear. When the Muslims appeared to be winning, most of the archers left their posts to collect spoils; Abd Allah and fewer than ten others stayed, and he reminded the rest of the Prophet's command, but they refused. Khalid ibn al-Walid saw that the hill was weakly held and charged with cavalry. Abd Allah shot until his arrows ran out, then fought with a spear until it broke, and then with a sword, until he was killed; Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl is named as his killer. The Quraysh mutilated his body. He is buried in the Uhud cemetery.

bio_sources.title: Arabic Wikipedia — Abd Allah ibn Jubayr
WikiShia (draft) — Abd Allah b. Jubayr

bio: Abdullah bin Ka'b (c. 594–650 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Amr al-Mazini was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Mazin of the Ansar, with the kunya Abu al-Harith. One version of his lineage is Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Amr ibn Awf ibn Mabdhul ibn Amr ibn Ghanm al-Mazini, though other versions exist. He fought at Badr, and the Prophet entrusted him with guarding the spoils on the return from Badr to Medina. He also fought at Uhud and in all the other campaigns alongside the Prophet. Al-Baghawi lists him in his dictionary of Companions as al-Mazini al-Ansari al-Badri. He died in 30 AH, and Uthman ibn Affan led the funeral prayer over him.

bio_sources.title: Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Amr
Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abd Allah ibn Ka'b al-Mazini al-Ansari al-Badri (al-Baghawi, Mu'jam al-Sahaba, index entry)

bio: Abdullah bin Makhramah Al-Amiri was one of the first companions to Islam. He immigrated to Abyssinia in the second migration, then immigrated to Yathrib, and witnessed all the scenes with the Prophet Muhammad. Then, after the death of the Prophet Muhammad, he participated in the wars of apostasy, and was killed in the Battle of Al-Yamamah.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Makhrama ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Abi Qays al-Amiri, known by the kunya Abu Muhammad, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy of Quraysh. His mother was Bahnana bint Safwan. He was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca. Sources differ on his emigration to Abyssinia. Ibn Ishaq lists him among those who went in the second emigration with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, al-Waqidi says he made both emigrations, and Musa ibn Uqba and Abu Ma'shar do not name him among the emigrants to Abyssinia. He later emigrated to Medina, where he stayed with Kulthum ibn al-Hidm, and the Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Farwa ibn Amr al-Bayadi of the Ansar. He fought at Badr at the age of thirty, and at Uhud, the Trench and all the other campaigns with the Prophet. Ibn al-Athir describes him as virtuous and devout. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Abi Hatim record that he prayed not to die until he had been wounded in every joint for God's cause, and that he was struck in his joints at Yamama. After the Prophet's death he fought in the Ridda wars, and he was killed at the Battle of Yamama in 12 AH, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, at the age of forty-one. Ibn Umar reported finding him mortally wounded there; he asked whether the fasting person had broken his fast, and Ibn Umar brought him water in a shield, but he died before he could drink. He left a son, Musahiq, whose mother was Zaynab bint Suraqa ibn al-Mu'tamir, and his descendants remained in Medina.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abdullah b. Makhrama b. Abd al-Uzza (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, Ibn Hibban, al-Baghawi, Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Abi Hatim)
Arabic Wikipedia — عبد الله بن مخرمة

bio: Abdullah bin Maz'un (c. 594–650 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Maz'un was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived from approximately 594 to 650 CE during the early formative period of Islam. He was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of Islamic history in seventh-century Arabia.

Abdullah belonged to the Jumahi clan of the Quraysh tribe in Mecca, the same tribal confederation as the Prophet Muhammad. His family name "bin Maz'un" indicates he was the son of Maz'un, connecting him to other notable early Muslim figures who shared this lineage. This tribal affiliation placed him within the social and political networks of Meccan society during the emergence of Islam.

He is most notably recognized as a participant in the Battle of Badr in 622 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against their Meccan opponents. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are accorded special recognition in Islamic tradition for their role in this pivotal moment.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Abdullah bin Maz'un was part of the close circle of early converts who directly witnessed the Prophet's teachings and actions. The companions collectively played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting the religious practices, sayings, and customs that would later form the foundation of Islamic jurisprudence and religious scholarship.

His lifespan of fifty-six years encompassed the most significant period of early Islamic expansion, from the initial revelations in Mecca through the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina and the subsequent spread of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. He lived through the Prophet's death in 632 CE and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the first caliphs.

While specific details about his individual contributions to Islamic jurisprudence or other religious sciences are not extensively documented in the most reliable historical sources, his status as a companion who participated in Badr places him among the revered early Muslims whose proximity to the Prophet Muhammad gave them authority in matters of religious practice and Islamic teaching.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Abdullah bin Mirba' bin Qayzi (c. 597–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Mirba' bin Qayzi was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the Prophet's time there.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Abdullah bin Mirba' bin Qayzi was part of the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community. The companions hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Abdullah bin Mirba' bin Qayzi is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, where he died in 636 CE and is honored as a martyr. The Battle of Uhud was a significant military engagement between the early Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces, taking place on the slopes of Mount Uhud near Medina. This battle was one of several key conflicts during the early expansion of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula.

His death at Uhud places him among those companions who made the ultimate sacrifice in defense of the early Muslim community during a critical period in Islamic history. The Battle of Uhud, while presenting challenges for the Muslim forces, was part of the series of events that ultimately led to the consolidation of Muslim power in the region and the eventual peaceful conquest of Mecca.

The companions who died at Uhud are remembered in Islamic tradition for their dedication and sacrifice during the formative years of the faith. Their participation in these early struggles helped establish the foundations upon which the later Islamic empire would be built. As with many of the early companions, Abdullah bin Mirba' bin Qayzi represents the first generation of Muslims whose commitment to their faith during its most vulnerable period was crucial to its survival and eventual flourishing.

His life span of approximately thirty-nine years encompassed the entire Meccan period of Muhammad's prophethood and the early Medinan period, making him a witness to the complete transformation of Arabian society during the rise of Islam.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdullah bin Mughfal al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Mughfal al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he belonged to the Muzayna tribe and became one of the Sahaba, the generation of Muslims who directly knew and followed the Prophet.

Abdullah bin Mughfal is most notably recognized as one of the participants in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree. This significant event took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah, near Mecca, when approximately 1,400 Muslims pledged their loyalty to Prophet Muhammad under a tree. The Quran references this pledge in verse 48:18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those who gave their allegiance. This event is considered pivotal in early Islamic history as it demonstrated the unwavering commitment of the early Muslim community during a tense period of negotiations with the Meccan tribes.

As a member of the Sahaba, Abdullah bin Mughfal would have been among those who transmitted the teachings and practices of the Prophet Muhammad to subsequent generations. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and passing down the hadith literature, which forms one of the fundamental sources of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. His contributions to hadith sciences represent part of the broader effort by the Prophet's companions to maintain the accuracy and authenticity of Islamic teachings.

Living in the Hijaz region, the heartland of early Islam that includes the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, Abdullah bin Mughfal witnessed the formative years of the Muslim community. This was a period of rapid expansion and consolidation of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions from this era are particularly revered in Islamic tradition for their direct connection to the Prophet and their role in establishing the foundations of the Muslim community.

Abdullah bin Mughfal al-Mazni died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate. His legacy, like that of other companions, rests primarily on his participation in key historical events such as the Pledge of Ridwan and his contribution to the preservation of Islamic teachings through the hadith tradition. His life represents the dedication of the early Muslim community during Islam's foundational period.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdullah bin Qatada ibn al-Nu'man (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_note: No source found for a longer biography

bio: Abdullah bin Qays (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Qays ibn Khalida ibn al-Harith ibn Sawad ibn Malik ibn Ghanm was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu al-Najjar branch of the Khazraj. One modern summary gives his lineage as Abdullah ibn Qays ibn Khalid ibn Khalda. He fought at the Battle of Badr and at the Battle of Uhud. Sources disagree about his death. Al-Waqidi, as reported by Ibn Sa'd, says he was not killed at Uhud but survived, took part in the Prophet's later campaigns, and died during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan. Ibn Umara al-Ansari, also reported by Ibn Sa'd, says instead that he was killed as a martyr at Uhud. Ibn Sa'd records that his wife Su'ad bint Qays ibn Makhlad was the mother of his sons Abd al-Rahman and Umayra, and that he also had a daughter, Umm Awn. Ibn Sa'd also notes that his line did not continue.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abdullah b. Qays (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: Abdullah b. Qays b. Khalida)
Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — عبد الله بن قيس بن خالد

bio: Abdullah bin Qays b Sakhr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Qays ibn Sakhr, whose lineage is also given as Abdullah ibn Qays ibn Sayfi ibn Sakhr, ibn Haram ibn Rabi'a ibn Adi ibn Ghanm ibn Ka'b ibn Salama, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the clan of Banu Salama. Ibn Ishaq, Abu Ma'shar, al-Waqidi and Ibn Umara al-Ansari list him among those who fought at the Battle of Badr, while Musa ibn Uqba does not include him in his list. His brother Ma'bad ibn Qays also fought at Badr. Abdullah also fought at the Battle of Uhud. Ibn Sa'd records that he left no descendants. The sources consulted give no date or place of his death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abdullah b. Qays (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: Abdullah b. Qays b. Sayfi b. Sakhr)
Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — عبد الله بن قيس بن صخر

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Abdullah bin Qayzi bin Qays (c. 597–635 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Qayzi bin Qays was a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the Muslims who lived in Medina during the Prophet's time there, making him part of the community that formed the foundation of the early Islamic state.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Abdullah bin Qayzi bin Qays would have been directly involved in the development of the Muslim community during its crucial early years. The companions played essential roles in supporting the Prophet's mission, participating in the establishment of Islamic practices, and helping to spread the faith throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Abdullah bin Qayzi bin Qays is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, one of the significant military engagements during the early Islamic period. This battle took place in 625 CE near Medina, where Muslim forces faced the Meccan army. The battle was a pivotal moment in early Islamic history, testing the resolve and faith of the Muslim community during a period of external pressure and conflict.

He earned the distinction of being known as the "Martyr of the Battle of Uhud," indicating that he died fighting in this engagement. In Islamic tradition, those who die in battle defending their faith and community are honored as martyrs (shahids), a status that carries particular religious significance.

His death in 635 CE, approximately ten years after the Battle of Uhud mentioned in his title, suggests either that the martyrdom reference relates to his participation and wounding in that battle rather than his death there, or that his association with Uhud reflects his distinguished service in that campaign even though he died later. The exact circumstances would require additional historical verification.

As one of the companions who lived through the Prophet's time in Medina, Abdullah bin Qayzi bin Qays represents the generation of early Muslims who directly witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community. These individuals played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam to subsequent generations, making their contributions fundamental to the religion's historical development and continuity.

bio: Abdullah bin Rabi' bin Qays (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn al-Rabi' ibn Qays ibn Amir ibn Abbad ibn al-Abjar was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. He belonged to the Banu Khudra, also called al-Abjar, of the Khazraj; Ibn al-Athir gives his great-grandfather's name as Amr rather than Amir. His mother was Fatima bint Amr ibn Atiyya of the Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar. According to Ibn Sa'd, he was present at the Pledge of al-Aqaba with the seventy Ansar. Ibn Ishaq lists him among the men of the Khazraj who fought at the Battle of Badr, and Urwa also names him as a Badr participant. Ibn Sa'd adds that he fought at the Battle of Uhud. He had two sons, Abd al-Rahman and Sa'd, whose mother was from the tribe of Tayy. Ibn Sa'd notes that his line later died out. The sources consulted do not give the date or place of his death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abdullah b. al-Rabi' b. Qays (Ibn Sa'd; Usd al-Ghaba)
Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — عبد الله بن الربيع

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdullah bin Sa'd bin Khaythama (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Khaythama al-Ansari al-Awsi, known by the kunya Abu Khaythama, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Amr ibn Awf of the Aws in Medina. Al-Baghawi gives his lineage as Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Khaythama ibn Ghanm ibn al-Salm ibn Malik ibn Aws ibn Haritha. He and his father were both Companions. His father, Sa'd ibn Khaythama, was killed at Badr, and his grandfather Khaythama was killed at Uhud. Reports differ on which events he attended. In a narration from al-Mughira ibn Hakim, he said he witnessed Badr, and al-Aqaba, riding behind his father; this version is recorded by al-Bukhari, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Nu'aym and al-Baghawi, and Ibn Hibban also says he witnessed Badr and al-Aqaba. Ibn Abd al-Barr prefers a version transmitted by Ibn al-Mubarak, in which he said he witnessed Uhud with the Prophet, riding behind his father. Al-Waqidi, quoted by al-Baghawi, held that the Badr report is a mistake and that he witnessed neither Badr nor Uhud, but was present with the Prophet at al-Hudaybiyya and Khaybar. Ibn Hibban states that he died in Medina. The sources consulted give no year of death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abdullah b. Sa'd b. Khaythama al-Ansari al-Awsi (al-Isti'ab, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Baghawi)

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Abdullah bin Sa'sa'a (c. 597–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Sa'sa'a ibn Wahb ibn Adi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Khazraj and then the Banu al-Najjar. He took part in the Battle of Uhud and the campaigns that followed it. He was later killed at the Battle of the Bridge of Abu Ubayd (Jisr Abi Ubayd). Ibn Hajar notes in al-Isaba that he was mentioned by al-Adawi, and that Ibn Fathun and Ibn al-Athir added him to the works on the Companions. He also has entries in Ibn al-Athir's Usd al-Ghaba and al-Dhahabi's Tajrid.

bio_sources.title: Ibn al-Amin, al-Istidrak 'ala al-Isti'ab — عبد الله بن صعصعة بن وهب (shamela.ws, citing al-Isaba, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Tajrid)

bio: Abdullah bin Sahl bin Zayd (c. 594–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Sahl bin Zayd was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he resided in Medina, the city that became the second holiest site in Islam and served as the base for the early Muslim community following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Abdullah bin Sahl is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and involved around 300 Muslim fighters facing a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory at Badr was considered pivotal in establishing the credibility and survival of the early Islamic state.

Those who fought at Badr alongside the Prophet Muhammad hold a special status in Islamic tradition, known as the Badr Companions or "Badriyyun." This group is particularly revered because they stood with the Muslim community during one of its most vulnerable and crucial moments, when the survival of Islam as a religious and political movement hung in the balance. Their participation in this battle is viewed as a testament to their faith and commitment to the early Muslim cause.

Abdullah bin Sahl's life span coincided with the most dynamic period of early Islamic expansion, witnessing the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established political entity in Medina. He lived through the Prophet's migration, the establishment of the first Muslim state, and the initial military campaigns that secured the community's survival against hostile neighboring tribes and cities.

His death in 626 CE occurred during the continued consolidation of Muslim power in the Arabian Peninsula, just a few years before the Prophet Muhammad's own death in 632 CE. Like many of the early companions, Abdullah bin Sahl's legacy rests primarily on his presence during these foundational years and his participation in the events that shaped the early trajectory of Islamic civilization. His status as a Badr Companion ensures his remembrance in Islamic historical accounts as one of those who supported the Prophet during a critical juncture in Islamic history.

bio: Abdullah bin Salma bin Malik (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Salma bin Malik was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formation of the Islamic community in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims residing in Medina during the crucial early years of Islam's development.

Abdullah bin Salma is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The encounter took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and involved roughly 300 Muslims facing a much larger Meccan army.

The participants in the Battle of Badr, known collectively as the Badr companions, hold a distinguished position within Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment. The battle's outcome helped establish the military credibility of the nascent Muslim state and marked a turning point in the relationship between the Muslim community in Medina and their opponents in Mecca.

As a resident of Medina, Abdullah bin Salma would have witnessed the transformation of the city following the Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina became the first Islamic state's capital and the center from which Islamic governance, law, and community practices developed. The companions who lived through this period played essential roles in preserving and transmitting the early Islamic teachings and practices.

Abdullah bin Salma's life was relatively brief, as he died in 625 CE, likely around the age of thirty. His death occurred during the formative period of the Islamic community, just a few years after the establishment of the Muslim presence in Medina and shortly after the significant victory at Badr.

While specific details about Abdullah bin Salma's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, his status as a companion of the Prophet Muhammad places him among those early Muslims who directly interacted with the Prophet and participated in the foundational events of Islamic history. The companions, collectively known as the Sahaba, are regarded as crucial links in the transmission of Islamic knowledge, practices, and historical accounts from the time of the Prophet to subsequent generations.

bio: Abdullah bin Sufyan (c. 593–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Sufyan was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 593 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early converts to Islam during its initial spread in Mecca.

Abdullah bin Sufyan is most notably remembered as one of the Muslims who participated in the emigration to Abyssinia (present-day Ethiopia), which occurred around 615 CE. This migration, known as the first Hijra, took place when the early Muslim community in Mecca faced increasing persecution from the Quraysh tribe and other opponents of the new faith. The Prophet Muhammad advised a group of his followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, whose ruler, the Negus, was known for his justice and tolerance.

The emigrants to Abyssinia included both men and women from various clans and social backgrounds, representing some of the most committed early believers who were willing to leave their homes and tribal protections for their faith. This migration demonstrated the international dimension of early Islam and the community's adaptability in seeking sanctuary beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

As a companion of the Prophet, Abdullah bin Sufyan would have been among those who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions, known as Sahaba in Arabic, hold a special place in Islamic history as the first generation of Muslims who learned directly from the Prophet and later transmitted Islamic knowledge and practices to subsequent generations.

Abdullah bin Sufyan is associated with the early ascetic tradition within Islam, suggesting he may have emphasized spiritual devotion, simplicity, and detachment from worldly concerns. This ascetic approach was present among some early Muslims who sought to focus intensively on worship and spiritual development.

He died in 636 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate period, when the Muslim community was expanding rapidly beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the leadership of the first four caliphs. His life span covered the crucial period from Islam's emergence through its establishment as a major force in the region, making him a witness to one of history's most significant religious and political transformations.

bio: Abdullah bin Suhayl (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Suhayl ibn Amr ibn Abd Shams al-Amiri, known by the kunya Abu Suhayl, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy of Quraysh. He was the son of the Qurashi leader Suhayl ibn Amr and the elder brother of Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl. His mother was Fakhita bint Amir ibn Nawfal. He accepted Islam in Mecca. Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi, as reported by Ibn Abd al-Barr, say he made the second emigration to Abyssinia; another account says he is reported to have gone in the first. When he returned to Mecca, his father held him back and pressured him to abandon his faith. He went out to Badr with his father in the Quraysh army while hiding his Islam, and when the Prophet camped at Badr he left the Meccans and joined the Muslims. He fought at Badr and in all the later campaigns with the Prophet. He was one of the witnesses to the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya. On the day of the Conquest of Mecca he asked the Prophet to grant his father safety, and the Prophet agreed. He was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Yamama in 12 AH, at the age of thirty-eight.

bio_sources.title: Tarajm — عبد الله بن سهيل بن عمرو (al-Isti'ab, al-Isaba)
Wikipedia — Abdullah ibn Suhayl (citing Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat vol. 3)

bio: Abdullah bin Suraqa bin Al-Mu'tamir Al-Adawi Al-Qurashi is a distinguished companion from Quraysh. Ibn Ishaq said that Abdullah witnessed the Battle of Badr with the Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings of God be upon him, and the scenes that followed it. Al-Waqidi and Musa bin Uqba said that he did not witness Badr, but he witnessed the Battle of Uhud and the scenes that followed it. He is the brother of the companion Amr bin Suraqa.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Suraqa ibn al-Mu'tamir ibn Anas al-Adawi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Banu Adi ibn Ka'b of Quraysh, the clan of Umar ibn al-Khattab. His brother was the Companion Amr ibn Suraqa. He emigrated from Mecca to Medina with his brother Amr and stayed with Rifa'a ibn Abd al-Mundhir. Sources disagree over whether he fought at Badr. Ibn Ishaq and al-Zubayr say that he did, while Musa ibn Uqba, Abu Ma'shar and al-Waqidi say he did not. He fought at Uhud, the Trench and all the later campaigns with the Prophet. He narrated the hadith "Take the pre-dawn meal (suhur), even if only with water." Ibn Sa'd, citing Ibn Ishaq, says he left no descendants. The classical sources consulted give no date of death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abdullah b. Suraqa b. al-Mu'tamir b. Anas (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Abu Nu'aym)
Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — عبد الله بن سراقة بن المعتمر

bio: Abdullah Bin Tariq was a companion of the Islamic Prophet Muhammad. He was killed during the Expedition of Al Raji. In 625 some men requested that Muhammad send instructors to teach them Islam, but the men were bribed by the two tribes of Khuzaymah who wanted revenge for the assassination of Khalid bin Sufyan by Muhammad's followers and they killed the Muslims After killing Asim ibn Thabit, Hudhayl wanted to sell his head.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Tariq ibn Amr ibn Malik al-Balawi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the tribe of Bali, of Quda'a, and an ally of the Banu Zafar of the Ansar in Medina. His maternal half-brother, Mu'attib ibn Ubayd, also fought at Badr. Abdullah fought at the Battles of Badr and Uhud. He was one of the small group of Muslims sent with men of the tribes of Adal and al-Qara to teach them Islam. At al-Raji', a watering place of Hudhayl, the group was betrayed and attacked. Abdullah was one of three men who surrendered and were taken as prisoners to be sold in Mecca, together with Khubayb and Zayd. At Marr al-Zahran he pulled his hand free from the rope and drew his sword, and his captors drew back from him and stoned him to death. He was buried at Marr al-Zahran. Ibn Sa'd dates these events to Safar, thirty-six months after the Hijra, while Ibn al-Athir places the mission at the end of 3 AH. Ibn Sa'd records that he left no descendants. The poet Hassan ibn Thabit mentioned the men of al-Raji' in his verse.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abdullah b. Tariq, ally of Banu Zafar (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Baghawi)
Wikipedia — Abd Allah bin Tariq

bio: Abdullah bin Tha'laba bin Hazama (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abdullah bin Tha'laba bin Hazama was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. He was among the early Muslims who lived in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community in the early 7th century.

Abdullah is historically recognized as one of the "Companions of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as it was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The battle took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the outnumbered Muslim forces led by Prophet Muhammad.

The participants in the Battle of Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as they were among the early supporters who stood with the Prophet during a critical moment when the survival of the nascent Muslim community was at stake. The Quranic revelation later praised the participants of this battle, cementing their elevated status among the companions.

As a resident of Medina, Abdullah would have witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic state and the development of many foundational Islamic practices and laws. The Medinan period, from 622 to 632 CE, was crucial for the consolidation of the Muslim community and the expansion of Islamic influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Abdullah bin Tha'laba bin Hazama died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. This places his death during the period of the Ridda Wars, when various Arabian tribes challenged the central authority of the Islamic state following the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

His life span covered the most transformative period in early Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's mission, the establishment of the Islamic community in Medina, and into the early expansion period under the first Caliph. As one of the Companions of Badr, he remains a recognized figure in Islamic historical records, representing the early generation of Muslims who directly supported and witnessed the foundational events of Islamic civilization.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdullah bin Yazid bin Zayd (c. 600 CE–692 CE, Kufa) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Yazid ibn Zayd al-Khatmi was a young Companion of the Prophet from the Ansar of Medina, of the Khatma clan of the Aws tribe. His father, Yazid ibn Zayd, was also a Companion. Ibn Abd al-Barr and al-Baghawi, citing al-Waqidi, report that he was present at al-Hudaybiya at the age of seventeen, and Abu Nu'aym counts him among those who took the Pledge of Ridwan. Scholars differed over his status: Abu Dawud noted that some described him as one who had seen the Prophet rather than a full Companion, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal did not consider his companionship sound, while Abu Hatim accepted it conditionally and al-Daraqutni affirmed it. His kunya is usually given as Abu Musa. He is recorded as fighting at the Battle of the Bridge, and later with Ali ibn Abi Talib at the Camel, Siffin and Nahrawan. He settled in Kufa and governed it on behalf of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr; Abu Nu'aym dates his appointment to 65 AH, and the scholar al-Sha'bi served as his secretary. He narrated hadith from the Prophet. Those who narrated from him include his daughter's son Adi ibn Thabit, Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, al-Sha'bi and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. He died in Kufa during Ibn al-Zubayr's rule. One entry places his death after 70 AH, while another account says he died before 70 AH, at about eighty years of age.

bio_sources.title: Arabic Wikipedia — عبد الله بن يزيد الخطمي
Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — al-Isti'ab, Ma'rifat al-Sahaba (Abu Nu'aym), al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil etc.: عبد الله بن يزيد الخطمي
Shamela narrator entry (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib / Taqrib / Tuhfat al-Tahsil) — عبد الله بن يزيد الخطمي

bio: Abdullah bin Zayd (c. 594–654 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Tha'laba ibn Abd Rabbih al-Ansari, known by the kunya Abu Muhammad, was a Companion of the Prophet from the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj of Medina. He is known as Sahib al-Adhan, 'the man of the call to prayer', because the adhan was shown to him in a dream. He was present at the Pledge of al-Aqaba and fought at the Battle of Badr. Al-Bukhari is reported to have known only one hadith from him, the one concerning the adhan, and a small number of his narrations appear in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah. According to Ibn Hibban, he died in Medina in 32 AH, and the caliph Uthman ibn Affan led his funeral prayer. A different report, mentioned by Ibn Hajar, says that he was martyred at Uhud. He is a different person from his namesake Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Asim al-Mazini, who narrated the hadith describing the Prophet's ablution.

bio_sources.title: Tohed narrator entry (Ibn Hibban, Ibn Hajar's Taqrib) — عبد الله بن زيد بن ثعلبة بن عبد ربه
Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — al-Kalabadhi's note distinguishing him from Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Asim

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdullah bin Zayd Mazni (c. 600 CE–681 CE, Madinah, al-Harrah) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Asim al-Ansari al-Mazini, known as Ibn Umm Umara and by the kunya Abu Muhammad, was a Companion of the Prophet from the Khazraj of Medina. His mother was Umm Umara, Nusayba bint Ka'b, and his brothers were Habib and Tamim. He fought at Uhud and other battles. Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym say he also fought at Badr, but Ibn Abd al-Barr says he did not, and Ibn al-Athir considered that the correct view. His brother Habib was killed by Musaylima, and at the Battle of al-Yamama Abdullah took part in killing Musaylima: Wahshi struck him with a spear and Abdullah struck him with his sword. He narrated the well-known hadith describing the Prophet's ablution, as well as reports on the prayer for rain. Those who narrated from him include his nephew Abbad ibn Tamim, Yahya ibn Umara, Wasi' ibn Habban and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. Most sources say he was killed at the Battle of al-Harra in Medina in Dhu al-Hijja 63 AH, under Yazid ibn Mu'awiya. Al-Suyuti gives his age as about seventy, and Ibn Hibban as seventy-three. Ibn Sa'd adds that two of his sons, Khallad and Ali, were killed with him. Al-Kalabadhi also records other reported death years, 32 AH and 64 AH. He is a different person from Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Abd Rabbih, who was shown the adhan in a dream.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd, al-Kalabadhi, Siyar etc.: عبد الله بن زيد بن عاصم المازني

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Abdullah ibn 'Amr bin Haram (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century CE. Born around 594 CE, he belonged to the Khazraj tribe, one of the two major Arab tribes that inhabited the city then known as Yathrib, which would later become Medina.

Abdullah ibn 'Amr is historically significant as one of the participants in the First Pledge of Aqabah, which took place around 621 CE. This pledge marked a crucial moment in early Islamic history when a group of men from Medina traveled to meet Muhammad during the annual pilgrimage season near Mecca. At a location called Aqabah, these individuals formally accepted Islam and pledged their allegiance to the Prophet, promising to worship Allah alone, avoid theft, adultery, infanticide, and slander, and to obey Muhammad in all righteous matters.

The First Pledge of Aqabah represented the initial formal acceptance of Islam by representatives of Medina's tribes and laid the groundwork for what would become the Hijra, the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. This event fundamentally changed the trajectory of the early Muslim community, providing them with a secure base of operations and local tribal protection.

As a member of the Khazraj tribe, Abdullah ibn 'Amr played a role in the political dynamics that allowed Islam to take root in Medina. The Khazraj, along with their rivals the Aws, had been engaged in prolonged tribal conflicts before the arrival of Islam. The new faith provided a unifying framework that helped resolve these internal disputes.

Abdullah ibn 'Amr died in 625 CE, likely during the early years of the Muslim community's establishment in Medina. His participation in the First Pledge of Aqabah places him among the earliest supporters of Islam outside of Mecca and demonstrates the appeal that Muhammad's message held for the Arab tribes of the Arabian Peninsula. His commitment to the new faith during its formative period contributed to the foundation upon which the larger Islamic community would develop.

full: Abd Allah ibn Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib al-Hashimi
primaryTitle: Hibr al-Umma — Scholar of the Umma; Father of Tafsir
titles: Hibr al-Umma · Tarjuman al-Quran · Ra's al-Mufassirin
bio: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, also known as Ibn ʿAbbās, was one of the cousins of the prophet Muhammad.
bio_full:
ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās (Arabic: عَبْد ٱللَّٰه ٱبْن عَبَّاس; c. 619 – 687 CE), also known as Ibn ʿAbbās, was one of the cousins of the prophet Muhammad.  He is considered to be the greatest mufassir (exegete) of the Qur'an.  
He was the son of Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, an uncle of Muhammad, and a nephew of Maymunah bint al-Harith, who later became Muhammad's wife. During the early struggles for the caliphate, he supported Ali, and was made governor of Basra. He withdrew to Mecca shortly afterwards. During the reign of Mu'awiya I he lived in Hejaz and often travelled to Damascus. After Mu'awiya I died in 680 CE he migrated to At-Ta'if, where he is resting from around 687 CE.
'Abd Allah ibn Abbas was highly regarded for his knowledge of traditions and his critical interpretation of the Qur'an. From early on, he gathered information from other companions of Muhammad and gave classes and wrote commentaries.

Early life

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās was born in 3 BH (619–620 C.E.). He was the third son of a wealthy merchant, Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, a paternal uncle of the Islamic prophet Muhammad His mother, Umm al-Fadl Lubaba, was a close friend of Khadijah bint Khuwaylid and is traditionally regarded as the second woman to convert to Islam.
As a member of the Banu Hashim, Ibn ʿAbbās shared a direct lineage with Muhammad through their grandfather, ʿAbd al-Muttalib. Shortly after his birth, his mother brought him to Muhammad, who reportedly placed some of his saliva on the infant's tongue before he began to suckle, marking the beginning of their close relationship.

Muhammad's era
As he grew up, he was by Muhammad's side doing different services like fetching water for ablution (Arabic: wudu). He would pray (Arabic: salat) with Muhammad and follow him on his assemblies, journeys and expeditions. It is said that Muhammad would often draw him close, pat him on the shoulder and pray, "O God! Teach him (the knowledge of) the Book (Qur'an) ". Muhammad had also supplicated for him to attain discernment in religion. Ibn Abbas kept following Muhammad, memorizing and learning his teaching.
In 10 AH (631/632 CE), Muhammad fell into his last illness. During this period, the Hadith of the pen and paper was reported, with Ibn Abbas as the first-level narrator, at that time about twelve years old. Days after that, Abbas and Ali supported Muhammad's weight on their shoulder, as Muhammad was too weak to walk unaided.

Rashidun Caliphate

During the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman
After the death of Muhammad, Ibn Abbas dedicated himself to collecting and verifying Muhammad's teachings from the senior Sahaba. He was known for his rigorous methodology, often consulting as many as thirty companions to verify a single matter. In one instance, he recounted waiting outside the door of a companion during the afternoon heat, allowing the dust to blow over him rather than disturbing the scholar's rest, famously telling the companion that "knowledge is sought, it does not just come."
This dedication earned him a prominent place in the consultative councils of the early Caliphate. Umar frequently invited him to sit with the veterans of the Battle of Badr, which drew objections from some elders who questioned why a youth was included when they had sons of similar age. Umar justified his decision by citing Ibn Abbas's religious status and knowledge. To demonstrate this to the council, Umar once asked them to interpret the statement of Allah in Surah an-Nasr: "When comes the Help of Allah and the conquest." While some companions interpreted the verse literally as a command to praise God upon victory and others remained silent, Ibn Abbas stated that the verse was actually a sign of Muhammad's approaching death. Umar publicly endorsed this view, stating that he knew nothing of the verse other than what Ibn Abbas had said. Sa`d ibn Abi Waqqas corroborated this standing, noting that he had never seen anyone quicker in understanding or wiser in council than Ibn Abbas, even in the presence of the veterans of Badr.
As his reputation grew, Ibn Abbas’s home in Medina became a center of higher learning, often compared to a university. He organized his teaching by subject, dedicating specific days to Tafsir, Fiqh, Halal and Haraam, military expeditions, poetry, and inheritance laws. His classes were so well-attended that crowds would block the roads leading to his house. To manage the volume of students, he would admit them in shifts based on their field of study, personally elucidating the pronunciation of the Qur'an for one group before clearing the house to discuss interpretation (tafsir) for the next, consistently providing more information than was requested.
During the caliphate of Uthman, Ibn Abbas took on a more active military and administrative role. In 647 CE, he joined the expedition to North Africa under the command of Abd Allah ibn Sa'd, which culminated in the Battle of Sufetula (647). He served in this campaign alongside other prominent members of the Banu Hashim and the wider Qurayshite youth.

During the caliphates of Ali and Hasan
During the First Fitna, Ibn Abbas remained a staunch supporter of his cousin, the Caliph Ali. Following the Battle of the Camel, Ali appointed him as the governor of Basra. He later fought prominently at the Battle of Siffin. After the fighting at Siffin ceased, Ali initially sought to appoint Ibn Abbas as his representative for the arbitration. However, this choice was rejected by Al-Ash'ath and the Iraqi qurra. They demanded a negotiator who was not a member of the Banu Hashim and who remained equally distant from both Ali and Muawiyah. Following the assassination of Ali in 661 CE, Ibn Abbas pledged allegiance to his eldest son, Hasan ibn Ali, and remained a loyal supporter throughout Hasan's short caliphate, maintaining his allegiance until Hasan’s abdication in favor of Muawiyah later that year.

Debate with the Kharijites
A large group of Ali's army were discontented with the outcome of Ali's war with Muawiyah, and broke off into a separate group that became known as the Kharijites. Ibn Abbas played a key role in convincing a large number of them to return to Ali; 20,000 of 24,000 according to some sources. He did so using his knowledge of Muhammad's biography. According to the Siyar A'lam al-Nubala by al-Dhahabi, 'Kitāb al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kabīr by Ibn Sa'd, Al-Mustadrak ala al-Sahihayn, Musannaf Abd al-Razzaq and many other medieval sources, there are three issues which pointed out by the Kharijites for the reason they rebelled:

Ali's policy for appointing Abu Musa Al-Ashari as arbitrator in the dispute with Mu'awiyah. The Kharijites consider it as religious transgression, citing chapters Al-An'am Quran 6:57–7 (Translated by Pickthall) and Yusuf Quran 12:40–7 (Translated by Pickthall): "The decision rests with Allah only.". Ibn Abbas responded by pointing out chapter Al-Ma'idah Quran 5:95–7 (Translated by Pickthall). "the judge to be two men among you known for justice", arguing it is  permitted to appoint arbitrator for dispute.
Ali's decision to not include his  caliphal title during the arbitration with Mu'awiyah's faction. Argued by Ibn Abbas, citing the Treaty of al-Hudaybiya when Muhammad does not include his honorific as Prophets and messengers in Islam when negotiating with Suhayl ibn Amr.
Spoils of war and captives, which was not taken by Ali after the Battle of the Camel, Ibn Abbas responded that since among the defeated was Aisha, the widow of Muhammad, it was impermissible for a Muslim to take another Muslim woman as a captive or to confiscate her property.

Umayyad Caliphate
In 680 CE (60 AH), following the death of Muawiyah, Ibn Abbas attempted to dissuade Husayn ibn Ali from his planned expedition to Kufa.

bio: Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib was the father of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He was the son of Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim and Fatima bint Amr of the Makhzum Clan.
bio_full:
Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib (; Arabic: عبد الله بن عبد المطلب, romanized: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; c. 545-570) was the father of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He was the son of Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim and Fatima bint Amr of the Makhzum Clan.
He was married to Aminah bint Wahb. Muhammad was their only child.

Name
ʿAbd Allāh means "servant of God" or "slave of God". His full name was ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim ('Amr) ibn Abd Manāf (al-Mughīra) ibn Qusayy (Zayd) ibn Kilāb ibn Murra ibn Ka`b ibn Lu'ayy ibn Ghālib ibn Fahr (Quraysh) ibn Mālik ibn an-Naḑr (Qays) ibn Kinānah ibn Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah ('Āmir) ibn Ilyas ibn Muḍar ibn Nizār ibn Ma'ādd ibn 'Adnān.

Marriage
His father chose for him Āminah, the daughter of Wahb ibn 'Abd Munāf who was the grandson of Zuhrah ibn Kilab, the brother of his great-great-grandfather Qusayy ibn Kilāb. Wahb had been the chief of Banu Zuhrah as well as its eldest and noblest member but had died some time previously and Āminah became a ward of his brother Wuhaib, who had succeeded him as chief of the clan.
His father went with him to the quarter of Banū Zuhrah. There, he sought the residence of Wuhayb and went in to ask for the hand of Wahb's daughter for his son. 'Abdullāh's father fixed his marriage with Aminah. It was said that a light shone out of his forehead and that this light was the promise of a Prophet as offspring. Many women approached 'Abdullāh, who is reported to have been a handsome man, so that they might gain the honor of producing his offspring. However it is believed that, as decided by God, the light was destined to be transferred to Āminah through 'Abdullāh after consummating the marriage.
After marrying Aminah Bint Wahb, Abdullah Ibn Abd al-Muttalib lived with her for three days; it was their custom that a man could live for three nights only with his wife in her father's family.

Wedding
At the wedding ceremony, Abd al-Muttalib chose Wuhayb's daughter Halah for himself. When Abd al-Muttalib proposed to Wuhayb, he agreed. And so on the same occasion Abd al-Muttalib and Abdullah married Halah and Amina respectively. Later, Halah gave birth to Hamza, who was both Muhammad's uncle and foster brother.

Death

Soon after his marriage, 'Abdullāh was called to Syria (in what is Ash-Shām or the Levant) on a trading caravan trip. When he left, Āminah was pregnant. He spent several months in Gaza, and on his return trip he stopped for a longer rest with the family of his paternal grandmother, Salma bint Amr, who belonged to the Najjar clan of the Khazraj tribe in Medina. 'Abdullāh was preparing to join a caravan to Mecca when he fell ill. The caravan went on without him to Mecca with news of his illness. Upon the caravan's arrival in Mecca, 'Abdul-Muttalib immediately sent his eldest son Al-Harith to Medina. However, by the time al-Harith arrived, 'Abdullāh had died. Al-Harith returned to Mecca to announce 'Abdullāh's death to his aged father and his pregnant wife Āminah. According to Ibn Sa'd, Abdullah died three months after his marriage and was twenty-five years old when he died.
He was buried in Dar-ul-Nabeghah in Medina (today Saudi Arabia), and his mausoleum was demolished on the 20th or 21 January 1978. Reportedly he was reburied in Al-Baqee' Graveyard, next to Muhammad's son Ibrahim.

Estate
'Abdullāh left five camels, a herd of sheep and goats, and an Abyssinian slave nurse, called Umm Ayman, who was to take care of his son Muhammad. This patrimony does not prove that 'Abdullāh was wealthy, but at the same time it does not prove that he was poor. Rather, it shows that Muhammad was his heir. Furthermore, 'Abdullāh was still a young man capable of working and of amassing a fortune. His father was still alive and none of his wealth had as yet been transferred to his sons. 

Fate in the afterlife
Islamic scholars have long been divided over the religious beliefs of Muhammad's parents and their fate in the afterlife. One transmission by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah states that Allah (God) refused to forgive Āminah for her kufr (disbelief). According to another sahih (authentic) hadith Muhammad clarified that his own father was in the Fire. Another transmission in Musnad al-Bazzar states that Muhammad's parents were brought back to life and accepted Islam, then returned to the Barzakh. Some Ash'ari and Shafi'i scholars argued that neither would be punished in the afterlife, as they were Ahl al-fatrah, or "People of the interval" between the prophetic messages of 'Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad. The concept of Ahl al-fatrah is not universally accepted among Islamic scholars, and there is debate concerning the extent of salvation available for active practitioners of Shirk (Polytheism), though the majority of scholars have come to agree with it, and disregard  the hadith (narrations)  that state that Muhammad's parents were condemned to hell.
While a work attributed to Abu Hanifah, an early Sunni scholar, stated that both Āminah and 'Abdullāh died upon their innate nature (Mata 'ala al-fitrah), some later authors of mawlid texts related a tradition in which Āminah and 'Abdullāh were temporarily revived and embraced Islam. Scholars like Ibn Taymiyyah stated that this was a lie, though Al-Qurtubi stated that the concept did not disagree with Islamic theology. According to Ali al-Qari, the preferred view is that both the parents of Muhammad were Muslims. According to Al-Suyuti, Isma'il Haqqi, and other Islamic scholars, all of the narrations indicating that the parents of Muhammad were not forgiven were later abrogated when they were brought to life and accepted Islam.  Shia Muslims believe that all of Muhammad's ancestors, Āminah included, were monotheists who practiced the shariah of Abraham, and were therefore entitled to Paradise.

bio: Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa al-Sahmi was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He is best known in Islamic tradition for his role as the courier of a letter from Muhammad to Khosrow II, the King of Persia, and for his imprisonment and torture by Heraclius, the Byzantine Emperor.
bio_full:
Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa al-Sahmi (Arabic: عبد الله بن حذافة السهمي, romanized: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥudhāfa al-Sahmī; died 653) was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He is best known in Islamic tradition for his role as the courier of a letter from Muhammad to Khosrow II, the King of Persia, and for his imprisonment and torture by Heraclius, the Byzantine Emperor.

In Prophet Muhammad's era

Letter to Khosrow II
Abd Allah bin Hudhafa al-Sahmi carried the letter of Muhammad to Khosrow II, the emperor of the Sassanid Empire (Persia). When Abd Allah entered the kingdom, Khosrow sent his messenger to get the letter off him but Abd Allah refused, saying Muhammad had ordered him to present the letter to the King only and he was not going to break the instructions of Muhammad. Khosrow was enraged by the letter, tearing it into shreds. When Muhammad heard Khosrow had torn his letter, he made a prayer that Allah tears his kingdom. Khosrow sent a couple of troopers to arrest Muhammad and bring him to his presence. As soon as the men reached Madina, Muhammad was informed by Divine Revelation that Khosrow, the emperor of Persia, had been murdered by his own son, which Muhammad disclosed to the troopers.

The leader of an expedition

Muslim scholars says that, and according to hadith of Sihah Sittah and Tafsir Ibn Kathir, the verse of Obedience about uli al-Amr was revealed about an incident of sahaba Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa. Muhammad once sent him as a military leader of  some sahabas, on the way he became furious and told them to make coils of fire, and to plunge into it. However, Imam Asakir Zuhri said, Abdullah was a humorous person. He made this order in jest. After returning from the expedition, the Islamic prophet Muhammad said, obedience to the leader is only wajib in those matters which Allah has permitted.

In Caliph Umar's era
In 639 (19AH), during the Caliphate of Umar, he sent an army to Rome. There, Heraclius, the emperor of the Byzantine Empire, attempted to convert Abd Allah to Christianity with bribery and torture, but Abd Allah refused to recant. Heraclius attempted all sorts of torture, such as boiling other sahaba in front of him. He attempted to send a prostitute to Abd Allah's cell, but his firm belief in Islam led him to run around in his cell to get away from the woman. She eventually grew bored and gave up. Heraclius then attempted to scare him, by ordering his soldiers to shoot arrows at him, but not hit him. Again, this didn't faze Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa. When Heraclius boiled the other sahaba in front of Abd Allah, Abd Allah began to cry. Heraclius thought he had finally broken him and mocked him. Abd Allah, then declared that he wasn't crying out of fear, rather he was crying that he knew he could only die once, and proclaimed that he wishes he was blessed with 1000 lives in order to die in the same way, due to the strength of his faith in Islam. After all this, Heraclius tried on the last attempt. He told Abd Allah, "If you kiss my head, I will let you go." Abd Allah refused and said, "I wouldn't let you kiss my head". Heraclius then said, "Kiss my forehead and I will let go of 60 sahaba and you." Abd Allah refused. This kept on going until Heraclius said: "Kiss my forehead and I will let go of 300 sahaba". Abd Allah agreed.
Abd Allah and the Sahaba were freed and made their way back to the Muslim lands.

full: Abd Allah ibn Masud ibn Ghafil al-Hudhali
primaryTitle: First Hafiz of the Quran — Closest to the Prophet
titles: Hafiz al-Quran · Shaykh al-Kufiyyeen
bio: Abu Abd al-Rahman Abdullah bin Masoud bin Ghafil bin Habib al-Sahili al-Hudhali, the jurist of the nation, a great companion, a minister, a reciter and a narrator of the Prophet’s hadith. He is one of the first to Islam, the sixth to convert to Islam, one of the missionaries of Paradise, the owner of the Prophet Muhammad’s sandals and his siwaks, one of those who emigrated in the two migrations to Abyssinia and to Medina, and one of those who realized the two qiblahs. He was the first to recite the Qur’an aloud in Mecca and witness all the scenes. With the Prophet Muhammad. He was the one who killed Abu Jahl and beheaded him in the Battle of Badr and presented him to the Prophet Muhammad. He took over the judiciary, the ministry of Kufa, and its treasury during the caliphate of Omar and was issued during the caliphate of Othman.
bio_full:
Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud (Arabic: عبد الله بن مسعود, romanized: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd; c. 594 – c. 653) was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad whom Sunni Islamic tradition regards as the greatest interpreter of the Quran of his time and the second ever. He was also known by the kunya Abu Abd al-Rahman.

Early years
Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud was born in Mecca in about 594, a son of Mas'ud ibn Ghafil and Umm Abd bint Abd Wadd, both of whom were from the Hudhayl tribe,
Abd Allah had a brother, Utba, and at least one wife in Muhammad's lifetime. A craftswoman who supported Abd Allah and their child through her hand-crafts. She was Zaynab bint Abd Allah from the Thaqif tribe with whom he had several daughters. Some people called her also Rayta bint Abd Allah. Based on authentic hadiths, both Rayta and Zaynab was the same woman, referto Abd Allah's age and his age of marriage due to his difficult economy. He specified in his will that none of his daughters should be married off without their own knowledge. He also had a son named Abd al-Rahman.
He is described as a thin, short man with very dark skin, and smooth hair reaching his shoulders. Abd Allah wore white clothes, and could be recognized in the dark by his distinctive, high-quality perfume. He was reported to be sociable and willing to speak out to put people at ease. In his character and goals, he was said to be the person "most like Muhammad".

Conversion to Islam
Ibn Masʿūd was an early follower of Islam, having converted before 616. He appears nineteenth on Ibn Ishaq's list of people who were converted by Abu Bakr.
As a youth, he worked as a shepherd for Uqba ibn Abu Mu'ayt, one of the principal adversaries of Islam. He first met Muhammad and Abu Bakr while watching his flocks when they were "fleeing from the idolators". They asked him for milk, but Abd Allah said he could not steal from his employer. According to Masʿūd, Muhammad then asked for an unmated ewe and stroked its udder, whereupon milk poured out. Abd Allah immediately asked to be taught "some of these words", and Muhammad began to teach him the Qur'an. Abd Allah later said that he learned 70 surahs from Muhammad.
Later his mother and brother also converted to Islam.
Around 614 the Quraysh began a campaign to suppress Islam through the oppression of Muslims of lower social status. Abd Allah, as a foreigner whose allies had withdrawn their protection, was vulnerable to this persecution. Abu Jahl—one of the high-status leaders among the Quraysh—once "clawed at him and punched him".
The Muslims remarked one day that the Quraysh had never heard the Qur'an being recited clearly, and that someone needed to make them listen to it. Abd Allah volunteered. His friends reminded him that he had no protector and therefore the crowds might attack him, but Abd Allah replied, "Allah will protect me." He stood in front of the Kaaba and began to recite Surah Ar-Rahman from the Qur'an. When the Quraysh realised that he was reciting Muhammad's teaching, they began to hit his face, but he continued to recite. He returned to the Muslims with the bruises on his face, saying, "I have never despised Allah's enemies more than I do now, and if you like I will go and do the same thing tomorrow." The Muslims told him that he had already done enough, "for you have made them listen to what they don't want to hear".
Abd Allah and his brother Utba were among those who emigrated to Abyssinia in 616. Abd Allah returned to Mecca in 619 with Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf.

Emigration to Medina
When the Muslims emigrated to Medina in 622, Abd Allah lodged with Muadh ibn Jabal or Saad ibn Khaythama. One tradition states that Muhammad made a pact of brotherhood between Abd Allah and Muadh ibn Jabal; but according to another, Abd Allah's brother in Islam was al-Zubayar ibn Al-Awwam. When land in Medina was allocated to the immigrants, the Zuhra clan was given an area behind the mosque, which included plots for Abd Allah and his brother Utba.

Relationship with Muhammad
Outsiders perceived Abd Allah and his mother as members of Muhammad's household. He worked as a personal servant, taking care of Muhammad's bedding, toothbrush, sandals and travelling hygiene. "He used to screen him when he bathed and wake him when he slept and walk with him in a wild land." He was said to be the "keeper of secrets". Muhammad once told him to climb a tree and bring him a twig. The companions laughed at how thin Abd Allah's legs were. Muhammad said: "Why are you laughing? Abd Allah's foot will be heavier than Mount Uhud in the scales on the Day of Resurrection."
Muhammad recognized Abd Allah as one of the four foremost experts on the Qur'an. He once asked him to recite; when Abd Allah protested, "Should I recite it to you when you are the one to whom it was sent down and revealed?" Muhammad replied, "I love to hear it from someone else." Abd Allah then recited it until Muhammad wept.

Military career
Abd Allah fought at the Battle of Badr. After the battle, Muhammad ordered the warriors to search among the corpses for his enemy Abu Jahl, who could be recognised by a distinctive scar on his knee.
Abd Allah found Abu Jahl Amr "at his last gasp" with his leg cut off. He seized his beard and asked, "Are you Abu Jahl?" Abu Jahl replied, "Can there be a man superior to the one you have killed or one whom his own folk has killed?" Abd Allah then placed his foot on Abu Jahl Amr's neck, and asked, "Allah's enemy, has Allah put you to shame?" Abu Jahl Amr replied, "How has he shamed me? Am I anything more than a man whom you have killed? Tell me how the battle went." Abd Allah told him that the Muslims had won. Abu Jahl Amr responded, "You have climbed high, you little shepherd!" Then Abd Allah struck off his head. He brought it to Muhammad, proclaiming, "This is the head of Allah's enemy Abu Jahl!".
Abd Allah also fought at the Battle of Uhud, the Battle of the Trench and "all the battles", including Tabuk. Twenty years later, he said he wished he had died at Tabuk.

Caliphates of Abu Bakr and Umar
After the death of Muhammad, Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud became the eighth-most prominent transmitter of hadith with a total of 848 narrations. Umar called him "a box full of knowledge". The following traditions are among those attributed to him.

I asked Allah's Messenger which deed was the best. He replied: "Prayer at its appointed hour." I said: "Then what?" He replied: "Kindness to the parents." I said: "Then what?" He replied: "Jihad in the cause of Allah." And I would not have ceased asking more questions but out of regard.
A man said: "Allah's Messenger, which offence is the most grievous in Allah's eye?" He replied: "That you associate a partner with Allah, who created you." He said: "What next?" He replied: "That you kill your child out of fear that he would join you in food." He said: "What next?" He replied: "That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." And the Almighty and Exalted Lord testified it: All those who call not unto another god along with Allah, and slay not any soul which Allah has forbidden, except in the cause of justice, nor commit fornication, and he who does this shall meet a requital of sin. [ Qur'an 25:68]
We were along with Allah's Messenger at Mina, that moon was split up into two. One of its parts was behind the mountain and the other one was on this side of the mountain. Allah's Messenger said to us: "Bear witness to this."
Umar allotted Abd Allah a pension of 6,000 dirhams, and he was said to be very generous with his money. His mother was also granted a pension of 1,000 dirhams.
Around 642 Umar appointed him as a preacher, treasurer and magistrate (qāḍī) in Kufa, saying: "I have preferred you with him over myself, so take him."

Conflict with the Government
Abd Allah, in his capacity as treasurer, lent a sum of money to Saad ibn Abi Waqqas, the Governor of Kufa, and when he was unable to repay it, they quarrelled.

bio: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad also known as al-Ṭāhir and al-Ṭayyib was one of the sons of Muhammad and Khadija. He died in childhood.
bio_full: Abdullah ibn Muhammad was a son of the Prophet Muhammad and his first wife, Khadija bint Khuwaylid. He was born in Mecca and was named after the Prophet's own father, Abdullah. He is also known by the titles al-Tahir, 'the pure', and al-Tayyib, 'the good'. Most biographers and genealogists hold that these were titles of Abdullah, though some considered them the names of other sons. Sources differ on when he was born. According to al-Qastallani, he was given these titles because he was born after the start of the prophethood. One modern account, drawing on the early biographies, places his birth before the first revelation in 610 CE, most likely between 605 and 608. His full brother was al-Qasim, the eldest son, and his sisters included Fatima. He died in early childhood in Mecca; one account, citing al-Qastallani, gives 614 CE, while another places his death around 610, at about four years of age. He is reported to have been buried in the Jannat al-Mu'alla cemetery in Mecca. After his death, al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi said of the Prophet that his line had been cut off and that he was 'abtar', without male heirs. Al-Qastallani's account links this to the revelation of the final verse of Surat al-Kawthar: 'Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off' (Qur'an 108:3).

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abdur Rahman bin 'Aqeel al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Abdur Rahman bin 'Aqeel al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE in the Hijaz region of the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he belonged to the Mazin tribe and died around 640 CE during the early period of Islamic expansion.

Al-Mazni is historically significant as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a pivotal moment in early Islamic history that occurred in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge, referenced in Quran 48:18, took place when approximately 1,400 Muslims accompanying the Prophet Muhammad on what was intended to be a pilgrimage to Mecca were prevented from entering the city by the Meccan authorities. When rumors spread that the Prophet's envoy Uthman ibn Affan had been killed during negotiations, the Muslim community gathered under a tree where they pledged their loyalty to Muhammad, vowing to fight to the death if necessary.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular importance in Islamic tradition because the Quran explicitly mentions God's pleasure with those who participated in this oath of allegiance. The verse states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged their allegiance under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts. This divine approval gave the participants, including Abdur Rahman bin 'Aqeel al-Mazni, special recognition within the early Muslim community.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, al-Mazni was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly knew and followed Muhammad. The companions hold a unique position in Islamic history as the primary transmitters of the Prophet's teachings and practices, and as the foundation of the early Muslim community that would spread Islam across vast territories following Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

While specific details about al-Mazni's individual contributions beyond his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, his recognition as a companion and participant in this significant event establishes his place among the early Muslims who helped establish the foundations of the Islamic community during its formative period in seventh-century Arabia.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Abdur Rahman bin al-Habib (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Abdur Rahman bin al-Habib was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE in the Hijaz region, he witnessed and participated in the emergence of the Muslim community during one of the most pivotal periods in Islamic history.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Abdur Rahman was among the early Muslims who directly interacted with Muhammad and experienced the foundational years of the Islamic faith. The companions held a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of believers who received religious teachings directly from the Prophet and helped establish the early Muslim community.

Abdur Rahman's life was cut short during the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, where he died as a martyr. The Battle of Uhud was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces, taking place approximately three years after the Prophet's migration from Mecca to Medina. This battle occurred on the slopes of Mount Uhud, near Medina, and represented a crucial moment in early Islamic history as the young Muslim community faced external military pressure.

The battle itself was significant for several reasons: it tested the resolve and unity of the early Muslim community, demonstrated the challenges faced during Islam's expansion, and produced numerous martyrs who became remembered figures in Islamic historical memory. Those who died fighting alongside the Prophet at Uhud were accorded special recognition as martyrs, a status that carried deep spiritual significance in Islamic belief.

Abdur Rahman's sacrifice at Uhud places him within the broader narrative of early Islamic struggle and community formation. His death at approximately twenty-eight years of age reflects the youth of many early companions who gave their lives during this formative period. The companions who died at Uhud are remembered collectively as having made the ultimate sacrifice for their faith and community during a critical juncture when the survival of the early Muslim community was not assured.

His legacy, like that of other companions who died at Uhud, is preserved within Islamic historical tradition as part of the foundational generation that helped establish Islam during its earliest and most vulnerable years.

famous: Abdur Rahman bin Hassan ibn Thabit
full: Abdur Rahman bin Hassan ibn Thabit
dob_s: c. 655 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: 722 CE (al-Isabah / Usd al-Ghabah / Siyar / Tabaqat (AI-extracted 2026-06, spot-verified))
bio: Abdur Rahman bin Hassan ibn Thabit (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Poet-Companion.
bio_full: Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan ibn Thabit al-Ansari was a poet of Medina and the son of the Prophet's poet Hassan ibn Thabit, of the Banu al-Najjar of the Khazraj. His kunya was Abu Muhammad, or Abu Sa'id in some reports. His mother was Sirin, a Coptic woman and sister of Mariya, the mother of the Prophet's son Ibrahim, which made Abd al-Rahman a maternal cousin of Ibrahim. Al-Askari and al-Ja'abi say he was born during the Prophet's lifetime, and Ibn Mandah, Abu Nu'aym, al-Askari and others therefore listed him among the Companions, although al-Askari notes that he narrated nothing from the Prophet. Others classed him as a Successor: Ibn Sa'd placed him in the second generation of the Successors of Medina, and Ibn Hibban and Ibn Ma'in also counted him among the Successors. He narrated a small number of reports from his father Hassan, his mother Sirin and Zayd ibn Thabit. His son Sa'id and Abd al-Rahman ibn Bahman narrated from him. Ibn Sa'd described him as 'a poet who narrated little hadith', and al-Dhahabi called him 'the poet, son of the poet' and recorded that he was considered reliable. Khalifa ibn Khayyat, al-Tabari, Ibn Qani' and Ibn Hibban give his death as 104 AH. Reports of his age at death differ: Ibn Hibban gives seventy-two, while al-Dhahabi reports that he lived to over ninety.
