titles: Abu Hudhayfah · Father of Salim (by adoption)
_merge_notes: merged from F0128 on 20260422_193715: dob 594->580; filled=['titles']
bio: Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah (c. 580–633 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abū Ḥudhayfa ibn ʿUtba (Arabic: أبو حذيفة بن عتبة; died 633), full name Qays ibn Utba ibn Rabi'a ibn Abd Shams ibn Abd Manaf ibn Qusay ibn Kilab al-Qurashī al-ʿAbshamī was from the early companions of the prophet Muhammad and the leader of his tribe, Banu 'Absham. He participated in several battles such as the battle of Badr.

Biography
Abū Ḥudhayfah bin ʿUtbah converted to Islam before entering the House of Al-Arqam, it was said that he was  tall, handsome, with even teeth, and was said that he was known as ‘the squinting one’. 
He was the maternal uncle of the martyr Mus'ab ibn Umayr and of the Caliph Muawiyah. 
Some narrations recorded that his name was "Muhasham" however Al-Suhayli refutes those narrations stating that " Ibn Hisham said: His name is Muhasham, but this is an error according to genealogists, for Muhasham is actually Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughira, the brother of Hashim and Hisham, the sons of al-Mughira ibn Abdullah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum. As for Abu Hudhayfah ibn Utbah, his name is Qays, as they [scholars] have mentioned." 
He emigrated twice to Abyssinia where his son, Muhammad ibn Abi Hudhayfah, was born and his mother was Sahla bint Suhayl ibn Amr who later married Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.
His brother, Abu Hisham bin ʿUtbah embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Makkah, it was recorded that he had a good belief, he fought for Islam and settled in Syria where he became pious and devout. He died during the Caliphate of Uthman.
His brother narrated on the authority of the Prophet where his narrations can be found in Sunan Al-Tirmidhi, Al-Nasa’i, and Ibn Majah.
Abū Ḥudhayfah had a servant named Salim ibn Ma'qal who was freed by Thubayta bint Ya'ar, the wife of Abū Ḥudhayfah, and was adopted in the islamic way by Abū Ḥudhayfah. 
Abū Ḥudhayfah participated in the battle of Badr where Abu al-Zinad said that he called his father to a duel, in other narrations it was said that Abū Ḥudhayfah stood to face him, but the Prophet told him: ‘Sit down.’ Then, when the men stood up to duel, Abū Ḥudhayfah aided in striking his father. 
After the death of Abū Ḥudhayfah, Uthman took care of his son, Muhammad ibn Abi Hudhayfah. Muhammad later went to Egypt during the Caliphate of Uthman and became one of the fiercest agitators against him and was nicknamed "The Rebel" however Muawiyah tricked him and imprisoned him for his rebellion against the Caliph. Muhammad was later killed however some narrators such as Ibn Qutaybah said that he was killed by Rushdin, the freed slave of Muawiyah, while Ibn al-Kalbi said that Muhammad was killed by Malik ibn Hubayrah al-Sakuni. 

Death
Abū Ḥudhayfah was martyred at the Battle of Yamama alongside his freed slave Salim.

full: Abd al-Rahman ibn Sakhr al-Dawsi al-Yamani
titles: Abu Hurairah · Hafiz al-Sahaba
bio: Abū Hurayra ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ṣakhr al-Dawsī al-Zahrānī, commonly known as Abu Hurayra, was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and considered the most prolific hadith narrator. Born in al-Jabur, Arabia to the Banu Daws clan of the Zahran tribe, he converted to Islam around 7 AH following the Battle of Khaybar, and later became a member of the Suffah after migrating to Medina.
bio_full:
Abū Hurayra ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ṣakhr al-Dawsī al-Zahrānī (Arabic: أبُو هُرَيْرَة عَبْد ٱلرَّحْمَٰن بْن صَخْر ٱلدَّوْسِيّ ٱلزَّهْرَانِيّ; c. 603–679), commonly known as Abu Hurayra (Arabic: أبُو هُرَيْرَة; lit. 'father of a kitten'), was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and considered the most prolific hadith narrator. Born in al-Jabur, Arabia to the Banu Daws clan of the Zahran tribe, he converted to Islam around 7 AH (c. 629 CE) following the Battle of Khaybar, and later became a member of the Suffah after migrating to Medina. 
Under prophet Muhammad, Abu Hurayra was sent as a muezzin to al-Ala al-Hadhrami in Bahrain. During the reign of the Rashidun caliph Umar (r. 634-644), he briefly served as a governor of Bahrain.
He memorized over 5,000 hadiths, which later produced more than 500,000 narrator chains, making him an example followed by Sunni Hadith scholars today. The four major Sunni madhahib have all used hadith narrated by Abu Hurayra in major jurisprudential decisions. However, non-Sunni scholars, including some Shia scholars, have regarded Abu Hurayra as not always reliable.

Life

Ancestry
Abu Hurairah's personal name (ism) is unknown, and so is his father's. The most popular opinion, voiced by Al-Dhahabi and Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, is that it was 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Ṣakhr (عبد الرحمن بن صخر). According to Al-Dhahabi, Abu Hurairah hailed from the prominent Banu Daws clan of the Arab tribe of Zahran, and was born in the region of Al-Bahah. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani traced the lineage of the Banu Daws to Azd, a Nabatean ancestor of the southern Arabs, through Zahran. Al-Qalqashandi reported the Zahran as a descendant of Khalid ibn Nasr, while Ibn Hazm reported Zahran was a descendant of Malik ibn Nasr, a Qahtanite. One hadith records Muhammad as having a favorable view of the Banu Daws, viewing them as on par with his tribe, the Quraysh, the Ansar of Medina, and Banu Thaqif.

Conversion to Islam and life in Medina
Abu Hurairah embraced Islam through Tufayl ibn 'Amr, the chieftain of his tribe in 629, 7AH. Tufayl had returned to his village after meeting Muhammad in Mecca and converting to Islam in its early years. Abu Hurairah was one of the first to accept Islam from his tribe, unlike the majority of Tufayl's tribesmen who embraced Islam later. Abu Hurairah accompanied Tufayl to Madina to meet Muhammad who renamed him Abdurrahman. It was said that he found a stray kitten, so he took it in his sleeve, which is the reason he was named Abu Hurairah (father of the kitten).

After the hijrah (migration to Medina), Abu Hurairah became one of the inhabitants of the Suffah. Abu Hurairah stuck closely to Muhammad, and went on expeditions and journeys with him. Abu Hurairah was recorded as having participated in the Expedition of Dhat al-Riqa, which took place in Najd in the year 4 AH or 5 AH. The consensus of Muslim scholars considers Abu Hurairah's military career as having begun after the Battle of Khaybar, after which he was present in the Battle of Mu'tah, during the Conquest of Mecca, at Hunayn, and in the Expedition of Tabuk. Later, Abu Hurairah was sent as a muezzin to al-Ala al-Hadhrami in Bahrayn.
Abu Hurairah was father-in-law of the prominent tabi' (pl. tabi'un) Said ibn al-Musayyib (d. 715), who confessed that he had married Abu Hurairah's daughter in order to get closer with her father and learn the hadith he possessed. Hammam ibn Munabbih (d. 748), another prominent tabi' and disciple of Abu Hurairah compiled the hadith narrated to him by Abu Hurairah in his hadith collection Sahifah Hammam ibn Munabbih, one of the earliest hadith collections in history. There is little mention of the family of Abu Huraira, but it is known that he had a wife named Basra bint Ghazwan.

After Muhammad, later years and death
According to Ahmad ibn Hanbal, after the death of Muhammad, Abu Hurairah participated in the Ridda Wars under the first Rashidun caliph, Abu Bakr. After Abu Bakr's death, during Umar's reign, Abu Hurairah actively participated in the Muslim conquest of Persia. Later, he became governor of Bahrayn. During this time, Abu Hurairah is noted to have become wealthy, amassing close to 10,000 gold dinars through breeding horses and spoils of war, which he brought to Medina. This raised Umar's suspicion, who accused him of corruption. Abu Hurairah was later found innocent and Umar asked him again to govern Bahrayn once again, an offer he turned down. After leaving the governorship, Abu Hurairah returned to Medina and worked as a qadi (judge), issuing fatāwā (sing. fatwa). Abu Hurairah was one of the defenders of the third Rashidun caliph, Uthman, during his assassination. Abu Hurairah continued to work as mufti after Uthman's death. In the early Umayyad era, Abu Hurairah was tasked with assessing the authenticity of the hadith circulated within the caliphate.
Abu Hurairah died in the year 679 (59 AH) at the age of 76 and was buried at al-Baqi'. His funeral prayer was led by Al-Walid ibn Utba, who was the governor of Medina, and was attended by Abd Allah ibn Umar and Abu Sa'id al Khudri. Al-Walid wrote to Mu'awiya I about his death, who made a concession of 10,000 dirhams to Abu Hurairah's heirs and commanded Al-Walid to take care of them. In 1274 (673 AH) the Mausoleum of Abu Hurairah was constructed in Yibna, at the order of the Mamluk Sultan Baibars. The mausoleum has been described as "one of the finest domed mausoleums in Palestine." Following the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, the mausoleum was designated a shrine for Jews dedicated to Gamaliel II by the Israeli government, although neither Abu Hurairah nor Gamaliel II are likely to have been buried in the tomb.

Legacy and influence
The hadith reported by Abu Hurairah are diverse, being used by Islamic scholars specializing in hadith, 'aqīdah, fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence), ijtihād, tafsīr (Quranic exegesis), and Islamic eschatology.
In his Kitab al-Iman, a book on 'aqīdah, Ibn Taymiyyah (d. 1328) uses hadith narrations from Abu Hurairah to study tawḥīd. Ibn Kathir uses Abu Hurairah's narrations in Al-Nihāyah fī al-Fitan wa al-Malaḥim, a work on Islamic eschatology. References to Abu Hurairah's narrations can be found in Al-Tabari's Tafsir al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir's Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti's collaborative Tafsir al-Jalalayn, and Al-Qurtubi's Tafsir al-Qurtubi, all of which are works of tafsīr, or Quranic exegesis. They also refer to Abu Hurairah's ijtihād and the resulting fatāwā as their resources.
Abu Hurairah was among the few companions of Muhammad who issued jurisprudential rulings or fatāwā (sing. fatwa), and he was personally requested by his contemporary companion Ibn Abbas to do so. As the Sunni madhahib (sing. madhhab, schools of jurisprudence) were structurally based on the rulings or narrations from companions of Muhammad, the ruling jurisprudence for the four main Sunni madhahib heavily relied on Abu Hurairah's fatāwā and his numerous narrations. Taqi al-Din al-Subki compiled the fatāwā of Abu Hurairah in his book, Fatawa Abu Hurairah. Abu Hurairah was one of the six prominent companions of Muhammad involved in jurisprudential rulings during the Rashidun era, the others being Ali, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Darda, Saʽid al-Khudri, and Abu Shafiah. Abd al-Rahman Jaziri, a professor at Al-Azhar University, has concluded that on certain issues, the four madhahib reached ijmā' (consensus) on Abu Hurairah's ruling.
The four major Sunni madhahib, have all used hadith narrated by Abu Hurairah in major jurisprudential decisions. Muwatta Imam Malik, the hadith collection of the founder of the Maliki madhhab, Malik ibn Anas, contains various hadiths narrated by Abu Hurairah wherein they form the basis for jurisprudential rulings. Bulugh al-Maram, a hadith collection by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani pertaining to the Shafi'i madhhab also contains many hadith narrated by Abu Hurairah. Al-Nawawi's Al-Arba'ūn an-Nawawiyyah also contain narrations from Abu Hurairah.

titles: Shaykh al-Mashaikh · Qutb al-Chisht
bio: Abu Ishaq Shami was a Muslim scholar who is often regarded as the founder of the Sufi Chishti Order. He was the first in the Chishti lineage (silsila) to live in Chisht and to adopt the name "Chishti", so that, if the Chishti order itself dates back to him, it is one of the oldest recorded Sufi orders. His original name, Shami, implies he came from Syria (ash-Sham). He died in Damascus and lies buried on Mount Qasiyun, where Ibn Arabi was later buried.
bio_full:
Abu Ishaq Shami (ابو اسحاق شامی چشتی; died 940) was a Muslim scholar who is often regarded as the founder of the Sufi Chishti Order. He was the first in the Chishti lineage (silsila) to live in Chisht and to adopt the name "Chishti", so that, if the Chishti order itself dates back to him, it is one of the oldest recorded Sufi orders. His original name, Shami, implies he came from Syria (ash-Sham). He died in Damascus and lies buried on Mount Qasiyun, where Ibn Arabi was later buried.

Masters and students
Abu Ishaq Shami's teacher was Mumshad Al-Dinawari, whose own teacher was Abu Hubayra al-Basri, a disciple of Huzaifah Al-Mar'ashi who was in turn a disciple of Ibrahim ibn Adham (Abu Ben Adhem In the western tradition.) The Chishtiyyah silsila continued through Abu Ishaq Shami's disciple Abu Aḥmad Abdal Chishti. In South Asia, Moinuddin Chishti, whose silsila goes back to Abu Ishaq Shami, was the founding father who brought Chishti teaching to the region.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Abu Jubayra bin al-Dahhak (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Abu Jubayra bin al-Dahhak was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 600 CE. As one of the Sahabah, he belonged to the generation of Muslims who lived during the Prophet's lifetime and had direct contact with him, making him part of the foundational community of early Islam.

Abu Jubayra is historically recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event in early Islamic history that took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge, also known as Bay'at al-Ridwan, is referenced in the Quran in verse 48:18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those believers who pledged their allegiance under the tree. The pledge occurred when the Prophet Muhammad and approximately 1,400 Muslims were traveling to Mecca for pilgrimage but were stopped by the Meccan tribes. When rumors spread that the Prophet's envoy had been killed, the companions pledged their loyalty and readiness to fight if necessary, demonstrating their unwavering commitment to Islam and their leader.

Based in Medina, Abu Jubayra lived during the formative period of the Islamic community, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim state and the development of Islamic practices and governance. His presence during this crucial era meant he was part of the community that helped shape the early traditions and practices of Islam.

Abu Jubayra's association with hadith sciences indicates his role in the preservation and transmission of the Prophet's teachings and sayings. The companions played a vital role in collecting, memorizing, and passing down the hadith literature that would later become fundamental sources of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran.

He died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the second Caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab. This period marked the rapid expansion of the Islamic empire beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Abu Jubayra's significance lies primarily in his status as a Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan and his contribution to the early Islamic community in Medina. His participation in this pivotal moment demonstrates the dedication and loyalty that characterized the early Muslim community during a critical period in Islamic history.

bio: Abu Kabsha (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Persia. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abu Kabsha was a freedman (mawla) of the Prophet Muhammad. Khalifa ibn Khayyat gives his name as Sulaym, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr reports that it was said to be Sulaym, and Ibn Hibban gives it as Aws. His origin is reported differently: Ibn Hisham said he was from Persia (Fars), others said he was born in the land of Daws, and some said he was born in Mecca. According to Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, the Prophet bought him and then set him free.

He fought at Badr and in all the Prophet's later battles, according to Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir record two reports of his death. One, the account they give first, places it in 13 AH (634 CE), on the very day that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab became caliph; Ibn Hibban also dates his death to that day. The other says he died later, in 23 AH, during 'Umar's caliphate.

He is a different person from Abu Kabsha al-Anmari, a Companion of the tribe of Anmar who settled in Syria. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr also discusses why Quraysh called the Prophet 'Ibn Abi Kabsha'; the explanations he records refer to other men, such as a maternal ancestor of the Prophet or the husband of his wet-nurse Halima, not to this freedman.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Abu Kalab bin Abi Sa'sa'a (c. 597–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Abu Kalab bin Abi Sa'sa'a was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative years of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he witnessed the emergence and early expansion of the Islamic community during the late 6th and early 7th centuries.

As a Sahaba, Abu Kalab belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and played crucial roles in establishing the early Islamic community. The Sahaba were instrumental in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, participating in the religion's foundational events, and supporting the development of the first Muslim society.

Abu Kalab's life was centered in Medina, the city that became the political and spiritual center of the early Islamic state after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the base from which the Muslim community defended itself against various tribal coalitions and expanded its influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Abu Kalab is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, fought in 625 CE near Medina. This battle was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community and the Meccan forces led by the Quraysh tribe. The battle proved to be a significant test for the early Muslim community, as it followed their victory at the Battle of Badr and demonstrated both the challenges and resolve of the growing Islamic movement.

His death in 634 CE occurred during a pivotal period in Islamic history, coinciding with the end of the Prophet Muhammad's life and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr. This was a time of rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula and the consolidation of Muslim political authority.

The designation of Abu Kalab as a martyr of Uhud places him among those early Muslims who made ultimate sacrifices during the formative military campaigns that helped secure the survival and growth of the Islamic community. The Battle of Uhud, despite its mixed outcomes for the Muslims, became an important event in Islamic historical memory, representing themes of perseverance, faith under trial, and commitment to the community's defense.

Abu Kalab's life span of approximately 37 years encompassed the entire public ministry of Prophet Muhammad and the initial establishment of Islamic civilization, making him a witness to one of history's most significant religious and social transformations.

famous: Abu Khuzayma bin Aws bin Zayd
full: Abu Khuzayma bin Aws bin Zayd
bio: Abu Khuzayma bin Aws bin Zayd (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abu Khuzayma bin Aws bin Zayd was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the residents of Medina who encountered the Prophet after his migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Abu Khuzayma is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr." This battle, fought between the early Muslim community and the Meccan Quraysh tribe, holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim forces. The battle took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory despite the Muslims being significantly outnumbered.

The designation "Companion of Badr" carries special weight in Islamic tradition, as those who participated in this pivotal engagement are regarded as holding a distinguished position among the Prophet's companions. The battle marked a turning point for the nascent Muslim community, establishing their military capability and strengthening their position in the Arabian Peninsula.

As a companion of the Prophet, Abu Khuzayma would have been part of the close-knit community that formed around Muhammad in Medina. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam during and after the Prophet's lifetime. They served as witnesses to the Prophet's words and actions, contributing to the foundation of Islamic knowledge and jurisprudence.

Abu Khuzayma lived through the rapid expansion of Islam during the Prophet's lifetime and into the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate. His death in 634 CE occurred during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just two years after the Prophet's passing, placing him among those early companions who witnessed the initial consolidation of the Islamic state but did not see its later territorial expansions.

While specific details about Abu Khuzayma's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in historical sources, his status as a companion places him among the foundational figures of early Islamic history whose presence and participation helped establish the Muslim community during its crucial formative years.

bio: Abu Lubaba bin 'Abdul Mundhir (b. c. 570) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abu Lubaba bin 'Abdul Mundhir was a prominent companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 570 CE, he was among the Ansar, the Muslim converts from Medina who provided crucial support to the early Muslim community.

Abu Lubaba is historically significant as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. This battle holds particular importance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the resilience of the early Muslim state and is frequently referenced in Islamic sources as a defining moment for the community.

His full name, Abu Lubaba bin 'Abdul Mundhir, follows the Arabic naming convention where "Abu Lubaba" serves as his kunya (honorific name), while "bin 'Abdul Mundhir" indicates his paternal lineage. As a companion of the Prophet, he belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the revelation and early implementation of Islamic teachings.

The companions, known collectively as the Sahaba, hold a special position in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of hadith literature and Islamic knowledge to subsequent generations. Their testimonies and accounts form the foundation of much Islamic jurisprudence and historical understanding of the Prophet's life and teachings.

Abu Lubaba lived through the crucial transition period that saw the establishment of the first Islamic state in Medina, the expansion of Muslim influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula, and the beginning of the larger Arab conquests. He died in 634 CE, during the early years of the first Caliphate under Abu Bakr, having witnessed the complete transformation of Arabian society and the emergence of Islam as a major religious and political force.

While specific details about his individual contributions to hadith transmission or particular roles in the early Muslim community require further verification through primary sources, his status as a Badr veteran and companion places him among the foundational figures of early Islamic history whose experiences helped shape the religious and historical narratives that would influence Muslim communities for generations to come.

full: Ja'far ibn Muhammad Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi
titles: Albumasar (Latin) · Ja'far ibn Muhammad
bio: While he was not a major innovator, his practical manuals for training astrologers profoundly influenced Muslim intellectual history and, through translations, that of western Europe and Byzantium.
bio_full:
Abu Ma‘shar al-Balkhi, Latinized as Albumasar (also Albusar, Albuxar, Albumazar; full name Abū Maʿshar Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar al-Balkhī  ابومَعْشَر جعفر بن محمد بن عمر بلخی;
10 August 787 – 9 March 886, AH 171–272), was an early Persian Muslim astrologer, thought to be the greatest astrologer of the Abbasid court in Baghdad. While he was not a major innovator, his practical manuals for training astrologers profoundly influenced Muslim intellectual history and, through translations, that of western Europe and Byzantium.

Life
Abū Maʿshar was a native of Balkh, a town in the Balkh province of Afghanistan, approximately 74 kilometres (46 mi) south of the Amu Darya, one of the main bases of support of the Abbasid revolt in the early 8th century. Its population, as was generally the case in the frontier areas of the Arab conquest of Persia, remained culturally dedicated to its Sasanian and Hellenistic heritage. He probably came to Baghdad in the early years of the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn (r. 813–833). According to al-Nadim's  Al-Fihrist (10th century), he lived on the west side of Baghdad, near Bab Khurasan, the northeast gate of the original city on the west bank of the Tigris.
Abū Maʿshar was a member of the third generation (after the Arab Conquest) of the Pahlavi-oriented Khurasani intellectual elite, and he defended an approach of a “most astonishing and inconsistent” eclecticism. His reputation saved him from religious persecution, although there is a report of one incident where he was whipped for his practice of astrology under the caliphate of al-Musta'in (r. 862–866).
He was a scholar of hadith, and according to biographical tradition, he only turned to astrology at the age of forty-seven (832/3).
He became involved in a bitter dispute with al-Kindi (c. 796–873), the foremost Arab philosopher of his time, who was versed in Aristotelism and Neoplatonism. It was his confrontation with al-Kindi that convinced Abū Maʿshar of the need to study “mathematics” in order to understand philosophical arguments.
His foretelling of an event that subsequently occurred earned him a lashing ordered by the displeased Caliph al-Musta'in. "I hit the mark and I was severely punished."
Al-Nadim includes an extract from Abū Maʿshar's book on the variations of astronomical tables, which describes how the Persian kings gathered the best writing materials in the world to preserve their books on the sciences and deposited them in the Sarwayh fortress in the city of Jayy in Isfahan. The depository continued to exist at the time al-Nadim wrote in the 10th century.
Amir Khusrav mentions that Abū Maʿshar came to Benaras (Varanasi) and studied astronomy there for ten years. 
Abū Maʿshar is said to have died at the age of 98 (but a centenarian according to the Islamic year count) in Wāsiṭ in eastern Iraq, during the last two nights of Ramadan of AH 272 (9 March 866). 
Abū Maʿshar was a Persian nationalist, studying Sasanian-era astrology in his "Kitab al-Qeranat" to predict the imminent collapse of Arab rule and the restoration of Persian rule.

Works

Science of astrology
His work Kitāb al-madkhal al-kabīr (English: The Great Introduction to the Science of Astrology) provides an introduction to astrology which received many translations to Latin and Greek starting from the 11th century.
In one part of this book he records the rising of tides in relation with the position of the Moon, noticing that there are two high-tides in a day. He rejected Greek thought that moonlight influenced the tides and considered that the Moon had some astrological virtue that attracted the sea. These ideas were discussed by European medieval scholars.  It had significant influence on European medieval scholars, like Albert the Great who developed his own theory of tides based on a mix of both light and Abū Ma'shar virtue.

Other work
His works on astronomy are not extant, but information can still be gleaned from summaries found in the works of later astronomers or from his astrology works.

Kitāb mukhtaṣar al-madkhal, an abridged version of the above, later translated to Latin by Adelard of Bath.
Kitāb al-milal wa-ʾl-duwal ("Book on religions and dynasties"), probably his most important work, commented on in the major works of Roger Bacon, Pierre d'Ailly, and Pico della Mirandola.
Fī dhikr ma tadullu ʿalayhi al-ashkhāṣ al-ʿulwiyya ("On the indications of the celestial objects"),
Kitāb al-dalālāt ʿalā al-ittiṣālāt wa-qirānāt al-kawākib ("Book of the indications of the planetary conjunctions"),
Kitāb al-ulūf ("Book of thousands"), preserved only in summaries by Sijzī.
Kitāb taḥāwīl sinī al-ʿālam (Flowers of Abu Ma'shar), uses horoscopes to examine months and days of the year. It was a manual for astrologers. It was translated in the 12th century by John of Seville.
Kitāb taḥāwil sinī al-mawālīd ("Book of the revolutions of the years of nativities"). translated into Greek in 1000, and from that translation into Latin in the 13th century.
Kitāb mawālīd al-rijāl wa-ʾl-nisāʾ ("Book of nativities of men and women"), which was widely circulated in the Islamic world.  ʻAbd al-Ḥasan Iṣfāhānī copied excerpts into the 14th century illustrated manuscript the Kitab al-Bulhan (ca.1390).

Latin and Greek translations

Albumasar's "Introduction" (Kitāb al-mudkhal al-kabīr, written c. 848) was first translated into Latin by John of Seville in 1133, as Introductorium in Astronomiam, and again, less literally and abridged, as De magnis coniunctionibus, by Herman of Carinthia in 1140.
Lemay (1962) argued that the writings of Albumasar were very likely the single most important original source for the recovery of Aristotle for medieval European scholars prior to the middle of the 12th century.
Herman of Carinthia's translation, De magnis coniunctionibus, was first printed by Erhard Ratdolt of Augsburg in 1488/9.
It was again printed in Venice, in 1506 and 1515.
Modern editions:

full: Abu Madyan Shu'ayb ibn al-Husayn al-Ansari al-Andalusi
primaryTitle: Shu'ayb al-Andalusi — Patron Saint of Tlemcen
titles: Patron Saint of Tlemcen · Teacher of the West
bio: Abu Madyan Shu'ayb ibn al-Husayn al-Ansari al-Andalusi (c. 1126–1198) was a mystic of the Qadiriyya tradition, based in Seville. Known as Shu'ayb al-Andalusi — Patron Saint of Tlemcen.
bio_full:
Abu Madyan Shuʿayb ibn al-Husayn al-Ansari al-Andalusi (Arabic: ابو مدين شعيب بن الحسين الأنصاري الأندلسي; c. 1126 – 1198 CE), commonly known as Abū Madyan, was an influential Andalusian mystic and a great Sufi master.
Some even refer to him as the national figure of Maghreb mysticism as he was such a forerunner of Sufism in this geographical area. Devoted to the fervent service of God, he helped introduce looking into oneself and harmonizing internal occurrences with the external observances through asceticism.
Among his most famous students were Ibn 'Arabi (d. 637/1240) and the historian Ibn Hammad (d. 628/1230).

Life
Abu Madyan was born in Cantillana, a small town about 35 km away from Seville, in 1126. He came from an obscure family and his parents were poor. As he grew up, he learned the trade of a weaver as it was a popular practice at the time. His insatiable hunger for knowledge, however, piqued his interest in the Qur'an and the study of religion and mysticism. After crossing the Strait of Gibraltar, he worked for a while in Sabta (Ceuta) with fishermen. Afterwards, he went to Marrakesh, where he served in the Almoravid army defending the city.
Soon after, Abu Madyan traveled to Fez to complete his education. He left for Fez at about the end of the Almoravid era or at the beginning of the founding of the Almohad state. There, he studied under Abu Ya’azza al-Hazmiri, ‘Ali Hirzihim, and al-Dakkak. It was al-Dakkak that provided him with the khirka, the cloak passed from Master to student in the study of Sufism. Abu Madyan was particularly fascinated with mysticism by Sidi Ali Ibn Harazem. After finishing his studies with his master Abu Ya'za, he traveled to the Orient. During his time in the Orient, he became familiar with the works of Al-Ghazali, one of the most prominent theologians, philosophers, and mystics of Sunni Islam regarded as one of the renewers of the religion.
Abu Madyan went to Mecca where he met the great Muslim saint, Jilani, and completed his spiritual training under him. On his return, he went to the town of Béjaïa where he practiced very strict asceticism and acquired an honorable reputation for his knowledge. People would come far to both listen to his public lectures and consult him on certain manners. People believed he could even perform miracles.
His beliefs were in opposition to the Almohade doctors of that town. The Almohads were disturbed at his increasing reputation and wanted to get rid of him.
Eventually, Madyan settled in the town of Béjaïa where he established a mosque-school (zawiya). The sheer amount of fame and influence that Abu Madyan evoked raised serious concern from the political powers of the time. The Almohad Caliph Ya’qub al-Mansur summoned Abu Madyan to Marrakesh for this reason so he could talk to Abu Madyan himself. Upon his summoning to Marrakesh, Abu Madyan was taken ill and died before he reached his destination in 594/1198, near the river of Ysser (يسر). His last sigh was supposedly "Allah al-Haqq." He was buried in al-‘Ubbad near Tlemcen, Algeria. His funeral was widely commemorated by the people of Tlemcen and he has been considered the patron saint and protector of Tlemcen ever since. A mausoleum was built by the order of the Almohade sovereign, Muhammad al-Nasir, too shortly after his death. Many princes and kings of Tlemcen have contributed to this mausoleum since his demise. Many monuments, a good number of them still well preserved, were built in his honor next to his tomb by the Marinid kings, who controlled Tlemcen in the 14th century. One such monument is the Mosque of Madrasa. His tomb became the center of fine architecture and is still a place of pilgrimage for many Sufis today.

Teachings
The basic principles and virtues taught at Madyan’s school in Bejaia were repentance (tawba), asceticism (zuhd), paying visits to other masters, and service to experienced masters. He emphasized futuwa (youth/chivalry) but only when accompanied by the obedience of devotees to their master, the avoidance of disagreements between devotees, justice, constancy, nobility of mind, the denunciation of the unjust, and a feeling of satisfaction with the gifts of God. Because of his focus on the acceptance of one’s emotions, Madyan and his followers refused to confine themselves to only asceticism and meditation alone, but instead lived day to day by maintaining close relationships with the people around them. Along with sharing his knowledge and ideas with his disciples, Abu Madyan wrote many poems and spoke in proverbs in order to connect with the masses and not just the intellectuals.
According to Yahya ibn Khaldun, Abu Madyan's teachings may all be summed up in this verse which he often repeated, 
"Say Allah! and abandon all that is matter, or is connected with it, if though desirest to attain the truth goal."

Legacy
Aside from attaining Ghawth status and teaching hundreds and hundreds of disciples, Abu Madyan left his mark in more ways than one. He gained immense popularity because he was relatable, despite his high scholarly status. He had a personality and way of speaking that united people from all walks of life, from the common people to the academics. Even to this day, scholars say that no one of the time surpassed him in religious and intellectual influence. His school produced hundreds of saints and out of the 46 Sufi saints in the Rif region, 15 were his disciples. People still visit his tomb today for asking God through him, which is called tawassul, they visit him from all around the world.

Sayings
There are very few surviving writings from Abu Madyan, and of those that do still exist, there are mystical poems, a testament (wasiyya) and a creed (aqida). He encouraged the free expression of emotions rather than rigidity, but also made known his support of asceticism complete devotion to God and a minimalist lifestyle.

Works

Diwan, (collection of his poems) édit. Chaouar of Tlemcen, Damascus, 1938.
Ouns al Wahid, Ms 2-105 (8) fol. 337–343, Bibliot. Nat. Paris, ed. in Cairo 1301–1884, with a commentary by Ahmed Bâ'chan.

bio: Abu Marthad al-Ghanvi (c. 570–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abu Marthad al-Ghanvi was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 570 CE in the Hijaz region, he belonged to the Ghanm tribe and became one of the early converts to Islam in Mecca.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Abu Marthad was among those who directly interacted with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community. He participated in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, the first major military encounter between the early Muslim community and the Meccan tribes. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as it marked a turning point for the nascent Muslim state in Medina, and those who participated became known as the "Companions of Badr," a designation that carried special honor within the early Islamic community.

Abu Marthad was recognized as part of the early ascetic tradition within Islam, representing those companions who emphasized spiritual discipline and withdrawal from worldly concerns. This ascetic approach was characterized by simple living, frequent prayer, and dedication to religious devotion, reflecting one strand of early Islamic spirituality that developed alongside the community's expansion.

Like many of the early companions, Abu Marthad experienced the major transitions of early Islamic history, including the migration period between Mecca and Medina, the establishment of the first Islamic polity, and the initial expansion of Muslim influence in Arabia. He lived through the Prophet's death in 632 CE and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr.

Abu Marthad died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, having witnessed the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to the dominant force in the Arabian Peninsula. His participation in Badr and his status as a direct companion of Muhammad secured his place in early Islamic historical memory, particularly among those who valued the ascetic dimensions of Islamic practice. His life span coincided almost exactly with the emergence and initial consolidation of Islam as both a religious and political force in seventh-century Arabia.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Abu Mas'ud al-Badri ( , (b. c. 591 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Abu Mas'ud al-Badri, 'Uqba ibn 'Amr ibn Tha'laba al-Ansari, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj of Medina. His father was 'Amr ibn Tha'laba and his mother Salama bint 'Azib. Ibn Qani' and Ibn Manzur trace his descent through Judara ibn 'Awf ibn al-Harith of the Khazraj; Ibn Manjuwayh spells the name Khudara.

He was present at the Second Pledge of al-'Aqaba. Whether he fought at Badr is disputed. Al-Bukhari listed him among the people of Badr, but al-Waqidi and Ibn Hibban say he did not fight there, and this is said to be the view of most biographers. They explain the name 'al-Badri' by his having lived at the water of Badr.

He settled in Kufa and built a house there. He was one of the companions of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who appointed him over Kufa when he marched to Siffin. He was a well-known narrator of hadith, quoted in Sahih al-Bukhari. Those who transmitted from him include his son Bashir, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, 'Alqama ibn Qays, Abu Wa'il Shaqiq and Rib'i ibn Kharash.

Accounts of his death differ. Ibn al-Athir gives 41 or 42 AH, adding that others said after 60 AH, and al-Waqidi said he died in Medina during Mu'awiya's caliphate. Yahya al-Qattan said he died in Kufa around the time 'Ali was killed, al-Mada'ini gave 40 AH, Khalifa said before 40, and Ibn Qani' said 39; Ibn Hibban says only that he died in the days of 'Ali.

bio: Abu Mulayl bin al-'Az'ar (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Abu Mulayl bin al-'Az'ar was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who joined the growing community in Medina during the Prophet's lifetime.

Abu Mulayl is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr came to be known as the "Badriyyun" or "Companions of Badr," a designation that carried special honor and recognition within the early Muslim community.

As a Sahabi (companion of the Prophet), Abu Mulayl belonged to the generation that had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the revelation and early implementation of Islamic teachings. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet, which later formed the basis of hadith literature—the second most important source of Islamic law and guidance after the Quran.

Abu Mulayl was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Islamic state after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the political and spiritual capital during this foundational period, and its residents, both the indigenous Ansar (helpers) and the immigrant Muhajirun (emigrants), formed the core of the early Muslim community.

His death in 634 CE occurred during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just two years after the Prophet's passing. This places him among the companions who lived through the critical transition period when the Muslim community was establishing its identity and governance structure following the Prophet's death.

While specific details about Abu Mulayl's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in available historical sources, his status as a companion and participant in this pivotal battle marks him as part of the foundational generation that helped establish Islam as both a religious and political force in seventh-century Arabia. His life span of approximately forty years coincided with the emergence and early expansion of the Islamic community from its origins in Mecca to its establishment in Medina.

full: Abd Allah ibn Qays ibn Sulaym al-Ash'ari
primaryTitle: Ahsan al-Nas Sawtan — Most Beautiful Voice for Quran
titles: Ahsan al-Nas Sawtan · Governor of Basra and Kufa
bio: Prominent Companion of the Prophet, praised for his beautiful Quran recitation. Served as governor of Basra under Umar and governor of Kufa under Uthman. Participated in the conquests of Persia. Served as arbitrator during the First Fitna after the Battle of Siffin. Ancestor of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari.

full_name_ar: أبو موسى عبد الله بن قيس بن سليم الأشعري
bio_full:
Abu Musa Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ash'ari (Arabic: أبو موسى عبد الله بن قيس الأشعري, romanized: Abū Mūsā ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qays al-Ashʿarī), better known as Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (Arabic: أبو موسى الأشعري, romanized: Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī) (died c. 662 or 672) was a companion of Muhammad and an important figure in early Islamic history. He was at various times governor of Basra and Kufa and was involved in the early Muslim conquest of Persia.

Life
Abu Musa came originally from Zabid, in the region of Yemen, where his tribe, the Asha'ir, lived in the pre-Islamic period. He accepted Islam at Mecca prior to the hijra and returned to his native Yemen to propagate the faith. He lived in Habasha for some time until following the conquest of Khaybar in 628, when he came to Muhammad in Medina with more than fifty converts from Yemen, including his two brothers Abu Ruhm and Abu Burdah.
Following the conquest of Mecca in 629, Abu Musa was named among those sent by Muhammad on the expedition to Awtas. Two years later he was appointed as one of the governors over Yemen, where he remained until the caliphate of Abu Bakr, whom he joined in fighting the local leader of the ridda (lit. apostasy) movement.

During Muhammad's era

He was present during the Expedition of Dhat al-Riqa. Some scholars claim that the expedition took place in Nejd (a large area of tableland in the Arabian Peninsula) in Rabi‘ Ath-Thani or Jumada Al-Ula, 4 A.H (or beginning of 5AH). They substantiate their claim by saying that it was strategically necessary to carry out this campaign in order to quell the rebellious bedouins in order to meet the exigencies of the agreed upon encounter with the polytheists, i.e. minor Badr Battle in Sha‘ban, 4 A.H. Muhammad received the news that certain tribes of Banu Ghatafan were assembling at Dhat al-Riqa with suspicious purposes.
Muhammad proceeded towards Nejd at the head of 400 or 700 men, after he had mandated Abu Dhar - in the Umayyad version, the Umayyad chief : Uthman ibn Affan was given this honor- to dispose of the affairs of Madinah during his absence. The Muslim fighters penetrated deep into their land until they reached a spot called Nakhlah where they came across some bedouins of Ghatfan.
The most authentic opinion according to "Saifur Rahman al Mubarakpuri", however, is that Dhat Ar-Riqa's campaign took place after the fall of Khaibar (and not as part of the Invasion of Nejd). This is supported by the fact that Abu Hurairah and Abu Musa Ashaari witnessed the battle. Abu Hurairah embraced Islam only some days before Khaibar, and Abu Musa Al-Ash‘ari came back from Abyssinia (Ethiopia) and joined Muhammad at Khaibar. The rules relating to the prayer of fear which Muhammad observed at Dhat Ar-Riqa's campaign, were revealed at the Asfan Invasion which scholars say, took place after Al-Khandaq (the Battle of the Trench).

After the Caliphate of Abu Bakr
The appointments of Abu Musa to the governorates of Basra and Kufa were made during the caliphates of Umar and Uthman, but the exact dates and circumstances are not clear. However, during the period that he was governor of one or the other of the two Muslim garrison towns in Iraq, Abu Musa is frequently mentioned in connection with the early Muslim conquest of the Sasanian Empire. In the Siege of Shushtar (642) he distinguished himself as a military commander. The Persian commander, Hormuzan, had withdrawn his forces to the fortified city of Shushtar. The Caliph Umar did not underestimate the strength of the enemy and he mobilized a force to confront Hormuzan. Among the Muslim forces were dedicated veterans like Ammar ibn Yasir, Al-Baraa ibn Malik al-Ansari, and his brother Anas, Majra'a al-Bakri, and Salamah ibn Rajaa. Umar appointed Abu Musa as commander of the army. Tostar was impossible to take by storm and several unsuccessful attempts were made to breach the walls. However, a Persian defector opened the city's gates from within making way for Abu Musa's army.
When Basra was established during 'Umar's period, he started building some canals for conveying drinking water and for irrigation. Al-Tabari reports that 'Utba ibn Ghazwan built the first canal from the Tigris River to the site of Basra when the city was in the planning stage. After the city was built, 'Umar appointed Abu Musa al-Ash'ari as the first governor. Al-Ash'ari governed during the period 17-29/638-650. He began building two important canals linking Basra with the Tigris River. These were the al-Ubulla River and the Ma'qil River. The two canals were the basis for the agricultural development of the whole Basra region and were used for drinking water. 'Umar also devised the policy of cultivating barren lands by assigning such lands to those who undertook to cultivate them. This policy continued during the Umayyad period and it resulted in the cultivation of large areas of barren lands through the construction of irrigation canals by the state and by individuals.
During the time of Caliph Uthman, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari was replaced by Abdullah ibn Aamir as governor of Basra. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari didn't show resentment about his replacement, instead he praised Abdullah Ibn Aamir as his worthy and adequate successor.

Following the assassination of Uthman
There are many unresolved issues regarding the First Fitna (literally "trial") period of dissension and civil war, which split the Muslim community following the assassination of the Caliph Uthman. When Ali arrived in Kufa in 656 seeking support against Aisha bint Abi Bakr and the Basrans it is agreed that Abu Musa (then the governor of Kufa), urged his subjects not to support Ali and avoid participation in the upcoming battle. When his advice was rejected and the people of Kufa supported Ali, Abu Musa was forced to leave and Ali disposed him from his Governorate.
However, the next year Abu Musa was named as the arbitrator (hakam) chosen by defactors in Ali's party by the terms agreed between Ali and Muawiyah after the battle of Siffin. There are many historical versions of the result of the arbitration court. According to academic research done by Khalid Kabir Alal at the University of Algeria, the most authentic version is that both Abu Musa and 'Amr ibn al-'As, the arbitrator appointed by Muawiyah I, decided that Muawiyah will be deposed, and the fate of the murderers of Uthman will be decided by the remaining of The Ten Promised Paradise.
After this Abu Musa died in Mecca and some say in Kufa. There are several different dates given for his death, the most common being 662 and 672.

Contributions to Islamic learning
Despite Abu Musa's reputation as a soldier and politician, he was also praised for his beautiful recitation of the Qur'an, and he is associated with one of the early versions (mashahef), which was superseded by Uthman's recension. Some of the variants of Abu Musa's version have been preserved. He was also a respected faqih and was regarded among the leading judges in early Muslim history.

famous: Abu Na'yla bin Salaama bin Waqash ( ,
full: Abu Na'yla bin Salaama bin Waqash ( ,
bio: Abu Na'yla bin Salaama bin Waqash ( , (b. c. 597 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Poet-Companion.
bio_full:
Abu Na'yla bin Salaama bin Waqash was a companion (sahabi) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early decades of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 597 CE, he was among the Muslims who formed the early community in Medina during the formative period of Islamic history.

As one of the sahaba, Abu Na'yla belonged to the generation of Arabs who directly encountered Prophet Muhammad and accepted Islam during the Prophet's lifetime. The companions played a crucial role in the establishment and early expansion of the Muslim community, serving as both witnesses to Islamic teachings and participants in the religion's foundational events.

Abu Na'yla is distinguished among the companions for his reputation as a poet, earning him recognition as a "Poet-Companion." Poetry held significant cultural importance in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society, serving as a primary means of artistic expression, historical record-keeping, and social commentary. Poets were highly regarded for their linguistic skills and ability to preserve tribal memories and values through verse.

The combination of his status as a companion and his poetic abilities would have made Abu Na'yla an important figure in the early Muslim community. Poet-companions often used their literary talents to support and promote Islamic ideals, creating verses that celebrated the new faith and its principles. Their works contributed to the cultural transformation occurring as Arabian society adapted to Islamic teachings.

Abu Na'yla's presence in Medina placed him at the center of early Islamic political and religious developments. Medina served as the first Muslim city-state and the base from which Islam spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Companions residing there witnessed the establishment of Islamic governance, legal principles, and community practices that would later influence Muslim societies across different regions and centuries.

His death around 637 CE occurred during the early period of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs, as Muslim armies were extending Islamic rule beyond the Arabian Peninsula into surrounding territories. Abu Na'yla represents the generation of early Muslims who experienced both the initial establishment of Islam under Prophet Muhammad and the beginning of its transformation into a major world religion and political force.

While specific details about his individual contributions and works may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, his recognition as a Poet-Companion indicates his valued role in the literary and religious culture of early Islam.

primaryTitle: Founder of the Suhrawardi Path — Uncle and Teacher of Shihab al-Din
classif: Sufi master and founder of the Suhrawardi school
titles: Shaykh al-Shuyukh · Imam al-Tasawwuf
bio: Ḍiyāʾ al-Dīn Abū Najīb al-Suhrawardī (1097–1168) was a mystic of the Suhrawardiyya tradition, based in Baghdad. Known as Founder of the Suhrawardi Path — Uncle and Teacher of Shihab al-Din.
bio_full:
Ḍiyāʾ al-Dīn Abū Najīb al-Suhrawardī was a prominent Islamic mystic who lived from 1097 to 1168 CE during the Abbasid period. Born in Suhraward, a town in northwestern Iran, he later established himself in Baghdad, which served as the center of his religious and educational activities.

Abu Najib is most significant as the founder of the Suhrawardiyya Sufi order, one of the major mystical traditions in Islam. This tariqa (Sufi path) would become influential across the Islamic world, particularly in Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and parts of the Middle East. The order emphasized a balance between mystical experience and adherence to Islamic law, promoting spiritual discipline while maintaining orthodox religious practice.

As a teacher and spiritual guide, Abu Najib attracted numerous disciples to his circle in Baghdad. His most notable student was his nephew, Shihab al-Din Abu Hafs Umar al-Suhrawardi, who would later become even more famous as the systematizer and main propagator of the Suhrawardiyya teachings. Under Shihab al-Din's influence, the order expanded significantly and developed its distinctive doctrines and practices.

Abu Najib's approach to Sufism emphasized the importance of spiritual guidance, structured religious education, and the cultivation of both inner purification and outward conformity to Islamic principles. He established a khanqah (Sufi lodge) in Baghdad that served as a center for teaching and spiritual practice, creating an institutional framework that would be replicated by later Suhrawardi establishments.

The Suhrawardiyya order founded by Abu Najib differed from some other Sufi traditions in its more moderate approach to mystical practices and its emphasis on maintaining harmony with mainstream Islamic scholarship. This characteristic helped ensure the order's acceptance within broader Islamic society and contributed to its longevity and influence.

Abu Najib's legacy extends beyond his immediate disciples through the continued presence of the Suhrawardiyya order, which remains active in various parts of the Islamic world today. His contributions to Islamic mysticism represent an important chapter in the development of organized Sufism during the classical period of Islamic civilization.

titles: Imam Ahl al-Tasawwuf (Imam of the Sufi Community) · Compiler of Sufi Doctrine
bio: Abu Nasr 'Abd Allah al-Sarraj al-Tusi (c. 920–988) was a scholar of the Khorasan School tradition, based in Tus. Known as Imam Ahl al-Tasawwuf.
bio_full:
Abu Nasr 'Abd Allah al-Sarraj al-Tusi was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from approximately 920 to 988 CE in the city of Tus, located in the Khorasan region of present-day Iran. He belonged to the influential Khorasan School of Islamic scholarship, which flourished during the early medieval period and produced many notable religious thinkers.

Al-Sarraj earned the honorific title "Imam Ahl al-Tasawwuf," meaning "Leader of the People of Sufism," indicating his recognized authority in Islamic mysticism and spiritual practice. This designation reflects his significant contributions to the development and systematization of Sufi thought during a formative period in Islamic mystical tradition.

Living during the 10th century, al-Sarraj witnessed and participated in a crucial era of Islamic intellectual development. This period saw the consolidation of various Islamic sciences and the emergence of distinct schools of thought across the Muslim world. The Khorasan region, where he was based, served as an important center of learning that connected the Islamic heartlands with Central Asia and India.

His work contributed to the broader scholarly environment of Khorasan, which was known for producing influential jurists, theologians, and mystics who shaped Islamic thought. The region's strategic location along trade routes facilitated the exchange of ideas and made it a vibrant intellectual hub during al-Sarraj's lifetime.

As a scholar of the Khorasan School, al-Sarraj was part of a tradition that emphasized rigorous scholarship combined with spiritual insight. This approach sought to balance external religious observance with internal spiritual development, a synthesis that became characteristic of mature Sufi thought.

The recognition of al-Sarraj as an imam of the Sufi community indicates that his contemporaries viewed him as a reliable guide in matters of Islamic mysticism. During this period, Sufism was developing its distinctive vocabulary, practices, and institutional forms, making the work of scholars like al-Sarraj crucial for establishing the intellectual foundations of the tradition.

His life spanned nearly seven decades during a dynamic period of Islamic civilization, when the Muslim world was experiencing significant cultural and intellectual flourishing. Through his scholarly activities in Tus, al-Sarraj contributed to the rich tradition of Islamic learning that characterized the Khorasan region and influenced the broader development of Islamic mystical thought.

primaryTitle: Faris Rasul Allah — Cavalry Commander of the Prophet
titles: Faris Rasul Allah · Elite cavalryman
bio: al-Harith ibn Rib'i al-Ansari al-Khazraji (c. 600–674) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Faris Rasul Allah — Cavalry Commander of the Prophet.
bio_full:
Abu Qatada al-Ansari, whose full name was al-Harith ibn Rib'i al-Ansari al-Khazraji, was a prominent companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived from approximately 600 to 674 CE. He belonged to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who supported Muhammad and the early Muslim community after the migration from Mecca in 622 CE. Specifically, he was from the Khazraj tribe, one of the two main Arab tribes of Medina that embraced Islam.

Abu Qatada earned the distinguished title "Faris Rasul Allah," meaning "Cavalry Commander of the Prophet," reflecting his important military role in the early Islamic community. This designation indicates his expertise in mounted warfare and his trusted position in the Prophet's military campaigns. During the formative years of Islam, when the Muslim community faced numerous military challenges, skilled cavalry commanders like Abu Qatada played crucial roles in defending and expanding the nascent Islamic state.

As one of the Ansar, Abu Qatada represented the Medinan Muslims who provided critical support to the Prophet and the immigrant Muslims from Mecca. The Ansar were instrumental in establishing Islam's first political community and are remembered for their loyalty and sacrifices during Islam's early, vulnerable period.

Beyond his military contributions, Abu Qatada is associated with the early ascetic tradition in Islam. This suggests he was among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline, simplicity, and devotion to worship alongside their worldly duties. The early ascetic movement in Islam emphasized renunciation of excessive material pleasures and focus on spiritual development, representing an important strand of early Islamic spirituality.

Abu Qatada's significance in Islamic history lies in his representation of the Ansar's dedication to the Prophet and the early Muslim community, his military leadership during critical formative battles, and his embodiment of early Islamic spiritual values. His life spanned the entire prophetic period and extended into the early expansion of the Islamic empire, making him a witness to and participant in some of the most pivotal moments in Islamic history. His dual role as both military leader and spiritual exemplar illustrates the integrated nature of worldly service and religious devotion that characterized many of the Prophet's companions.
