bio: al-Namr bin Tulab al-'Akli (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Poet-Companion.
bio_full:
al-Namr bin Tulab al-'Akli was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the early seventh century. Born around 595 CE, he was among the generation that witnessed the emergence and early expansion of the Islamic community in the Arabian Peninsula.

As indicated by his epithet "Poet-Companion," al-Namr was recognized for his literary abilities, particularly in poetry, which held significant cultural importance in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society. Poetry served not only as artistic expression but also as a means of preserving tribal history, conveying religious and moral teachings, and strengthening community bonds. The combination of his status as a companion of the Prophet and his poetic talents would have made him a notable figure within the early Muslim community.

Al-Namr's association with hadith sciences reflects the broader role that many companions played in the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings. The companions, having direct contact with Prophet Muhammad, were crucial sources for recording and passing down his sayings, actions, and teachings to subsequent generations. This transmission process formed the foundation of hadith literature, which became one of the primary sources of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran.

His presence in the Hijaz region places him at the geographical heart of early Islamic developments. The Hijaz, encompassing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was where the Prophet Muhammad received his prophetic calling and where the first Muslim community was established. Being based in this region would have provided al-Namr with direct exposure to the central events and personalities of early Islamic history.

Al-Namr bin Tulab al-'Akli died around 635 CE, during the period of the early Islamic expansion under the first caliphs. His relatively short life span of approximately forty years was characteristic of his era, yet it encompassed the entire prophetic period and the beginning of Islam's rapid spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about his individual contributions may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, his recognition as both a companion and a poet indicates his participation in the cultural and religious life of the early Muslim community during one of the most significant periods in Islamic history.

full: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb al-Nasa'i
primaryTitle: Imam al-Naqd — Most Precise of the Six Masters
titles: Imam al-Naqd · Most precise criteria among the six canonical masters
bio: Al-Nasāʾī, full name Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Aḥmad ibn Shuʿayb ibn ʿAlī ibn Sinān ibn Baḥr ibn Dīnar al-Khurasānī al-Nasāʾī, was a noted collector of hadith, from the city of Nasa, and the author of "As-Sunan", one of the six canonical hadith collections recognized by Sunni Muslims. From his "As-Sunan al-Kubra " he wrote an abridged version, "Al-Mujtaba" or Sunan al-Sughra. Of the fifteen books he is known to have written, six treat the science of hadīth.
bio_full:
Al-Nasāʾī (215 – 303 AH; c. 830 – 915 CE), full name Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Aḥmad ibn Shuʿayb ibn ʿAlī ibn Sinān ibn Baḥr ibn Dīnar al-Khurasānī al-Nasāʾī (Arabic: أبو عبد الرحمن أحمد بن شعيب النَّسائي), was a noted collector of hadith (sayings of Muhammad), from the city of Nasa (early Khorasan and present day Turkmenistan), and the author of "As-Sunan", one of the six canonical hadith collections recognized by Sunni Muslims. From his "As-Sunan al-Kubra (The Large Sunan)" he wrote an abridged version, "Al-Mujtaba" or Sunan al-Sughra (The Concise Sunan). Of the fifteen books he is known to have written, six treat the science of hadīth.

Biography
Of Persian origin, Al-Nasa'i himself states he was born in the year 830 (215 h.) - although some say it was in 829 or 869 (214 or 255 h.) - in the city of Nasa in present-day Turkmenistan - part of Khorasan, a region in Western Asia and Central Asia known for its many centres of Islamic learning. There he attended the gatherings and circles of knowledge, known as "halaqat". His facination with knowledge began at an early age. In the year 230 AH, at about 15 years old, he began his travels with his first journey to Qutaibah b. Saʿīd where he stayed in the city of Baghlan for a year and two months. He covered the whole Arabian Peninsula seeking knowledge from scholars in Iraq, Kufa, the Hijaz, Syria and Egypt, where he eventually settled and where scholars would travel to to visit him. He was an unparalleled scholar of his time.  A habit of his was to fast every other day, as this was a habit of Dawud.
He had a radiant face, well into his old age. He came from a wealthy background and would often wear Nubian clocks. Imam Dhahabī narrates a story about Imam Nasāʾi of when he went to the circle of al-Hārith b. Miskīn and he refused to let Imam Nasāʾi enter fearing he was a government spy due to his elevated apparel uncommon for students of Islamic knowledge of the time. Imam Nasāʾi then sat behind a door and listened to al-Hārith b. Miskīn read hadith. 

Death
In 302 AH/915 AD, he stopped by in the city of Damascus in between his long journey from Cairo to Mecca just as a stopping point. Near the time of his death, he had become a renowned scholar in the Islamic world and decided to give a speech in the Umayyad Mosque as a scholar of his repute tends to do. The lecture he did was on the virtues of the companions of Muhammad, specifically throughout the lecture he recited the virtues of Ali that he had heard of throughout his life. His narrating the virtues of Ali railed up the crowd due to the anti-Alid sentiments in Damascus. In opposition, the crowd felt that there was nothing about Mu'awiya I in the lecture and asked him to narrate something related to the Umayyad caliph. He responded back by saying the only narration that he had heard about him about Mu'awiya by Muhammed was when Muhammed prayed to Allah saying "May Allah not fill his stomach". The crowd took this narration as a demerit from Muhammad leading the crowd to beat him. Those anti-Alid Syrians crushed Imam an-Nasa'i's testicles and cut open his stomach because of which Imam got martyred. It is said he was buried between Safā and Marwā or in Palestine. 

Teachers
According to the hafiz Ibn Hajr Alaih, al-Nasa'i's teachers were too numerous to name, but included:

Ishaq Ibn Rahwayh
Imam Abu Daud Al-Sijistani (author of Sunan Abu Dawood)
Qutayba ibn Sa'id
Hafiz ibn Hajr and others claimed that Imam Bukhari was among his teachers.  However Al-Mizzi, refutes that the Imam ever met him.  As-Sakhawi gives the reasons in great detail for al-Mizzi's claim that they never met, but argues these must apply also to his claim that An-Nasa'i heard from Abu Dawud. Moreover, Ibn Mundah narrates the following: We were informed by Hamzah, that an-Nasa'i, Abu Abd-ur-Rahman informed us saying, 'I heard Muhammad Ibn Isma'il Al-Bukhari...' Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub al-Juzajani was also an influence.
In Egypt an-Nasa'i began to lecture, mostly narrating ahadith (hadith plural) to the extent that he became known by the title "Hafizul Hadeeth".  His lectures were well attended and among his many students were the scholars:

Imam Abul Qasim Tabrani
Imam Abu Bakr Ahmed ibn Muhammad, also known as Allamah ibn Sunni
Sheikh Ali, the son of the Muhaddith, Imam Tahawi.

School of Thought
Imam Izzakie was a follower of the Shafi'i fiqh (jurisprudence) according to Allamah as-Subki, Shah Waliullah, Shah Abdulaziz and many other scholars.

bio: al-Nu'man bin 'Abdu 'Amr bin Mas'ud (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: al-Nu'man ibn Abd Amr ibn Mas'ud was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Hibban and Abu Nu'aym give his lineage as ibn Mas'ud ibn Abd al-Ashhal ibn Haritha ibn Dinar ibn al-Najjar, placing him in the clan of Banu Dinar ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj; another version gives Mas'ud ibn Ka'b ibn Abd al-Ashhal. He fought at the Battle of Badr together with his brother, al-Dahhak ibn Abd Amr. He also fought at Uhud, where he was killed; Ibn Abd al-Barr records that he was killed on the day of Uhud as a martyr. Abu Nu'aym notes that neither he nor his brother al-Dahhak left descendants.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — al-Nu'man ibn Abd Amr (Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym, al-Isti'ab)
Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — al-Nu'man ibn Abd Amr

bio: al-Nu'man bin 'Adiy bin Nadla (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
al-Nu'man bin 'Adiy bin Nadla was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the early seventh century. Born around 593 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca during a time when the nascent Muslim community faced significant persecution from the established Meccan tribes.

al-Nu'man is most notably remembered as one of the emigrants to Abyssinia, a group of early Muslims who sought refuge in the Christian kingdom of Aksum in present-day Ethiopia. This migration, known in Islamic history as the first hijra, occurred around 615 CE when the situation for Muslims in Mecca became increasingly difficult. The Prophet Muhammad advised a group of his followers to seek protection under the Christian king Najashi (the Negus), who was known for his justice and tolerance.

The decision to emigrate to Abyssinia was significant for the early Muslim community, as it represented the first major test of their commitment to their faith. Those who made this journey, including al-Nu'man, demonstrated considerable courage and dedication by leaving behind their homes, families, and familiar surroundings to preserve their religious beliefs. The emigrants found safety and were able to practice their faith freely under the protection of the Abyssinian ruler.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, al-Nu'man belonged to the generation of Muslims who directly witnessed and participated in the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions, known as sahaba in Arabic, hold a special place in Islamic history as the first generation of Muslims who learned directly from the Prophet and helped establish the foundations of the Muslim community.

al-Nu'man's classification within the tradition of early ascetics suggests that he was among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline and devotion in their religious practice. This ascetic tendency was characteristic of some of the earliest Muslim converts who sought to purify themselves through rigorous spiritual practices and simple living.

He died in 633 CE, just one year after the death of the Prophet Muhammad, during the period when the Muslim community was transitioning under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. His relatively short life span of about forty years encompassed the entire prophetic period and the earliest years of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

bio: al-Nu'man bin 'Amr bin Rifa'a (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: al-Nu'man ibn Amr ibn Rifa'a, known by the diminutive Nu'ayman, was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd gives his lineage as ibn Rifa'a ibn al-Harith ibn Sawad ibn Malik ibn Ghanm, and names his mother as Fatima bint Amr ibn Atiyya of Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar. Ibn Ishaq counts him among the seventy Ansar at the second pledge of al-Aqaba. He fought at Badr, Uhud and al-Khandaq, and Ibn Sa'd says he took part in all the battles with the Prophet. Ibn Sa'd reports that the Prophet had him flogged several times for drinking nabidh, and that a man cursed him on that account. Ibn Abd al-Barr suggests he may be the man who was flogged more than five times for drinking. Later accounts remember him for his humour and pranks. Ibn Sa'd names several children, among them Muhammad, Amir, Sabra, Lubaba and Kabsha, but states that his line did not continue. According to al-Waqidi, he lived on until his death during the caliphate of Mu'awiya.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — al-Nu'man ibn Amr ibn Rifa'a (Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Ibn Sa'd)
Wikipedia (Wikiwand mirror) — Al-Nuayman ibn Amr

bio: al-Nu'man bin 'Asar (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: al-Nu'man ibn 'Asr al-Balawi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the tribe of Bali, of Quda'a. Ibn Abd al-Barr gives his lineage as al-Nu'man ibn 'Asr ibn al-Rabi' ibn al-Harith ibn Udaym al-Balawi, with an alternative line through 'Ubayd ibn Wa'ila ibn Haritha. He was an ally (halif) of the Ansar, specifically of Banu Mu'awiya ibn Malik ibn Amr ibn Awf. Ibn Ishaq lists 'al-Nu'man al-Balawi' among the men of Banu Mu'awiya who fought at Badr, and Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr both say he took part in Badr and all the other battles with the Prophet. Ibn Makula adds that he was said to have been present at al-Aqaba. Early authorities differed over his name: al-Waqidi, Musa ibn 'Uqba, Ibn Ishaq and Abu Ma'shar read it as 'Asr, Hisham al-Kalbi read it as 'Asar, and Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Umara called him Laqit ibn 'Asr. He was killed as a martyr at al-Yamama.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — al-Nu'man ibn 'Asr (Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab)

bio: al-Nu'man bin Abi Khadhma (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Al-Nu'man ibn Abi Khadhma was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early converts who became part of the Muslim community in Medina following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Al-Nu'man is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle, fought between the early Muslim community and the Meccan Quraysh tribe, holds particular significance in Islamic history as it was the first major military victory for the Muslims and helped establish their presence in the Arabian Peninsula. Those who participated in this battle are given special recognition in Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment.

As one of the Sahaba, or companions of the Prophet Muhammad, al-Nu'man was part of the generation that directly witnessed the Prophet's teachings and the early development of Islamic practices and community life. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's sayings and actions, which would later form important sources for Islamic law and practice.

Al-Nu'man lived during a period of rapid change in Arabian society, witnessing the transformation from the pre-Islamic tribal system to the emergence of the Islamic community. His life spanned the final years of the Jahiliyyah period and the early decades of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

He died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr and shortly after the death of Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. This placed him among the early companions who did not live to see the major territorial expansions of Islam that would occur under the later caliphs.

While specific details about al-Nu'man's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in the historical sources, his status as a companion places him among the foundational generation of Muslims whose collective experiences and testimonies helped shape the early Islamic community and its understanding of prophetic teachings.

primaryTitle: Among the First Judges (Qudah) of Islam
bio: al-Nu'man bin Bashir ibn Sa'd (c. 623 CE–685 CE, Hims) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Among the First Judges of Islam.
bio_full: al-Nu'man ibn Bashir ibn Sa'd al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj of Medina. His father was the Companion Bashir ibn Sa'd and his mother was Amra bint Rawaha, sister of Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. He was born in Medina in 2 AH (c. 623 CE), and Abu Nu'aym describes him as the first child born to the Ansar after the Hijra. In the First Fitna he sided with Mu'awiya and sought vengeance for the killing of Uthman; he fought at Siffin in 657 and in 659 led an unsuccessful raid on Ali's garrison at Ayn al-Tamr. Al-Dhahabi reports that he served as judge of Damascus, succeeding Fadala. Mu'awiya made him governor of Homs in 666 and of Kufa in 679. Yazid I replaced him in 680 with Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad, partly because of his lax response to Muslim ibn Aqil's activity on behalf of Husayn ibn Ali. He transmitted hadith; his son Muhammad and al-Sha'bi are among those who narrated from him. After Yazid's death he recognised Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who returned him to Homs. Following the Battle of Marj Rahit he fled Homs and was killed nearby; al-Dhahabi places this at the village of Birin, and one account he gives dates it to late 64 AH (684 CE). Abu Nu'aym gives 60 AH instead.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: al-Nu'man bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
al-Nu'man bin Maqrin al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early decades of Islam in the seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he belonged to the Mazin tribe and became one of the notable Sahaba, the generation of Muslims who personally knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad.

Al-Nu'man's most significant recorded participation in Islamic history was his involvement in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree. This crucial event took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers were prevented from performing pilgrimage to Mecca. Under a tree, approximately 1,400 Muslims pledged their loyalty to the Prophet, promising to fight to the death if necessary. This pledge is specifically mentioned in the Quran in verse 48:18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds special significance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the unwavering commitment of the early Muslim community to their faith and leader during a moment of uncertainty and potential conflict. Those who participated in this pledge are considered to hold a distinguished status among the companions of the Prophet.

Al-Nu'man lived during the foundational period of Islam, witnessing the religion's establishment in the Hijaz region of the Arabian Peninsula. His lifetime spanned the final years of the Prophet Muhammad's mission and the early expansion of Islam under the first caliphs. He died around 640 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, when the Muslim community was rapidly expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

As one of the companions, al-Nu'man would have been among those who transmitted knowledge of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and passing down the traditions and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, forming the foundation of what would later become the formal science of Hadith literature.

While specific details about al-Nu'man's individual contributions beyond his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan are limited in historical records, his status as a companion who participated in this pivotal moment ensures his place in early Islamic history as one of the dedicated followers who helped establish the Muslim community during its formative years.

bio: al-Numan bin Sinan (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: al-Nu'man ibn Sinan was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir record him as a client (mawla) of Banu Ubayd ibn Adi ibn Ghanm ibn Ka'b ibn Salama, of the Khazraj. Abu Nu'aym instead calls him an ally (halif) of Banu Ubayd ibn Adi and gives a different line for that clan, while a report he cites from Ibn Shihab calls him their client. He fought at Badr and Uhud. Ibn Sa'd states that he died leaving no descendants. None of the classical entries gives the date or place of his death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — al-Nu'man ibn Sinan (Ibn Sa'd, al-Isti'ab, Usd al-Ghaba, Abu Nu'aym)
Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — al-Nu'man ibn Sinan

bio: al-Nuwwar bint Malik bin Sirma (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
al-Nuwwar bint Malik bin Sirma was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet and witnessed the foundational period of Islamic history.

As a resident of Medina, al-Nuwwar would have experienced the crucial years following the hijra (migration) of the Prophet Muhammad from Mecca in 622 CE. This period marked the establishment of the first Muslim community and the development of Islamic practices and teachings. Like other companions of the Prophet, she was positioned to observe and learn directly from Muhammad's words and actions during this formative time.

al-Nuwwar is recognized in Islamic tradition as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and teachings of the Prophet Muhammad. Women companions played important roles in preserving and transmitting hadith literature, often providing unique perspectives on the Prophet's behavior in domestic and social settings that male companions might not have witnessed. Female narrators were particularly valuable sources for matters relating to family life, women's religious obligations, and the Prophet's interactions within household contexts.

Her contribution to hadith sciences represents part of the broader participation of women in early Islamic scholarship and religious transmission. The companions, both male and female, served as the crucial link between the Prophet's lifetime and subsequent generations of Muslims, ensuring the preservation of Islamic teachings and practices.

The early Muslim community in Medina included numerous women who, like al-Nuwwar, served as witnesses to the Prophet's conduct and teachings. Their testimonies became integral to the body of hadith literature that would later be compiled, authenticated, and used by Islamic scholars to understand religious law and practice.

al-Nuwwar's death around 635 CE places her among the companions who died during the early expansion of Islam under the first caliphs. Her relatively short life span of approximately forty years was typical of the era, yet her role as a hadith narrator ensured that her observations and memories of the Prophet's time contributed to the preservation of Islamic tradition for future generations.

Through her participation in hadith transmission, al-Nuwwar bint Malik bin Sirma represents the important but often understudied role of women in early Islamic history and religious scholarship.

dob_s: c. 590 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)

bio: al-Nuwwar bint Qays bin al-Harith (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
al-Nuwwar bint Qays bin al-Harith was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia during the formative period of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the term used for the inhabitants of Medina who supported Muhammad and the early Muslim community after their migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, al-Nuwwar belonged to the generation of Muslims who witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic community and state. The Ansar played a crucial role in early Islamic history by providing refuge and support to the Muslim emigrants (muhajirun) who fled persecution in Mecca. This period, known as the Hijra, marked a turning point in Islamic history and the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

Her designation as a sahabiyya places her among the women who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and were part of the earliest Muslim community. The female companions hold a special status in Islamic tradition as they were witnesses to the revelation of the Quran and the development of Islamic practices and social structures.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's time meant that al-Nuwwar would have experienced the rapid transformation of Arabian society as Islam spread throughout the peninsula. The early Muslim community in Medina faced numerous challenges, including military conflicts with Meccan forces and the establishment of new social and legal frameworks based on Islamic principles.

The female companions like al-Nuwwar contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings and practices, particularly those related to women's roles in the new faith. Their experiences and testimonies became part of the historical record that helped shape Islamic jurisprudence and social customs.

al-Nuwwar's death around 635 CE occurred during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, just a few years after Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. She lived through the foundational decades of Islam, witnessing its emergence from a small community in Mecca to a major force that would soon expand beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Her inclusion in historical records as a named companion reflects the Islamic tradition's recognition of women's contributions to the early Muslim community, though detailed accounts of her specific activities and contributions have not been extensively preserved in the historical sources that have reached us today.

full: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qabisi
titles: Imam al-Maliki
bio: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qabisi (935–1012) was a scholar of the Islamic Sciences tradition, based in Qayrawan. Known as Imam al-Maliki of Qayrawan.
bio_full: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Khalaf al-Ma'afiri, known as al-Qabisi or Ibn al-Qabisi, was a Maliki jurist and hadith scholar of Qayrawan in Ifriqiya. He was born in 324 AH (935 CE). One account links his name to the village of al-Ma'afiriyyin near Qabis (Gabes); Qadi Iyad reports instead that it came from an uncle who wound his turban in the style of Qabis. His teachers included Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani, Hamza al-Kinani and Ali ibn Masrur al-Dabbagh. He travelled east for the Hajj and to study in Egypt and Mecca, spending about five years away; in Mecca he heard Sahih al-Bukhari from Abu Zayd al-Marwazi. He was blind, and some sources say this came in old age. He became a leading Maliki authority of Ifriqiya, and is reported to have accepted the role of mufti only reluctantly. His students included Abu Imran al-Fasi, Abu Amr al-Dani and Makki ibn Abi Talib. His works include al-Mulakhkhas, a collection of the connected hadiths of Malik's Muwatta in the transmission of Ibn al-Qasim, and al-Risala al-Mufassala, on the conduct of teachers and pupils. He died in Qayrawan in Rabi' al-Akhir 403 AH (1012 CE) and was buried at Bab Tunis.

bio_sources.title: Tarajm — Abu al-Hasan al-Qabisi (compiles Siyar A'lam al-Nubala, Tabaqat al-Fuqaha, Shajarat al-Nur al-Zakiyya, al-A'lam)
Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Khalaf Ibn al-Qabisi

full: Abu al-Fadl 'Iyad ibn Musa al-Yahsubi al-Maliki
titles: al-Qadi Iyad (The Judge Iyad) · Imam al-Maghrib · Qadi of Ceuta
bio: Abū al-Faḍl ʿIyāḍ ibn Mūsā ibn ʿIyāḍ ibn ʿAmr ibn Mūsā ibn ʿIyāḍ ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā ibn ʿIyāḍ al-Yaḥṣubī al-Sabtī, better known as Qāḍī Iyāḍ (1083–1149), was a Sunni polymath and considered the leading scholar in Maliki fiqh and hadith in his time. In addition, he specialized in theology, legal theory, scriptural exegesis, Arabic language, history, genealogy, and poetry.
bio_full:
Al-Qadi Iyad ibn Musa al-Yahsubi (1083-1149) was one of the most influential Islamic scholars of the 12th century, renowned for his expertise in Islamic jurisprudence, hadith studies, and numerous other fields of Islamic learning. Born in Ceuta in present-day Morocco, he lived during the height of the Almoravid dynasty in Al-Andalus and the Maghreb.

Iyad served as a judge (qadi) in his native Ceuta and later in Granada, demonstrating his practical application of Islamic law alongside his theoretical scholarship. He became the preeminent authority on Maliki jurisprudence of his era, the legal school that dominated North Africa and Islamic Spain. His mastery extended beyond law to encompass hadith studies, theology, Quranic exegesis, Arabic linguistics, history, genealogy, and poetry, marking him as a true polymath of medieval Islamic civilization.

His most celebrated work is "Al-Shifa bi Ta'rif Huquq al-Mustafa" (The Healing through Recognition of the Rights of the Chosen One), a comprehensive study of the Prophet Muhammad's life, character, and the respect due to him. This text became one of the most widely read and influential works in Islamic literature, copied and studied throughout the Muslim world for centuries. The work systematically addresses the Prophet's attributes, miracles, and the proper conduct of Muslims toward prophetic traditions.

Iyad also authored "Mashaariq al-Anwar" (The Rising Places of Lights), an important collection and explanation of prophetic traditions found in the two most authoritative hadith collections of Bukhari and Muslim. This work served as a crucial reference for scholars seeking to understand difficult or ambiguous hadith texts.

His scholarly contributions extended to biographical literature, particularly his work on the scholars and judges of Al-Andalus, providing valuable historical records of Islamic intellectual life in medieval Iberia. Through his teaching and writing, Iyad trained numerous students who carried forward his scholarly methods across North Africa and beyond.

Al-Qadi Iyad died in 1149 in Marrakech, having spent his final years under the Almohad dynasty. His works continued to be studied and referenced by subsequent generations of Islamic scholars, cementing his reputation as one of the great intellectual figures of medieval Islam and a pivotal contributor to the preservation and interpretation of Islamic religious sciences.

full: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Abī Bakr al-Qurṭubī al-Andalusī
city: Cordoba, Spain / Munya Bani Khasib, Egypt
bio: Abū ʿAbdullāh Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Abī Bakr al-Anṣārī al-Qurṭubī was an Andalusian Sunni Muslim polymath, Maliki jurisconsult, mufassir, muhaddith and an expert in the Arabic language. Prominent scholars of Córdoba, Spain, taught him, and he is well known for his classical commentary of the Quran named Tafsir al-Qurtubi.
bio_full:
Abū ʿAbdullāh Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Abī Bakr al-Anṣārī al-Qurṭubī (Arabic: أبو عبدالله القرطبي) (1214 – 29 April 1273) was an Andalusian Sunni Muslim polymath, Maliki jurisconsult, mufassir, muhaddith and an expert in the Arabic language. Prominent scholars of Córdoba, Spain, taught him, and he is well known for his classical commentary of the Quran named Tafsir al-Qurtubi.

Biography
He was born in Qurtubah (modern-day Córdoba), Al-Andalus, in the 13th century. His father was a farmer and died during a Spanish attack in 1230. During his youth, he contributed to his family by carrying clay for use in potteries. He finished his education in Qurtubah (Córdoba), studying from renowned scholars Ibn Abu Hujja and Abdurrahman ibn Ahmed Al-Ashari. After the fall of Cordoba in 1236, he left for Alexandria, where he studied hadith and tafsir. He then passed to Cairo and settled in Munya Abi'l-Khusavb, where he spent the rest of his life. In Egypt, he studied under notable teachers, including Aḥmad b. ʿUmar b. Ibrāhīm al-Qurṭubī, better known as Ibn al-Muzayyin (511–573/1117–1178), with whom he is sometimes confused; ʿAbd al-Muʿṭī b. Muḥammad al-Iskandarānī; Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī b. Hibat Allāh al-Lakhmī; and others.
Known for his modesty and humble lifestyle, he was buried in Munya Abi'l-Khusavb, Egypt, in 1273. His grave was carried to a mosque where a mausoleum was built under his name in 1971, still open for visiting today.

Views
He was very skilled in commentary, narrative, recitation and law, which is evident in his writings, and the depth of his scholarship has been recognized by many scholars. In his works, Qurtubi defended the Sunni point of view and criticised the Mu'tazilah.

Reception
The hadith scholar Dhahabi said of him, "...he was an imam versed in numerous branches of scholarship, an ocean of learning whose works testify to the wealth of his knowledge, the width of his intelligence and his superior worth."
Ibn Farḥūn said of him, “He was among the righteous servants of God — a learned scholar, knowledgeable, scrupulous, and ascetic in worldly matters; preoccupied with what concerned him of the affairs of the Hereafter. His time was fully occupied between devotion, worship, and writing.”
Ibn al-ʿImād said of him, “He was a learned imam, one who delved deeply into the meanings of hadith, skilled in composition, and precise in transmission.”
Muḥammad Makhlūf said of him:, “The learned imam — distinguished, virtuous, jurist, exegete, accomplished scholar, meticulous, and complete — he was among the righteous servants of God and the scholars who acted upon their knowledge.”
Islamic scholar Nuh Ha Mim Keller said of him:

Imam Qurtubi is Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abu Bakr ibn Farah, Abu Abdullah al-Ansari al-Qurtubi, of Cordova (in present-day Spain). A Maliki scholar and hadith specialist, he was one of the greatest Imams of Koranic exegesis, an ascetic who divided his days between worship and writing. Educated in hadith by masters like Ali ibn Muhammad al-Yahsabi and al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Bakri, he wrote works in the sciences of hadith and tenets of faith. However, his enduring contribution is his twenty volume al-Jami li Ahkam al-Qur’an [The compendium of the rules of the Koran], from which he mainly omitted the stories and histories customary in other commentaries, and recorded instead the legal rulings contained in the Koran and how scholars have inferred them, together with canonical readings (qira’at), Arabic grammar, and which verses abrogate others and which are abrogated (nasikh wa mansukh). Scholars have used it extensively ever since it was written. It is related to Qurtubi's disdainful airs, and how he used to walk about in a simple caftan with a plain cap (taqiyya) on his head. He travelled east and settled in Munya Abi al-Khusayb in upper Egypt, where he died in 671/1273

Works
Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: The most important and famous of his works, this 20-volume commentary has raised great interest and has had many editions. It is often referred to as al-Jamī' li-'Aḥkām, meaning "All the Judgements." Contrary to what this name implies, the commentary is not limited to verses dealing with legal issues, but is a general interpretation of the Quran with a Maliki point of view. Any claims made about a verse are stated and thoroughly investigated.
al-Tadhkirah fī Aḥwāl al-Mawtà wa-Umūr al-Ākhirah (Reminder of the Conditions of the Dead and the Matters of the Hereafter): a book dealing with the topics of death, the punishments of the grave, the end times and the day of resurrection
Al-Asnà fi Sharḥ al-Asmā' al-Ḥusnà
Kitāb ut-Tadhkār fi Afḍal il-Adhkār
Kitab Sharḥ it-Taqaṣṣi
Kitab Qam' il-Ḥirṣ biz-Zuhd wal-Qanā'ah: Ibn Farḥūn said: “I have not come across a work better than it in its field.”
At-Takrāb li-Kitāb it-Tamhīd
al-Mufhim lima Ushkila min Talkhis Sahih Muslim
Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān wa-adab al-tilāwa (“Merits of the Qurʾān and of the art of Qurʾānic recitation”)
Kitāb al-tadhkira fī aḥwāl al-mawtā wa-umūr al-ākhira/aḥwāl al-ukhrā (“The reminder about the circumstances of the deceased and issues of the afterlife”). Judging by the large number of extant manuscripts and its many modern editions, this was an extremely popular work on Islamic eschatology, second only to the Jāmiʿ.

titles: Imam al-Qushayri · Defender of Orthodox Sufism
bio: Abu al-Qasim 'Abd al-Karim al-Qushayri al-Naysaburi (986–1072) was a scholar of the Khorasan School tradition, based in Nishapur. Known as Defender of Orthodox Sufism.
bio_full:
'Abd al-Karīm ibn Hawazin Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī al-Naysābūrī (Persian: عبدالکریم قُشَیری‎, Arabic: عبد الكريم بن هوازن بن عبد الملك بن طلحة أبو القاسم القشيري; 986 – 30 December 1072) was an Arab Muslim scholar, theologian, jurist, legal theoretician, commentator of the Qur’an, muhaddith, grammarian, spiritual master, orator, poet, and an eminent scholar who mastered a number of Islamic sciences. Al-Qushayri, combined the routine instruction of a Shafi'i law specialist and Hadith expert (muhaddith) with a solid slant to mysticism and ascetic lifestyle.
He was born in Nishapur which is in Khorasan province in Iran. This region was widely known as a center of Islamic civilization up to the 13th Century CE. He was the grandfather of the hadith scholar Abd al-Ghafir al-Farsi, a student of Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni.

Biography
Al Qushayri was born into a privileged Arab family from among the Banu Qushayr who had settled near Nishapur. As a young man he received the education of a country squire of the time: adab, the Arabic language, chivalry and weaponry (istiʿmāl al-silāḥ), but that all changed when he journeyed to the city of Nishapur and was introduced to the Sufi shaykh Abū ʿAlī al-Daqqāq. Daqqaq was a student of al-Nasrabadhi (d. 367/977), who was the foremost ascetic of his time in Khorasan. Al-Nasrabadhi himself was a student of Abu Bakr al-Shiblì (d. 946), the student of Junayd Al-Baghdadi.
Daqqāq later became the master and teacher of the mystical ways to Qushayri. He later married the daughter of Daqqāq, Fatima. After the death of Daqqāq, Qushayri became the successor of his master and father-in-law and became the leader of mystic assemblies in the madrasa that Abu Ali al-Daqqāq built in 1001 CE, which later became known as al-Madrasa al-Qushayriyya or "the school of the Qushayri family". Qushayri was also the student of Al-Sulami, another student of al-Nasrabadhi (d. 367/977).
In later years Qushayri performed the pilgrimage in the company of Abu Muhammad al-Juwayni (d. 438/1047), the father of the great Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni, as well as traveling to Baghdad and the Hijaz. During these travels he heard Hadith from various prominent Hadith scholars. Upon his return he began teaching Hadith, which is something he is famous for. He returned to Baghdad where the Caliph al-Qa'im had him perform hadith teachings in his palace. After his return to Khurāsān, political unrest in the region between the Ḥanafī and Ashʿarī-Shāfiʿī factions in the city forced him to leave Nishapur, but he was eventually able to return and lived there until his death in 1072/465, when the Seljuq vizier Nizam al-Mulk re-established the balance of power between the Ḥanafīs and the Shāfiʿīs. He left behind six sons and several daughters between Fatima and his second wife and was buried near al-Madrasa al-Qushayriyya, next to his father in-law Abū ʿAlī al-Daqqāq

Influence
Laṭā'if al-Isharat bi-Tafsīr al-Qur'ān is a famous work of al-Qushayri that is a complete commentary of the Qur'an. He determined that there were four levels of meaning in the Qur'an. First, the ibara which is the meaning of the text meant for the mass of believers. Second, the ishara, only available to the spiritual elite and lying beyond the obvious verbal meaning. Third, laṭā’if, subtleties in the text that were meant particularly for saints. And finally, the ḥaqā’iq, which he said were only comprehensible to the prophets. This text placed him among the elite of the Sufi mystics and is widely used as a standard of Sufi thought.
His fame however, is due mostly to his al-Risala al-Qushayriyya (or the Epistle on Sufism). This text is essentially a reminder to the people of his era that Sufis had authentic ancestral tradition, as well as a defence of Sufism against the doubters that rose during that time of his life. Al-Qushayri repeatedly acknowledges his debt to, and admiration for, his
Sufi master throughout his Risala. Daqqaq was instrumental in introducing Qushayri to another outstanding Sufi authority of Khurasan, al-Sulami, who is quoted on almost every page of the Risala. It has sections where al-Qushayrī discusses the creed of the Sufis, mentions important and influential Sufis from the past, and establishes fundamentals of Sufi terminology, giving his own interpretation of those Sufi terms. Al-Qushayrī finally goes through specific practices of Sufism and the techniques of those practices. This text has been used by many Sufi saints in later times as a standard, as is obvious from the many translations into numerous languages.

Legacy

Abd al-Ghafir al-Farsi said about his grandfather (Al-Qushayri):

The absolute Imam, jurist, theologian, legal theorist, the interpreter of the Qu'ran, a man of letters, grammarian, writer/poet, the master of his time, God's secret among His creation, the axis of reality, source of happiness, the pole of masterhood, one who joined the Shari'a and the Truth. He was knowledgeable in the foundations of the Ash'ari creed and in the branches of the Shafi'i school of though.
Abu al-Hasan al-Bakhirzi, the author of the book Dimyah al-Qasr, said about him:

[He was] one who gathered all kinds of goodness, the one to whom all things were facilitated, and who held the bridle of every lowly thing. So, if he were to shout at a stone, it would dissolve. And if Iblis were to attend his gathering of remembrance, he would repent. He was extremely distinguished with sound logic, and an expert in the theology of the school of al-Ash’ari. The breadth of his knowledge was almost beyond human capacity. His words were beneficial and precious gems for the seekers of benefit. Verily, the feet of his pulpit are the pillows of the Gnostics.
When the Sufi Shaykhs had agreed upon the favor he possessed and saw his nearness and allotment from the al-Haqq, they faded before him and disappeared in comparison with him. His carpet rolled them up in its margins. They were divided between looking at him and contemplating him. He has poems that crown the heads of his noble ministers. Thus, his furthest hopes are achieved through him.
Shaykh Amin considers Imam al-Qushayri's work to be an inspiration to the better-known work of Al-Ghazali:

If you understand the times of Imam al-Qushayri, I think it is a prelude to Imam al-Ghazali, and his book [al-Risala al-Qushayriyya], actually is, I would say, a blueprint for Imam al-Ghazali’s Ihya 'Ulum al-Din.

Works
Among Imam al-Qushayri's writings besides al-Risala al-Qushayriyya and Laṭā'if al-Isharat bi-Tafsīr al-Qur'an include the following:

Arba’un fi al-Hadith
Istifadah al-Muradat
Balaghah al-Maqasid 
Al-Ta’khir fi 'Ilm al-Tadhkir fi Ma’ani Ism Allah Ta’ala
Al-Taysir fi 'Ilm al-Tafsir
Uyun al-Ujubah fi Funun al-As’ilah
Al-Fusul fi al-Usul
Kitab al-Mi’raj, an account of the Night Journey
Al-Muntaha fi Nukat Ula al-Nuha.
Nasikh al-Hadith wa Mansukhihi
Nahw al-Qulub
Hayat al-Arwah wa al-Dalil ila Tariq al-Salah
Shikayah Ahl al-Sunnah bi Hikayah Ma Nalahum min al-Mihnah
Manthur al-Khitab fi Shuhud al-Albab

Sayings
I heard the master Abu Ali al-Daqqaq say: “Al-Jurayri saw al-Junayd in a
dream [after his death] and asked him: ‘How are you, Abu al-Qasim?’ He answered:
‘Gone are all those allegorical allusions (isharat), and all those unequivocal
expressions ('ibarat) have vanished. Only those praises of God that we used to
utter in the morning have benefited us [in the Hereafter]!’ ”

bio: al-Rabab bint Haritha bin Sinan (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
al-Rabab bint Haritha bin Sinan was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early decades of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the local inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, al-Rabab would have been among the Medinan women who embraced Islam and pledged their allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. The Ansar played a crucial role in the establishment of the early Muslim community, providing shelter, protection, and material support to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca. This partnership between the Ansar and Muhajirun formed the foundation of the first Islamic society in Medina.

The female companions of the Prophet Muhammad, known collectively as the Sahabiyyat, were instrumental in the early Islamic community. They participated in religious life, supported the community during times of conflict, and helped transmit Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations. Women like al-Rabab contributed to the social fabric of early Islamic society through their roles as believers, community members, and participants in the religious and social life of Medina.

Living during the formative period of Islam, al-Rabab would have witnessed the establishment of Islamic religious practices, the development of the Muslim community's social structures, and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime coincided with the Prophet's ministry in Medina, the early military campaigns, and the consolidation of Islamic authority in the region.

al-Rabab's significance lies in her status as one of the Sahabiyyat, a group revered in Islamic tradition for their direct connection to the Prophet Muhammad and their role in the early Muslim community. The female companions are remembered for their faith, dedication, and contributions to the preservation and transmission of Islamic values and practices. Her identification as an Ansari companion specifically connects her to the pivotal moment when Medina became the center of the growing Islamic movement, marking her as a participant in one of the most important chapters of early Islamic history.

The classical entries do not give the dates of her birth or death.

full: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariyya al-Razi al-Rayy
primaryTitle: Galen of the Arabs — Father of Clinical Medicine
titles: Rhazes (Latin) · Galen of the Arabs · First to distinguish smallpox from measles
bio: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariyya al-Razi al-Rayy (854–925) was a scientist of the Islamic Sciences tradition, based in Ray (near Tehran). Known as Galen of the Arabs — Father of Clinical Medicine.
bio_full:
Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariyya al-Razi was a Persian physician, philosopher, and scholar who lived from 854 to 925 CE in the city of Ray, located near present-day Tehran. Al-Razi became one of the most influential medical practitioners and theorists of the Islamic Golden Age, earning recognition as both a clinical physician and medical educator.

Al-Razi's approach to medicine emphasized careful observation, systematic record-keeping, and evidence-based treatment. He maintained detailed case studies of his patients and was among the first physicians to distinguish between smallpox and measles, providing accurate clinical descriptions of both diseases. His medical writings demonstrated a methodical approach that combined Greek medical traditions with his own empirical observations and innovations.

His most famous medical work, "Al-Hawi" (The Comprehensive Book), served as an encyclopedic compilation of medical knowledge that included Greek, Persian, Indian, and Arab medical traditions alongside his own clinical experiences. The work was later translated into Latin as "Liber Continens" and remained influential in European medical education for centuries.

Beyond medicine, al-Razi contributed to chemistry and philosophy. His chemical writings described laboratory techniques and equipment, and he classified substances into categories that influenced later alchemical and chemical studies. As a philosopher, he wrote on ethics and metaphysics, though fewer of these works have survived.

Al-Razi directed hospitals in Ray and later in Baghdad, where he established clinical teaching methods that became models for medical education. He trained students through direct patient care and emphasized the importance of studying both theory and practice.

His influence on Islamic medicine was substantial, as his works were widely copied and studied throughout the Islamic world. The clinical methods he developed, particularly his emphasis on observation and documentation, contributed to the advancement of medical practice during the Islamic Golden Age. His writings were eventually translated into Latin, Greek, and other languages, making his medical knowledge accessible to physicians beyond the Islamic world and contributing to the development of medieval European medicine.

Al-Razi's legacy lies in his systematic approach to clinical medicine and his integration of theoretical knowledge with practical experience, establishing principles that influenced medical practice for centuries after his death.

bio: al-Rubbayi' bint al-Nadr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
al-Rubbayi' bint al-Nadr was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early 7th century. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with the Prophet and witnessed the foundational period of Islam.

As a resident of Medina, al-Rubbayi' would have experienced the significant transformation of the city following the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina became the center of the early Muslim community, and companions like al-Rubbayi' played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices they observed.

al-Rubbayi' is primarily recognized for her contributions to hadith literature as a narrator of prophetic traditions. In the early Islamic community, both men and women served as transmitters of hadith, preserving the sayings, actions, and tacit approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. These oral traditions formed a critical foundation for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and practice alongside the Quran.

Her role as a hadith narrator reflects the broader participation of women in the preservation of Islamic knowledge during this formative period. Female companions often had unique access to certain aspects of the Prophet's life and teachings, particularly those related to domestic matters, family interactions, and guidance given specifically to women in the community.

The fact that al-Rubbayi' is remembered specifically for her role in hadith transmission indicates that her narrations were considered reliable and were passed down through subsequent generations of Islamic scholars. The preservation of her name and recognition of her contributions demonstrates the value placed on authenticated chains of transmission in early Islamic scholarship.

Living during the crucial decades of Islam's establishment, al-Rubbayi' would have witnessed major events including the early military campaigns, the development of Islamic law and governance, and the expansion of the Muslim community. Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

al-Rubbayi' bint al-Nadr represents the important but often understudied contributions of female companions to the preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge. Her inclusion in hadith literature ensures that her voice and observations from Islam's foundational period remain part of the historical record.

bio_full:
al-Rubbayi' bint Haritha bin Sinan was a female companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Sahabiyya, the female companions of the Prophet, al-Rubbayi' was part of the foundational generation of Muslims who directly witnessed and participated in the establishment of the early Islamic community in Medina. The Ansar played a crucial role in Islamic history by providing refuge and assistance to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca, helping to secure the survival and growth of the nascent Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

Like other women of her generation in Medina, al-Rubbayi' would have experienced the significant social and religious transformations that occurred during the Prophet's residence in the city from 622 to 632 CE. This period saw the development of key Islamic practices, the revelation of important Quranic verses, and the consolidation of the Muslim community as both a religious and political entity.

The designation of al-Rubbayi' as an Ansari Companion indicates her family's local Medinan origins and their decision to embrace Islam and support the Prophet's mission. The Ansar are remembered in Islamic tradition for their hospitality and sacrifice, sharing their homes, resources, and community with the Muslim emigrants in an act of solidarity that became a model of Islamic brotherhood.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This means she lived through the initial period of Islamic expansion under the first caliph, Abu Bakr, and witnessed the beginning of Islam's spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about al-Rubbayi's individual contributions are limited in the historical record, her recognition as a Sahabiyya places her among the women who were part of the formative community that established the practices and traditions that would guide Islamic civilization for centuries to come. Her inclusion in the ranks of the Prophet's companions reflects the important, though often understated, role that women played in the early development of Islam.

bio: al-Sa'ba bint Sahl bin Zayd (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
al-Sa'ba bint Sahl bin Zayd was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the Ansar, the indigenous population of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari woman, al-Sa'ba belonged to one of the Arab tribes of Medina that played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community. The Ansar were distinguished from the Muhajirun (the migrants from Mecca) and were highly regarded for their hospitality and support during Islam's earliest and most vulnerable years. Her tribal affiliation through her father Sahl bin Zayd connected her to the established social networks of pre-Islamic Medina.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime in Medina, al-Sa'ba would have witnessed the foundational events of early Islamic history, including the establishment of the first Muslim state, the construction of the Prophet's mosque, and the development of Islamic law and community practices. The female companions of this era played important roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, particularly those related to family life, women's religious obligations, and social customs.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing means she lived through both the prophetic period and the beginning of Islam's rapid expansion under the first caliphs.

The preservation of her name in historical records reflects the early Muslim community's recognition of the contributions made by female companions. While specific details of her individual actions or sayings may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her inclusion among the recognized sahabiyya indicates her acceptance of Islam and her role within the Medinan Muslim community.

al-Sa'ba bint Sahl bin Zayd represents the many women of the Ansar who supported the early Muslim community during its formative period in Medina, contributing to the foundation upon which Islamic civilization would develop and spread across the known world.

bio: al-Sa'ib bin al-Harith (c. 593–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: al-Sa'ib ibn al-Harith ibn Qays ibn Adi ibn Sa'd ibn Sahm was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Sahm clan of Quraysh. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Umm al-Hajjaj, of the Banu Shanuq. He was among the Muslims who emigrated to Abyssinia, in the second migration according to Ibn Sa'd, together with his brothers Bishr, al-Harith, Ma'mar and Abd Allah, the sons of al-Harith ibn Qays, as Ibn Abd al-Barr lists them. He took part in the campaign of Ta'if, where Ibn Abd al-Barr reports he was wounded. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir say he was later killed as a martyr at the Battle of Fihl in Jordan, in the land of al-Sham. Ibn al-Kalbi dated Fihl to 14 AH; Ibn Abd al-Barr places it in Dhu al-Qa'da 13 AH, at the start of Umar's caliphate. A different report, given by Ibn Manda and attributed by Ibn al-Athir to Ibn Ishaq, says he was martyred at Ta'if itself. Ibn Sa'd states that he left no descendants, and Ibn al-Athir notes that the line of al-Harith ibn Qays ibn Adi died out.

bio: al-Sa'ib ibn Uthman bin Maz'un (c. 594–633 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Al-Sāʾib bin ʿUthmān bin Maẓʿūn (Arabic: السائب بن عثمان بن مظعون الجمحي; died 632 AD) was the son of the sahabi Uthman ibn Maz'un and Khawlah bint Hakim. He was among the companions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, who participated in the battles of Badr, Uhud, Khandaq and Al-Yamama, and he was a well-known archer.

Biography
Al-Sāʾib bin ʿUthmān bin Maẓʿūn participated in the second migration to Abyssinia, alongside his family (Banu Maẓʿūn) and sahaba. He returned to Medina after the Hijrah occurred and participated in the Battle of Badr, Uhud and Khandaq alongside his father and uncles, Qudāmah ibn Maẓʿūn and ʿAbdullāh bin Maẓʿūn.
Muhammad established a bond of brotherhood between Al-Sāʾib and Ḥārithah bin Suraqah al-Anṣārī, who was martyred at Badr.

full: Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn Khalīl ibn Aybak al-Ṣafadī
bio: Khalīl ibn Aybak al-Ṣafadī, or Ṣalaḥ al-Dīn al-Ṣafadī (Arabic: صلاح الدين الصَّفديّ; full name - Ṣalaḥ al-Dīn Abū al-Ṣafa Khalīl ibn Aybak ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Albakī al-Ṣafari al-Damascī Shafi'i. was a Turkic Mamluk author and historian. He studied under the historian and Shafi'i scholar, al-Dhahabi.
bio_full:
Khalīl ibn Aybak al-Ṣafadī, or Ṣalaḥ al-Dīn al-Ṣafadī (Arabic: صلاح الدين الصَّفديّ; full name - Ṣalaḥ al-Dīn Abū al-Ṣafa Khalīl ibn Aybak ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Albakī al-Ṣafari al-Damascī Shafi'i.  (1296 – 1363) was a Turkic Mamluk author and historian. He studied under the historian and Shafi'i scholar, al-Dhahabi.
He was born in Safad, Palestine under Mamluk rule. His wealthy family afforded him a broad education, memorising the Quran and reciting the books of Hadith.  He excelled in the social sciences of grammar, language, philology and calligraphy. He painted on canvas, and was especially passionate about literature. He taught himself poetry, its systems, transmitters and meters.

His teachers
Among Ṣafadī’s many teachers from Safad, Damascus, Cairo and Aleppo were:

Al-Ḥāfīz  Fatḥ al-Dīn ibn Sayyid al-Nās (d.734AH / 1333), with whom he studied literature in Cairo.
Ibn al-Nabatah Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Farqī al-Maṣrī (d.768AH / 1367)
Abū Hayyan al-Gharnatī (d.745AH / 1345); with whom he studied grammar and philology.
Maḥmūd ibn Salmān Ibn Fahd (d.725AH / 1325-26), author of Ḥusn al-tawassul ilá ṣināʻat al-tarassul  (حسن التوسل إلى صناعة الترسل) and narrated much of his poetry.
Judge Badr al-Dīn ibn Jamāt, Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Sa’d al-Kattanī (d. 733AH / 1333-34).
Taqi al-Din al-Subki (d.756AH / 1356-57)
The Ḥadīth Abū Al-Nūn Yūnus ibn Ibrāhīm al-Dabusi (d.729AH / 1329-30)
Hafiz Jamal al-Din Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Mizzi (d.742AH / 1342), and studied by the Ḥadīth in Dar al-Hadith Ashrafieh in Damascus.
Al-Ḥafiz Shams al-Dīn Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Uthman al-Dhahabī (d.749AH / 1347-48); with whom he studied the Hadith and history.

Books
Ikhtirāʿ al-Khurāʿ ("Invention of Absurdity"); on scholastic pedantry, a satirical work in the tradition of Arabic parodies, it is one of his most famous works.
Kitāb al-Wāfī bi-l-Wafayāt (كتاب الوافي بالوفيات) (29 vols.); biographical dictionary of notable people.
Nakt al-Humyān fī Nukat al-Umyān, biographies of notable blind people, with a section on the causes of blindness.
Al-Ghayth al-Musajam fi Sharh Lamiyyat-Ajam (Flowing Desert Rains in the Commentary upon the L-Poem of the Non-Arabs); an encyclopedic commentary on Togharayi's Lamiyyat al-Ajam.
al-Ḥusn aṣ-ṣarīḥ fī miʾat malīḥ ('Pure Beauty: on one hundred handsome lads'), also a solo-authored maqāṭīʿ-collection composed between 1337 and 1338
Al-Rawḍ al-bāsim wa-l-ʿarf an-nāsim ('The Smiling Garden and the Wafting Fragrance'), a 444-poem solo-authored maqāṭīʿ-collection in forty-six chapters composed sometime before 1355
Alḥān as-sawājiʿ bayn al-bādī wa-l-murājiʿ ('Tunes of Cooing Doves, between the Initiator and Responder [in Literary Correspondence]'), an epistolary anthology
Kashf al-ḥāl fī waṣf al-khāl ('Revealing the Situation about Describing Beauty Marks')
Rashf al-zulāl fī waṣf al-hilāl ('A Sip of Pure Water: describing the crescent moon')
Ladhdhat al-samʿ fī waṣf al-dam ('Pleasing the Ears by Describing the Tears'), also known as Kitāb Tashnīf as-samʿ bi-nsikāb ad-damʿ

Notes
The Internet Archive hosts a copy of كتاب الوافي بالوفيات (Kitab Al-Wafi Bi-Al-Wafayat) at https://archive.org/details/FP49931.

bio: al-Sahmus bint Malik bin Qays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
al-Sahmus bint Malik bin Qays was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early period of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the community of Medinan Muslims who provided crucial support to the Prophet and the early Muslim emigrants from Mecca.

As an Ansari companion, al-Sahmus was part of the indigenous population of Medina who embraced Islam and welcomed the Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE. The Ansar played a vital role in the establishment and growth of the early Muslim community, offering not only political and military support but also economic assistance and social integration for the new arrivals.

Her designation as a sahabiyya places her among the women who personally knew, met, or interacted with Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime while maintaining their faith in Islam until their death. This status holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are regarded as the direct transmitters of the Prophet's teachings and the primary witnesses to the formative period of the Islamic community.

Living in Medina during the 620s and 630s CE, al-Sahmus would have witnessed the critical early decades of Islamic expansion and consolidation. This period saw the establishment of the first Islamic state, the codification of Islamic law and practice, and the beginning of the rapid spread of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

The female companions like al-Sahmus played important but often less documented roles in early Islamic society. While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively recorded in the historical sources, her recognition as a companion indicates her active participation in the early Muslim community and her direct connection to the foundational period of Islam.

al-Sahmus died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the rule of the first caliph, Abu Bakr, and shortly before or during the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate. Her life spanned the crucial transition from the pre-Islamic period through the Prophet's mission and into the early expansion of the Islamic state, making her part of the generation that witnessed and participated in one of history's most significant religious and social transformations.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: al-Saib bin al-'Awwam bin Khuwaylid (c. 597–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: al-Sa'ib ibn al-Awwam ibn Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Qusayy was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Asad clan of Quraysh and a brother of al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam. According to Ibn Sa'd his mother was Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's paternal aunt; Ibn al-Athir mentions a report naming his mother as Hala bint Uhayb, but judges the first view more accurate. Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr state that he took part in Uhud, the Battle of the Trench and the other campaigns with the Prophet. He was killed as a martyr at the Battle of al-Yamama in 12 AH, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, as Ibn Sa'd records; Ibn Manda and Abu Nu'aym also report his death at al-Yamama. Ibn Sa'd notes that he left no descendants. Abu Nu'aym corrects an error made by some writers, stating that al-Sa'ib belonged to the Banu Asad, not the Banu Abd al-Dar.

bio: Shams al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn ‘Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sakhāwī was a Shafi‘i Muslim hadith scholar and historian who was born in Cairo. Al-Sakhawi refers to the village of Sakha in Egypt, where his relatives belonged. He was a prolific writer that excelled in the knowledge of hadith, tafsir, literature, and history. His work was also anthropological. For example, in Egypt he recorded the marital history of 500 women, the largest sample on marriage in the Middle Ages, and found that at least a third of all women in the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the Bilad al-Sham married more than once, with many marrying three or more times. According to al-Sakhawi, as many as three out of ten marriages in 15th century Cairo ended in divorce. His proficiency in hadith has its influences trace back heavily on his Shaykh al-Hafiz, ibn Hajar al-`Asqalani. He died in Medina.
bio_full:
Shams al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn ‘Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sakhāwī (Arabic: شمس الدين محمد بن عبدالرحمن السخاوي, 1428/831 AH – 1497/902 AH) was a Shafi‘i Muslim hadith scholar and historian who was born in Cairo. Al-Sakhawi refers to the village of Sakha in Egypt, where his relatives belonged. He was a prolific writer that excelled in the knowledge of hadith, tafsir, literature, and history. His work was also anthropological. For example, in Egypt he recorded the marital history of 500 women, the largest sample on marriage in the Middle Ages, and found that at least a third of all women in the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the Bilad al-Sham married more than once, with many marrying three or more times. According to al-Sakhawi, as many as three out of ten marriages in 15th century Cairo ended in divorce. His proficiency in hadith has its influences trace back heavily on his Shaykh al-Hafiz, ibn Hajar al-`Asqalani. He died in Medina.

Sharḥ al-Taqrīb wa al-Taysīr li-Maʿrifat al-Bashīr wa al-Nadhīr lil-Nawawī (Explanation of Al-Taqrib and Al-Taysir for Knowing the Bearer of Glad Tidings and Warnings by Al-Nawawi)

Fatḥ al-Mughīth bi-Sharḥ Alfiyyat al-Ḥadīth (The Enlightening Opening: Commentary on the Thousand Verses on Hadith), a monumental commentary on Alfiyya of al-Iraqi by Zain al-Din al-Iraqi.

bio: al-Sakran bin 'Amr b 'Abd Shams (c. 593–620 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: al-Sakran ibn Amr ibn Abd Shams ibn Abd Wadd was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from Quraysh. Ibn Abd al-Barr describes him as the full brother, through both father and mother, of Suhayl ibn Amr. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Hubba bint Qays ibn Dubays. He was among the Muslims who emigrated to Abyssinia, taking with him his wife Sawda bint Zam'a. The sources differ on where he died. Musa ibn Uqba and Abu Ma'shar said he died in Abyssinia; Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi said he returned to Mecca and died there before the emigration to Medina. After his death the Prophet married his widow Sawda; Ibn Sa'd says she was the first woman the Prophet married after the death of Khadija. Ibn Sa'd records that al-Sakran had a son named Abd Allah.
