bio: al-Sama' bint Basr al-Maazni (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
al-Sama' bint Basr al-Maazni was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formation of the Islamic community in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Maazni tribe and was based in the Hijaz region, which encompassed the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

As a sahabiyya, al-Sama' held the distinguished status of having personally encountered and interacted with Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime. This direct connection to the Prophet placed her among the most revered generation in Islamic history, as the companions are considered the primary witnesses to Muhammad's teachings, actions, and character.

al-Sama' is particularly recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial source of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions like al-Sama' played an essential role in preserving and transmitting these prophetic traditions, especially those related to matters concerning women's religious practices, family life, and social conduct.

The participation of women like al-Sama' in hadith transmission demonstrates the early Islamic community's recognition of women as reliable sources of religious knowledge. Female narrators were particularly valued for their ability to report on the Prophet's private conduct and teachings within domestic settings, areas where male companions had limited access.

Living during the pivotal period of Islamic revelation and community formation, al-Sama' witnessed the transformation of Arabian society under Islamic teachings. Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, just after the initial wave of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about the number and content of hadiths transmitted by al-Sama' are not extensively documented in widely available sources, her inclusion among recognized female hadith narrators reflects her contribution to the preservation of prophetic traditions. The recognition of female companions as hadith transmitters underscores their integral role in maintaining the continuity of Islamic teachings from the prophetic generation to subsequent Muslim communities.

al-Sama' bint Basr al-Maazni represents the broader contribution of female companions to early Islamic scholarship and religious transmission, embodying the active participation of women in preserving the foundational teachings of Islam for future generations.

full: Shams al-Aʾimma Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Abī Sahl al-Sarakhsī
primaryTitle: Sun of the Imams — Greatest Hanafi Jurist
titles: Shams al-Aʾimma
bio: Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Abi Sahl Abu Bakr al-Sarakhsi, was a Persian jurist and also an Islamic scholar of the Hanafi school of thought. He was traditionally known as Shams al-A'imma.
bio_full:
Muhammad b. Ahmad b. Abi Sahl Abu Bakr al-Sarakhsi (Persian: محمد بن احمد بن ابي سهل ابو بكر السرخسي), was a Persian jurist and also an Islamic scholar of the Hanafi school of thought. He was traditionally known as Shams al-A'imma (شمس الأئمة; transl. The sun of the leaders).
He is an influential jurist in the Hanafi school where the tradition is reported to have been that: "when in doubt, follow Sarakhsi". Both Al-Kasani and Burhan al-Din al-Marghinani, in their flagship fiqh books of Bada'i' al-Sana'i' and Al-Hidaya, have extensively drawn upon the discussions and legal reasonings presented in al-Sarakhsi's Al-Mabsut and Usul al-Sarakhsi.
The Indian Muslim scholar of the 19th century, Abd al-Hayy al-Lucknawi, classifies al-Sarakhsi in the second grade of mujtahids, along with scholars such as Al-Tahawi, who are believed to be the seminal jurists after Abu Hanifa's students (i.e. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani).

Background Information
Al-Sarakhsi was born in Sarakhs, a city in Greater Khorasan, which is presently located at the border between Iran and Turkmenistan. He died in 483/1090 or in 490/1096, according to different sources.
He studied under the great Hanafi jurist, 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Halwani (d. 448/1056) who was also a teacher to Al-Bazdawi.
Not much is known about his early life, though some clues are found in his works. It is said that al-Sarakhsi was imprisoned due to his opinion on a juristic matter concerning a ruler; he criticized the king by questioning the validity of his marriage to a slave woman. He spent around fifteen years in prison. While he was imprisoned he wrote the Mabsut and some of his other most important works. He is known for his remarkable memory, (he was able to recall many texts when he was held in prison) as well as his intelligence.
Al-Sarakhsi's opinions on law have been widely cited and he has been thought of as a distinctive writer. His main works are the Usul al-Fiqh, the Kitab al-Mabsut, and the Sharh al-Siyar al-Kabir.

Important works
Al-Sarakhsi's most important works are 

Usul al-Fiqh
Kitab al-Mabsut
Sharh al-Siyar al-Kabir.

Usul al-Fiqh
This work deals with Islamic jurisprudence and the exercise of ra’y in systematic reasoning and juristic preference. To write this work, al-Sarakhsi incorporated information from many different sources, including Abu’l-Hasan al-Karkhi, Ahmad b. Muhammad al-Shashi, al-Djassas, Abū ʿAbdullāh Muhammad ibn Idrīs al-Shafiʿī and major works from the other law traditions.

Kitab al-Mabsut
Al-Sarakhsi's Mabsut is a commentary on the mukhtasar (epitome) by Muhammad b. Muhammad al-Marwazi, which in turn summarized some of the foundational texts of the Hanafi school written by Muhammad al-Shaybani. Al-Shaybani was a companion of Abū Ḥanīfah, the founder of the Hanafi school. In his Mabsut, Al-Sarakhsi reworks many of the concepts from al-Shaybani's works. He organized his work around points of scholarly divergence (ikhtilaf) and incorporated more information from the Hanafi school, as well as other schools of law. The Mabsut is well-organized, covers topics comprehensively, explores points of dispute thoroughly, and manipulates hermeneutical argument well. These factors make the Mabsut a very influential piece of juristic literature: it was an important work of furū‘ in the Hanafi school until the 19th century. (The furū‘, literally “branches”, are particular legal rulings built upon the usūl, or “roots”, which are the Principles of Islamic jurisprudence.) Its significance in earlier times is reflected in the statement of the 15th-century Hanafi jurist, 'Ala' al-Din al-Tarabulusi (d. 1440): “Whoever memorizes al-Mabsut and the doctrine of the ancient scholars becomes thereby a mujtahid." Al-Sarakhsi deals with many themes in his Mabsut, these include juristic preference, the legality of doing activities with illegally obtained objects, zakat (alms tax, one of the Five Pillars of Islam) and land reclamation. In the Mabsut he defines the doctrine of istihsān, or juristic preference, as the "abandonment of the opinion to which reasoning by the doctrine of ...systematic reasoning would lead, in favor of a different opinion support by stronger evidence and adapted to what is accommodating to the people. Thereby, Sarakhsi neither undermines the importance of the exercise of the doctrine of systematic reasoning nor rejects it in any sense." In addition, al-Sarakhsi deals with the dilemma of doing a legal activity with an illegally obtained object, opining that the fact that the object was obtained illegally does not mean that the legal activity becomes illegal. Al-Sarakhsi also deals with issues concerning zakat in the Mabsut. For example, if the collector comes and a person denies that something is taxable, he does not have to pay the tax on that item, since it is a duty to God. This is explained in the following passage from the Mabsut, which is quoted in Classical Islam: A Sourcebook of Religious Literature, by Norman Calder, Jawid Ahmad Mojaddedi, and Andrew Rippin:

"He then swears that this is so. He is believed in all cases. This is because he is responsible for zakat duties that are obligatory on him. Zakat is an act of worship purely for the sake of God, and the word of a responsible person is always acceptable in regard to acts of worship that are obligatory as being due to God."
Al-Sarakhsi also mentions the views of Abu Hanifa on land reclamation. This passage is from al-Sarakhsi's Mabsut, as quoted by Sherman A. Jackson:

“'In the view of Abu Hanifa, God show him mercy, reclaimed land becomes the property of one who restores it only after he receives permission from the Imam'... Al-Sarakhsi goes on to explain Abu Hanifa's reasoning. Abu Hanifa relied on the statement of
the Prophet 'A person may have only that which his Imam is content with giving him.' This statement even if it is general, [is for him probative] since he maintains that statements universally accepted as general take precedence over those that are specific. Then the Prophet said, ‘... except desolate plots of land; for these belong to God, His messenger then to you.' Now, that
which has been designated as God's and His messenger's falls under the jurisdiction of the Imam. It is thus not permissible for anyone to act independently regarding such things without the latter's permission, just as is maintained in the case of the one-
fifth portion of booty.... And the Prophet's statement, 'Whoever reclaims a desolate plot of land ...’ merely clarifies the fact-
which we accept-that the means by which one gains ownership over restored land is reclamation, after he obtains permission from
the Imam. The Imam's permission remains a necessary precondition in all of this".

Sharh al-Siyar al-Kabir
This work is a commentary on the Kitab al-Siyar al-kabir of al-Shaybani. It demonstrates the role of juristic preference in sharia law.

full: Abu Nasr Abd Allah ibn Ali al-Sarraj al-Tusi
titles: Imam al-Sufiyya
bio: Abu Nasr Abd Allah ibn Ali al-Sarraj al-Tusi (c. 900–988) was a scholar of the Khorasan School tradition, based in Tus. Known as First Encyclopaedist of Sufism.
bio_full:
Abu Nasr Abd Allah ibn Ali al-Sarraj al-Tusi was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from approximately 900 to 988 CE in the city of Tus, located in the Khorasan region of present-day Iran. He belonged to the influential Khorasan School tradition of Islamic scholarship that flourished during the classical period of Islamic civilization.

Al-Sarraj is most renowned for his systematic approach to documenting and organizing Sufi teachings and practices, earning him recognition as the first encyclopaedist of Sufism. During the 10th century, Sufi mystical traditions were largely transmitted through oral teaching and scattered writings. Al-Sarraj undertook the pioneering work of collecting, categorizing, and presenting these diverse mystical teachings in a comprehensive written format.

His most significant contribution was the creation of structured documentation of Sufi doctrine, practices, and the sayings of early Sufi masters. This systematic approach helped preserve important mystical teachings that might otherwise have been lost and provided a foundation for future scholars to build upon. His work represented an early attempt to bring academic rigor to the study of Islamic mysticism.

The Khorasan School, to which al-Sarraj belonged, was known for its scholarly approach to Islamic learning and its synthesis of various intellectual traditions. Scholars from this school played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge during a period of significant cultural and intellectual development in the eastern Islamic world.

Al-Sarraj's efforts to systematize Sufi knowledge came at a time when Islamic mysticism was evolving from a largely informal spiritual movement into a more organized tradition with defined practices and teachings. His encyclopedic work helped establish a scholarly framework for understanding Sufism that would influence subsequent generations of mystics and scholars.

Living in Tus, a city that produced several notable Islamic scholars, al-Sarraj was part of a vibrant intellectual environment that encouraged scholarly inquiry and documentation. His work represents an important milestone in the development of Islamic mystical literature and the preservation of early Sufi teachings. Through his systematic documentation efforts, he helped ensure that the wisdom and practices of early Sufi masters would be available to future generations of seekers and scholars.

bio: al-Shifa' bint 'Abdullah b. 'Abd Shams (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: al-Shifa' bint Abd Allah ibn Abd Shams was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Adi clan of Quraysh. Ibn Abd al-Barr gives her mother as Fatima bint Abi Wahb of the Makhzum clan, and reports that her given name was said to be Layla, though al-Shifa' became the name she was known by. Her kunya was Umm Sulayman, after her son Sulayman ibn Abi Hathma. She accepted Islam in Mecca before the Hijra, pledged allegiance to the Prophet there, and was among the early women emigrants to Medina. Before Islam she had practised ruqya, healing by recitation; according to a report in al-Isti'ab the Prophet asked her to teach this ruqya to his wife Hafsa. Later works add that she could read and write, a rare skill in Mecca, and taught writing to Hafsa. The Prophet granted her a house in Medina, where she lived with her son Sulayman, and he used to visit her there. Ibn Abd al-Barr records that the caliph Umar gave weight to her opinion and sometimes put her in charge of some matters of the market. She narrated hadith, and her grandsons Abu Bakr and Uthman, sons of Sulayman ibn Abi Hathma, narrated from her. Her husband is named as Abu Hathma ibn Hudhayfa and her sons as Sulayman and Masruq. The sources consulted do not give her date of death.

full: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abd Allah al-Shushtari
titles: Shaykh al-Malamatiyya
bio: Al-Shustari was an Andalusī Sufi poet, sufi mystic, and scholar known for his contributions to Islamic mysticism and religious poetry.
bio_full: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Abd Allah al-Numayri al-Shushtari was an Andalusian Sufi poet. He came from Shushtar, a village in the district of Wadi Ash (Guadix), near Granada, and belonged to a prominent family of the Arab tribe of Banu Numayr. A classical biographical entry dates his birth to 610 AH (1213 CE); another account gives c. 1203. He received a traditional education in Qur'anic exegesis, hadith, jurisprudence and grammar. The same classical entry says he was of the emirs and sons of emirs before he took up the life of a dervish. His first teacher on the Sufi path was Ibn Suraqa al-Shatibi. In 1248 he met Ibn Sab'in in Bijaya (Bougie), and he served Ibn Sab'in and became his disciple, receiving his cloak of initiation. He travelled widely in North Africa and the Middle East, including Damascus and Mecca, and was followed on his journeys by more than four hundred dervishes. He is known for his Diwan of qasidas, muwashshahat and zajal poems, and is credited with pioneering vernacular zajal for religious expression. He also wrote prose treatises, among them al-Risala al-Baghdadiyya and al-Risala al-Mi'rajiyya. In his later years his disciples increasingly identified with the Shadhiliyya order, into which his teaching was absorbed after his death. He died on 17 Safar 668 AH (16 October 1269) at al-Tina near Damietta in Egypt.

full: Abū Sulaymān Muḥammad ibn Ṭāhir ibn Bahrām al-Sijistānī
primaryTitle: Philosopher of Baghdad — Custodian of Philosophy
bio: Abū Sulaymān Muḥammad ibn Ṭāhir ibn Bahrām al-Sijistānī (912–c. 985) was a philosopher of the Islamic Philosophy tradition, based in Baghdad. Known as Philosopher of Baghdad — Custodian of Philosophy.
bio_full: Abu Sulayman Muhammad ibn Tahir ibn Bahram al-Sijistani, known as al-Mantiqi ("the Logician"), was a philosopher of tenth-century Baghdad. His name refers to Sijistan (Sistan), where he spent his early years; the mature part of his career took place in Baghdad. George Atiyeh, in the Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, dates his life to c. 932 to c. 1000 CE; another account gives c. 912 to c. 985, and the Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage gives his death as c. 985. He was one of the Muslim students of the Christian philosopher Yahya ibn Adi. In the second half of the tenth century he was a leading figure of philosophy in Baghdad, gathering a circle of philosophers, scientists and men of letters who met in regular sessions. He preferred teaching orally to writing, and most of what is known of his views comes from his student and protégé Abu Hayyan al-Tawhidi. He held that religion and philosophy are both true but differ in method and substance and cannot be reconciled; he rejected the claim of the kalam theologians that reason proved their theology, and the Brethren of Purity's attempt to combine philosophy and religion. The history of philosophy Siwan al-Hikma ("Vessel of Wisdom") is attributed to him, though W. al-Qadi questioned the attribution and Joel Kraemer argued that it came from his school; only selections survive. Short treatises, including one on the first mover, are also ascribed to him.

full: Taj al-Din Abd al-Wahhab ibn Taqiyy al-Din al-Subki
titles: Taj al-Din · Qadi al-Qudat
bio:
Al-Subki is a surname. Notable people with the surname include:Taqi al-Din al-Subki (1284–1355), Egyptian scholar
Taj al-Din al-Subki (1327–1370), Egyptian scholar, his son
bio_full:
Taj al-Din al-Subki (1327-1370) was a prominent Egyptian Islamic scholar and jurist who made significant contributions to Islamic jurisprudence during the Mamluk period. Born Abd al-Wahhab ibn Ali ibn Abd al-Kafi al-Subki, he was the son of the renowned scholar Taqi al-Din al-Subki, following in his father's footsteps to become one of the leading Islamic legal authorities of his time.

Al-Subki belonged to the Shafi'i school of Islamic jurisprudence, one of the four major Sunni legal traditions. He lived during a period of intellectual flourishing in medieval Islamic civilization, when Cairo served as a major center of Islamic learning under Mamluk rule. The Mamluk sultanate, which controlled Egypt and the Levant, was known for its patronage of scholars and the establishment of numerous madrasas and libraries.

He is best known for his extensive writings on Islamic law, theology, and biography. Among his most significant works is "Tabaqat al-Shafi'iyya al-Kubra," a comprehensive biographical dictionary of Shafi'i scholars that remains an important source for historians studying Islamic intellectual history. This work documented the lives and contributions of hundreds of jurists, preserving valuable information about the development of Islamic legal thought.

Al-Subki also wrote extensively on legal methodology and specific jurisprudential issues. His works demonstrate a deep engagement with the classical sources of Islamic law and showcase his ability to address complex legal questions with scholarly rigor. He was particularly noted for his expertise in the principles of Islamic jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) and his ability to reconcile different legal opinions within the Shafi'i tradition.

Beyond his scholarly writings, al-Subki held important judicial and teaching positions in Cairo, contributing to the training of the next generation of Islamic scholars. His relatively short life of 43 years was remarkably productive, and his works continued to be studied and referenced by later generations of Muslim jurists.

Al-Subki's significance lies in his role as both a preserver and developer of Islamic legal tradition. His biographical works serve as crucial historical sources, while his jurisprudential writings contributed to the ongoing development of Islamic law. He represents the high level of scholarship achieved during the Mamluk period and the continuity of Islamic intellectual tradition across generations.

full: Abū al-Ḥusayn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUmar al-Ṣūfī
primaryTitle: Azophi — First to Describe the Andromeda Galaxy
titles: Azophi (Latin)
bio: Abu Al-Hussein Abdul Rahman bin Omar bin Sahl Al-Sufi Al-Razi. He was a Persian Muslim astronomer of the 10th century AD. Balari was born in Persia on 9 Muharram 291 AH. He came into contact with Ad-Dawla al-Buwaihi. He was one of those who said that the Earth was spherical after Eratosthenes, who had proven its sphericity before Christ, and was one of the leading astronomers. He is one of the greatest astronomers of Islam, according to the historian George Sartoun. He was a friend of the Buyid Sultan Adud al-Dawla, who took him as an astronomer and his teacher to know the positions of the various stars and planets and the movement of astronomical bodies. Adud al-Dawla built a special observatory for the Sufi in Shiraz, which helped him carry out his astronomical achievements. His language was Persian, but he wrote his scientific books in Arabic because it was the language of science in the Golden Age of Islam at that time. The Sufi died on Muharram 8, 376 AH, at the age of 83.
bio_full:
ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (full name: Abū’l-Ḥusayn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUmar ibn Sahl al-Ṣūfī al-Rāzī —Arabic: أَبُو الحُسَين عَبدُ اَلرَّحمَن بن عُمَر بن سَهل اَلصُّوفِي اَلرَّازِي; Persian: ابوالحسن عبدالرحمن صوفی رازی — 7 December 903 – 25 May 986) was a Persian astronomer.
His work, Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib ("The Book of Fixed Stars"), completed in 964, included both textual descriptions and illustrations. The Persian polymath Al-Biruni noted that al-Ṣūfī's work on the ecliptic was conducted in Shiraz. Al-Ṣūfī lived at the Buyid court in Isfahan.

Biography
ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī was one of the nine famous Muslim astronomers. He lived at the court of Emir 'Adud al-Dawla in Isfahan and worked on translating and expanding ancient Greek astronomical works, especially the Almagest of Ptolemy. He made corrections to Ptolemy's star list, and his estimations of star brightness and magnitude deviated from those of Ptolemy; just over half of al-Ṣūfī's magnitudes were identical to Ptolemy's. A Persian, al-Ṣūfī wrote in Arabic, the lingua franca of the scientific Muslim world.
Al-Ṣūfī was a major contributor to the translation into Arabic of Hellenistic astronomy, which had been centered in Alexandria, Egypt. He was among the first to attempt to relate Greek star names with the traditional Arabic names and constellations, which were largely unrelated and overlapped in complex ways.

Astronomy
Al-Ṣūfī made his astronomical observations at a latitude of 32.7° N in Isfahan. It has been claimed that he identified the Large Magellanic Cloud, but this appears to be a misunderstanding of a reference to some stars south of Canopus, which he admits he did not observe. He also made the earliest recorded observation of the Andromeda Galaxy in 964, describing it as a "small cloud". This was the first galaxy other than the Milky Way to be mentioned in writing.

Astrolabe
Al-Ṣūfī also wrote about the astrolabe, identifying numerous additional uses for it. According to American Near Eastern scholar Adam L. Bean, al-Ṣūfī's work describes over 1,000 different uses in areas as diverse as astronomy, astrology and horoscopes, navigation, surveying, timekeeping, determining the Qibla, and performing Salat prayer.

Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib ("The Book of Fixed Stars")

Al-Ṣūfī published Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib ("The Book of Fixed Stars") in 964, and dedicated it to Adud al-Dawla, the ruler of Buwayhid at the time. This book describes 48 constellations and the stars within them.
Al-Ṣūfī compared Greek constellations and stars as described in Ptolemy’s Almagest with Arabic ones, linking those that were the same. He included two illustrations of each constellation, one showing the orientation of the stars from the perspective outside the celestial globe, and the other from the perspective of looking at the sky while standing on the Earth. He separated them into three groups; 21 seen from the north, 15 seen from the south, and the 12 zodiac constellations. He included a complete set of star charts, that included the names and numbers of the individual stars in each of the 48 constellations, and each star's longitudinal and latitudinal coordinates, magnitude, and location north or south of the ecliptic. 
Scribal errors within the 35 surviving copies of The Book of Fixed Stars have caused the value of the magnitude for a particular star to vary from manuscript to manuscript. Al-Ṣūfī organized the stars in each of his drawings into two groups: those that form the image depicted, and others that are in close proximity to the image. He identified and described stars not included by Ptolemy, but he did not include them in his own star charts. Stating that his charts were modelled after Ptolemy, he left the stars excluded in Ptolemy's catalogue out of his charts as well.
To allow for the longitudinal placement of the stars within constellations having changed over the eight centuries since the Almagest was written, Al-Ṣūfī added 12° 42' to all the longitudes values provided by Ptolemy. Al-Ṣūfī differed from Ptolemy by having a three level scale to measure the magnitude of stars instead of a two level scale. This extra level increased the precision of his measurements. His methodology for determining these magnitude measurements cannot be found in any of his extant texts.
Despite the importance of The Book of Fixed Stars in the history of astronomy, it took more than 1000 years until the first partial English translation of the book was published in 2010.

Legacy

Al-Ṣūfī's astronomical work was subsequently used by many other astronomers, including Ulugh Beg who was both a prince and astronomer.
The lunar crater Azophi and the minor planet 12621 Alsufi are named after Al-Ṣūfī.
The Astronomy Society of Iran – Amateur Committee has held international Sufi Observing Competitions in memory of the astronomer. The first competition was held in 2006 in the north of Semnan Province, and the second was held in the summer of 2008 in Ladiz near the Zahedan. More than 100 attendees from Iran and Iraq participated in these events.
Google Doodle commemorated Al-Ṣūfī's 1113th birthday on 7 December 2016.

full: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Sulami al-Naysaburi
primaryTitle: Imam al-Tasawwuf — Master of the Sufi Sciences
titles: Shaykh al-Islam · Hafiz al-Khorasan
bio: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Sulami al-Naysaburi (937–1021) was a scholar of the Khorasan School tradition, based in Nishapur. Known as Imam al-Tasawwuf — Master of the Sufi Sciences.
bio_full:
Abu 'Abd al-Rahman Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Sulami al-Naysaburi was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from 937 to 1021 CE in Nishapur, a major center of learning in the Khorasan region of present-day Iran. He belonged to the influential Khorasan School tradition and earned recognition as "Imam al-Tasawwuf," meaning Master of the Sufi Sciences, reflecting his expertise in Islamic mysticism.

Al-Sulami lived during a period of significant intellectual and spiritual development in the Islamic world, when Nishapur served as a crucial hub for religious scholarship and Sufi thought. The city attracted scholars from across the Muslim world and was known for producing influential figures in various Islamic disciplines.

As a scholar of Sufism, al-Sulami contributed to the systematization and transmission of mystical Islamic knowledge. His work focused on documenting and preserving the teachings, practices, and biographical accounts of earlier Sufi masters, helping to establish a more formal framework for understanding Islamic mysticism. This scholarly approach was characteristic of the Khorasan School, which emphasized both the theoretical foundations and practical applications of Sufi teachings.

Al-Sulami's significance lies in his role as a bridge between the earlier, more informal tradition of Sufi teaching and the later, more systematized approach to Islamic mysticism. His efforts to document and organize Sufi knowledge helped preserve important spiritual teachings that might otherwise have been lost. Through his scholarly work, he contributed to the development of Sufism as a recognized branch of Islamic learning with its own literature, methodology, and educational practices.

His long life span of 84 years allowed him to witness and participate in nearly a century of Islamic intellectual development. Working within the Khorasan School tradition, he helped establish Nishapur's reputation as a center for Sufi scholarship. His title as Master of the Sufi Sciences indicates that he was recognized by his contemporaries as an authority in this field, suggesting that his contributions were both substantial and widely acknowledged within the scholarly community of his time.

full: Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā al-Ṣūlī
primaryTitle: Greatest Chess Master of the Medieval Islamic World
bio: Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn al-‘Abbās al-Ṣūlī was a Turkic scholar and a court companion of three Abbāsid caliphs: al-Muktafī, his successor al-Muqtadir, and later, al-Radi, whom he also tutored. He was a bibliophile, wrote letters, editor-poet, chronicler, and a shatranj (chess) player. His contemporary biographer Isḥāq al-Nadīm tells us he was "of manly bearing." He wrote many books, the most famous of which are Kitāb Al-Awrāq and Kitāb al-Shiṭranj.
bio_full:
Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn al-‘Abbās al-Ṣūlī (Arabic: أبو بكر محمد بن يحيى بن العباس الصولي) (born c. 870 Gorgan – died between 941 and 948 Basra) was a Turkic scholar and a court companion of three Abbāsid caliphs: al-Muktafī, his successor al-Muqtadir, and later, al-Radi, whom he also tutored. He was a bibliophile, wrote letters, editor-poet, chronicler, and a shatranj (chess) player. His contemporary biographer Isḥāq al-Nadīm tells us he was "of manly bearing." He wrote many books, the most famous of which are Kitāb Al-Awrāq and Kitāb al-Shiṭranj.

Life
Abū Bakr al-Ṣūlī was born into an illustrious family of Turkic origin, his great-grandfather was the Turkic prince Sul-takin and his uncle was the poet Ibrahim ibn al-'Abbas as-Suli.
Al-Marzubānī, a principal pupil of al-Ṣūlī, who admired him and copied him in the art of compilation, borrowed much of al-Ṣūlī's material for his Kitāb al-Muwashshaḥ. Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣbahānī made extensive use of his material in his Kitāb al-Aghānī.                          
On Caliph al-Rāḍī's death in 940, al-Ṣūlī fell into disfavour with the new ruler due to his Shi'a sympathies and he died hiding at al-Baṣrah,  for having quoted a passage about ‘Alī, which caused a public scandal.

Chess
Al-Ṣūlī was among a group of tenth-century chess players who wrote books about the game of shaṭranj, i.e. "chess".
Al-Ṣūlī's books were:

Kitāb al-Shiṭranj al-Nisḥa al-Awala (كتاب الشطرنج النسخة الاولة) ‘Chess, the first manuscript’;
Kitāb al-Shiṭranj al-Nisḥa ath-Thānīa (كتاب الشطرنج النسخة الثانية) Chess, the second manuscript; Book on chess strategy, common chess openings, standard problems in middle game, annotated end games and the first known description of the knight's tour problem.
Sometime between 902 and 908, al-Ṣūlī played and beat the reigning shaṭranj champion, al-Mawardī, at the court of Caliph al-Muktafī, and the Caliph of Baghdad. When al-Muktafī died, al-Ṣūlī retained the favour of the succeeding rulers, Caliph al-Muqtadir and Caliph al-Radi.
His biographer Ibn Khallikan, (d. 1282), relates that even in his lifetime the phrase "to play like al-Ṣūlī" was to show great skill at shaṭranj. His endgame strategies are still studied. Contemporary biographers mention his skill in blindfold chess. Al-Ṣūlī also taught shaṭranj. Many later European writers based their work on modern chess on al-Suli's work.

Other Chess players/authors in the Group
Al-‘Adlī (العَدْلى) wrote:
 – Kitāb al-Shiṭranj (كتاب الشطرنج) ‘Chess’, the first book on chess, and;
 – Al-Nard, wa Isbābha wa-al-La’ab bīha (كتاب النرد واسبابها واللعب بها). 'Al-Nard Its Elements and Play'.

Al-Rāzī (الرازى) was a chess rival of al-‘Adlī and the caliph Al-Mutawakkil attended their matches. He wrote:
 – Kitāb latīf fī al- Shiṭranj (كتاب لطيف في الشطرنج) ‘A Delightful Book about Chess.’

Abū al-Faraj Muḥammad ibn ‘Ubayd Allāh al-Lajlāj ("the stammerer") (ابو الفرج محمد بن عبيد الله اللَجْلاج), whom Isḥāq al-Nadīm had met, was his best known pupil. He excelled at chess at the Būyid court of king ‘Aḍud al-Dawlah in Shīrāz, where he died sometime after 970/71 [360 AH]. He wrote:
 – Manṣūbāt al-Shiṭranj (منصوبات الشطرنج) ‘The Stratagems of Chess.’

Ibn al-Uqlīdasī Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ, one of the most skilful chess players, who wrote A Collection of the Stratagems of Chess.

Al-Suli's Diamond

Al-Ṣūlī's shaṭranj endgame study, called "Al-Ṣūlī's Diamond", went unsolved for over a thousand years. Shatranj is the predecessor to modern chess, where the "ferz" or "vizier", meaning counsellor, is a very weak piece, able to move and attack only a single square diagonally. It is possible to win in shaṭranj by capturing all pieces except the king, unless the opponent is able to do the same on the next move.

This position is ancient old, yet neither al-‘Adlī nor any one else has said whether it is drawn or can be won. Nor has any one interpreted it, or pointed (diagrammed) it because of its difficulty. There is no one on earth who has solved it unless he was taught it by me. I have never learnt that there was any one before; for if any one had solved it, he would either have written down the solution, or have taught it to some one else. This is the word of as-Ṣūlī. (9th century)
David Hooper and Ken Whyld studied this problem in the mid-1980s, but the solution published in the first edition of The Oxford Companion to Chess in 1984 overlooked Black's strongest defensive line on move 3 and was considered incorrect. The first correct solution was reconstructed from the three manuscript positions and is credited to the leading endgame theoretician, grandmaster, and former chairman of the USSR Chess Federation, Yuri Averbakh, who first published his solution in the 10th bulletin of the 1986 Chess Olympiad in Dubai.
According to the second edition of The Oxford Companion to Chess, published in 1992, mathematician John Beasley provided the first computer-generated solution using the stronger defence 6...Kf8 instead of 6...Kg8. The first move of the solution had already been given by Al-Ṣūlī in the Istanbul manuscript discussed by Murray in A History of Chess. The full solution to Al-Ṣūlī's Diamond, beginning with 1.Kb4, is given in Averbakh's writings later collected in In Search of Truth, in Ree's The Human Comedy of Chess, and in online analyses. The full solution to Al-Ṣūlī's Diamond, beginning with 1.Kb4, is given in Averbakh's writings later collected in In Search of Truth, in Ree's The Human Comedy of Chess, and in online analyses. The position can be tried under historical shatranj rules on the shatranj.ai play board by entering the FEN position.
A video walkthrough of the solution along with the historical sources of the discovery story, produced as part of the Shatranj.ai Erasmus+ educational curriculum project and including a reproduction of the relevant page from the 10th bulletin of the 1986 Chess Olympiad in Dubai, is available online.
Subsequent computer analysis has produced related positions. In 2015, John Tromp described "Suli's Rough Diamond", a related four-piece shaṭranj position with a distance-to-win of 53 plies, which transposes into the canonical Suli's Diamond with 39 plies distance-to-win after best play from both sides. In 2026, the endgame study association ARVES listed additional related positions by Tamer Karatekin, shah+ferz vs. shah+ferz, including the Suli-Karatekin Tough Diamond with 63 plies, Suli-Karatekin Concave Tough Diamond, Suli's Little Diamond, and Suli's Flipped Diamond, with their FEN positions and links to a longer technical article. Explanations of the code and tablebase-generation methods used for Suli's Diamond and related four-piece shaṭranj positions are available in the shatranj.ai curriculum materials.

Works

Kitāb Al-Awrāq
Kitāb Al-Awrāq (كتاب الاوراق) ‘Leaves’ or ‘Folios’;  unfinished  work on the traditions of the caliphs and the poets;  the poems and chronicles of the sons of the caliphs, from al-Saffāḥ to Ibn al-Mu‘tazz (750–908) and poems of other members of the Banū al-‘Abbās who were neither caliphs nor sons of caliphs in rank.  This included the poetry of ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Alī (عبد الله بن على), the poetry of Abū Aḥmad Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Ismā’īl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn ‘Īsā ibn al-Manṣūr (ابو احمد محمد بن احمد بن اسمعيل بن ابراهيم بن عيسى بن المنصور), the poems of members of the family of Abū Ṭālib the descendants of al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, the descendants of al-‘Abbās ibn ‘Alī, the descendants of ‘Umar ibn ‘Alī, and the descendants of Ja‘far ibn Abī Ṭālib; poems of the descendants of al-Ḥārith ibn ‘Abd al-Muṭṭalib; traditions about, and selected poems by, Ibn Harmah;  traditions about al-Sayyid al-Ḥimyarī (السيد الحميرى), with a selection of his poetry;  traditions about, and selected poems by, Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf (احمد بن يوسف); traditions about Sudayf with a selection of his poetry.

bio: al-Sumayra' bint Qays bin Malik (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
al-Sumayra' bint Qays bin Malik was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan inhabitants who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, al-Sumayra' was part of the indigenous population that embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the first Islamic state in Medina, offering both material and moral support to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca.

Her lineage traces back to Qays bin Malik, indicating her connection to one of the established tribal families in Medina. During the early decades of Islam, women like al-Sumayra' participated actively in the religious and social life of the Muslim community, though the specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the historical sources that have survived.

The period of her life, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompasses the most critical era in early Islamic history, including the Prophet's ministry in Mecca, the Hijra (migration) to Medina, the establishment of the first Muslim state, and the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate following the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

Female companions like al-Sumayra' represent an important dimension of early Islamic society, demonstrating that women were recognized participants in the early Muslim community. Their designation as Sahabiyya acknowledges their direct connection to the Prophet Muhammad and their role in the transmission and preservation of Islamic teachings and practices.

al-Sumayra' died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, when the Islamic state was beginning its rapid expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. While detailed accounts of her specific deeds may not have been preserved in the historical record, her status as a companion places her among those early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational period of Islamic civilization.
