bio: Amira bint Hubbasha bin Jwaybit (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amira bint Hubbasha bin Jwaybit was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim community following the migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Amira would have been among the local inhabitants who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the early Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the first Islamic state in Medina, offering their homes, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca.

The female companions of the Prophet Muhammad, known collectively as the sahabiyyat, occupied important positions within the early Muslim community. They participated in religious life, supported the propagation of Islam, and often served as transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations. Many sahabiyyat were noted for their piety, knowledge, and contributions to the preservation and transmission of Islamic traditions.

Living during the foundational period of Islam, Amira witnessed the crucial early decades of the faith's development. Her lifetime spanned the Prophet Muhammad's mission in Medina, the establishment of the first Muslim state, and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate following the Prophet's death in 632 CE. She died around 635 CE, during the early years of the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab.

The significance of companions like Amira lies in their role as the first generation of Muslims who directly learned from and interacted with the Prophet Muhammad. Their acceptance of Islam and support for the early Muslim community was essential to the religion's survival and growth. The Ansari companions, in particular, demonstrated the importance of hospitality, solidarity, and sacrifice in Islamic values.

While specific details about Amira's individual contributions may not be extensively documented in historical sources, her status as a sahabiyya places her among the revered first generation of Muslims whose faith and dedication helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization. Her life represents the important but often under-documented role of women in early Islamic history.

bio: Amira bint Kultum bin al-Hadm (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amira bint Kultum bin al-Hadm was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who provided crucial support to the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra (migration) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, Amira bint Kultum lived through the pivotal early decades of Islamic history, witnessing the establishment and consolidation of the first Muslim community. The Ansar played a fundamental role in the survival and growth of Islam, offering sanctuary, resources, and military support to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca and forming the backbone of the early Islamic state in Medina.

Her designation as a sahabiyya places her among the female companions who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and participated in the early Muslim community. The female companions of this era contributed to various aspects of religious and social life, though the specific details of individual contributions often remain limited in historical sources.

Living during a time of rapid social and religious transformation, Amira bint Kultum would have experienced the major events that shaped early Islam, including the various military campaigns, the gradual conversion of Arabian tribes, and the development of Islamic law and social practices. Her lifetime, spanning approximately forty years from 595 to 635 CE, encompassed the entire prophetic mission of Muhammad and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr.

The significance of companions like Amira bint Kultum lies in their role as the foundational generation of Muslims who preserved and transmitted Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations. full: Ammar ibn Yasir ibn Amir al-Ansi al-Makhzumi
primaryTitle: First Martyr Family — Symbol of Early Persecution
titles: Ibn al-Shahidayn (Son of Two Martyrs) · First Builder of Mosque
bio: Ammar ibn Yasir was a Sahabi (Companion) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, and a commander in the early Muslim conquests. His parents, Sumayya and Yasir ibn Amir, were the first martyrs of the Ummah. Ammar converted to Islam by the invitation of Abu Bakr and was amongst the muhajirun. After the migration to Medina, he participated in building the Prophet's Mosque and fought in most of the early Muslim expeditions.
bio_full:
Ammar ibn Yasir (Arabic: عَمَّار بْن يَاسِر, romanized: ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir; c. 567/570 – July 657 CE) was a Sahabi (Companion) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, and a commander in the early Muslim conquests. His parents, Sumayya and Yasir ibn Amir, were the first martyrs of the Ummah. Ammar converted to Islam by the invitation of Abu Bakr and was amongst the muhajirun. After the migration to Medina, he participated in building the Prophet's Mosque and fought in most of the early Muslim expeditions.
He fought in the Ridda wars under Caliph Abu Bakr (r. 632–634) and in the Muslim conquest of Iran under Caliph Umar (r. 634–644). Ammar served as governor of Kufa under Umar. Following Uthman's assassination, Ammar became a devout partisan of Caliph Ali (r. 656–661) and died while fighting on Ali's side in the Battle of Siffin.

Before Islam
Ammar belonged to the Malik clan of the Madhhij tribe in Yemen. He later lived in the Hijaz region (in present-day Saudi Arabia). Born in or around the Year of the Elephant—the same year as Muhammad—he grew up in Mecca and served as one of the intermediaries in Muhammad's marriage to Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. His father, Yasir ibn Amir, came from the tribe of Qahtan in Yemen and migrated to Mecca, where he settled after marrying Sumayya, a slave woman. Ammar and his parents, Yasir and Sumayya, were slaves to Abu Huzaifa, and after his death they came under the control of Abu Jahl, who later became one of Islam's fiercest enemies and the notorious torturer of the family. Ammar's trust in and knowledge of Muhammad's credibility—even before his prophethood—encouraged him to follow Muhammad's prophetic visions as one of the earliest converts.

After conversion to Islam
Belonging to the Banu Makhzum, Ammar was born in 567 to Yasir ibn Amir and Sumayya, both of whom were later brutally killed. At an early age, Ammar converted to Islam by the invitation of Abu Bakr, becoming one of the earliest Muslims. He became one of Muhammad's most prominent companions, participating in all his military campaigns and battles. Historically, Ammar ibn Yasir was the first Muslim to build a mosque.
ʿAmmār converted to Islam in 614 or 615 CE. This was during the period when the Quraysh were persecuting lower-class Muslims. As Ammar later recounted to his grandson: "I met Suhayb ibn Sinan at the door of the house of Al-Arqam while the Messenger of Allah was inside. I asked him, 'What do you want?' He replied, 'What do you want?' I answered, 'I want to go to Muhammad and listen to what he says.' He said, 'That is what I want.' We entered, and he presented Islam to us. We became Muslim and spent the day until evening, then went out concealing ourselves". Ammar's father, mother, and brother also became Muslims, though not at Abu Bakr's invitation.
When the Quraysh learned of Yasir's family's conversion, they became among "the victims who were tortured at Mecca to make them recant". The Makhzum clan would expose Ammar, his father, and his mother to the scorching heat of the day and torture them over open fire. Muhammad would pass by and say, "Patience, O family of Yasir! Your meeting-place will be Paradise" and "O fire! Be cool and harmless for ‘Ammar in the same manner in which you became cool and harmless for Ibrahim.” As a result, Ammar bore scars from this torture for the rest of his life.
Ammar was tortured "until he did not know what he was saying," as was his friend Suhayb. In this state, he temporarily maligned Muhammad and praised the pagan gods. Afterwards, he confessed to Muhammad. When asked, "How do you find your heart?" Ammar replied that he was still a Muslim at heart. Muhammad said all was well. The Qur'an verse "someone forced to do it whose heart remains at rest in its faith" (16:106) refers to Ammar. His mother was murdered by Abu Jahl for refusing to abandon Islam and is regarded as the first Muslim martyr. The opening verses of Surat Al-Ankabut (chapter 29: The Spider) were revealed in response to this event.
To escape the Meccans' torture, ibn Saad and Ibn Ishaq report that Ammar went to Abyssinia in 616.

Battles under Muhammad

'Ammar was one of the few warriors to participate in the first major Islamic battle, the Battle of Badr, despite harsh conditions; and he continued to fight in all Muslim battles even after Muhammad's death.
In addition to his military role, Ammar's life illustrates a historically significant incident: while helping to build the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, he complained of being overloaded with bricks. Umm Salama, Muhammad's wife, witnessed Muhammad, who ran his hand through Ammar's curly hair and said: "Alas Ibn Sumayya! It is not they who will kill you but a wicked band of men." He took a stick in his hand, angry, and said, "What is wrong between them and Ammar? He invites them to Paradise while they invite him to hell." These reports, regarded as valid by both Sunnis and Shi'is, were later significant in discussions of succession and in interpreting Ammar's death at the Battle of Siffin.

Role after Muhammad's death
Under Umar, he became governor of Kufa, however he was later removed from power.
During Uthman ibn Affan's election by the shura and before his eventual overthrowal, Ammar warningly predicted the upcoming conflict if anyone but Ali got elected and said that "If you do not want to cause a dispute among the Muslims, you have to give the pledge of allegiance to Ali". Ammar's relationship with Uthman ibn Affan deteriorated; although the details of their hostilities towards each other are debatable.

Battle of the Camel

Prior to the events of the Battle of the Camel, a shura was set up in an attempt to decide a successor after Uthman's death; at this meeting, attendees were not in agreement regarding whether retaliation for Uthman's murder was necessary or not. A report of ʻAlqama b. Waqqas al-Laythi of Kinana indicates that Ammar said that they should not seek revenge. Madelung interprets Ammar's behavior at this meeting indicating his desire to keep Talha from gaining power because Talha was in favor of seeking retaliation. Ammar would not have wanted this since "he had been the most active in inciting the rebels to action".
As the battle was developing, Ammar continued to show his support for Ali in multiple ways. Ali first sent him along with al-Hasan to Kufa in order to try to rally the Kufans to help during the upcoming battle. According to one report recorded by Al-Tabari, Ammar was questioned upon arrival for participating in Uthman's murder; however, he continued to try to convince the governor, Abu Musa, to take a stance instead of remaining impartial in the conflict. Al-Tabari reports how Abu Musa had encouraged the Kufans to remain neutral because he did not want to participate in inter-Muslim fighting, and he also believed that the Muslim community still owed their allegiance to Uthman because no new successor had been named. An additional transmission of the same event does not mention Ammar's actions against Uthman and instead focuses on his intentions to sway Abu Musa into action. 
During the actual battle, Ammar fought on Ali's side. Al-Tabari includes in his history an account in which al-Zubayr is told that Ammar is fighting alongside Ali, and this knowledge causes al-Zubayr to be fearful because he had been with Muhammad and Ammar when Muhammad had told Ammar that he would be killed by "transgressing group". Al-Tabari again includes multiple reports of the same event, which in this case is a moment during the battle in which Ammar and al-Zubayr confront each other. In both accounts Ammar approaches al-Zubayr to attack him, when al-Zubayr speaks. In the report from 'Umar b. Shabbah, al-Zubayr asks Ammar, "Do you want to kill me?" whereas in that from 'Amir b. Hafs, al-Zubayr asks, "Are you going to kill me, Abu al Yaqzan?" In both reports, Ammar's response is negative.

dod_s: c. 650 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
bio: Amna bint Qurat bin Khansa' (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amna bint Qurat bin Khansa' was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. As an Ansari companion, she belonged to the indigenous Muslim community of Medina who supported and assisted the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) who came from Mecca.

The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were the residents of Medina who embraced Islam and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad when he migrated there in 622 CE. This migration, known as the Hijra, marked a pivotal moment in early Islamic history, and the Ansar played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community in Medina. Amna bint Qurat bin Khansa' was among these early supporters who helped lay the foundation of the nascent Islamic state.

As a Sahabiyya, Amna lived during the formative period of Islam, witnessing firsthand the revelation of the Quran and the development of Islamic practices and community life. The companions of the Prophet Muhammad, both male and female, hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who received religious instruction directly from the Prophet and participated in the early Islamic community.

Her designation as an Ansari companion of Medina indicates that she was part of the local community that provided essential support to the growing Muslim population. The Ansar's contributions were vital to the survival and growth of the early Muslim community, as they shared their resources, homes, and protection with the Muslim emigrants who had left their possessions behind in Mecca.

Amna bint Qurat bin Khansa' died around 635 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate that followed the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. Her life span encompassed the entire Meccan and Medinan periods of the Prophet's mission, making her a witness to the complete transformation of Arabian society through the emergence of Islam.

While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the surviving historical sources, her recognition as a companion reflects her participation in the early Muslim community and her role among the women who supported the establishment of Islam in Medina. The female companions collectively contributed to various aspects of early Islamic society, from religious learning to community support.

bio: Amr b Suraqa (c. 594–650 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Amr ibn Suraqa ibn al-Mu'tamir ibn Anas was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Banu Adi ibn Ka'b of Quraysh. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Amina bint Abd Allah ibn Umayr, while Khalifa ibn Khayyat calls her Qudlama bint Abd Allah ibn Umayr. His brother was Abd Allah ibn Suraqa. When the two brothers emigrated from Mecca to Medina, they stayed with Rifa'a ibn Abd al-Mundhir, brother of Abu Lubaba. Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq, Abu Ma'shar and al-Waqidi all list Amr among those who fought at Badr, and Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr add that he fought at Uhud, the Trench and all the other campaigns with the Prophet. A report from Amir ibn Rabi'a, preserved by Ibn al-Athir, describes him as a tall man with a slender belly, and Ibn al-Athir rejects Ibn Manda's description of him as an Ansari as a mistake. Khalifa ibn Khayyat states that no hadith from Amr is known. He died during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan; Ibn Abd al-Barr adds that his brother Abd Allah died in the same period.

bio: Amr bin 'Uthman bin 'Amr (c. 593–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Amr ibn Uthman al-Taymi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Quraysh clan of Taym ibn Murra. Ibn Hajar gives his lineage as Amr ibn Uthman ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Taym ibn Murra. His mother was Hind bint al-Bayya' of the Banu Layth. Ibn Ishaq lists him among the Muslims who emigrated from Mecca to Abyssinia. According to Ibn al-Athir, he came back with the emigrants who returned on the two ships. He was later killed at the Battle of al-Qadisiyya in Iraq, fighting alongside Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, in 15 AH (636 CE). The classical sources state that he left no descendants.

bio_sources.title: Tarajm.com — Amr ibn Uthman ibn Ka'b al-Taymi (texts of al-Isaba, Ibn Hajar; Usd al-Ghaba, Ibn al-Athir)

bio: Amr bin al-Harith bin Zuhayr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Zuhayr al-Fihri was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Quraysh clan of Fihr. Ibn al-Athir gives his full lineage as Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Zuhayr ibn Abi Shaddad ibn Rabi'a ibn Hilal ibn Malik ibn Dabba ibn al-Harith ibn Fihr, while Ibn Ishaq records a slightly different chain. Some gave his name as Amir rather than Amr. His kunya was Abu Nafi'. He accepted Islam early, in Mecca. Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi list him among those who emigrated to Abyssinia, although Musa ibn Uqba and Abu Ma'shar do not include him among the emigrants. Both Musa ibn Uqba and Ibn Ishaq list him among the Muslims who fought at the Battle of Badr. The classical entry on him gives no date or place of death.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Amr bin al-Jamuh bin Zayd (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Amr ibn al-Jamuh ibn Zayd ibn Haram al-Ansari al-Salami was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Salima of the Khazraj in Medina. Before Islam he was a chief and noble of the Banu Salima and kept a wooden idol in his house, which Ibn al-Athir names Manaf. His son Mu'adh and Mu'adh ibn Jabal, among others, repeatedly threw the idol away; after it was found tied to a dead dog, he abandoned it and accepted Islam. Ibn al-Kalbi said he was the last of the Ansar to accept Islam. Ibn Hajar and Ibn al-Athir record reports that the Prophet asked the Banu Salima who their chief was. When they named al-Jadd ibn Qays while noting his stinginess, the Prophet replied that there was no worse illness than stinginess and named Amr ibn al-Jamuh as their chief; a report from al-Zuhri names Bishr ibn al-Bara' instead. Amr was lame in one leg. One opinion holds that he was present at Badr, but Ibn Ishaq does not list him, and Ibn al-Kalbi reported that his sons kept him from going because of his lameness. Before Uhud he pleaded to join the fighting although he had been excused, and he was killed in that battle in 625 CE. Ibn al-Athir reports that the Prophet said he saw him walking in Paradise on his lame leg. He also reports that Amr's wife, Hind bint Amr, aunt of Jabir ibn Abd Allah, carried his body and that of her brother Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Haram, and that the two were buried in one grave. One report says his son Khallad was killed with him at Uhud.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Amr bin Ghaziyah bin 'Amr (b. c. 591 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Amr bin Ghaziyah bin 'Amr was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 591 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the Prophet's time there.

His most notable historical distinction was his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan (Bay'at al-Ridwan), a significant oath of allegiance taken by the Prophet's companions. This pledge occurred at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE, when approximately 1,400 Muslims had traveled with Muhammad toward Mecca for pilgrimage but were prevented from entering the city. When rumors spread that the Prophet's envoy Uthman ibn Affan had been killed by the Meccans, Muhammad called upon his followers to pledge their loyalty and readiness to fight if necessary. The companions who took this oath became known as the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan.

This event holds particular significance in Islamic history because it is referenced in the Quran, specifically in verse 48:18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree. The Quranic reference has given special recognition to all those who participated in this pledge, including Amr bin Ghaziyah bin 'Amr.

As one of the sahaba, Amr bin Ghaziyah would have been part of the early Muslim community that witnessed the revelation of the Quran and participated in the establishment of the first Islamic society. The companions hold a revered position in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who learned directly from the Prophet Muhammad and helped transmit his teachings to subsequent generations.

Amr bin Ghaziyah bin 'Amr died in 631 CE, during the final years of the Prophet Muhammad's life or shortly after the Prophet's death. His inclusion among the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan places him within a select group of early Muslims who demonstrated their commitment to the faith and the Prophet during a crucial moment in Islamic history. While specific details about his individual contributions or activities beyond this pledge are not well-documented in historical sources, his status as a companion and participant in this significant event marks his place in the foundational period of Islam.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Amr bin Iyas (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Amr bin Iyas was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he witnessed the emergence and early expansion of the Islamic community during the Prophet's mission.

As one of the Sahaba, the term used for the companions of Prophet Muhammad, Amr bin Iyas was among those who directly interacted with the Prophet and supported the early Muslim community. His presence in Medina places him within the crucial period following the Hijra, the migration of Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, which marked the beginning of the Islamic calendar and the establishment of the first Muslim community.

Amr bin Iyas is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, which took place in 625 CE near Medina. This battle was the second major military engagement between the Muslim community and the Meccan forces, occurring approximately one year after the Muslim victory at the Battle of Badr. The Battle of Uhud proved to be a significant test for the early Muslim community, as it resulted in heavy casualties and served as a learning experience about military discipline and strategy.

During this battle, Amr bin Iyas made the ultimate sacrifice for his faith and community, dying as a martyr at the young age of approximately 28 years. His death at Uhud places him among the notable companions who gave their lives during this pivotal engagement, which is remembered as a defining moment in early Islamic history.

The Battle of Uhud and the sacrifices made by companions like Amr bin Iyas are significant in Islamic historical memory as they demonstrate the challenges faced by the early Muslim community and the dedication of those who supported the Prophet's mission. While the Muslims faced setbacks in this battle, the event became an important lesson in perseverance and faith for the growing Islamic community.

Amr bin Iyas represents the generation of early Muslims who lived through Islam's foundational period and whose commitment helped establish the religion during its most vulnerable early years. His martyrdom at Uhud contributes to the collective memory of sacrifice and devotion that characterizes the accounts of the Prophet's companions in Islamic tradition.

bio: Amr bin Iyyas bin Zayd (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Amr bin Iyyas bin Zayd was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslim community that established itself in Medina following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Amr bin Iyyas is most notably recognized for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement marked a turning point for the early Muslim state, demonstrating their ability to defend themselves against more numerous opposition forces. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as they were present during this crucial early test of the Muslim community's survival.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Amr bin Iyyas belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and played fundamental roles in the establishment and early expansion of Islam. The companions are considered vital sources for understanding early Islamic teachings, practices, and historical events, as they witnessed and participated in the formative moments of the religion.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's time there, Amr bin Iyyas would have been part of the diverse community that the Prophet worked to unite under Islamic principles. This period saw the development of many foundational Islamic institutions and practices that would shape the religion's future development.

Amr bin Iyyas died in 634 CE, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. His death occurred during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr, as the Muslim community was beginning its expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his status as a Companion of Badr places him among the early Muslims who helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization during its most crucial formative years.

bio: Amr bin Jahm bin Qays (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Amr bin Jahm bin Qays was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam. Born around 593 CE, he was among the early Muslims in Mecca who faced persecution for their new faith during the initial years of the Islamic message.

Amr bin Jahm is most notably remembered as one of the emigrants to Abyssinia, a group of early Muslims who undertook what Islamic history records as the first hijra (migration) around 615 CE. When the persecution of Muslims in Mecca intensified, the Prophet Muhammad advised a small group of his followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, present-day Ethiopia, under the protection of the Negus (king). This migration preceded the more famous migration to Medina by several years.

The emigrants to Abyssinia faced the difficult decision of leaving their homeland, families, and tribal connections to preserve their religious beliefs. This group, which included Amr bin Jahm, demonstrated remarkable commitment to their faith during a period when Islam was still in its earliest stages and Muslims were a small, vulnerable community.

As a sahaba (companion), Amr bin Jahm belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community. The companions who participated in the Abyssinian migration hold a special position in Islamic history as they were among the first to sacrifice worldly comforts for their religious convictions.

Amr bin Jahm bin Qays died in 633 CE, shortly after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. His relatively short life span of about forty years encompassed the entire period of early Islamic revelation and community formation. Like many of the early companions, his life exemplified the ascetic tradition that characterized some of the earliest Muslims, who prioritized spiritual commitment over material concerns.

While detailed accounts of his specific activities and contributions are limited in historical sources, his inclusion among the emigrants to Abyssinia marks him as one of the early Muslims who played a role in establishing the precedent for religious migration when faced with persecution, a concept that would become significant in Islamic jurisprudence and history.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Amr bin Mutarrif bin 'Alqama (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Amr ibn Mutarrif al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the clan of Banu Amr ibn Mabdhul. His name is reported in several forms. Ibn Ishaq's list of the martyrs of Uhud, as transmitted by Yunus ibn Bukayr and Salama, calls him Amr ibn Mutarrif ibn Amr, while al-Bakka'i's transmission gives Amr ibn Mutarrif ibn Alqama. Ibn Abd al-Barr also records the form Mutarrif ibn Alqama. Musa ibn Uqba, citing Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, uses the 'ibn Alqama' form and lists him among the martyrs of Banu Amr ibn Awf. All of these sources agree that he was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Uhud. The classical entries record no further details of his life.

bio: Amr bin Qays bin Zayd (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Amr ibn Qays ibn Zayd ibn Sawad ibn Malik ibn Ghanm al-Ansari al-Najjari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu al-Najjar of the Ansar in Medina. His kunya is given as Abu Amr and also Abu al-Hakam. Abu Ma'shar, al-Waqidi and Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Umara state that he fought at Badr, but this is reported only by some scholars. There is no disagreement that he was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Uhud, together with his son Qays. It is said that he was killed by Nawfal ibn Mu'awiya al-Dili, who later accepted Islam in the year of the conquest of Mecca.

famous: Amr bin Talaq b Zayd b Umayya
full: Amr bin Talaq b Zayd b Umayya
bio: Amr bin Talaq b Zayd b Umayya (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Amr ibn Talaq ibn Zayd ibn Umayya was a companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who resided in Medina, the city that became the center of the nascent Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Amr ibn Talaq is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the Muslims despite being significantly outnumbered.

The Companions of Badr, including Amr ibn Talaq, hold a special status within Islamic tradition due to their participation in this pivotal battle. Islamic sources indicate that approximately 313 to 317 Muslims participated in the Battle of Badr, facing a Meccan force of around 1,000 warriors. The victory at Badr was seen as a turning point that established the Muslims as a formidable force in the Arabian Peninsula and validated their cause in the eyes of many tribal communities.

As a Sahaba, or Companion of the Prophet, Amr ibn Talaq was part of the generation that directly witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community. The Companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam to subsequent generations. Their experiences and testimonies became foundational sources for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and historical accounts.

Amr ibn Talaq died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph after Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. His death occurred during a period of rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula, as Muslim forces began their conquests in Syria, Iraq, and other regions. While specific details about his later life and activities remain limited in historical records, his participation in the Battle of Badr ensures his place among the notable early Muslims who contributed to the establishment and early development of the Islamic community.

bio: Amr bin Tha'laba (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Amr ibn Tha'laba ibn Wahb ibn Adi al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar, a clan of the Khazraj in Medina. Ibn Sa'd gives his kunya as Abu Hakim; Ibn Abd al-Barr gives Abu Hakim or Abu Hukayma and says he was better known by his kunya than his name, while Abu Nu'aym gives Abu al-Hakam. Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri states that he fought at Badr, and Ibn Abd al-Barr adds that he also fought at Uhud. Ibn al-Athir held that he was the same man as a Companion called Amr ibn Tha'laba al-Juhani, whom Ibn Manda had listed as a separate person. None of the classical entries records the date of his death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia (hawramani.com) — Amr ibn Tha'laba (Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd; Usd al-Ghaba; al-Isti'ab; Ma'rifat al-Sahaba, Abu Nu'aym)

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Amr bin Thabit bin Waqash (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Amr bin Thabit bin Waqash was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early years of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the early Muslims who supported the Prophet during the formative period of the Islamic community.

Amr bin Thabit lived during a crucial era in Islamic history when the Muslim community was establishing itself in Medina following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE. As one of the Sahaba, the term used for the companions of Prophet Muhammad, he was part of the close-knit group of early believers who witnessed the revelation of the Quran and participated in the foundational events of Islamic civilization.

He is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, where he lost his life fighting alongside the Muslim forces. The Battle of Uhud was the second major military encounter between the early Muslim community and the Meccan tribes who opposed them. This battle took place near Mount Uhud, close to Medina, and represented a significant test for the young Muslim community.

The battle itself was a complex engagement that initially favored the Muslims but later turned against them when some Muslim archers abandoned their assigned positions. Despite the challenging circumstances, companions like Amr bin Thabit demonstrated their commitment to the cause by remaining steadfast until the end.

His death at Uhud earned him recognition as one of the martyrs of this important battle. In Islamic tradition, those who die in defense of their faith and community are accorded special honor, and the martyrs of Uhud hold a particular place in Islamic historical memory.

Amr bin Thabit's significance lies in his representation of the early Muslim community's dedication during Islam's most vulnerable period. His life and sacrifice exemplify the commitment shown by the Sahaba during the foundational years when the survival of the Islamic message was far from assured. Like many early companions, his story reflects the personal costs borne by individuals who chose to support the Prophet Muhammad during a time when doing so required considerable courage and sacrifice.

His legacy is preserved within the broader narrative of the Sahaba and their role in supporting the establishment of Islam during its earliest and most challenging years.

bio: Amr bin Umayya bin al-Harith (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Amr ibn Umayya ibn al-Harith ibn Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Qusayy was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Quraysh clan of Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza. Ibn Sa'd records that he accepted Islam early in Mecca, emigrated to Abyssinia in the second emigration, and died there. Ibn Sa'd notes that all the accounts agree on this, and that he left no descendants. He is a different person from the better-known Companion Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri.

full: ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī
primaryTitle: Conqueror of Egypt — Governor of Egypt
titles: Fātiḥ Miṣr

relations.person: Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As

bio: Amr ibn al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi was an Arab commander and companion of Muhammad who led the Muslim conquest of Egypt and served as its governor in 640–646 and 658–664. The son of a wealthy Qurayshite, Amr embraced Islam in c. 629 and was assigned important roles in the nascent Muslim community by the Islamic prophet Muhammad. The first caliph Abu Bakr appointed Amr as a commander of what became the conquest of Syria. He conquered most of Palestine, to which he was appointed governor, and helped lead the Arabs to decisive victories over the Byzantines at the battles of Ajnadayn and the Yarmuk in 634 and 636.
bio_full:
Amr ibn al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi (c. 585 – 664) was an Arab commander and companion of Muhammad who led the Muslim conquest of Egypt and served as its governor in 640–646 and 658–664. The son of a wealthy Qurayshite, Amr embraced Islam in c. 629 and was assigned important roles in the nascent Muslim community by the Islamic prophet Muhammad. The first caliph Abu Bakr (r. 632–634) appointed Amr as a commander of what became the conquest of Syria. He conquered most of Palestine, to which he was appointed governor, and helped lead the Arabs to decisive victories over the Byzantines at the battles of Ajnadayn and the Yarmuk in 634 and 636.
Amr launched the expedition that conquered Egypt on his own initiative in late 639, defeating the Byzantines in a string of victories ending with the surrender of Alexandria in 641 or 642. It was the swiftest of the early Muslim conquests. This was followed by westward advances by Amr as far as Tripoli in present-day Libya. In a treaty signed with the Byzantine governor Cyrus, Amr guaranteed the security of Egypt's population and imposed a poll tax on non-Muslim adult men. He maintained the Coptic-dominated bureaucracy and cordial ties with the Coptic patriarch Benjamin. He founded Fustat as the provincial capital with the mosque later called after him at its center. Amr ruled relatively independently, acquired significant wealth, and upheld the interests of the Arab conquerors who formed Fustat's garrison in relation to the central authorities in Medina. After gradually diluting Amr's authority, Caliph Uthman (r. 644–656) dismissed him in 646 after accusations of incompetence from his successor Abd Allah ibn Sa'd.
After mutineers from Egypt assassinated Uthman, Amr distanced himself from their cause, despite previously instigating opposition against Uthman. In the ensuing First Fitna, Amr joined Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan against Caliph Ali (r. 656–661) due to promises of the governorship of Egypt and its tax revenues. Amr served as Mu'awiya's representative in the abortive arbitration talks to end the war. Afterward, he wrested control of Egypt from Ali's loyalists, killing its governor Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, and assumed the governorship instead. Mu'awiya kept him in his post after establishing the Umayyad Caliphate in 661 and Amr ruled the province until his death.

Early life and military career
Amr ibn al-As was born in c. 573. His father, al-As ibn Wa'il, was a wealthy landowner from the Banu Sahm clan of the Quraysh tribe of Mecca. Following the death of al-As in c. 622, Amr inherited from him the lucrative al-Waht estate and vineyards near Ta'if. Amr's mother was al-Nabigha bint Harmala from the Banu Jallan clan of the Anaza tribe. She had been taken captive and sold, in succession, to several members of the Quraysh, one of whom was Amr's father. As such, Amr had two maternal half-brothers, Amr ibn Atatha of the Banu Adi and Uqba ibn Nafi of the Banu Fihr, and a half-sister from the Banu Abd Shams. Amr is physically described in the traditional sources as being short with broad shoulders, having a large head with a wide forehead and wide mouth, long arms and a long beard.
There are conflicting reports about when Amr embraced Islam, with the most credible version placing it in 629/630, not long before the conquest of Mecca by Muhammad. According to this account, he converted alongside the Qurayshites Khalid ibn al-Walid and Uthman ibn Talha. According to Amr's own testimony, transmitted by his fourth-generation descendant Amr ibn Shu'ayb, he converted in Axum in the presence of King Armah (Najashi) and met Muhammad in Medina upon the latter's return from the Battle of Khaybar in 628. Amr conditioned his conversion on the forgiveness of his past sins and an "active part in affairs", according to a report cited by the historian Ibn Asakir (d. 1176).
Indeed, in October 629, Amr was tasked by Muhammad with leading the raid on Dhat al-Salasil, likely located in the northern Hejaz (western Arabia), a lucrative opportunity for Amr in view of the potential war spoils. The purpose of the raid is unclear, though the modern historian Fred Donner speculates that it was to "break up a gathering of hostile tribal groups" possibly backed by the Byzantine Empire. The historian Ibn Hisham (d. 833) holds that Amr rallied the nomadic Arabs in the region "to make war on [Byzantine] Syria". The tribal groups targeted in the raid included the Quda'a in general and the Bali specifically. Amr's paternal grandmother hailed from the Bali, and this may have motivated his appointment to the command by Muhammad as Amr was instructed to recruit tribesmen from the Bali and the other Quda'a tribes of Balqayn and Banu Udhra. Following the raid, a delegation of the Bali embraced Islam. Amr further consecrated ties with the tribe by marrying a Bali woman, with whom he had his son Muhammad.
Muhammad appointed Amr as the governor of Oman and he remained there until being informed of Muhammad's death in 632. Amr was personally chosen by Muhammad to deliver a letter calling the kings of Oman, the Julanda brothers Abd and Jayfa, to convert to Islam while being accompanied by Sa'id ibn Aws al-Ansari. Historian Al-Baladhuri reports that on their departure to Sohar, Muhammad said to them:

 "If these people (of Oman) accept the witness of truth and pledge obedience to Allah and his Prophet, Amr will be the commander, and Abu Zayd will officiate in prayer. Propagate Islam and teach the Qur'an and the institutions of the Prophet."
The death of Muhammad prompted several Arab tribes to defect from the nascent Medina-based Muslim polity in the Ridda wars. Muhammad's successor Caliph Abu Bakr (r. 632–634) appointed Amr to rein in the apostate Quda'a tribes, and among those targeted were the Hejazi branches of the Bali. Amr's campaigns, which were supported by the commander Shurahbil ibn Hasana, succeeded in restoring Medina's authority as far as the northern frontier with Syria.

Governor of Palestine and role in the Syrian conquest
Amr was one of four commanders dispatched by Abu Bakr to conquer Syria in 633. The focus of Amr's campaign was Palestine, to which he had been appointed governor by Abu Bakr before his departure. As a Qurayshite merchant Amr was likely already well-acquainted with the routes to Gaza, a principle terminal for Meccan caravans. He took the coastal route of the Hejaz, reaching Ayla, a Muslim possession since 630, before breaking west into the Negev desert or possibly the Sinai. He arrived near the villages of Dathin and Badan in Gaza's environs where he entered into talks with Gaza's Byzantine commander. After the negotiations broke down, Amr's men bested the Byzantines at the Battle of Dathin on 4 February 634 and set up headquarters at Ghamr al-Arabat in the middle of the Wadi Araba. Most accounts hold that Amr's army was 3,000-strong; the Muhajirun (emigrants from Mecca to Medina) and the Ansar (natives of Medina), who together formed the core of the earliest Muslim converts, dominated his forces according to al-Waqidi (d. 823), while the 9th-century historian Ibn A'tham holds that Amr's army consisted of 3,300 Qurayshite and allied horsemen, 1,700 horsemen from the Banu Sulaym and 200 from the Yemenite tribe of Madh'hij. The historian Philip Mayerson considers the troop figures to be "unquestionably exaggerated" but still representing the largest Arab fighting force to have ever been assembled in southern Palestine and the Sinai until then.
Amr conquered the area around Gaza by February or March 634 and proceeded to besiege Caesarea, the capital of Byzantine Palestine, in July. He soon after abandoned the siege upon the approach of a large Byzantine army.

bio: Amr ibn Mua'dh (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Amr ibn Mu'adh ibn al-Nu'man ibn Imru' al-Qays ibn Zayd ibn Abd al-Ashhal was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Abd al-Ashhal of the Ansar in Medina. He was the brother of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, chief of the Aws, and their mother was Kabsha bint Rafi' ibn Mu'awiya. His kunya is given as Abu Uthman. The Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Umayr ibn Abi Waqqas. He fought at Badr alongside his brother Sa'd, and at Uhud, where he was killed as a martyr. His killer was Dirar ibn al-Khattab al-Fihri, who later accepted Islam in the year of the conquest of Mecca. Ibn Abd al-Barr states that Amr was thirty-two years old when he was killed and that he left no descendants.

bio: Amr ibn Sa'id ibn al-'Aas (c. 593–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Amr ibn Sa'id ibn al-As ibn Umayya ibn Abd Shams, known as Abu Uqba, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Umayyad clan of Quraysh. His mother was Safiyya bint al-Mughira of the Banu Makhzum, an aunt of Khalid ibn al-Walid, and his brothers included Khalid, Aban and Abd Allah. He accepted Islam shortly after his brother Khalid, and Ibn Hajar preserves verses exchanged between him and his brother Aban, who at first rebuked them for their new religion. Musa ibn Uqba and Ibn Ishaq list him among the emigrants to Abyssinia, together with his wife, whom Ibn Ishaq names Fatima bint Safwan ibn Umayya. According to al-Waqidi, he reached Abyssinia two years after the first group and stayed until the emigrants returned by ship. He joined the Prophet at Khaybar in 7 AH, and al-Waqidi reports that he took part in the conquest of Mecca, Hunayn, al-Ta'if and Tabuk. The Prophet put him in charge of the date harvest of Khaybar, and Ibn Hajar says he was in charge of Wadi al-Qura and other places when the Prophet died. After the Prophet's death he and his brothers left their posts and went to Syria. Most early historians, including al-Waqidi, Musa ibn Uqba and Ibn Manda, say he was killed at the Battle of Ajnadayn during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, which Ibn al-Athir dates to Jumada I 13 AH (634 CE). Ibn al-Athir also notes a report from Ibn Ishaq that he died at Yarmuk, which others did not follow, and Khalifa ibn Khayyat placed his death at Marj al-Saffar. He left no descendants.

bio: Amra bint Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurayq al-Ansariyya (c. 646–c. 717) was a scholar of the Hadith Sciences tradition, based in Medina. Known as Foremost Female Jurist of Medina.
bio_full:
Amra bint Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurayq al-Ansariyya was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from approximately 646 to 717 CE in Medina. She belonged to the Ansar, the Medinan tribes who supported Prophet Muhammad after his migration from Mecca, as indicated by her tribal designation "al-Ansariyya."

Amra specialized in hadith sciences, the scholarly discipline concerned with collecting, preserving, and authenticating the sayings, actions, and tacit approvals of Prophet Muhammad. During the early Islamic period, hadith scholars played a crucial role in establishing the foundations of Islamic law and practice by carefully transmitting and verifying these prophetic traditions.

Living in Medina, the second holiest city in Islam and the Prophet's adopted home, Amra was positioned at the heart of Islamic scholarship. The city served as a major center of learning where scholars gathered to study and transmit religious knowledge. Her proximity to the original Muslim community and the companions of the Prophet provided her with access to authentic chains of transmission, which were essential for establishing the reliability of hadith narrations.

Amra earned recognition as the foremost female jurist of Medina, indicating her expertise extended beyond hadith collection to Islamic jurisprudence. This distinction highlights her significant role in the development of Islamic legal thought during the formative period of the religion. Female scholars like Amra were particularly important in transmitting traditions related to women's religious practices and domestic aspects of Islamic life, areas where they had unique access and authority.

Her scholarly career coincided with the Umayyad period, when Islamic civilization was expanding rapidly and systematic approaches to religious scholarship were being established. During this time, scholars were working to codify and preserve Islamic teachings for future generations, making the contributions of hadith specialists like Amra essential to the religion's intellectual development.

As one of the early female authorities in Islamic jurisprudence, Amra represents the important but often understudied role of women scholars in early Islamic history. Her recognition as Medina's leading female jurist demonstrates that women could achieve prominent positions in religious scholarship during this period, contributing to the preservation and interpretation of Islamic knowledge alongside their male counterparts.

bio: Amra bint Abi Ayoub (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Amra bint Abi Ayyub was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. She was the daughter of the well-known Companion Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Kulayb al-Ansari, and her mother was Umm Ayyub bint Qays ibn Sa'd. Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet, and Ibn al-Athir, citing Ibn Habib, also names her among those who gave the pledge. She married Safwan ibn Aws ibn Jabir and bore him a son, Khalid ibn Safwan. The classical entries on her record no hadith narrated by her and give no date of death.

bio: Amra bint Haritha bin al-Nu'man (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amra bint Haritha ibn al-Nu'man was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the Banu al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd gives her father's lineage as Haritha ibn al-Nu'man ibn Naf', traced back through Zayd, Ubayd, Tha'laba and Ghanm to Malik ibn al-Najjar. He names her mother as Umm Khalid bint Khalid, also of the Banu al-Najjar.

She was married first to Qays ibn Amr ibn Sahl ibn Tha'laba of the Banu al-Najjar. After him she married Uthman ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf of the Banu Amr ibn Awf. Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam and gave her pledge of allegiance (bay'a) to the Prophet. His entry names no children and gives no dates of birth or death for her.

bio: Amra bint Hazm ibn Zayd (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amra bint Hazm ibn Zayd was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra (migration from Mecca to Medina) in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Amra bint Hazm was part of the indigenous population of Medina that played a crucial role in establishing the early Islamic community. The Ansar were instrumental in providing shelter, protection, and material support to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca, forming the foundation of the first Islamic state in Medina.

Living during the formative period of Islam, Amra bint Hazm witnessed and participated in the development of the Muslim community during the Prophet's lifetime. Her status as a Sahabiyya indicates that she had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions, a designation that holds special significance in Islamic tradition.

The female companions of the Prophet Muhammad played important roles in the early Muslim community, contributing to religious, social, and educational aspects of Islamic society. They participated in community life, supported the spread of Islamic teachings, and served as role models for subsequent generations of Muslim women.

Amra bint Hazm's life spanned approximately forty years, ending around 635 CE, which places her death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's reign. This means she lived through the foundational period of Islam, from its early establishment in Medina through the initial expansion of the Islamic state beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Her recognition as an Ansari companion of Medina places her among the honored early supporters of Islam who facilitated the religion's growth and consolidation. While specific details of her individual contributions may not be extensively documented in historical sources, her status as a Sahabiyya ensures her place among the respected figures of early Islamic history, representing the important role that women played in the formation and development of the Muslim community.

bio: Amra bint Hazzal (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amra bint Hazzal was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, Amra bint Hazzal would have been part of the crucial support network that enabled the establishment and growth of the early Islamic community. The Ansar played a fundamental role in Islamic history by providing refuge, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca, helping to secure the survival and expansion of the nascent faith during its most vulnerable period.

Like other female companions of her era, Amra bint Hazzal lived through the critical decades that saw the revelation of the Quran, the establishment of Islamic law and governance, and the expansion of Muslim influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her presence in Medina during this transformative period placed her at the heart of early Islamic society, though specific details of her individual contributions or activities are not extensively documented in the historical sources that have survived.

Amra bint Hazzal's life span, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompassed the entire prophetic period and extended into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule. This timing means she witnessed the complete transformation of Arabian society and the emergence of Islam as a major religious and political force.

Her designation as a Sahabiyya places her among the women who are recognized in Islamic tradition as having direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and being part of the first generation of Muslims. This status carries particular significance in Islamic historical memory, as the companions are viewed as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations, helping to preserve and pass down the foundational elements of the faith during its earliest and most formative period.

bio: Amra bint Mas'ud #1 (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amra bint Mas'ud ibn Qays ibn Amr ibn Zayd Manat ibn Adi ibn Amr ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the Banu al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd has five numbered entries for women named Amra bint Mas'ud; she is the one he calls 'the First' (al-Ula). Her mother was Umayra bint Amr ibn Haram, of the same Banu al-Najjar line.

She married Zayd ibn Malik ibn Abd Wadd ibn Ka'b ibn Abd al-Ashhal and bore him two sons, Sa'd, who fought at Badr, and Thabit. Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam and gave her pledge of allegiance (bay'a) to the Prophet. His entry gives no dates for her.

She is not the same woman as Amra bint Mas'ud, mother of Sa'd ibn Ubada, whom Ibn Sa'd lists as 'the Fourth', nor Amra bint Mas'ud ibn Aws of the Banu Zafar, wife of Muhammad ibn Maslama.

bio: Amra bint Mas'ud bin Aws (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Scholar of Quranic Exegesis.
bio_full:
Amra bint Mas'ud bin Aws was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early 7th century CE. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with the Prophet and witnessed the foundational period of Islam.

As a resident of Medina, Amra would have been present during the crucial years following the Hijra in 622 CE, when the Muslim community was establishing itself and developing its religious and social practices. During this formative period, she gained recognition for her knowledge and understanding of Quranic exegesis, earning her a reputation as a female scholar in the interpretation of Islamic scripture.

The early Islamic community in Medina included several women who were noted for their religious learning and scholarship. Amra bint Mas'ud bin Aws was among those female companions who contributed to the preservation and interpretation of Islamic teachings during the religion's earliest decades. Her expertise in Quranic exegesis would have made her an important resource for the Muslim community, particularly for women seeking religious guidance and education.

Her role as a scholar of Quranic interpretation reflects the broader participation of women in the intellectual and religious life of early Islamic society. Female companions like Amra played significant roles in transmitting religious knowledge and understanding, contributing to the development of Islamic jurisprudence and scholarship that would influence future generations.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime and the early years of the Islamic community, Amra witnessed the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices. Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, just a few years after the Prophet's passing in 632 CE.

As one of the female scholars of the early Islamic period, Amra bint Mas'ud bin Aws represents the important contributions that women made to Islamic learning and religious scholarship during the formative years of the faith. Her expertise in Quranic exegesis positioned her as an influential figure in the preservation and interpretation of Islamic religious knowledge during this crucial historical period.

bio: Amra bint Rawaha (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Amra bint Rawaha was a woman of the Ansar from the Khazraj of Medina, the sister of the Companion Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. Khalifa ibn Khayyat gives her as the daughter of Rawaha ibn Imru' al-Qays of the Khazraj, and names her mother as Kabsha bint Waqid ibn Amr ibn al-Itnaba. She was the wife of Bashir ibn Sa'd and the mother of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.

She appears in a well-known report about a gift. Bashir gave their son al-Nu'man a gift, and Amra asked that the Prophet be made a witness to it. The Prophet asked whether Bashir had given the same to all his children. When Bashir said he had not, the Prophet declined to witness it; in one version he called it unjust, and in another he told Bashir to find a different witness.

Her son al-Nu'man also reported that when Abd Allah ibn Rawaha fainted, Amra wept aloud, calling out to him and listing his virtues. When he recovered, he told her that at every word she said he had been asked whether he was truly so.

Amra herself transmitted a hadith from the Prophet that going out (to the prayer) was obligatory for every woman who wore a waistband (nitaq).

bio: Amra bint Abd al-Rahman al-Ansariyya, a civilian follower, and one of the narrators of the Prophet’s hadith.
bio_full:
Amrah bint Abd al-Rahman al-Ansariyya (645-717 CE) was a prominent female scholar of the early Islamic period, belonging to the generation known as the Tabi'un—those who learned from the Companions of Prophet Muhammad but did not meet the Prophet themselves. She lived during the formative decades of Islamic scholarship in the late 7th and early 8th centuries.

Amrah is recognized as one of the important transmitters of hadith, the recorded sayings and traditions of Prophet Muhammad. Her role in hadith transmission places her among the notable female scholars who contributed to preserving and passing down Islamic religious knowledge during Islam's first century. As a member of the Tabi'un generation, she received her religious education from those who had direct contact with the Prophet's Companions, making her part of the crucial early chain of Islamic scholarly transmission.

Her designation as "al-Ansariyya" indicates a connection to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who supported Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community. This suggests she was part of the established Muslim community in the Arabian Peninsula's most important early Islamic centers.

During her lifetime, which spanned over seven decades, Amrah witnessed the rapid expansion of the Islamic empire under the Umayyad Caliphate and the corresponding development of Islamic legal and religious scholarship. The period in which she lived was crucial for the systematization of hadith collection and verification, processes that would later become formalized into the Islamic sciences of hadith criticism and authentication.

Her contribution to hadith transmission represents the broader participation of women in early Islamic scholarship, particularly in the preservation and teaching of religious knowledge. Female scholars like Amrah played essential roles in maintaining the continuity of Islamic learning during the religion's foundational period, often serving as links between different generations of scholars.

Amrah's work as a hadith narrator contributed to the larger project of preserving prophetic traditions that would eventually form the basis for Islamic law, theology, and practice. Her position among the recognized transmitters of the Tabi'un generation underscores the significance of her scholarly contributions to the development of Islamic religious sciences during this critical period of Islamic history.

bio: Amrah bint al-S'adi bin Waqdan (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Amrah bint al-S'adi bin Waqdan was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the early seventh century. Born around 593 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, she was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca during a time when the nascent Muslim community faced significant persecution from the ruling Quraysh tribe.

Amrah is historically significant as one of the Muslims who participated in the migration to Abyssinia (present-day Ethiopia), known in Islamic history as the first hijra. This migration occurred around 615 CE when the Prophet Muhammad advised a group of his followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Aksum under the protection of the Negus (king) Najashi. The emigrants, numbering approximately eighty individuals including men, women, and children, left Mecca to escape the intensifying persecution they faced for their religious beliefs.

The migration to Abyssinia represents a crucial moment in early Islamic history, demonstrating the severe challenges faced by the first Muslim community and the Prophet's strategic thinking in ensuring their survival. Those who made this journey, including Amrah, showed remarkable courage and commitment to their faith, as they left behind their homes, families, and familiar surroundings for an uncertain future in a foreign land.

As one of the female emigrants, Amrah would have faced particular challenges, as women's mobility was generally restricted in Arabian society. Her participation in this migration indicates her significant dedication to the Islamic faith and her recognition of the necessity of preserving the early Muslim community.

Amrah is also noted as being part of the early ascetic tradition within Islam, suggesting she may have been known for her pious lifestyle and spiritual devotion. She died in 633 CE, shortly after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE, making her one of the companions who witnessed the entire prophetic period and the immediate aftermath.

Her life represents the experiences of the earliest Muslim women who played important roles in the survival and establishment of the Islamic community during its most vulnerable period. While detailed records of her specific activities are limited, her status as a companion and emigrant to Abyssinia marks her as a significant figure in the foundational period of Islamic history.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Anas bin al-Nadr b. DamDam (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Anas ibn al-Nadr ibn Damdam was a Companion of the Prophet from the Khazraj of the Ansar in Medina. He was the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik, the Prophet's servant, and the brother of al-Rubayyi' bint al-Nadr.

He missed the Battle of Badr and was grieved by it. He told the Prophet that he had been absent from the first battle fought against the polytheists, and vowed that if God let him witness another, God would see what he would do.

At Uhud, when the Muslims fell back, he asked God to excuse what his companions had done and declared himself free of what the polytheists had done. He then went forward and met Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, telling him that he could smell the scent of Paradise from beyond Uhud. Sa'd later said he could not do what Anas did. Anas was killed in the battle. His body bore more than eighty wounds, and only his sister could recognise him, by his fingertips. Anas ibn Malik reported that they held the verse 'Among the believers are men who have been true to their covenant with God' (Qur'an 33:23) to refer to him and those like him. Ibn Hisham's Sira adds that when word spread that the Prophet had been killed, he found Companions who had stopped fighting and urged them to rise and die, and was then killed.

Al-Bukhari also records that when his sister al-Rubayyi' broke a woman's front tooth and the Prophet ordered retaliation, Anas swore that her tooth would not be broken. The other side accepted compensation, and the Prophet said that among God's servants are some whose oaths God fulfils when they swear by Him.

bio: Anas bin Mua'dh bin Anas (c. 594–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Anas ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas ibn Qays ibn Ubayd ibn Zayd ibn Mu'awiya ibn Amr ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar was a Companion of the Prophet from the Banu al-Najjar of the Khazraj in Medina. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Umm Anas bint Khalid ibn Khunays ibn Lawdhan of the Banu Sa'ida.

Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi all list him among those who fought at Badr. His name is reported in different forms: Urwa called him Unays, and in one account Ibn Ishaq called him Aws ibn Mu'adh.

Accounts differ on how his life ended. Al-Waqidi, as cited by Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr, says he fought at Badr, Uhud, the Trench and all the campaigns with the Prophet, and died during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan. Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Umara instead said he was killed as a martyr at Bi'r Ma'una, together with his full brother Ubayy ibn Mu'adh (Abu Muhammad); Ibn Abd al-Barr reports that Ibn Ishaq also placed his death there. Al-Waqidi and al-Zuhri both say he left no descendants.

bio: Anas ibn Mālik ibn Naḍr al-Khazrajī al-Anṣārī was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He was nicknamed Khadim al-Nabi for serving Muhammad for ten years.
bio_full:
Anas ibn Malik ibn Nadr al-Khazraji al-Ansari was a prominent companion of the Prophet Muhammad and one of the most prolific narrators of hadith in Islamic tradition. Born around 611 CE in Medina, he belonged to the Khazraj tribe, one of the two main Arab tribes of the city.

When Muhammad migrated to Medina in 622 CE, Anas was approximately ten years old. His mother, Umm Sulaym, brought him to serve the Prophet, beginning a decade-long period of close companionship that would define his life and historical significance. This service earned him the nickname "Khadim al-Nabi," meaning "servant of the Prophet."

During his years of service, Anas accompanied Muhammad on various journeys and witnessed many significant events in early Islamic history. His proximity to the Prophet's household provided him with intimate knowledge of Muhammad's daily practices, teachings, and personal conduct. This unique position made him an invaluable source of information about prophetic traditions.

Anas is most renowned for his role in hadith transmission. He is credited with narrating over 2,000 hadith, making him one of the most frequently cited sources in major hadith collections, including those of Bukhari and Muslim. His narrations cover diverse topics ranging from religious rituals and legal matters to the Prophet's personal habits and character traits.

After Muhammad's death in 632 CE, Anas continued to live in Medina and later moved to Basra in Iraq, where he served in various administrative capacities under the Umayyad caliphs. His longevity allowed him to witness the rapid expansion of the Islamic empire and the development of early Islamic institutions.

Anas lived an exceptionally long life, dying in Basra around 713 CE at approximately 102 years of age. His advanced age made him one of the last surviving companions of Muhammad, and scholars from across the Islamic world sought him out to learn prophetic traditions directly from someone who had witnessed them firsthand.

His contributions to Islamic scholarship extend beyond hadith narration. His detailed accounts of the Prophet's life and practices became fundamental sources for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and biographical literature. Modern Islamic scholarship continues to reference his narrations as primary sources for understanding early Islamic history and prophetic teachings.

bio: Anisa bint 'Adiy bin Nadla (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Anisa bint 'Adiy bin Nadla was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 593 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, she was among the earliest converts to Islam during its initial emergence in Mecca.

Anisa is historically recognized as one of the emigrants to Abyssinia (modern-day Ethiopia), participating in what Islamic sources term the first hijra or migration. This migration occurred around 615 CE when a group of early Muslim converts, facing persecution from the Meccan tribes, sought refuge in the Christian kingdom of Aksum under the protection of the Negus (king). The emigration to Abyssinia represented a crucial early chapter in Islamic history, demonstrating both the challenges faced by the nascent Muslim community and the pragmatic diplomatic relationships that developed between early Muslims and Christian rulers.

As an early convert and emigrant, Anisa belonged to a small but significant group of individuals who accepted Islam during its most vulnerable period, when the religion had few followers and faced considerable opposition from established tribal and religious authorities in Mecca. Her participation in the Abyssinian migration indicates her commitment to the new faith despite the personal costs of leaving her homeland and familiar social networks.

The emigrants to Abyssinia occupied a unique position in early Islamic history, as they maintained their religious practices in a foreign land while the Muslim community continued to develop in the Arabian Peninsula. This experience of early Muslim diaspora would later inform Islamic approaches to living as religious minorities in non-Muslim territories.

Anisa's identification with early ascetic traditions suggests she may have practiced forms of religious devotion that emphasized spiritual discipline and detachment from worldly concerns, though specific details of her ascetic practices are not definitively documented in available historical sources.

Her death in 633 CE places her among the generation of companions who witnessed both the prophetic period and the immediate aftermath of Muhammad's death in 632 CE. As a female companion from this earliest generation, she represents the often under-documented participation of women in the foundational period of Islamic history, particularly their role in the difficult early migrations that helped ensure the survival and eventual expansion of the Muslim community.

bio: Anisa bint Abi Talha (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Anisa bint Abi Talha was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Anisa bint Abi Talha lived during the formative period of Islam when the Muslim community was establishing itself in Medina. The Ansar played a crucial role in providing shelter, resources, and protection to the early Muslims who had migrated from Mecca, and they were instrumental in the survival and growth of the nascent Islamic community.

Like other female companions of her time, Anisa bint Abi Talha would have been part of the community of women who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and participated in the early Islamic society. The female companions, known collectively as the Sahabiyat, contributed to various aspects of community life, including religious learning, social support, and the preservation of Islamic teachings.

Her designation as an Ansari companion places her among those Medinan residents who converted to Islam and pledged their support to the Prophet Muhammad. The Ansar were particularly honored in Islamic tradition for their generosity and sacrifice in supporting the Muslim migrants from Mecca, sharing their homes, resources, and establishing bonds of brotherhood with the newcomers.

Anisa bint Abi Talha died around 635 CE, during the early period of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs following the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. Her life spanned the crucial decades when Islam transformed from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community in Medina and the beginning of a major religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula.

The preservation of her name in Islamic historical records reflects the recognition given to the female companions who witnessed and participated in the early development of Islam. While specific details of her individual contributions may not be extensively documented, her status as a Sahabiyya indicates her important place among the first generation of Muslims who helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization.
