bio: Anisa bint Raqeem bin al-Harith (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Anisa bint Raqeem bin al-Harith was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, Anisa bint Raqeem belonged to the crucial group of early Muslims who provided essential support during the establishment of the first Islamic community. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were the Medinan tribes who embraced Islam and offered protection and assistance to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca. This alliance was fundamental to the survival and growth of the early Muslim community.

Her designation as a sahabiyya indicates that she had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. The companions hold a revered position in Islamic tradition, as they were the first generation of Muslims who received Islamic teachings directly from the Prophet and helped transmit these teachings to subsequent generations.

Living during the pivotal decades of early Islamic expansion, Anisa bint Raqeem witnessed the transformation of Arabian society and the rapid spread of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime, ending around 635 CE, coincided with the period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the first four caliphs who succeeded Prophet Muhammad.

The inclusion of female companions like Anisa bint Raqeem in historical records reflects the active participation of women in the early Islamic community. These women contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings, participated in community affairs, and played significant roles in supporting the nascent Muslim society.

Her legacy, along with that of other companions, represents the foundational generation that helped establish the religious, social, and political frameworks that would define Islamic civilization. The companions collectively serve as important links in the chain of Islamic tradition, connecting later generations of Muslims to the origins of their faith and the authentic teachings of Islam as practiced during the Prophet's lifetime.

bio: Abbas ibn Firnas (810–887 CE) was a scientist of the Andalusian Sciences tradition, based in Cordoba. Known as Andalusian polymath and aviation pioneer.
bio_full:
Abū al-Qāsim ʿAbbās ibn Firnās ibn Wardās al-Tākurunnī (Arabic: أَبُو ٱلْقَاسِمِ، عَبَّاسُ بْنُ فِرْنَاسِ بْنِ وَرْدَاسَ ٱلتَّاكُرُنِّيُّ; c. 809/810 – 887 CE), known as ʿAbbās ibn Firnās (Arabic: عَبَّاسُ بْنُ فِرْنَاسٍ) was an Andalusi polymath: an inventor, astronomer, physician, chemist, engineer, musician, and poet. He was reported to have experimented with unpowered flight.
Ibn Firnas made various contributions in the field of astronomy and engineering. He constructed a device which indicated the motion of the planets and stars in the Universe. In addition, Ibn Firnas came up with a procedure to manufacture colourless glass and made magnifying lenses for reading, which were known as reading stones.

Early life
There's scholarly consensus that ibn Firnas – full name Abu al-Qasim Abbas ibn Firnas ibn Wirdas al-Takurini – was born in Ronda, in the Takurunna province; lived in Córdoba, and was an Umayyad mawlā (client) of Berber decent. His lineage may have been linked to the early Muslim conquests of the Iberian Peninsula. Later accounts emphasizing Arabic contributions to science may identify Abbas ibn Firnas in the broader frame of Islamic cultural heritage or as native muladí.

Work
Abbas ibn Firnas devised a means of manufacturing colourless glass, invented various glass planispheres, made corrective lenses ("reading stones"), devised an apparatus consisting of a chain of objects that could be used to simulate the motions of the planets and stars, and developed a process for cutting rock crystal that allowed Al-Andalus to cease exporting quartz to Egypt to be cut. He introduced the Sindhind to Al-Andalus, which had important influence on astronomy in Europe. He also designed the al-Maqata, a water clock, and a prototype for a kind of metronome.

Aviation
Some seven centuries after the death of Firnas, the Algerian historian Ahmad al-Maqqari (d. 1632) wrote a description of Ibn Firnas that included the following:

Among other very curious experiments which he made, one is his trying to fly. He covered himself with feathers for the purpose, attached a couple of wings to his body, and, getting on an eminence, flung himself down into the air, when according to the testimony of several trustworthy writers who witnessed the performance, he flew a considerable distance, as if he had been a bird, but, in alighting again on the place whence he had started, his back was very much hurt, for not knowing that birds when they alight come down upon their tails, he forgot to provide himself with one.
Al-Maqqari is said to have used in his history works "many early sources no longer extant", but in the case of Ibn Firnas, he does not cite his sources for the details of the reputed flight, though he does claim that one verse in a ninth-century Arab poem is actually an allusion to Ibn Firnas's flight. The poem was written by Mu'min ibn Said, a court poet of Córdoba under Muhammad I (d. 886), amir of the Emirate of Córdoba, who was acquainted with and usually critical of Ibn Firnas. The pertinent verse runs: "He flew faster than the phoenix in his flight when he dressed his body in the feathers of a vulture." No other surviving sources refer to the event.
It has been suggested that Ibn Firnas's attempt at glider flight might have inspired the attempt by Eilmer of Malmesbury between 1000 and 1010 in England, but there is no evidence supporting this hypothesis.

Armen Firman
According to some secondary sources, about 20 years before Ibn Firnas attempted to fly he witnessed a man named Armen Firman wrap himself in a loose cloak stiffened with wooden struts and jump from a tower in Córdoba, intending to use the garment as wings on which he could glide. The alleged attempt at flight was unsuccessful, but the garment slowed his fall enough that he sustained only minor injuries.
However, other secondary sources that deal exhaustively with Ibn Firnas' flight attempt make no reference at all to Armen Firman. Al-Maqqari's account of Ibn Firnas, being the sole primary source of the flight story, makes no mention of Firman. Since Firman's jump is said to have been Ibn Firnas' source of inspiration, the lack of any mention of Firman in Al-Maqqari's account may point to synthesis—the tower jump later confused with Ibn Firnas' gliding attempt in secondary writings. In fact, it is likely that Armen Firman is simply the Latinized name of Abbas ibn Firnas.

Legacy
In 1973, a statue of Ibn Firnas by the sculptor Badri al-Samarrai was installed at the Baghdad International Airport in Iraq.
In 1976, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) approved of naming a crater on the moon after him as Ibn Firnas. In 2011, one of the bridges going over the Guadalquivir river in Córdoba, Spain, was named the "Abbas ibn Firnás Bridge". A British one-plane airline, Firnas Airways, was also named after him.

bio: Ansa (c. 594–635 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Anasa, known by the kunya Abu Masruh, was a freedman (mawla) of the Prophet. Mus'ab al-Zubayri said he was born in al-Sarat. Musa ibn Uqba, citing Ibn Shihab, and Ibn Ishaq both list him among those who fought at Badr, and Abu Nu'aym says he was present at both Badr and Uhud. He was one of those who admitted people to the Prophet when he sat with his companions.

Reports about his death differ. Al-Mada'ini, through Ikrima from Ibn Abbas, reported that he was killed at Badr, naming him Abu Anasa; Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that the correct name is Anasa. Al-Waqidi did not accept this report, saying that scholars hold he fought at Uhud and lived for some time afterwards. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Abu Nu'aym both say he died during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, after the Prophet's death.

bio_sources.title: Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Isti'ab and Abu Nu'aym, Ma'rifat al-Sahaba — Anasa, mawla of the Prophet (Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia)

bio: Antara Mawla Salim bin 'Amr (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Antara Mawla Salim bin 'Amr was a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he lived during the crucial decades when Islam was first revealed and began to spread beyond the confines of Mecca.

As indicated by his name, Antara was a mawla, meaning he was likely a freed slave or client who had become affiliated with the tribe or family of Salim bin 'Amr. This social status was common in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society, where individuals could gain protection and tribal affiliation through such relationships. His inclusion among the Sahaba demonstrates that early Islamic society welcomed converts and followers from diverse social backgrounds.

Antara is historically significant as one of the Companions of Badr, meaning he participated in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds immense importance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, located between Mecca and Medina, and involved approximately 300 Muslim fighters facing a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory at Badr was seen as divine validation of their cause and marked a turning point in the early expansion of Islam.

The Companions of Badr, including Antara, hold a special place in Islamic tradition due to their participation in this pivotal battle. Their willingness to fight alongside the Prophet Muhammad during this critical moment demonstrated their commitment to the nascent Muslim community when its survival was far from guaranteed.

Antara's presence in Medina aligns with the period following the Hijra, when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers had migrated from Mecca and were establishing the first Muslim community. He died in 625 CE, just one year after the Battle of Badr, during the early years of the Islamic community's development in Medina.

While specific details about Antara's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not well-documented in historical sources, his recognition as a Sahaba places him among the early Muslims who directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization during its most formative period.

bio: Anūsh ibn Shīth (legendary–legendary) was a founding figure, based in Mesopotamia. Known as Ancestor of Prophet Muhammad. The sources record 2 teachers.
bio_full:
Anūsh ibn Shīth is a legendary figure in Islamic genealogical traditions, positioned as an early ancestor in the lineage leading to the Prophet Muhammad. According to Islamic historical sources, he was the son of Shīth (Seth), who is identified in Islamic tradition as a son of Adam and a prophet. These accounts place Anūsh in the earliest generations of humanity, in the region of Mesopotamia.

The chronological framework provided by traditional Islamic historians places Anūsh's lifetime in the fourth millennium BCE, though these dates reflect the legendary nature of the genealogies rather than verifiable historical records. Islamic sources describe him as part of the antediluvian generations that preceded the flood associated with the prophet Nūḥ (Noah).

Within Islamic genealogical literature, Anūsh serves as a crucial link in the prophetic lineage, connecting the earliest generations of humanity to later prophetic figures. The sources indicate he received instruction from two teachers, though the specific details of this education are not elaborated in the surviving records.

His significance in Islamic history lies primarily in his role within the sacred genealogy that traces the ancestry of the Prophet Muhammad back to Adam through the prophetic line. This genealogical tradition was important for establishing prophetic legitimacy and connecting Islamic sacred history to the broader narrative of human origins.

The figure of Anūsh appears in various Islamic historical and genealogical works, where he is consistently identified as a foundational ancestor. However, like other figures from this early legendary period, historical details about his life, teachings, or specific contributions are limited in the sources.

The preservation of Anūsh's name and position in Islamic genealogical traditions reflects the importance placed by Islamic scholars on maintaining chains of transmission and ancestry, particularly those connected to prophetic figures. While the specific historical details of his life remain within the realm of traditional accounts rather than documented history, his place in Islamic genealogical literature demonstrates the comprehensive nature of Islamic efforts to trace sacred lineages back to humanity's origins.

His legacy exists primarily through his position in these genealogical chains rather than through recorded teachings or historical actions, marking him as a transitional figure in the legendary period of Islamic historical tradition.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Aqeel bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Aqeel bin Maqrn al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE in the Hijaz region, he belonged to the Mazin tribe and lived during the critical decades when Islam was established and began its rapid expansion.

As one of the Sahaba, Aqeel was among those who directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community. His most notable distinction was his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, which took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This event is specifically referenced in the Quran (48:18), where God expresses His pleasure with those who pledged their allegiance to the Prophet under the tree. The pledge occurred when the Prophet and his followers were prevented from performing pilgrimage to Mecca and rumors spread that the Prophet's negotiator had been killed, prompting the companions to pledge their willingness to fight if necessary.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds special significance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the unwavering loyalty of the early Muslim community to their Prophet during a moment of uncertainty and potential conflict. Those who participated in this pledge are considered to have received divine approval according to Islamic belief, making Aqeel's participation a mark of his standing within the early Muslim community.

Aqeel's involvement in hadith sciences indicates that he was among those companions who transmitted sayings, actions, or approvals of Prophet Muhammad to subsequent generations. This role was crucial in preserving Islamic teachings and legal precedents during the period when Islamic law and practice were being established and codified.

Living through the final years of Prophet Muhammad's life and into the early period of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs, Aqeel witnessed the transformation of Islam from a local Arabian movement to a major political and religious force. He died around 640 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, having lived through the foundational decades of Islamic civilization. His legacy remains tied to his participation in one of the most significant pledges of loyalty in Islamic history and his contribution to the preservation of prophetic traditions.

bio: ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib, c. 580 – 670 or 683, was a cousin of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and an elder brother of Ali and Ja'far ibn Abi Talib.
bio_full:
ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib (lit. "Aqil the Son of Abu Talib"; full name Abū Yazīd ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib ibn Hāshim, Arabic: أبو يزيد عقيل بن أبي طالب بن عبد المطّلب بن هاشم), c. 580 – 670 or 683, was a cousin of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and an elder brother of Ali and Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. 
Having fought on the side of the Qurayshi rulers of Mecca against Muhammad and the early Muslims, he converted to Islam a few years before the death of Muhammad in 632. Under the second caliph Umar, he was appointed a position as an expert in the genealogy of the Quraysh. During the rivalry between his brother Ali (who reigned as the fourth caliph from 656 until his death in 661) and Mu'awiya (the first Umayyad caliph) Aqil first chose the side of his brother, but later may have deserted him in favor of Mu'awiya, as the latter is said to have offered him better financial incentives.
He was noted by later authors for his eloquence as well as for transmitting a number of hadith. Due to his close kinship with both Muhammad and with Ali, his descendants were sometimes reckoned among the Ahl al-Bayt (the extended family of Muhammad venerated by Shiite Muslims) by later generations. Most notably, the great majority of Somali clans claim to be descended from Aqil ibn Abi Talib, though this is historically untenable.

Biography
Aqil ibn Abi Talib is said to have been born 10 years after his elder brother Talib ibn Abi Talib (the first son of Muhammad's paternal uncle and guardian Abu Talib and Fatima bint Asad), and 10 and 20 years before his younger brothers Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and Ali ibn Abi Talib, respectively. After the death of his father Abu Talib in c. 619, Aqil and his older brother Talib inherited Abu Talib's great wealth.
Having initially fought against Muhammad at the Battle of Badr (624), in which he was taken prisoner and later bought free by his uncle Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, he converted to Islam around 629 or 630. He may have participated at the Muslim side in the battles of Mu'tah (629) and Hunayn (630).
After the victory of the Muslims and the death of Muhammad in 632, Aqil lived in the military encampments of Kufa and Basra for a while, supporting his brother Ali (who ruled from Medina as the fourth caliph, 656 – 661). However, later he may have abandoned Ali, as he moved to Syria in order to join the court of the first Umayyad caliph Mu'awiya I (r. 661–680). According to later tradition, Aqil's change of heart was motivated by the fact that Mu'awiya was more willing than Ali to pay his debts. While he may have given up the Hashimite claims to the caliphate and politically supported the rival claim of the Umayyads instead, he always defended his brother Ali against any criticism leveled against him at Mu'awiya's court.
Aqil was an expert on the genealogy of the Quraysh tribe (the leading tribe of Mecca, to which both the Hashimite and Umayyad families belonged). The second caliph Umar (r. 634–644) appointed him to record the names of the members of the Quraysh in the clan register (the dīwān), and to arbitrate disputes with regard to genealogy.
He was married to Fatima bint Utba, with whom he had several children (the most famous of them being Muslim ibn Aqil). Contrary to their father, a number of his sons decided to fight for the Hashimite cause and were martyred along with their cousin Husayn ibn Ali at the Battle of Karbala in 680. Aqil himself died in Medina, having become blind, either in 670 or (according to another report) in 683.

Legacy
Multiple prophetic traditions (hadiths) were transmitted on Aqil's authority, and he also figured in hadiths related by others. According to one of those, Muhammad had expressed his twofold love for Aqil: one love for him because of his kinship with him, and another love because Aqil was Abu Talib's favorite son (Muhammad himself had a close relationship with Abu Talib, who had adopted him after his own father Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib had died a few months before his birth).
Aqil was often cited by later writers for his eloquence and his witty rejoinders, addressed both against his wife Fatima bint Utba and against Mu'awiya. He seems to have been a rich man, owning multiple properties both in Mecca and in Medina. One of his properties in Medina, the Dār ʿAqīl (lit. 'the House of Aqil'), appears to have contained a graveyard where a number of notable early Muslims (especially members of the Hashimite family, such as Muhammad's daughter and Ali's wife Fatima) are said to have been buried.
Aqil's descendants through his son Muhammad, known by the name al-ʿAqīlī, were sometimes seen by later generations as members of the Ahl al-Bayt (the extended family of Muhammad, whom Shiites regarded as eligible for holding the title of caliph), much like the descendants of his brothers Ali (the Alids) and Ja'far (the Ja'farids), as well as the descendants of the three brothers' uncle Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib (the Abbasids).

Claims of ancestry by Somali clans
Most notably, the great majority of Somali clans trace their ancestry to Aqil ibn Abi Talib. The northern Darod clan trace their descent from Aqil directly through their purported forefather Darod. Northern pastoralist clans such as the Hawiye and the Dir trace their ancestry to Aqil through their common purported forefather Samaale (whose name also lies at the origin of the name 'Somali'). The Isaaq clan is sometimes regarded as having been descended from Aqil through a matrilineal connection with the Dir, but they themselves claim to be patrilineally descended from Aqil's brother Ali ibn Abi Talib instead. Finally, southern clans who practice agriculture such as the Rahanweyn trace their ancestry to Aqil through their common purported forefather Sab. One possible genealogical table may look as follows:

Aqil ibn Abi Talib
Darod
Darod clan
Samaale
Irir
Hawiye clan
Aji
Dir clan
(matrilineally) Isaaq clan
Sab
Digil
Rahanweyn clan
These genealogical claims, which are part of what Sada Mire has called "the Somali Islamic myth of origin", are historically untenable. However, they do reflect the longstanding cultural contacts between Somalia (especially, though not exclusively, its most northern part Somaliland) and Southern Arabia.

bio: Aqil bin al-Bukayr (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Aqil ibn al-Bukayr ibn Abd Yalil of the Banu Layth, a branch of Kinana, was an early Companion of the Prophet. His father al-Bukayr was an ally of Nufayl ibn Abd al-Uzza, grandfather of Umar ibn al-Khattab, so Aqil and his brothers were counted as allies of the Banu Adi. Ibn Sa'd says his name had been Ghafil and that the Prophet renamed him Aqil.

He was among the early converts in Mecca; one account says he was the first to accept Islam in the house of al-Arqam. His brothers Amir, Iyas and Khalid became Muslim with him and pledged allegiance there. The brothers emigrated to Medina with their families and stayed with Rifa'a ibn Abd al-Mundhir. The Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Mubashshir ibn Abd al-Mundhir; some accounts name al-Mujadhdhar ibn Ziyad instead.

All four brothers fought at Badr. Aqil was killed there, aged about 34, as was Mubashshir ibn Abd al-Mundhir. The accounts name Malik ibn Zuhayr al-Jushami as his killer.

bio: Ar-Rabab bint al-Bara' bin Ma'rur (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Ar-Rabab bint al-Bara' bin Ma'rur was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As the daughter of al-Bara' bin Ma'rur, she came from a prominent family among the Khazraj tribe, one of the two main Arab tribes of Medina. Her father was recognized as a leader who played a significant role in the early acceptance of Islam in Medina, which positioned her within an influential household during the formative years of the Muslim community.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's lifetime, Ar-Rabab would have witnessed the establishment and growth of the first Islamic state. The Ansar, including her family, were instrumental in providing the Muslim community with a secure base from which Islam could spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her presence among the companions places her within the generation that directly experienced the Prophet's teachings and guidance.

As a Sahabiyya, she holds a distinguished position in Islamic tradition. The companions of the Prophet are revered in Islamic history for their direct contact with Muhammad and their role in preserving and transmitting his teachings to subsequent generations. Female companions, in particular, are recognized for their contributions to early Islamic society, often serving as sources of religious knowledge and playing important roles in community life.

The limited historical records about individual female companions reflect the broader challenges of documenting women's lives in early Islamic history. However, her recognition as a companion indicates that she was known within the community and likely participated in the religious and social life of early Medina.

Ar-Rabab bint al-Bara' bin Ma'rur died around 635 CE, during the period of the Rashidun Caliphate that followed the Prophet's death in 632 CE. Her life spanned the crucial transition from the pre-Islamic period through the establishment of Islam as a major religious and political force in Arabia. As part of the founding generation of Muslims, she represents the Ansar's essential contribution to the survival and growth of the early Islamic community.

bio: Ar-Rabab bint an-Nu'man (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Al-Rabab bint al-Nu'man ibn Imru' al-Qays ibn Zayd ibn Abd al-Ashhal was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the Banu Abd al-Ashhal, and the paternal aunt of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Mu'adha bint Anas ibn Qays of the Banu Hudayla, a branch of the Banu al-Najjar.

She married first Zurara ibn Amr ibn Adi of the Banu Zafar, and bore him Mu'adh ibn Zurara. She later married Ma'rur ibn Sakhr ibn Khansa', and bore him al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, one of the twelve leaders (nuqaba') of the Ansar. Ibn Sa'd notes that al-Bara' died before the Prophet's emigration to Medina and that the Prophet prayed at his grave.

Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam and gave her pledge of allegiance (bay'a) to the Prophet; Ibn al-Athir also lists her among those who gave the pledge. No dates are recorded for her.

bio: ar-Rubbayi' bint Mu'awwidh bin 'Afra' (b. c. 600 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Ar-Rubbayi' bint Mu'awwidh bin 'Afra' was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early 7th century CE. Born around 600 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the Medinan Muslims who supported the Prophet and the early Muslim community after the migration from Mecca.

She is recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant oath of allegiance taken by Muhammad's followers under a tree at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge is commemorated in the Quran (48:18), which speaks of God's pleasure with those who pledged their allegiance. The event occurred during negotiations with the Meccan tribes and represented a crucial moment of unity and commitment among the early Muslim community.

As a sahabiyya, or female companion, ar-Rubbayi' was among the women who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the foundational period of Islam. Her inclusion in historical records reflects the active participation of women in the early Muslim community, both in religious and social contexts.

Her family connections place her within the Khazraj tribe of Medina, one of the two main Arab tribes that constituted the Ansar. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the Muslim community in Medina and supporting the Prophet's mission after the Hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

Ar-Rubbayi' lived through the formative decades of Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim state, the major battles that secured the community's survival, and the completion of the Quranic revelation. Her presence at Hudaybiyyah demonstrates her commitment to the Muslim cause during a period of significant political and military tension.

She died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the second Caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab. Her life spanned the prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about her individual contributions are limited in historical sources, her recognition as a companion and participant in the Pledge of Ridwan marks her as one of the foundational figures of the early Muslim community, representing the important role that women played in supporting and sustaining the nascent Islamic movement.

bio: Arfakhshadh ibn Sām (legendary–legendary) was a founding figure, based in Mesopotamia. Known as Ancestor of Prophet Muhammad. The sources record 2 teachers.
bio_full:
Arfakhshadh ibn Sam is a figure mentioned in Islamic genealogical traditions as an ancient ancestor in the prophetic lineage. According to Islamic historical sources, he lived in Mesopotamia during the legendary period corresponding to approximately 2200-1700 BCE, placing him in the post-Noahic era of biblical and Islamic chronology.

In Islamic tradition, Arfakhshadh is identified as a descendant of Sam (Shem), one of the sons of Prophet Nuh (Noah). His significance lies primarily in his position within the genealogical chain that Islamic historians trace from the early post-flood generations down to Prophet Muhammad. This genealogical framework forms part of the broader Islamic understanding of prophetic heritage and the continuity of monotheistic tradition through specific family lines.

The historical sources indicate that Arfakhshadh had contact with two teachers, though the specific details of his education or the nature of these relationships are not extensively documented in the available records. This suggests he was part of a learned tradition, consistent with Islamic accounts of knowledge transmission through the generations of righteous ancestors.

Mesopotamia, his reported base of activity, was during this period one of the world's earliest centers of civilization, home to developing urban centers and sophisticated cultural traditions. The region's significance as a crossroads of ancient Near Eastern civilizations makes it a fitting location for figures who occupy important positions in Islamic genealogical memory.

Arfakhshadh's importance to Islamic history is primarily genealogical rather than based on specific recorded deeds or teachings. He represents a link in the chain of ancestry that connects the immediate post-Noahic period to later prophetic figures, ultimately leading to Prophet Muhammad. This genealogical significance reflects the Islamic emphasis on the continuity of monotheistic faith and righteous lineage throughout history.

While the specific historical details of Arfakhshadh's life remain limited in the sources, his inclusion in Islamic genealogical traditions demonstrates the community's interest in tracing prophetic heritage back to the earliest generations after the flood, establishing connections between Islamic sacred history and the broader narrative of human civilization's renewal in the ancient Near East.

bio: Arwā bint ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was an aunt of Muhammad. She died in the year 15 AH during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab.
bio_full:
Arwa bint Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim was a paternal aunt of the Prophet Muhammad, from the Hashim clan of Quraysh. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Fatima bint Amr of the Makhzum clan; another account gives Safiyya bint Jundub. Before Islam she married Umayr ibn Wahb and bore him a son, Tulayb. Her second marriage is reported differently: Ibn Sa'd names Artat ibn Shurahbil, father of her daughter Fatima, while Ibn Abd al-Barr names Kalada ibn Abd Manaf.

Scholars differed over whether she accepted Islam. Ibn Ishaq held that Safiyya was the only one of the Prophet's aunts to do so, but Ibn Sa'd states that Arwa became Muslim in Mecca, and al-Uqayli counted her among the Companions. According to al-Waqidi, Tulayb accepted Islam at the house of al-Arqam and urged her to follow; she first said she would wait to see what her sisters did, then declared her faith. She went on to support the Prophet with her words and praised her son for defending him. When Tulayb struck Abu Jahl for harming the Prophet, Abu Lahab rebuked her, and she told him to stand by his nephew; he refused.

Ibn Sa'd reports that she emigrated to Medina. She composed poetry, including an elegy for her father and elegies for the Prophet. She died in Medina during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab and, according to one account, was buried in al-Baqi'. Al-Zirikli gives her death as 16 AH; other accounts give 15 AH.

bio: Arwā bint al-Ḥārith was an eloquent and rhetorically skilled sahabiya and the cousin of Muhammad and Ali. She was the daughter of Al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Ghaziyya bint Qays. She was married to Abu Wida'a (al-Harith) ibn Sabarah ibn Sa'id ibn Sa'd ibn Sahm al-Sahmi al-Qurayshi, and they had ten children. These ten children were: Wida'a, Abd Allah, al-Saib, al-Muttalib, Sufyan, Hakim, Abu Sufyan (Yazid), al-Rabi', Umm Kulthum (Rabi'a), Umm Jamil (Zaynab), and Umm Hakim (Fatima).

bio: Arwa bint al-Muqawwim (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca.
bio_full: Arwa bint al-Muqawwim was the daughter of al-Muqawwim ibn Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, a paternal uncle of the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd records her in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra and names her mother as Qulaba bint Amr ibn Ju'ana, whose lineage goes back to Sahm. Arwa married Abu Masruh, al-Harith ibn Ya'mar, of the Sa'd ibn Bakr branch of Hawazin, who was an ally of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib. She bore him a son, Abd Allah ibn Abi Masruh. Ibn Sa'd's short entry gives no details of her conversion, her later life or the date of her death.

bio: Arwa bint Kuraiz bin Rabi'a (c. 606 CE–654 CE, Medinah) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Arwa bint Kuraiz bin Rabi'a was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early decades of Islam. Born around 606 CE, she witnessed the emergence and establishment of the Islamic community during one of the most transformative periods in Arabian history.

As a contemporary of the Prophet Muhammad, Arwa belonged to the first generation of Muslims who directly encountered the foundational teachings of Islam. Her status as a sahabiyya places her among the respected group of individuals who lived during the Prophet's lifetime and had personal interaction with him, a distinction that holds particular significance in Islamic tradition.

Arwa is primarily recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial component of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice. Female hadith narrators played an essential role in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, particularly regarding matters that involved women's religious and social practices where male narrators might have had limited access or knowledge.

The preservation and transmission of hadith required individuals of recognized integrity, memory, and religious knowledge. That Arwa is specifically noted for this role indicates she possessed these qualities and was trusted by her community to accurately convey prophetic traditions. Female companions like Arwa contributed significantly to the early Islamic scholarly tradition, ensuring that various aspects of religious guidance were preserved for future generations.

Her life spanned approximately 48 years, during which she would have witnessed the Prophet's mission in Mecca, the migration to Medina, the establishment of the first Islamic state, and the early expansion of Islam under the first caliphs. Living until 654 CE, she experienced the reigns of the first three caliphs after the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

While specific details about her individual contributions or the particular hadith she narrated may not be extensively documented in widely available sources, her inclusion among recognized female hadith narrators demonstrates her participation in the foundational scholarship of Islam. The early Muslim community's recognition of her authority to transmit religious knowledge reflects the important role that women played in preserving Islamic teachings during this formative period.

Arwa bint Kuraiz bin Rabi'a represents the broader group of female companions whose contributions to early Islamic scholarship helped ensure the accurate transmission of religious knowledge across generations.

bio: Arwa bint Malik bin Khansa' (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Arwa bint Malik ibn Khansa' ibn Sinan ibn Ubayd was a woman of the Banu Salima clan of Medina. Ibn Sa'd records her in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra as the full sister of al-Tufayl ibn Malik, who is noted there as having been present at Badr. Their mother was Asma' bint al-Qayn ibn Ka'b, also of Banu Salima. Arwa married Amr ibn Adi ibn Sinan, and Ibn Sa'd names Khalid and Umm Mani' as their children. According to Ibn Sa'd, she accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. No date of death is recorded in this entry.

bio: As'ad bin Yazid bin al-Fakih (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
As'ad bin Yazid bin al-Fakih was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the early 7th century CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community in Medina following the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As'ad is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr" (Ashab Badr). This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The approximately 300 Muslims who fought at Badr are honored in Islamic tradition for their role in this pivotal moment that helped secure the survival of the early Muslim state.

As a resident of Medina, As'ad would have been part of the community that supported the Prophet during the crucial Medinan period of his mission. During these years, the basic structures of Islamic governance, law, and society were established, and the companions who lived through this period served as important witnesses to the Prophet's teachings and practices.

The companions of the Prophet hold a special status in Islamic historical consciousness as the first generation of Muslims who directly received Islamic teachings and witnessed the Prophet's example firsthand. Their accounts and testimonies became foundational sources for understanding Islamic law, theology, and practice in subsequent generations.

As'ad bin Yazid bin al-Fakih died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first caliph. His death came during a period of rapid Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula, though the specific circumstances of his death are not clearly documented in available historical sources.

While detailed biographical information about As'ad bin Yazid bin al-Fakih remains limited in the historical record, his recognition as a Companion of Badr places him among those early Muslims whose presence during the formative battles and events of early Islam contributed to the establishment and preservation of the Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Asʿad ibn Zurāra, often known by his kunya Abū Umāma, was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and the first chief in Medina to become a Muslim.
bio_full:
As'ad ibn Zurara, known by his kunya Abu Umama, was born around 589 CE in Medina and died in 623 CE. He belonged to the Khazraj tribe, one of the two major Arab tribes that inhabited Yathrib, the city that would later be renamed Medina.

As'ad holds the distinction of being the first chief or leader in Medina to embrace Islam. His conversion occurred during one of the early meetings between representatives from Medina and the Prophet Muhammad, which took place during the pilgrimage season in Mecca. These encounters were part of the preliminary discussions that would eventually lead to the historic migration of Muslims from Mecca to Medina.

Following his conversion, As'ad played a crucial role in spreading Islam among his people in Medina. He worked actively to convince members of both the Khazraj and Aws tribes to accept the new faith, helping to prepare the ground for what would become the Hijra, the migration of the Muslim community from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As'ad was among the participants in the pledges of Aqaba, the secret meetings between the Prophet Muhammad and representatives from Medina that established the terms for Muslim migration to their city. These agreements were fundamental in creating the alliance that would provide Muslims with a safe haven from persecution in Mecca.

His significance extends beyond his early conversion. As a tribal leader who embraced Islam, As'ad helped bridge the gap between the established social structures of Medina and the new Muslim community. His influence among the Khazraj was instrumental in creating the political and social conditions necessary for the successful establishment of the first Muslim state in Medina.

As'ad ibn Zurara died in 623 CE, relatively early in the Medina period of Islamic history. Despite his short time as a Muslim, his role as the first Medinan chief to accept Islam and his efforts in preparing his community for the arrival of the Muslim migrants from Mecca secured his place as an important figure among the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad. His legacy represents the critical local leadership that made the transformation of Medina into the center of early Islamic civilization possible.

bio: as-Sa'bah bint al-Hadrami (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
as-Sa'bah bint al-Hadrami was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 594 CE, she was based in Mecca during the time when the Islamic community was first establishing itself in the Arabian Peninsula.

As indicated by her name "bint al-Hadrami," she was the daughter of someone from Hadramaut, a region in what is now southern Yemen known for its ancient trade routes and tribal confederations. This suggests possible connections to the broader Arabian tribal networks that were significant in early Islamic society.

as-Sa'bah is recognized primarily for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial source of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. As a female narrator, she was part of the important tradition of women companions who preserved and transmitted the Prophet's teachings to subsequent generations. The science of hadith transmission relied heavily on trusted narrators who had direct contact with the Prophet, making the contributions of companions like as-Sa'bah fundamental to the preservation of Islamic teachings.

Her significance lies in her participation in the early Muslim community during its most crucial developmental phase and her role in the chain of transmission that helped preserve prophetic traditions. Female companions who served as hadith narrators were essential figures in Islamic scholarship, as they often had access to aspects of the Prophet's life and teachings that male companions might not have witnessed, particularly regarding family and domestic matters.

as-Sa'bah died in 634 CE, just two years after the Prophet's death in 632 CE, during the early period of the first Caliph Abu Bakr's rule. This places her death during the Ridda Wars period, when the early Muslim community was consolidating control over the Arabian Peninsula. Her relatively short life span of approximately forty years was typical for the era, and her contribution to hadith transmission represents the vital role that the earliest Muslim women played in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings during the religion's foundational period.

full: al-Sāʾib ibn Yazīd ibn Saʿīd ibn Thumāma al-Kindī al-Azdī al-Madanī
primaryTitle: The Child Who Made Hajj with the Prophet
titles: al-Sāʾib · Min Ṣighār al-Ṣaḥāba (Among the Young Companions)
source: al-Bukhāri — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhāri · Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr — al-Istīʿāb
bio: Al-Sa'ib bin Yazid Al-Hudhali. It was said that Al-Kindi and others were among the young companions. His father performed Hajj with the Prophet when he was seven years old, and he had a share of companionship and narration.
bio_full:
Al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid ibn Sa'id ibn Thumama, known by the kunya Abu Yazid and as Ibn Ukht Namir (son of Namir's sister), was a young Companion of the Prophet Muhammad. He is usually called al-Kindi: he was of Kinda and an ally (halif) of Quraysh; other sources call him al-Hudhali or al-Azdi. One report in Ibn Asakir's history of Damascus, as abridged by Ibn Manzur, places his birth in 3 AH. Al-Dhahabi states that both he and his father were Companions.

As a small boy he was brought by his aunt to the Prophet, who wiped his head and prayed for blessing for him; he drank from the water of the Prophet's ablution and saw the seal of prophethood between his shoulders. He was taken on Hajj with the Prophet at the age of seven, and he recalled going out with other boys to Thaniyyat al-Wada' to meet the Prophet returning from Tabuk. His freed slave Ata' said that the part of his hair the Prophet had touched stayed black while the rest turned white.

Umar ibn al-Khattab gave him minor duties, and he worked with Abd Allah ibn Utba ibn Mas'ud collecting tithes at the market of Medina. He narrated from the Prophet, Umar, Uthman, Talha, Sa'd and others, and al-Zuhri, Yahya al-Ansari and his son Abd Allah were among those who narrated from him. Al-Bukhari included his reports in his Sahih.

Ibn Hibban and al-Dhahabi give his death as 91 AH, Ibn Hibban placing it in Medina, and Abu Mushir gives his age as 88. Ibn Manzur's abridgement records other reports ranging from 80 to 97 AH.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid (al-Baji, Ibn Hibban's Mashahir, al-Baghawi's Mu'jam al-Sahaba, Ibn Manzur's Mukhtasar Tarikh Dimashq, al-Dhahabi's Siyar)

dod_s: c. 650 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
bio: Ash-Shamus bint 'Amr bin Haram (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Ash-Shamus bint 'Amr bin Haram was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who provided crucial support to the early Muslim community when the Prophet and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Ash-Shamus would have been among those who welcomed the Muslim emigrants and helped establish the foundational Muslim community in the city. The Ansar played a vital role in the early development of Islam, offering shelter, resources, and protection to the nascent Muslim community during a critical period when they faced persecution and challenges in Mecca.

Her lineage, indicated by her name "bint 'Amr bin Haram" (daughter of 'Amr son of Haram), suggests she came from an established Medinan family. During this period, women in the early Muslim community often played significant roles in supporting the religious and social aspects of the developing Islamic society, though specific details of individual contributions are not always well-documented in historical sources.

The designation of Sahabiyya indicates that she had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. This status held particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions were considered the first generation of Muslims who learned directly from the Prophet and helped preserve and transmit Islamic teachings.

Ash-Shamus lived during the formative decades of Islam, witnessing the religion's establishment and early expansion. Her lifetime, spanning approximately four decades until around 635 CE, covered the entire Medinan period of the Prophet's mission, his death in 632 CE, and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under the first caliph, Abu Bakr.

While specific details of her individual contributions to early Islamic history may not be extensively recorded, her recognition as a companion places her among the foundational generation of Muslims who supported the establishment and growth of the Islamic community in Medina. The Ansari companions collectively represent an essential element in Islamic history, demonstrating the inclusive nature of the early Muslim community that brought together people from different tribal and regional backgrounds under the banner of the new faith.

full: Ashraf 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Haqq al-Thanawi al-Chishti al-Imdadi
primaryTitle: Hakim al-Ummat — Physician of the Muslim Community
titles: Hakim al-Ummat (Physician of the Community) · Mujaddid of the 14th century AH · Deobandi-Chishti synthesis
bio: Ashraf 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Haqq al-Thanawi al-Chishti al-Imdadi (1863–1943) was a scholar of the Chishti tradition, based in Thana Bhawan. Known as Hakim al-Ummat — Physician of the Muslim Community.
bio_full:
Ashraf Ali Thanwi (often referred as Hakimul Ummat and Mujaddidul Millat; 19 August 1863 – 20 July 1943) was an Indian Sunni Muslim scholar, jurist, thinker, reformist and a revivor of classical Sufism in the Indian subcontinent during the British Raj. He was a central figure of Islamic spiritual, intellectual and religious life in South Asia and continues to be highly influential today. He wrote over a thousand works including Bayan Ul Quran and Bahishti Zewar. He was also one of the chief proponents of the Pakistan Movement. 
He graduated from Darul Uloom Deoband in 1883 and moved to Kanpur, then Thana Bhawan to direct the Khanqah-i-Imdadiyah, where he resided until his death. His training in Quran, hadith, fiqh studies and Sufism qualified him to become a leading Sunni authority among the scholars of Deoband. His teaching mixes Sunni orthodoxy, Islamic elements of belief and the patriarchal structure of the society. He offered a sketch of a Muslim community that is collective, patriarchal, hierarchical and compassion-based.

Views and ideology

Thanwi was a strong supporter of the Muslim League. He maintained correspondence with the leadership of All India Muslim League (AIML), including Muhammad Ali Jinnah. He also sent groups of Muslim scholars to give religious advice and reminders to Jinnah. His disciples Zafar Ahmad Usmani and Shabbir Ahmad Usmani were key players in religious support for the creation of Pakistan. During the 1940s, many Deobandi Ulama supported the Congress but Thanwi and some other leading Deobandi scholars including Muhammad Shafi and Shabbir Ahmad Usmani were in favour of the Muslim League. Thanwi resigned from Darul Uloom Deoband's management committee due to its pro-Congress stance. His support and the support of his disciples for Pakistan Movement were greatly appreciated by AIML.

Teaching and Education
After completing his education, with the permission of his father and teachers, he went to Kanpur and began teaching at Madrasa Faiz-e-Aam. For fourteen years, he continued to spread knowledge (faiz) there. In 1315 AH, he left Kanpur and returned to his ancestral home in Thana Bhawan. There, he revived the Khanqah of Haji Imdadullah Muhajir Makki and established an educational institution named Madrasa Ashrafiya, where he devoted himself until the end of his life to teaching, spiritual purification (tazkiya-e-nufoos), and social reform.
Upon his return, Haji Imdadullah Muhajir Makki sent him a letter, which stated: "It is better that you have moved to Thana Bhawan. I hope that many people will benefit from you, both outwardly and inwardly. You will restore our madrasa and mosque anew. I pray for you at all times."

Influence and legacy
He produced around 1000 trainees, to whom he permitted for Bay'ah and those spread their influences of Thanwi. Among them are: Sulaiman Nadvi, Shabbir Ahmad Usmani, Zafar Ahmad Usmani, Abdul Hai Arifi, Athar Ali Bengali, Shah Abdul Wahhab, Abdul Majid Daryabadi, Aziz al-Hasan Ghouri, Abrarul Haq Haqqi, Muhammadullah Hafezzi, Khair Muhammad Jalandhari, Masihullah Khan, Muhammad Shafi, Murtaza Hasan Chandpuri, Habibullah Qurayshi, Muhammad Tayyib Qasmi.

bio: Asim bin 'Adiy bin al-Jadd (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Asim bin 'Adiy bin al-Jadd was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late sixth and early seventh centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslim community based in Medina and died in 634 CE, shortly after the Prophet's death.

Asim is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, meaning he participated in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The participants in this battle are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as they were among the earliest supporters of the Prophet Muhammad during a critical period when the survival of the nascent Muslim community was uncertain.

As a Sahaba, or Companion of the Prophet, Asim belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. The Companions play a crucial role in Islamic historical and religious understanding, as they were the primary sources for transmitting the Prophet's sayings, actions, and teachings to subsequent generations.

Asim's connection to hadith sciences reflects the important role that many Companions played in preserving and transmitting the oral traditions that would later become foundational texts in Islamic jurisprudence and theology. The Companions' testimonies and recollections formed the basis for much of what Muslims know about the Prophet's life and teachings.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's time meant that Asim witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic community and the development of early Islamic governance and social structures. Medina served as the political and spiritual center of the early Muslim state, making its residents central figures in the historical narrative of Islam's origins.

The brief span of Asim's life corresponds with one of the most transformative periods in Arabian and world history, as Islam emerged from a local religious movement to a major force that would soon expand beyond the Arabian Peninsula. His death in 634 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death, placing him among those who witnessed the transition from the prophetic period to the era of the early caliphs.

bio: Asim bin Qays (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Asim ibn Qays ibn Thabit was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar, of the Banu Tha'laba ibn Amr ibn Awf, a branch of the Aws of Medina. Ibn al-Athir gives his lineage as Asim ibn Qays ibn Thabit ibn al-Nu'man ibn Umayya ibn Imru' al-Qays ibn Tha'laba, while Ibn Sa'd gives Asim ibn Qays ibn Thabit ibn Kulfa ibn Tha'laba. Early historians of the campaigns, including Musa ibn Uqba and Muhammad ibn Ishaq, list him among those who fought at Badr, and he also fought at Uhud. Ibn Sa'd notes that he left no descendants. The sources give no date of death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Asim ibn Qays (Ibn al-Athir, Usd al-Ghaba; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Abu Nu'aym, Ma'rifat al-Sahaba)
Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya — Asim ibn Qays

famous: Asim bin Thabit ibn Abi al-Aflah
full: Asim bin Thabit ibn Abi al-Aflah
bio: Asim bin Thabit ibn Abi al-Aflah (c. 594–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Asim ibn Thabit ibn Abi al-Aqlah, whose grandfather Abu al-Aqlah was named Qays ibn Isma, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar, of the Amr ibn Awf branch of the Aws in Medina. His kunya was Abu Sulayman. The Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Abd Allah ibn Jahsh.

He fought at Badr and at Uhud. Ibn Sa'd counts him among the noted archers and reports that at Uhud he stood firm with the Prophet when others fled. There he killed al-Harith and Musafi', sons of Talha ibn Abi Talha, and their mother Sulafa vowed to drink wine from his skull and offered a hundred camels for his head.

When men of Banu Lihyan of Hudhayl asked the Prophet for teachers, Asim was sent at the head of a small party; Abu Nu'aym's narration describes ten men sent as scouts under his command. At al-Raji' they were surrounded. Asim refused the polytheists' offer of surrender, saying he had vowed never to accept a polytheist's protection, and fought with arrows, spear and sword until he was killed. Ibn Sa'd dates this to Safar, thirty-six months after the Hijra (625 CE).

His enemies wanted his head, but a swarm of bees (dabr) shielded his body; a night flood later carried it away and it was never found. Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that the Prophet supplicated for a month against Ri'l, Dhakwan and Banu Lihyan. The poet al-Ahwas was among his descendants, through his son Muhammad.

bio_sources.title: Wikipedia — Asim ibn Thabit
Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Asim ibn Thabit (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Isti'ab; Abu Nu'aym, Ma'rifat al-Sahaba)
Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Asim ibn Thabit ibn al-Aqlah (al-Isti'ab; Ibn Hibban)

bio: Asim/'Amir bin al-'Ukayr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Asim bin al-'Ukayr, also known as 'Amir bin al-'Ukayr, was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE. He lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula and was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Asim bin al-'Ukayr is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces and holds profound significance in Islamic history. The Muslims, though significantly outnumbered, achieved a decisive victory that strengthened their position and validated their cause in the eyes of many Arabian tribes.

The Battle of Badr participants, known as the Badr veterans or "Ahl Badr," hold a special status in Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal engagement. Their participation demonstrated their commitment to the early Muslim community during a period of considerable uncertainty and danger. The battle's outcome marked a turning point in the relationship between the nascent Muslim state in Medina and the established powers in Mecca.

As a Sahabi, Asim bin al-'Ukayr was part of the generation that witnessed the revelation of the Quran and directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad. The companions collectively played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, participating in the early expansion of Islam, and establishing the foundations of Islamic governance and society.

Asim bin al-'Ukayr died in 634 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph. His death occurred during a time when the Muslim community was consolidating its control over the Arabian Peninsula and beginning the conquests that would eventually spread Islam across vast territories.

While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented, his status as a companion places him among the foundational generation of Muslims whose collective efforts established Islam as both a religious and political force in seventh-century Arabia.

bio: Asma bin al-Husain bin Wabara (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Asma bin al-Husain bin Wabara was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of the Islamic community.

Asma is historically recognized as one of the Sahaba, the Arabic term for the companions of Prophet Muhammad who met him, believed in his message, and died as Muslims. This designation places him among a select group of individuals who had direct contact with the Prophet and were part of the first generation of Muslims.

He is particularly known for his participation in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE near the town of Badr in the Hejaz region of present-day Saudi Arabia. This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the early Muslim community against the Meccan tribes. The Muslims, despite being significantly outnumbered, achieved a decisive victory that helped establish the political and military credibility of the nascent Islamic state in Medina.

Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are collectively known as the "Badr Companions" and hold a special status in Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment. The battle is considered a turning point that helped secure the survival and growth of the early Muslim community.

Based in Medina, Asma would have been part of the community that developed around the Prophet after the Hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. Medina served as the center of the early Islamic state and the base from which the Muslim community expanded throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Asma bin al-Husain bin Wabara died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph after the Prophet's death. His death occurred during a period of rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula, as the Muslim armies began their conquests in Iraq, Syria, and other neighboring regions.

As one of the Badr Companions, Asma represents the generation of early Muslims whose dedication and sacrifice during Islam's most vulnerable period helped ensure the religion's survival and eventual spread across vast territories.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Asma bin Ri'ab bin Hunayf (c. 600–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Asma bin Ri'ab bin Hunayf was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he was present during the crucial decades when the Islamic community was establishing itself, first in Mecca and later in Medina.

Asma is historically significant as one of the companions who participated in the Pledge of Ridwan (Bay'at al-Ridwan), also known as the Pledge of the Tree, which took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge is mentioned in the Quran in verse 48:18, which refers to God's pleasure with those believers who pledged their allegiance under the tree. The historical context of this pledge was a tense moment when the Muslim community, having traveled from Medina to perform pilgrimage in Mecca, found themselves in a standoff with the Meccan tribes. The companions who participated in this pledge demonstrated their loyalty and commitment to the Prophet Muhammad during this critical diplomatic moment.

As a Sahabi, Asma was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the revelation and early development of Islamic teachings. The Sahaba hold a special position in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of the Prophet's sayings, actions, and approvals, which form the basis of the Sunnah literature that guides Muslim practice alongside the Quran.

Asma's life spanned the period from before the Islamic revelation through the early expansion of the Muslim community. He lived through the migration (Hijra) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, the establishment of the first Islamic state, and the various treaties and conflicts that shaped the early Muslim community's relationship with surrounding tribes and communities.

He died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This places his death during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, when the Muslim community was consolidating its position in the Arabian Peninsula and beginning the expansion that would eventually spread Islamic civilization across vast regions of the known world.

full: Asmāʾ bint Abi Bakr ibn Abi Quḥāfa al-Qurashiyya al-Taymiyya
primaryTitle: Dhāt al-Niṭāqayn — She of the Two Belts
dod_s: 692 CE (73 AH; Usd al-Ghabah — lived ~100 lunar years)
titles: Dhāt al-Niṭāqayn (She of the Two Belts) · Last of the Muhājirūn · Mother of Caliph ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · al-Dhahabī — Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ · Ibn Kathīr — al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
bio: Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr was a follower and Sahabiyya of prophet Muhammad and the elder half-sister of his wife Aisha. Her nickname Dhat an-Nitaqayn was given to her by Muhammad during the migration to Medina. She is regarded as one of the most prominent Islamic figures, as she helped Muhammad during the Hijrah from Mecca to Medina.
bio_full:
Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr (Arabic: أسماء بنت أبي بكر; c. 594/595 – 692/693 CE) was a follower and Sahabiyya of prophet Muhammad and the elder half-sister of his wife Aisha. Her nickname Dhat an-Nitaqayn (meaning she with the two belts) was given to her by Muhammad during the migration to Medina. She is regarded as one of the most prominent Islamic figures, as she helped Muhammad during the Hijrah from Mecca to Medina.

Family
She was Abu Bakr's daughter. Her mother was Qutaylah bint Abd al-Uzza, and she was the full sister of Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr. Her half-sisters were Aisha and Umm Kulthum bint Abi Bakr, and her half-brothers were Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr and Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. She also had a stepmother from the Kinana tribe, Umm Ruman bint Amir, and a stepbrother, al-Tufayl ibn al-Harith al-Azdi. The historians Ibn Kathir and Ibn Asakir cite a tradition that Asma was ten years older than Aisha; but according to Al-Dhahabi, the age difference was thirteen to nineteen  years.

Biography

Early life: 603/604–610
Asma's parents were divorced before Muhammad started preaching the message of Islam. Because of this she remained at her father's house.

Islam in Mecca: 610–622
Asma was one of the first to accept Islam, being listed fifteenth on Ibn Ishaq's list of those who accepted Islam at the invitation of Abu Bakr.
She was married to Zubayr ibn al-Awwam shortly before the Hijra. She joined him in Medina a few months later.
When Muhammad and Abu Bakr sought refuge in Jabal Thawr outside Mecca on their migration to Medina in 622, Asma used to carry food to them under cover of dark. When the two men left the cave, Asma tied the goods with the two belts of her cover, and for this ingenuity she received from Muhammad the title Dhat an-Nitaqayn, meaning "She of the Two Belts".
After it was discovered that Muhammad and Abu Bakr had escaped, Abu Jahl, one of the biggest enemies of Islam, marched to Asma's house, demanding her to reveal the location of her father and the Prophet. Asma, then heavily pregnant, refused to respond. Out of rage, Abu Jahl violently slapped her so hard that the earring she was wearing fell off. Despite this, she did not stagger and Abu Jahl left in anger.

Medina: 623 onwards
Asma found her new neighbours to be "sincere women". She was a poor baker, and they used to make bread for her. She and Al-Zubayr arrived in Medina with "neither property nor slave nor any possession in the earth other than his horse." Asma used to feed the horse, taking it out to graze and grinding date-stones for it. Muhammad gave Al-Zubayr (a land with) some date-palms in Medina, and Asma used to carry date-stones on her head from the garden to their home, a journey of about two miles. One day, while carrying the date-stones on her head she passed Muhammad (along with some of his companions), who offered her a lift home on his camel (by directing his camel to kneel down and indicating to her to ride behind him, but out of shyness to travel with the men, and fearing her husband's jealousy, she hesitated. Noticing that she felt shy, he moved on. When she narrated about running into the Prophet to her husband, he told her, however, that it shamed him more that she had been carrying such a heavy load (and she was seen by the Prophet in such a state) than her riding with him. When her father, Abu Bakr, eventually sent her a servant to look after the horse, Asma said that "it was as if he had set me free". 
Her mother Qutaylah came to visit her in Medina, bringing gifts of dates, ghee, and mimosa leaves. Asma would not admit her to the house or accept the gifts until she had sent her sister Aisha to consult with Muhammad. Muhammad advised that it was correct for Asma to show hospitality to her mother”.
Asma and Al-Zubayr had eight children:

Abd Allah
al-Mundhir.
Asim.
al-Muhajir.
Khadija.
Umm al-Hasan.
A’isha.
Urwah, a major transmitter of hadith.
Asma at one point had marital issues with Zubayr, as he was rigid and "the most jealous of people". She complained to her father, who advised her: "My daughter, be patient. When a woman has a righteous husband and he dies and she does not remarry after him, they will be reunited in the Garden [Paradise]". Another of al-Zubayr's wives, Umm Kulthum bint Uqba, also complained of his "harshness" and pestered him into divorcing her after only a few months.
Al-Zubayr eventually divorced Asma "and took Urwa, who was young at that time".

The Battle of Yarmouk
The Battle of the Yarmuk in 636 is regarded as one of the most decisive battles in military history. The Muslims were hugely outnumbered by the Byzantines but, with the help of the women and the young boys amongst them, they drove the Byzantine Empire out of Syria.
Women like Hind bint Utbah and Asma bint Abi Bakr were instrumental in the Battle of the Yarmuk. The earliest histories pay great tribute to Asmā's bravery there. Al-Waqidi wrote that the Quraysh women fought harder than the men. Every time the men ran away, the women fought, fearing that if they lost, the Byzantines would enslave them.

Asma's opposition to Yazid
Asma's son, Abdallah, and his cousin, Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, were both grandsons of Abu Bakr and nephews of Aisha. When Husayn ibn Ali was martyred in Karbala, Abdallah, who had been Husayn's friend, collected the people of Mecca and rose up against Yazid. When he heard about this, Yazid had a silver chain made and sent to Mecca with the intention of having al-Walid ibn Utbah arrest Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr with it. In Mecca and Medina Hussein's family had a strong support base, and the people were willing to stand up for them. Hussein's remaining family moved back to Madina. Eventually Abdullah consolidated his power by sending a governor to Kufa. Soon Abdullah established his power in Iraq, southern Arabia, the greater part of Syria and parts of Egypt.
Yazid tried to end Abdallah's rebellion by invading the Hejaz, and he took Medina after the Battle of al-Harrah followed by the siege of Mecca. His sudden death ended the campaign and threw the Umayyads into disarray, with civil war eventually breaking out. After the Umayyad civil war ended, Abdullah lost Egypt and whatever he had of Syria to Marwan I. This, coupled with the Kharijite rebellions in Iraq, reduced his domain to only the Hejaz.
Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr was finally defeated by Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, who sent Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf. Abdallah asked his mother what he should do, then left to take on Hajjaj. Abdullah's army was defeated and Abdallah died on the battlefield in 692 CE. The defeat of Abdallah ibn al-Zubayr re-established Umayyad control over the Empire.
A few years later in 740 CE the people of Kufa called Zayd ibn Ali, the grandson of Hussein, over to Kufa. Zaydis believe that in Zayd's last hour, he was also betrayed by the people of Kufa,."

692: Death
Asma died a few days after her son who was killed on Tuesday 17 Jumada al-Ula in 73 AH". Asma died when she was 100 years (lunar) old. 

Asma was 17th person who became Muslim and she was 10 years older than her sister, Aisha. She passed away ten days after death of her son while she was 100 years old and all of her teeth were healthy.
