full: Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays ibn Maʿad al-Khathʿamiyya
primaryTitle: Dhāt al-Hijratayn — Woman of Two Migrations
titles: Dhāt al-Hijratayn (Woman of Two Migrations) · al-Akhawāt al-Muʾmināt (The Believing Sisters — with Maymunah and Umm al-Faḍl)
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · al-Dhahabī — Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ · Ibn Ḥajar — al-Iṣāba
bio: Asma bint Umays Al-Khathamiyya is a companion who converted to Islam in the past along with her sister Salma bint Umays. Asmaa was the wife of Jaafar bin Abi Talib, then of Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq, then of Ali bin Abi Talib. She migrated to Abyssinia and then to Yathrib, and was nicknamed “the woman of the two migrations.”
bio_full:
Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays (Arabic: أَسْمَاء بِنْت عُمَيْس) was a female disciple (known in Arabic as Sahaba or Companions of the Prophet) of Muhammad, the prophet of Islam.
She is known for having married three famous companions of Muhammad, namely, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, Abu Bakr, and Ali.

Early life and family
Asma's birth year is unknown, however, being the firstborn of her mother's third marriage, narrows down her birth year to around 597 to 600 CE. She was born apparently in Mecca as the daughter of immigrants. Her father was Umays ibn Ma'ad from the Khath'am tribe, and her mother was Hind bint Awf from the Himyar tribe.
Her full siblings were Salma bint Umays, wife of Hamza ibn Abdul Muttalib, and Awn ibn Umais. Her maternal half-siblings included two of Muhammad's wives, Zaynab bint Khuzayma and Maymunah bint al-Harith, as well as Umm Faḍl, the wife of Abbas ibn Abdul Muttalib, Al-Sa'ib ibn al-Harith, Qatn ibn al-Harith, and the community treasurer Mahmiyah ibn Al-Jaz'.
Asma and her sister Salma both converted to Islam "after the Messenger of Allah had entered the house of al-Arqam", i.e., between late 614 and early 616 CE. She is notable for having been the wife of three of Muhammad's close companions.

Married life

Marriage to Jafar
Asma's first marriage was probably to Rabia ibn Riyab al-Hilali from Banu Hilal tribe in Hejaz, who either died before Islam or divorced her.
Shortly afterwards, she was married to Ja'far ibn Abi Talib from the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh tribe. In 616 she emigrated with him to Abyssinia, where she gave birth to their three sons, Abdullah, Muhammad and Awn. Asma disliked living in Abyssinia and she later referred to "fear" and "harm" that she had suffered there while "far away and banished," though she did not elaborate on the nature of these difficulties.
They returned to Medina in 628, at the time of the Muslim conquest of Khaybar.
Ja'far fought at the Battle of Mu'tah against the Ghassanids, who were aided by the Byzantines, in September 629 and, Ja'far along with Zayd ibn Haritha and Abdullah ibn Rawahah, was killed there.
Asma narrated how she heard the news of her husband's death. "The Prophet came to me. I had prepared forty mann of 'dip' [tanned forty skins] and kneaded the dough. I took my two sons and I washed their faces and put oil on them. The Messenger of God came to me and said, 'O Asma, where are the sons of Ja'far?' I brought them to him and he embraced them and smelt them, then his eyes welled up and he cried. I said, 'Why, Messenger of God, perhaps [you have news] about Ja'far.' He replied, 'Yes, he was killed today.' I stood up and screamed, and the women came to me. The Prophet began to say, 'O Asma, do not speak obscene words or beat your chest!'" Her son Abd Allah remembered: "He said, 'O Asma, will you not rejoice? Indeed, God most high has made two wings for Ja'far, that he may fly with them in Paradise!'" Then Muhammad told his daughter Fatimah, "Prepare food for the family of Ja'far, for they are preoccupied today."

Marriage to Abu Bakr
After Ja'far's death, Asma married Abu Bakr. She gave birth to his son Muhammad in 632 at al-Baydaa while on the way to the Farewell Pilgrimage. Abu Bakr planned to send Asma and their child back to Medina, but Muhammad told him to let her make the major ablution and then rededicate herself in offering the pilgrimage.
The dying Abu Bakr left instructions that Asma should wash his corpse and that she should not fast on that day. She only remembered this instruction towards sunset, when she called for water to drink so that she would not have technically disobeyed him. As it was a very cold day, it was agreed that she did not have to perform an ablution after washing the body.

Marriage to Ali
When Abu Bakr died, the new caliph Umar allotted Asma a pension of 1,000 dirhams. Soon afterwards, Ali ibn Abu Talib, the younger brother of Ja'far, married her and brought up Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr as his own son. Asma bore two more sons, Yahya and Awn to Ali.

Death and burial

There is no record about the exact date of her demise. However, 38/658-9 and after 60/679-80 were mentioned in some sources.

In an account, it is only mentioned that she was alive after the martyrdom of Imam Ali (a) (40/661). 

It is believed that Asma's qabr (Arabic: قَـبْـر, grave) is at the Maqbarah al-Bāb aṣ-Ṣaghīr (Arabic: مَـقْـبَـرَة الْـبَـاب الـصَّـغِـيْـر, Bab al-Saghir Cemetery) in Damascus, present-day Syria.

Legacy
Asma narrated ahadith from Muhammad. According to a report deemed authentic, she is considered one of the women of Paradise.

Historical controversy
The following historians state that Asma was present at Fatima's wedding ceremony in 1 AH:

The author of Kashf Al-Ghummah
Hadhrami in Rashfat al-Sadi, p. 10
Ahmad ibn Hanbal in al-Manaqib.
Nur al-Din al-Haythami in Majma al-Zawa'id
Nisaee in Khasaes, pg 31
Muhib Ad-Din Tabari in Dhakhaer al-Uqbi
They depend on the narrations of: Abu Abbas Khawarazmi from Husayn ibn Ali, Sayid Jalal al-Din Abu al-Hamid Ibn Fakhr al-Musawi, and Dulabi from Imam Baqir and his father. This is a historical problem that has not yet been solved despite the various attempts made by Majlisi in Bihar al-Anwar vol. 10.
One theory states that Asma Bint Umais had actually immigrated with her husband to Abyssinia, but repeatedly returned to Mecca and Medina. The distance between Jeddah and Abyssinia is limited to that of the width of the Red Sea, which is not very difficult for a journey.

full: Asmāʾ bint Yazīd ibn al-Sakan al-Anṣāriyya al-Awsiyya
primaryTitle: Khaṭībat al-Nisāʾ — Orator of the Women
titles: Khaṭībat al-Nisāʾ (Orator of the Women) · Safīrat al-Nisāʾ (Spokesperson of the Women)
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · al-Dhahabī — Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ · Ibn Ḥajar — al-Iṣāba
bio: Asmāʾ bint Yazīd ibn al-Sakan al-Anṣāriyya al-Awsiyya (approximate–approximate) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Damascus. Known as Khaṭībat al-Nisāʾ — Orator of the Women.
bio_full:
Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan ibn Rafi' ibn Imru' al-Qays ibn Abd al-Ashhal was a woman Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar, of the Abd al-Ashhal clan of the Aws in Medina. Her kunya is given as Umm Salama, and also as Umm Amir. She was a cousin of Mu'adh ibn Jabal. She is known by the title Khatibat al-Nisa', 'the orator of the women', given to her by al-Khatib al-Baghdadi and followed by Ibn Hajar, because she spoke up for women and asked the Prophet about religious rulings, often on their behalf.

She accepted Islam in the first year of the Hijra and pledged allegiance to the Prophet; some reports say she was present at the Pledge of Ridwan. She took part in the campaign of Khaybar, and Ibn Hajar records that she was present at the Battle of Yarmuk, where, according to historians' reports, she killed nine Byzantine soldiers with a tent pole.

Ibn Hibban, al-Dhahabi and Ibn Hajar all count her as a Companion. Ibn Hajar notes a report from her in Abu Dawud with a good (hasan) chain, and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi held that a report in Sahih Muslim giving a woman a different father's name in fact refers to her. She settled in Damascus and lived into the reign of Yazid ibn Mu'awiya. One account places her death between 61 and 70 AH.

famous: Asma' bint Makhrabah b. Jandal al-Tamimi
full: Asma' bint Makhrabah b. Jandal al-Tamimi
bio: Asma' bint Makhrabah b. Jandal al-Tamimi (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Asma' bint Makhrabah b. Jandal al-Tamimi was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, she belonged to the Tamim tribe, one of the prominent Arabian tribal confederations of the time.

As a sahabiyya, Asma' was among the women who personally encountered Prophet Muhammad and embraced Islam during his lifetime. Her presence in Mecca, the birthplace of Islam and center of early Muslim community life, positioned her as a direct witness to the foundational period of the Islamic faith. The early Muslim community in Mecca was relatively small and faced significant challenges, making the role of each companion particularly significant in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings.

Asma' is recognized primarily for her contribution to hadith literature as a narrator of prophetic traditions. Hadith, which comprises the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad, forms the second most important source of Islamic guidance after the Quran. Female companions played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting these traditions, particularly those relating to matters involving women, family life, and domestic practices that male companions might not have witnessed directly.

Her relatively short life span, ending around 634 CE, meant that she lived through the Prophet's entire ministry in Mecca and Medina, as well as the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr. This timeline suggests she witnessed the major transformative events of early Islamic history, from the initial revelations through the establishment of the first Islamic state.

The preservation of her name and recognition as a hadith narrator indicates that her contributions were valued by the early Muslim community. Female companions who served as hadith narrators were essential in ensuring that the comprehensive body of prophetic traditions was maintained for future generations. Their testimonies provided crucial perspectives on the Prophet's character and teachings, particularly in contexts where women had unique access and insight.

While specific details about her individual narrations or particular contributions may not be extensively documented in widely available historical sources, her identification as a hadith narrator places her within the important tradition of early Islamic scholarship and religious preservation that would become fundamental to Islamic jurisprudence and practice.

bio: Asma' bint Murshida bin Jabir (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Asma' bint Murshida ibn Jabr ibn Malik ibn Huwayratha was a woman of the Banu Haritha of Medina. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Salama bint Mas'ud, also descended from Haritha. She married al-Dahhak ibn Khalifa, of the line of Abd al-Ashhal, and their children were Thabit, Abu Jubayra, Abu Bakr, Umar, Thubayta, Bakra, Hamada and Safiyya; Thubayta later married Muhammad ibn Maslama. According to Ibn Sa'd, Asma' accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad.

Ibn al-Athir, who calls her al-Harithiyya, records one hadith attributed to her about irregular bleeding: she asked the Prophet about bleeding that returned some days after she had become pure, and he told her to wait three days, then purify herself and pray. Ibn Abd al-Barr judged this report not authentic, because only Haram ibn Uthman transmitted it and all the critics considered him weak.

bio: Asma' bint Qurat bin Khansa' (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Asma' bint Qurat bin Khansa' was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim community after the Hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Sahabiyya, the female companions of the Prophet, Asma' bint Qurat lived through the crucial early decades of Islamic history in Medina. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the first Muslim community, providing shelter, resources, and protection to the early Muslims who had migrated from Mecca. Her presence in Medina during this period means she would have witnessed the development of the early Islamic community and the establishment of many fundamental Islamic practices and institutions.

The female companions of the Prophet Muhammad hold a significant place in Islamic history as they participated in the religious and social life of the early Muslim community. These women were involved in various aspects of community life, from learning and transmitting religious knowledge to supporting the community during times of hardship and conflict.

Asma' bint Qurat's identity as an Ansari companion connects her to the broader narrative of Medinan support for the nascent Muslim community. The Ansar's acceptance of Islam and their assistance to the Muhajirin (the migrants from Mecca) was crucial for the survival and growth of the early Islamic community. Their homes, resources, and local knowledge helped establish Medina as the first Islamic city-state.

She lived during a transformative period that saw the revelation of much of the Quran, the establishment of Islamic law and social practices, and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's passing in 632 CE.

While specific details about her individual contributions and activities are not extensively documented in the historical sources, her recognition as a companion of the Prophet indicates her acceptance and practice of Islam during its foundational period, making her part of the generation that directly received and preserved the teachings of Islam for future generations.

bio: Asma' bint Salama/Makhrabah (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Asma' bint Salama, also known as Asma' bint Makhrabah, was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 594 CE, she was among the early Muslims in Mecca during the formative period of Islam.

As a sahabiyya, Asma' belonged to the distinguished group of individuals who personally knew, interacted with, and learned directly from the Prophet Muhammad. This status placed her within the most revered generation in Islamic tradition, as the companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Asma' is particularly recognized for her role in hadith transmission, serving as a narrator of prophetic traditions. In Islamic scholarship, hadith literature forms one of the fundamental sources of religious guidance alongside the Quran, preserving the sayings, actions, and tacit approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. Female companions like Asma' played crucial roles in this transmission process, particularly in preserving traditions related to private religious practices and domestic aspects of the Prophet's life that male companions might not have witnessed.

Her contribution to hadith sciences reflects the broader participation of women in early Islamic scholarship and religious transmission. During the earliest period of Islam, women actively engaged in learning, teaching, and preserving religious knowledge, establishing precedents for female participation in Islamic intellectual life.

Living during the rapid expansion of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to a established community, Asma' witnessed the foundational developments of Islamic society. Her death in 634 CE occurred during the early caliphate period, just two years after the Prophet's death, placing her among those who experienced both the prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic political expansion under the first caliph, Abu Bakr.

The preservation of her name and recognition as a hadith narrator in Islamic historical sources demonstrates the early Muslim community's acknowledgment of women's contributions to religious scholarship. Her inclusion in biographical dictionaries of companions and hadith narrators reflects the systematic efforts of later Islamic scholars to document and preserve the chain of transmission that connected them to the Prophet's teachings through figures like Asma' bint Salama.

bio: Asma' bint Zayd ibn al-Khattab (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Asma' bint Zayd ibn al-Khattab was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative years of Islam in the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the generation that witnessed the emergence and early expansion of the Islamic community in the Arabian Peninsula.

As indicated by her name, Asma' was the daughter of Zayd ibn al-Khattab, making her a member of a prominent family within the early Muslim community. Her connection to this influential lineage placed her among the notable figures of early Islamic society in Medina, the city that became the center of the growing Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca.

Asma' is primarily remembered for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and teachings of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial component of Islamic religious and legal tradition. As a female narrator, she contributed to the preservation and transmission of prophetic traditions at a time when such documentation was essential for establishing the foundations of Islamic practice and belief. Her participation in hadith transmission reflects the important role that women played in the early preservation of Islamic knowledge and religious teachings.

The inclusion of women like Asma' in the hadith transmission process demonstrates the significance placed on their testimonies and religious understanding within the early Muslim community. Female companions who served as hadith narrators were recognized as reliable transmitters of religious knowledge, contributing to the comprehensive documentation of prophetic guidance that would later inform Islamic jurisprudence and spiritual practice.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime and the immediate aftermath, Asma' was witness to the rapid transformation of Arabian society and the establishment of the first Islamic state. Her life span, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompassed the crucial forty-year period that saw the revelation of the Quran, the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, and the beginning of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Though specific details about her individual contributions and personal circumstances remain limited in historical records, Asma' bint Zayd ibn al-Khattab represents the broader group of female companions whose participation in early Islamic society helped establish the religious and social foundations that would guide the Muslim community for generations to come.

full: Ata ibn Abi Rabah al-Qurashi al-Makki
titles: Mufti Mecca · Imam al-Hajj · Sheikh of Tawaf
bio: Ata ibn Abi Rabah was a prominent early Muslim jurist and hadith transmitter of Nubian origin who served as the mufti of Mecca in the late seventh and early eighth centuries. He is considered a leading figure of the early Meccan school of fiqh.
bio_full:
Ata ibn Abi Rabah (Arabic: عطاء بن أبي رباح, romanized: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ; c. 646 – c. 733) was a prominent early Muslim jurist and hadith transmitter of Nubian origin who served as the mufti of Mecca in the late seventh and early eighth centuries. He is considered a leading figure of the early Meccan school of fiqh.

Early life
Ata was born in the town of Muwalladi l-Janad in Yemen. Although early biographical sources differ on the exact year of his birth, it is generally accepted he was born towards the beginning of Uthman ibn Affan's reign, c. 25 AH/646 CE. His mother was a Nubian basket weaver while his father, named Aslam, is described as being dark-skinned and flat-nosed. Ata was a cripple and possessed a limp, and while he was born with one healthy eye, he later went completely blind.

Life as a scholar
Ata was raised in Mecca as a mawla (client) of the Qurayshi Abu Khuthaym al-Fihri, where he worked as a Quran teacher, before being recognised for his expertise in fiqh. He was later appointed mufti of the city by the Umayyads and taught in the Great Mosque, in which he also lived during the latter years of his life. While in Mecca, Ata met with and transmitted hadith from several companions of Muhammad, including Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurairah and Jabir ibn Abd Allah.
As a jurist, Ata was considered an authority on the rites of Hajj. Among his most prominent students were Qays ibn Sa'd and Ibn Jurayj, the latter being the primary transmitter of his legal opinions. When giving legal verdicts, Ata largely relied on his own independent reasoning (ra'y). Less frequently, he referred to the opinions of Muhammad's companions and Qur'anic verses, and he rarely referred to hadith.
An early Quranic exegete, the commentaries of Ata are preserved in the tafsir works of Ibn Mujahid, Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani and al-Tabari. Ata's style of commentary has been described as simple and concise, eschewing linguistic analysis for explaining the meanings of Quranic verses.
Ata fought for Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr during the Second Fitna and lost a hand in battle. In 93 AH/711 CE, he was imprisoned on suspicion of being a murji' at the behest of Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, but was later released. Biographical sources disagree on the year of his death, but it is likely he died c. 115 AH/733 CE. He was survived by one son named Yaqub.

Legacy

Piety
Narrations in biographical works present Ata as a pious and virtuous man. He reportedly only wore simple clothing, performed the Hajj over seventy times, and, despite reaching an advanced age, was able to recite 200 verses of Al-Baqarah in salah without moving.

Hadith
Many of the hadith transmitted by Ata lack an isnad. Early hadith scholars, such as Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan, were critical of hadith that Ata had transmitted in mursal form, suspected he may have engaged in tadlis and noted that his intellectual faculties declined towards the end of his life. However, he was generally perceived as a reliable transmitter and later hadith critics such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal exonerated him from tadlis. Several of Ata's students, including his son Yaqub and Ibn Jurayj, transmitted hadith from him in writing.

Musannaf of Abd al-Razzaq
Ata is frequently cited as one of Ibn Jurayj's authorities in the Musannaf of Abd al-Razzaq. In a sample of 3,810 narrations selected by Harald Motzki, 39% of those ascribed to Ibn Jurayj are adduced from Ata. Ata relates a tradition in only 20% of these narrations, with the remaining 80% being his own ra'y. Of the authorities cited in his traditions, 15% are companions of Muhammad, 10% are Quranic verses and 5% are hadith from Muhammad. According to Motzki, Ibn Jurayj attempted to reproduce Ata's narrations faithfully and the corpus lacked signs of fabrication.

Further reading
Motzi, Harald (2002). The Origins of Islamic Jurisprudence: Meccan Fiqh Before the Classical Schools. Translated by Katz, Marion H. Brill. Chapter 3.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Atik b. Qays b. Haysha (c. 597–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Atik b. Qays b. Haysha was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the early Muslims who became part of the growing community in Medina during the first decades of the 7th century.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, Atik b. Qays was part of the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the establishment of the early Islamic community. The Sahaba hold a particularly revered position in Islamic tradition as the individuals who helped establish and spread the new faith during its earliest and most crucial period.

Atik b. Qays is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, where he died as a martyr in 634 CE. The Battle of Uhud was the second major military engagement between the early Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan tribes, taking place approximately one year after the Battle of Badr. This battle was significant in early Islamic history as it tested the resilience of the nascent Muslim community and demonstrated both the challenges and commitment involved in establishing the new religious and political order.

The battle itself was a complex engagement where the Muslim forces initially appeared to gain the upper hand before experiencing significant casualties due to tactical complications. Many companions of the Prophet, including Atik b. Qays, lost their lives during this confrontation. Those who died fighting in defense of the early Muslim community at Uhud are remembered as martyrs in Islamic historical accounts.

Atik b. Qays represents the numerous early Muslims whose individual stories may not be extensively documented but who played important roles in the survival and establishment of Islam during its most vulnerable period. His life span coincided with the prophetic period and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate, making him a witness to the transformation of Arabian society and the emergence of Islam as a major religious and political force. His sacrifice at Uhud exemplifies the dedication of the early Muslim community members who contributed to the faith's survival during its formative years.

bio: Atika bint Abdul Muttalib bin Hashim Al-Qurashi Al-Hashimiya, she is the aunt of the Prophet Muhammad, the daughter of Abdul Muttalib bin Hashim, the sister of Abu Talib and Abdullah, and her mother is Fatima bint Amr bin Aidh. There was disagreement about her conversion to Islam, and some mentioned her among the Companions. It was narrated that she saw a vision that frightened her, and she told her brother Abbas bin Abdul Muttalib about the Battle of Badr.
bio_full:
Atika bint Abd al-Muttalib was a paternal aunt of the Prophet Muhammad, a daughter of Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim of Quraysh. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Fatima bint Amr ibn A'idh of the Makhzum clan, which made her a full sister of Abu Talib and Abd Allah, the Prophet's father. Before Islam she married Abu Umayya ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and Ibn Sa'd names their children as Abd Allah, Zuhayr and Qurayba; through this marriage she was stepmother to Umm Salama.

She is best known for a dream she had shortly before the Battle of Badr in 624. As Ibn Sa'd and Abu Nu'aym report it, she saw a rider who shouted a warning to Quraysh and then threw a rock that broke apart, its pieces falling into nearly every house in Mecca. She told her brother al-Abbas, who asked her to keep it secret, but the story spread and Abu Jahl mocked it. Days later the call came to defend the Meccan caravan, and Quraysh marched to Badr. Al-Dhahabi reports that her dream was one reason her brother Abu Lahab stayed behind. Abu Nu'aym, citing Ibn Ishaq, preserves verses she composed after Badr saying her dream had come true, and Ibn Sa'd also attributes to her an elegy for the Prophet.

Whether she accepted Islam is disputed. Ibn Sa'd and al-Dhahabi state that she became Muslim in Mecca and later emigrated to Medina. Ibn Abd al-Barr says her conversion is disputed and that most scholars reject it, and Ibn Manda says that among the Prophet's aunts only Safiyya's Islam is agreed upon. The sources consulted do not record the date of her death.

bio: Atika bint Zayd al-Adawiyya was a 7th-century Islamic scholar and poet. She was a disciple (ṣaḥābiyyah) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. She was also one of the wives of Umar, the second Caliph. Famously, all five of her husbands became shaheed (martyrs).
bio_full:
Atika bint Zayd al-Adawiyya (Arabic: عاتكة بنت زيد, romanized: ʿĀtika bint Zayd) was a 7th-century Islamic scholar and poet. She was a disciple (ṣaḥābiyyah) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. She was also one of the wives of Umar, the second Caliph. Famously, all five of her husbands became shaheed (martyrs).

Early life
Atika bint Zayd was born c. 600, the daughter of Umm Kurz Safiya bint al-Hadrami and Zayd ibn Amr, a member of the Adi clan of the Quraysh in Mecca. Sa'id ibn Zayd was her brother. Their father was murdered in 605.
Atika was probably still a child when Muhammad's prophethood began in 610. Sa'id was among the early converts to Islam, and Atika became a Muslim too.

Personal life
Atika married five times in her lifetime.

First marriage
Her first husband was her cousin, Zayd ibn al-Khattab, who was at least twenty years older than her. He was also a Muslim, and it was presumably in his company that Atika joined the general immigration to Medina in 622.
This marriage apparently ended in divorce, for Atika had already remarried by the time of Zayd's death at the Battle of Yamama in December 632.

Second marriage
Her second marriage was to Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr. It was said that Abdullah deferred to Atika's judgment and spent so much time with her that he was too busy to fight in the Islamic army.

Divorce
Abu Bakr punished his son by ordering him to divorce her. According to Al-Baladhuri, the reason Abu Bakr ordered the divorce was because Atika was barren. Abdullah did as he was told but was grief-stricken. He wrote poetry for her:

In the end Abdullah was allowed to take Atika back before her waiting period was completed.

Death of Muhammad
When Muhammad died in 632, Atika composed an elegy for him.

Death of Abdullah
Abdullah settled a large amount of property on Atika on the condition that she would not remarry after his death. He died in Medina in January 633 from an old battle wound incurred at the Siege of Ta'if. Atika composed an elegy for him.

She refused several suitors in the following months.

Third marriage

Courtship
Umar, the future second Caliph and Atika's first cousin, told her that she had been wrong to renounce her right to remarry, "denying yourself what God has permitted".

The broken vow
After Umar became Caliph, when Aisha learned that Atika had broken her vow of celibacy, she sent her a message:

Return our property to us!"
When Ali also recited this poem to them, Umar told Atika to return the land. He settled an equivalent sum of money on her, which she distributed in alms to expiate the breaking of her vow to Abd Allah.

Married life
From her marriage to Umar, Atika gave birth to a son named Iyad.
Atika asked Umar's permission to attend public prayers at the mosque. Umar preferred his wives to remain at home and expressed his displeasure with silence. Atika told him that she was not going to stop asking permission, and that she would go to the mosque unless he specifically forbade her. He remained silent, presumably because he could not forbid something that Muhammad had permitted, and so Atika continued to attend.

Death of Umar
Atika was present at the mosque when Umar was assassinated there in November 644. She composed elegies for him.

Fourth marriage

Courtship
After Umar's death, Atika married Zubayr ibn al-Awwam. She made it a condition of their marriage contract that he would not beat her, that he would continue to permit her to visit the mosque at will, and that he would not withhold "any of her rights".

Death of Zubayr
Zubayr was killed at the Battle of the Camel in December 656. Atika also composed an elegy for him.

It was at this point that people began to say: "Let a man who wants to be a shahid marry Atika bint Zayd!"
Afterwards, the fourth caliph of Islam Ali himself proposed to her, but she told him, "I would not want you to die, O cousin of the Prophet." Despite that, Ali ended up dying a shaheed anyway, which changed her as well as people's views.

Last marriage
Atika's fifth and final husband was Ali's own son, Husayn, who was over twenty years younger than she was.

famous: Attab bin Usayd bin Abi al-'Is
full: Attab bin Usayd bin Abi al-'Is
primaryTitle: Among the First Judges (Qudah) of Islam
bio: Attab bin Usayd bin Abi al-'Is (c. 606 CE–634 CE, Jamadi II, Makkah) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Among the First Judges of Islam.
bio_full:
Attab bin Usayd bin Abi al-'Is was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived from approximately 606 to 634 CE. Born in Mecca during the pre-Islamic period, he witnessed the emergence and early expansion of Islam during his relatively short life of twenty-eight years.

As a Sahaba, Attab belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and accepted Islam during the Prophet's lifetime. His full name indicates his tribal lineage within the Quraysh, the dominant tribe of Mecca, suggesting he came from a prominent family background that would have been significant in the social structure of early seventh-century Arabian society.

Attab is historically recognized as one of the early figures in Islamic jurisprudence, earning recognition as among the first judges in Islam. This role was crucial during the formative period of the Muslim community, when legal precedents and judicial procedures were being established. The position of judge in early Islamic society required not only knowledge of Islamic principles but also the trust and respect of the community, indicating Attab's standing among his contemporaries.

His appointment as a judge reflects the practical needs of the rapidly growing Muslim community, which required institutional structures to resolve disputes and maintain social order according to Islamic principles. The early judges played a vital role in interpreting and applying Islamic law in real-world situations, helping to establish legal traditions that would influence Islamic jurisprudence for centuries to come.

Attab's death in 634 CE occurred during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death. His relatively early death meant that his contributions to Islamic legal thought occurred during the very foundational period of Islamic civilization. The fact that he died in Mecca, his birthplace, suggests he remained connected to the religious and administrative center of early Islam.

While specific details of his judicial decisions or legal opinions have not been extensively preserved in historical records, his recognition as one of Islam's first judges establishes his importance in the development of Islamic legal institutions. His role represents the transition from the direct guidance of the Prophet to the systematic development of Islamic law through qualified interpreters and judges in the early Muslim community.

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Auf bin 'Afra' (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Awf ibn al-Harith ibn Rifa'a was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar of Khazraj. He was known as Awf ibn Afra after his mother, Afra bint Ubayd ibn Tha'laba, and was a brother of the Companions Mu'adh and Mu'awwidh, who were also called after her. Ibn Sa'd notes that Ibn Ishaq added a fourth brother, Rifa'a, though another family source did not accept this.

According to al-Waqidi, quoted by Ibn Sa'd, Awf was among the six men of the Ansar who were the first to accept Islam in Mecca, and he attended both pledges of Aqaba; Ibn Ishaq lists him among the seventy at the second pledge. Al-Dhahabi also notes that some counted him among the first six.

He fought at Badr in 624 alongside his brothers and was killed there. Abu Nu'aym reports that during the battle Awf asked the Prophet what makes the Lord laugh with delight at His servant, and the Prophet answered: a servant who plunges into the enemy without armour. Awf took off his coat of mail, threw it aside, and fought until he was killed. Some accounts give this exchange to his brother Mu'adh instead. Ibn Sa'd reports that Awf and Mu'awwidh attacked Abu Jahl, the Meccan leader, and that Abu Jahl killed Awf.

full: Awhad al-Din Hamid ibn Abi al-Fakhr al-Kirmani
titles: Qutb al-Aqtab
bio: Awhad al-Din Hamid ibn Abi al-Fakhr al-Kirmani (c. 1164–1238) was a mystic of the Akbarian tradition, based in Kirman. Known as Qutb al-Aqtab of Kirman.
bio_full:
Awhad al-Din Hamid ibn Abi al-Fakhr al-Kirmani was a prominent Islamic mystic who lived from approximately 1164 to 1238 CE. Based in the city of Kirman in present-day Iran, he became one of the notable figures in the Akbarian tradition of Sufism, which followed the mystical teachings associated with the great Andalusian mystic Ibn Arabi.

Al-Kirmani lived during a transformative period in Islamic history, spanning the late Ayyubid period and the early years of the Mongol invasions that would reshape much of the Islamic world. His lifetime coincided with the flourishing of various Sufi orders and mystical traditions across the Islamic lands, particularly in Persia, where mystical poetry and philosophy were experiencing remarkable development.

Within the Akbarian school of Sufism, al-Kirmani was recognized for his spiritual attainments and was honored with the title "Qutb al-Aqtab," meaning "Pole of Poles." In Sufi cosmology, the qutb or spiritual pole represents the highest rank in the invisible hierarchy of saints who are believed to maintain the spiritual order of the world. The title "Qutb al-Aqtab" suggests that al-Kirmani was regarded as holding supreme spiritual authority among the mystics of his region and time.

The Akbarian tradition, named after Ibn Arabi, emphasized metaphysical speculation, the concept of the unity of being, and sophisticated mystical philosophy. Practitioners of this school developed complex theoretical frameworks for understanding the relationship between the divine and creation, often expressed through intricate symbolic language and mystical terminology.

Al-Kirmani's significance lies in his role as a representative of the Akbarian mystical tradition in the eastern Islamic world, particularly in the Persian cultural sphere. His recognition as a leading spiritual figure of Kirman indicates his influence within the local Sufi community and suggests that he played an important role in transmitting and developing Akbarian teachings in his region.

The city of Kirman itself was an important center of Islamic learning and culture during this period, situated along trade routes that connected various parts of the Islamic world. Al-Kirmani's presence there contributed to the city's reputation as a hub of mystical learning and spiritual practice during the medieval period.

full: ʿĀlamgīr I: Abū al-Muẓaffar Muḥyī al-Dīn Muḥammad Awrangzīb
titles: ʿĀlamgīr (Conqueror of the World)

relations.source: Mughal court chronicles; Ain-i-Akbari (Abu al-Fadl Allami)

bio: Alamgir I, commonly known by the title Aurangzeb, was the sixth Mughal emperor, reigning from 1658 until his death in 1707.
bio_full:
Alamgir I (Muhi al-Din Muhammad; 3 November 1618 – 3 March 1707), commonly known by the title Aurangzeb, was the sixth Mughal emperor, reigning from 1658 until his death in 1707. Under his reign, the Mughal Empire reached its greatest extent, with territory spanning nearly the entirety of the Indian subcontinent.
Aurangzeb and the Mughals belonged to a branch of the Timurid dynasty.  He held administrative and military posts under his father Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658) and gained recognition as an accomplished military commander. Aurangzeb served as the viceroy of the Deccan in 1636–1637 and the governor of Gujarat in 1645–1647. He jointly administered the provinces of Multan and Sindh in 1648–1652 and continued expeditions into the neighbouring Safavid territories. In September 1657, Shah Jahan nominated his eldest and liberalist son Dara Shikoh as his successor, a move repudiated by Aurangzeb, who proclaimed himself emperor in February 1658. In April 1658, Aurangzeb defeated the allied army of Shikoh and the Kingdom of Marwar at the Battle of Dharmat. Aurangzeb's decisive victory at the Battle of Samugarh in May 1658 cemented his sovereignty and his suzerainty was acknowledged throughout the Empire. After Shah Jahan recovered from illness in July 1658, Aurangzeb declared him incompetent to rule and imprisoned his father in the Agra Fort. Following this, Aurangzeb had Dara Shikoh executed by beheading and his head was placed in a box and presented to their imprisoned father.
Aurangzeb's reign is characterised by a period of rapid military expansion, with several dynasties and states being overthrown by the Mughals. The Mughals also surpassed Qing China as the world's largest economy and biggest manufacturing power. The Mughal military gradually improved and became one of the strongest armies in the world. A staunch Muslim, Aurangzeb is credited with the construction of numerous mosques and patronising works of Arabic calligraphy. He successfully imposed the Fatawa-i Alamgiri as the principal regulating body of the empire and prohibited religiously forbidden activities in Islam. Although Aurangzeb suppressed several local revolts, he maintained cordial relations with foreign governments.
His empire was also one of the largest in Indian history. However, his emperorship has a complicated legacy. He is often criticized for his actions against non-Muslims, including his ordering of the demolition of non-Muslim schools and temples and the reimposition of the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims, which had been suspended for the previous 100 years by his great-grandfather Akbar. He has also been criticized for his conservative view of Islam, with some arguing that he abandoned the legacy of pluralism and tolerance of the earlier Mughal emperors. Others, however, reject these assertions, arguing that he opposed bigotry against Hindus, Sikhs and Shia Muslims and that he employed significantly more Hindus in his imperial bureaucracy than his predecessors.

Early life

Aurangzeb was born in Dahod on 3 November 1618. He was the sixth child of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal. Aurangzeb was a descendent of Timur through his father.
In June 1626, after an unsuccessful rebellion by his father, eight-year-old Aurangzeb and his brother Dara Shikoh were sent to the Mughal court in Lahore as hostages of their grandfather Jahangir and his wife, Nur Jahan, as part of their father's pardon deal. After Jahangir died in 1627, Shah Jahan emerged victorious in the ensuing war of succession to the Mughal throne. Aurangzeb and his brother were consequently reunited with Shah Jahan in Agra in 1628. Aurangzeb's daily allowance was fixed at 500 rupees.
As a Mughal prince, Aurangzeb received an education covering subjects like combat, military strategy, and administration. His curriculum also included areas like Islamic studies, Turkic and Persian literature. Aurangzeb grew up fluent in the Hindustani language. He was also fluent in his ancestral language of Chagatai Turkic, but similar to his predecessors, he preferred to use Persian. He had mastered the Quran and the hadith.

On 28 May 1633, a war elephant stampeded through the Mughal imperial encampment. Aurangzeb rode against the elephant and threw his spear at its head. He was unhorsed but escaped death. For his courage, Aurangzeb's father conferred on him the title of Bahadur (brave) and presented him with gifts. When chided for his recklessness, Aurangzeb replied:

If the fight had ended fatally for me it would not have been a matter of shame. Death drops the curtain even on emperors; it is no dishonor. The shame lay in what my brothers did!
Historians have interpreted this as an unjust taunt with cowardice against his brothers. Shuja had also faced the elephant and wounded it with his spear. Dara had been too far away to come to their assistance.
Three days later Aurangzeb turned fifteen. Shah Jahan weighed him and presented him 5,000 Mohars, the elephant Sudhakar, along with other presents worth Rs. 200,000. His bravery against the elephant was documented in Persian and Urdu verses.

Ancestry

Career as prince

In December 1634, he was assigned to his first post with the rank of ten thousand horse and four thousand troopers, also was allowed to use the royal prerogative of red tent. Aurangzeb was nominally in charge of the force sent to Bundelkhand with the intent of subduing the rebellious ruler of Orchha, Jhujhar Singh, who had attacked another territory in defiance of Shah Jahan's policy and was refusing to atone for his actions. By arrangement, Aurangzeb stayed in the rear, away from the fighting, and took the advice of his generals as the Mughal Army gathered and commenced the siege of Orchha in 1635. The campaign was successful and Singh was removed from power.

First Deccan governorate (1636–1644)

Aurangzeb was appointed viceroy of the Deccan in 1636. After Shah Jahan's vassals had been devastated by the alarming expansion of Ahmednagar during the reign of the Nizam Shahi boy-prince Murtaza Shah III, the emperor dispatched Aurangzeb, who in 1636 brought the Nizam Shahi dynasty to an end. The Mughal provinces of Deccan at that time were Khandesh, Berar, Telangana and Daulatabad. The entire region with 64 forts, were in charge of Aurangzeb, while ten more forts had yet to be conquered by the Mughals. In 1637, Aurangzeb married the Safavid princess Dilras Banu, posthumously known as Rabia-ud-Daurani. She was his first wife and chief consort as well as his favourite. He also had an infatuation with a slave girl, Hira Bai, whose death at a young age greatly affected him. In his old age, he was under the charms of his concubine, Udaipuri Mahal. The latter had formerly been a companion to Dara Shukoh.
In the same year, 1637, Aurangzeb was placed in charge of annexing the small Rajput kingdom of Baglana, which he did with ease. In 1638, Aurangzeb married Nawab Bai, later known as Rahmat al-Nisa. That same year, Aurangzeb dispatched an army to subdue the Portuguese coastal fortress of Daman, however his forces met stubborn resistance and were eventually repulsed at the end of a long siege. At some point, Aurangzeb married Aurangabadi Mahal, who was a Circassian or Georgian.
Aurangzeb arrived in Agra on 2 May 1644 to see his sister Jahanara who was severely burnt in an accident two months prior. 
Shah Jahan was outraged to see Aurangzeb enter the interior palace compound in military attire and immediately dismissed him from his position of viceroy of the Deccan; Aurangzeb was also no longer allowed to use red tents or to associate himself with the official military standard of the Mughal emperor. Other sources state that Aurangzeb was dismissed from his position because Aurangzeb left the life of luxury and became a faqir.
Aurangzeb's first viceroyalty of the Deccan lasted eight years from 14 July 1636 to 28 May 1644 before his dismissal.

Governor of Gujarat (1645–1647)
In 1645, he was barred from the court for seven months.

bio: Aus bin As-Samit (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Aws ibn al-Samit ibn Qays was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Awf ibn al-Khazraj, and a brother of the Companion Ubada ibn al-Samit. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Qurrat al-Ayn bint Ubada ibn Nadla. After the emigration the Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Marthad ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi.

He fought at Badr, and Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr say he also fought at Uhud, the Trench and the Prophet's other campaigns. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir describe him as a poet.

He is remembered as the husband of Khawla (also called Khuwayla) bint Tha'laba, the woman of Surat al-Mujadila. Ibn Sa'd reports that his was the first case of zihar in Islam: he told his wife that she was to him like his mother's back, and then regretted it. Khawla went to the Prophet and pleaded her case repeatedly until the opening verses of Surat al-Mujadila were revealed, setting out the expiation for zihar. Abu Nu'aym reports that the Prophet helped Aws pay the expiation of feeding sixty poor people, and Khawla added food of her own. Ibn Sa'd names their son as al-Rabi'.

He lived on after the Prophet. Ibn Hibban says he died in Medina during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, aged eighty-five; Ibn Sa'd reports more cautiously that he is said to have lived into Uthman's time. Ibn Abd al-Barr names Hassan ibn Atiyya as one who narrated from him.

bio_sources.title: Aws ibn al-Samit — entries from Ibn Sa'd (Tabaqat), Ibn Abd al-Barr (al-Isti'ab), Ibn al-Athir (Usd al-Ghaba), Ibn Hibban (al-Thiqat; Mashahir), Ibn Qani', Abu Nu'aym — hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com

bio: Aus bin Thabit (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Aws ibn Thabit ibn al-Mundhir ibn Haram was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Amr ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar of Khazraj. He was the brother of the poet Hassan ibn Thabit and the father of the Companion Shaddad ibn Aws. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Sakhta bint Haritha.

He was one of the seventy Ansar who took the second pledge of Aqaba, and he fought at Badr. After the emigration, Ibn Sa'd reports on the authority of Ibn Ishaq and Musa ibn Muhammad, the Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Uthman ibn Affan. Al-Waqidi adds that he took part in Uhud, the Trench and the other campaigns.

The sources disagree about his death. Al-Waqidi says he died in Medina during the caliphate of Uthman, and Ibn Hibban gives the year as 35 AH (655 CE). Ibn Ishaq and others, followed by Abu Nu'aym, say he was killed at the Battle of Uhud in 625, and Ibn Abd al-Barr says he prefers this view. Ibn Sa'd notes that al-Waqidi did not know of a death at Uhud and that al-Waqidi reported descendants of his living in Jerusalem, while Ibn Ishaq says he left no children; his son Shaddad, however, is named by Ibn Abd al-Barr and Abu Nu'aym.

bio_sources.title: Aws ibn Thabit ibn al-Mundhir — entries from Ibn Sa'd (Tabaqat), Ibn Abd al-Barr (al-Isti'ab), Ibn al-Athir (Usd al-Ghaba), Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym — hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Aus/Anas bin Arqam (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Aws ibn Arqam ibn Zayd ibn Qays ibn al-Nu'man was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj. Ibn al-Athir identifies him as a brother of the well-known Companion Zayd ibn Arqam.

He was killed at the Battle of Uhud in 625. His name appears in Ibn Ishaq's list of the men of Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj who fell at Uhud, as recorded by Ibn al-Athir (through Yunus ibn Bukayr) and by Abu Nu'aym; Ibn Abd al-Barr also states that he was martyred at Uhud. The sources consulted record no further details of his life.

bio_sources.title: Aws ibn al-Arqam ibn Zayd ibn Qays — Ibn al-Athir, Usd al-Ghaba — hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com
Aws ibn al-Arqam — Ibn Abd al-Barr (al-Isti'ab), Abu Nu'aym (Ma'rifat al-Sahaba) — hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com

bio: Aws bin Khawli (c. 594–655 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Aws bin Khawli was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he lived through the early decades of Islamic history until his death in 655 CE, spanning both the prophetic period and the early caliphate.

Based in Medina, Aws bin Khawli became one of the Sahaba, the term used for the companions of Prophet Muhammad who met him, believed in his message, and remained Muslim until their death. His most notable distinction was his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as a "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces, and those who participated in it are held in special regard within Islamic tradition.

The Battle of Badr was a pivotal moment that helped establish the nascent Muslim community's legitimacy and survival in the Arabian Peninsula. The companions who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are considered to hold a unique status among the Sahaba due to their early commitment and sacrifice during this crucial period when Islam's future remained uncertain.

As a companion of the Prophet, Aws bin Khawli would have been part of the community that received direct teachings from Muhammad and witnessed the revelation of the Quran. The companions played essential roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, practices, and the prophetic traditions known as hadith to subsequent generations.

Aws bin Khawli's association with hadith sciences reflects the important role many companions played in the oral transmission of the Prophet's sayings, actions, and approvals. The companions served as the primary sources for Islamic scholarship and jurisprudence that developed in the centuries following the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

Living until 655 CE, Aws bin Khawli witnessed the expansion of Islam beyond Arabia under the first three caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Uthman ibn Affan. His lifetime encompassed the transformation of Islam from a local Arabian religious movement to a major force that had spread across significant portions of the Byzantine and Sassanian empires. The knowledge and experiences of companions like Aws bin Khawli became foundational sources for later Islamic scholarship and religious understanding.

famous: Ayadh bin Zuhayr b Abi Shaddad
full: Ayadh bin Zuhayr b Abi Shaddad
bio: Ayadh bin Zuhayr b Abi Shaddad (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ayadh bin Zuhayr b Abi Shaddad was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. As one of the Sahaba, he belonged to the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islam.

Ayadh is most notably recognized as a participant in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition, as they demonstrated their commitment to the faith during a critical and dangerous period for the early Muslim community.

The Battle of Badr represented a turning point for Islam, transforming it from a persecuted religious movement into a recognized political and military force in the Arabian Peninsula. Companions like Ayadh who participated in this engagement played crucial roles in establishing the foundations of the Islamic state and ensuring the survival of the Muslim community during its most vulnerable years.

Ayadh is associated with the early ascetic tradition within Islam, suggesting he was among those companions who emphasized spiritual discipline, simple living, and devotion to worship. This ascetic orientation reflected one of the key spiritual currents in early Islamic society, where some companions chose to focus intensively on prayer, contemplation, and detachment from worldly concerns.

His death in 634 CE places him among the companions who died during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph after Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing means Ayadh witnessed the immediate transition period following the Prophet's death, when the Muslim community faced the challenge of maintaining unity and continuing the expansion of Islam under new leadership.

While specific details about Ayadh's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in historical sources, his status as a Sahaba automatically grants him significant respect within Islamic tradition. The companions as a group are revered for their direct knowledge of the Prophet's teachings and their role in preserving and transmitting Islamic practices to subsequent generations. Ayadh bin Zuhayr represents the dedication and sacrifice of those early Muslims who helped establish Islam during its formative decades.

primaryTitle: Supreme Leader — Founder of the Islamic Republic of Iran
titles: Imām · Marja al-Taqlīd
bio: Ruhollah Mostafavi Musavi Khomeini was an Iranian political revolutionary and Shia cleric who served as the first supreme leader of Iran from 1979 until his death in 1989. He was the leader of the Iranian Revolution, which overthrew Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, ended the Pahlavi era, and transformed the country into an Islamic republic. As supreme leader, he implemented policies that came to be known as Khomeinism.
bio_full:
Ruhollah Mostafavi Musavi Khomeini (17 May 1900 – 3 June 1989) was an Iranian political revolutionary and Shia cleric who served as the first supreme leader of Iran from 1979 until his death in 1989. He was the leader of the Iranian Revolution, which overthrew Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, ended the Pahlavi era, and transformed the country into an Islamic republic. As supreme leader, he implemented policies that came to be known as Khomeinism.
Born in the city of Khomeyn, in what is now Iran's Markazi province, Khomeini's father was murdered when he was two years old. He began studying the Quran and Arabic from a young age  assisted by his relatives. Khomeini became a high ranking cleric in Twelver Shi'ism, an ayatollah, a marja' ("source of emulation"), a mujtahid, faqīha and a hafiz (an expert in fiqh), and author of more than 40 books. His opposition to the White Revolution resulted in his state-sponsored expulsion to Bursa in 1964. Nearly a year later, he moved to Najaf, where speeches he gave outlining his religiopolitical theory of Guardianship of the Jurist were compiled into the book Islamic Government.
After the success of the Iranian Revolution, Khomeini served as the country's de facto head of state from February 1979 until his appointment as supreme leader in December of that same year. Khomeini was Time magazine's Man of the Year in 1979 for his international influence and in the next decade was described as the "virtual face of Shia Islam in Western popular culture". He was known for his support of the hostage takers during the Iran hostage crisis; his fatwa calling for the murder of Indian-born British novelist Salman Rushdie for Rushdie's description of the Islamic prophet Muhammad in his novel The Satanic Verses, which Khomeini considered blasphemous; pursuing the overthrow of Saddam Hussein in the Iran–Iraq War; and for referring to the United States as the "Great Satan" and Israel as the "Little Satan".
The subject of a pervasive cult of personality, Khomeini held the title Ayatollah and is officially known as Imam Khomeini inside Iran and by his supporters internationally. His state funeral was attended by up to 10 million people, one fifth of Iran's population at the time, and is considered the second-largest funeral in history.
Khomeini's legacy is controversial. In Iran, he is legally considered "inviolable"—insulting him is punishable with imprisonment; his gold-domed tomb in Tehran's Behesht-e Zahra cemetery has become a shrine for his adherents. While some view him as a champion of Islamic revival, independence, anti-imperialism, and resistance to foreign influence in Iran, Khomeini has been criticized for anti-Western and antisemitic rhetoric, anti-democratic actions, numerous human rights violations including the Iranian Cultural Revolution purges, 1981–1982 Iran massacres, 1988 mass executions of Iranian political prisoners, and for using child soldiers extensively during the Iran–Iraq War for human wave attacks. There were many protests during his rule, including in 1979 and 1981.

Early years

Background

Ruhollah Mostafavi Musavi Khomeini came from a lineage of small land owners, clerics, and merchants. His ancestors migrated towards the end of the 18th century from their original home in Nishapur, then part of Khorasan province, in northeastern Iran for a short stay to the Kingdom of Awadh, a region in the present-day Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, whose rulers were Twelver Shi'a Muslims of Persian origin. During their rule, they extensively invited and received a steady stream of Persian scholars, poets, jurists, architects, and painters. The family eventually settled in the small town of Kintoor, near Lucknow, the capital of Awadh.
Khomeini's paternal grandfather, Ahmad Hindi, was born in Kintoor. He left Lucknow in 1830 on a pilgrimage to the tomb of Ali in Najaf, Ottoman Iraq (now Iraq), and never returned. According to biographer Baqer Moin, this migration was to escape from the spread of British power in India. In 1834, Seyyed Ahmad Musavi Hindi visited Iran, and in 1839, he settled in Khomein. Although he stayed and settled in Iran, he continued to be known as Hindi, indicating his stay in India, and Ruhollah Khomeini even used Hindi as a pen name in some of his ghazals. Khomeini's grandfather, Mirza Ahmad Mojtahed-e Khonsari was the cleric who issued a fatwa to forbid usage of tobacco during the Tobacco Protest.

Childhood
According to his birth certificate, Ruhollah Mostafavi Musavi Khomeini, whose first name means "spirit of Allah", was born on 17 May 1900 in Khomeyn, Markazi province, although his brother Mortaza (later known as Ayatollah Pasandideh) gives his birth date of 24 September 1902, the birth anniversary of Muhammad's daughter, Fatima. He was raised by his mother, Agha Khanum, and his aunt, Sahebeth, following the murder of his father, Mustafa Musawi, over two years after his birth in 1903.
Ruhollah began to study the Quran and elementary Persian at the age of six. The following year, he began to attend a local school, where he learned religion, noheh khani (lamentation recital), and other traditional subjects. Throughout his childhood, he continued his religious education with the assistance of his relatives, including his mother's cousin, Ja'far, and his elder half-brother, Morteza Pasandideh, a cleric and poet.

Education and lecturing

After World War I, arrangements were made for him to study at the Islamic seminary in Isfahan, but he preferred the seminary in Arak. He was placed under the leadership of Ayatollah Abdolkarim Haeri Yazdi. In 1920, Khomeini commenced his studies in Arak. The following year, Ayatollah Haeri Yazdi transferred to the Islamic seminary in the holy city of Qom, southwest of Tehran, and invited his students to follow. Khomeini accepted the invitation and took up residence at the Dar al-Shafa school in Qom. Khomeini's studies included Islamic law (sharia) and jurisprudence (fiqh), but by that time, Khomeini had also acquired an interest in poetry and philosophy (irfan). So, upon arriving in Qom, Khomeini sought the guidance of Mirza Ali Akbar Yazdi, a scholar of philosophy and mysticism. Yazdi died in 1924, but Khomeini continued to pursue his interest in philosophy with two other teachers, Javad Aqa Maleki Tabrizi and Rafi'i Qazvini. However, Khomeini's biggest influences were Mohammad Ali Shah Abadi, and historic Sufi mystics Mulla Sadra and Ibn Arabi.
Khomeini studied ancient Greek philosophy and was influenced by both the philosophy of Aristotle, whom he regarded as the founder of logic, and Plato, whose views "in the field of divinity" he regarded as "grave and solid". Among Islamic philosophers, Khomeini was mainly influenced by Avicenna and Mulla Sadra. Apart from philosophy, Khomeini was interested in literature and poetry. His poetry collection was released after his death. Beginning in his adolescent years, Khomeini composed mystic, political and social poetry. His poetry works were published in three collections: The Confidant, The Decanter of Love and Turning Point, and Divan. His knowledge of poetry is further attested by the modern poet Nader Naderpour (1929–2000), who "had spent many hours exchanging poems with Khomeini in the early 1960s". Naderpour remembered: "For four hours we recited poetry. Every single line I recited from any poet, he recited the next."
Ruhollah Khomeini was a lecturer at Najaf and Qom seminaries for decades before he was known on the political scene. He soon became a leading scholar of Shia Islam. He taught political philosophy, Islamic history and ethics. Several of his students, for example Morteza Motahhari, later became leading Islamic philosophers and also marja'. As a scholar and teacher, Khomeini produced numerous writings on Islamic philosophy, law, and ethics.

bio: Ayman bin 'Ubiad (c. 594–630 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca.
bio_full:
Ayman bin 'Ubiad was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Mecca during the early seventh century. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed the initial development of the Islamic community during its formative years in the Arabian Peninsula.

As one of the Sahaba, Ayman bin 'Ubiad belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct personal contact with Prophet Muhammad and received religious instruction firsthand. This status holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Ayman bin 'Ubiad is noted as being part of the early ascetic tradition within Islam. This suggests he was among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline, self-restraint, and devotion to worship as central aspects of their religious practice. The early ascetic movement in Islam represented those believers who sought to deepen their spiritual connection through practices such as extended prayer, fasting, and withdrawal from worldly pursuits.

Living in Mecca during this period placed Ayman bin 'Ubiad at the center of significant historical developments. Mecca was not only the birthplace of Islam but also the location where the early Muslim community faced considerable challenges, including persecution from the established tribal and commercial interests that dominated the city. The early Meccan period of Islam, roughly from 610 to 622 CE, was characterized by the gradual revelation of the Quran and the steady growth of the Muslim community despite opposition.

His death in 630 CE occurred during a pivotal moment in Islamic history, coinciding with the period when Muslim influence was expanding throughout the Arabian Peninsula. By this time, the Muslim community had established itself in Medina and was in the process of consolidating its position across the region.

The legacy of companions like Ayman bin 'Ubiad lies in their role as foundational figures who helped establish and preserve the earliest Islamic traditions. Their direct experience with the Prophet Muhammad and their participation in the early Muslim community provided crucial continuity for the transmission of Islamic knowledge and practices to future generations of Muslims.

bio: Aymen bin Khuraym bin Fatik (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Poet-Companion.
bio_full:
Aymen bin Khuraym bin Fatik was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE in the Hijaz region, he belonged to the generation that witnessed the emergence and establishment of the Islamic community.

As one of the Sahaba, Aymen was among those who personally knew and interacted with Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime. This direct association placed him within the most revered circle in Islamic tradition, as the companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and the earliest witnesses to the Prophet's example.

Aymen is particularly distinguished by his recognition as a "Poet-Companion," indicating his dual role as both a religious figure and a literary contributor to early Islamic culture. Poetry held significant cultural importance in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society, serving as a primary means of communication, documentation, and artistic expression. Poets were highly respected for their linguistic skills and their ability to preserve and transmit cultural memory through verse.

His involvement in hadith sciences reflects the crucial role that companions played in preserving and transmitting the sayings, actions, and teachings of Prophet Muhammad. The companions served as the first generation of Islamic scholarship, responsible for collecting and passing down the foundational texts and practices that would later develop into formal Islamic sciences.

Living during the pivotal decades of Islamic expansion, Aymen's lifetime spanned the period from the pre-Islamic era through the early caliphate. His death around 635 CE occurred during the reign of the second caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab, a time when the Islamic community was rapidly expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

The significance of figures like Aymen lies in their role as bridges between the prophetic period and subsequent Islamic generations. As both companions and early transmitters of Islamic knowledge, they helped establish the foundations upon which later Islamic scholarship, jurisprudence, and literary traditions would develop. Their testimonies and preserved accounts became essential sources for understanding the early Islamic period and the authentic teachings of Islam.

While specific details about his individual contributions to poetry or hadith transmission may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, his recognition as both a companion and poet-contributor represents the diverse ways in which early Muslims participated in building and preserving their religious and cultural heritage.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Ayyadh bin Ghanm bin Zuhayr (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Ayyadh bin Ghanm bin Zuhayr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community.

Ayyadh is historically recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event that took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge, referenced in the Quran (48:18), involved approximately 1,400 Muslims who swore allegiance to Prophet Muhammad under a tree, demonstrating their loyalty and commitment during a tense diplomatic situation with the Meccan tribes. The Quranic verse specifically praises those who participated in this pledge, stating that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance.

As a sahabi (companion of the Prophet), Ayyadh belonged to the generation of Muslims who directly interacted with Muhammad and learned Islamic teachings firsthand. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's sayings and practices, which later formed the foundation of hadith literature. Their testimonies and narrations became essential sources for understanding Islamic law, theology, and the early history of the Muslim community.

Ayyadh's participation in the Pledge of Ridwan places him among a select group of companions who demonstrated unwavering loyalty during a critical moment in early Islamic history. The Hudaybiyyah expedition marked a turning point in relations between the Muslim community and the Meccan tribes, ultimately leading to the peaceful conquest of Mecca two years later.

The companions who participated in this pledge were held in special regard within the Muslim community, as their commitment was specifically acknowledged in the Quran. Their role extended beyond their lifetime, as later generations of Muslims looked to their example and teachings as authoritative sources for religious guidance.

Ayyadh bin Ghanm bin Zuhayr died around 640 CE, during the early period of Islamic expansion under the Rashidun Caliphate. His legacy, like that of other companions, lies primarily in his role as a witness to the Prophet's teachings and his contribution to the preservation of early Islamic tradition through the generation that directly experienced the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of the first Muslim community.

bio: Ayyash bin Abi Rabi'a (c. 593–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Makhzum clan of Quraysh in Mecca. His father, Abu Rabi'a, was Amr ibn al-Mughira, and his mother was Asma bint Makhraba of the Tamim tribe. Through her he was a half-brother of Abu Jahl and al-Harith ibn Hisham, and Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabi'a was his full brother. His kunya is given as Abu Abd al-Rahman or Abu Abd Allah.

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr say he accepted Islam early, before the Prophet began meeting his followers in the house of al-Arqam. They report that he emigrated to Abyssinia with his wife Asma bint Salama, and that their son Abd Allah was born there, though Musa ibn Uqba and Abu Ma'shar did not list him among those emigrants. He later returned to Mecca and emigrated to Medina with Umar ibn al-Khattab. Soon after, Abu Jahl and al-Harith came to him claiming his mother had vowed not to comb her hair or sit in shade until she saw him. Against Umar's warning he went back with them, and on the road they tied him up and brought him to Mecca as a prisoner. The Prophet prayed for his rescue, together with Salama ibn Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Walid, in a supplication reported by Abu Hurayra in Sahih al-Bukhari.

Accounts of his death differ. Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Hibban say he was killed at the Battle of Yarmouk; al-Bukhari and Ibn Abi Hatim say he died in Syria during Umar's conquests, and Ibn Qani' gives 15 AH (636 CE). Ibn Sa'd and al-Tabari instead report that he died in Mecca. His sons Abd Allah and al-Harith narrated from him.
