primaryTitle: Sabir — The Patient, Model of Endurance
titles: Ayyub · Job · al-Sabir · model of patience and gratitude amid suffering
dating_source: Book of Job; Islamic tradition places Ayyub among descendants of Ishaq
dating_note: Ayyub/Job; dating uncertain, tradition varies widely.
bio: Ayyūb ibn Maws ibn Rā'il ibn 'Isāw (c. 1600–c. 1500 BCE) was a prophet, based in Hauran. Known as Sabir — The Patient, Model of Endurance.
bio_full:
Job (Arabic: أيوب, romanized: ʾAyyūb) is a prophet in Islam mentioned in the Quran. Job's story in Islam is parallel to the Hebrew Bible's story, although the main emphasis is on Job remaining steadfast to God; there is no mention of Job's discussions with friends in the Qur'anic text, but later Muslim literature states that Job had brothers, who argued with the man about the cause of his affliction. Some Muslim commentators also spoke of Job as being the ancestor of the Romans. Islamic literature also comments on Job's time and place of prophetic ministry, saying that he came after Joseph in the prophetic series and that he preached to his own people rather than being sent to a specified community. Tradition further recounts that Job will be the leader in Heaven of the group of "those who patiently endured".

In the Quran
ʾAyyūb (Job) is first mentioned in the Quran in the following verse:  Indeed, We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And we revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Descendants, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and to David We gave the book [of Zabur]. 
The Quran describes Job as a righteous servant of God, who was afflicted by suffering for a lengthy period of time. However, it clearly states that Job never lost faith in God and forever called to God in prayer, asking Him to remove his affliction:

 And [mention] Job, when he called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and you are the Most Merciful of the merciful."
The narrative goes on to state that after many years of suffering, God ordered Job to "Strike with thy foot!". At once, Job struck the ground with his foot and God caused a cool spring of water to gush forth from the Earth, from which Job could replenish himself. The Quran states that it was then that God removed his pain and suffering and He returned Job's family to him, blessed him with many generations of children and granted him great wealth. In addition to the brief descriptions of Job's narrative, the Quran further mentions Job twice in the lists of those whom God had given special guidance, wisdom and inspiration (4:163) and as one of the men who received authority, the gift of prophethood (6:84).
After Satan had given up trying to turn Job away from the Lord, God removed Job's affliction and returned his family to him, doubling them in number. He returned Job's wealth and showered Job with gold. Once Job's wife had seen her husband restored to prosperity and health, she prayed thanks to God but then worried over the oath her husband had taken earlier, in which he had promised to strike her with a hundred lashes. Job was also deeply grieved over the oath he had taken, amidst his suffering. God, however, sent a revelation to Job, which told him to not beat his wife but to hit her once, using a bundle of a hundred blades of grass.
(this above part is no where mentioned in Quran)
and, 'Take in thy hand a bundle of rushes, and strike therewith, and do not fail in thy oath.' Surely We found him a steadfast man. How excellent a servant he was! He was a penitent.
[We said], "And take in your hand a bunch [of grass] and strike with it and do not break your oath." Indeed, We found him patient, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was one repeatedly turning back [to Allah]. 

Qur'anic commentary and Muslim tradition
Ibn Kathir narrates the story in the following manner. Job was a very rich person with much land, and many animals and children — all of which were lost and soon he was struck with skin disease as a test from God.  He was afflicted with sores that crawled with worms.  He remained steadfast and patient all along, so God eventually relieved him of the disease.

Job's lineage was an important field of study for many of the early Islamic scholars. A prevalent belief among early commentators was that Job descended from the line of Esau, the son of Ishaq. Although various commentators gave different genealogies relating to Job, all of them traced his ancestry to Abraham through Isaac's son Esau. Those scholars who traced Job's lineage back to Abraham did so by using the following Qur'anic verse as the basis for their view:"That was the reasoning about Us which We gave to Abraham (to use) against his people. We raise whom We will in degree, for thy Lord is full of wisdom and knowledge. We bestowed upon him [Abraham] Isaac and Jacob, all (three) We guided; and before him We guided Noah and among his progeny David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron. Thus do We reward those who do good."
Muslim historical literature fleshes out Job's story and describes him as being a late descendant of the patriarch Noah. Similar to the Hebrew Bible's narrative, Ibn Kathir mentions that Satan heard the angels of God speak of Job as being the most faithful man of his generation. Job, being a chosen prophet of God, would remain committed in daily prayer and would frequently call to God, thanking God for blessing him with abundant wealth and a large family. But Satan planned to turn the God-fearing Job away from God and wanted Job to fall into disbelief and corruption. Therefore, God allowed Satan to afflict Job with distress and intense illness and suffering, as God knew that Job would never turn away from his Lord. Although Job's possessions were destroyed and he suffered many calamities, he remained steadfast in his worship of God and remained committed to his religion. Satan then appeared to Job in the guise of an old man and suggested that God was not rewarding Job for his prayer. Job, however, rebuked Satan and told him that God is all-knowing and does what He thinks is best. It is said that then Satan, having failed at tempting Job, turned to Job's wife, who was also a faithful woman. Satan reminded Job's wife of her life before Job's affliction and how they were abundant in family and fortune. Job's wife, although she did not lose faith, burst into tears and asked Job to tell God to remove this suffering from the household. Job, in his misery, rebuked his wife and told her that this suffering had been for a relatively short period of time and, without thinking, swore that he would beat her with 100 strokes for complaining. After Job was cured, God ordered him to take some grass and to hit her once with 100 blades of grass. By doing this, Job fulfilled his promise to God but didn't hurt her. This Islamic narrative has now become symbolic and is often used by Islamic preachers as a reminder to be kind with wives.
Philip K. Hitti asserted that the subject was an Arab and the setting was Northern Arabia.

The plant known in English as Job's tears (Coix lacryma-jobi) takes its name from Arabic دموع أيوب (dumūʿ ʾAyyūb), the name used by Arab merchants who introduced the plant to Europe in the Middle Ages.

full: Ayyūb ibn Abi Tamīma Kaysān al-Sakhtiyānī al-Baṣrī
primaryTitle: Abū Bakr al-Baṣrī — Imām of the Hadith Scholars of Basra
titles: Abū Bakr al-Baṣrī · Sayyid Aḥdāth al-Baṣra (Master of the Youth of Basra — per Hasan al-Basri) · Imām Ahl al-Baṣra
source: al-Dhahabī — Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ · Ibn Ḥajar — Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb · al-Mizzī — Tahdhīb al-Kamāl
bio: Ayyūb ibn Abi Tamīma Kaysān al-Sakhtiyānī al-Baṣrī (approximate–certain) was a historical figure of the Hadith Sciences tradition, based in Basra. Known as Abū Bakr al-Baṣrī — Imām of the Hadith Scholars of Basra.
bio_full:
Ayyūb ibn Abi Tamīma Kaysān al-Sakhtiyānī al-Baṣrī was a prominent scholar of hadith sciences who lived from approximately 687 to 748 CE. Based in the important Iraqi city of Basra, he became known by the honorary title Abū Bakr al-Baṣrī and earned recognition as an imam among the hadith scholars of his city.

Al-Sakhtiyānī belonged to the generation known as the Tabi'un, the "Followers" who came after the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad but who had the opportunity to learn directly from them. This positioned him as a crucial link in the early transmission of Islamic knowledge, particularly in the developing science of hadith collection and verification.

Basra, where al-Sakhtiyānī spent his scholarly career, was one of the major intellectual centers of the early Islamic world. The city served as a hub for religious learning and attracted scholars from across the Islamic territories. In this environment, al-Sakhtiyānī established himself as a leading authority in hadith sciences, the discipline concerned with collecting, authenticating, and transmitting the sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad.

As a member of the Tabi'un generation, al-Sakhtiyānī's work was particularly significant because he helped bridge the gap between the earliest Islamic community and later generations of Muslims. His scholarly activities contributed to the systematic preservation of prophetic traditions during a critical period when the oral transmission of religious knowledge was being supplemented by more formal methods of collection and documentation.

The title "Imam of the Hadith Scholars of Basra" indicates the high regard in which his contemporaries held him. This recognition suggests that he played a leadership role among the religious scholars of his city and that his expertise in hadith sciences was widely acknowledged. His work would have been essential in establishing the methodological foundations that later hadith scholars would build upon.

Al-Sakhtiyānī's contributions to Islamic scholarship occurred during the Umayyad period, a time when Islamic legal and religious sciences were still in their formative stages. His efforts in hadith sciences helped establish the scholarly traditions that would become central to Islamic religious education and jurisprudence in subsequent centuries.

bio: Az-Zubair ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. The sources record 2 family or contemporary relations.
bio_full:
Az-Zubair ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Mecca during the early seventh century. Born around 595 CE, he was part of the Hashemite clan of the Quraysh tribe and died in 635 CE, shortly after the death of the Prophet.

As a member of the Sahaba, Az-Zubair was among those who personally knew and interacted with Muhammad during his prophetic mission. The Sahaba constitute a foundational generation in Islamic history, as their testimonies and accounts form a crucial part of the hadith literature that preserves the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad.

Az-Zubair's connection to hadith sciences reflects the important role that companions played in transmitting Islamic teachings to subsequent generations. The companions served as the primary witnesses to the Prophet's conduct and teachings, and their reports became essential sources for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and practice. Through their testimonies, later scholars were able to compile comprehensive collections of prophetic traditions.

Living in Mecca, Az-Zubair would have witnessed the early development of the Islamic community during a period of significant social and religious transformation. Mecca was the birthplace of Islam and the center of the Prophet's initial preaching, making it a crucial location for understanding the origins and early spread of the faith.

The historical sources indicate that Az-Zubair had family and contemporary relationships that connected him to the broader network of early Muslims. These social connections were significant in the early Islamic community, as they often determined patterns of support, alliance, and the transmission of religious knowledge.

Az-Zubair's significance lies primarily in his status as a direct witness to the prophetic period and his role in the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings. Like other companions, he represents a vital link between the time of revelation and the later Islamic scholarly tradition. His contributions to hadith sciences helped ensure that the teachings and example of Prophet Muhammad were accurately preserved for future generations of Muslims.

The companion's relatively brief life span, ending just three years after the Prophet's death in 632 CE, places him squarely within the foundational period of Islamic history when the basic principles and practices of the faith were being established and codified.

bio: Āzar ibn Nāhūr ibn Sārūgh (legendary–legendary) was a founding figure, based in Ur of the Chaldees. Known as Father of Ibrahim — Named in the Quran.
bio_full:
Azar ibn Nahur ibn Sarugh is a figure mentioned in the Quran as the father of the prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). According to Islamic sources, he lived in Ur of the Chaldees, an ancient city in Mesopotamia, during what would correspond to approximately the 18th century BCE based on traditional chronologies.

The Quran identifies Azar as Ibrahim's father in Surah Al-An'am, where Ibrahim confronts his father about idol worship, saying "O Azar, do you take idols as gods?" This places Azar within the broader Quranic narrative of Ibrahim's rejection of polytheism and his call to monotheism. Islamic tradition presents Azar as an idol maker or seller, representing the polytheistic practices that Ibrahim would later challenge.

Azar's significance in Islamic history stems primarily from his role as the father of Ibrahim, who is revered as one of the most important prophets in Islam and is called "Khalil Allah" (Friend of God). The relationship between Azar and Ibrahim serves as a foundational narrative illustrating the tension between old polytheistic traditions and the emerging monotheistic message that would become central to Abrahamic faiths.

The Quranic account describes Ibrahim's attempts to guide his father away from idol worship, highlighting themes of filial respect balanced with religious conviction. Despite Ibrahim's efforts, the text suggests that Azar remained committed to his traditional beliefs, creating a paradigmatic story about the challenges faced by those who call others to monotheism.

While Azar appears in the Quran, his historicity and the details of his life remain within the realm of religious narrative rather than documented historical fact. The biblical tradition refers to Abraham's father as Terah rather than Azar, representing one of the differences between Islamic and Judeo-Christian scriptural accounts.

In Islamic tradition, Azar's story is primarily understood through his relationship with Ibrahim and serves as an early example of the conflict between established religious practices and prophetic calls to reform. His mention in the Quran establishes him as a significant figure in the genealogy of prophetic history, even as he represents opposition to the monotheistic message that would define Ibrahim's mission and legacy.

titles: Hazret-i Hudayi · Pir-i Tarikat
_merge_notes: merged from F1945 on 20260422_193715: dob kept 1541; filled=[]
bio: Aziz Mahmud Hüdayi (1541–1628), was one of the most renowned Sufi saints of the Ottoman Empire. A mystic, poet, composer, and influential Hanafi-Maturidi scholar, he served as a spiritual advisor to several
bio_full:
Aziz Mahmud Hüdayi (1541–1628), (b. Şereflikoçhisar, d. Üsküdar) was one of the most renowned Sufi saints of the Ottoman Empire. A mystic, poet, composer, and influential Hanafi-Maturidi scholar, he served as a spiritual advisor to several

Sultans. while popular tradition often links him to the Ottoman imperial family, he is most celebrated as the founder of the Jelveti Sufi Order.

Born in Central Anatolia, Aziz Mahmud Hudayi completed his studies in a medrese in Istanbul. He became the Sheikh of Sultan Ahmed I who constructed the famous Blue Mosque and so read the first Friday prayer there on its opening. He was also especially respected by Sultan Murad III. He is a descendant of Junayd of Baghdad, and, as a descendant of Husayn ibn 'Ali, can be called a sayyid.

He founded the Jelveti (Turkish: Celveti) order of sufis and served as a qadi (Islamic judge, kadı in Turkish) in Edirne, Egypt, Sham (Syria), and Bursa. A murid (disciple) and khalifah (successor) of Üftade Hazretleri of Bursa, he wrote about thirty works, seven of them in Turkish. Mustafa Gaibi, a prominent sufi from Ottoman Bosnia, was one of his disciples.

His supplication prompted many sailors of the Ottoman Navy to visit his grave before going out to sea: Those who visit us when we are alive, and those who visit our grave after our death and read the Fatiha when passing by our tomb are ours. May those who love us not drown at sea, may they not suffer poverty in their old age, and may they not pass away without saving their faith.

He died in Üsküdar, Istanbul and was buried on a site which is now enclosed within a mosque complex that remains a site of pilgrimage and devotion. By 1855 it was in ruins but was restored and expanded by Sultan Abdülmecid I.

The small stone house in which he lived is a few miles away from the complex. The 19th-century Üsküdar-born artist Hoca Ali Riza painted a watercolour of the house standing alone in what was then countryside. A foundation named after him now maintains the house which has become the Çilehane Mescid overlooked by the large new Çilehane Cami.

Along with Yahya Efendi, Telli Baba, and Yuşa (Joshua), Aziz Mahmud Hudayi is considered to be one of the Four Patron Saints of the Bosphorus.

Mustafa Devati, a successor

full: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad Baba Kuhi al-Shirazi
titles: Patron Saint of Shiraz · Qutb al-Aqtab of Fars
bio: Baba Kuhi of Shiraz was a 10th- and 11th-century Persian Sufi mystic. Probably born in Shiraz. As a young man he met the Arab poet Al-Mutanabbi and the well-known Sufi Abū ʿAbdallāh Moḥammad.
bio_full:
Baba Kuhi of Shiraz was a Persian Sufi mystic and poet who lived from 948 to 1037 CE, spanning the late 10th and early 11th centuries. He was likely born in Shiraz, the major city in the Fars province of present-day Iran, during a period when Persian Islamic culture was flourishing under various regional dynasties.

As a young man, Baba Kuhi encountered significant literary and spiritual figures of his time, including the renowned Arab poet Al-Mutanabbi, one of the most celebrated poets in Arabic literature, and the Sufi master Abū ʿAbdallāh Moḥammad. These encounters likely influenced his development as both a poet and a mystic, connecting him to the broader intellectual networks of the Islamic world.

Baba Kuhi belonged to the Khorasan School of Persian poetry, a literary tradition that emerged in the eastern regions of the Islamic world and played a crucial role in developing Persian as a literary language. This school was instrumental in establishing many of the forms and themes that would characterize Persian poetry for centuries to come.

As a Sufi mystic, Baba Kuhi participated in the rich tradition of Islamic mysticism that sought direct spiritual experience of the divine. Sufism during this period was becoming increasingly organized and influential throughout the Islamic world, with practitioners like Baba Kuhi contributing to its literary and spiritual development.

His significance lies in his contribution to the early development of Persian Sufi poetry, which would later reach its zenith with figures like Rumi and Hafez. The 10th and 11th centuries were formative periods for Persian literature, as poets were establishing Persian as a vehicle for sophisticated religious and mystical expression alongside Arabic.

Baba Kuhi lived during a time of political fragmentation in the Islamic world, when the Abbasid Caliphate's central authority was weakening and regional powers were asserting independence. Despite this political instability, or perhaps because of it, this period saw remarkable cultural and literary productivity, particularly in Persian-speaking regions.

His work represents an important link in the chain of Persian mystical poetry, bridging earlier Arabic Sufi traditions with the distinctively Persian voice that would come to dominate Islamic mystical literature. Through his poetry and spiritual practice, Baba Kuhi contributed to the rich tapestry of Islamic intellectual and cultural life during a pivotal period in its development.

full: Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur ibn Umar Shaykh Mirza
primaryTitle: Founder of the Mughal Empire — The Tiger
titles: Zahir al-Din · Padshah
bio: Babur was the founder of the Mughal Empire in the Indian subcontinent. He was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan through his father and mother respectively. He was also given the posthumous name of Firdaws Makani.
bio_full:
Babur (Persian: ببر, Persian: [bɑː.βuɾ]; 14 February 1483 – 26 December 1530; born Zahīr ud-Dīn Muhammad) was the founder of the Mughal Empire in the Indian subcontinent. He was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan through his father and mother respectively. He was also given the posthumous name of Firdaws Makani ('Dwelling in Paradise').
Born in Andijan in the Fergana Valley (now in Uzbekistan), Babur was the eldest son of Umar Shaikh Mirza II (1456–1494, Timurid governor of Fergana from 1469 to 1494) and a great-great-great-grandson of Timur (1336–1405). Babur ascended the throne of Fergana in its capital Akhsikath in 1494 at the age of twelve and faced rebellion. He conquered Samarkand two years later, only to lose Fergana soon after. In his attempt to reconquer Fergana, he lost control of Samarkand. In 1501, his attempt to recapture both the regions failed when the Uzbek prince Muhammad Shaybani defeated him and founded the Khanate of Bukhara.
In 1504, he conquered Kabul, which was under the putative rule of Abd ur-Razaq Mirza, the infant heir of Ulugh Beg II. Babur formed a partnership with the Safavid emperor Ismail I and reconquered parts of Turkestan, including Samarkand, only to again lose it and the other newly conquered lands to the Shaybanids.
After losing Samarkand for the third time, Babur turned his attention to India and employed aid from the neighbouring Safavid and Ottoman empires. He defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the Sultan of Delhi, at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 and founded the Mughal Empire. Before the defeat of Lodi at Delhi, the Sultanate of Delhi had been a spent force, long in a state of decline.
The ruler of the adjacent Kingdom of Mewar, Rana Sanga, advanced on Babur with a grand coalition of Rajput and Afghan warlords, engaging Babur in the Battle of Khanwa. Babur achieved a decisive victory due to his skillful troop positioning and use of gunpowder. The battle was one of the most decisive events in Indian history and was a watershed event in the Mughal conquest of North India.
Religiously, Babur started his life as a staunch Sunni Muslim, but he underwent significant evolution. Babur became more tolerant as he conquered new territories and grew older, allowing other religions to peacefully coexist in his empire and at his court. He also displayed a certain attraction to theology, poetry, geography, history, and biology—disciplines he promoted at his court—earning him a frequent association with representatives of the Timurid Renaissance. His religious and philosophical stances are characterized as humanistic.
Babur married several times. Notable among his children were Humayun, Kamran Mirza, Hindal Mirza, Masuma Sultan Begum, and the author Gulbadan Begum. Babur died in 1530 in Agra and Humayun succeeded him. Babur was first buried in Agra but, as per his wishes, his remains were moved to Kabul and reburied. He ranks as a national hero in Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Many of his poems have become popular folk songs. He wrote the Baburnama in Chaghatai Turkic; it was translated into Persian during the reign (1556–1605) of his grandson, the emperor Akbar.

Name
Ẓahīr-ud-Dīn is Arabic for "Defender of the Faith" (of Islam), and Muhammad honours the Islamic prophet. The name was chosen for Babur by the Sufi saint Khwaja Ahrar, who was the spiritual master of his father. The difficulty of pronouncing the name for his Central Asian Turco-Mongol army may have been responsible for the greater popularity of his nickname Babur, also variously spelled Baber, Babar, and Bābor. The name is generally taken in reference to the Persian word babur (ببر), meaning "tiger" or "panther". The word repeatedly appears in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and was borrowed into the Turkic languages of Central Asia.

Background

Babur's memoirs form the main source for details of his life. They are known as the Baburnama and were written in Chagatai, his first language, though, according to Dale, "his Turkic prose is highly Persianized in its sentence structure, morphology or word formation and vocabulary." Baburnama was translated into Persian during the rule of Babur's grandson Akbar.
Babur was born on 14 February 1483 in the city of Andijan, Fergana Valley, contemporary Uzbekistan. He was the eldest son of Umar Shaikh Mirza II, ruler of the Fergana Valley, the son of Abū Saʿīd Mirza (and grandson of Miran Shah, who was himself son of Timur) and his wife Qutlugh Nigar Khanum, daughter of Yunus Khan, the ruler of Moghulistan and a descendant of Genghis Khan.
Babur hailed from the Turkic Barlas tribe, which was of Mongol origin and had embraced the Turco-Persian tradition They had also converted to Islam centuries earlier and resided in Turkestan and Khorasan.
Aside from the Chaghatai Turkic, Babur was equally fluent in Classical Persian, the lingua franca of the Timurid elite.
Some of Babur's relatives, such as his uncles Mahmud Khan (Moghul Khan) and Ahmad Khan, continued to identify as Mongols, and allowed him to use their Mongol troops to help recover his fortunes in the turbulent years that followed.
Hence, Babur, though nominally a Mongol (or Moghul in Persian language), drew much of his support from the local Turkic and Iranian people of Central Asia, and his army was diverse in its ethnic makeup. It included Sarts, Tajiks, ethnic Afghans, Arabs, as well as Barlas and Chaghatayid Turko-Mongols from Central Asia.

Ruler of Central Asia

As Timurid ruler of Fergana

In 1494, eleven-year-old Babur became the Timurid ruler of Fergana, in present-day Uzbekistan, after his father Umar Sheikh Mirza died "while tending pigeons in an ill-constructed dovecote that toppled into the ravine below the palace". During this time, two of his uncles from the neighbouring kingdoms, who were hostile to his father, and a group of nobles who wanted his younger brother Jahangir to be the ruler, threatened his succession to the throne. His uncles were relentless in their attempts to dislodge him from this position as well as from many of his other territorial possessions to come. Babur was able to secure his throne mainly because of help from his maternal grandmother, Aisan Daulat Begum, although there was also some luck involved.
Most territories around his kingdom were ruled by his relatives, who were descendants of either Timur or Genghis Khan, and were constantly in conflict. At that time, rival princes were fighting over the city of Samarkand to the west, which was ruled by his paternal cousin. Babur had a great ambition to capture the city. 

In 1497, he besieged Samarkand for seven months before eventually gaining control over it. He was fifteen years old and for him the campaign was a huge achievement. Babur was able to hold the city despite desertions in his army, but he later fell seriously ill. Meanwhile, a rebellion back home, approximately 350 kilometres (220 mi) away, amongst nobles who favoured his brother, robbed him of Fergana. As he was marching to recover it, he left Samarkand to Sultan Mahmud Mirza, leaving him with neither territory in his possession. He had held Samarkand for 100 days, and he considered this defeat as his biggest loss, obsessing over it even later in his life after his conquests in India.
For three years, Babur concentrated on building a strong army, recruiting widely amongst the Tajiks of Badakhshan in particular. In 1500–1501, he again laid siege to Samarkand, and indeed he took the city briefly, but he was in turn besieged by his most formidable rival, Muhammad Shaybani, Khan of the Uzbeks. The situation became such that Babur was compelled to give his sister, Khanzada, to Shaybani in marriage as part of the peace settlement. Only after this were Babur and his troops allowed to depart the city in safety. Samarkand, his lifelong obsession, was thus lost again.

full: Badīʿ al-Zamān Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Hamadhānī
primaryTitle: Wonder of the Age — Inventor of the Maqama Literary Form
titles: Badīʿ al-Zamān (Wonder of the Age)
bio: Badi' al-Zamān al-Hamadānī or al-Hamadhānī was a medieval poet and man of letters. He is best known for his work the Maqamat Badi' az-Zaman al-Hamadhani, a collection of 52 episodic stories of a rogue, Abu al-Fath al-Iskandari, as recounted by a narrator, 'Isa b. Hisham. His Persian name, Hamedani, translates to "from the city of Hamedan." His Arabic name translates into "The Wonder of the Age".
bio_full:
Badi al-Zaman al-Hamadhani was a medieval Arabic writer and poet whose innovative literary contributions helped shape the development of Arabic prose literature. Born in 968 CE and dying in 1008 CE, he lived during the later Abbasid period, a time when Arabic literature was flourishing across the Islamic world. His name translates to "The Wonder of the Age," reflecting the high regard in which his contemporaries held his literary talents.

Al-Hamadhani hailed from Hamadan, a city in western Iran, as indicated by his nisba (geographical surname). Despite his Persian origins, he wrote primarily in Arabic, which was the dominant literary language of the Islamic world during his era. He represents the cosmopolitan nature of Islamic civilization, where scholars and writers from diverse ethnic backgrounds contributed to a shared Arabic literary tradition.

His most significant and enduring contribution to Arabic literature is the Maqamat, a collection of 52 episodic stories that introduced a new literary genre to Arabic prose. These tales feature a clever rogue named Abu al-Fath al-Iskandari, whose adventures and schemes are recounted by a narrator called Isa ibn Hisham. The stories are characterized by their elaborate rhetorical style, wordplay, and the protagonist's ability to talk his way out of difficult situations through eloquence and wit.

The Maqamat genre that al-Hamadhani pioneered became extremely influential in Arabic literature. His work established a template that would be followed and refined by later writers, most notably al-Hariri of Basra, whose own Maqamat became even more famous. The genre's emphasis on linguistic virtuosity, entertaining narratives, and social commentary made it a popular form that persisted for centuries.

Al-Hamadhani's literary innovation lay in combining entertainment with linguistic artistry. His stories served both as showcases for Arabic rhetorical skills and as vehicles for social observation. The episodic nature of the Maqamat, with their recurring characters and varied settings, provided a flexible framework that allowed for both linguistic experimentation and social commentary.

His work represents an important development in the evolution of Arabic prose literature, moving beyond the more formal historical and religious texts that had previously dominated the field toward a more creative and entertaining form of literary expression that would influence Arabic writing for generations to come.

full: Baha ud-Din Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Bakri
titles: Sultan al-Ulama
bio: Baha ud-Din Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Bakri (1148–1231) was a mystic of the Khorasan School tradition, based in Balkh. Known as Sultan al-Ulama — Father of Rumi.
bio_full:
Baha ud-Din Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Bakri (1148–1231) was a prominent Islamic mystic and scholar who belonged to the Khorasan School of Sufism. Born in the mid-12th century, he established himself as a respected religious teacher in Balkh, a major center of Islamic learning in present-day Afghanistan.

Known by the honorific title "Sultan al-Ulama" (King of Scholars), Baha ud-Din Walad gained recognition for his deep knowledge of Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and mystical teachings. He attracted numerous students and followers who gathered around him to study both the exoteric and esoteric dimensions of Islam. His scholarship encompassed traditional Islamic sciences while emphasizing the inner spiritual dimensions of the faith characteristic of the Khorasan mystical tradition.

The political upheavals of his time, including the advancing Mongol invasions that would eventually devastate much of Central Asia, forced Baha ud-Din to leave Balkh with his family and followers. This migration took them through various cities across the Islamic world, including Nishapur, Baghdad, Mecca, Damascus, and eventually to Konya in Anatolia, where they settled under the patronage of the Seljuk rulers.

Baha ud-Din's most enduring legacy lies in his role as the father and first spiritual teacher of Jalal ud-Din Rumi, who would become one of the most celebrated mystic poets in Islamic history. The mystical foundation that Baha ud-Din provided to his son significantly influenced Rumi's later spiritual development and poetic expression. Through his teachings and personal example, he transmitted the spiritual traditions of the Khorasan School to a new generation.

His written works include the "Ma'arif," a collection of mystical discourses and teachings that provide insight into his spiritual methodology and understanding of the mystical path. These texts reveal his emphasis on divine love, spiritual purification, and the importance of a qualified spiritual guide in the mystical journey.

Baha ud-Din Walad died in Konya in 1231, where he had spent his final years teaching and guiding his community. His influence extended beyond his immediate circle through his son Rumi and the subsequent establishment of the Mevlevi Sufi order, which would preserve and propagate many of the spiritual principles he embodied and taught.

full: Khwaja Muhammad Baha al-Din Shah Naqshband al-Bukhari
titles: Shah Naqshband (King of the Engraved Heart) · Qutb al-Zaman · Founder of Naqshbandiyya
bio: Baha' al-Din Muhammad Naqshband was the eponymous founder of what became one of the largest Sufi Sunni orders, the Naqshbandi.
bio_full:
Baha' al-Din Muhammad Naqshband (Persian: بهاءالدین محمد نقشبند; 1318–1389) was the eponymous founder of what became one of the largest Sufi Sunni orders, the Naqshbandi.

Baha al-Din was born in March 1318 in the village of Qasr-i Hinduvan, near Bukhara. Like the majority of the region's sedentary population, Baha al-Din was a Tajik, i.e. a speaker of Persian and a participant in its culture. According Encyclopædia Iranica, the texts that claim Baha al-Din was descended from the Islamic prophet Muhammad through Ja'far al-Sadiq (died 765), should be "treated with reserve". Early texts do not mention Baha al-Din's supposed ancestry to Muhammad, but they do imply that his teacher Amir Kulal (died 1370) was a descendant of Muhammad through Ja'far al-Sadiq, which may suggest that their genealogies were later conflated.

Annemarie Schimmel highlights the descent of Bahauddin from Hasan al-Askari, referring to Khwaja Mir Dard's family and "many nobles, from Bukhara; they led their pedigree back to Baha al-Din Naqshband, after whom the Naqshbandi order is named, and who was a descendant, in the 13th generation of the 11th imam al-Hasan al-Askari".

Three days after his birth, Baha al-Din was adopted as a spiritual son by Baba Mohammad Sammasi, a master of the Khwajagan, a Sufi order founded by Yusuf Hamadani (died 1140). Baha al-Din's paternal grandfather brought him to Sammasi, where he was the latter's murid (novice). Sammasi later entrusted Baha al-Din's training to his distinguished student Amir Kulal.

Early texts do not mention how Baha al-Din gained the nickname "Naqshband", nor its meaning. An agreement was later partly reached that it referred to the naqsh (imprint) of the name of Allah that is embedded in the heart through constant prayer. In Bukhara, Baha al-Din became its patron saint and was commonly referred to as "Khwaja Bala-gardan" by its inhabitants.

Some historians agree that the original Naqshbandi had a particularly Iranian or Khurasanian attitude, which according to Encyclopædia Iranica is supported by the fact that Baha al-Din was surrounded by a company of urban dwellers who mostly spoke Tajik. However, the Naqshbandi had been influenced by Turkic Sufi order, the Yasawiyya. Three generations after Baha al-Din's death, the Naqshbandi started receiving support among the Turkic inhabitants of Central Asia, thus displaying an all-inclusive appeal.

Baha al-Din died on 2 March 1389 in Qasr-i Hinduvan, which was later renamed Qasr-i Arifan out of respect to him.

Algar, H. (1988a). "Bahāʾ-al-Dīn Naqšband". Encyclopædia Iranica, online edition, Vol. III, Fasc. 4. New York. pp. 433–435.{{cite encyclopedia}}:  CS1 maint: location missing publisher (link)

Algar, H. (1988b). "Bābā Sammāsī". Encyclopædia Iranica, online edition, Vol. III, Fasc. 3. New York. pp. 294–295.{{cite encyclopedia}}:  CS1 maint: location missing publisher (link)

full: Baha al-Din Zakariya ibn Muhammad al-Multani
titles: Shaykh al-Islam of Multan · Imam of Suhrawardiyya in South Asia
bio: Bahauddin Zakariya, also known as Baha-ul-Haq, was a Sunni Muslim scholar, saint and poet who established the Suhrawardiyya order of Baghdad in medieval South Asia, later becoming one of the most influential spiritual leaders of his era.
bio_full:
Bahauddin Zakariya (c.1170 – 1262), also known as Baha-ul-Haq, was a Sunni Muslim scholar, saint and poet who established the Suhrawardiyya order of Baghdad in medieval South Asia, later becoming one of the most influential spiritual leaders of his era.

Life
Zakariya was born in 1161 or 1182. His family was of Hashimid lineage, and thus traced their descent back to Asad ibn Hashim, one of the ancestors of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Baha al-Din's family was originally from the Khwarazm region in Central Asia, but had settled in Kut Karur in the Punjab region, near the city of Multan. His father was Wajih al-Din Muhammad, while his mother was the daughter of Husam al-Din Tirmidhi.
For fifteen years, Zakariya travelled to different cities in southern Punjab, where the order was able to attract large numbers of converts from Hinduism. Zakariya finally settled in Multan in 1222. Under his influence, Multan became known as "Baghdad of the East," and is referred by Zakariya in his Persian poetry:

Zakariya became a vocal critic of Multan's ruler at the time, Nasir-ud-Din Qabacha, and sided with Iltutmish, the Mamluk Sultan of Delhi when he overthrew Qabacha in 1228. Zakariya's support was crucial for Iltutmish's victory, and so he was awarded the title Shaikh-ul-Islam by Iltutmish to oversee the state's spiritual matters, in gratitude for his support. Zakariya was also granted official state patronage by the Sultan.
During his lifetime, Zakariya befriended Lal Shahbaz Qalandar - a widely revered Sufi saint from Sindh, and founder of the Qalandariyya order of wandering dervishes. As Shaikh-ul-Islam, Zakariya was able to assuage orthodox Muslims, who were offended by the Lal Shahbaz Qalandar's teachings. Zakariya, Shahbaz Qalandar, Baba Farid and Syed Jalalauddin Bukhari, together became the legendary Haq Char Yaar, or "Four friends" group, which is highly revered among South Asian Muslims.

Spiritual philosophy
Zakariya's Tariqat, or Sufi philosophical orientation, was to the renowned Persian Sufi master Shahab al-Din Abu Hafs Umar Suhrawardi of Baghdad. The Suhrawardi order rejected a life of poverty, as espoused by the Chisti order that was more prevalent in the Lahore region. Instead, the Suhrawardis believed in ordinary food and clothing, and rejected the Chisti assertion that spirituality lay upon a foundation of poverty. The Suhrawardis also rejected the early Chisti practice of dissociation from the political State.
Zakariya's preachings emphasized the need to conform to usual Islamic practices like fasting (roza) and alms-giving (zakat), but also advocated a philosophy of scholarship (ilm) combined with spirituality. His emphasis on teaching all humans, regardless of class or ethnicity, set him apart from his contemporary Hindu mystics.
He did not reject the traditional of spiritual music that was heavily emphasized in Chisti worship, but only partook in it on occasion. He rejected the Chisti tradition of bowing in reverence to religious leaders - a practice that may have been borrowed from Hinduism.

Impact
Zakariya's teachings spread widely throughout southern Punjab and Sindh, and drew large numbers of converts from Hinduism. His successors continued to exert strong influences over southern Punjab for the next several centuries, while his order spread further east into regions of northern India, especially in Gujarat and Bengal.

Shrine

Baha-ud-Din Zakariya died in 1268 and his mausoleum (Darbar) is located in Multan. The mausoleum is a square of 51 ft 9 in (15.77 m), measured internally. Above this is an octagon, about half the height of the square, which is surmounted by a hemispherical dome. The mausoleum was almost completely ruined during the Siege of Multan in 1848 by the British, but was soon afterward restored by local Muslims.
Many pilgrims visit his shrine at the time of his urs from different parts of Pakistan and beyond.

Writings
Awrad-e-Shaikhush Shuyukh: Al-Awrad : Awrad-e-Suhrawardy
( اوراد شيخ‌ الشيوخ‌  : الاوراد : اوراد سهروردي‌)

Commemorative honors
Bahauddin Zakaria Express train is named after him, which runs between Karachi and Multan.
Bahauddin Zakariya University located in Multan is named after him which is the largest institution in southern Punjab.

Notes

References

Sources
Arya, Gholam-Ali (2015). "Bahāʾ al-Dīn Abū Muḥammad Zakariyyāʾ Multānī". In Fleet, Kate; Krämer, Gudrun; Matringe, Denis; Nawas, John; Rowson, Everett (eds.). Encyclopaedia of Islam (3rd ed.). Brill Online. ISSN 1873-9830.

bio: Bahhath bin Tha'laba bin Hazama (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Bahhath bin Tha'laba bin Hazama was a companion (sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE. He lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula and was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Bahhath is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE. This battle was the first major military encounter between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces, and it holds profound significance in Islamic history. The Muslim victory at Badr, despite being significantly outnumbered, was interpreted by early Muslims as divine confirmation of their cause and marked a turning point in the establishment of Islam as a political and religious force in Arabia.

As a "Companion of Badr," Bahhath belonged to a distinguished group within early Islamic society. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr were held in special esteem by later Muslim generations, as this battle demonstrated their early commitment to Islam and their willingness to risk their lives for the nascent Muslim community. The Qur'an references this battle and its participants, further cementing their status in Islamic tradition.

Bahhath's tribal lineage traces to the Hazama clan, indicating his integration into the complex tribal structure of Arabian society during the early seventh century. His presence in Medina suggests he was either among the local inhabitants who accepted Islam or was part of the community that formed around the Prophet after the migration from Mecca.

He died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. This places his death during a period of rapid Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula, though his specific role, if any, in these later developments is not clearly documented in available historical sources.

Bahhath's significance lies primarily in his status as an early supporter of Islam and his participation in one of the most consequential battles in Islamic history. His life span encompasses the entire prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic expansion, making him a witness to the transformation of Islam from a local religious movement to a major political force.

primaryTitle: Sultan of Poets — Greatest Ottoman Divan Poet
titles: Sulṭānu l-Şuʿarāʾ (Sultan of Poets)
bio: Bâḳî (باقى) was the pen name of the Ottoman Turkish poet Mahmud Abdülbâkî. Bâkî came to be known as Sultânüş-şuarâ, or "Sultan of poets".
bio_full:
Mahmud Abdulbaki, known by his pen name Bâkî (Arabic: باقي, 1526-1600 CE / 932-1008 AH), was an Ottoman poet of the classical period and one of the most celebrated literary figures of the sixteenth century. He was given the official title Sultanü'ş-Şuara — 'Sultan of Poets' — by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent and is considered, alongside Fuzuli, the supreme poet of Ottoman classical literature.

Born in Istanbul to a humble family — his father was a muezzin at the Fatih Mosque — he received his initial training as a saddle-maker before his evident literary talent led him into the medrese system. He studied under leading scholars of the age, including Karamanizade Mehmed Efendi and Kadiri Hamid Efendi, and entered government service through the patronage of Sultan Suleiman, who personally admired his poetry.

His diwan contains some of the most refined examples of the Ottoman ghazal — short, polished, intensely musical lyric poems on themes of love, wine, beauty, and the transience of worldly power. His most famous single work is the Kanunî Mersiyesi, the elegy on the death of Sultan Suleiman in 1566, which remains a touchstone of Ottoman elegiac literature for its restrained grief and meditation on the impermanence of empire.

Bâkî held a series of major religious-judicial offices, rising through the Ottoman ulema hierarchy to become Kazasker (Chief Military Judge) of both Anatolia and Rumelia — the second-highest religious-judicial post in the empire. He was a candidate for the office of Sheikh ul-Islam several times but was passed over, in part because of court rivalries.

His verse drew on the full Persian classical tradition — Hafiz, Sa'di, Jami — and on earlier Ottoman masters, but transformed it into a distinctly Ottoman idiom of urbane wit and aristocratic precision. He is buried in Eyüp, Istanbul. His influence on later Ottoman court poetry was decisive.

full: Muhammad Bali ibn Yusuf al-Shumuznawi al-Sofyawi
titles: Sultans' Shaykh
bio: Muhammad Bali ibn Yusuf al-Shumuznawi al-Sofyawi (c. 1490–1552) was a mystic of the Naqshbandiyya tradition, based in Sofia. Known as Sultans' Sufi — Shaykh of Sokollu.
bio_full:
Muhammad Bali ibn Yusuf al-Shumuznawi al-Sofyawi, known as Bali Efendi, was an influential Islamic mystic who lived from approximately 1490 to 1552. He belonged to the Naqshbandiyya Sufi order, one of the major mystical traditions in Islam, and was based in Sofia, which was then part of the Ottoman Empire.

Bali Efendi earned the distinctive title "Sultans' Sufi," reflecting his notable connections to Ottoman imperial circles. This designation suggests he held a position of considerable respect and influence within the religious hierarchy of the empire. His epithet as "Shaykh of Sokollu" indicates his role as spiritual guide to members of the prominent Sokollu family, who would later produce significant Ottoman statesmen including Grand Vizier Mehmed Pasha Sokollu.

As a representative of the Naqshbandiyya tradition, Bali Efendi was part of a Sufi order known for its emphasis on silent dhikr (remembrance of God), adherence to Islamic law, and often close relationships with political authorities. The Naqshbandiyya had spread throughout the Islamic world and was particularly influential in Central Asia, Anatolia, and the Balkans during this period.

His base in Sofia placed him in a strategically important city within the Ottoman Empire's European territories. Sofia served as a significant administrative and cultural center in the Balkans, making it a suitable location for a religious figure with connections to the imperial court and prominent families.

The period of Bali Efendi's life coincided with the height of Ottoman expansion under sultans like Selim I and Suleiman the Magnificent. During this era, Sufi orders played important roles in the empire's religious and social life, often serving as bridges between the state and various communities.

Bali Efendi's significance lies in his representation of the integration between Sufi mysticism and Ottoman political culture during the empire's classical period. His connections to influential families and his designation as "Sultans' Sufi" illustrate the important role that mystical teachers played in Ottoman society, serving not only as spiritual guides but also as figures who helped maintain the religious legitimacy and cultural cohesion of the empire's diverse populations.

full: Banū Mūsā: Muḥammad, Aḥmad, al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā ibn Shākir
primaryTitle: Three Brothers — Pioneers of Mechanics and Mathematics
bio: Banū Mūsā: Muḥammad, Aḥmad, al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā ibn Shākir (c. 800–c. 873) was a scientist of the Islamic Sciences tradition, based in Baghdad. Known as Three Brothers — Pioneers of Mechanics and Mathematics.
bio_full:
The Banū Mūsā, literally the Sons of Musa, refers to a Persian family of polymaths, astronomers, mathematicians, and engineers active in 9th century Baghdad. Both their own contributions and their direct connections to other prominent scholars of the House of Wisdom mark them as one of the most preeminent figures of the Islamic Golden Age.
The term Banū Mūsā is derived from the name of Mūsā ibn Shākir, and most commonly refers to his three sons; Muḥammad ibn Mūsā (before 803 – February 873); Aḥmad ibn Mūsā (d. 9th century); and Al-Ḥasan ibn Mūsā (d. 9th century). 
Mūsā ibn Shākir  was a renowned astronomer serving directly under the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun. After his death, his three sons received an education under al-Ma'mun’s direct orders, and were enrolled at the House of Wisdom in  Baghdad. There they undertook the translation of ancient Greek works acquired from Byzantium, which they used to develop their own technological, mathematical and astronomical ideas. They were some of the earliest scholars to adopt Greek mathematics, but innovative in their approach to the concepts of area and circumference by expressing them using numerical values instead of ratios. They made geodesic measurements to determine the length of a degree of latitude, and so obtained a relatively accurate value for the circumference of the Earth.
The Banū Mūsā wrote almost 20 books, all but three of which are now lost. The most important of all their works was a treatise on geometry, Kitāb Maʿrifah masāḥat al-ashkāl al-basīṭah wa-al-kuriyyah ("Book on the Measurement of Plane and Spherical Figures"), which was used extensively by medieval mathematicians. Their most famous extant work (of which the oldest and most reliable copy is in the Topkapi Sarayi in Istanbul) is Kitab al-Hiyal al-Naficah ("Book of Ingenious Devices"). It describes 100 inventions, many of which were pouring vessels, intended to entertain party guests. Some of their innovations, such as those that involved 
fluid pressure variations and valves, remained unsurpassed until the modern period. One of those inventions includes an automatic flute player that may have been the first programmable machine or computer.

Biographical details

Early years
The Banu Musa were the three sons of Mūsā ibn Shākir, who earlier in life had been a highwayman and astronomer in Khorasan of unknown pedigree. After befriending al-Ma'mun, who was then a governor of Khorasan and staying in Merv, Musa was employed as an astrologer and astronomer. 
After Musa's death, the three orphaned children were cared for at the court of al-Maʾmūn, who made the senior Baghdad official Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Mus'abi their guardian. Al-Ma’mun recognized their abilities, and enrolled them in the House of Wisdom, an institution created by him as a centre for collecting, translating and studying books from other lands. In Baghdad, where they apparently lived for the rest of their lives, the three brothers studied geometry, mechanics, music, mathematics and astronomy, trained by a senior court astrologer, Yaḥyā bin Abī Manṣūr.
The three brothers, Moḥammad, Aḥmad, and Ḥasan, are often listed in what is assumed to be their order of seniority.

Accomplishments under the Abbasid Caliphate
The Banū Mūsā assisted al-Ma'mun's in his obsession to obtain and translate works from Greek into Arabic. They sent for Greek texts from the Byzantines, or travelled themselves to Byzantium to acquire them. During their working lives they used their wealth and energy towards the translation of these works. On his way home to Baghdad from Byzantium, Muhammad met and recruited Thābit ibn Qurra, a money changer from Harran. Thābit went on to make important discoveries in algebra, geometry, and astronomy.
Under the direction of al-Ma'mun, the Banū Mūsā worked with the most talented men available, including al-Khwarizmi, al-Kindi, Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf ibn Maṭar, and the mathematician and translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq, who became a close friend of one of the brothers, Muhammad. Of  the translators, three were paid about 500 dinars a month. None of the brothers were medically trained, and relied upon Ishaq bin Hunayn and Thabit bin Qurra to translate Greek medical works. They exchanged ideas with other experts, including the astrologer Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi, with whom Muhammed was in continuous contact.
The brothers are likely to have used portable instruments such as armillary spheres or dials when making their observations, which were recorded from around 847 to 869. From their Baghdad home, they observed stars in the constellation Ursa Major In 847–848, and measured the maximum and minimum altitudes of the Sun in 868–869. They also observed the September equinox in the city of Samarra. To calculate the difference in latitude between Samarra and Nishapur, they organized simultaneous observations of a lunar eclipse.
Whilst working for al-Ma’mun, the Banū Mūsā travelled to a desert near Sanjar, in northern Mesopotamia, with the aim of measuring the length of a degree of latitude along a meridian, and from that verifying a value of 25,000 miles (40,000 km) obtained by the Greeks for the Earth's circumference. They first measured the altitude of the Pole Star, and then, using pegs and a rope as they moved north, stopped again when the altitude of the star changed by one degree. They repeated the same measurement, this time travelling southwards. The process was repeated at al-Kufa. From their measurements, the brothers obtained a value for the circumference of the Earth of 24,000 miles (39,000 km).
Under the patronage of the caliphs that followed al Ma’mun—al-Mu'tasim, al-Wathiq, and al-Mutawakkil—the brothers continued to acquire great wealth and become influential in court. They used much of their wealth to collect the works of ancient writers, a practise that was later copied by other scholars at the House of Wisdom. The brothers were very active during the reign of al-Mutawakkil, who was interested in mechanics, and asked the Banū Mūsā to write on this subject. A son of al-Mu'tasim was educated by Ahmad, but the brothers' relations with the caliph are otherwise unknown. When close to death, al-Mu'tasim's successor al-Wathiq called together his astrologers, including Muhammed, who erroneously pronounced that the caliph would live for another 50 years.

Involvement in politics
The Banū Mūsā's employment by the caliphs for different civil engineering projects, including their involvement in the building of the city of al-D̲j̲aʿfariyya for al-Mutawakki, led to them becoming involved in court politics. In 860, the Banū Mūsā and Mutawakkil’s architects were involved in obtaining land for a new city. The caliph’s advisor suggested that Muhammed and Ahmad bin Musa should be forced to contribute towards the expense of a new palace nearby.
The peak of Muhammad's political activity came towards the end of his life, when Turkish commanders were starting to take control of the state. After the death of al-Mutawakkil, Muhammad helped al-Mustaʿīn to become nominated as caliph. Denied the throne, Al-Mustaʿīn's brother besieged Baghdad, and Muhammad was sent to estimate the size of the attacking army. After the siege, he was sent to find out the terms for al-Mustaʿīn to abdicate.

Jaʻfariyya canal
It was during the reigns of al-Wathiq and al-Mutawakkil that internal rivalries arose between the scholars there. The Banū Mūsā became enemies of al-Kindi, and assisted in his persecution by al-Mutawakkil. They criticized and ridiculed his treatise on the astrolabe, and caused al-Mutawakkil to have him beaten, removed from court, and his library confiscated.

bio: Baraka bint Yasar (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Baraka bint Yasar was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and a freedwoman (mawla) of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb of Quraysh. Abu Nu'aym, citing Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri through Musa ibn Uqba, lists her among those who emigrated from Mecca to Abyssinia, travelling with her husband Qays ibn Abd Allah al-Asadi. Ibn Abd al-Barr, citing Ibn Ishaq and Musa ibn Uqba, likewise says she emigrated to Abyssinia with her husband, whom he names Qays ibn Abd al-Asad.

Ibn Abd al-Barr also discusses a report about a woman named Baraka who served Umm Habiba bint Abi Sufyan and came with her from Abyssinia. He first suggests she might be Umm Ayman, who was also named Baraka, then identifies her as Baraka bint Yasar. The sources consulted give no details of her children or her death.

bio: Barira, the client of 'Aisha (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Emigrant and Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Barira was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. Originally enslaved, she became the client (freed slave) of 'Aisha bint Abi Bakr, the Prophet's wife, through the Islamic institution of manumission that encouraged the freeing of slaves.

As one of the early converts to Islam, Barira was among the emigrants (muhajirun) who left Mecca for Medina during the hijra period, demonstrating her commitment to the nascent Muslim community despite the social and economic challenges this entailed. Her status as both a freed slave and female emigrant places her among a significant group of early Muslims who sacrificed material security for religious conviction.

Barira's most lasting contribution to Islamic scholarship lies in her role as a narrator of hadith. She transmitted sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad, contributing to the body of prophetic traditions that would later form one of the primary sources of Islamic law and theology. Her narrations were considered reliable by early Islamic scholars, reflecting the trust placed in her character and memory by the Muslim community.

Her close association with 'Aisha, one of the most prominent figures in early Islam and herself a major hadith narrator, likely provided Barira with unique access to prophetic traditions and Islamic teachings. This relationship exemplifies the complex social dynamics of early Islamic society, where bonds of clientage created networks of religious and social transmission that transcended traditional hierarchies.

The preservation of Barira's name and status in Islamic historical sources reflects the early Muslim community's recognition of contributions made by individuals regardless of their social origins. Her inclusion among the companions acknowledged by Islamic tradition demonstrates how the faith provided pathways for social mobility and religious authority for formerly enslaved individuals.

Barira's death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, meaning she witnessed both the prophetic period and the initial expansion of Islamic governance beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her legacy endures primarily through the hadith literature, where her narrations continue to be studied as part of the foundational texts of Islamic jurisprudence and theology.

bio: Barra bint Abi Tajra (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Yemen. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Barra bint Abi Tajra was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in the Arabian Peninsula during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she died in 635 CE, making her a contemporary of the foundational years of Islam.

Barra is historically significant as one of the female narrators of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial component of Islamic religious guidance alongside the Quran. Her role as a hadith narrator places her among the women who contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings during the religion's formative period.

As a sahabiyya, Barra belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad, a status that holds particular reverence in Islamic tradition. The companions, both male and female, are considered the primary sources for understanding the Prophet's teachings and the early Islamic community's practices.

Her association with Yemen indicates the geographic spread of early Islamic influence beyond the Hijaz region of western Arabia where Islam first emerged. Yemen's inclusion in the early Muslim community demonstrates the religion's expansion throughout the Arabian Peninsula during Prophet Muhammad's lifetime and immediately following his death in 632 CE.

The preservation of Barra's name and her identification as a hadith narrator reflects the recognized role that women played in the early Islamic scholarly tradition. Female companions who transmitted religious knowledge were acknowledged contributors to Islamic learning, and their narrations were considered legitimate sources of religious guidance.

Barra's death in 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following Prophet Muhammad's death when the first four caliphs led the Muslim community. Her relatively short life span, dying at approximately forty years of age, was not uncommon for the era.

While specific details about the content of her hadith narrations or the extent of her scholarly activities are not well-documented in widely available historical sources, her inclusion among recognized female hadith narrators indicates her participation in the crucial early process of Islamic knowledge transmission. This role contributed to the broader foundation of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice that would develop in subsequent generations.

bio: Barrah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca.
bio_full:
Barra bint Abd al-Muttalib was a paternal aunt of the Prophet Muhammad, a daughter of Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim of Quraysh. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Fatima bint Amr ibn A'idh of the Makhzum clan, so she was a full sister of Abd Allah, the Prophet's father, and of Abu Talib.

In the pre-Islamic period she married Abd al-Asad ibn Hilal of Makhzum and bore him Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Asad, a Companion who fought at Badr and was the husband of Umm Salama before she married the Prophet. She later married Abu Ruhm ibn Abd al-Uzza of the Amir ibn Lu'ayy clan and bore him Abu Sabra, who also fought at Badr.

Whether she lived to see Islam is uncertain. Ibn Sa'd's entry does not say that she accepted Islam, and al-Dhahabi states that she did not live to see the start of the Prophet's mission. The date of her death is not recorded in the sources consulted.

bio: Basbas bin 'Amr bin Tha'laba (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Basbas bin 'Amr bin Tha'laba was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE. He lived in Medina during the early period of Islam and was among those who directly interacted with and followed the Prophet during his lifetime.

Basbas is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle, fought between the early Muslim community and the Meccan Quraysh tribe, holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are held in special esteem within Islamic tradition due to their early commitment to Islam and their willingness to risk their lives for the nascent Muslim community when its survival was uncertain.

As a sahabi, Basbas belonged to the generation that witnessed the revelation of the Quran and observed the Prophet's teachings firsthand. The companions are considered by Muslims to be crucial transmitters of Islamic knowledge, practices, and traditions that would later be compiled into hadith literature and Islamic jurisprudence. Their direct experience with the Prophet's example (sunnah) made them invaluable sources for understanding proper Islamic conduct and worship.

Living in Medina, Basbas would have been present during the formative years of the first Muslim community, when the basic institutions and practices of Islam were being established. This period saw the development of the Muslim calendar, the codification of prayer practices, the establishment of social welfare systems, and the formation of the constitutional framework known as the Constitution of Medina.

Basbas died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the rule of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. His death came just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's passing, during a period when the Muslim community was consolidating its position in the Arabian Peninsula and beginning its expansion beyond the region.

While specific details about Basbas's individual contributions or particular roles within the early Muslim community are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his status as a Companion of Badr ensures his place in Islamic historical memory as one of those who supported the Prophet during a critical moment in the religion's early development.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Basheer bin 'Atik (c. 597–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Basheer bin 'Atik was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the early Muslims who became part of the close circle of followers surrounding the Prophet during the establishment of the Islamic community in Medina.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Basheer bin 'Atik was witness to the crucial early decades of Islamic history when the religion was taking shape and the Muslim community was establishing itself in the Hijaz region of Arabia. The companions held special significance in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly received teachings from Prophet Muhammad and participated in the foundational events of the faith.

Basheer bin 'Atik is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, fought in 625 CE near Medina between the Muslim community and the Meccan forces. This battle was one of the significant early military engagements that helped define the survival and growth of the nascent Islamic state. The battle proved challenging for the Muslim forces, with the tide of conflict shifting multiple times throughout the engagement.

During this battle, Basheer bin 'Atik lost his life while fighting alongside his fellow Muslims, earning him recognition as a martyr. In Islamic tradition, those who die in defense of the faith and community are honored with the designation of shahid, or martyr, which carries special religious significance.

His death in 634 CE, the same year as the Prophet Muhammad's passing, places him among those companions who lived through the entire Medinan period of Islamic history but did not witness the rapid expansion that would follow under the subsequent Caliphate. The companions who died during these early conflicts are remembered for their sacrifice in defending the early Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

Basheer bin 'Atik represents the dedication of the early Muslim community members who committed themselves to the defense of their faith and society during a time of significant challenge and transformation in Arabian society. His story reflects the experiences of many early Muslims who made personal sacrifices during Islam's foundational era.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Basheer bin 'Unbus bin Zayd (c. 597–635 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Basheer bin 'Unbus bin Zayd was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he lived during the transition from the pre-Islamic period to the establishment of the early Muslim community.

As one of the Sahaba, Basheer was among those who personally knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime. The companions played a crucial role in the early Islamic community, serving as direct witnesses to the Prophet's teachings and participating in the foundational events that shaped the religion. Their testimonies and accounts became essential sources for understanding Islamic doctrine and the Prophet's example.

Basheer was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the political and spiritual heart of the expanding Islamic state, and those who lived there during this period were witnesses to the development of Islamic law, governance, and community practices.

Basheer is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, where he died as a martyr in 635 CE. The Battle of Uhud was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces, taking place in 625 CE near Medina. This battle was significant in early Islamic history as it tested the resolve of the Muslim community and provided important lessons about unity and obedience to leadership during warfare.

The concept of martyrdom (shahada) holds special significance in Islamic tradition, and those who died fighting in defense of the early Muslim community are honored for their sacrifice. Basheer's death at Uhud places him among those companions who gave their lives during the crucial early conflicts that determined the survival and expansion of Islam.

His relatively short life span of approximately 38 years encompassed the entire prophetic period and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate. Like many of the early companions, Basheer represents the generation that directly experienced the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices, making the Sahaba collectively important as the first Muslim community and the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings to subsequent generations.

bio: Abu al-Nu'man Bashir ibn Sa'd al-Ansari was a prominent companion (Sahaba) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and a leader of the Banu Khazraj tribe in Medina. A veteran of the Battle of Badr, Bashir was among the early converts from the Ansar and was one of the few individuals of his era literate in Arabic.
bio_full:
Abu al-Nu'man Bashir ibn Sa'd al-Ansari (Arabic: بَشِيرٍ بْنُ سَعْدٍ, romanized: Abū al-Nuʿmān Bashīr ibn Saʿd al-Anṣārī; died 633 CE) was a prominent companion (Sahaba) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and a leader of the Banu Khazraj tribe in Medina. A veteran of the Battle of Badr, Bashir was among the early converts from the Ansar and was one of the few individuals of his era literate in Arabic.
Bashir is historically best known for his decisive role during the Saqifah gathering following Muhammad's death in 632 CE. He was the first member of the Ansar to pledge allegiance (Bay'ah) to Abu Bakr, an act credited with breaking the tribal deadlock between the Khazraj and Banu Aws and ensuring the stability of the early Rashidun Caliphate. He served as a military commander in several expeditions during Muhammad's lifetime and was later martyred during the Muslim conquest of Persia at the Battle of Ayn al-Tamr while serving under Khalid ibn al-Walid.

Family and lineage
Bashir belonged to the Al-Harith branch of the Banu Khazraj. His full lineage is recorded as Bashir ibn Sa’d ibn Tha‘laba ibn Khallas ibn Zayd ibn Malik al-Agharr ibn Tha‘laba ibn Ka‘b. His mother was Unaysa bint Khalifa ibn ‘Adi ibn ‘Amr. Bashir was married to Amra bint Rawaha, the sister of the poet-commander Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. They had two children: a son, Nu'man ibn Bashir, and a daughter, Ubayya.
He had a full brother, Simak ibn Sa'd al-Ansari, who was also a companion of Muhammad and a veteran of the battles of Badr and Uhud. Bashir was notable for being literate, a rare skill in the Jahiliyya period, and was known to write in Arabic before the advent of Islam.

Biography

Era of Muhammad
Bashir participated in the Battle of Badr (624 CE). The Muslim forces included figures such as Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and Zubayr ibn al-Awwam. The army famously relied on limited transport, with seventy camels and two horses shared among the men. 
In Shaban 7 AH (December 628 CE), Bashir commanded the Expedition of Bashir Ibn Sa’d al-Ansari (Fadak) against the Banu Murra. During the encounter, thirty Muslims were ambushed; twenty-nine were killed, and Bashir was severely wounded in the heel. He was initially presumed dead but managed to recover after being sheltered by a local resident in Fadak.
In Shawwal 7 AH, he led a second mission to the region of Yemen and al-Jabar against the Banu Ghatafan, which resulted in the capture of spoils and a safe return to Medina. Later that year, during the First Pilgrimage, Muhammad appointed him to oversee the Muslim army's weaponry.

Succession at Saqifa

Upon the death of Muhammad in 632 CE, a leadership dispute arose at the Saqifah of Banu Sa'ida. While many of the Ansar favored Sa'd ibn Ubadah, Bashir intervened to advocate for unity. Despite the tensions between the Muhajirun and Ansar, Bashir was the first of the Ansar to offer his Bay'ah (oath of allegiance) to Abu Bakr. His support was pivotal, as it prompted members of the rival Banu Aws tribe to also pledge allegiance, effectively securing Abu Bakr's position as the first Caliph.

Death
During the caliphate of Abu Bakr, Bashir joined the conquest of Iraq. He was martyred in 633 CE (12 AH) at the Battle of Ayn al-Tamr while serving under the command of Khalid ibn al-Walid.

Hadith narration
Bashir is the subject of a foundational Hadith concerning parental equity. His son, Nu'man ibn Bashir, reported that Bashir once attempted to give him a specific gift and sought Muhammad's blessing:

Bashir said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have given this son of mine a slave who belonged to me as a present." The Messenger of Allah said: "Have you given a present to all your children?" He said: "No." He said: "Then take (your present) back."
This report serves as a primary source for the Islamic jurisprudence requirement that parents treat all their children with fairness.

See also
List of expeditions of Muhammad
Expedition of Bashir Ibn Sa’d al-Ansari (Fadak)

Bibliography

bio: Bashira bint al-Harith (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Bashira bint al-Harith was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the helpers of Medina who supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra (migration) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions based in Medina, Bashira bint al-Harith would have witnessed and participated in the crucial early decades of Islamic history when the Muslim community was establishing itself as both a religious and political entity. The Ansar played a vital role in providing refuge, support, and resources to the Prophet Muhammad and the Meccan emigrants (Muhajirun) who had fled persecution in their hometown.

The designation of sahabiyya places Bashira bint al-Harith among the women who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime and embraced Islam during this foundational period. Female companions held significant positions within the early Muslim community, often serving as teachers, transmitters of religious knowledge, and active participants in community affairs.

Living during the pivotal years between approximately 595 and 635 CE, Bashira bint al-Harith's lifespan encompassed the revelation of the Quran, the establishment of the first Muslim state in Medina, and the early expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, just a few years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

The historical record of individual female companions from this period is often limited, reflecting the documentary practices and priorities of early Islamic historiography. However, the recognition of Bashira bint al-Harith as a notable companion indicates her meaningful participation in the early Muslim community. The preservation of her name and basic biographical details in historical sources demonstrates the important role that women of the Ansar played in supporting and sustaining the nascent Islamic community during its most critical formative years in Medina.
