bio_full:
Dara Shikoh  (20 March 1615 – 30 August 1659), also transliterated as Dara Shukoh, was the eldest son and heir-apparent of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. Dara was designated with the title Padshahzada-i-Buzurg Martaba (lit. 'Prince of High Rank') and was favoured as a successor by his father and his elder sister, Princess Jahanara Begum. He had been given the title of 'Shah-e-Buland Iqbal' by Shah Jahan. In the war of succession which ensued after Shah Jahan's illness in 1657, Dara was defeated by his younger brother Prince Muhiuddin (later, the Emperor Aurangzeb). He was executed in 1659 on Aurangzeb's orders after a bitter struggle for the imperial throne.
Dara was a liberal-minded unorthodox Muslim as opposed to the orthodox Aurangzeb; he authored the work The Confluence of the Two Seas, which argues for the harmony of Sufi philosophy in Islam and Vedanta philosophy in Hinduism. A great patron of the arts, he was also more inclined towards philosophy and mysticism rather than military pursuits. The course of the history of the Indian subcontinent, had Dara Shikoh prevailed over Aurangzeb, has been a matter of some conjecture among historians.

Early life

Muhammad Dara Shikoh was born on 20 March 1615 in Ajmer, Rajasthan. He was the first son and third child of Prince Shahib-ud-din Muhammad Khurram and his second wife, Mumtaz Mahal. The prince was named by his father. 'Dara' means owner of wealth or star in Persian while the second part of the prince's name is commonly spelled in two ways: Shikoh (terror) or Shukoh (majesty or grandeur). Thus, Dara's full name can be translated as "Of the Terror of Darius" or "Of the Grandeur of Darius", respectively. Historian Ebba Koch favours 'Shukoh'.
Dara Shikoh had thirteen siblings of whom six survived to adulthood: Jahanara Begum, Shah Shuja, Roshanara Begum, Aurangzeb, Murad Bakhsh, and Gauhara Begum. He shared a close relationship with his  sister, Jahanara. As part of his formal education, Dara studied the Quran, history, Persian poetry and calligraphy. He was a liberal-minded unorthodox Muslim unlike his father and his younger brother Aurangzeb. Persian was Dara's native language, but he also learned Hindi, Arabic and later Sanskrit.
In October 1627, Dara's grandfather Emperor Jahangir died, and his father ascended the throne in January 1628 taking the regnal name 'Shah Jahan'. In 1633, Dara was appointed as the Vali-ahad (heir-apparent) to his father. He and his older sister Jahanara were Shah Jahan's favourite children.

Marriage

During the lifetime of his mother Mumtaz Mahal, Dara Shikoh was betrothed to his half-cousin, Princess Nadira Banu Begum, the daughter of his paternal uncle Sultan Parvez Mirza. He married her on 1 February 1633 at Agra amidst great celebrations, pomp and grandeur. By all accounts, Dara and Nadira were devoted to each other and Dara's love for Nadira was so profound that unlike the usual practice of polygyny prevalent at the time, he never contracted any other marriage. The imperial couple had seven children together; among them three sons, Sulaiman Shikoh, Mumtaz Shikoh, and Sipihr Shikoh, and a daughter, Jahanzeb Banu Begum, survived to play important roles in future events.
A great patron of the arts, Dara ordered for the compilation of some refined artwork into an album which is now famous by the name of 'Dara Shikoh Album'. This album was presented by Dara to his wife, Nadira Banu Begum, in 1641. It is one of the few Mughal albums that have their original miniatures, calligraphy, and original covers intact. 
Dara had at least two concubines, Gul Safeh (also known as Rana Dil) and Udaipuri Mahal (a Georgian or Armenian slave girl). Udaipuri later became a part of Aurangzeb's harem after her master's defeat.

Military service

 On 10 September 1642, Shah Jahan formally confirmed Dara Shikoh as his heir, granting him the title of Shahzada-e-Buland Iqbal ("Prince of High Fortune") and promoting him to command of 20,000-foot and 20,000 horse. In 1645, he was appointed as subahdar (governor) of Allahabad. He was promoted to a command of 30,000-foot and 20,000 horse on 18 April 1648, and was appointed Governor of the province of Gujarat on 3 July.

The struggle for succession

On 6 September 1657, the illness of emperor Shah Jahan triggered a desperate struggle for power among the four Mughal princes, though realistically only Dara Shikoh and Aurangzeb had a chance of emerging victorious. Shah Shuja was the first to make his move, declaring himself Mughal Emperor in Bengal and marching towards Agra from the east. Murad Baksh allied himself with Aurangzeb.

Intellectual pursuits

Dara Shikoh is widely renowned as an enlightened paragon of the harmonious coexistence of heterodox traditions on the Indian subcontinent. He was an erudite champion of mystical religious speculation and a poetic diviner of syncretic cultural interaction among people of all faiths. This made him a heretic in the eyes of his orthodox younger brother and a suspect eccentric in the view of many of the worldly power brokers swarming around the Mughal throne. Dara Shikoh was a follower of the Armenian Sufi-perennialist mystic Sarmad Kashani, as well as Lahore's famous Qadiri Sufi saint Mian Mir, whom he was introduced to by Mullah Shah Badakhshi (Mian Mir's spiritual disciple and successor). Mian Mir was so widely respected among all communities that he was invited to lay the foundation stone of the Golden Temple in Amritsar by the Sikhs.
Dara Shikoh subsequently developed a friendship with the seventh Sikh Guru, Guru Har Rai. Dara Shikoh devoted much effort towards finding a common mystical language between Islam and Hinduism. Towards this goal he completed the translation of fifty Upanishads from their original Sanskrit into Persian in 1657 so that they could be studied by Muslim scholars. His translation is often called Sirr-i-Akbar ("The Greatest Mystery"), where he states boldly, in the introduction, his speculative hypothesis that the work referred to in the Qur'an as the "Kitab al-maknun" or the hidden book, is none other than the Upanishads. His most famous work, Majma-ul-Bahrain ("The Confluence of the Two Seas"), was also devoted to a revelation of the mystical and pluralistic affinities between Sufic and Vedantic speculation. The book was authored as a short treatise in Persian in 1654–55.
In 1006 A.H, the prince had commissioned a translation of Yoga Vasistha, after both Vasistha and Rama appeared  in his dream. Translation was undertaken by Nizam al-Din Panipati and came to be known as the Jug-Basisht, which has since become popular in Persia among intellectuals interested in Indo-Persian culture. The Safavid-era mystic Mir Findiriski (d. 1641) commented on selected passages of Jug-Basisht.
The library established by Dara Shikoh still exists on the grounds of Ambedkar University, Kashmiri Gate, Delhi, and is now run as a museum by Archaeological Survey of India after being renovated.

Patron of arts

He was also a patron of fine arts, music and dancing, a trait frowned upon by his younger sibling Muhiuddin, later the Emperor Aurangzeb. The 'Dara Shikoh' is a collection of paintings and calligraphy assembled from the 1630s until his death. It was presented to his wife Nadira Banu in 1641–42 and remained with her until her death after which the album was taken into the royal library and the inscriptions connecting it with Dara Shikoh were deliberately erased; however not everything was vandalised and many calligraphy scripts and paintings still bear his mark.
Among the existing paintings from the Dara Shikoh Album, are two facing pages, compiled in the early 1630s just before his marriage, showing two ascetics in yogic postures, probably meant to be a pair of yogis, Vaishnava and Shaiva. These paintings are attributed to the artist Govardhan.

bio: Darar bin al-Khattab (b. c. 606 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Poet-Companion.
bio_full:
Darar bin al-Khattab was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early 7th century CE. Born around 606 CE, he was based in Mecca during the formative period of Islam and died in 646 CE, placing his life span during the crucial decades of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs.

Darar is distinguished among the companions primarily for his literary abilities, earning him recognition as a poet-companion. This designation reflects the important role that poetry played in Arabian society of the time, where skilled poets held positions of respect and influence. Poetry served not only as entertainment but also as a means of preserving tribal history, expressing cultural values, and engaging in political discourse.

As one of the Sahaba, the term used for companions of Prophet Muhammad, Darar belonged to the generation that witnessed the emergence and early development of Islam firsthand. The Sahaba are considered highly significant in Islamic tradition as they were direct witnesses to the Prophet's teachings and practices, making their accounts and experiences foundational to Islamic scholarship and jurisprudence.

The combination of Darar's status as both a companion and a poet suggests he may have contributed to the early Islamic literary tradition, though specific details about his poetic works or their content cannot be definitively established. During this period, many poets who embraced Islam used their skills to support and promote the new faith, creating works that celebrated Islamic values and defended the Muslim community against criticism.

Darar's life span covered the period of Islamic revelation, the early Muslim community's struggles in Mecca, and the subsequent expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula and beyond. His death in 646 CE occurred during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, by which time the Islamic state had expanded significantly beyond its original boundaries in the Hijaz region.

The preservation of Darar's name and his identification as a poet-companion indicates his recognized standing within the early Muslim community, though the specific nature of his contributions to Islamic literature and society remains within the broader context of the collective role played by the Sahaba in establishing and transmitting Islamic tradition to subsequent generations.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Darar bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Darar bin Maqrn al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early 7th century CE in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he belonged to the Mazni tribe and was active in the Hijaz region during the formative period of Islam.

Darar is most notably recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event in early Islamic history that took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge, also known as the Bay'at al-Ridwan, is referenced in the Quran in verse 48:18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those who pledged their allegiance under the tree. The historical context of this pledge relates to a critical moment when the Muslim community faced potential conflict, and the companions demonstrated their loyalty and commitment to the Prophet Muhammad.

As a sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Darar would have been among those early Muslims who had direct personal contact with Muhammad and played a role in the establishment and early expansion of the Islamic community. The companions held a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who witnessed the revelation of the Quran and participated in the foundational events of the faith.

Darar lived through the crucial period of Islamic history that included the Prophet's migration to Medina, the establishment of the first Muslim community, and the early military campaigns that secured the position of Islam in Arabia. His participation in the Pledge of Ridwan places him among those companions who were present during one of the most symbolically important moments of unity and commitment in early Islamic history.

He died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate period, when the Islamic state was rapidly expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the leadership of the first caliphs. Like many of the early companions, his life spanned the entire prophetic period and the beginning of Islam's expansion, making him a witness to the transformation of a small religious community into a major political and spiritual force in the region.

primaryTitle: Khalifa of God on Earth — Prophet-King and Psalmist
titles: Dawud · David · Khalifat Allah · recipient of the Zabur · slayer of Jalut (Goliath)
dating_source: Tel Dan Stele (1993 discovery) confirms 'House of David'; Finkelstein
dating_note: Dawud/David; now archaeologically attested via Tel Dan.
bio: David was, originally, leader of the Tribe of Judah who became the first king of the united Kingdom of Israel according to the Hebrew Bible and Old Testament.
bio_full: Dawud (David) is honoured in Islam as a prophet and messenger of God and as a righteous king of the Children of Israel. The Qur'an mentions him by name sixteen times. It relates that Dawud killed Jalut (Goliath), and that God then gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed (Q 2:251). God gave him the scripture called the Zabur, identified with the Psalms (Q 4:163, 17:55). The Qur'an calls Dawud "the man of strength" who constantly turned to God (Q 38:17). God commanded the mountains and the birds to echo His praise along with him (Q 21:79, 34:10), made iron mouldable for him, and taught him to make coats of armour (Q 21:80, 34:10–11). God made him a khalifa, a vicegerent, on earth (Q 38:26), a title the Qur'an otherwise gives only to Adam (Q 2:30). God gave both Dawud and his son Sulayman (Solomon) sound judgment and knowledge (Q 21:78–79), and gave Dawud the ability to distinguish truth from falsehood in judging (Q 38:20). The Qur'an also alludes to a test after which Dawud sought forgiveness, bowed down in repentance, and was forgiven (Q 38:24–25). According to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad said that the prayer and fasting most beloved to God were those of Dawud: he slept half the night, prayed for a third of it and slept for a sixth, and he fasted on alternate days.

titles: Shaykh al-Islam · Amir al-Muhaqqiqin
bio: Dawud ibn Mahmud al-Kayseri (c. 1261–c. 1350) was a scholar of the Akbarian tradition, based in Kayseri. Known as Shaykh al-Islam of the Ottomans.
bio_full:
Dawud ibn Mahmud al-Kayseri was a prominent Islamic scholar and mystic who lived during the 13th and 14th centuries, roughly from 1261 to 1350. Based in the Anatolian city of Kayseri, he became one of the most significant figures in the Akbarian tradition of Islamic mysticism, which followed the teachings of the renowned Sufi master Ibn Arabi.

Al-Kayseri distinguished himself as a leading interpreter and systematizer of Ibn Arabi's complex mystical philosophy. He authored several important works that helped make Ibn Arabi's teachings more accessible to subsequent generations of scholars and mystics. His most notable contribution was his commentary on Ibn Arabi's "Fusus al-Hikam" (The Bezels of Wisdom), which became one of the standard interpretive texts for understanding this foundational work of Islamic mysticism.

As a scholar of the Akbarian school, al-Kayseri focused on the metaphysical dimensions of Islamic thought, particularly concepts related to the unity of being and the relationship between the divine and creation. His writings demonstrate deep engagement with both the theoretical aspects of mystical philosophy and its practical applications for spiritual development.

Al-Kayseri's influence extended beyond purely academic circles. He held the prestigious title of Shaykh al-Islam among the early Ottomans, indicating his recognition as a supreme religious authority. This position placed him at the intersection of scholarly learning and practical governance during a formative period in Ottoman history, when the emerging empire was establishing its religious and legal institutions.

His work contributed significantly to the preservation and transmission of Ibn Arabi's teachings throughout the Islamic world. Through his commentaries and original writings, al-Kayseri helped establish a systematic approach to understanding Akbarian mysticism that influenced subsequent generations of scholars across various regions of the Islamic world.

The scholarly tradition that al-Kayseri helped establish continued to flourish long after his death, with his interpretive methods and philosophical insights being studied and developed by later mystics and theologians. His position as both a mystical teacher and an official religious authority exemplifies the integration of esoteric Islamic knowledge with mainstream religious scholarship that characterized much of medieval Islamic intellectual life.

full: Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn Nusayr al-Ta'i al-Kufi
primaryTitle: Imam al-Wara' — The Jurist Who Chose the Cave
titles: Imam al-Wara' (Imam of Scrupulous Piety) · Student of Imam Abu Hanifa
bio: Abū Sulaymān Daʾūd ibn Nuṣayr al-Ṭā'ī, usually referred to as Dawud Taʾi, was a scholar of Islam and Sufi mystic. He resided in Kufa and was a prominent student of Abu Hanifa. His disciples included many influential figures in Islamic mysticism, such as Ma'ruf al-Karkhi. His master was Habib al-Ajami.
bio_full:
Abū Sulaymān Daʾūd ibn Nuṣayr al-Ṭā'ī, (Arabic: ابو سلیمان داؤد بن نصیر الطائي) usually referred to as Dawud Taʾi, (died between 776 and 783) was a scholar of Islam and Sufi mystic. He resided in Kufa and was a prominent student of Abu Hanifa. His disciples included many influential figures in Islamic mysticism, such as Ma'ruf al-Karkhi. His master was Habib al-Ajami.

Biography
Ta'i studied hadith and fiqh for many years with Abu Hanifa in Kufa, and being one of his favorite students, he reached a high level in science and fiqh. He also had an effective speaking ability and was probably a bit offensive too. As a matter of fact, once when he hit someone with a stick, his teacher Abu Hanifa had to scold him: "Abu Suleiman, your hand and tongue are growing long!" Dawud al-Tai was highly affected by this warning and did not speak in the last year of his studentship; he neither asked nor answered any questions. Although al-Tai was "the most fluent speaker of his time and the one who knew Arabic best", and "one of the leading imams in fiqh and opinion", he threw his books into the Euphrates River for some reasons that are shown differently in the sources and retreated to zuhd and worship. He completely distanced himself from the public and worldly affairs, locked himself in his house, and joined the congregation only at prayer times.
Among the people he met were Fudayl b. Iyaz, Jafar al-Sadiq and Ibrahim ibn Adham. He also met the Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid according to Imam Abu Yusuf. According to Fariduddin Attar, Fudayl b. Iyaz was proud to have had the honor of meeting him twice. One of his contemporaries in describing his greatness said, "If Dawud al-Tai had lived in the Age of Bliss [the Holy Prophet's time], the Qur'an would certainly have mentioned his zuhd and taqwa." 
Maruf Karkhi, his best-known disciple, introduces his master by saying, “I have never seen anyone who does not value the world as much as Tai.” The fact that he used the expression "May your death be your celebration" while wishing someone well and that he saw death as salvation from the prison of this world reflects the characteristic feature of the life of asceticism at that time. This optimistic understanding about death turned into Shab-i Arus (Wedding Night) in later periods. Dawud al-Tai, who bequeathed his grave to be built in a deserted place and thus wanted the seclusion in the world to continue there, used to attach great importance to worship, but said that one should not see one's worship as perfect and should not trust their worship. According to him, the worship of a person who does not have generosity and muruwa  is incomplete. As a matter of fact, after he turned to Sufism, he spent the money left by his father with his friends.
Al-Tai died while reading the Qur'an in his house, which was in ruins.

bio: Dhafra bint Ghalib al-Rasiyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Dhafra bint Ghalib al-Rasiyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE in the Hijaz region of the Arabian Peninsula, she was among the women who encountered and interacted with the Prophet during the formative period of Islam.

As a sahabiyya, Dhafra belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad, a status that held particular significance in early Islamic society. The companions, both male and female, were considered crucial links in preserving and transmitting the teachings, sayings, and practices of the Prophet to subsequent generations.

Dhafra is primarily recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a fundamental source of Islamic guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions like Dhafra played an important role in the early transmission of Islamic knowledge, particularly regarding matters that pertained to women's religious practices, family life, and social customs where they had direct access and observation.

The preservation and transmission of hadith required careful memorization and accurate reporting, making the narrators essential figures in maintaining the integrity of Islamic teachings. As someone who lived during the Prophet's lifetime and in his geographical vicinity, Dhafra would have been positioned to observe and later recount authentic accounts of prophetic traditions.

Her death around 635 CE places her among the early Muslims who witnessed both the initial spread of Islam during the Prophet's lifetime and the beginning of the rapid expansion that followed after his death in 632 CE. This generation of companions experienced the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca and Medina to a growing force that would soon extend beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

The inclusion of female narrators like Dhafra in the hadith tradition demonstrates the active participation of women in early Islamic scholarship and religious transmission. Their contributions helped ensure that the full spectrum of prophetic guidance, including aspects of daily life and religious practice that women were uniquely positioned to observe, was preserved for future Muslim generations.

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Dhakwan bin 'Abdu Qays bin Khalada (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Dhakwan bin 'Abdu Qays bin Khalada was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he died in 625 CE at approximately thirty-one years of age, making him one of the earlier companions to pass away during the Prophet's lifetime.

Dhakwan is historically recognized as one of the participants in the First Pledge of Aqabah, a pivotal event in early Islamic history that took place around 621 CE. This pledge was made by a group of individuals from the tribes of Aws and Khazraj from the city of Yathrib, later known as Medina, who had encountered the Prophet Muhammad during the annual pilgrimage season in Mecca. The First Pledge of Aqabah, also known as the First Pledge of the Women due to its peaceful nature, involved these early converts promising to worship only Allah, avoid theft, adultery, infanticide, and slander, and to obey the Prophet in all righteous matters.

The significance of Dhakwan's participation in this pledge extends beyond the personal commitment it represented. The First Pledge of Aqabah was a crucial step in establishing the foundation for what would become the Muslim community in Medina. Those who took this pledge were among the earliest supporters of Islam outside of Mecca and helped pave the way for the eventual migration of the Prophet and the Meccan Muslims to Medina in 622 CE, known as the Hijra.

As a companion who was present during these formative years, Dhakwan would have witnessed the early development of Islamic practices and community structures. His presence in Medina during this period means he was part of the community that welcomed the migrating Muslims from Mecca and participated in the establishment of the first Islamic state.

The early death of Dhakwan in 625 CE means he lived through the critical transition period of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community in Medina, but he passed away during the early years of the Medinan period. His participation in the First Pledge of Aqabah ensures his place among the early supporters who helped make the survival and growth of the early Muslim community possible.

famous: Dhakwan or Kisan or Tahman or Mihran
full: Dhakwan or Kisan or Tahman or Mihran
dob_s: c. 590 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)

bio: Dhakwan or Kisan or Tahman or Mihran (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina.
bio_full:
Dhakwan, also known by the names Kisan, Tahman, or Mihran, was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam. Born around 595 CE, he was among the generation that witnessed the emergence and establishment of the Islamic community in the Arabian Peninsula during the early seventh century.

As a sahabi, Dhakwan belonged to the distinguished group of individuals who personally knew, met, or encountered the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime and died as believers. This status holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are regarded as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings, practices, and the sayings of the Prophet known as hadith.

Dhakwan was based in Medina, the city that became the political and spiritual center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the capital of the expanding Islamic state and was home to many of the Prophet's closest companions who played crucial roles in the development and preservation of Islamic knowledge and practice.

The multiple names associated with this figure—Dhakwan, Kisan, Tahman, and Mihran—reflect the naming conventions of the time, where individuals might be known by different names or have various appellations used in different contexts or by different groups.

His association with hadith sciences indicates his role in the transmission of prophetic traditions, though the specific details of his contributions to this field require careful historical verification. The hadith sciences became fundamental to Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and practice, making the early companions who participated in this transmission process significant figures in Islamic intellectual history.

Dhakwan died around 635 CE, during the period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the second caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab. This places his death during the rapid expansion of Islamic rule beyond the Arabian Peninsula, a time when the foundations laid by the Prophet and his companions were being extended to new territories and populations.

His life span coincided with one of the most transformative periods in world history, as he witnessed the birth of Islam, the establishment of the first Islamic state, and the beginning of Islamic expansion that would eventually influence vast regions of Africa, Asia, and Europe.

bio: Dhu'l-Shimalyn 'Umair bin 'Abd 'Amr (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Dhu'l-Shimalyn 'Umair bin 'Abd 'Amr was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 594 CE in Mecca, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of Islamic history.

'Umair is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr" (Sahabi Badri). This battle, fought between the early Muslim community and the Meccan Quraysh tribe, is considered one of the most significant military encounters in early Islamic history. The Muslim victory at Badr was viewed as divine validation of their cause and marked a turning point in the relationship between the emerging Muslim community and the established tribal powers of the Arabian Peninsula.

The companions who fought at Badr held special status within the early Muslim community. Their participation in this crucial battle demonstrated their commitment to the new faith during a period when Islam faced existential threats from opposing tribal forces. These early supporters of Muhammad were later revered for their sacrifices and dedication during Islam's most vulnerable period.

'Umair died in 624 CE, the same year as the Battle of Badr, though the specific circumstances of his death are not clearly documented in available historical sources. His relatively short life span, ending at approximately thirty years of age, reflects the challenging and often dangerous conditions faced by early Muslims in seventh-century Arabia.

As one of the sahaba, 'Umair belongs to the generation of Muslims who had direct personal contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions as a group are considered important figures in Islamic tradition, as they served as the primary transmitters of Islamic knowledge and practices to subsequent generations.

While detailed biographical information about 'Umair beyond his participation at Badr remains limited in historical records, his inclusion among the Companions of Badr ensures his place in Islamic historical memory as one of the early supporters who stood with Muhammad during a critical moment in the establishment of the Muslim community.

primaryTitle: Man of the Pledge — Patient and Righteous Prophet
titles: Dhul-Kifl · possibly identified with Ezekiel or Elisha · man of the double portion
dating_source: Ibn Kathir; often identified with Ezekiel in Islamic tradition
dating_note: Dhul-Kifl; identity debated, Ezekiel identification places him in Babylonian exile.
bio: Dhu'l-Kifl, also spelled Dhu al-Kifl, Dhu l-Kifl, Dhul-Kifl, Zu al-Kifl, Zul Kifl, or Zu l-Kifl, is an Islamic prophet. Although his identity is unknown, his identity has been theorised and identified as various Hebrew Bible prophets and other figures, most commonly Ezekiel. Dhu'l-Kifl is believed to have been raised by Allah to a high station in life and is chronicled in the Qur'an as a man of the "Company of the Good". Although not much is known of Dhu'l-Kifl from other historical sources, all the writings from classical commentators, such as Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir, speak of Dhu'l-Kifl as a prophetic, saintly man who remained faithful in daily prayer and worship.
bio_full:
Dhu'l-Kifl (Arabic: ‏ذُو الْكِفْل‎, romanized: ḏū l-kifl, lit. 'Possessor of the Portion'), also spelled Dhu al-Kifl, Dhu l-Kifl, Dhul-Kifl, Zu al-Kifl, Zul Kifl, or Zu l-Kifl, is an Islamic prophet. Although his identity is unknown, his identity has been theorised and identified as various Hebrew Bible prophets and other figures, most commonly Ezekiel. Dhu'l-Kifl is believed to have been raised by Allah to a high station in life and is chronicled in the Qur'an as a man of the "Company of the Good". Although not much is known of Dhu'l-Kifl from other historical sources, all the writings from classical commentators, such as Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir, speak of Dhu'l-Kifl as a prophetic, saintly man who remained faithful in daily prayer (Arabic: صلاة, romanized: ṣalāh) and worship (Arabic: عبادة, romanized: ʿibāda).
A tomb in the Ergani province of Diyarbakir, Turkey is believed by some to be the resting place of Prophet Dhu'l-Kifl. It is located 5 km from the city centre on a hill called Makam Dağı.

Etymology
The name Dhu'l-Kifl literally means "the possessor of kifl ", using a type of name where ذُو dhū ("possessor of") precedes some characteristically associated feature. Such names were used of other notable figures in the Quran, for example Dhu'l-Qarnayn (Arabic: ذُو ٱلْقَرْنَيْن, lit. 'He of the Two Horns/He of the Two Times'), and Dhu'l-Nun (Arabic: ذُو ٱلْنُّون, lit. 'the One with the Fish'), referring to Yunus. Kifl (Arabic: كِفْل) is an archaic Arabic word meaning "double" or "duplicate", from the root ka-fa-la (ك-ف-ل) meaning "to double" or "to fold"; it was also used for a fold of cloth. The name is generally understood to mean "one of a double portion." Some scholars have suggested that the name means "the man with the double recompense" or rather "the man who received recompense twice over", that is to say that it is a title for Job, as his family was returned to him according to the Qur'an and the Book of Job.

In the Qur'an
Dhu'l-Kifl has been mentioned twice in the Qur'an, in the following verses:

And ˹remember˺ Ishmael, Enoch, and Ⱬul-Kifl. They were all steadfast.We admitted them into Our mercy, for they were truly of the righteous.
Also remember Ishmael, Elisha, and Ⱬul-Kifl. All are among the best.
In both cases, Dhu'l-Kifl is mentioned in the context of a list of Qur'anic prophets, including many others not mentioned in the ayatayn quoted above.

Identifications

Ezekiel

Some identify Dhu'l-Kifl is Ezekiel. When the exile, monarchy, and state were annihilated, political and national life was no longer possible. In conformity with the two parts of his book, his personality and his preaching are alike, and the title Dhu'l-Kifl means "the one to double" or "to fold."
In a story repeated in a fragment from the Cairo Geniza and a work by the 12th century Jewish scholar Moses ben Jacob of Coucy, the tomb of Ezekiel is at al-Kifl and was visited by Jews. 
In his Qur'anic commentary, Abdullah Yusuf Ali says:

Dhu al-Kifl would literally mean "possessor of, or giving, a double requital or portion"; or else, "one who used a cloak of double thickness," that being one of the meanings of Kifl. The commentators differ in opinion as to who is meant, why the title is applied to him. I think the best suggestion is that afforded by Karsten Niebuhr in his Reisebeschreibung nach Arabien, Copenhagen, 1778, ii. 264–266, as quoted in the Encyclopaedia of Islam under Dhul-Kifl. He visited Meshad 'All in 'Iraq, and also the little town called Kifl, midway between Najaf and Hilla (Babylon). Kefil, he says, is the Arabic form of Ezekiel. The shrine of Ezekiel was there, and the Jews came to it on pilgrimage.
If we accept "Dhu al-Kifl" to be not an epithet, but an Arabicised form of "Ezekiel", it fits the context, Ezekiel was a prophet in Israel who was carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar after his second attack on Jerusalem (about B.C. 599). His Book is included in the English Bible (Old Testament). He was chained and bound, and put into prison, and for a time he was dumb. He bore all with patience and constancy, and continued to reprove boldly the evils in Israel. In a burning passage he denounces false leaders in words which are eternally true: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed the flocks? Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock. The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken......".
Al-Kifl is a town in southeastern Iraq on the Euphrates between Najaf and Hillah. Variant names for the shrine within al-Kifl are the Dhu'l-Kifl Shrine, Marqad Dhu'l-Kifl, Qubbat Dhu'l-Kifl, Qabr al-Nabi Dhu'l-Kifl, Dhu'l-Kifl Shrine, Zul-Kifl Shrine, Qabr Hazqiyal, Hazqiyal Shrine. Hazqiyal (Arabic: حزقيال) is the Arabic version of the Hebrew name for Ezekiel, which was mostly utilized by Arabic-speaking Sephardic Jews. This indicates that the Jews equated Ezekiel and Dhu'l-Kifl, and Muslim exegetes followed suit.
The Iraqi authorities assert that in 1316 (715–16 AH), the Il khan Öljaitü acquired the rights of guardianship over the tomb of Dhu'l-Kifl from the Jewish community. Consequently, the shrine was renamed according to the Islamic nomenclature for the same prophet. Öljaitü added to the structure by building a mosque and a minaret and restored the shrine, implementing some alterations made clear by comparing its present state with pre-Ilkhanid travelers' descriptions.
The site remained a Muslim pilgrimage place until the beginning of the nineteenth century, when Menahem ibn Danyal, a wealthy Jew, successfully converted it back to a Jewish site and restored it. The minaret remained as the only witness to its tenure as an Islamic site.

bio: Dhū'l-Nūn al-Miṣrī, often rendered in English literature as Dhū'n-Nūn al-Miṣrī or Zūl-Nūn al-Miṣrī, was an early Egyptian Sufi mystic and alchemist. His surname al-Miṣrī means "the Egyptian".
bio_full:
Dhū'l-Nūn al-Miṣrī (d. Giza, 859-862), often rendered in English literature as Dhū'n-Nūn al-Miṣrī or Zūl-Nūn al-Miṣrī, was an early Egyptian Sufi mystic and alchemist. His surname al-Miṣrī means "the Egyptian".
He was born in Akhmim, Upper Egypt in 796 and is said to be of Nubian descent. Dhu'l-Nun is said to have made some study of the scholastic disciplines of alchemy, medicine, and Greek philosophy in his early life, before coming under the mentorship of the mystic Saʿdūn of Cairo, who is described in traditional accounts of Dhu'l-Nun's life as both "his teacher and spiritual director."
Celebrated for his legendary wisdom both in his own life and by later Islamic thinkers, Dhu'l-Nun has been venerated as one of the greatest saints of the early era of Sufism.

Name
It has been speculated by scholars whether "Dhu'l-Nun" was an honorific (laqab) for the mystic rather than his name proper, which is sometimes believed to be Thawbān. As "Dhu'l-Nun," literally meaning "the one of the fish [or whale]," or an abbreviation of "from Nineveh" as in the Quranic reference to the Hebrew prophet Jonah in Islamic tradition, it is sometimes believed that this title was given to Dhu'l-Nun in commemoration of Jonah.

Life
Dhu'l-Nun is one of the most prominent saints of early Islamic tradition, appearing "in the earliest accounts of Ṣūfism as the leading figure of his generation." Often depicted as the spiritual master of Sahl al-Tustari (c. 818–896), the traditional hagiographies relate that the latter refused to engage in mystical discourse until after Dhu'l-Nun's death, on account of his recognition of Dhu'l-Nun's elevated rank in wisdom and gnosis.

Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri is considered among the most prominent saints of early Sufism and holds a position in the Sufi chronicles as high as Junayd Baghdadi (d. 910) and Bayazid Bastami (d. 874). He studied under various teachers and travelled extensively in Arabia and Syria. The Muslim scholar and Sufi Sahl al-Tustari was one of Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri's students. In 829 he was arrested on a charge of heresy and sent to prison in Baghdad, but after examination he was released on the caliph's orders to return to Cairo, where he died in 859; his tombstone has been preserved.
Dhu'l-Nun's name came about in relation to an incident on a sea voyage. He was falsely accused of stealing a
jewel from a merchant. He cried out "O Creator, Thou knowest best", whereupon a large number of fish raised their heads above the waves, each bearing a jewel in its mouth.
A legendary alchemist and thaumaturge, he is supposed to have known the secret of the Egyptian hieroglyphs. His sayings and poems, which are extremely dense and rich in mystical imagery, emphasize knowledge or gnosis (marifah) more than fear (makhafah) or love (mahabbah), the other two major paths of spiritual realization in Sufism. None of his written works have survived, but a vast collection of poems, sayings, and aphorisms attributed to him continues to live on in oral tradition.
Osho mentions him as "an Egyptian Sufi mystic, one of the greatest who has ever walked on the earth".
Contemporary Sufi Llewellyn Vaughan-Lee mentions an incident from the life of Dhu'l-nun in his work Catching the Thread:

A story from the life of the ninth-century Sufi, Dhu-l-Nun, the Egyptian, illustrates this: 
I was wandering in the mountains when I observed a party of afflicted folk gathered together.
"What befell you?" I asked.
"There is a devotee living in a cell here," they
answered. "Once every year he comes out and
breathes on these people and they are all
healed. Then he returns to his cell, and does not
emerge again until the following year."
I waited patiently until he came out. I beheld
a man pale of cheek, wasted and with sunken
eyes. The awe of him caused me to tremble. He
looked on the multitude with compassion. Then
he raised his eyes to heaven, and breathed
several times over the afflicted ones. All were
healed.
As he was about to retire to his cell, I seized
his skirt. "For the love of God," I cried. "You
have healed the outward sickness; pray heal the
inward sickness."
"Dhu-l-Nun," he said, gazing at me, "take
your hand off me. The Friend is watching from
the zenith of might and majesty.

bio: Duba'a bint 'Amr bin Mihsan (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Duba'a bint 'Amr bin Mihsan was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet and the early Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Sahabiyya, the female companions of the Prophet, Duba'a lived during the formative period of Islam in Medina. The Ansar played a crucial role in the establishment and growth of the early Muslim community, providing shelter, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca. These Medinan supporters were instrumental in creating the social and political foundation that allowed Islam to flourish during its earliest decades.

The historical records regarding Duba'a bint 'Amr bin Mihsan are limited, which reflects the broader challenge of documenting women's lives from this early period of Islamic history. What is established is her status as a companion, indicating that she lived during the Prophet's lifetime and was part of the Muslim community in Medina. Her lineage, identified through her father 'Amr bin Mihsan, places her within the tribal structure of Medina's society.

The designation of companion carries significant weight in Islamic tradition, as the Sahaba are considered the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad. Their experiences, testimonies, and actions are viewed as important sources for understanding early Islamic practices and teachings. Female companions like Duba'a contributed to the transmission of Islamic knowledge and the development of the early Muslim community, though their specific contributions are often less detailed in historical sources compared to their male counterparts.

Duba'a's death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This timing means she witnessed not only the Prophet's ministry in Medina but also the initial expansion of the Islamic community under the first caliphs. Her life span encompasses the most crucial formative years of Islam, from its establishment in Medina through its early growth as a major religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula.

bio: Duba'a bint 'Amr bin Qurat (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Emigrant — Makkah to Madinah.
bio_full:
Duba'a bint 'Amr ibn Qurat was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE in Mecca, she was among the early converts to Islam during the formative period of the Muslim community.

As one of the Meccan Muslims, Duba'a experienced the social and economic pressures that the early Muslim community faced in their home city. The growing tensions between the Muslim minority and the established Meccan society created increasingly difficult conditions for those who had embraced the new faith. Like many of her fellow believers, she made the significant decision to participate in the hijra, the historic migration from Mecca to Medina that took place in 622 CE.

This migration marked a pivotal moment in Islamic history, representing not merely a physical relocation but a fundamental transformation in how the Muslim community was organized and governed. By joining this migration, Duba'a demonstrated her commitment to the nascent Muslim community and her willingness to abandon familiar surroundings for an uncertain future in Medina.

Her status as a muhajirun (emigrant) placed her among a distinguished group within early Islamic society. The emigrants who made this journey were later recognized for their sacrifice and dedication, having left behind their homes, tribal protections, and economic networks to preserve their faith and support the development of the Muslim community in Medina.

The inclusion of women like Duba'a in the migration underscores the fact that the early Islamic movement encompassed believers across gender and social lines. Female companions played important roles in the establishment and growth of the Muslim community, though historical records often provide limited details about their individual experiences and contributions.

Duba'a's life spanned the crucial early decades of Islamic history, from the initial revelations to the Prophet Muhammad through the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina. She died around 635 CE, during the period of the Rashidun Caliphate, having witnessed the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to the foundation of a rapidly expanding Islamic state. Her participation in the hijra connects her to one of the most significant events in Islamic history and marks her as part of the foundational generation of Muslims.

bio: Duba'a bint al-Zubayr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Cousin of the Prophet.
bio_full: Duba'a bint al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, from the Hashim clan of Quraysh. Her father, al-Zubayr, was the Prophet's paternal uncle, and her mother was Atika bint Abi Wahb of the Makhzum clan. Al-Dhahabi counts her among the women who emigrated (muhajirat). Ibn Sa'd states that the Prophet arranged her marriage to al-Miqdad ibn Amr, who was known as al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad because al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth al-Zuhri, his ally, had adopted him. She bore him Abd Allah and Karima. Abd Allah was killed at the Battle of the Camel on the side of Aisha. Ibn Sa'd also records that the Prophet allotted Duba'a forty wasq of produce from Khaybar. She narrated a few hadiths from the Prophet. The best known concerns the pilgrimage: the Prophet told her to perform Hajj and to make a condition on entering ihram, that her place of release would be wherever she was held back. Other reports from her include an account, transmitted through her sister, of the Prophet eating meat from a shoulder and praying without renewing his ablution, and one in which, embarrassed to send him only the neck of a slaughtered sheep, she was told to send it, as it was the nearest to good and the farthest from harm. Those who narrated from her include Ibn Abbas, Jabir ibn Abd Allah, Anas ibn Malik, Aisha, Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-A'raj and her daughter Karima. Al-Dhahabi believed she lived until after the year 40 AH (c. 660 CE).

Living during the foundational period of Islam, Dubayya witnessed the development of the Muslim community from its early struggles to its establishment as a recognized political and religious force in the Arabian Peninsula. The designation of Sahabiyya indicates that she had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. This status holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are considered the first generation of Muslims who learned directly from the Prophet and transmitted his teachings to subsequent generations.

bio: Durrah bint Abi Lahab (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca.
bio_full: Durra bint Abi Lahab was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad and one of the women who emigrated from Mecca to Medina. Her father was Abu Lahab (Abd al-Uzza) ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and her mother was Umm Jamil bint Harb ibn Umayya; Surat al-Masad (Q 111) was revealed about her parents. The classical sources differ about her marriages. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir say she was married to al-Harith ibn Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib and bore him Utba (or Uqba), al-Walid and Abu Muslim. Ibn Sa'd instead names her husband as al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Nawfal, who was killed at Badr as a disbeliever, and says she bore him al-Walid, Abu al-Hasan and Muslim, and afterwards married Dihya ibn Khalifa al-Kalbi. In Medina she stayed at the house of Rafi' ibn al-Mu'alla al-Zuraqi. Women of the Banu Zurayq taunted her as the daughter of Abu Lahab, whom the Qur'an condemns, asking what her emigration could do for her. She complained to the Prophet, who, after leading the noon prayer, addressed the people from the minbar, asking why he was being hurt through his family, and saying that his intercession would reach his relatives. She narrated a small number of hadiths. In one, a man asked the Prophet who the best of people were, and he answered: those who recite the Qur'an most, fear God most, most enjoin good and forbid evil, and most keep the ties of kinship. Another, transmitted from her through Ali ibn Abi Talib, states that the living are not harmed by the dead. One account, cited by al-Zirikli, says she died around 20 AH (c. 640 CE).

bio: Durrah bintt Abi Salamah (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Makkah or Medinah. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Durrah bint Abi Salamah was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the crucial decades when Islam was first revealed and established as a religious community in the Arabian Peninsula.

As a sahabiyya, Durrah was among the generation of women who personally knew and interacted with Prophet Muhammad, placing her within the most revered category of Islamic historical figures. The companions, both male and female, hold special significance in Islamic tradition as the direct recipients and first transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices.

Durrah's primary historical importance lies in her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a fundamental source of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. Female hadith narrators played a crucial but sometimes overlooked role in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge during the religion's earliest period. These women served as vital links in the chain of transmission that allowed Islamic teachings to be preserved and passed down to subsequent generations.

The early Islamic community in Makkah and Madinah provided opportunities for women to participate in religious learning and transmission of knowledge. Female companions like Durrah were positioned to observe and later recount important aspects of the Prophet's teachings and conduct, particularly in domestic and social contexts that male companions might not have witnessed.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the first Caliphate under Abu Bakr, just a few years after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This timing meant that her role as a hadith narrator occurred during the critical period when the early Muslim community was working to collect and preserve the Prophet's teachings for future generations.

While specific details about her individual contributions to hadith literature require further scholarly verification, Durrah bint Abi Salamah represents the important category of female companions who served as early authorities in Islamic knowledge transmission. Her inclusion among recognized hadith narrators reflects the significant role that women played in preserving Islamic teachings during the religion's foundational period, contributing to the vast corpus of prophetic traditions that continue to guide Muslim practice and understanding today.

full: Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Mustafa al-'Imadi Ebussuud Efendi
primaryTitle: Shaykh al-Islam of the Golden Age
titles: Shaykh al-Islam · Qadi al-Qudat al-Rum
bio: Ebussuud Efendi, was a Hanafi Maturidi Ottoman jurist and Quran exegete, served as the Qadi (judge) of Istanbul from 1533 to 1537, and the Shaykh al-Islām of the Ottoman Empire from 1545 to 1574. He was also called "El-İmâdî" because his family hailed from Imâd, a village near İskilip.
bio_full:
Ebussuud Efendi (Turkish: Mehmed Ebüssuûd Efendi, 30 December 1490 – 23 August 1574), was a Hanafi Maturidi Ottoman jurist and Quran exegete, served as the Qadi (judge) of Istanbul from 1533 to 1537, and the Shaykh al-Islām of the Ottoman Empire from 1545 to 1574. He was also called "El-İmâdî" because his family hailed from Imâd, a village near İskilip.
Ebussuud was the son of Iskilipli Sheikh Muhiddin Muhammad Efendi. In the 1530s, Ebussuud served as a judge in Bursa, Istanbul and Rumelia, where he brought local laws into conformity with Islamic divine law (sharia). Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent promoted him to Shaykh al-Islām – the supreme judge and highest official – in 1545, an office Ebussuud held until his death and which he brought to the peak of its power. He worked closely with the Sultan, issuing judicial opinions that legitimised Suleiman's killings of Yazidis and his successor Selim's attack on Cyprus. Ebussuud also issued legal rulings (fatwās) which labeled the Qizilbash, regardless of whether they lived on Iranian or Ottoman soil, as "heretics", and declared that killing them would be viewed as praiseworthy, rather than just being allowed according to the law.
Together with Suleiman, the "Lawgiver", Ebussuud reorganized Ottoman jurisprudence and brought it under tighter governmental control, creating a legal framework joining sharia and the Ottoman administrative code (qānūn). While the previously prevailing opinion held that judges were free to interpret sharia, the law that even the ruler was subject to, Ebussuud instituted a framework in which the judicial power was derived from the Sultan and which compelled judges to follow the Sultan's qānūn-nāmes, "law-letters", in their application of the law.
In addition to his judicial reforms, Ebussuud is also remembered for the great variety of fatwās he issued. His opinions allowing Karagöz plays and the consumption of coffee, a novelty at the time, are particularly celebrated. He is also known for a widely-contested fatwā permitting monetary dealings involving riba (interest) in certain situations. This opinion is often referenced by contemporary Muslim modernists.

Fatwā Compilation
Ebussuud’s work includes Tafsir of the Quran, jurisprudential commentaries, dictionaries and treatises on mysticism, Arabic grammar, literature and poetry. He is best known for his juristic opinions in thousands of fatwās that he composed during his thirty-year career as the Shaykh al-Islām.
Ebussuud formed a department (fatwā-khāna) in the office of Shaykh al-Islām and systematized the process of issuing fatwās which was largely informal before his period in office. The chief function of SHaykh al-Islām was to issue fatwās in response to legal questions from the Sultan, his ministers, governors or judges, or from members of the public seeking out-of-court settlements or simply answers to queries. Ebussuud established a high level of bureaucratic division of labor, where scribes (fatwā katibi) with legal training and experience drafted questions according to predetermined technical and rhetorical standards, and clerks (fatwā emini), legal scholars with high-level madrasa appointments, sometimes provided provisional answers to these questions before they were presented to the SHaykh al-Islām. Ebussuud composed a manual, titled ‘Advice to Fetva Scribes’ (Fetva Katiblerine Tenbih), about how to draft fatwās in ways that would allow queries to be answered precisely, unequivocally, and in the fewest possible words. Ebussuud’s reform of the procedure of composing fatwas allowed the office of SHaykh al-Islām to develop a standardized style of Ottoman fatwā documents and issue large volumes of them in relatively short periods of time.
Ebussuud’s fatwās collections, known as Ma‘ruḍāt, have received considerable attention in modern scholarship and were heavily cited and quoted by generations of legal scholars who came after him. Ebussuud wrote fatwās on contemporary issues of various kinds such as ritual prayer, ablution, contracts, religious foundations, and the practices of Ṣūfīs.  The importance of his fatwās lies in the systematization of Ottoman jurisprudence. He formulated the imperial land and tax systems and aligned them with Hanafi jurisprudential traditions. He also shaped many aspects of Ottoman legal practices including the institution of cash-waqf.  His legal opinions in fatwās did not always legitimize or side with state preferences. He, for example, declared that certain regulations in Ottoman law contradicted religious law, such as collection of poll tax from peasants without lands, torturing suspected criminals, and levying taxes on pigs. While Ebussuud’s contributions to the Ottoman land and tax codes have garnered great interest in modern historiography, his opinions on those issues occupied a limited space in his fatwas. Instead, two broadly defined foci in Ebussuud’s fatwās were economic concerns, such as contractual and property-related issues, and religious-doctrinal, communal (including non-Muslims) and family matters.
Scholars refer to collections of Ebussuud’s fatwās as Mecmuatu¨’l Fetava (‘Collection of Fatwās’) by Ebussuud, Fetava Ebussuud, or Fetava-yı Ebussuud. Multiple versions of Ebussuud’s fatwās compiled by different individuals exist in Turkish archives and manuscript libraries.
In addition to his fatwā compilation, Ebussuud was also outstanding as an exegete. He completed a commentary on the whole of the Qurʾān, Irshādu-l-‘Aqqli-s-Saleem ilā Mazāyā Al-Kitaabi-l-Kareem in 1566. For this, Sultan Suleiman granted him awards and sent copies of this work to Mecca and Medina to spread his fame outside of the Ottoman world. Later scholars like Sayyid Muhammad Anwar Shah Kashmiri, Sayyid Muhammad Yusuf Banuri, and Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani considers his Tafseer one of the top four commentaries of the Qur'an. He also wrote commentaries and super-commentaries on theological texts like al-Taftazānī's Talweeḥ and al-Nasafī's Manār.
