bio: Firas bin al-Nadr b al-Harith (c. 593–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Firas ibn al-Nadr ibn al-Harith was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Quraysh clan of 'Abd al-Dar, from which comes his nisba al-'Abdari. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr gives his lineage as Firas ibn al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn 'Alqama ibn Kalada ibn 'Abd Manaf ibn 'Abd al-Dar, and Ibn al-Athir continues it to Qusayy ibn Kilab ibn Murra. Abu Musa placed Kalada before 'Alqama in the line, but Ibn al-Athir notes that Ibn al-Kalbi, Ibn Habib, Ibn Makula and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar agree with Ibn 'Abd al-Barr's order.

He was among those who emigrated to Abyssinia. Ibn al-Athir notes that Ibn Ishaq mentioned him, while Musa ibn 'Uqba did not. Both Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir record that he was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Yarmuk. The sources do not give his year of birth or the year of his death.

bio_sources.title: al-Isti'ab; Usd al-Ghaba — Firas ibn al-Nadr (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

primaryTitle: Homer of the East — Author of the Shahnameh
titles: Ḥakīm Firdawsī
bio: Abu al-Qasim al-Firdawsi al-Tusi, known simply as “Firdawsi,” is one of the greatest Persian poets and the author of the famous poetic epic “The Shahnameh,” which is the longest poem in the world. He had a great impact in reviving the Persian language and preserving it from extinction, and he is considered one of the most influential figures in the history of literature. Among his nicknames are “Hakim al-Kalam” or “Hakim Tus.”
bio_full:
Abolqasem Mansour bin Hassan Tusi (940–1025), better known by his pen name Ferdowsi, was a Persian poet and the author of Shahnameh ("Book of Kings"), which is one of the world's longest epic poems created by a single poet, and the greatest epic of Persian-speaking countries. Ferdowsi is celebrated as one of the most influential figures of Persian literature and one of the greatest in the history of literature.
Researchers believe that Ferdowsi began composing the Shahnameh based on the Abu-Mansuri Shahnameh at the age of 30. The only poem that has been clarified about him is the Shahnameh itself. The Shahnameh is Ferdowsi's most famous poem and one of the greatest writings of ancient Persian literature. Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh in 944, three years before Mahmud's accession to the throne. In 1010, Ferdowsi completed the second edition. Other poems have also been attributed to Ferdowsi, most of which are baseless. The most famous of them are the Masnavi of Yusuf and Zulaikha. Another poem that is known to be by Ferdowsi is a satire in condemnation of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni.
Ferdowsi came from a family of landed gentry. He spent the beginning of his life in the Samanid era and at the same time as the movement for independence and identity among Iranians. The Samanid kings, with the support of the Persian language, prepared a brilliant time for the cultivation of the Persian language and thought, and Ferdowsi is clearly indebted to his predecessors and all those who reached the pinnacle of the Persian language in the ninth and tenth centuries, and he was able to use that capital to express his speech so brilliantly. In a comprehensive look at Ferdowsi's knowledge and learnings, it can be said that he knew the Arabic language, but he did not dominate Arabic literature. In the "Baysunghur Shahnameh", Ferdowsi's name is associated with the title of "Hakim", which according to some refers to the wisdom of Khosravani.
In the Shahnameh, Ferdowsi links the culture of pre-Islamic Iran with the culture of post-Islamic Iran. It can be concluded from the Shahnameh that Ferdowsi was influenced by ancient Iranian religions such as Zoroastrianism, Zurvanism and Mithraism, although some researchers consider the source of these influences to be the themes of Ferdowsi's work, to which he was very loyal. Also, due to his peasant origins, he was familiar with the ancient culture and rituals of Iran, and later increased the scope of this knowledge, so that this knowledge established his poetic worldview. What Ferdowsi was dealing with was not only poetic, but also intellectual; he did not write fiction. Ferdowsi considers wisdom as the source and capital of all goodness. He believes that a person with wisdom recognizes good and evil from each other, and in this way, he reaches the happiness of this world and the salvation of that world. Ferdowsi carefully examined his motifs, most of which were from the Abu-Mansuri Shahnameh. He was able to gather an excerpt from the vast wealth of knowledge he had at his disposal to have a legacy carried by the Persians, Turks, and Indians.

Ethymology
Except for his kunya (ابوالقاسم – Abul-Qâsem, meaning 'father of Qasem') and his pen name (فِردَوسی – Ferdowsī, meaning 'paradisic'), nothing is known with any certainty about his full name. According to Djalal Khaleghi-Motlagh, the information given by the 13th-century author Bundari about Ferdowsi's name should be taken as the most reliable. Bundari calls the poet al-Amir al-Hakim Abu'l-Qasem Mansur ibn al-Hasan al-Ferdowsi al-Tusi. From an early period on, he has been referred to by different additional names and titles, the most common one being حکیم / Hakīm ("philosopher"). Based on this, his full name is given in Persian sources as حکیم ابوالقاسم فردوسی توسی / Hakīm Abol-Qâsem Ferdowsī Tusī. Due to the non-standardised transliteration from Persian into English, different spellings of his name are used in English works, including Firdawsi, Firdusi, Firdosi, Firdausi, etc. The Encyclopaedia of Islam uses the spelling Firdawsī, based on the standardised transliteration method of the German Oriental Society. The Encyclopædia Iranica, which uses a modified version of the same method (with a stronger emphasis on modern Persian intonations), gives the spelling Ferdowsī. The modern Tajik transliteration of his name in Tajik Cyrillic is Ҳаким Абулқосим Фирдавсӣ Тӯсӣ (Hakim Abdulqosim Firdavsí Tŭsí).

Life

Family
Ferdowsi (Persian: ابوالقاسم فردوسی توسی) was born into a family of Persian landowners (dehqans) in 940 in the village of Paj, near the city of Tus, in the Khorasan region of the Samanid Empire, which is located in the present-day Razavi Khorasan province of northeastern Iran. Little is known about Ferdowsi's early life. The poet had a wife, who was probably literate and came from the same dehqan class. The dehqans were landowning Iranian gentry who had flourished under the Sasanian dynasty (the last pre-Islamic dynasty to rule Iran) and whose power, though diminished, had survived into the Islamic era which followed the Islamic conquests of the 7th century. The dehqans were attached to the pre-Islamic literary heritage, as their status was associated with it (so much so that dehqan is sometimes used as a synonym for "Iranian" in the Shahnameh). Thus they saw it as their task to preserve the pre-Islamic cultural traditions, including tales of legendary kings.
He had a son, who died at the age of 37, and was mourned by the poet in an elegy which he inserted into the Shahnameh.

Background
The Islamic conquests of the 7th century brought gradual linguistic and cultural changes to the Iranian Plateau. By the late 9th century, as the power of the caliphate had weakened, several local dynasties emerged in Greater Iran. Ferdowsi grew up in Tus, a city under the control of one of these dynasties, the Samanids, who claimed descent from the Sasanian general Bahram Chobin (whose story Ferdowsi recounts in one of the later sections of the Shahnameh). The Samanid bureaucracy used the New Persian language, which had been used to bring Islam to the Eastern regions of the Iranian world and supplanted local languages, and commissioned translations of Pahlavi texts into New Persian. Abu Mansur Muhammad, a dehqan and governor of Tus, had ordered his minister Abu Mansur Mamari to invite several local scholars to compile a prose Shahnameh ("Book of Kings"), which was completed in 1010. Although it no longer survives, Ferdowsi used it as one of the sources of his epic. Samanid rulers were patrons of such important Persian poets as Rudaki and Daqiqi, and Ferdowsi followed in the footsteps of these writers.
Details about Ferdowsi's education are lacking. While it is likely that he learned Arabic in school, there is no evidence in the Shahnameh that he knew either Arabic or Pahlavi.
Ferdowsi was a Shia Muslim, although varying views exist on what Shiite sect he belonged to. Khaleghi-Motlagh, following Theodor Nöldeke, notes that Ferdowsi displays a contradictory attitude towards religion in the Shahnameh: on the one hand, he shows a "lenient" attitude towards religion, but on the other hand, he believed that his sect was the "only true Islamic one." Khaleghi-Motlagh concurs with Nöldeke that Ferdowsi was "above all a deist and monotheist who at the same time kept faith with his forbears." Ferdowsi criticized philosophers and those who tried to prove the existence of God. He saw God's creation as the only evidence of His existence and believed everything in life to be the product of God's will. Khaleghi-Motlagh and others have suggested that a certain fatalism in Ferdowsi's work contradicts his "absolute faith in the unicity and might of God," and that this may have been the legacy of the Zurvanism of the Sasanian period.

Life as a poet

It is possible that Ferdowsi wrote some early poems which have not survived.

titles: Shaykh 'Isa · Sheikh of the Maryamiyya
bio: Frithjof Schuon was a Swiss philosopher and spiritual leader, belonging to the Traditionalist School of Perennialism. He was the author of more than twenty works in French on metaphysics, spirituality, religion, anthropology, and art. He was also a painter and a poet.
bio_full:
Frithjof Schuon ( SHOO-on; German: [ˈfʁɪtjɔf ˈʃuːɔn]; 18 June 1907 – 5 May 1998) was a Swiss philosopher and spiritual leader, belonging to the Traditionalist School of Perennialism. He was the author of more than twenty works in French on metaphysics, spirituality, religion, anthropology, and art. He was also a painter and a poet.
With René Guénon and Ananda Coomaraswamy, Schuon was one of the major 20th-century representatives of the philosophia perennis. Like them, he affirmed the reality of an absolute Principle – God – from which the universe emanates, and maintained that all divine revelations, despite their differences, possess a common essence: one and the same Truth. He also shared with them the certitude that man is potentially capable of supra-rational knowledge, and undertook a sustained critique of the modern mentality severed, according to him, from its traditional roots. Following Plato, Plotinus, Adi Shankara, Meister Eckhart, Ibn Arabī, and other metaphysicians, Schuon sought to affirm the metaphysical unity between the Principle and its manifestation.
Initiated by Sheikh Ahmad al-Alawī into the Sufi Shādhilī order, he founded the Tarīqa Maryamiyya. His writings emphasize the universality of metaphysical doctrine, along with the necessity of practicing a religion; he also insists on the importance of the virtues and of beauty.
Schuon cultivated close relationships with a large number of personages of diverse religious and spiritual horizons. He had a particular interest in the traditions of the North American Plains Indians, maintaining firm friendships with a number of their leaders and being adopted into both a Lakota Sioux tribe and the Crow tribe. Having spent a large part of his life in France and Switzerland, at the age of 73 moved to Bloomington, Indiana, where he had a community of disciples.

Life and work

Basel, Switzerland (1907–1920)
Frithjof Schuon was born in Basel, in the German-speaking part of Switzerland, on 18 June 1907. He was the younger of the two sons of Paul Schuon and Margarete Boehler, both of whom were of German origin (the former from Swabia and the latter from Alsace). His father was a concert violinist, and the household was one in which not only music but literary and spiritual culture were present. The Schuons, themselves raised as Catholics, brought their sons up as Protestants, though not in hostility to the Catholic Church.
At primary school, Schuon met the future author Titus Burckhardt, who remained a lifelong friend. From the age of ten, he began to read the Bible, the Upanishads, the Bhagavad-Gītā and the Quran, as well as Plato, Emerson, Goethe and Schiller. Schuon would later say that in his early youth four things had always moved him most profoundly: "the holy, the great, the beautiful, the childlike."

France (1920–1940)
In 1920, Schuon's father died and his mother decided to return with her young sons to her family in nearby Mulhouse, France, where Schuon became a French citizen, consequent upon the Treaty of Versailles. One year later, when he was 14, he was baptized as a Catholic. In 1923 his brother entered a Trappist monastery, and Schuon left school in order to provide for the family, finding work as a textile designer.
He then began an intense study of the Bhagavad-Gītā and the Vedānta. In 1924, while still living in Mulhouse, he discovered the works of the French philosopher René Guénon, which had a significant impact on his thought, confirming the intuitions of his youth. Schuon would later say of Guénon that he was "the profound and powerful theoretician of all that he loved".

In 1930, after 18 months in Besançon on military service in the French army, Schuon settled in Paris. There he resumed his profession as a textile designer, and began to study Arabic in the local mosque school. Living in Paris also gave him the opportunity to be exposed to various forms of traditional art to a much greater degree than before, especially the arts of Asia with which he had had a deep affinity since his youth. 
At the end of 1932 he completed his first book, Leitgedanken zur Urbesinnung, which would be published in 1935 and later translated into English under the title Primordial Meditation: Contemplating the Real. His desire to leave the West, whose modern values he rejected, combined with his growing interest in Islam, prompted him to go to Marseille, a port of departure for the East. There he made the acquaintance of two disciples of Sheikh Ahmad al-Alawī, a Sufi in Mostaganem, Algeria. Schuon saw the sign of his destiny in these encounters, and embarked for Algeria. In Mostaganem he entered Islam, and spent nearly four months in the Sheikh's zāwiya. The Sheikh gave him initiation and named him `Īsā Nūr ad-Dīn. However, Schuon was soon forced to return to Europe under pressure from the French colonial authorities.
Schuon did not consider his affiliation to Islam as a conversion, since he did not disavow Christianity; in each revelation he saw the expression of one and the same truth, in different forms. But for him, in the Guenonian perspective that he held at the time, Western Christianity no longer seemed to offer the possibility of following a "path of knowledge" under the guidance of a spiritual master, whereas such a path was still open within the framework of Sufism, Islamic esoterism.
Schuon reported that one night in July 1934, while reading the Bhagavad-Gītā, the divine Name Allāh took hold of him, and that for three days he could do nothing but invoke it ceaselessly. Shortly afterwards, he learned that his Sheikh had died on the same day.
In 1935 he returned to the zāwiya of Mostaganem, where Sheikh Adda ben Tounes, Sheikh al-Alawī's successor, conferred on him the function of muqaddam, thus authorizing him to initiate aspirants into the Alawī brotherhood. Returning to Europe, Schuon founded a zāwiya in Basel, another in Lausanne and a third in Amiens. He resumed his profession as a textile designer in Alsace for the next four years.

One night towards the end of 1936, after a spiritual experience, Schuon sensed, without a shadow of a doubt, that he had been invested with the function of spiritual master, of sheikh. This was confirmed, he later related, by visionary dreams that several of his disciples reported having had the same night. The differences of perspective between Schuon and the Mostaganem zāwiya gradually led to Schuon's assuming independence, supported by Guénon.
In 1938, Schuon traveled to Egypt, where he met Guénon, with whom he had been in correspondence for 7 years. In 1939, he embarked for India with two disciples, making a long stopover in Cairo, where he saw Guénon again. Shortly after his arrival in Bombay, World War II broke out, forcing him to return to Europe. Serving in the French army, he was interned by the Nazis, who were planning to incorporate all soldiers of Alsatian origin into the German army to fight on the Russian front. Schuon escaped to Switzerland, which was to be his home for forty years.

Lausanne, Switzerland (1941–1980)
He settled in Lausanne, where he continued contributing to the Guénonian journal Études Traditionnelles, as he had done since 1933. In 1947, after reading Black Elk Speaks by John G. Neihardt, Schuon, who had always been interested in the North American Indians, was convinced that Black Elk knew much more about Sioux tradition than was contained in the book. He asked his American friends to seek out the old chief. Following this initiative, the ethnologist Joseph E. Brown collected from Black Elk the description of the seven Sioux rites which would form the content of The Sacred Pipe.
In 1948 Schuon published his first book in French, De l'Unité transcendante des religions. Of this book, T. S.

titles: Imam al-Haramayn · Qudwat al-Zuhhad
bio: Abu 'Ali al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad al-Tamimi (c. 730–803) was a mystic of the Sufi tradition, based in Khorasan. Known as Imam al-Haramayn — Imam of the Two Sanctuaries.
bio_full:
Al-Fudayl bin Ayadh, one of the prominent figures of the Sunnis in the second century AH, was nicknamed “the worshiper of the Two Holy Mosques” (107 AH - 187 AH).

Al-Fudayl bin Ayadh bin Masoud bin Bishr Abu Ali Al-Tamimi Al-Yarbu’i Al-Khorasani. He was born in Samarkand in the year 107 AH and grew up in Abiward.

Ibn Asakir narrated with his chain of transmission on the authority of Al-Fadl ibn Musa, who said: Al-Fudayl was a wanderer crossing the road between Abiward and Sarakhs, and the reason for his repentance was that he fell in love with a slave girl. While he was climbing the walls to her, he heard someone reciting, “Has not the time come for those who believe that their hearts should be humbled by the remembrance of God?” He said: “O Lord, the time has come.” So he returned, and the night took him to a ruin, where he found a company in it. Some of them said: “We will travel,” and some people said: “Until we arrive, then Fudail is on the road, cutting us off.” He said: So I thought and said: I strive at night in sin, and there are some Muslims here who fear me, and I do not see God leading me to them except to be deterred. Oh God, I have repented to You and made my repentance adjacent to the Sacred House.

It was narrated on the authority of Al-A'mash, Al-Thawri, Mansour bin Al-Mu'tamir, Hisham bin Hassan, Sulaiman Al-Taymi, Awf Al-Arabi, Husayn bin Abdul Rahman, Laith bin Abi Salim, Suleiman bin Fayrouz Al-Shaibani, Awf bin Abi Jamila Al-Arabi, Yahya bin Ubaidullah bin Mawhib, Ata bin Al-Sa'ib and others.

Al-Thawri, Ibn Uyaynah, Al-Shafi’i, Ibn Al-Mubarak, Al-Humaydi, Yahya Al-Qattan, Abdul-Rahman bin Mahdi, Qutaybah bin Saeed, and Bishr Al-Hafi narrated from him.

Ibn Uyaynah said: “Fadil is trustworthy and used to kiss his hand.”

Al-Nasa’i said: “Mamun is trustworthy, a righteous man.”

Ibn Al-Mubarak said: “There is nothing better left on the face of the earth than Fudayl bin Iyad.”

Al-Dhahabi said: “The proven imam is the Sheikh of Islam.”

Ibn Hajar said: “Abid Imam is trustworthy.”

Many eminent people testified to him about his morals, and he received many praises from them

The Caliph “Harun al-Rashid” said about him: (I have not seen among scholars more fearsome than “Malik,” nor more pious than “Al-Fadhil”).

Ibn Al-Mubarak also says: There is nothing left on the face of the earth better than Al-Fudayl bin Iyad.

He said: “Whoever fears God, no one will harm him, and whoever fears other than God, no one will benefit him.”

He said: “Fear is better than hope as long as the man is healthy.

bio: Fukayha bint 'Ubayd b. Dulaim (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Fukayha bint 'Ubayd ibn Dulaym was a woman of the Ansar from the Banu Sa'ida branch of the Khazraj in Medina. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Fukayha bint 'Ubayd ibn Dulaym ibn Haritha ibn Abi Huzayma ibn Tha'laba ibn Tarif ibn al-Khazraj ibn Sa'ida. Ibn al-Athir describes her as a paternal cousin of Sa'd ibn 'Ubada, and Ibn Sa'd records that Sa'd ibn 'Ubada married her. She bore him Qays ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ubada and Umama bint Sa'd.

Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad, and Ibn al-Athir also records her pledge. The sources record no narrations from her and give no dates of birth or death.

bio: Fukayha bint al-Muttalib bin Khalada (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Fukayha bint al-Muttalib bin Khalada was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the crucial decades when Islam emerged and established itself as a major religious movement in the region.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, Fukayha belonged to the community of local supporters who welcomed and aided the Prophet Muhammad and his followers after their migration from Mecca in 622 CE. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" or "supporters," played a vital role in the early Muslim community by providing shelter, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants during a critical period when the new faith faced persecution and opposition.

Fukayha's presence in Medina during this transformative era means she would have witnessed firsthand the establishment of the first Muslim community, the construction of the Prophet's mosque, and the development of early Islamic social and legal frameworks. The companions of this generation, both male and female, are particularly revered in Islamic tradition as they had direct access to the Prophet's teachings and example.

Her designation as a sahabiyya places her among the women who directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and contributed to the early Muslim community. Female companions played important roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, supporting the community through various challenges, and participating in the social and religious life of early Medina.

Living until approximately 635 CE, Fukayha would have experienced not only the Prophet's lifetime but also the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule. This period saw the rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula and the consolidation of Muslim political authority.

The historical record of individual female companions from this era is often limited, reflecting the documentary practices and social priorities of the time. However, their collective importance to the preservation and transmission of Islamic tradition is well-established in Islamic historical sources. Fukayha's recognition as a companion indicates her accepted status within the early Muslim community and her contribution to the foundational period of Islamic civilization.

bio: Fukayha bint al-Sakan bin Zayd (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Fukayha bint al-Sakan bin Zayd was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca following the Hijra in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions based in Medina, Fukayha lived during the formative period of early Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim community and the development of Islamic teachings and practices. Her life spanned the pre-Islamic period, the early years of Muhammad's prophetic mission, and the crucial decades when Islam was taking root in the Arabian Peninsula.

The designation "Ansari Companion of Madinah" indicates her significant role within the early Muslim community. The Ansar held a special position in Islamic history as the original supporters who provided refuge and assistance to the Muslim community when it migrated from Mecca to Medina. Their support was instrumental in the survival and growth of the early Islamic state.

Like other female companions of her era, Fukayha would have participated in the religious and social life of the early Muslim community in Medina. The female companions played important roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, supporting community welfare, and contributing to the establishment of Islamic social practices.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the caliphate of Abu Bakr or the early years of Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule, a period when the Muslim community was expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula. This timing suggests she witnessed the Prophet's death in 632 CE and lived through the initial phase of Islamic expansion under the Rashidun Caliphate.

Fukayha represents the broader group of early Muslim women who, while not always prominently featured in historical accounts, formed the backbone of the early Islamic community. Her recognition as a companion acknowledges her contribution to the preservation and transmission of Islamic values during the religion's foundational period. Her Ansari heritage connects her to the pivotal moment when Medina became the center of the growing Muslim community, making her part of the essential support network that enabled Islam's early development and spread.

bio: Furay'a bint 'Amr b. Khunays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Furay'a bint 'Amr b. Khunays was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the foundational period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she was among the early Muslim community that formed in Medina following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Furay'a belonged to the group of Medinan Muslims who provided crucial support to the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim emigrants from Mecca. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were the indigenous tribes of Medina who embraced Islam and offered protection and assistance to the Muslim community during its most vulnerable early years. Their role was essential in establishing Islam's first stable base and allowing the religion to grow and develop.

Furay'a lived through the most transformative period of early Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim community in Medina, the development of Islamic law and practice, and the expansion of the faith throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her presence in Medina during this time meant she would have been part of the community that experienced the revelation of much of the Quran and observed the Prophet's teachings and practices firsthand.

The companions of the Prophet, known as the Sahaba, hold a special place in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly received religious instruction from Muhammad himself. Female companions like Furay'a played important roles in the early Muslim community, participating in religious life and serving as transmitters of Islamic knowledge and practices to subsequent generations.

Furay'a's life span, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompasses the pre-Islamic period, the emergence of Islam, and the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate that followed the Prophet's death in 632 CE. Her death around 635 CE places her among those early companions who witnessed the initial expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula but did not live to see its later dramatic territorial conquests.

While specific details about her individual contributions or particular roles within the early Muslim community are not well-documented in available historical sources, her recognition as a Sahabiyya reflects her standing as one of the women who helped establish and maintain the foundational Muslim community in Medina during Islam's crucial formative years.

bio: Fushum bint Aws bin Khawli (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Fushum bint Aws bin Khawli was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Muslim women who witnessed and participated in the foundational years of the Islamic community during the 7th century.

As a Sahabiyya, Fushum belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and lived during his lifetime. This status holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Fushum is primarily recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that serve as a crucial source of Islamic guidance alongside the Quran. During the early Islamic period, both men and women served as transmitters of these prophetic traditions, with female companions playing an essential role in preserving and passing down religious knowledge, particularly regarding matters that concerned women's religious and social practices.

Her contribution to hadith sciences places her within the broader network of early Islamic scholars and knowledge transmitters who were responsible for collecting, memorizing, and accurately conveying the Prophet's teachings to future Muslim generations. The hadith tradition relies heavily on chains of transmission (isnad) that trace back to direct witnesses of the Prophet's words and actions, making the testimony of companions like Fushum invaluable to Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

Fushum's life spanned a critical period in Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's ministry in Medina and the early expansion of the Muslim community. Her death around 635 CE occurred during the caliphate of the first Rashidun caliph, Abu Bakr, just a few years after the Prophet's passing in 632 CE.

The preservation of her name and recognition of her role as a hadith narrator reflects the important position that knowledgeable women held in early Islamic society as religious authorities and teachers. Her legacy contributes to the historical record of women's participation in the development and transmission of Islamic religious knowledge during the religion's formative period.

titles: Fuzuli — The Virtuous
bio: Muhammad bin Suleyman, better known by his pen name Fuzuli, was a 16th-century poet who composed works in his native Azerbaijani, as well as Persian and Arabic. Fuzuli's work was widely known and admired throughout the Turkic cultural landscape from the 16th to the 19th centuries, with his fame reaching as far as Central Asia and India.
bio_full:
Muhammad bin Suleyman (Azerbaijani: Məhəmməd Süleyman oğlu, مَحمد سلیمان اوغلی; 1483–1556), better known by his pen name Fuzuli (Füzuli, فضولی), was a 16th-century poet who composed works in his native Azerbaijani, as well as Persian and Arabic. He is regarded as one of the greatest poets of Turkic literature and a prominent figure in both Azerbaijani and Ottoman literature. Fuzuli's work was widely known and admired throughout the Turkic cultural landscape from the 16th to the 19th centuries, with his fame reaching as far as Central Asia and India.
Born in 1483 in modern-day Iraq, Fuzuli studied literature, mathematics, astronomy, and languages as a child. During his lifetime, his homeland changed hands between the Aq Qoyunlu, Safavid, and Ottoman states. He composed poetry for officials in all three empires, writing his first known poem to Shah Alvand Mirza of the Aq Qoyunlu. Fuzuli wrote most of his poetry during the Ottoman rule of Iraq, which is why he is also sometimes called an Ottoman poet. Throughout his life, he had several patrons but never found one that fully satisfied him—as he wrote—and his desire to join a royal court was never realised. Despite wishing to see places like Tabriz in modern-day Iran, Anatolia, and India, he never travelled outside Iraq. In 1556, Fuzuli died from the plague and was buried in Karbala.
Fuzuli is best known for his Azerbaijani works, especially his ghazals (a form of love poem) and his lyric poem Leylī va Macnūn, which is an interpretation of a Middle Eastern story of tragic love. He also wrote dīvāns (collections of poems) in Azerbaijani, Persian, and possibly Arabic. His style has been described as being distinguished by his "intense expression of feelings" and his use of mystic metaphors and symbols. His poetry shows influences from Persian poets like  Nizami, Jami, and Hafez, as well as Azerbaijani poets like Habibi and Nasimi.
Fuzuli played a role in the development of the Azerbaijani language, with his writings being described as elevating Azerbaijani poetry and language to new heights. His work has been characterised as a reconciliation of Azerbaijani, Persian, and Arabic literary practices, as well as of Shia and Sunni beliefs. He remains a popular poet in Azerbaijan, Turkey, Iran, and Iraq.

Life
Fuzuli, whose given name was Muhammad and whose father's name was Suleyman, was born in 1483. He wrote under the name Fuzuli, which can be translated either as "presumptuous, superfluous" or "exalted, superior, virtuous". In his Persian dīvān (a collection of poems), he wrote that he picked this name to stand out, knowing that no one else would choose such a pen name. Little is known about Fuzuli's youth. He was probably a Shia Muslim of Azerbaijani Turkic origin, descending from the Bayat tribe. Although some contemporary sources refer to him as Fuz̤ūlī-yi Baghdādī (lit. 'Fuzuli of Baghdad'), suggesting he was born or raised in that city or its surroundings, other sources cite the nearby cities of Najaf, Hilla, or Karbala as his birthplace. His father was reported to have once been a mufti (Islamic jurist) in Hilla, which suggests that Fuzuli likely came from an educated family. As a child, he studied literature, mathematics, astronomy, and languages, learning Persian and Arabic in addition to his native Azerbaijani. He had an interest in poetry since his childhood, with his poems suggesting that his initial inspiration was drawn from the works of the late-15th-century Azerbaijani poet Habibi.
Fuzuli lived in Iraq under the Aq Qoyunlu confederation, which ruled the region between 1470 and the conquest of the region by Shah Ismail I of the Iranian Safavid dynasty in 1508. By the time of the Safavid takeover, Fuzuli was already a popular young poet and had dedicated his first known poem, a Persian qaṣīdah (eulogy), to Shah Alvand Mirza of the Aq Qoyunlu. After 1514, the poet received patronage from Ibrahim Khan Mawsillu, the Safavid administrator of Baghdad, whom he met during Mawsillu's visit to Najaf and Karbala. He dedicated his first known Azerbaijani poem, a mas̱navī (a poem written in rhyming couplets) entitled Bang va Bādah (lit. 'Hashish and Wine'), to Ismail I and two qaṣīdahs and one tarjī'band (a poem with repeating verses) to Mawsillu. After Mawsillu was murdered by his own nephew in 1527, Fuzuli lost his patron and moved to either Hilla or Najaf, likely because he could not find another reliable patron among the Safavid nobles. During this time, he worked as a custodian of the Imam Ali Shrine in Najaf. Despite his employment, he did not have much money and relied on different patrons for support. His life between 1527 and 1534 is largely unknown.

When Sultan Suleiman I of the Ottoman Empire captured Baghdad in 1534, Fuzuli was already in his fifties. He presented the sultan with a long qaṣīdah and also wrote qaṣīdahs to Ottoman officials in his entourage in order to earn their favour. One of these officials, Celalzade Mustafa Çelebi, was appointed nişancı (head of the Ottoman Empire's imperial chancery) while in Baghdad and arranged for the poet to receive a daily grant of nine akçes from the excess of donations made to Shia shrines. When Fuzuli was unable to obtain the money from the officers of the Ministry of Evkaf, who were responsible for distributing it, he expressed his disappointment in a poetic letter called Şikāyatnāmah (lit. ''Complaint''), written in Azerbaijani and addressed to Çelebi. In the letter, he declared that he had abandoned all hope, explaining that he had been greatly affected by the political and theological instability of his age. His stipend was restored following the letter. At the time, he was working as a candle-lighter at the Bektashi convent in the Imam Husayn Shrine in Karbala. He wrote in his poems that he had never found a patron who satisfied his needs and his desire to join a royal court had never been realised. Despite expressing a strong desire to see places like Tabriz in modern-day Iran, Anatolia, and India, he never travelled outside modern-day Iraq. In 1556, he died from the plague, either in Baghdad or Karbala, and was buried in Karbala near the Imam Husayn Shrine, in a türbah (a small tomb-mausoleum). According to Bektashi oral tradition, the türbah was built by Abdü'l-mü'min Dede, the Bektashi sheikh (a spiritual guide) of Fuzuli, and the poet was buried next to him.

Poetry
Fuzuli composed poetry and prose in Azerbaijani, Persian and Arabic. Fifteen of his works are extant. The Encyclopædia Iranica distinguishes his work by "the way in which he integrates the mystic and the erotic, in the combination of the conventionality of his topics with the sincerity of his style, and in his intense expression of feelings of passionate love, of pity for the unfortunate, and of patience in the face of adversity". His frequent use of love themes in his poetry has earned him the nickname poet of love by scholars. Abdülkadir Karahan, a scholar of medieval Turkic literature, notes that what distinguished Fuzuli was his "sincerity, enthusiasm, simplicity, sensitivity, and power of expression". Alireza Asgharzadeh, an academic studying Iranian and Azerbaijani culture, describes Fuzuli's poetry as having "manifested the spirit of a profound humanism, reflecting the discontent of both the masses and the poet himself towards totalitarianism, feudal lords, and establishment religion". His poems have also been described by the literary researcher Muhsin Macit as having a "multi-layered structure" because of his "skillful use of metaphors and mystic symbols". Macit has also stated that Fuzuli's poems in Azerbaijani "have a multi-faceted structure, which, combined with perfection of expression, gives them permanence".

full: Esrar Mehmed, known as Şeyh Gālib
primaryTitle: Last Great Classical Ottoman Poet — Hüsn ü Aşk
titles: Şeyh Gālib
bio: Esrar Mehmed, known as Şeyh Gālib (1757–1799) was a poet of the Mawlawiyya tradition, based in Istanbul. Known as Last Great Classical Ottoman Poet — Hüsn ü Aşk.
bio_full:
Esrar Mehmed, known by his pen name Şeyh Gālib, was an Ottoman poet and member of the Mawlawiyya Sufi order who lived from 1757 to 1799. Born in Istanbul during the reign of Mustafa III, he became one of the most celebrated literary figures of the late Ottoman period and is widely regarded as the last great poet of the classical Ottoman tradition.

Gālib entered the Mawlawiyya order, also known as the Whirling Dervishes, which followed the mystical teachings of the 13th-century Persian poet and Sufi master Jalal ad-Din Rumi. This spiritual tradition profoundly influenced his poetic work, infusing it with Sufi themes of divine love, spiritual transformation, and the quest for unity with God. As a member of this order, he would have participated in the ritual practices of dhikr and sama, the ceremonial whirling that characterizes Mawlawiyya worship.

His masterwork, "Hüsn ü Aşk" (Beauty and Love), completed in 1782, stands as one of the finest examples of Ottoman mystical poetry. This allegorical narrative poem tells the story of Beauty and Love's spiritual journey, weaving together complex metaphors and Sufi symbolism to explore themes of divine love and spiritual awakening. The work demonstrates his mastery of classical Persian and Ottoman poetic forms while incorporating the philosophical depth characteristic of Islamic mystical literature.

Gālib's poetry represents the culmination of centuries of Ottoman literary development, synthesizing Persian, Arabic, and Turkish influences within an Islamic framework. His work bridged the classical tradition with emerging literary sensibilities, maintaining the sophisticated court style while expressing deeply personal spiritual experiences. His verses display remarkable technical skill in traditional meters and forms, particularly the ghazal and masnavi.

Beyond his literary achievements, Gālib held religious authority within the Mawlawiyya order, eventually attaining the rank of sheikh. This position involved guiding other Sufis in their spiritual development and preserving the order's traditions and teachings. His dual role as both poet and religious guide exemplifies the integration of artistic expression and spiritual practice that characterized Islamic civilization.

Gālib died in Istanbul in 1799 at the age of 42. His relatively short life produced a body of work that continued to influence Turkish and Islamic literature long after his death, establishing him as a central figure in the Ottoman cultural and religious landscape of the 18th century.

full: Gawhar Shād Āghā bint Ghiyāth al-Dīn Tarkhān
primaryTitle: Timurid Queen — Patron of Herat's Golden Age Architecture
bio: Kuhrshad Bekum, known as the “Upper Cradle,” was the queen and principal consort of Shahrukh, the emperor of the Timurid Empire.
bio_full:
Gawhar Shad (Persian: گوهرشاد, romanized: Gawaršād; meaning "joyful jewel" or "shining jewel"; also Gawhar Shad Begum, Gohar Shād or Gawharshâd; died 19 July 1457) was the chief consort of Shah Rukh, the emperor of the Timurid Empire.

Life
She was the daughter of Giāth ud-Din Tarkhān, an important and influential noble during Tīmur's reign. Her ancestor, Qishliq of the Suldus tribe, had been granted the title Tarkhān personally by Genghis Khan for his services, and was later a commander of a thousand under Chagatai Khan. The Tarkhān title descended down the family and they enjoyed significant prestige.

Marriage
Gawhar Shad was married to Shah Rukh probably in 1388, certainly before 1394 when their son, Ulugh Beg was born. It was a successful marriage, according to the ballads of Herat which sing of Shah Rukh's love for her. But little is known of their first forty years together, except what concerns her buildings.
Along with her brothers who were administrators at the Timurid court in Herat, Gawhar Shad played a very important role in the early Timurid history. In 1405 she moved the Timurid capital from Samarkand to Herat.
She was instrumental in the construction of Herat's Mousallah Complex.

Under her patronage, the Persian language and Persian culture were elevated to a main element of the Timurid dynasty. She and her husband led a cultural renaissance by their lavish patronage of the arts, attracting to their court artists, architects and philosophers and poets acknowledged today among the world's most illustrious, including the poet Jami. Many exquisite examples of Timurid architecture remain in Herat today.

Later years

After the death of her husband in 1447 Gawhar Shad maneuvered her favorite grandson to the throne. For ten years she became the de facto ruler of an empire stretching from the Tigris to the borders of China. When she was well past 80, she was executed on 19 July 1457 on the order of Sultān Abū Sa'īd.
According to legend, Gawhar Shad once inspected a mosque and a religious school (madrasah) in Herat accompanied by two hundred female attendants, after it had been cleared of its students, all of whom were male. One youth remained, having fallen asleep in his cell, and was discovered by an attendant and seduced. When Gawhar Shad found out, she ordered that all two hundred of her attendants be married to the students.

Burial
Gawhar Shad's tomb, the Gawhar Shad Mausoleum, is located within to the Gawhar Shad Madrasa that she had built, of which one minaret and the mausoleum remain until this day.

Legacy
A women's university in Kabul that opened in 2003 bears the name of Gawhar Shad [1]
Gawhar Shad had a mosque ("Masjid-e Goharshād") built in 1418 in Mashhad, Khorasan, and another one, Gawhar Shad Mosque built in Herat. Her sister, Gowhar-Tāj also has a tomb in Khorasan.

Personal life

Consort

Shah Rukh, Timurid Emperor

Sons
Ulugh Beg (1394–1449). Viceroy of Transoxiana, later succeeded his father.
Baysunghur (1397–1433). Shah Rukh's artistic third son never had a vice-royal position, but played an important part in his father's government in Samarqand.
Muhammad Juki Mirza (1402–1444). Viceroy of Garmsir and Khuttal.

Daughters
Maryam Sultan Agha (d. 1441).

titles: Hoca Efendi
bio: Ismail Gelenbevi was an Ottoman Turkish mathematician, Hanafi Maturidi theologian, logician, philosopher and Professor of Geometry at the Naval College in Istanbul, Turkey.
bio_full:
Ismail (bin Mustafa bin Mahmûd) Gelenbevi (1730 – 1790 or 1791) was an Ottoman Turkish mathematician, Hanafi Maturidi theologian, logician, philosopher and Professor of Geometry at the Naval College in Istanbul, Turkey.

His life and work are well documented in several scholarly works in English and Turkish

such as the thesis by Alaettin Avci "Turkiyede Askeri Okullar Tarihcesi" (History of the Military Schools in Turkey), 1963, published by the Research and Development Office of the Turkish General Staff,

and Mehmet Karabela's "The development of dialectic

and argumentation theory in

post-classical Islamic

intellectual history",

Born in 1730 in the town of Gelenbe, near Manisa, at that time in the province of Aydin in Western Anatolia, he is known under the name "Gelenbevi" (English: "from Gelenbe"), which means "de Gelenbe" in French, and "von Gelenbe" in German. He studied in Istanbul where he rose through the Ottoman examination system to the rank of "Müderris"  or professor, at the age of 33.

At the request of the Sadrazam or Grand Vizier Halil Hamit Pasha ("Paşa" in modern Turkish) (1782–1785),  and of the Fleet Admiral Cezayirli Hasan Pasha, he was appointed to a professorship in mathematics at the new Naval College in Kasımpaşa, on the Golden Horn, in Istanbul where he worked with other Ottoman reformers such as the Franco-Hungarian military engineer and aristocrat François Baron de Tott. Gelenbevi received an award from the Emperor Sultan Selim III for his very accurate ballistic computations.

Gelenbevi Ismail published some thirty five scientific treatises,  including a monograph on the game of chess written in Turkish and Arabic. He is credited with the introduction of logarithms in Turkey. The late Ottoman era Cabinet Minister Mehmet Cemaleddin Efendi  (1848–1917) (Turkish: Mehmet Cemâlüddin Efendi), senior judge of the Ottoman Empire and Şeyhülislam or Cabinet Minister in charge of religious and legal matters, the Ottoman period Minister of Education and Director of the Imperial School of Commerce, Gelenbevizade Mehmet Said

(1863–1937), the Turkish cinema pioneer and photographer Baha Gelenbevi (1907–1984), and Professor Erol Gelenbe are direct descendants of Gelenbevi Ismail. A selective public high school in the Fatih district of Istanbul

bears the family name.

titles: Bande Nawaz (Benefactor of Servants) · Khwaja-e-Deccan · Most prolific Chishti writer
bio: Sayyid Muhammad al-Husayni 'Gesu Daraz' al-Gulbargawi (1321–1422) was a mystic of the Chishti tradition, based in Delhi. Known as Bande Nawaz — Benefactor of Servants.
bio_full:
Sayyid Muhammad al-Husayni, known as Gesu Daraz (meaning "long locks") and Bande Nawaz ("Benefactor of Servants"), was a prominent Sufi mystic of the Chishti order who lived from 1321 to 1422. Born into a family with scholarly traditions, he spent his early life in Delhi, which was then a major center of Islamic learning and Sufi activity in the Indian subcontinent.

Gesu Daraz received his spiritual training in the Chishti tradition, a Sufi order known for its emphasis on love, devotion, and service to humanity. The Chishti order had been established in the Indian subcontinent in the 12th century and had become one of the most influential Sufi movements in the region. As a spiritual teacher, Gesu Daraz attracted numerous disciples and became recognized for his scholarship in both Islamic jurisprudence and mystical practices.

During the political upheavals of his time, including the invasions of Timur in the late 14th century, Gesu Daraz eventually migrated southward to the Deccan region. He settled in Gulbarga, which was then part of the Bahmani Sultanate, where he spent his later years. This relocation proved significant for the spread of Chishti Sufism in southern India, as his presence helped establish the order's influence beyond its traditional strongholds in northern India.

Gesu Daraz was known for his literary contributions, having authored works in Persian and Arabic on Sufi doctrine and practice. His writings reflect the traditional Chishti emphasis on spiritual purification, devotion, and the importance of a spiritual guide in the mystical path. He maintained the order's characteristic practices of meditation, remembrance of God, and service to the poor and needy.

His significance in Islamic history lies in his role as a bridge figure who helped transmit Chishti Sufi traditions from Delhi to the Deccan, contributing to the geographical expansion and cultural adaptation of this important Sufi order. His tomb in Gulbarga became a center of pilgrimage and continued to serve as a focal point for Chishti activities in the region. Through his disciples and literary legacy, Gesu Daraz influenced the development of Islamic mysticism in medieval India and contributed to the rich tapestry of Sufi culture in the subcontinent.

bio: Ghalib ibn Fihr, is counted among the direct ancestors of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. In the lineage of Muhammad from Adnan, Fihr precedes Muhammad by ten generations. He is the son of Fihr ibn Malik who lived in Makkah. He died and was buried in Makkah, which was also his birth place.
bio_full:
Ghalib ibn Fihr (Arabic: غَالِب ٱبْن فِهْر, romanized: Ghalib ibn Fihr, fl. c. 230–240 CE), is counted among the direct ancestors of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. In the lineage of Muhammad from Adnan, Fihr precedes Muhammad by ten generations. He is the son of Fihr ibn Malik who lived in Makkah. He died and was buried in Makkah, which was also his birth place.

It is said that Muhammad's lineage is:

Muḥammad bin ʿAbd Allāh bin ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib (Shayba) bin Hāshim (born ʿAmr al-ʿUlā) bin ʿAbd Manāf (al-Mughīrah) bin Qusayy (Zayd) bin Kilāb bin Murrah bin Kaʿb bin Luʿayy bin Ghalib bin Fihr bin Mālik bin al-Naḍr bin Kinanah bin Khuzaymah bin Mudrikah (ʿAmir) bin Ilyas bin Muḍar bin Nizar bin Maʿadd bin Adnan bin Add bin Udad bin Humaysi bin Hamayda bin Salaman bin Thalabah bin Bura bin Shuha bin Yarbah bin Kasdana bin Awwam bin Nashid bin Muqawwam bin Muhtamil bin Badlana bin Ayqan bin Alaha bin Shahdud bin Makhai bin Ayfa bin Aqir bin Al Daʿa bin Abdai bin Hamdan bin Bashmani bin Bathrani bin Bahrani bin Anud bin Raʿwani bin Aqara bin Dayshan bin Naydawan bin Ayyamah bin Bahami bin Hisn bin Nizal bin Qumayr bin Mujashshir bin Mazzi bin Adwa bin Arram bin Qaydar bin Ismail bin Ibrahim, the Friend of God.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Ghaziyah bin 'Amr Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Ghaziyah bin 'Amr Mazni was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community.

Ghaziyah is historically recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event in early Islamic history that took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, occurred when approximately 1,400 Muslims accompanying the Prophet Muhammad on a pilgrimage to Mecca were prevented from entering the city by the Meccan authorities. When rumors spread that the Prophet's envoy Uthman ibn Affan had been killed during negotiations, the companions pledged their loyalty to Muhammad, promising to fight to the death if necessary. This moment of unity and devotion is commemorated in the Quran in verse 48:18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular significance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the unwavering commitment of the early Muslim community to their faith and their leader during a moment of potential crisis. Those who participated in this pledge are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as the Quranic verse explicitly expresses divine approval of their actions.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Ghaziyah would have been among the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with and learned from the Prophet during his lifetime. The companions are considered by Muslims to be important transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices, having witnessed the development of the early Muslim community firsthand.

Ghaziyah bin 'Amr Mazni died around 640 CE, during the early period of Islamic expansion under the Rashidun Caliphate. Like many of the Prophet's companions, his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan remains his most documented contribution to early Islamic history, marking him as one of those who demonstrated loyalty and commitment during a pivotal moment in the formation of the Muslim community.

dob_s: c. 590 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: c. 650 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
bio: Ghaziyya bint Sa'd ibn Khalifa (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Ghaziyya bint Sa'd ibn Khalifa was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca following the Hijra in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Ghaziyya would have witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic community and the development of early Islamic practices and governance. The Ansar played a crucial role in the survival and growth of Islam during its formative years, providing shelter, resources, and military support to the nascent Muslim community when it faced persecution and opposition from Meccan tribes.

The designation of sahabiyya indicates that Ghaziyya had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. Female companions held significant positions within early Islamic society, often serving as transmitters of religious knowledge, participants in community affairs, and supporters of military campaigns. They were instrumental in preserving and passing down Islamic teachings, particularly those related to family life, women's issues, and daily religious practices.

Ghaziyya lived through the most transformative period of early Islamic history, from the initial revelations and persecution in Mecca through the establishment of the Islamic state in Medina. Her lifetime, ending around 635 CE, encompassed the entire prophetic mission of Muhammad and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under the first Caliph, Abu Bakr.

The historical significance of companions like Ghaziyya lies in their role as the first generation of Muslims who directly received Islamic teachings and helped establish the religious and social foundations that would shape Islamic civilization. As an Ansari woman, she represented the local Medinan support that was essential for Islam's survival and expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as a sahabiyya places her among the founding members of the Islamic community whose collective witness and participation authenticated the transmission of Islamic teachings to subsequent generations.

bio: The companion Habbar bin Sufyan bin Abdul-Assad bin Hilal bin Abdullah bin Omar bin Makhzum Al-Qurashi Al-Makhzoumi, from Bani Makhzum, his paternal uncle is Abu Salamah bin Abdul-Assad, his mother is the daughter of Abd bin Abi Qais bin Abd Wad bin Nasr bin Malik bin Hasal bin Amer bin Luay, and she is the sister of Amr bin Abd Wad, who was killed by Ali bin Abi Talib in the Battle of the Trench, and Habbar was an old man of Islam in Mecca. He migrated to the land of Abyssinia in the second migration, and was killed on the day of Ajnadayn in the Levant in the year 13 AH, and it was said: He was martyred in Yarmouk. It was said that he was dead.
bio_full:
Habbar ibn Sufyan ibn 'Abd al-Asad ibn Hilal was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Makhzum clan of Quraysh. Ibn al-Athir identifies him as the nephew of Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad. According to Ibn Sa'd, his mother was a daughter of 'Abd ibn Abi Qays and a sister of 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd, who was killed by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib at the Battle of the Trench.

Ibn Sa'd describes him as an early Muslim in Mecca. He was among the emigrants to Abyssinia, and Ibn Sa'd specifies that he went in the second emigration, according to all the accounts available to him.

Ibn Sa'd, Abu Nu'aym, al-Waqidi and al-Hasan ibn 'Uthman place his death at the Battle of Ajnadayn in Syria, which Abu Nu'aym dates to the caliphate of Abu Bakr. Some reported instead that he was killed at Mu'ta, but Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, followed by Ibn al-Athir, considered Ajnadayn more likely. Abu Nu'aym notes that he left no descendants.

He is distinct from Habbar ibn al-Aswad of the Banu Asad, who accepted Islam only after the conquest of Mecca.

bio_sources.title: Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd; Usd al-Ghaba; al-Isti'ab; Abu Nu'aym — Habbar ibn Sufyan (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

full: Abu Muhammad Habib ibn Muhammad al-Ajami al-Basri
primaryTitle: First Persian Sufi — Student of Hasan al-Basri
titles: al-Ajami (The Persian) · First Persian Sufi · Khalifa of Hasan al-Basri
bio: Habib ibn Muhammad al-‘Ajami al-Basri known also as Habib al-Ajami and Habib al-Farsi was a Muslim Sufi mystic, saint, and traditionalist of Persian descent. Different dates for his death are given in the sources, such as 113 AH, 120 (738), 125 (743), and 130 (747-48). Habib-i Ajami settled in Basra, where his shrine is. He is a disciple of Hasan al-Basri. His disciple is Dāwūd al-Tai.
bio_full:
Habib ibn Muhammad al-‘Ajami al-Basri (Arabic: حبيب بن محمد العجمي البصري) known also as Habib al-Ajami (حبيب العجمي) and Habib al-Farsi (حبيب الفارسي) was a Muslim Sufi mystic, saint, and traditionalist of Persian descent. Different dates for his death are given in the sources, such as 113 AH (731 CE), 120 (738), 125 (743), and 130 (747-48). Habib-i Ajami settled in Basra, where his shrine is. He is a disciple of Hasan al-Basri. His disciple is Dāwūd al-Tai.
According to Ibn Hajar, Habib is a solid hadith narrator. Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirrin, Abu Tamima al-Hujaymi and Bakir bin Abdullah narrated hadiths from him, and Sulayman al-Taymi, Hammad bin Salama, Jafar bin Sulayman and Mu'tamir bin Sulayman reported from him. Bukhari also mentioned him in al-Adab al-Mufrad (I, 366) and al-Tarikh al-Kabir (II, 326). Although Ibn al-Jawzi says that Habib, the narrator of the hadith, is another person, this information should be viewed with caution unless it is confirmed by other sources.

Biography
There is insufficient information about his family and life, but he was originally from Persia. Abu al-Fayd al-Manufi records that he was the son of a king without citing the source. It is rumored that Habib was engaged in trade and usury before turning to Sufism (tasawwuf), and collected a messenger's fee from the debtor if they were not able to pay when he went to collect his debt. It is said that once when he was about to eat a beggar asked him for alms and he harshly scolded him. Meanwhile, when his wife told him that his food had become bloodied, Habib regretted what he had done and decided to become an honest merchant and quit usury. According to the legend, Habib was extremely upset when the children who were playing games while he was passing by, ran away from him because they were fearful, and he went to the assembly of Hasan al-Basri and repented. 
Fariduddin Attar records that Habib-i Ajami received knowledge from Hasan-i Basri during the day and was busy with worship at night in the zawiya he had built on the edge of the Euphrates. According to the rumor, Hasan-i Basri thought that it would not be possible to pray behind him because Habib mispronounced Quranic verses while praying. However, in his dream, he was warned that all the prayers he performed would be accepted for the sake of the prayer he would offer behind Habib, because there was a big difference between correcting the tongue and correcting the heart. This narration is important in that it is one of the first characteristic examples of the mystical understanding that prioritizes the inward over the outward.

Significance
Another feature of Habib is that he is a person whose prayers are accepted according to common opinion. Attar mentions various legends on this subject. Habib's wife Amra was also one of the women ascetics of the time. 
The main importance of Habib in terms of the history of tasawwuf is that he takes place after Hasan al-Basri in the chain of succession (silsila) of the tariqas that were formed in the centuries after the period of asceticism (zuhd). Dawud al-Tai is seen as his disciple in these chains.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Habib bin 'Amr bin Mihsan (c. 597–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Habib ibn 'Amr ibn Mihsan al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar of the Ansar of Medina. Ibn al-Athir gives his lineage as Habib ibn 'Amr ibn Mihsan ibn 'Amr ibn 'Atik ibn 'Amr ibn Mabdhul ibn Ghanm ibn Mazin ibn al-Najjar, while Ibn 'Abd al-Barr places him in the line of 'Amr ibn Mabdhul ibn Ghanm ibn Mazin ibn al-Najjar. Ibn Hibban describes him as the brother of Abu 'Amra.

During the caliphate of Abu Bakr he set out with the Muslims against al-Yamama, but, as Ibn Hibban relates, he was killed on the road before the battle took place. Because he died on the way there, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir count him among the martyrs of al-Yamama. The sources give no year of birth or death.

bio_sources.title: Mashahir 'Ulama' al-Amsar (Ibn Hibban); al-Isti'ab; Usd al-Ghaba — Habib ibn 'Amr ibn Mihsan (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

bio: Habib bin al-Aswad (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Habib bin al-Aswad was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who migrated to Medina and became part of the growing Muslim community there.

Habib bin al-Aswad is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds immense significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The participants in this battle, numbering around 300 Muslims, are held in special reverence within Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment that helped establish the early Muslim state.

As one of the Sahabah, Habib bin al-Aswad was among those who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge, customs, and religious practices to subsequent generations. Their accounts and experiences form an important foundation for understanding early Islamic history and the implementation of Islamic principles in the nascent Muslim community.

Living in Medina, Habib bin al-Aswad would have been part of the diverse community that included both the Muhajirun (emigrants from Mecca) and the Ansar (local Medinan supporters). This period was marked by the establishment of the Constitution of Medina, the construction of the first mosque, and the development of early Islamic law and governance structures.

Habib bin al-Aswad died in 634 CE, which coincided with the end of the Rashidun Caliphate's first phase under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate. His death occurred during a period of rapid expansion of the Islamic state beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation in Badr are limited in historical records, his status as a Sahabi places him among the foundational figures of early Islam. The companions collectively represent the first generation of Muslims who helped establish the religious, social, and political frameworks that would influence Islamic civilization for centuries to come.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Habib bin Taym (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Habib ibn Taym was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad who was killed at the Battle of Uhud. The hadith critic Abu Hatim al-Razi, as recorded by his son Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil, said that he was from the people of Ratij and that he "witnessed Uhud and was killed."

Al-Sakhawi, in his history of the people of Medina, lists him as an Ansari and repeats Ibn Abi Hatim's report that he was martyred at Uhud. He adds the view of his teacher Ibn Hajar, who suggested that the man had been named after his grandfather and that he may be Habib ibn Zayd ibn Taym ibn Usayd ibn Khifaf al-Ansari al-Bayadi. The sources give no further details of his life.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Habib bin Zaid Mazni (c. 591–632 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Habib ibn Zayd ibn 'Asim al-Mazini al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar of Medina. Abu Nu'aym gives his lineage as Habib ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn 'Asim ibn 'Amr al-Mazini al-Najjari. His father was Zayd ibn 'Asim and his mother was Nusayba bint Ka'b, known as Umm 'Umara. Al-Baghawi describes him as the brother of 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn 'Asim, the uncle of 'Abbad ibn Tamim.

Abu Nu'aym records that he was present at the pledge of al-'Aqaba, and one account says he went there with his parents and his brother. Al-Baghawi, citing Ibn Sa'd, states that he took part in Uhud, the Trench and all the campaigns; another account says instead that he was considered too young to fight at Badr and Uhud, and took part in the later campaigns.

The Prophet sent him with a letter to Musaylima, the claimant to prophethood among the Banu Hanifa. Musaylima seized him and repeatedly demanded that he testify that Musaylima was a messenger of God. Habib affirmed that Muhammad was the Messenger of God but refused to say the same of Musaylima, and Musaylima had him cut apart, limb by limb, until he died. His mother later fought at the Battle of al-Yamama in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, in which Musaylima was killed. The sources consulted give no date for his death.

bio: Habiba bint Abi Tajra (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Yemen. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Habiba bint Abi Tajra was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she was based in Yemen during the early period of Islamic expansion into the Arabian Peninsula.

As a sahabiyya, Habiba belonged to the generation of women who personally knew and interacted with the Prophet Muhammad, making her part of the foundational community of early Islam. Her status as a companion placed her among those whose accounts of the Prophet's words and actions would later be considered authoritative sources in Islamic scholarship.

Habiba is primarily remembered for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial component of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice. Female companions like Habiba played important roles in preserving and transmitting religious knowledge, particularly regarding matters that pertained to women's religious and social practices, areas where male companions might have had limited access or knowledge.

Her Yemeni background places her within the context of Islam's spread beyond the Hijaz region into the broader Arabian Peninsula. Yemen's incorporation into the early Islamic community represented a significant expansion of the faith's geographical reach and demonstrated the religion's appeal across different Arabian tribal and regional groups.

The preservation of Habiba's name in Islamic historical records, despite the limited documentation of many early female figures, suggests she held a recognized position within her community as a reliable transmitter of religious knowledge. Her contributions to hadith literature would have been particularly valuable for later generations of Muslim scholars seeking to understand proper Islamic conduct and belief.

Habiba's death around 635 CE places her within the first generation of Muslims who witnessed both the Prophet's lifetime and the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule. This timing meant she lived through the crucial formative period when Islamic practices and teachings were being established and systematized for future generations.

Her legacy lies in her contribution to the preservation of Islamic religious knowledge through the hadith tradition, representing the important but often underrecorded role of women in early Islamic scholarship and religious transmission.

bio: Habiba bint As'ad bin Zurara (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Habiba bint As'ad ibn Zurara was a female Companion from the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj in Medina, and the daughter of As'ad ibn Zurara, known as Abu Umama. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Habiba bint As'ad ibn Zurara ibn 'Udus ibn 'Ubayd ibn Tha'laba ibn Ghanm ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar, and names her mother as 'Umayra bint Sahl ibn Tha'laba, also of the Banu al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad.

She married Sahl ibn Hunayf of the Aws and bore him a son. According to Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir, the Prophet named the child As'ad, after his grandfather, and gave him the kunya Abu Umama. Her sister al-Fari'a was married to Nubayt ibn Jabir of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir record a report from Zaynab bint Nubayt, the wife of Anas ibn Malik, that Abu Umama As'ad had entrusted her mother and her aunt to the Prophet, and that the Prophet adorned them with earrings of gold and pearls. Zaynab said she later saw some of that jewellery among her family. Abu Nu'aym gives a shorter version. One version of the report names the two women as Habiba and her sister Kabsha. The sources give no dates of birth or death.

bio: Habiba bint Kharijah ibn Zayd (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Habiba bint Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Abi Zuhayr was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the Khazraj clan of Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj. Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that she is also called Mulayka, and Abu Nu'aym gives her name as Habiba bint Zayd ibn Kharija. Ibn Hibban and Abu Nu'aym both identify her as the wife of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. According to a note in one manuscript of Malik's al-Muwatta, she had earlier been married to Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' al-Ansari, who was killed at Uhud, after which Abu Bakr married her. Abu Nu'aym records a report from Aisha that Abu Bakr asked the Prophet's permission to go to the house of Kharija, and the Prophet allowed it. Al-Muwatta preserves Abu Bakr's words to Aisha before his death that Habiba was pregnant and that he expected a girl. The same note says she gave birth to a daughter after his death, whom Aisha named Umm Kulthum; Umm Kulthum later married Talha ibn Ubayd Allah and bore him Aisha bint Talha. The note adds that after Abu Bakr she married Habib ibn Yisaf al-Ansari. Abu Nu'aym says she is mentioned in the sources, but no narration from her is known.

Her mother was al-Shumus bint Amr ibn Haram of the Banu Salama. She married Sinan ibn Amr ibn Talq of the Banu Salaman ibn Sa'd Hudhaym, an ally of her clan, and bore him al-Miqna' and Umm al-Harith. Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and gave her pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd also records a second woman of the same name, Habiba bint Mas'ud ibn Khalida of the Banu Zurayq, who is a different person. bio_full:
Habiba bint Mas'ud bin Khalada was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Habiba would have witnessed and participated in the crucial early decades of Islamic history when the Muslim community was establishing itself in Medina. The Ansar played a vital role in providing shelter, support, and protection to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca, helping to ensure the survival and growth of the early Islamic community during its most vulnerable period.

The designation of sahabiyya indicates that Habiba had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions, a status that holds special significance in Islamic tradition. Female companions like Habiba were part of the foundational generation of Muslims who received religious instruction directly from the Prophet and helped transmit Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Living in Medina during this period, Habiba would have experienced the rapid transformation of Arabian society as Islam spread throughout the region. She lived through the establishment of the first Islamic state, the various military campaigns, and the codification of Islamic law and social practices that occurred during the Prophet's lifetime and the early caliphate period.

Habiba died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, having lived through both the Prophetic period and the beginning of the Rashidun caliphate. Her life span encompassed the entire Meccan period of Islamic revelation, the migration to Medina, and the early expansion of the Islamic state beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about her individual contributions or particular roles are not extensively documented in the historical sources, her recognition as a companion places her among the foundational figures of early Islamic history. The female companions collectively played important roles in the early Muslim community, contributing to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings and supporting the development of the nascent Islamic society in Medina.

bio: Habiba bint Mulayl bin Wabara (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Habiba bint Mulayl bin Wabara was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Habiba bint Mulayl would have been part of the established population of Medina, originally known as Yathrib, who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community. The Ansar played a vital role in the early development of Islam, offering protection, resources, and solidarity to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) who had left their homes and possessions in Mecca.

The designation "bint Mulayl bin Wabara" indicates her lineage, following the traditional Arabic naming convention where individuals are identified through their paternal ancestry. Her father was Mulayl, whose father was Wabara, placing her within the tribal and family structures that were central to Arabian society of the early seventh century.

Living during the formative period of Islam, Habiba bint Mulayl would have witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic community in Medina under the Prophet's leadership. This era, spanning roughly from 622 to 632 CE, saw the development of Islamic law, governance, and social structures that would become foundational to the religion.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing means she lived through both the Prophetic period and the initial expansion of Islamic rule under the first caliph, Abu Bakr.

As a sahabiyya, Habiba bint Mulayl holds significance in Islamic history as part of the generation that directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and participated in the early Muslim community. The companions, both male and female, are revered in Islamic tradition for their role in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam to subsequent generations. While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the available historical sources, her status as an Ansari companion places her among those who played essential supporting roles in the establishment and early growth of the Islamic faith.
