bio: Ḥabība bint Sahl ibn Thaʿlaba al-Anṣāriyya al-Khazrajiyya al-Madaniyya (unknown–unknown) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Anṣārī Companion — First Khulʿ Case in Islam.
bio_full: Habiba bint Sahl ibn Tha'laba ibn al-Harith was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Amra bint Mas'ud ibn Qays, also of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd and Abu Nu'aym report that the Prophet Muhammad considered marrying her but then left the idea; Ibn Sa'd links this to his not wishing to distress the Ansar, given their jealousy over their women. She married Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas. Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and gave her pledge of allegiance to the Prophet. One report, given by Abu Nu'aym, says Thabit had a harsh temper and struck her, and that she came to the Prophet's door at dawn; another says she disliked him. The Prophet asked whether she would return the garden Thabit had given her as her dowry; she agreed, Thabit took it back, and they were separated. Abu Nu'aym's report calls this the first khul' (divorce sought by the wife) in Islam. Ibn Sa'd adds that Ubayy ibn Ka'b later married her. Her account was transmitted by Amra bint Abd al-Rahman and appears in Malik's al-Muwatta and other hadith collections. Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that other reports name Thabit's wife in a khul' case as Jamila bint Ubayy ibn Salul, and says both women may have separated from Thabit.

The preservation of hadith narrations from female companions like Habiba bint Shareeq demonstrates the active participation of women in the intellectual and religious life of early Islam. These women served as bridges between the Prophet's immediate circle and later generations of Muslims, ensuring that authentic teachings were passed down through reliable chains of transmission.

Habiba bint Shareeq died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate that followed the Prophet's death in 632 CE. Her contributions to hadith literature represent part of the collective effort by the Prophet's companions to preserve Islamic teachings for future generations, making her an important figure in the development of Islamic scholarly tradition and religious authority.

bio: Habiba bint Ubayd Allah was the daughter of Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh and Umm Habiba Ramla bint Abi Sufyan.
bio_full: Habiba bint Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh was the daughter of Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh and Umm Habiba Ramla bint Abi Sufyan, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad; Ibn al-Athir therefore describes Habiba as the Prophet's stepdaughter. Ibn Ishaq, Musa ibn Uqba and others report that she went with her mother to Abyssinia among the Muslim emigrants, and later returned with her to Medina. Her father became a Christian in Abyssinia and died there as a Christian. According to Ibn al-Athir, she narrated from her mother a hadith known as one passed along by four female Companions in succession, and Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym recorded it. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir both give her an entry among the female Companions. No date of birth or death is recorded in these sources.

bio: Hafez Shirazi (1325–1390) was a Persian lyric poet whose collected works are regarded by many Iranians as one of the highest pinnacles of Persian literature. bio_full:
Hafez Shirazi (1325–1390) was a Persian lyric poet whose collected works are regarded by many Iranians as one of the highest pinnacles of Persian literature. His works are often found in the homes of Persian speakers, who learn his poems by heart and use them as everyday proverbs and sayings. His life and poems have become the subjects of much analysis, commentary, and interpretation, influencing post-14th century Persian writing more than any other Persian author. He is also known by his sobriquet Lisan al-Ghayb (Tongue of the Unseen).
Hafez is best known for his Divān, a collection of his surviving poems probably compiled after his death. His works can be described as "antinomian" and with the medieval use of the term "theosophical"; the term "theosophy" in the 13th and 14th centuries was used to indicate mystical work by "authors only inspired by the Islamic holy books" (as distinguished from theology). Hafez primarily wrote in the literary genre of lyric poetry or ghazals, which is the ideal style for expressing the ecstasy of divine inspiration in the mystical form of love poems. He was a Sufi.
Themes of his ghazals include the beloved, faith and exposing hypocrisy. In his ghazals, he deals with love, wine and taverns, all presenting religious ecstasy and freedom from restraint, whether in actual worldly release or in the voice of the lover. His influence on Persian speakers appears in divination by his poems (Persian: فال حافظ, romanized: fāl-e hāfez, somewhat similar to the Roman tradition of Sortes Vergilianae) and in the frequent use of his poems in Persian traditional music, visual art and Persian calligraphy. His tomb is located in his birthplace of Shiraz and is regularly visited by locals. Adaptations, imitations, and translations of his poems exist in all major languages.

Life

Khājeh Shams-od-Dīn Moḥammad Ḥāfeẓ-e Shīrāzī was born in Shiraz, and identified as a Sufi Muslim. Few details of his life are known and accounts of his early life rely upon traditional anecdotes. Early tazkiras (biographical sketches) mentioning Hafez are generally considered unreliable. At an early age, he memorized the Quran. He was given the title of Hafez because of this, which he later used as his pen name. The preface of his Divān, in which his early life is discussed, was written by an unknown contemporary whose name may have been Moḥammad Golandām. Two of the most highly regarded modern editions of Hafez's Divān are compiled by Allame Mohammad Qazvini and Qāsem Ghani (495 ghazals) and by Parviz Natel-Khanlari (486 ghazals).
Modern scholars generally agree that he was born either in 1315 or 1317, although Gulfishan Khan suggests he was born in 1320. According to an account by Jami, Hafez died in 1390. He was supported by patronage from several successive local regimes: Shah Abu Ishaq, who came to power while Hafez was in his teens; Timur at the end of his life; and even the strict ruler Shah Mubariz ud-Din Muhammad (Mubariz Muzaffar). Though his work flourished most under the 27-year rule of Jalal ud-Din Shah Shuja (Shah Shuja), it is claimed Hāfez briefly fell out of favor with Shah Shuja for mocking inferior poets (Shah Shuja wrote poetry himself and may have taken the comments personally), forcing Hāfez to flee from Shiraz to Isfahan and Yazd, however, no historical evidence to corroborate this is available. Hafez also exchanged letters and poetry with Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah, the Sultan of Bengal, who invited him to Sonargaon though he could not make it. Hafez was also a contemporary of the famous Sunni Shaf'iite theologian Adud al-Din al-Iji - who he praised as one of the five notables of Fars.
Twenty years after his death, a tomb was erected to honor Hafez in the Musalla Gardens in Shiraz. The current mausoleum was designed by André Godard, a French archeologist and architect, in the late 1930s, and the tomb is raised on a dais amidst rose gardens, water channels, and orange trees. Inside, Hafez's alabaster sarcophagus bears the inscription of two of his poems.

Legends

Many semi-miraculous mythical tales were woven around Hafez after his death. It is said that by listening to his father's recitations, Hafez had accomplished the task of learning the Quran by heart at an early age (that is the meaning of the word Hafez). At the same time, he is said to have known by heart the works of Rumi, Saadi, Attar Neyshapuri, and Nizami Ganjavi.
According to one tradition, before meeting his self-chosen Sufi master Hajji Zayn al-Attar, Hafez had been working in a bakery, delivering bread to a wealthy quarter of the town. There, he first saw Shakh-e Nabat, a woman of great beauty, to whom some of his poems are addressed. Ravished by her beauty but knowing that his love for her would not be requited, he allegedly held his first mystic vigil in his desire to realize this union. Still, he encountered a being of surpassing beauty who identified himself as an angel, and his further attempts at union became mystic; a pursuit of spiritual union with the divine.
At 60, he is said to have begun a chilla-nashini, a 40-day-and-night vigil by sitting in a circle that he had drawn for himself. On the 40th day, he once again met with Zayn al-Attar on what is known to be their fortieth anniversary and was offered a cup of Shirazi wine. It was there where he is said to have attained "Cosmic Consciousness". He hints at this episode in one of his verses in which he advises the reader to attain "clarity of wine" by letting it "sit for 40 days".
In one tale, Timur angrily summoned Hafez to account for one of his verses:

Samarkand was Timur's capital and Bukhara was the kingdom's finest city. "With the blows of my lustrous sword", Timur complained, "I have subjugated most of the habitable globe... to embellish Samarkand and Bokhara, the seats of my government; and you would sell them for the black mole of some girl in Shiraz!"
Hafez, the tale goes, bowed deeply and replied, "Alas, O Prince, it is this prodigality which is the cause of the misery in which you find me". So surprised and pleased was Timur with this response that he dismissed Hafez with handsome gifts.

Influence

Intellectual and artistic legacy

Hafez was acclaimed throughout the Islamic world during his lifetime, with other Persian poets imitating his work, and offers of patronage from Baghdad to India.
European scholars began to translate Hafez's work from the 17th Century. The earliest translation of Hafez's poetic compositions is by Francois de Mesgnien Meninski who was the first court interpreter for the government of the Ottoman Empire, or Ottoman Porte. Thomas Hyde, Laudian Professor of Arabic at the University of Oxford translated Hafez's work into Latin in around 1690, according to Gulfishan Khan. Hyde taught himself Persian and translated the work with the assistance of a Turkish commentary.
His work was first translated into English in 1771 by William Jones. It would leave a mark on such Western writers as Thoreau, Goethe, W. B. Yeats, in his prose anthology book of essays, Discoveries, as well as gaining a positive reception within West Bengal, in India, among some of the most prolific religious leaders and poets in this province, Debendranath Tagore, Rabindranath Tagore's father, who knew Persian and used to recite from Hafez's Divans and in this line, Gurudev himself, who, during his visit to Persia in 1932, also made a homage visit to Hafez's tomb in Shiraz  and Ralph Waldo Emerson (the last referred to him as "a poet's poet"). Sir Arthur Conan Doyle has his character Sherlock Holmes state that "there is as much sense in Hafiz as in Horace, and as much knowledge of the world" (in A Case of Identity). Friedrich Engels mentioned him in an 1853 letter to Karl Marx.

bio: Hafsa bint bin Hatib bin 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Hafsa bint Hatib bin 'Amr was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the indigenous inhabitants of Medina who provided crucial support to the Muslim community during its establishment in the city.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Hafsa belonged to the community that welcomed Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, an event known as the Hijra. The Ansar played a pivotal role in Islamic history by offering sanctuary and assistance to the early Muslim community during a critical period when they faced persecution in Mecca.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime, Hafsa would have witnessed the rapid transformation of Medina into the center of the growing Muslim community. The Ansari companions like her were integral to the social and religious fabric of early Islamic society, providing stability and support that allowed the new faith to flourish and expand.

Her designation as a Sahabiyya indicates that she had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. The female companions of the Prophet held important positions within the early Muslim community, often serving as transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations, particularly in matters relating to women's religious and social roles.

Hafsa's relatively short lifespan, ending around 635 CE, means she lived through the most crucial decades of early Islamic history, from the initial revelations through the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina and the beginning of Islam's expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. She died during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following the Prophet's death when his closest companions led the Muslim community.

As an Ansari companion, Hafsa bint Hatib bin 'Amr represents the essential contribution of Medina's indigenous population to the foundation and early development of Islamic civilization. Her recognition in Islamic historical sources reflects the important role that women companions played in the formative period of the faith, serving as witnesses to and participants in the events that shaped early Islamic society.

full: Ḥafṣah bint Sīrīn al-Baṣriyya, Mawlāt Anas ibn Mālik
primaryTitle: Umm Hudhayl — Pioneer of Female Asceticism in Islam
titles: Umm Hudhayl · Iyas ibn Muʿāwiya's verdict: 'I have met no one I prefer over her'
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · al-Dhahabī — Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ · al-Mizzī — Tahdhīb al-Kamāl
bio: Hafsa bint Sirin was an early female scholar of Islam. She has been called one of the "pioneers in the history of female asceticism in Islam".
bio_full:
Umm al-Hudhayl ​​Hafsa bint Sirin al-Ansariyya al-Basriyah, a jurist and hadith narrator.

Umm Attiya, Umm Al-Raih, her master Anas bin Malik, and Abu Al-Aaliyah.

Her brother Muhammad, Qatada, Ayoub, Khaled Al-Hadha, Ibn Aoun, and Hisham bin Hassan.

The mention of death would never leave her, for she knew that the world had a number of days, and if a day passed, some of them also disappeared. Therefore, she expected death at every moment, until it was reported that she used to keep a permanent shroud for herself, which was part of her clothing. So, if she performed Hajj and entered ihram, she would wear it, and if the last ten days of Ramadan came, she would wear it and stay in it.

She used to say: O young people! Take care of yourselves while you are young, for I have seen work in youth.

She read the Qur’an and contemplated its meanings when she was twelve years old. Whenever her brother, Muhammad ibn Sirin, had difficulty with something in the Qur’an, he would say: Go to Hafsa and ask her how she reads? Hafsa was famous for her asceticism and beautiful patience in obedience to God and worshiping Him. She fasted a lot and stood for a long time. She would enter her mosque and pray in it, and worship by reading the Qur’an, and would not leave her house except For a need or to meet those who come to question it and learn from it.

She was a modern scholar, and she had six brothers besides her, all of whom recited the Qur’an and were busy with hadith.

Hafsa loved knowledge and sacrificed everything for its sake. Hafsa was also known for her strong adherence to the true teachings of Islam and her obedience to God and His Messenger. On the authority of Asim Al-Ahwal, he said: We used to go to Hafsa bint Sirin, and she had made the jilbab like this and was wearing her veil, and we would say to her, may God have mercy on you. God Almighty said: “As for the women who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame on them if they remove their clothes and do not adorn themselves with adornment. If they behave chastely, it is better for them, and God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing (Al-Nur: 60). If they remain chaste, it is better for them.) She says, “It is the proof of the jilbab.”

On the authority of Hisham bin Hassan. He said: Al-Hudhayl ​​bin Hafsa used to collect firewood in the summer, peel it and take the reeds. So he splits it.

Hisham said: He had an impotence.

full: Ḥafṣah bint ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb al-ʿAdawiyya al-Qurashiyya
primaryTitle: Umm al-Muʾminīn — Custodian of the Quran
titles: Umm al-Muʾminīn · Ḥāfiẓat al-Muṣḥaf (Guardian of the Quran Manuscript) · Ṣawwāma Qawwāma (Devoted to Fasting and Prayer)
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · al-Bukhāri — Ṣaḥīḥ · al-Dhahabī — Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ
bio: Hafsa bint Umar was the fourth wife of Muhammad and a daughter of the second caliph Umar. In Islamic writings, her name is thus often prefixed by the title "Mother of the Believers".
bio_full:
Hafsa bint Umar was a prominent figure in early Islamic history, known primarily as the fourth wife of the Prophet Muhammad and the daughter of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who would later become the second Caliph of Islam. Born around 605 CE in Mecca, she lived during the formative period of the Islamic community and died in 665 CE in Medina.

Before her marriage to Muhammad, Hafsa was married to Khunays ibn Hudhafa, a companion of the Prophet who died from wounds sustained at the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE. Following her period of mourning, she married Muhammad in 625 CE, becoming one of the Mothers of the Believers, a title of honor given to the Prophet's wives in Islamic tradition.

Hafsa's most significant contribution to Islamic history lies in her role in preserving the Quran. After the Prophet's death, she was entrusted with keeping one of the earliest complete written compilations of the Quranic text. This compilation had been assembled during the caliphate of Abu Bakr under the supervision of Zayd ibn Thabit. When the third Caliph Uthman ibn Affan initiated the project to create a standardized version of the Quran, Hafsa's copy served as a crucial reference manuscript. Her careful preservation of this text played an essential role in maintaining the integrity of the Quranic revelation for future generations.

As one of the Mothers of the Believers, Hafsa held a respected position within the early Muslim community. She was known for her literacy, which was relatively uncommon among women of her time, and her strong character. Islamic historical sources indicate that she was active in religious discussions and was consulted on various matters related to Islamic law and practice.

Hafsa's life spanned the Prophet's era, the period of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, and into the early Umayyad period. Her longevity allowed her to witness and participate in the crucial formative decades of Islamic civilization. Through her preservation of the Quranic text and her position as a Mother of the Believers, she remains an important figure in Islamic religious and historical consciousness, representing both the intimate circle of the Prophet's household and the broader community of early Muslim women who contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings.

full: Muhammad Imdad Allah ibn Muhammad Hafiz al-Thanawi al-Makki al-Chishti
primaryTitle: Spiritual Father of Both Deoband and Barelvi
titles: Haji Sahib · Amir of the 1857 Rebellion · Spiritual master of founders of both Deobandi and Barelvi movements
bio: Imdadullah Muhajir Makki was an Indian Islamic scholar. A Sufi saint who followed the Chishti order, his disciples were Pir Meher Ali Shah,Muhammad Anwarullah Farooqui, and some who abandoned his method & path and formed their own new sect, include Muhammad Qasim Nanawtawi, Rashid Ahmad Gangohi and Ashraf Ali Thanwi. In the Indian Rebellion of 1857, he led the Muslims in Thana Bhawan to fight against the British. Imdadullah is also referred to by the Persian title A'la Hazrat.
bio_full:
Imdadullah Muhajir Makki (1817 – 1899) was an Indian Islamic scholar. A Sufi saint who followed the Chishti order, his disciples were Pir Meher Ali Shah,Muhammad Anwarullah Farooqui,Muhammad Qasim Nanawtawi, Rashid Ahmad Gangohi and Ashraf Ali Thanwi. In the Indian Rebellion of 1857, he led the Muslims in Thana Bhawan to fight against the British. Imdadullah is also referred to by the Persian title A'la Hazrat.

Early life
Imdadullah Muhaajir Makki was born in Nanauta, British India in 1817. His father Muhammad Amīn named him Imdad Hussain. However, Shah Muhammad Ishaq gave him the name of Imdādullah.
Aged seven, Imdādullah lost his mother who wrote her will that none shall touch her kid after her, and kept Imdādullah more beloved to her in those seven years; this became a hurdle that no one took care of Imdādullah's education. He then started memorizing the Quran on his own but failed to do so. Aged 16, he traveled to Delhi with Mamluk Ali Nanautawi to seek education.

Religious work and travels
At the age of eighteen, his bay'at was accepted by Nasiruddin Naqshbandi. Later he went to study under Mianji (Noor Mohammad Jhanjhanvi), as an initiate of the Chishti-Sabiri Sufi order, but after Mianji's death he temporarily became a semi-recluse. After wandering in the wilderness for six months he was overcome by a strong urge to travel to Medina. On 7 December 1845, he arrived at Banares. From there, he departed for Ottoman Arabia for Hajj and pilgrimage of the tomb of shrine of Muhammad.
After the completion of his hajj, Imadadullah remained with Ishaq Muhajir Makki and others. Shah informed him that, after his pilgrimage to Medina, he should return to India. Sayyid Qudratullah Banarasi Makki sent several of his murids to accompany him to Medina.

Freedom struggle against the British
In Thana Bhawan, the local Sunnis declared Imdadullah their leader. In May 1857 the Battle of Shamli took place between the forces of Imdadullah and the British.

Disciples
Disciples include:

Maulana Peer Syed Shah Muhammad Meher Ali Quadri Qummaisi
Ahmad Hasan Amrohi
Asghar Hussain Deobandi
Ashraf Ali Thanwi
Muhammad Qasim Nanautawi
Rashid Ahmad Gangohi
Muhammad Anwaarullah Farooqui
Muhammad Yaqub Nanautawi
Mahmud Hasan Deobandi
Maulana Badruddin Phulwarvi
Sayyid Muhammad Abid
Najib Ali Choudhury

Marriages
Imdadullah married for the first time at the age of 48. After the death of his first wife, he married a blind widow. Because she was blind, she could not manage all household work, so she requested him to take another wife so all household work. Imdadullah then married for the 3rd time. None of his three wives bore him children.

Literary works
His books include:

Faisla Haft Masala
Kulliyat-e-Imdadiya
Hashiya Mathnavi Moulana Rumi: This is an annotation in Persian on the Mathnawi-i Ma’nawi by Rumi. During Imadadullah's lifetime, only two parts could be printed. The remainder was printed after his death.
Ghiza-e-Ruh (The Nourishment of the Soul): Imadadullah wrote this book in 1264 AH. Mianji Noor Mohammad Jhanjhanvi is also discussed. It consists of 1600 verses of poetry.
Ikleelul Quran (Tafseer Quran in Arabi). First Published in Bahraich by Taj Offcet Press formerly Aqeel Press NazirPura Bahraich
Jihad-e-Akbar (The Greater Jihad): He composed this book in 1268 AH. It is a poetic work in Persian that he translated it into Urdu. It consists of 17 pages with 679 verses.
Mathnavi Tuhfatul Ushshaq (Mathnavi – A Gift for Lovers): This consists of 1324 poetic verses and was compiled in 1281 AH.
Risala Dard Ghamnak (The Treatise of Painful Sorrow): It consists of 5 pages with 175 verses.
Irshad-e-Murshid (The Directive of the Murshid): This book deals with wadha'if, muraaqabaat, aurad, and shajaraat of the four silsilas. It was written in 1293 AH.
Zia ul Quloob (Glitter of the Hearts): This book is in Persian. He wrote this kitab in Makkah in 1282 AH on the request of Hafiz Muhammad Yusuf, the son of Hafiz Muhammad Zamin.

Death and legacy
Imdadullah died at Mecca in 1899. He was buried in the Jannat al-Mu'alla cemetery besides the grave of Rahmatullah Kairanwi. His biographical works include: Imdadul Mustaq Ila Asraful Akhlaq by Ashraf Ali Thanwi, Shamaem Emdadiya by Muhammad Murtaza Khan Qanauji. 

Eponyms
Jamia Arabia Imdadul Uloom, Faridabad, Bangladesh

See also
Muhammad Mian Mansoor Ansari

References

Bibliography
Kugle, Scott (2007). Body Revived The Heart of Ḥājji Imdādullah', Sufis & Saints' Bodies: Mysticism, Corporeality, and Sacred Power in Islam. Chapel Hill, NC: University of North Carolina Press. ISBN 9781469602684.
Mawlāna Abd al-Rashīd Arshad. "Hadhrat Hāji Imdādullah Muhājir Makki". In Deobandi, Nawaz (ed.). Sawaneh Ulama-e-Deoband (in Urdu). Vol. 1 (January 2000 ed.). Deoband: Nawaz Publications. pp. 342–376.
Tareen, SherAli (2013). "FAYSALA-YI HAFT MAS'ALA (A RESOLUTION TO THE SEVEN CONTROVERSIES): Haji Imdadullah's Hermeneutics of Reconciliation". SAGAR: South Asia Graduate Research Journal. 21. hdl:2152/28002. Retrieved 7 November 2021.

titles: Sultan al-Awliya · Haji Bektash
bio: Haji Bektash Veli was an Islamic scholar, mystic, saint and philosopher from Khorasan who lived and taught in Anatolia. His original name was Muhammad. He is also referred to as the "Sultan of Hearts" and the "Dervish of the Dervishes".
bio_full:
Haji Bektash Veli (Persian: حاجی بکتاش ولی, romanized: Ḥājī Baktāš Valī; Turkish: Hacı Bektaş Veli; Albanian: Haxhi Veli Bektashi; c. 1209–1271) was an Islamic scholar, mystic, saint and philosopher from Khorasan who lived and taught in Anatolia. His original name was Muhammad. He is also referred to as the "Sultan of Hearts" and the "Dervish of the Dervishes". 
He is revered among Alevis for an Islamic understanding that is esoteric, rational and humanistic. He was one of the many figures who flourished in the Sultanate of Rum and had an important influence on the culture of Turkic nomads of Asia Minor.

Identity
Bektash is generally believed to be of Persian or Turkic origin, and his name is considered to be of Turkic origin. Bektash belonged to a group of Khorasani migrants in Anatolia who had left their homeland during the Mongol conquests. According to the Vilâyet-Nâme, Bektash was the son of Sayyed Muhammad ibn Musa, a great-grandson of Musa al-Kazim; this is impossible, given the fact that Bektash lived in the 7th/13th century. Genealogies encountered in later sources and designed to fill the obvious gap in time are all questionable and may well have been inspired by a wish—analogous to that of the fabricators of the Safavid genealogy—to give Bektash, as the eponym of a nominally Shia order, Imami descent.
According to "The history of Aşıkpaşazade" (Aşıkpaşazade Tarihi), written by one of the grandsons of "Aşık Pasha" who was the son of "Muhlis Paşa" (Muhlees Pāshā) who was the son of renowned Baba Ilyas al-Khorasani, "Sayyeed Muhammad ibn Sayyeed Ebrāheem Ātā" had come to Sivas, Anatolia from Khorasan with his brother "Menteş" (Mantash) to become affiliated with the tariqat of Baba Ilyas al-Khorasani. On the other hand, the famous reference book of Bektaşi order, Valāyat-Nāma-i Hādjī Baktāsh-ī Wālī, claims that "Bektash" was the murshid of Bābā (Bābā Eliyās al-Khorāsānī).
The name attributed to him by his followers can be translated as "The Pilgrim Saint Bektash." The Haji title implies that he had made the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina to perform Hajj. He is the eponym of the Bektashi Sufi order and is considered one of the principal teachers of Alevism. According to the Encyclopaedia of Islam, the "center and source of his teachings" was ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, whom Alevis believe to be the righteous successor of Muhammad while also "acknowledging the twelve Shia Imams" and "holding Jafar as-Sadiq in high esteem". Despite his Shia belief and his unorthodox teachings, he is considered a renowned figure in the history and culture of both the Ottoman Empire and the modern nation-state of Turkey. On the other hand, Ibn Khallikan reports that Shī'ite tendencies belonged not to him but rather to his murids, who took refuge in his tekke at Suluca Kara Oyuk in Kırşehir after the Babai Revolt.

Origins

Born in Nishapur. Legends state that Bektash was a khalifa of Ahmad Yasawi, the eponymous founder of the Yasawi order that had a wide following among Turkic nomads in Central Asia. Though chronogically impossible, supposedly Yasawi sent him to Anatolia to propagate his order there. Not much is known about him, his origins are shrouded in mystery and much of his biography is based on legends.

Silsila connecting to Hoja Ahmad Yasawi

The sisilah of Hadji Baktāsh Wālī reaches to the Yasawi Order through another but a similar tariqah, which is well known as the Wafā'īyyah Order of Abu’l Wafā al-Khwarazmī, who was a murid of Ahmad Yasawi and the murshid of Dede Ğarkhen, who was in turn the murshid of Bābā Eliyās al-Khorāsānī († 1240), an influential mystic from Eastern Persia. Modern research connects him to another important religious movement of that time: to the Qalandariyya and to Bābā Eliyās al-Khorāsānī, who was the murshid of Aybak Bābā, who was in turn the murshid of one of the leading actors of the Babai revolt, Baba Ishak, as well. Eventually, Bābā Eliyās Khorāsānī was held responsible for the Babai revolt organized by Baba Ishak, and consequently executed by Mubāriz’ud-Dīn-i Armāğān-Shāh, the supreme commander-in-chief of the armies of the Sultanate of Rum.
The original Bektashi teachings in many ways resemble the teachings of the Khorasanian Qalandariyya and that of Bābā Eliyās. Haji Baktash Veli was the murid of Lokhmānn Bābā (Lokhmānn Sarakhsī), who was one of the four most famous murids of Bābā Eliyās al-Khorāsānī as well. Lokhmānn Bābā, on the other hand, was also a murid of the renowned Qalandari Qutb ad-Dīn Haydar, who was the murid of Ahmad Yasawi. For these reasons, his silsila gets connected to Ahmad Yasawi through two different channels, one by means of the Wafā’i and the other through Qutb ad-Dīn Haydar. He was highly respected by the Sultanate of Rum due to his amicable attitude during the Babai revolt, and his khanqah in Suluca Kara Oyuk was permitted to remain open during and after it, thereby saving most of the lives of the Alevi survivors.

From the Vilayetname
From the Vilayetname (or: The Saintly Exploits of Hacı Bektaş Veli):
After Lokman Perende had returned from the hajj, the erenler (saints) of Khorasan came to offer him their respects. When they saw a spring flowing from the middle of the mekteb, they said, "We have been here before many times and had never seen such spring." Lokman Perende replied, "This is by the blessings of Hunkar Haji Bektash." The erenler asked, "Who is this Hunkar Haji Bektash?" Lokman Perende said, "Haji Bektash Hunkar is this beloved one," and he then pointed to the young Bektash. The erenler said, "That one is still a child. How on earth could he become a haji?" Lokman Perende then described to the gathering all of the miracles of Haji Bektash one by one and then said, "While I was performing my prayer at the Kaabah, Bektash was always there praying next to me. When we completed our prayer, he would vanished." The erenler said, "Where could this boy have found this extraordinary capability?" Then Hunkar Haji Bektash opened his blessed mouth and said, "I am the secret of the exalted Imam Ali, who is the dispenser of the River Kawthar and who is the Lion of Allah, the Emperor of Sainthood and the Commander of the Faithful. My origin and family line is from him. These many miracles are my inheritance which is granted by Allah. It should not be surprising to anyone that miracles like these appear from me, for this is the Power of God."
The erenler of Khorasan said, "If, in reality, you are the secret of the Shah, he has marks. Show these marks to us and we shall believe." Now the sign of Hazreti Ali was this; in the middle of his blessed hand he had a beautiful mole of emerald tone. So Hazreti Hunkar Haji Bektash Veli opened his sanctified hand and showed his palm. They all saw that there, in the middle his palm, was a beautiful emerald mole. The erenler said, "The Commander of the Faithful also had a beautiful emerald mole on his blessed forehead." Hunkar Haji Bektash Veli removed the skull cap from his blessed head and all saw a divinely illuminated mole of emerald tint between his brow. All of the erenler begged for forgiveness, saying, "O Dervish of the Dervishes, we have been sorely mistaken." They surrendered to him asserting, "These are indeed miracles."

Spread of the Bektashi order

Bektashism spread from Anatolia through the Ottoman Turks primarily into the Balkans, where its leaders (known as dedes or babas) helped convert many to Islam. The Bektashi Sufi order became the official order of the elite Janissary corps after their establishment. The Bektashi Order remained very popular among Albanians, and Bektashi tekkes can be found throughout Albania, Kosovo and the Republic of Macedonia to this day. During the Ottoman period Bektashi tekkes were set up in Egypt and Iraq, but the order did not take root in these countries.

primaryTitle: al-Hakim — Imam of the Science of Sainthood
titles: al-Hakim (The Sage) · Imam 'Ilm al-Wilaya
bio: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi (c. 820–c. 910) was a scholar of the Khorasan School tradition, based in Tirmidh. Known as al-Hakim — Imam of the Science of Sainthood.
bio_full:
Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from approximately 820 to 910 CE in the city of Tirmidh, located in present-day Uzbekistan along the Amu Darya River. He belonged to the Khorasan School tradition, an influential intellectual movement that flourished in the eastern regions of the Islamic world during the early medieval period.

Al-Tirmidhi earned the honorific title "al-Hakim," meaning "the wise one," reflecting his reputation for profound spiritual insight and religious knowledge. He is most notably remembered as a pioneer in the systematic study of Islamic mysticism and sainthood, earning him recognition as the "Imam of the Science of Sainthood." His work represented an early attempt to codify and analyze the spiritual dimensions of Islamic religious experience.

Operating during a period of significant intellectual development in the Islamic world, al-Tirmidhi contributed to the emerging field of Sufi literature and theory. The Khorasan region, where he lived and taught, served as a crucial center for Islamic learning and spiritual development during the ninth and tenth centuries, attracting scholars from across the Muslim world.

His scholarly output focused primarily on questions of spiritual development, the nature of sainthood, and the relationship between religious knowledge and mystical experience. Al-Tirmidhi's approach combined rigorous adherence to Islamic law and tradition with deep exploration of the inner dimensions of faith, helping to establish frameworks that would influence later Islamic mystical thought.

The city of Tirmidh, strategically positioned along major trade routes, provided al-Tirmidhi with exposure to diverse intellectual currents and religious traditions. This cosmopolitan environment likely influenced his scholarly development and contributed to the breadth of his intellectual interests.

Al-Tirmidhi's legacy lies in his role as an early systematizer of Islamic mystical concepts and his contribution to the theoretical foundations of Sufism. His work helped establish scholarly methodologies for examining spiritual experience within an Islamic context, influencing subsequent generations of Muslim mystics and scholars. While specific details of his life remain limited, his intellectual contributions mark him as a significant figure in the development of Islamic spiritual thought during the classical period.

bio: Halima/Jamila bint 'Urwa bin Mas'ud (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Halima bint 'Urwa bin Mas'ud was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the crucial decades that witnessed the emergence and initial expansion of the Islamic community.

As an Ansari companion, Halima belonged to the group of Medinan supporters who welcomed and aided the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were the residents of Medina who embraced Islam and provided essential support to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) who had migrated from Mecca. This designation indicates that she was among the local population of Medina who played a vital role in establishing the early Islamic community in that city.

Her father, 'Urwa bin Mas'ud, connects her to the prominent Thaqif tribe, suggesting she came from a family of some standing in Arabian society. During this period, tribal affiliations and family lineages were significant markers of identity and social position in Arabian culture.

Halima lived during one of the most transformative periods in Arabian and Islamic history, witnessing the Prophet's migration to Medina, the establishment of the first Muslim community, and the early expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime, spanning approximately four decades until around 635 CE, encompassed the entire Medinan period of Islamic history and extended into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate.

The inclusion of female companions like Halima in historical records reflects the important roles women played in the early Islamic community, even when specific details of their individual contributions may not be extensively documented. As part of the Ansar, she would have been among those who provided the foundational support necessary for the survival and growth of the early Muslim community in Medina.

Her recognition as a Sahabiyya places her within the most revered generation in Islamic tradition—those who lived during the time of the Prophet Muhammad and directly participated in the formative years of the Islamic community. This status acknowledges her as part of the foundational generation that helped establish Islam as both a religious and social system.

primaryTitle: Sultan al-Tarikain — King of the Two Paths
titles: Sultan al-Tarikain
bio: Hamid al-Din Muhammad Sufi Nagori (1192–1274) was a mystic of the Chishti tradition, based in Nagaur. Known as Sultan al-Tarikain — King of the Two Paths.
bio_full:
Hamid al-Din Muhammad Sufi Nagori was a prominent Islamic mystic who lived from 1192 to 1274 CE during the Delhi Sultanate period in medieval India. He belonged to the Chishti order, one of the most influential Sufi traditions that played a crucial role in spreading Islam throughout the Indian subcontinent.

Nagori was based in Nagaur, a city in present-day Rajasthan, India, which served as an important center of Islamic learning and spirituality during his lifetime. The city's strategic location along trade routes made it a crossroads of cultural and religious exchange, providing an ideal environment for his mystical teachings and practices.

He earned the distinctive title "Sultan al-Tarikain," meaning "King of the Two Paths," though the precise meaning of this epithet remains a subject of scholarly discussion. The title suggests he may have been recognized for mastering different aspects of Sufi doctrine or practice, or for his ability to guide disciples along multiple spiritual approaches within the Chishti tradition.

As a Chishti mystic, Nagori would have emphasized the core principles of this Sufi order, which typically included poverty, humility, and service to humanity regardless of religious background. The Chishti tradition was known for its inclusive approach and its focus on music and poetry as means of spiritual expression, though specific details about Nagori's particular methods and teachings are not well-documented in widely available historical sources.

His lifetime coincided with a significant period of Islamic expansion and consolidation in northern India. The early 13th century saw the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate, and Sufi masters like Nagori played important roles in the peaceful spread of Islamic culture and religious practice among local populations.

Nagori's eight-decade lifespan allowed him to witness and participate in the formative years of Islamic mysticism in India. His presence in Nagaur contributed to the establishment of the region as a notable center of Sufi activity, though detailed records of his specific contributions to Islamic scholarship or the number of disciples he trained are limited in accessible historical documentation.

His legacy represents the broader pattern of Chishti influence in medieval India, where Sufi masters served as bridges between Islamic traditions and local cultures, facilitating religious and cultural synthesis that would characterize much of the subcontinent's Islamic heritage.

bio: Hamnah bint Jahsh (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Hamnah bint Jahsh or Hammnah (Arabic: حمنة بنت جحش), was a companion of Muhammad.

Biography
She was the daughter of Jahsh ibn Riyab, an immigrant to Mecca from the Banu Asad  tribe, and Umayma bint Abd al-Muttalib, a member of the Hashim clan of the Quraysh tribe who was Muhammad's aunt. Hence Hammanah was a first cousin of Muhammad and Ali, a  sister of Abd-Allah ibn Jahsh, Ubayd-Allah ibn Jahsh and Zaynab bint Jahsh, and a niece of Hamza ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib.
She was married to Mus`ab ibn `Umair when she converted to Islam. She migrated to Medina, and when the women of Ansar and Muhajirun took the oath of allegiance at the hands of Muhammad, she was amongst them.
She participated in the battle of Uhud, providing water and treating the injured. Her husband Mus`ab was killed in this battle. When Muhammad returned from Uhud, the women began to ask after the battle casualties. He said, "O Hamnah! Expect that your brother Abdullah will be rewarded!" She replied, "To Allah we belong and to him we shall return. May Allah's mercy be upon him and may Allah forgive him." Then Muhammad said, "Expect that your uncle, Hamza ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib, will be rewarded!" Again she remained calm and gave the same reply. He then said, "O Hammanah! Expect that your husband, Mus`ab ibn `Umair, will be rewarded!"  Upon this she shrieked and wailed. Muhammad remarked, "The woman's husband holds a special place with her, as you can see from her self-control at the death of her brother and her uncle and her shrieking over her husband."
Hammanah then married the prominent Muslim general Talha ibn Ubayd-Allah. Talha was amongst the Asharah Mubasharah, the ten people to whom Muhammad promised Paradise while they were still alive. Hammanah had two children by Talha, Muhammad ibn Talha, known as Sajjad, and Imran.
The year of Hammanah's death is unknown; however, she outlived her sister Zaynab, who died in the year 20 A. H.

bio: Hamza bin al-Humayyir (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Hamza bin al-Humayyir was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early 7th century CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community.

Hamza bin al-Humayyir is historically recognized for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The Muslims who fought at Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as this engagement marked a crucial turning point in the early expansion and consolidation of Islam.

As a Sahabi, Hamza bin al-Humayyir was part of the generation that directly witnessed and participated in the establishment of the early Muslim community under the Prophet's guidance. The companions played essential roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam to subsequent generations, serving as primary sources for understanding the Prophet's words and actions.

His presence in Medina places him within the community that emerged after the Hijra, the migration of Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. This period saw the development of the first Islamic society and the establishment of many foundational Islamic practices and institutions.

Hamza bin al-Humayyir died in 634 CE, during the era of the first Caliph Abu Bakr, when the Muslim community was beginning its rapid expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. His death occurred during a period of significant transition, as the Islamic community was adapting to life after the Prophet's passing in 632 CE and beginning the military campaigns that would eventually establish a vast Islamic empire.

While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in the historical record, his status as a companion who fought at this pivotal battle ensures his place in early Islamic history. The companions of Badr are remembered as individuals who supported the Prophet during a critical moment when the survival of the early Muslim community was at stake.

primaryTitle: First Sufi Poet of the Malay World
titles: Shaykh al-Islam of Malay Sufism
bio: Hamzah Fansuri was a 16th-century Sumatran Sufi writer, and the first writer known to write mystical panentheistic ideas in the Malay language. He wrote poetry as well as prose. He has been called the "first Malay poet" and the first known poet to have written in the Malay poetic form syair.
bio_full:
Hamzah Fansuri (Jawi: حمزه فنسوري; also spelled Hamzah Pansuri, d. c. 1590 ?) was a 16th-century Sumatran Sufi writer, and the first writer known to write mystical panentheistic ideas in the Malay language. He wrote poetry as well as prose. He has been called the "first Malay poet" and the first known poet to have written in the Malay poetic form syair.

Life
Information on Hamzah's life comes largely from the takhallus bait (pen-name stanza) that ends his poetry (syair), as well as from the work of his disciple Hasan Fansuri and commentaries on Hamzah's poems. However, many of his biographical details are uncertain. His name indicates that he may be from Barus (also known as Fansur to the Arabs), or have spent a large part of his life there. A link to the Siamese Ayutthaya (Shahr-i-Naw) has also been proposed, although it may be that he travelled to Ayutthaya rather than that being his birthplace. He was inducted into a Sufi order and it is thought that he may have worked at the court of the Aceh Sultanate.
Hamzah travelled widely, and was known to have visited the Malay Peninsula, Mughal India, Mecca and Medina, and Baghdad.  He was one of the earliest Southeast Asians to have completed the hajj during the early 16th century. The date of his death is generally assumed to be around 1590 or earlier, although a later date during the reign of Sultan Iskandar Muda has also been proposed. However, an inscription on a gravestone found in Mecca for a Shaykh Hamza b. Abd Allah al-Fansuri recorded a date of April 11, 1527, although that identification has been challenged. Such an early date, if confirmed, may suggest that Hamzah did not live or work in Aceh, rather he was in Barus before leaving for Mecca where he died.

Panentheism
Hamzah Fansuri's panentheism was derived from the writings of the medieval Islamic scholars. He was influenced by Ibn Arabi's doctrine of Waḥdat al-Wujūd popular in Persia and Mughal India during the 16th century. Ibn Arabi taught that all reality is one and everything that exists is part of the divine. He perceived God as immanent within all things, including the individual, and sought to unite one's self with the indwelling spirit of God. He employed the doctrine of seven stages of emanation (martabat) in which God manifests Himself in this world, ending in the Perfect Man, a doctrine widespread in Indonesia at the time. His teachings were promoted by Aceh theologian Shamsuddin al-Sumatrani.
However, his views were later deemed heretical by Nuruddin ar-Raniri for not conforming to the Islamic belief that God remained unchanged by His creation. Nuruddin travelled to Aceh and under his influence, the Sultana Taj ul-Alam attempted to eradicate Hamzah's works and name, and his writings were burnt.

Works
The poetry, syair or ruba'i, of Hamzah Fansuri are usually not more than 13-15 stanzas, but some may be up to 21. 32 of his poems have survived, and Hamzah included in each poem his name and information about himself in the last stanza (takhallus bait).  Scholars have commented on his technical skill and mastery in his rhymes, the effective blending Arabic words into Malay poetic structure. They also noted a fondness for pun in his works that displays his humour and poetical flair. He also wrote prose, and his three surviving works in prose are:

Sharab al-'ashiqin ("The Lovers' Beverage")
Asrar al-'arifin ("The Secrets of the Gnostics")
Kitab al-Muntahi ("The Adept") – a collection of Arabic and Persian quotations with discussions in Malay.
He was the first writer to write about Sufi doctrines poetically in the Malay language, or indeed any other languages of the Malay archipelago.

See also
Syed Muhammad Naquib al-Attas

References

Further reading
Muhammad Naguib al-Attas. The mysticism of Hamzah Fansuri. Kuala Lumpur: University of Malaya Press, 1970.
G.W.J. Drewes and L.F. Brakel (eds. and tr.). The poems of Hamzah Fansuri. Dordrecht and Cinnaminson: Foris Publications, 1986.

bio: Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib was a foster brother, paternal uncle, maternal second-cousin, and companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
bio_full:
Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib (Arabic: حَمْزَة إبْن عَبْد ٱلْمُطَّلِب, romanized: Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; c. 568 – 625) was a foster brother, paternal uncle, maternal second-cousin, and companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
Hamza embraced Islam around 616 CE following an altercation with Abu Jahl and soon became one of Muhammad’s strongest supporters. He took part in early expeditions, notably fighting at the Battle of Badr, and was killed in the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE. His death was widely mourned, and Islamic tradition honors him as Asadullah (lit. 'Lion of God') and the "leader of the martyrs".

Ancestry
Ibn Sa'd, citing al-Waqidi, and Ibn Sayyid, quoting Zubayr, both reported that Hamza was four years older than Muhammad. His father was Abdul Muttalib, a member of the Quraysh tribe of Mecca, and his mother was Halah bint Wuhayb of the Zuhrah clan of Quraysh.  Al-Tabari cites two traditions regarding their marriage: in one account, al-Waqidi relates that Abdul Muttalib accompanied his son Abdullah to the house of Wahb ibn Abd Manaf to propose marriage to Wahb’s daughter Amina. During the visit, Abdul Muttalib noticed Wahb’s niece, Halah bint Wuhayb, and also asked for her hand. Wahb agreed, and both Abdullah and Abdul Muttalib were married on the same day in a double-marriage ceremony.

Family tree

* indicates that the marriage order is disputed
Note that direct lineage is marked in bold.

Life and Martyrdom

Conversion to Islam
Hamza showed little interest in Islam during its early years and converted in late 616 CE. According to early sources, after returning to Mecca from a hunting trip, he was informed that Abu Jahl had insulted Muhammad. Hamza went to the Kaaba, struck Abu Jahl with his bow, and declared his support for Muhammad. When members of Abu Jahl’s clan intervened, he reportedly told them to leave Hamza alone, admitting he had insulted Muhammad.
Following the incident, Hamza entered the House of Al-Arqam and formally embraced Islam.  His conversion was seen as a turning point by the Quraysh, who shifted from direct harassment to attempts at negotiation, which he refused. One account states that Hamza once asked to see the angel Jibril in his true form. When Jibril appeared with feet like emeralds, Hamza lost consciousness. In 622, he joined the emigration to Medina, where he stayed with either Kulthum ibn al-Hidm  or Sa'd ibn Khaythama.  Muhammad paired him in brotherhood with Zayd ibn Haritha.

Military expeditions
In his first expedition, Muhammad appointed Hamza to lead a raid against a Quraysh caravan. He commanded a force of thirty riders to intercept a merchant convoy returning from Syria along the coastal route in Juhayna territory.  At the seashore, Hamza encountered the caravan led by Abu Hisham, accompanied by 300 riders. Conflict was averted when Majdi ibn Amr al-Juhani, who had ties to both parties, intervened and negotiated a peaceful resolution. Sources differ on whether Hamza or his cousin Ubayda ibn al-Harith was the first Muslim to whom Muhammad entrusted a banner. However, Hamza's role as a standard-bearer was further solidified during the expedition against the Banu Qaynuqa, where he again carried the banner of Muhammad.
At the Battle of Badr, Hamza fought alongside the Muslims, sharing a camel with Zayd ibn Haritha and wearing an ostrich feather to make himself identifiable in combat. Prior to the battle, the Muslims blocked access to the wells at Badr. Al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad approached the cistern, vowing to drink from it, destroy it, or die trying. Hamza confronted him and struck his leg, causing him to fall. Al-Aswad crawled into the water before Hamza killed him near the cistern. During a duel with Utba ibn Rabi'a, Hamza is reported to have referred to himself as the "Lion of Allah and His Messenger". Accounts differ on whether Utba was killed by Hamza or Ali. Hamza later carried Muhammad’s banner during the expedition against Banu Qaynuqa.

Death

Hamza was killed in the Battle of Uhud on Saturday, 23 March 625 (7 Shawwal 3 AH), at the age of approximately 57 to 59. Fighting at the front line with two swords, he was fatally struck in the abdomen by a javelin thrown by Wahshi ibn Harb, an Abyssinian slave promised manumission by Hind bint Utba in retaliation for the death of her father at the Battle of Badr. Some sources report that Hind attempted to chew Hamza’s liver after the battle but was unable to swallow it. Ibn Hisham narrates that Muhammad expressed deep grief upon seeing Hamza’s body and stated that the angel Jibril had called him the "Lion of the Prophet" in the seven heavens. Hamza and his nephew, Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, were buried in the same grave. Ibn Masud reported that Muhammad led multiple funeral prayer for Hamza, each time with another fallen companion laid beside him. He was widely mourned and later referred to as the "leader of the martyrs" by Muhammad, as narrated by Jabir ibn Abd Allah.

Marriages and children
Hamza married three times and had seven children.

Salmah bint Umays ibn Ma'd, the half-sister of Maymunah bint al-Harith.
Umama bint Hamza, wife of Salama ibn Abi Salama.
Zaynab bint Al-Milla ibn Malik of the Aws tribe in Medina.
Amir ibn Hamza.
Bakr ibn Hamza, who died in childhood.
Khawla bint Qays ibn Amir of the An-Najjar clan.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Hanzala bin Abi 'Amir al-Rahib (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Hanzala bin Abi 'Amir al-Rahib was a companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the residents of Medina who encountered the Prophet after the migration from Mecca.

Hanzala is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, which took place in 625 CE near Medina. This battle was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community and the Meccan forces led by Abu Sufyan. The conflict arose as a follow-up to the Muslim victory at the Battle of Badr the previous year, with the Meccans seeking to restore their prestige and inflict a decisive defeat on the growing Muslim community.

During the Battle of Uhud, Hanzala fought alongside other Muslim defenders and was killed in combat, earning him recognition as one of the martyrs of this significant early Islamic battle. The Battle of Uhud itself was a complex engagement that initially favored the Muslims but ultimately resulted in heavy casualties for the Muslim forces, including the near-fatal wounding of Prophet Muhammad himself.

Hanzala's participation in this battle places him among the early Muslims who directly supported the establishment of the Islamic community in Medina during its formative years. His death at approximately twenty-eight years of age reflects the dangerous circumstances faced by the early Muslim community as it struggled to survive against the opposition of established Meccan tribes and their allies.

The Battle of Uhud holds particular significance in Islamic history as it demonstrated both the challenges faced by the early Muslim community and the dedication of individuals like Hanzala who gave their lives in defense of their faith and community. Those who died at Uhud are remembered in Islamic tradition as martyrs who made the ultimate sacrifice during a critical period when the survival of the nascent Islamic state was far from assured.

Hanzala's story represents the experiences of many early Muslims who converted to Islam and subsequently faced the military conflicts that characterized the religion's early expansion in the Arabian Peninsula. His martyrdom at Uhud places him within the broader narrative of sacrifice and commitment that marked the founding generation of the Islamic community.

titles: Katib al-Wahy (Scribe of Revelation)
bio: Hanzala bin al-Rabi' al-Usaydi (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in HIjaz. Known as Katib al-Wahy — Scribe of the Revelation.
bio_full:
Hanzala bin al-Rabi' al-Usaydi was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE in the Hijaz region, he became one of the scribes responsible for recording the Quranic revelations, earning him the distinguished title "Katib al-Wahy" (Scribe of the Revelation).

As one of the Sahaba—the companions who lived during the time of Prophet Muhammad—Hanzala occupied a position of considerable trust and responsibility within the early Muslim community. The role of recording divine revelations required not only literacy, which was relatively rare in seventh-century Arabia, but also impeccable character and reliability, as these scribes were entrusted with preserving the exact words believed to be revealed from God.

The scribes of revelation played a crucial role in the preservation and transmission of the Quran. In an era when oral tradition was predominant, having written records provided an additional layer of authenticity and helped ensure accurate preservation of the text. These scribes would write down verses as they were revealed, using available materials such as palm leaves, stones, and pieces of leather or bone.

Hanzala's work as a scribe contributed to the foundation of what would later become the formal compilation of the Quran into a single book during the caliphates of Abu Bakr and Uthman ibn Affan. The careful documentation by scribes like Hanzala provided source material that was essential for these later compilation efforts.

His death in 635 CE places him during the early years of the first caliphate under Abu Bakr, when the Muslim community was expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula. This was a critical period in Islamic history when the foundations established during the Prophet's lifetime were being consolidated and extended.

While specific details about Hanzala's other activities or contributions remain limited in available historical sources, his role as a scribe of revelation represents one of the most significant functions in early Islamic history. The work of preserving the Quranic text would prove fundamental to the development of Islamic civilization and religious practice for centuries to come.

full: Hanzala ibn Abi Amir ibn Sayfi al-Ansari al-Awsi
primaryTitle: Ghasil al-Mala'ika — Washed by the Angels
titles: Ghasil al-Mala'ika (Washed by Angels) · Martyr of Uhud
bio: Hanzala Ibn Abi Amir was one of the companions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He belonged to the Banu Aus tribe of the Ansar. His father, Abu Aamir was said to be a Christian. Hanzala was just 24 years old when he died in the Battle of Uhud while fighting against the polytheists. Hanzala, being a foot soldier, attacked Abu Sufyan ibn Harb's horse. However, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb was saved by Shaddād bin al-Aswad who then killed Hanzala.
bio_full:
Hanzala Ibn Abi Amir (Arabic: ﺣﻨﻈﻠـة ﺍﺑﻦ ﺍﺑﻲ ﻋﺎﻣﺮ) (c. 601 – 625) was one of the companions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He belonged to the Banu Aus tribe of the Ansar. His father, Abu Aamir was said to be a Christian. Hanzala was just 24 years old when he died in the Battle of Uhud while fighting against the polytheists. Hanzala, being a foot soldier, attacked Abu Sufyan ibn Harb's horse. However, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb was saved by Shaddād bin al-Aswad (also known as Ibn Sha'ub) who then killed Hanzala.
Hanzala had left for the battlefield to respond to the call of Jihad leaving his wife Jamila, daughter of Abd-Allah ibn Ubayy, on their wedding night. He did not have time to carry out Ghusl (ablution). Muhammad is said to have seen angels giving Hanzala a bath in between heaven and earth with fresh rainwater kept in silver vessels. Because of this honour, Hanzala earned the title of Ghaseel al-Malāʾika (Arabic: غسيل الملائكة) or the one cleansed by the angels.

bio: Haram bin Milhan was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He was one of the Ansari people from Medina.
bio_full:
Haram bin Milhan (Arabic: حرام بن ملحان; died 625) was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He was one of the Ansari people from Medina.
Being a member of Najjar clan from Banu Khazraj, he was brother of Umm Haram and Umm Sulaym (the mother of Anas bin Malik). During the Expedition of Bir Maona, Muslims sent him as a messenger with a letter of Muhammad to Amir ibn al-Tufayl, the nephew of Abu Bara and the chief of Banu Amir.

titles: al-Muhasibi (The Self-Examiner) · Imam 'Ilm al-Batin
bio: Al-Muḥāsibī was a Muslim Arab, theologian, philosopher and ascetic. He is considered to be the founder of the Baghdad School of Islamic philosophy which combined Kalam and Sufism, and a teacher of the Sufi masters Junayd al-Baghdadi and Sirri Saqti.
bio_full:
Al-Muḥāsibī (Arabic: المحاسبي) (781–857 CE) was a Muslim Arab, theologian, philosopher and ascetic. He is considered to be the founder of the Baghdad School of Islamic philosophy which combined Kalam and Sufism, and a teacher of the Sufi masters Junayd al-Baghdadi and Sirri Saqti.
His full name is Abu Abdullah Harith bin Asad bin Abdullah al-Anizi al-Basri, and he hailed from the Arab Anazzah tribe. He was born in Basra in about 781. Muhasibi means self-inspection or audit. He was a founder of what later became the mainstream Sufi doctrine, and influenced many subsequent theologians, such as al-Ghazali.
The author of approximately 200 works, he wrote about theology and Tasawwuf (Sufism), among them Kitab al-Khalwa and Kitab al-Ri`aya li-huquq Allah ("Obeying God's Permits").

Life
Al-Muhasibi was born in Basra, and his parents later moved to Baghdad, which had become the Abbasid capital. His father accumulated considerable wealth, which al-Muhasibi is reported to have rejected due to theological disagreements concerning his father’s views on the createdness of the Qur'an. Despite this background, al-Muhasibi adopted an ascetic lifestyle and was influenced by the teachings of al-Hasan al-Basri.
Al-Muhasibi wrote extensively on ethical self-discipline and spiritual introspection. He addressed contemporary Sufi practices such as wearing woolen garments, night recitation of the Qur'an, and dietary restraint, arguing that while such practices could aid in controlling the passions, they could also foster hypocrisy or pride if they became outward displays of piety rather than expressions of inner reform. He emphasised the importance of continual self-examination in preparation for the Day of Judgement as a means of purifying the inner self.
He studied jurisprudence under al-Shafi'i before later associating with a group of theologians led by Abdullah ibn Kullāb. This circle opposed the doctrines of the Jahmis, Mu'tazilis, and anthropomorphist theologians. Ibn Kullab argued against the Mu'tazilite position that the Qur'an was created, introducing a distinction between God’s eternal speech and its temporal expression.
In 848 (or possibly 851), the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil formally ended the Mihna, the inquisition enforcing Mu'tazilite doctrine, and subsequently prohibited Mu'tazilite theology.
In his work al-Khalwa, al-Muhasibi discussed the themes of fear and hope, advocating renunciation of worldly attachment as a prerequisite for spiritual discipline:

Know that the first thing that corrects you and helps you correct others is renouncing this world. For renunciation is attained by realisation, and consideration is attained by reflection...

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Harith bin Abi Sa'sa'a (c. 597–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Harith bin Abi Sa'sa'a was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed the establishment and growth of the Islamic community in Medina following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Harith bin Abi Sa'sa'a was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with Islam's founder and participated in the crucial early events that shaped the religion. The companions hold a revered position in Islamic tradition as the individuals who received Islamic teachings firsthand and helped transmit them to subsequent generations.

Harith bin Abi Sa'sa'a is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, where he died as a martyr in 634 CE. The Battle of Uhud was a significant military engagement fought between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan tribes, taking place on the slopes of Mount Uhud near Medina. This battle was one of the major early conflicts that tested the resilience and faith of the nascent Muslim community.

His death at Uhud places him among those early Muslims who made the ultimate sacrifice in defense of their faith and community during Islam's foundational period. In Islamic tradition, those who die in battle defending the faith are honored as martyrs, a status that carries particular religious significance.

The Battle of Uhud itself was a pivotal moment in early Islamic history, serving as both a military challenge and a spiritual test for the Muslim community. The engagement demonstrated the difficulties faced by the early Muslim state and the personal sacrifices made by individual believers like Harith bin Abi Sa'sa'a.

While specific details about his life, family background, or individual contributions beyond his participation in this battle are not extensively documented in widely accessible historical sources, his inclusion among the companions and his martyrdom at Uhud mark him as one of the early Muslims who played a role in Islam's formative years. His life span of approximately thirty-seven years encompassed the critical period of Islam's emergence and early expansion in the Arabian Peninsula.

bio: Harith bin Qays bin Khalid (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Harith bin Qays bin Khalid was a companion (Sahabi) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community in Medina following the Prophet's migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

Harith is historically recognized as one of the "Companions of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military encounter between the early Muslim community and the Meccan tribes. The battle resulted in a decisive victory for the Muslim forces despite being significantly outnumbered, and those who participated alongside the Prophet are held in special regard within Islamic tradition.

As a resident of Medina, Harith would have been present during the crucial decade when the foundational practices and institutions of Islam were being established. The Medinan period saw the development of the first Muslim political community, the codification of Islamic law and practices, and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

The companions of Prophet Muhammad, including Harith bin Qays bin Khalid, played essential roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam to subsequent generations. They served as direct witnesses to the Prophet's words and actions, making their testimonies crucial sources for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and historical understanding.

Harith bin Qays bin Khalid died in 634 CE, which places his death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. This period marked the beginning of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula, though the specific circumstances of Harith's death are not clearly documented in available historical sources.

His legacy, like that of other companions, lies primarily in his role as a bridge between the prophetic period and the subsequent development of Islamic civilization. The companions collectively represent the foundational generation that helped establish Islam as both a religious and political force in the region.

bio: Haritha bin al-Nu'man (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Haritha bin al-Nu'man was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islamic history in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who resided in Medina and witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim community.

Haritha is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan tribes, and those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition. The companions who participated in this battle are specifically mentioned in Islamic sources as having a distinguished status among the early Muslim community.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Haritha belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and learned Islamic teachings firsthand. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's sayings, actions, and teachings, which later formed the basis of hadith literature. This body of oral tradition became fundamental to Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and practice.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's time, Haritha would have been present during the critical years when Islamic law and community practices were being established. The Medinan period, from 622 to 632 CE, saw the development of the first Islamic state and the codification of many religious and social practices that became central to Muslim civilization.

Haritha died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr's leadership. His death occurred during a period of rapid Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Like other companions of his generation, his life bridged the prophetic period and the subsequent era of Islamic conquests and institutional development.

His significance lies primarily in his status as a Badr veteran and his role in the early Muslim community of Medina. The companions of this generation served as living links between the Prophet's teachings and later Muslim generations, making their testimonies and experiences invaluable sources for understanding early Islamic history and religious practice.

bio: Harmala bint 'Abd bin al-Aswad (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Harmala bint Abd al-Aswad, also called Huraymila and known by the kunya Umm Harmala, was an early Muslim woman of the tribe of Khuza'a. Ibn Hajar gives her lineage as Huraymila bint Abd ibn al-Aswad ibn Jadhima ibn Qays of the Khuza'a, and the classical sources differ over the names in her family line. Ibn Sa'd, as quoted by Ibn Hajar, says she accepted Islam early and emigrated to Abyssinia with her husband Jahm ibn Qays, and bore him Abd Allah, Amr and Harmala; she was called Umm Harmala and died there. Ibn Ishaq, cited by Ibn al-Athir, likewise lists Umm Harmala among the emigrants to Abyssinia with her husband Jahm ibn Qays; Ibn Abd al-Barr also lists her with her husband. Musa ibn Uqba names Jahm's wife on this emigration as Khawla bint al-Aswad; Ibn al-Athir notes that Musa ibn Uqba gives her name while Ibn Ishaq gives only her kunya. Al-Tabari, cited by Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn Hajar, also reports that she died in Abyssinia. No date is given for her death.

primaryTitle: Wazir Musa — Minister and Brother of Moses
titles: Harun · Aaron · brother and minister of Musa · Wazir al-Nabi
dating_source: Merneptah Stele (1208 BCE); Exodus dating consensus
dating_note: Harun/Aaron, brother of Musa.
bio: Hārūn ibn 'Imrān (c. 1395–c. 1275 BCE) was a prophet, based in Egypt. Known as Wazir Musa — Minister and Brother of Moses.
bio_full: Harun ibn Imran (Aaron) is honoured in Islam as a prophet and messenger of God and the elder brother of the prophet Musa (Moses). Islamic tradition names his father as Imran and his mother as Yukabid, and Maryam (Miriam) was their sister. The Qur'an tells that when Musa was sent to Pharaoh, he prayed for a helper from his own family, asking that his brother Harun share in his mission, and his prayer was granted (20:29-36). Musa described Harun as more eloquent than himself and asked that he be sent with him as a supporter (28:34), and God says He granted Musa his brother Harun as a prophet out of His mercy (19:53). The two brothers were sent together to Pharaoh and his chiefs (10:75). When Musa went to meet his Lord for forty nights, he left Harun in his place among the Israelites (7:142). During that time the Samiri led the people into worshipping a calf. Harun warned them that they were being tested by it and urged them to follow him, but they refused to stop until Musa returned (20:85-91). When Musa returned and seized him by the head, Harun, calling him 'son of my mother', explained that the people had overpowered him and nearly killed him, and that he had feared being blamed for dividing the Children of Israel (7:150; 20:94). The Qur'an sends peace upon Musa and Harun together (37:120). In the hadith of the Night Journey, the Prophet Muhammad is reported to have met Harun in the fifth heaven. One Islamic tradition places his tomb on Jabal Harun near Petra, in present-day Jordan.
