bio: Jamila bint 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Jamila is a woman of the Ansar of Medina whose parentage the classical sources dispute. Ibn al-Athir has an entry for Jamila bint Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, daughter of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, whom the sources call the head of the hypocrites. Elsewhere in the same work, and in Abu Nu'aym's dictionary, she is described instead as Abd Allah's sister, Jamila bint Ubayy ibn Salul, and the claim that she was his daughter is called a mistake. Ibn al-Athir concludes that the two entries refer to one woman. She was first married to Hanzala ibn Abi Amir, known as 'the one washed by the angels', who was killed at Uhud. She then married Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas. In a report from Ibn Abbas, she told the Prophet that she found no fault in Thabit's religion or character, 'but I dislike kufr in Islam'; in another report she said she disliked only his appearance. The Prophet asked whether she would return the garden Thabit had given her; she agreed, and he separated them. Abu Nu'aym describes this as a khul', a separation sought by the wife in return for giving back the dower. Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that narrators of Basra name this woman Jamila bint Ubayy, while those of Medina name her Habiba bint Sahl. After Thabit she married Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, and then Habib (or Khubayb) ibn Isaf. The sources consulted do not record her death.

bio: Jamila bint Abi Sa'sa'a (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Jamila bint Abi Sa'sa'a was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the clan of Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj. Ibn Sa'd gives her father's lineage as Amr ibn Zayd ibn Awf ibn Mabdhul ibn Amr ibn Ghanm ibn Mazin ibn al-Najjar, and names her mother as Unaysa bint Asim, of the same clan. Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir both record that she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet. According to Ibn Sa'd, she was first married to the Companion Ubada ibn al-Samit, to whom she bore a son, al-Walid ibn Ubada. She then married al-Rabi' ibn Suraqa and bore him Abd Allah, Muhammad and Buthayna. Her third husband was Khalda ibn Abi Khalid of the Khazraj. The sources consulted do not record any hadith narrated by her, nor the date of her death.

bio: Jamila bint Khuzayma bin Hazma (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Jamila bint Khuzayma bin Hazma was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she witnessed the emergence and establishment of the Islamic community in Medina during the early seventh century.

As an Ansari companion, Jamila belonged to the Medinan tribes who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca following the Hijra in 622 CE. The Ansar, meaning "helpers," played a crucial role in providing sanctuary and assistance to the early Muslim community when they faced persecution in Mecca and needed a new base for their religious and social movement.

Jamila lived during one of the most significant periods in Islamic history, spanning the final decades of the pre-Islamic era through the foundational years of the Muslim community. Her lifetime coincided with the Prophet's ministry, the revelation of the Quran, and the establishment of the first Islamic state in Medina. She would have witnessed the major events that shaped early Islam, including the various military campaigns, the consolidation of tribal alliances, and the expansion of Islamic influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

The female companions of the Prophet Muhammad, known collectively as the sahabiyyat, hold an important place in Islamic historical consciousness. They are recognized for their early acceptance of Islam, their support of the Prophet's mission, and their contributions to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings to subsequent generations. Many female companions played active roles in the community, participating in religious, social, and sometimes military activities alongside their male counterparts.

Jamila's designation as an Ansari companion places her among those Medinan residents who made the crucial decision to embrace Islam and support the Prophet Muhammad's community during its most vulnerable early years. This support proved essential for the survival and growth of Islam beyond its birthplace in Mecca.

She died around 635 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, having lived to see Islam transform from a small religious movement into a major force that would soon extend far beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her life spanned the entire prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs.

bio: Jamila bint Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi' (b. c. 625 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Jamila bint Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi' was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia during the formative period of Islam. Born around 625 CE in Medina, she belonged to the generation that witnessed the establishment and early expansion of the Muslim community.

As a companion of the Prophet, Jamila would have had direct contact with Muhammad during his lifetime, placing her among the revered first generation of Muslims whose testimonies and accounts formed crucial source material for Islamic religious and historical knowledge. Her designation as a sahabiyya indicates that she not only encountered the Prophet but was recognized as a Muslim during his lifetime.

Jamila is particularly noted for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that became fundamental sources of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions like Jamila played significant roles in preserving and transmitting these prophetic traditions, especially regarding matters that concerned women's religious practices, family life, and social interactions where male narrators might have had limited access or knowledge.

The science of hadith transmission, in which Jamila participated, became one of the most sophisticated scholarly disciplines in Islamic civilization. Narrators were subject to rigorous evaluation of their reliability, memory, and moral character. That Jamila is remembered as a hadith narrator suggests she met the strict criteria established by later hadith scholars for trustworthy transmission.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's time would have placed Jamila at the center of the rapidly developing Muslim community. Medina served as the political and spiritual capital of early Islam, where the fundamental institutions and practices of the religion were established. Female companions in this environment often played active roles in community life, religious education, and the preservation of Islamic teachings.

Jamila's death around 665 CE places her passing during the early Umayyad period, when the Islamic empire was expanding rapidly beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her contributions to hadith preservation helped ensure that prophetic guidance remained available to Muslim communities as they spread across diverse geographical and cultural territories.

While specific details about Jamila's individual narrations or particular areas of expertise in hadith transmission are not definitively documented in widely available sources, her recognition as a narrator indicates her valued contribution to the foundational period of Islamic scholarship and religious preservation.

bio: Jamila bint Sayfi bin 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Jamila bint Sayfi bin 'Amr was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions based in Medina, Jamila witnessed and participated in the establishment of the first Islamic community. The Ansar played a crucial role in Islamic history by providing refuge, material support, and military assistance to the early Muslims during a critical period when the nascent faith faced opposition from Meccan tribes and other adversaries.

The designation "Sahabiyya" indicates that Jamila was among the female companions who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime. These companions, both male and female, hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who received teachings directly from the Prophet and helped transmit Islamic knowledge and practices to subsequent generations.

Women among the Ansar typically contributed to the early Muslim community through various means, including providing hospitality to migrants, participating in community affairs, and supporting the social and economic needs of the growing Muslim population in Medina. The presence of female companions like Jamila in historical records reflects their recognized participation in the early Islamic community, though specific details about individual contributions often remain limited in available sources.

Jamila lived through the most transformative period of early Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic era through the establishment of Islam as the dominant force in the Arabian Peninsula. Her life span of approximately forty years coincided with the Prophet's ministry and the initial expansion of the Muslim community. She died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, when the Islamic state was consolidating its authority and beginning its expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

The historical significance of companions like Jamila lies in their role as the foundational community that preserved and transmitted Islamic teachings, customs, and practices to future generations, helping to establish the religious and social framework that would guide Islamic civilization.

bio: Jamila bint Thabit ibn Abi al-Aflah (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Jamila bint Thabit was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. She was the daughter of Thabit ibn Abi al-Aqlah and al-Shamus bint Abi Amir, of the clan of Amr ibn Awf of the Aws, and the sister of Asim ibn Thabit, who fought at Badr. Her name was originally Asiya, meaning 'disobedient'. When she accepted Islam, the Prophet renamed her Jamila; Ibn al-Athir reports this from Ibn Umar, while one version in Abu Nu'aym has Umar renaming her first and the Prophet confirming it. Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir date her marriage to Umar ibn al-Khattab to 7 AH. She bore him a son, Asim ibn Umar, and was called Umm Asim after him. Umar later divorced her, and she married Yazid ibn Jariya, to whom she bore Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid. Ibn Abd al-Barr relates that Umar once took the young Asim from his grandmother al-Shamus at Quba, and that Abu Bakr told him to return the child to her. The sources consulted do not record when she died.

titles: Yusuf al-Umma (The Joseph of This Umma) · Destroyer of Dhu al-Khalasa
bio: Jarir ibn Abd Allah ibn Jabir al-Bajali (c. 607–678) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Kufa. Known as Yusuf al-Umma — Most Handsome of the Companions.
bio_full: Jarir ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Yemeni tribe of Bajila, of its Ahmas branch. His kunya is given as Abu Amr or Abu Abd Allah, and Ibn Manjawayh gives his lineage as Jarir ibn Abd Allah ibn Jabir ibn Malik. He came to the Prophet late in the Prophet's life: Ibn Abd al-Barr reports Jarir's own statement that he accepted Islam forty days before the Prophet's death, and Ibn al-Athir states the same, while Ibn Hibban places his arrival in Ramadan of the year 10 AH. Before he entered, the Prophet described him as among the best men of Yemen, with 'the trace of an angel' on his face, and told his Companions to honour a people's noble when he came to them. The Prophet sent him with fifty (in another report 150) riders to destroy the idol-shrine of Dhu al-Khalasa, which he burned, and prayed for him and his horsemen. He pledged to give sincere counsel to every Muslim. Umar ibn al-Khattab called him 'the Yusuf of this community' for his good looks. He took part in the conquest of al-Mada'in and settled in Kufa, where he had a house. Ali sent him as an envoy to Mu'awiya. During the civil strife he left Kufa and settled at Qarqisiya. Ibn Abd al-Barr gives his death there in 54 AH (c. 674 CE); Ibn Hibban and Ibn Manjawayh give 51 AH. Those who narrated from him include Anas ibn Malik, Qays ibn Abi Hazim, al-Sha'bi and his own sons.

bio: Jariyya bint 'Amr bin Mu'mil (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Early Muslim — Tortured for Faith.
bio_full:
Jariyya bint 'Amr bin Mu'mil was one of the early female companions of Prophet Muhammad, known in Islamic tradition as a Sahabiyya. Born around 594 CE in Mecca, she lived during the transformative period of early Islam's emergence in the Arabian Peninsula.

As an early convert to Islam in Mecca, Jariyya experienced the persecution that characterized the faith's initial years. The early Muslim community in Mecca faced significant opposition from the established tribal and religious authorities, who viewed the new monotheistic message as a threat to their social and economic order. Like many early converts, particularly those from vulnerable social positions, Jariyya endured torture and harassment for her religious beliefs.

Her experience reflects the broader pattern of persecution faced by early Muslims in Mecca before the community's migration to Medina in 622 CE. The Meccan period of Islamic history was marked by the gradual conversion of individuals who often faced social ostracism, economic boycotts, and physical violence from their families and tribes. Women converts were particularly vulnerable, as they often lacked the tribal protection that men might enjoy.

Jariyya is remembered within the tradition of early Islamic ascetics, suggesting she embraced a lifestyle of spiritual discipline and devotion that characterized some of the Prophet's companions. This ascetic tradition emphasized simplicity, devotion to worship, and detachment from worldly concerns, values that were particularly significant during the challenging early years of the Islamic community.

Her death in 634 CE, just two years after Prophet Muhammad's passing, places her among the companions who witnessed both the Prophet's ministry and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr. This timing means she lived through the entire Meccan period of persecution, the migration to Medina, the establishment of the Muslim community there, and the faith's eventual return to and conquest of Mecca.

Jariyya's story, while not extensively documented in historical sources, represents the experiences of many early Muslim women who accepted Islam despite facing severe consequences. Her inclusion among the recognized companions acknowledges her role in the foundational period of Islamic history and her steadfastness in maintaining her faith under difficult circumstances. Her life exemplifies the sacrifices made by the earliest Muslim community members during Islam's formative decades.

full: Jawhar ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ṣiqillī al-Rūmī
primaryTitle: Fatimid General — Founder of Cairo and al-Azhar
bio: Al-Qaid Jawhar ibn Abdallah was a Fatimid general of Croatian origin who led the conquest of Maghreb, and subsequently the conquest of Egypt, for the 4th Fatimid Imam-Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah. He served as viceroy of Egypt until al-Mu'izz's arrival in 973, consolidating Fatimid control over the country. After that, he retired from public life until his death.
bio_full:
Al-Qaid Jawhar ibn Abdallah (Arabic: جوهر  بن عبد الله, romanized: Jawhar ibn ʿAbd Allāh, better known as Jawhar  al Siqilli, al-Qaid al-Siqilli, "The Sicilian General", or al-Saqlabi, "The Slav" or the slave; born in Sicily and died 28 April 992) was a Fatimid general of Croatian origin who led the conquest of Maghreb, and subsequently the conquest of Egypt, for the 4th Fatimid Imam-Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah. He served as viceroy of Egypt until al-Mu'izz's arrival in 973, consolidating Fatimid control over the country. After that, he retired from public life until his death.
He is variously known with the nisbas al-Siqilli (Arabic: الصقلي, romanized: al-Ṣiqillī, lit. 'The Sicilian'), al-Saqlabi (Arabic: الصقلبي, lit. The Slav or the slave), al-Rumi (Arabic: الرومي, romanized: al-Rūmī, lit. 'the Roman'); and with the titles al-Katib (Arabic: الكَاتِب, romanized: al-Kātib, lit. 'the Secretary') and al-Qa'id (Arabic: القائد, romanized: al-Qāʾid, lit. 'the General').

Biography
The birth date of Jawhar is not known, but as he died in 992, and the peak of his career was between 950 and 975, he cannot have been born earlier than the 900s. Jawhar is either born to Croatian parents in Sicily or Zachlumia.
Jawhar's father, Abdallah, was a slave from Dubrovnik-Konavle area, and Jawhar is first mentioned as a slave-soldier (ghulām) and possibly a secretary to the third Fatimid caliph, al-Mansur bi-Nasr Allah (r. 946–953). In 958, al-Mansur's son and successor, al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah (r. 953–975) chose Jawhar to lead a campaign to restore Fatimid control over the central and western parts of North Africa. In this campaign, Jawhar first gave proof of his exceptional military talents. He first led the Fatimid armies to victory over the Zenata tribe that had allied with the Fatimids' rivals, the Umayyads of the Caliphate of Córdoba, defeating and killing their leader, Ya'la ibn Muhammad al-Yafrani. He then turned southeast towards Sijilmasa, capturing and killing its ruler Muhammad ibn al-Fath ibn Maymun ibn Midrar. It was not until a year later, in October 960, that he moved north towards Fez, taking the city by storm on 13 November and capturing its Umayyad governor, Ahmad ibn Abi Bakr al-Judhami. With this victory, all of the Maghreb, apart from Tangier and Ceuta, came under Fatimid control, or recognized Fatimid suzerainty. As a token of his victory, Jawhar is said to have sent jars filled with live fish from the Atlantic Ocean to the Caliph in Ifriqiya.
It is reported that Al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah would spend hours discussing tactics and strategy with Al-Qaid Jawhar in his tent before the campaign of North Africa began, and when they finally parted, Al-Mu'izz granted Al-Qaid Jawhar with very high honors requiring all soldiers to disembark their horse as a sign of respect for the commander-in-chief.
After the Western borders had been secured, Jawhar led the Fatimid invasion of Ikhshidid Egypt (969). He approached Egypt from the direction of Alexandria and marched towards the capital, Fustat. His army encountered little resistance and the country was secured by a treaty with the Ikhshidid vizier Abu Ja'far Muslim. Some divisions of the Ikhshidid army mutinied in protest and took up positions on Roda Island in the Nile, to defend the river crossing and prevent the Fatimid army from gaining access to Fustat. Jawhar stormed the island with his Kutama troops and cleared away the enemy soldiers before proceeding to peacefully enter Fustat.
As Jawhar pacified Egypt the Fatimid army began its invasion of Ikhshidid Syria (970) under the Kutama general Ja'far ibn Falah. After initial successes this army was destroyed near Damascus in August 971 by a coalition of Ikhshidid soldiers and Arab tribesmen led by the Qarmatians of Bahrain. Egypt was left defenceless and was invaded by the coalition in September. Jawhar had few troops at hand so he mobilised the entire population of Fustat to build a defensive line consisting of a wall and a ditch at a bottleneck north of the city. As the coalition army stalled in the Nile Delta Jawhar managed to finish his preparations in time. The invaders' attempt to take Fustat was foiled by the defences and Jawhar routed them in battle outside the city with his raw troops.

Last campaign
Jawhar played at least a formal role in the designation of al-Mu'izz's younger son, Nizar, as designated heir a few days before the caliph's death in December 975: Jawhar and the court physician accompanied Nizar out of the room in which al-Mu'izz lay dying and placed him on a throne, thus signifying his designation. The new caliph, al-Aziz, was confronted with the problem of Syria, where a series of Fatimid attempts to expand into the region failed due to the opposition of the local urban militias (ahdath) and the Banu Uqayl Bedouin, the intervention of the Turkic commander Alptakin, who ousted the Fatimids from Damascus and became its ruler, and the Qarmatians, who allied with Alptakin. In the first half of 976, the Qarmatians occupied Palestine, while the Fatimids only held isolated coastal cities, under threat from the Qarmatians and Alptakin.
In response to this situation, and on the advice of Ya'qub ibn Killis, in May al-Aziz entrusted Jawhar with leading an army of 20,000 men—the largest Fatimid force hitherto sent to Syria—to confront the Qarmatians and Alptakin. The Qarmatians quickly retreated before the Fatimid advance, leaving only a small part of their number to join Alptakin at Tiberias. From Ramla, Jawhar sent a letter to Alptakin promising pardon, as well as a robe of honour and money—effectively an offer to enter the Fatimid service, which the Turk refused. Nevertheless, Alptakin too was forced to withdraw to Damascus before the numerically stronger Fatimid army. Jawhar's army arrived before Damascus in July 976, erected a fortified camp, and began a siege that lasted for several months, punctuated by skirmishes. As Alptakin had gathered the entire harvest of the region into the city, the Fatimid army suffered from hunger with the onset of winter. When news of a Qarmatian army under al-Hasan al-A'sam approaching the city, Jawhar decided to lift the siege and withdrew from Damascus in December/January, as the Fatimids were now outnumbered by their opponents.
Jawhar retreated south, first to Tiberias and then towards Ramla, closely followed by his enemies, who were now joined by the numerous Banu Tayy tribes—the medieval chroniclers speak of 50,000 Bedouin—under the leadership of the Jarrahid family. Jawhar lost many men to the freezing cold and snow, and after a defeat in a bloody battle on the Yarkon River, found himself besieged at Ramla. There the Fatimid army was further debilitated by lack of supplies and even water. Jawhar was forced to abandon Ramla for the coastal fortress of Ascalon. The Qarmatians entered Ramla on 12 March 977, and soon, joined by the forces of Alptakin, placed Ascalon under siege as well. The blockade lasted for fifteen months, during which time Jawhar lost the bulk of his army to starvation. At long last, Jawhar was obliged to enter into negotiations with the more receptive Alptakin—the Qarmatians vehemently opposed any deal and proposed to maintain the siege until their enemies died of hunger—and was allowed to leave in March/April 978 after a humiliating capitulation: the surviving Fatimid troops marched out of Ascalon passing under Alptakin's sword, which had been slung at the city gate. Jawhar agreed to abandon all Fatimid claims to rule lands north of Gaza, while Alptakin retained rule of the rest of Syria; whether he accepted a Fatimid suzerainty, as reported by Yahya of Antioch, or not, he was de facto independent.

Death
The capitulation at Ascalon put an end to Jawhar's military career. He died on 28 April 992. He is presumed to be buried in Cairo, Egypt, but his resting place is unknown as of yet.

bio: Jubayr bin Iyas bin Khalid (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Jubayr bin Iyas bin Khalid was a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the Prophet's time there.

Jubayr is most notably recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the town of Badr, southwest of Medina, and marked a turning point in the early Muslim community's struggle for survival and recognition in the Arabian Peninsula.

The designation "Companion of Badr" carries special reverence in Islamic tradition, as those who fought alongside the Prophet in this crucial battle are held in high esteem by Muslims. The battle involved approximately 300 Muslims facing a much larger Meccan army, and their victory was seen as divinely blessed and strategically decisive for the future of Islam.

As a Sahaba, Jubayr belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and received Islamic teachings firsthand. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings, practices, and sayings to subsequent generations, forming the foundation for Islamic scholarship and jurisprudence.

Jubayr's life spanned the critical decades when Islam emerged from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community in Medina. He witnessed the major developments of early Islamic history, including the various military campaigns, the establishment of the first Muslim state, and the codification of Islamic practices and laws.

He died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, the first successor to Prophet Muhammad. This places his death during the period when the Muslim community was beginning its expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the leadership of the Rashidun Caliphs.

While specific details about Jubayr's individual contributions beyond his participation in the Battle of Badr are not extensively documented in the historical record, his status as a companion places him among the foundational figures of Islamic history who helped establish and spread the early Muslim community.

bio: Judhama bint Jandal al-Asadiyya (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Emigrant — Makkah to Madinah.
bio_full:
Judhama bint Jandal al-Asadiyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, she belonged to the Banu Asad tribe, as indicated by her nisba "al-Asadiyya."

Like many early Muslims in Mecca, Judhama faced the challenges of practicing the new faith in an environment that was often hostile to the growing Muslim community. The difficulties experienced by early converts eventually led to the historic migration known as the Hijra, when Muslims moved from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE to establish the first Islamic community under more favorable conditions.

Judhama was among those who participated in this significant migration from Mecca to Medina, earning her recognition as one of the Muhajirun (emigrants). This group of early Muslims who left their homes, property, and tribal protection in Mecca to follow the Prophet Muhammad held a special status in early Islamic society. Their sacrifice and commitment to the faith despite personal hardship became a model for future generations of Muslims.

As a sahabiyya, Judhama was part of the generation that directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices and principles. The female companions played important roles in the early Muslim community, often serving as transmitters of religious knowledge, particularly regarding matters that concerned women's religious and social practices.

The companions who made the journey from Mecca to Medina were instrumental in helping to establish the first Islamic state and community. Their experiences during this foundational period provided crucial precedents for Islamic law, social organization, and religious practice that would influence Muslim societies for centuries to come.

Judhama's life spanned the crucial early decades of Islamic history, from the initial revelations to Muhammad through the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina. She died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, having witnessed the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to a major force that would soon expand beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her status as both an early convert and an emigrant places her among the most respected figures in Islamic historical memory.

bio: Junadah bin Sufyan bin Ma'mar (c. 593–646 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Junadah bin Sufyan bin Ma'mar was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late sixth and early seventh centuries CE. Born around 593 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca during the religion's initial phase of growth.

Junadah is primarily remembered for his participation in the migration to Abyssinia, one of the most significant early events in Islamic history. When the Muslim community in Mecca faced increasing persecution from the Quraysh tribe, the Prophet Muhammad advised some of his followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, located in present-day Ethiopia. This migration, which occurred around 615 CE, represented the first major test of the young Muslim community's resilience and their ability to find sanctuary beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

The migration to Abyssinia was particularly notable because it demonstrated early Islamic diplomacy and the religion's capacity to coexist with other monotheistic faiths. The migrants, including Junadah, were received by the Negus, the Christian ruler of Abyssinia, who provided them protection after hearing their testimony about their faith. This event established important precedents for Muslim communities living under non-Muslim rule and highlighted the shared values between Islam and Christianity.

As a sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Junadah belonged to the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions hold special significance in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of prophetic teachings and as exemplars of early Islamic devotion.

Junadah's association with the early ascetic tradition suggests he was among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline and detachment from worldly concerns. This ascetic approach would later influence the development of Islamic mysticism and spirituality.

He lived through the crucial early decades of Islamic expansion, witnessing the religion's growth from a small community in Mecca to a major force in the Arabian Peninsula. Junadah died in 646 CE, during the period of the early caliphates when Islam was rapidly expanding beyond its Arabian origins. His life span encompassed the entire prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic territorial expansion, making him a witness to one of history's most significant religious and political transformations.

full: Abu al-Qasim Junayd ibn Muhammad al-Khazzaz al-Baghdadi
primaryTitle: Sayyid al-Ta'ifa — Master of the Sufi Group
titles: Sayyid al-Ta'ifa · Qutb al-'Arifin · Imam al-Sohw (Imam of Sobriety)
bio: Junayd of Baghdad was a mystic and one of the most famous of the early Islamic saints. He is a central figure in the spiritual lineage of many Sufi orders.
bio_full:
Junayd of Baghdad (Persian: جُنیدِ بَغدادی; Arabic: الجنيد البغدادي; c. 830 – 910) was a mystic and one of the most famous of the early Islamic saints. He is a central figure in the spiritual lineage of many Sufi orders.
Junayd taught in Baghdad throughout his lifetime and was an important figure in the development of Sufi doctrine. Like Hasan of Basra before him, was widely revered by his students and disciples as well as quoted by other mystics. Because of his importance in Sufi theology, Junayd was often referred to as the "Sultan".

Early life and education
The exact birth date of Abu-l-Qāsim al-Junayd ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Junayd al-Khazzāz al-Qawārīrī (Arabic: أبو القاسم الجنيد بن محمد الخزاز القواريري) is disputed and ranges from 210 to 215 AH according to Abdel-Kader. His death is more certain and ranges from 296 to 298 AH (908 to 910 CE). Junayd was a Persian, with his ancestors originating in Nihawand in modern-day Iran. Al-Junayd was raised by his uncle Sirri Saqti after being orphaned as a boy. Al-Junayd's early education included teachings from Abū Thawr, Abū 'Ubayd, al-Ḥārith al-Muḥãsibī, and Sarī ibn Mughallas.

Hagiography
As to the hagiography by Attar of Nishapur, the Tazkirat al-Awliya, had felt the pain of divine separation since childhood. Regardless of spiritual sorrow, he was known for his quick understanding and discipline when Sirri Saqti accepted him. 
According to Attar, Junayd was only seven years of age when Sirri Saqti took him along for the Hajj. In al-Masjid an-Nabawi, there were 400 sheikhs discussing the concept of ‘thankfulness’ whereby each expounded his own view. When Sirri Saqti told him to present his definition, Junayd said, "Thankfulness means that should not disobey God by means of the favour which he has bestowed upon you nor make of His favour a source of disobedience." The sheikhs unanimously agreed that no other words could define the term better. Sirri Saqti asked Junayd from where he could learn all this. Junayd replied, "From sitting with you."

Spiritual journey
His traditional hagiography continues by stating that Junayd went back to Baghdad and took up selling glasses. However, he spent most of his time in prayer. Hence, he retired to the porch of Sirri Saqti's house and kept himself away from worldly matters, devoting his thoughts solely to God. People need to "relinquish natural desires, to wipe out human attributes, to discard selfish motives, to cultivate spiritual qualities, to devote oneself to true knowledge, to do what is best in the context of eternity, to wish good for the entire community, to be truly faithful to God, and to follow the Prophet in the matters of the Shari’a." This starts with the practice of asceticism (zuhd) and continues with withdrawal from society, intense concentration on devotion (ibadah) and remembrance (dhikr) of God, sincerity (ikhlas), and contemplation (muraqaba) respectively; contemplation produces fana.
Junayd spent 40 years on his mystic course praying while sacrificing his sleep and any other worldly desires, but then a conceit in his heart arose that he had achieved his goal. By then he was inspired by God that "He who is not worthy of union, all his good works are but sins." This meant that the prayers which become a source of pride are useless, as true prayer makes a person more humble and devoted to God. His name became famous in many parts of the world despite the persecution he faced and the tongues of slander shot at him. Even then, he did not start preaching until 30 of the great saints indicated to him that he should now call men to God. However, he chose not to preach yet, saying, "While the master is there, it is not seemly for the disciple to preach." After witnessing Muhammad in his dream commanding him to preach, he had to listen to Sirri Saqti. The intensity of ishq poured out of the speech of Junayd such that out of the 40 people he first preached, 18 died and 22 fainted. His caliph and dearest disciple was Abu Bakr Shibli.

Works by Junayd
Junayd helped establish the "sober" school of Sufi thought, which meant that he was very logical and scholarly about his definitions of various virtues, tawhid, etc.  Sober Sufism is characterized by people who "experience fana [and] do not subsist in that state of selfless absorption in God but find themselves returned to their senses by God.  Such returnees from the experience of selflessness are thus reconstituted as renewed selves," just like an intoxicated person sobering up. For example, Junayd is quoted as saying, "The water takes on the color of the cup."  While this might seem rather confusing at first, ‘Abd al-Hakeem Carney explains it as: "When the water is understood here to refer to the Light of Divine self-disclosure, we are led to the important concept of 'capacity,' whereby the Divine epiphany is received by the heart of any person according to that person’s particular receptive capacity and will be 'colored' by that person’s nature".
Also, according to Sells, "Junayd seems to presuppose that his hearer or reader has had the experience about which he is speaking – or, even more radically, that the hearer or reader is able to enter that experience, or some re-creation of it – at the moment of encounter with Junayd's words." This statement makes it seem like Junayd was writing to a specific sect of the elite that he described earlier. The elite that he refers to are the elect, or "a tightly knit group of 'brethren' that Junayd designates by such phrases as 'the choice of believers' or 'the pure ones'. They play significant roles in the community of believers."

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Jundub bin Makayth (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Jundub bin Makayth was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam and became part of the close circle of followers who supported Muhammad during the formative years of the Islamic community.

Jundub is most notably remembered for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event in Islamic history that took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge, also known as the Bay'at al-Ridwan, occurred when approximately 1,400 Muslims accompanying Muhammad on what was intended to be a pilgrimage to Mecca pledged their loyalty and willingness to fight, if necessary, when it appeared that the Prophet's envoy to the Meccan leaders might have been killed. The Quran later commemorated this event in verse 48:18, expressing divine approval of those who participated in this demonstration of faith and solidarity.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, Jundub belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions held a special status in Islamic tradition as the first recipients and transmitters of Islamic knowledge, serving as crucial links between the Prophet's teachings and subsequent generations of Muslims.

Jundub lived and participated in the Muslim community during its most transformative period, witnessing the growth of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community in Medina. His presence during key events like the Pledge of Ridwan placed him among those who directly experienced the challenges and pivotal moments that shaped early Islamic history.

He died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, having lived through the Prophet's death in 632 CE and the beginning of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs. Like many companions of his generation, Jundub represents the foundational community of believers whose commitment and participation were essential to the establishment and preservation of the early Islamic tradition. His inclusion in the Quranic reference to the Pledge of Ridwan ensures his continued remembrance in Islamic historical memory.

full: Juwayriya bint al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar al-Mustaliqqiyya
primaryTitle: Juwayriya bint al-Harith — Her Marriage Freed a Hundred Families
titles: Umm al-Muminin (Mother of the Believers)
bio: Juwayriya bint al-Harith was the eighth wife of Muhammad and so, considered to be a Mother of the Believers. She was from the Banu Mustaliq clan, and her father al-Harith was the chief of the clan.
bio_full:
Juwayriya bint al-Harith (Arabic: جويرية بنت الحارث, romanized: Juwayriyyah bint al-Ḥārith; c. 608–676) was the eighth wife of Muhammad and so, considered to be a Mother of the Believers. She was from the Banu Mustaliq clan, and her father al-Harith was the chief of the clan.

Family background
She was the daughter of Al-Hārith ibn Abi Dirar, the chief of the Banu Mustaliq clan, who was defeated with his tribe in a battle.

Conflict between Muslims and Banu Mustaliq

Two months after Muḥammad returned from the Expedition of Dhū Qarad, he began to hear rumours that the Banū al-Muṣṭaliq were preparing to attack him, so he sent a spy, Buraydah ibn Al-Ḥasīb Al-Aslamī, to confirm this. The Banū al-Muṣṭaliq also believed that Muḥammad was preparing to attack them. So they in turn sent a spy reconnoiter to explore the positions of the Muslims, but he was captured and killed by them.
The two armies were stationed at a well called Al-Muraysī', near the sea, a short distance from Mecca. They fought with bows and arrows for an hour, and then the Muslims advanced rapidly, they surrounded the al-Muṣṭaliq and took the entire tribe as prisoners, with their families, herds and flock. The battle ended in full victory for the Muslims. Two hundred families were taken as captives, two hundred camels, five thousand sheep, goats, as well as a huge quantity of household goods which were captured as booty. The household goods were sold in an auction to the highest bidder.
The Mustaliq lost a total of ten men. Only one Muslim was killed by mistake by a Helper. Juwayrīyah bint al-Ḥārith, daughter of the Banū al-Muṣṭaliq chief was one of the captives.

Marriage to Muhammad
After minimal casualties, the Muslim forces were victorious. Among the many captives was Juwayriya, whose husband Mustafa bin Safwan, had been killed in the battle. She initially fell among Muhammad's companion Thabit ibn Qays ibn Al-Shammas. Troubled by this, Juwayriya sought a deed of redemption from Muhammad. Muhammad proposed to marry her and, as a result, freed her from the bondage of Thabit ibn Qais and consequently ameliorated the condition of her captured tribe.
This incident was described in more detail:
"At the first opportunity (after her capture) she went to the Prophet, and pleaded her case with him. She told him that she was the daughter of a chieftain and used to command and because of her unfortunate circumstance she found herself in this helpless position. From a throne made of gold she had fallen into dust. ......How could she possibly live the life as a slave? She pleaded with the Prophet, to take notice of the pitiful and desperate condition in which she found herself.
The Prophet, was moved by her sorrowful plea and asked her if she would like to live as a free woman and be part of his household if he paid her ransom. She had never in her dreams expected this offer. Moved deeply by this unexpected elevation in her status, she exclaimed she would be more than happy to accept."
Some time later her father and all the men of her tribe who had been freed also accepted Islam as their religion.
Consequently, she was married to Muhammad, the Islamic prophet when he was 57 years old and she was 19,  thus placing the marriage in 627-628.
She was married to the prophet for four years, and died 44 years later.

Death and burial
She died at the age of sixty-five in the 50th year after migration and was buried with the other wives of Muhammad in Jannatul Baqi'.

Her qualities
Juwayriya was described as being very beautiful and refined:

She was brought up in the lap of luxury, and had all the refinements and graces of a princess. Intelligent and wise, she mastered language and literary style. This was an accomplishment much prized by contemporary Arabs.
All who saw [Juwayriya] were stunned by her exceptional beauty.

bio: K'ab bin 'Amr bin 'Ubbad (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
K'ab bin 'Amr bin 'Ubbad was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. He lived during the formative period of Islam in the early 7th century and was among those who personally knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime.

K'ab is most notably recognized as a participant in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE near the wells of Badr in present-day Saudi Arabia. This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The Muslims, though significantly outnumbered, achieved a decisive victory that is considered pivotal in establishing Islam's presence in the Arabian Peninsula. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition and are collectively known as the "Badriyyun" or "Companions of Badr."

As a sahabi, K'ab belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and could serve as sources for hadith - the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet that form a crucial component of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice alongside the Quran. The companions' testimonies and narrations became fundamental sources for understanding Islamic teachings and the Prophet's example.

K'ab lived in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Islamic state after the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the base from which Islam expanded throughout the Arabian Peninsula and beyond. Living in this environment, K'ab would have witnessed the development of the first Muslim community and the establishment of Islamic governance and social structures.

He died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, the first caliph after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This places his death during the early expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula and the consolidation of Islamic rule over the various Arab tribes.

K'ab's historical significance lies primarily in his status as a Companion of Badr and his role as a direct witness to the Prophet's teachings and conduct. His generation of companions formed the crucial link between the Prophet's lifetime and subsequent generations of Muslims, serving as the human carriers of Islamic knowledge and tradition.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Ka'b bin 'Ajra al-Salmi, al-Ansari (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Ka'b bin 'Ajra al-Salmi, al-Ansari was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 600 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. As indicated by his name "al-Ansari," he belonged to the Ansar, the Muslim inhabitants of Medina who supported and gave refuge to the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

Ka'b bin 'Ajra is most notably remembered as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan (Bay'at al-Ridwan), a significant event in early Islamic history that took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge, referenced in the Quran (48:18), occurred when approximately 1,400 Muslims accompanying the Prophet on a pilgrimage to Mecca were prevented from entering the city. Under a tree at Hudaybiyyah, these companions pledged their loyalty to the Prophet, demonstrating their unwavering commitment even in the face of potential conflict with the Meccan tribes.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular importance in Islamic tradition because it represented a moment of absolute trust and devotion by the early Muslim community. The Quranic verse states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree, making those who participated in this event especially honored in Islamic history.

As a companion of the Prophet, Ka'b bin 'Ajra would have been among those who directly received teachings from Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Muslim community in Medina. The companions serve as crucial links in the transmission of Islamic knowledge, including hadith (prophetic traditions) and early Islamic practices.

Ka'b bin 'Ajra lived during the formative period of Islam, witnessing the religion's establishment and early expansion throughout the Arabian Peninsula. He died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, when the Muslim community was consolidating its presence in Arabia and beginning its expansion beyond the peninsula.

His inclusion among the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan ensures his place in Islamic historical memory as one of the early believers who demonstrated exceptional loyalty during a critical moment in the Prophet's mission. This designation connects him to both Quranic text and the broader narrative of early Islamic community formation.

bio: Ka'b bin Jimaz bin Tha'laba (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ka'b bin Jimaz bin Tha'laba was a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslim community that established itself in Medina following the Prophet's migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

Ka'b is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as it was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The Companions of Badr, numbering around 300 men, are held in special regard within Islamic tradition due to their participation in this pivotal engagement that helped secure the survival of the early Muslim state.

As a member of the Ansar—the local inhabitants of Medina who supported and assisted the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca—Ka'b would have been part of the community that provided crucial support during Islam's early expansion. The Ansar played a fundamental role in establishing the first Muslim society in Medina and defending it against external threats.

His tribal lineage traces to the Tha'laba clan, connecting him to the broader tribal structure of pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society. Like many of his contemporaries among the Companions, Ka'b would have witnessed and participated in the rapid transformation of Arabian society as Islam spread throughout the peninsula during the Prophet's lifetime and the early Caliphate period.

Ka'b died in 634 CE, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE, during the early reign of the first Caliph Abu Bakr. This places his death during the initial period of the Rashidun Caliphate, when the Muslim community was consolidating its position in Arabia and beginning the conquests that would eventually extend Islamic rule beyond the peninsula.

His significance lies primarily in his status as a Companion of the Prophet and his participation in the Battle of Badr, making him part of the foundational generation that established and preserved the early Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

famous: Ka'b bin Zayd bin Qays bin Malik
full: Ka'b bin Zayd bin Qays bin Malik
bio: Ka'b bin Zayd bin Qays bin Malik (c. 594–627 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Ka'b ibn Zayd ibn Qays ibn Malik ibn Ka'b ibn Haritha ibn Dinar ibn al-Najjar was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Dinar branch of the Najjar clan of the Khazraj. Ibn Hibban gives his kunya as Abu Amir. Musa ibn Uqba and Ibn Ishaq list him among those who fought at the Battle of Badr, and Ibn Ishaq is also cited as placing him at Uhud. He was present at Bi'r Ma'una, where, according to Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir, he alone survived while all his companions were killed. He was later killed as a martyr at the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq). The accounts differ on how he died: al-Waqidi says Dirar ibn al-Khattab killed him, while Ibn Ishaq says an arrow struck and killed him, and it is reported that the arrow was shot by Umayya ibn Rabi'a ibn Sakhr al-Du'ali.

bio: Kaab bin Luay, the seventh grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad bin Abdullah, was the master of the Kenana tribe. His nickname was Abu Husays.
bio_full:
Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy  (Arabic: كَعْب ٱبْن لُؤَيّ) was an ancestor of the Islamic prophet Muhammad in Arabic tradition.

Ka'b Lu'ayy was born in c. 305, in Mecca, Saudi Arabia to Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib and Ma'wiya bint Ka`b ibn al-Qayn ibn Jasr ibn Shay' Allah ibn Asad ibn Wabara ibn Taghlib ibn Hulwan ibn Imran ibn al-Haf ibn Quda'a. Her (Ma'wiyah's) mother was 'Atikah bint Kahil Ibn 'Udhrah.

Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy had two full brothers ('Amir and Samah); the three of them were known as the Banu Najiyah.

They also had a paternal half-brother whose descendants regarded themselves as part of the Banu Ghatafan, becoming a part of them. This brother was called 'Awf ibn Lu'ayy and his mother was al-Baridah bint 'Awf ibn Ghanm ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ghatafan. It is said that when her husband, Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib died, she went back with her son 'Awf to her own tribe (Banu Ghatafan) and married Sa'd ibn Dhubyan ibn Baghid, who adopted 'Awf ibn Lu'ayy. Addressing 'Awf, Fazara ibn Dhubyan is reported to have said:

Son of Lu'ayy, turn your camel aside to me;

Your own people have abandoned you and you have

no dwelling place.

Also, Ka'b had two more paternal half-brothers. One of these was Khuzaymah, known as A'idhat Quraish after his mother, A'idhah bint al-Khims ibn Quhafah ibn Kath'am. The other was Sa'd, whose descendants were known as the Bunanah, after Sa'd's mother, Bunanah.

primaryTitle: Poet-Companion Who Repented from Tabuk Absence
titles: Sha'ir al-Nabi · One of Three Who Stayed Behind at Tabuk
bio: Ka'b bin Malik Al-Ansari Al-Sulami, the poet of Islam, converted to Islam in the past and witnessed Aqaba but not Badr. He was one of the three whom God accepted after their failure to participate in the Battle of Tabuk. He died in the year 50 AH, or it was said 51 AH.
bio_full: Ka'b ibn Malik ibn Abi Ka'b was an Ansari Companion of the Banu Salima, a clan of the Khazraj in Medina. His mother was Layla bint Zayd ibn Tha'laba, also of the Banu Salima. His usual kunya was Abu Abd Allah; Abu Abd al-Rahman is also recorded, and Abu Nu'aym reports that before Islam he was called Abu Bashir. He was among the Medinans who took the pledge of al-Aqaba. Most accounts say he did not fight at Badr, though Ibn al-Kalbi and Ibn Hibban report that he did. At Uhud he fought and was badly wounded (seventeen wounds in one report, eleven in Ibn Abd al-Barr's), and one account says he was the first to recognise the Prophet after the Muslim ranks broke. He was one of the poets who defended the Prophet in verse, named with Hassan ibn Thabit and Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. He is best known as one of the three men, with Hilal ibn Umayya and Murara ibn al-Rabi', who stayed behind from the Tabuk expedition without excuse. The Prophet ordered the Muslims not to speak to them until God revealed that they were forgiven. Late in life, during the caliphate of Mu'awiya, he lost his sight. His sons included Abd Allah, Ubayd Allah and Abd al-Rahman. Al-Waqidi dates his death to 50 AH at the age of 77; other reports give 51 or 53 AH, and al-Haytham and al-Mada'ini give 40 AH.

Kabsah bint Ma'n bin 'Asim was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Kabsah lived during the formative period of early Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim community and the development of Islamic practices and teachings. Her lifetime spanned the crucial decades when Islam transformed from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community in Medina, and eventually to a significant force across the Arabian Peninsula.

The Ansar held special significance in Islamic history as they provided crucial support to the early Muslim community during a vulnerable period. They offered refuge, protection, and resources to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca, demonstrating remarkable generosity and commitment to the new faith. This act of welcome and support was so valued that it earned them lasting recognition in Islamic tradition.

Kabsah's designation as a Sahabiyya places her among the women who directly encountered and interacted with Prophet Muhammad, a distinction that carries particular reverence in Islamic tradition. Female companions played important roles in the early Muslim community, contributing to its social fabric, religious life, and cultural development, though specific details of individual contributions often remain undocumented in historical sources.

She lived through the period of the Ridda wars and the early expansion of Islam under the first Caliph Abu Bakr, dying around 635 CE during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab. Her death occurred during a time when the Islamic state was rapidly expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula into the territories of the Byzantine and Sassanian empires.

While specific details of Kabsah's individual activities and contributions are not extensively documented in available historical sources, her recognition as a companion of the Prophet Muhammad indicates her presence and participation in the foundational period of the Islamic community in Medina. Her status reflects the broader role of Ansari women in supporting and participating in the early development of Islamic society.

bio: Kabsha bint As'ad bin Zurara (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Kabsha bint As'ad ibn Zurara ibn Udus was a woman of the Ansar of Medina and a daughter of As'ad ibn Zurara. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Umayra bint Sahl ibn Tha'laba and says that Kabsha was the youngest of As'ad's daughters. Ibn al-Athir records that As'ad entrusted his daughters to the Prophet, who raised them and arranged their marriages. Ibn al-Athir and Abu Nu'aym name one of her sisters as al-Fari'a (also given as Furay'a), who, according to Ibn al-Athir, was married to Nubayt ibn Jabir. These entries record no hadith narrated by her and give no dates for her birth or death.

bio: Abd al-Hayy al-Lucknawi (1848–1886 CE) was a scholar of the Hanafi tradition, based in Lucknow. Known as Indian Hanafi jurist and hadith critic.
bio_full:
Abdul Hayy Lucknawi Firangi Mahali (24 October 1848 - 27 December 1886) was an Indian Sunni Islamic scholar of Hanafi school of Islamic thought.

Abdul Hayy was born in Banda, India. He was an Indo-Arab and a descendant of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari RadiAllahi ‘Anhu from Madinah through the lineage of the Sufi saint of Herat, Abdullah Ansari.

After his father's death, he studied mathematics under his father's tutor, Muhammad Niamatullah. He taught for a while in Hyderabad. Subsequently, he left for Lucknow where he remained for the rest of his life.

The Grand Mufti of Makkah Ahmad Zayni Dahlan granted him permission for all isnad (chains of narration) from al-Hidayah of Burhan al-Din al-Marghinani, Muhammad ibn Abdullah Hanbali of Makkah and Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Gharbi. Abdul Ghani Dehlwi also granted him permission for various isnad.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Kabsha bint Rafi' bin Mu'awiya (b. c. 600 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Kabsha bint Rafi' bin Mu'awiya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE, she was among the Muslim women who witnessed and participated in the formative period of Islamic history in the Arabian Peninsula.

Kabsha is historically significant as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a pivotal event in Islamic history that took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, occurred when approximately 1,400 Muslims, including Kabsha, pledged their loyalty to Prophet Muhammad under a tree. The event is commemorated in the Quran in verse 48:18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree.

The Pledge of Ridwan took place during a tense moment when the Muslims had traveled from Medina to Mecca to perform pilgrimage but were prevented from entering the city. When rumors spread that the Prophet's emissary Uthman ibn Affan had been killed by the Meccan tribes, the Muslim community gathered to pledge their willingness to fight if necessary. This demonstration of unity and loyalty became a defining moment in early Islamic history, showing the strong bonds between the Prophet and his followers.

As a resident of Medina, Kabsha would have been part of the Muslim community during its crucial early development following the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the base for the expanding Muslim community and the seat of the first Islamic state.

Kabsha's inclusion among those specifically remembered for taking the Pledge of Ridwan highlights the active participation of women in the early Muslim community's significant events. Her recognition in Islamic historical sources demonstrates that women were present and acknowledged as important participants in key moments of Islamic history, not merely passive observers.

She died around 640 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, having lived through the Prophet's lifetime and the initial expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her life spanned the foundational decades of Islamic civilization, from its origins in Mecca and Medina to its emergence as a major force in the region.

bio: Kabsha bint Thabit (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Ibn Sa'd records two Ansari women named Kabsha bint Thabit, and says that both accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet. The better documented is Kabsha bint Thabit ibn al-Mundhir ibn Haram of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar, the paternal half-sister of the poet Hassan ibn Thabit. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Sakhta bint Haritha of the Banu Sa'ida. She married Amr ibn Muhsin, by whom she had Tha'laba, Abu Amra and Abu Habiba; then al-Harith ibn Tha'laba, by whom she had Ramla (Umm Thabit), who also gave the pledge; and then Haritha ibn al-Nu'man. Ibn Abd al-Barr, citing Ahmad ibn Zuhayr, says she was of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar and was a Companion. Through Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Amra she narrated that the Prophet drank standing from a hanging waterskin, and that she then cut off its mouth. Abu Aruba identifies this narrator as Hassan's sister, but Khalifa ibn Khayyat attributes the report to the other woman, Kabsha bint Thabit ibn Haritha of the Khazraj, whom he calls the grandmother of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Amra. Some transmitters call the narrator al-Barsa' or Kulthum. No dates for her birth or death are recorded.

The designation of Sahabiyya places Kabsha among the female companions who lived during the Prophet's lifetime and had direct contact with the early Muslim community. These women formed an important part of the foundational generation of Muslims, contributing to the establishment and development of Islamic society in its earliest phase.

Kabsha's position as an Ansari companion of Medina indicates that she was part of the local community that facilitated the transformation of Medina into the first Islamic city-state. The Ansar were instrumental in providing the political, social, and economic foundation that allowed Islam to establish itself as more than just a religious movement, evolving into a comprehensive social and political system.

Her life span, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompasses the pre-Islamic period, the entire prophetic mission of Muhammad, and the beginning of the rapid Islamic expansion under the first caliphs. This places her among those who witnessed the complete transformation of Arabian society from tribal paganism to a unified Islamic community.

While specific details about Kabsha's individual contributions are not extensively documented in available historical sources, her recognition as a companion reflects her participation in the early Muslim community during its most formative period. The preservation of her name in Islamic historical tradition indicates that she held some significance within the community of believers in Medina, contributing to the collective effort of establishing and maintaining the first Muslim society under the Prophet's guidance and in the immediate aftermath of his death.

full: Kamāl al-Dīn Abū al-Ḥasan Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Fārisī
primaryTitle: Discoverer of the Correct Explanation of the Rainbow
bio: Kamal al-Din Hasan ibn Ali ibn Hasan al-Farisi or Abu Hasan Muhammad ibn Hasan was a Persian Muslim scientist. He made two major contributions to science, one on optics, the other on number theory. Farisi was a pupil of the astronomer and mathematician Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, who in turn was a pupil of Nasir al-Din Tusi.
bio_full:
Kamal al-Din Hasan ibn Ali ibn Hasan al-Farisi  or Abu Hasan Muhammad ibn Hasan (1267– 12 January 1319, long assumed to be 1320; Persian: كمال‌الدين فارسی) was a Persian Muslim scientist. He made two major contributions to science, one on optics, the other on number theory. Farisi was a pupil of the astronomer and mathematician Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, who in turn was a pupil of Nasir al-Din Tusi.
According to Encyclopædia Iranica, Kamal al-Din was the most advanced Persian author on optics.

Optics

His work on optics was prompted by a question put to him concerning the refraction of light. Shirazi advised him to consult the Book of Optics of Ibn al-Haytham (Alhacen), and Farisi made such a deep study of this treatise that Shirazi suggested that he write what is essentially a revision of that major work, which came to be called the Tanqih. Qutb al-Din Al-Shirazi himself was writing a commentary on works of Avicenna at the time.
Farisi is known for giving the first mathematically satisfactory explanation of the rainbow, and an explication of the nature of colours that reformed the theory of Ibn al-Haytham Alhazen. Farisi also "proposed a model where the ray of light from the sun was refracted twice by a water droplet, one or more reflections occurring between the two refractions." He verified this through extensive experimentation using a transparent sphere filled with water and a camera obscura.
His research in this regard was based on theoretical investigations in dioptrics conducted on the so-called Burning Sphere (al-Kura al-muhriqa) in the tradition of Ibn Sahl (d. ca. 1000) and Ibn al-Haytham (d. ca. 1041) after him.  As he noted in his Kitab Tanqih al-Manazir (The Revision of the Optics), Farisi used a large clear vessel of glass in the shape of a sphere, which was filled with water, in order to have an experimental large-scale model of a rain drop. He then placed this model within a camera obscura that has a controlled aperture for the introduction of light.  He projected light unto the sphere and ultimately deducted through several trials and detailed observations of reflections and refractions of light that the colors of the rainbow are phenomena of the decomposition of light. His research had resonances with the studies of his contemporary Theodoric of Freiberg (without any contacts between them; even though they both relied on Ibn al-Haytham's legacy), and later with the experiments of Descartes and Newton in dioptrics (for instance, Newton conducted a similar experiment at Trinity College, though using a prism rather than a sphere).
In his Kitab Tanqih al-Manazir (The Revision of the Optics), Farisi also saved the latest advancements in color theory by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi on color ordering. In contrast to Aristotle (d. 322 BCE), who had suggested that all colors can be aligned on a single line from black to white, Ibn-Sina (d. 1037) had described that there were three paths from black to white, one path via grey, a second path via red and the third path via green. Al-Tusi (ca. 1258) elaborated on this by stating that there are no less than five of such paths, via lemon (yellow), blood (red), pistachio (green), indigo (blue) and grey. No less than 23 intermediate colors on these paths were explicitly mentioned in this text. Fortunately this text was saved since Farisi included it in his Kitab Tanqih al-Manazir (The Revision of the Optics), which was copied numerous times until at least the nineteenth century as part of the textbook Revision of the Optics (Tanqih al-Manazir). Tusi's description of the relations between various colors effectively made color space two-dimensional. 
Robert Grosseteste (d. 1253) proposed an effectively three-dimensional model of color space.

Number theory
Farisi made a number of important contributions to number theory. His most impressive work in number theory is on amicable numbers. In Tadhkira al-ahbab fi bayan al-tahabb ("Memorandum for friends on the proof of amicability") introduced a major new approach to a whole area of number theory, introducing ideas concerning factorization and combinatorial methods. In fact Farisi's approach is based on the unique factorization of an integer into powers of prime numbers. While the Greek mathematician Euclid took the first step on the way to the existence of prime factorization, al-Farisi took the final step and stated for the first time the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

Works
Asas al-qawa'id fi usul al-fawa'id (The base of the rules in the principles of uses) which comprises an introduction and five chapters dealing with arithmetic, notarial and sales rules, and the areas of surfaces and solids, while the last two essays are on algebra. The book is a commentary on the treatise of Al-Baha'i uses in the arithmetic rules of Al-Khawam al-Baghdadi.
Tanqih al-Manazir (Arabic: تنقيح المناظر; The Revision of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics). He completed the writing of this book in Ramadan 708 H.E. (Feb-Mar 1309 A.D.). The autograph manuscript of this work has newly discovered. Before the discovery, the completion date of the Tanqih had been controversial, placed from sometime before 1290 (M. Nazif) to after 1302, but before Quṭb al-Dīn Shīrāzī's death in 710/1311 (Wiedemann).
Tadhkira al-ahbab fi bayan al-tahabb (Memorandum for friends on the proof of amicability)
Al-Basa'ir fi 'ilm al-manazir (Insights Into the Sciences of Optics), a textbook for students of optics, presenting the conclusion of the Tanqih without the proofs or experiments. He completed the writing of this book in 708 H.E. (1309 A.D.).

bio: Kathir ibn al-'Abbas (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. The sources record 3 family or contemporary relations.
bio_full: Kathir ibn al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib al-Hashimi, known as Abu Tammam, was a son of the Prophet's uncle al-Abbas and a brother of Abd Allah, al-Fadl, Ubayd Allah, Qutham and Tammam. His mother was an umm walad; Ibn Abd al-Barr says she was a Roman woman named Saba, or else from Himyar. He was born a few months before the Prophet's death, which several authors place in 10 AH, though Ibn Hajar regards this date as not established. Ibn Abd al-Barr says he had no companionship with the Prophet, and al-Dhahabi classes him as a Successor; Ibn Abd al-Barr includes him in his work on the Companions only under his own criterion. A report that the Prophet lined up Kathir and his cousins and promised a reward to whoever reached him first is questioned by Ibn al-Athir. He lived in Medina. He narrated from his father, from Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman, and from his brother Abd Allah; al-Zuhri, Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj and Abu al-Asbagh al-Sulami narrated from him. Classical authors describe him as a jurist, virtuous and trustworthy, who narrated few hadiths. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Hibban and Ibn al-Athir say he left no descendants. He died in Medina during the caliphate of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan; al-Dhahabi places his death between 81 and 90 AH.
