full: Mustafa ibn Abd Allah Katip Celebi
titles: Haji Khalifa · Katip Celebi
bio: Kâtip Çelebi or Ḥājjī Khalīfa was a Turkish polymath and author of the 17th-century Ottoman Empire.
bio_full:
Kâtip Çelebi (كاتب جلبي) or Ḥājjī Khalīfa (حاجي خليفة)  (1017 AH/1609 AD – 1068 AH/1657 AD) was a Turkish polymath and author of the 17th-century Ottoman Empire. He compiled a vast universal bibliographic encyclopaedia of books and sciences, the Kaşf az-Zunūn, and wrote many treatises and essays. “A deliberate and impartial historian… of extensive learning”, Franz Babinger hailed him "the greatest encyclopaedist among the Ottomans."
Writing with equal facility in Alsina-i Thalātha—the three languages of Ottoman imperial administration, Arabic, Turkish and Persian –  principally in Arabic and then in Turkish, his native tongue— he also collaborated on translations from French and Latin. The German orientalist Gustav Flügel published Kaşf az-Zunūn in the original Arabic with parallel Latin translation, entitled Lexicon Bibliographicum et Encyclopaedicum  (7 vols.) The orientalist Barthélemy d'Herbelot produced a French edition of the Kaşf az-Zunūn principally with additional material, in the great compendium, Bibliothèque orientale.

Life
He was born Muṣṭafa ibn 'Abd Allāh (مصطفى بن عبد الله) in Istanbul in February 1609 (Dhu’l-Qa‘da 1017 AH). His father was a sipahi (cavalrist) and silāhdār (sword bearer) of the Sublime Porte and secretary in the Anadolı muhasebesi (Anatolian finance accountancy) in Istanbul. His mother came from a wealthy Istanbul family. From age five or six he began learning the Qur’ān, Arabic grammar and calligraphy, and at the age of 14 his father found him a clerical position in the imperial financial bureaucracy. He excelled in penmanship, accountancy and siyāqat ("Treasury cipher"). As the accountant of the commissariat department of the Ottoman army in Anatolia, he fought alongside his father on the Terjan campaign (1624) and in the failed expedition to recapture Baghdād from Persian control in 1625. On the return home his father died at Mosul, and his uncle died a month later. In 1626–1627 he was at the siege of Erzurum.
Çelebi had a love of learning from his father, and on his return to Istanbul in 1628 he attended the sermons of the charismatic preacher Qādīzāde, who inspired him to resume his studies. An inheritance allowed him to settle permanently in Istanbul. He continued for 34 years, interrupted only for military service on campaigns to Baghdād (1629) and Hamadan (1630). In 1633 he left his corps' winter quarters in Aleppo to make the Hajj, earning the title Hajji. He rejoined the imperial army at Diyarbakr, where he associated with scholars.  He took part in the recapture of Erivan by Sultan Murad IV, and expeditions to Tabriz and Baghdād (1629-1631).
On his return in 1635 to Istanbul, Mehmed Kalfa, an old associate of his father's, secured him an apprentice position as Khalifa (second clerk), in the Audit Office of the Cavalry. He later obtained a post in the head office of the Commissariat Department. In 1645 a legacy left to him by a wealthy relative enabled him to dedicate himself full-time to scholarship and acquire books. With his master and friend A'rej Mustafa Efendi, he studied the commentary of al-Baydawi, The Roots of Law, commentaries on Ashkāl al-ta’sīs  (Ideal Forms), al-Mulakhkhas (Summary) of Chaghmīnī, ‘arūd (prosody) of Andalusī, and Ulugh Beg’s Zīj (Almanac). He also attended the ders-i 'amm (lecturers), Kurd 'Abd Allāh Efendi at Ayia Sophia and Kechi Mehmed Efendi at the Suleymānīye.  In 1642, in order to carry on the chain of oral teaching, he attended Veli Efendi's lectures on the Nukhba, the Alfiya, and The Principles of Tradition. He also studied the Tawdīh, Isfahānī, Qādī-Mīr, al-Maqāsid (Object of Search), the Ādāb al-bahth (Rules of Disputation), Fanārī, the Tahdhīb and the Shamsiya.
He taught medicine, geography, geometry, the Sí fasl ('Thirty Sections') and the Bīst bāb ('Twenty Chapters') on the astrolabe, Elements of Accidence, al-Fanārī, the Shamsīya on logic, Jāmī, Mukhtasar, Farā’id, Multaqā, Durar, and Ali Qushji's treatises titled al-Muhammadiya on arithmetic and al-Fathīya on astronomy.  He wrote that his teaching method was “to enter every plurality by way of unity, and to master first principles by comprehending universals.” The astronomer Mevlana Mehmed ibn Ahmed Rumi al-Aqhisar was among those who attended his lectures.
His research ranged across lexicology, fiqh (jurisprudence), logic, rhetoric, tafsīr (Qur’ānic exegesis) and hadīth (Prophetic tradition), mathematics, medicine, mysteries of religion, astronomy, genealogy, history and chronicling.
Among his academic circle, he acquired the sobriquet “Kâtip Çelebi” (Learned Scribe). "Khatib" refers to a government clerk and "Chelebi" was used either for Ottoman princes or for scholars not part of the official hierarchy. His theology is described as Islamic orthodoxy combined with adherence to Ishrāqī (Illuminationist philosophy). The politician Köprülü Mehmed Paşa was a friend. It seems his tireless dedication to an arduous study regime, may have contributed to ill health and premature death in 1657 from a heart-attack, aged just 49. On his death, Kâtip Çelebi left unfinished works. His only son died young and, in 1659, after his widow was deceased, his library was partly acquired by Levinus Warner for Leiden University (Legatum Warnerianum). 
Çelebi’s taste for book acquisition had begun in Aleppo, and he would later expend a substantial part of his inheritance building his famous library, which came to be the largest in Istanbul in its day.

Works

Kâtip Çelebi was most productive in the decade up to his death in 1657. He authored at least 23 books, in addition to shorter essays and treatises:

Fadhlakat al-Tawārīkh ('Compendium History') (1639); summary account of 150 dynasties. Fadhlakat; i) Arabic edition from Creation to c. 1639.  Fezliké; ii) Turkish edition from 1000 AH to c. 1655. Index of 1,300 sources from original manuscript is lost.
Taqwīm at-Tawārikh (تقويم التواريخ), ('Calendar of Histories' or ‘Chronological Tables’) (1648); Universal history from Creation of Adam until the year 1648.  Written as an index to Fadhlaka partly in Turkish and partly in Persian. In 1697 Gio. Rinaldo Carli’s Italian translation was published titled Cronologia Historica.
Cihânnümâ, (var., Djihān-numā, Jihannuma ) (جهان نما) (‘View of the World’); Two-part geographic dictionary begun in 1648: part I - seas, their configuration and islands; part II - countries, rivers, mountains, roads and lands newly discovered since the 15th century (i.e. America). Çelebi based the work on Lawāmi’ al-Nūr (‘Flashes of Light’) a translation by Mehmed Ikhlāsī’ from the Latin work Atlas Minor by Gerardus Mercator (in the version published by Jodocus Hondius in Arnhem in 1621) ; the first use of European atlases and sources in Ottoman literature.
Kashf aẓ-Ẓunūn ‘an 'asāmī ‘l-Kutub wa'l-funūn (كشف الظنون عن أسامي الكتب والفنون) (‘The Removal of Doubt from the Names of Books and the Arts’). Begun in Aleppo in 1042 AH/1632 AD and completed in about 1062 AH/1652 AD, it is a vast bibliographic-biographical dictionary in Arabic, and a research-tool for scholars. Its list, approx. 15,000 Arabic, Persian and Turkish titles, 9500 authors and 300 arts and sciences, comprises among the most extensive bibliographical dictionaries of Islamic literature.

titles: Alp Eren · Kaygusuz
bio: Kaygusuz Abdul (1341–1444) was a Turkish folk poet of the 14th century.
bio_full:
Kaygusuz Abdul (1341–1444) was a Turkish folk poet of the 14th century.

In the fourteenth century, the city of Alaia was the capital of the small Emirate of Alaia. Gegusuz Abdul was born either in or near Alaya (present-day Alanya, Antalya Province in Türkiye). His name was Aladdin Jayebi and Kigosuz Abdel was his alias. According to tradition he was the son of a Bey (i.e. a prince). But instead of politics, he chose to be a dervish. His teacher was Abdul Musa.

Details of his life and travels are mysterious. Most of the stories attributed to him are unreliable. His works indicate that he traveled to many places. He traveled to Mecca for Hajj. He also visited Damascus, Najaf, and Karbala. There are unreliable accounts of his visits to cities in the Balkans such as Yambol, Plovdiv (now both in Bulgaria), Bitola (now in the Republic of Macedonia), and Edirne (now in Turkey). In Egypt, he earned the nickname Abdullah Al-Majarafi (“the servant of God who lives in a cave”) after spending several years in isolation.

Among his poetic works are:

Diwan

Golestan

Misnevi Baba Kaigozoz (Volume Three)

Jewel name

Minbar's name

His other works are:

Bodala name

Trials book

Your real name

The name of the palace

Delgosha

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Kaysan (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Kaysan was a freedman (mawla) of the Ansar who was killed at the Battle of Uhud. Ibn Ishaq lists him among the Muslims martyred there, and Ibn al-Athir, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn Hajar all record him in their works on the Companions. The sources differ on whose freedman he was: one account makes him a mawla of the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar, another of the Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar, and Ibn Abd al-Barr suggests that these may refer to two different men. Nothing more is recorded of his life.

primaryTitle: Among the First Seven — Early Martyr of Torture
titles: Among the First Seven Muslims · Tortured for Faith
bio: Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt, c. 585 – c. 660, was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad whom Islamic tradition regards as one of the ten earliest converts to Islam. Born as a slave in Mecca, he later became a swordsmith and was able to build up enough of a reputation to eventually get freed by his master. His beautiful recitation of the Quran is said to have been the direct cause of Umar ibn al-Khattab's conversion to Islam in c. 616.
bio_full:
Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt (Arabic: خبّاب بن الأرتّ), c. 585 – c. 660, was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad whom Islamic tradition regards as one of the ten earliest converts to Islam. Born as a slave in Mecca, he later became a swordsmith and was able to build up enough of a reputation to eventually get freed by his master. His beautiful recitation of the Quran is said to have been the direct cause of Umar ibn al-Khattab's (died 644, reigned as the second caliph 634–644) conversion to Islam in c. 616.

Biography
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt's background is uncertain, as medieval sources give widely different accounts. While some accounts regarded him in various ways as a mawlā (non-Arab client) of the Arab Banu Zuhra tribe, his descendants claimed that his father (whose name they gave as al-Aratt ibn Jandala ibn Saʿd ibn Khuzayma ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd) belonged to the Banu Sa'd branch of the Arab Banu Tamim tribe. However, he most likely was the son of a non-Arab inhabitant of the Sawād (southern Iraq), perhaps an Iraqi Nabataean, who was brought to Mecca as a slave and sold to someone belonging to the Arab Banu Khuza'ah tribe. His name al-Aratt, which literally means 'afflicted by a speech impairment', likely points to someone who did not master Arabic like a native speaker would.
As a slave and early convert Khabbab suffered heavily from the persecution of early Muslims by the Meccan elite, which would lead later tradition to see him as a symbol of Islam's power to emancipate and to reward steadfast belief regardless of origin or status. In 622 Khabbab was able to escape Mecca by participating in the migration (Hijra) of Muhammad and the early Muslims to Medina. He fought at the Battle of Badr in 624 and was highly regarded by Umar during his reign in 634–644. He died a rich man, in the year 657/658 (37 AH) or 659/660 (39 AH), and was buried outside of a village near Kufa where he had his estate. His son Abd Allah ibn Khabbab was murdered by the Kharijites.
Khabbab later figured as a transmitter of reports about Muhammad that were collected by the 8th/9th-century scholars of hadith, thirteen of which appeared in the Six Books recognized as most authoritative by Sunni Muslims.

References

Sources

bio: Khabbab, the client of Utbah ibn Ghazwan, a companion of Badri. He and his client Utbah were allies of the Banu Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf in pre-Islamic times. Khubayb and Utbah migrated to Yathrib, and the Prophet Muhammad made a brotherhood between him and Tamim, the client of Kharash ibn al-Samma. Khabbab participated with the Prophet Muhammad in all his conquests. Khabbab died in the year 19 AH in Medina, at the age of 50, and Caliph Omar bin Al-Khattab prayed for him.
bio_full: Khabbab, known as Abu Yahya, was the freedman (mawla) of the Companion Utba ibn Ghazwan. With his master he was an ally of the Banu Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf, and Ibn Ishaq lists him among the Badr fighters counted with that clan. According to Ibn Sa'd, the Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Tamim, the freedman of Khurash ibn al-Simma. He fought at Badr alongside Utba, and Ibn Sa'd adds that he took part in Uhud, the Trench and all the other battles with the Prophet. He died in Medina in 19 AH at the age of fifty, and Umar ibn al-Khattab led the funeral prayer over him. Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir note that no narration from him is known, and Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir add that he left no known descendants. Some authors confused him with the better-known Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, calling the latter Utba's freedman; Ibn al-Athir rejects this and treats the freedman of Utba, who died in 19 AH, as a different man.

famous: Khadij bin Salama bin Aus bin 'Amr
full: Khadij bin Salama bin Aus bin 'Amr
primaryTitle: Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Khadij bin Salama bin Aus bin 'Amr (b. c. 591 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Khadij bin Salama bin Aus bin 'Amr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islamic history in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 591 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam from the city of Medina, then known as Yathrib.

Khadij is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Second Pledge of Aqabah, a pivotal event that took place around 622 CE. This pledge was a crucial agreement between the Prophet Muhammad and a delegation of representatives from Medina, occurring before the famous migration (Hijra) of the Muslim community from Mecca to Medina. The Second Pledge of Aqabah involved a larger group than the first pledge and included commitments of protection and support for the Prophet and the Muslim community.

As a member of the Aws tribe, one of the two major Arab tribes in Medina alongside the Khazraj, Khadij belonged to a community that would play a significant role in the establishment of the first Muslim state. The Aws and Khazraj tribes had been engaged in prolonged conflicts before Islam, and their conversion and unity under the new faith marked a transformative moment in Arabian society.

The companions who participated in the pledges of Aqabah, known collectively as the Ansar (helpers), held a special status in early Islamic history as they provided sanctuary and support to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca. Their commitment enabled the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina and the development of the first Islamic political entity.

Khadij lived during the Prophet's lifetime and the early expansion of Islam, witnessing the transformation of Arabian society and the establishment of Islamic principles and governance. He died in 631 CE, shortly before the death of Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE, during a period when Islam had begun to extend beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details of his individual contributions beyond his participation in the Second Pledge of Aqabah are not extensively documented in historical sources, his status as a companion and early supporter places him among the foundational figures of the Islamic community. The companions of this generation are collectively remembered for their role in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of early Islam to subsequent generations.

dob_s: c. 616 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)

bio: Khadija bint al-Husayn ibn al-Harith (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Khadija bint al-Husayn ibn al-Harith ibn al-Muttalib ibn Abd Manaf was a woman of the clan of al-Muttalib, descended from Qusayy. Her father, al-Husayn ibn al-Harith, was a brother of Ubayda ibn al-Harith and fought at Badr. Ibn Sa'd records that Khadija accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet, and that at Khaybar the Prophet assigned her and her sister Hind an allowance of one hundred wasq. Ibn Hibban lists her among the women who emigrated (al-muhajirat). Neither author names her mother or husband, records any hadith from her, or gives dates for her birth or death.

full: Khadīja bint Khuwaylid ibn Asad al-Qurashī
primaryTitle: Mother of the Believers — First Believer
titles: Khadīja al-Kubrā · Ṭāhira (the Pure) · Sayyidat Nisāʾ al-ʿĀlamīn
bio: Khadija bint Khuwaylid was the first wife of Muhammad. Born into an aristocratic clan of the Quraysh, she was an affluent merchant in her own right and was known to have a noble personality within her tribe. She employed Muhammad to manage a trade caravan to Syria and, impressed by his skills, subsequently offered him marriage, which he accepted.
bio_full:
Khadija bint Khuwaylid (Arabic: خَدِيجَة بِنْت خُوَيْلِد) (c. 554 – November 619) was the first wife of Muhammad. Born into an aristocratic clan of the Quraysh, she was an affluent merchant in her own right and was known to have a noble personality within her tribe. She employed Muhammad to manage a trade caravan to Syria and, impressed by his skills, subsequently offered him marriage, which he accepted. 
The couple had two sons, Qasim and Abd Allah, and four daughters, Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthum and Fatima. In the aftermath of Muhammad's first revelation, Khadija is credited to have been the first convert to Islam. She continued to support her husband throughout her life and died in November 619 (Ramadan BH 3); the year was reportedly termed the "Year of Sorrow" by Muhammad. Her remains are located at the al-Mu'alla in Mecca and attract many Muslims for ziyarat.

Honored by Muslims as one of the "Mother of the Believers", Khadija is considered as one of the four "ladies of heaven" alongside Fatima, Asiya, the wife of the Pharaoh, and Mary, mother of Jesus. According to Sunni Muslim tradition, Khadija had married thrice before Muhammad.

Profession
Khadija's mother, Fatima bint Za'idah, who died in 575, was a member of the Amir ibn Luayy clan of the Quraysh and a third cousin of Muhammad's mother, Amina.
Khadija's father, Khuwaylid ibn Asad, was a merchant and leader. According to some accounts, he died c. 585 in the Sacrilegious War, but according to others, he was still alive when Khadija married Muhammad in 595. Khuwaylid also had a sister named Ume Habib binte Asad.
Khadija was a very successful merchant. It is said that when the Quraysh's trade caravan travellers gathered to embark upon their summer journey to Syria or winter journey to Yemen, Khadija's caravan equaled the caravans of all other traders of the Quraysh put together. Khadija was given many honorifics, including 'The Pious One', 'Princess of Quraysh' (Ameerat-Quraysh), and 'Khadija the Great' (Khadija al-Kubra). It is said that she fed and clothed the poor, assisted her relatives financially, and provided marriage portions for poor relations. Khadija was said to have neither believed in nor worshipped idols, which was atypical for pre-Islamic Arabian culture.
Khadija did not travel with her trade caravans; instead, she employed others to trade on her behalf for a commission. Khadija needed a co-worker for a transaction in Syria. She hired young Muhammad, who was in his early twenties at that time, for the trade in Syria, sending word that she would pay to double her usual commission. With the permission of Abu Talib ibn Muttalib, his uncle, Muhammad was sent to Syria with one of Khadija's servants. This caravan experience earned Muhammad the honorifics of al-Sadiq ('the Truthful') and al-Amin ('the Trustworthy').
She sent one of her servants, Maysarah, to assist him. Upon returning, Maysarah gave accounts of the honourable way in which Muhammad had conducted his business, bringing back twice as much profit as Khadija had expected.

Differing views on previous marriages

Sunni version
Most Sunnis accept that Khadija married three times and had children from all her marriages. While the order of her marriages is debated, it is generally believed that she first married Atiq ibn 'A'idh ibn' Abdullah Al-Makhzumi, followed by Malik ibn Nabash ibn Zargari ibn at-Tamimi. To Atiq, Khadija bore a daughter named Hindah. This marriage left Khadija a widow. With Malik, she had two sons, who were named Hala and Hind. Malik also left Khadija a widow, dying before his business became a success. Khadija subsequently proposed to Muhammad. Her respect for him had taken a place in her heart.

Shia version
Ibn Shahrashub quoted from al-Sayyid al-Murtada in al-Shafi and al-Shaykh al-Tusi in al-Talkhis, that Khadija was a virgin when she married Muhammad. Considering the cultural and intellectual situation in Hijaz, and the high position and status Khadija al-Kubra enjoyed, among other people, it is improbable that she would have married men from Banu Tamim or Banu Makhzum tribes (the two 'low'; see the Sunni version above). Some believe the two children attributed to Khadija were the children of Hala, Khadija's sister. After the death of Hala's husband, Khadija took care of Hala and (after Hala's own death) Hala's children.

Marriage to Muhammad

Khadija entrusted a friend named Nafisa to approach Muhammad and ask if he would consider marriage. When Muhammad hesitated because he had no money to support a wife, Nafisa asked if he would consider marriage to a woman who had the means to provide for herself. Muhammad agreed to meet with Khadija, and after this meeting they consulted their respective uncles. The uncles agreed to the marriage, and Muhammad's uncles accompanied him to make a formal proposal to Khadija. It is disputed whether it was Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib, Abu Talib, or both who accompanied Muhammad on this errand. Khadija's uncle accepted the proposal, and the marriage took place. At the time of the marriage, Muhammad was around 22 to 25 years old.
Khadija was 40 years old at that time according to some sources. However, other sources claim that she was approximately 28 years old during the marriage. Muhammad's father and grandfather had died before Muhammad reached the age of maturity, leaving him without financial resources. With this proposal, Muhammad moved into Khadija's house.

Children

Muhammad and Khadija may have had six or eight children. Sources disagree about the number of children: Al-Tabari names eight; the earliest biography of Muhammad by Ibn Ishaq, names seven children; most sources only identify six.
Their first son was Qasim, who died after his third birthday (hence Muhammad's kunya Abu Qasim). Khadija then gave birth to their daughters Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Kulthum and Fatima; and lastly to their son Abd Allah. Abd Allah was known as at-Tayyib ('the Good') and at-Tahir ('the Pure'). Abd-Allah also died in childhood.
Two other children also lived in Khadija's household: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the son of Muhammad's uncle; and Zayd ibn Harithah, a boy from the Kalb tribe who had been kidnapped and sold into slavery. Zayd was a slave in Khadija's household for several years, until his father came to Mecca to take him home. Muhammad insisted that Zayd be given a choice about where he lived, and Zayd decided to remain.

Becoming the first follower of Muhammad
According to the traditional Sunni narrative, when Muhammad reported his first revelation from the Angel Gabriel (Jibril), Khadija was the first person to accept Al-Haqq (The Truth), i.e. she accepted Islam. After his experience in the cave of Hira, Muhammad returned home to Khadija in a state of terror, pleading for her to cover him with a blanket. After calming down, he described the encounter to Khadija, who comforted him with the words that Allah would surely protect him from any danger and would never allow anyone to revile him as he was a man of peace and reconciliation and always extended the hand of friendship to all. According to some sources, it was Khadija's Christian cousin, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who confirmed Muhammad's prophethood soon afterwards.
Yahya ibn 'Afeef is quoted saying that he once came, during the period of Jahiliyyah (before the advent of Islam), to Makkah to be hosted by 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, one of Muhammad's uncles mentioned above. "'When the sun started rising', he said, 'I saw a man who came out of a place not far from us, faced the Kaaba and started performing his prayers. He hardly started before being joined by a young boy who stood on his right side, then by a woman who stood behind them. When he bowed down, the young boy and the woman bowed, and when he stood up straight, they, too, did likewise. When he prostrated, they, too, prostrated.' He expressed his amazement at that, saying to Abbas: 'This is quite strange, O Abbas!' 'Is it, really?' responded al-Abbas.

primaryTitle: Physician and polymath who wrote a pioneering account of Egypt
bio: Khadija bint Khuwaylid was the first wife of Muhammad. Born into an aristocratic clan of the Quraysh, she was an affluent merchant in her own right and was known to have a noble personality within her tribe. She employed Muhammad to manage a trade caravan to Syria and, impressed by his skills, subsequently offered him marriage, which he accepted.
bio_full: Muwaffaq al-Din Abu Muhammad Abd al-Latif ibn Yusuf al-Baghdadi was a physician, philosopher, historian, Arabic grammarian and traveller, born in Baghdad around 1162. As a young man he studied grammar, law, hadith, medicine, alchemy and philosophy, giving special attention to ancient authors, above all Aristotle. He first took Ibn Sina as his guide in philosophy, but in Cairo Abu al-Qasim al-Shari'i introduced him to al-Farabi, Alexander of Aphrodisias and Themistius, which by his own account turned him away from Ibn Sina and from alchemy. He travelled to Mosul in 1189, Damascus in 1190, and Saladin's camp outside Acre in 1191, and in 1192 he met Saladin in Jerusalem and received his patronage before returning to Damascus and Cairo. He later served at the Mengujekid court in Erzincan until the Seljuk ruler of Rum, Kayqubad, conquered the city, and he returned to Baghdad in 1229. He died there on 9 November 1231. Most of his many works, as listed by Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, concern medicine; he also wrote a commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics and two pamphlets against alchemy. He is best known for his two-part Account of Egypt (Kitab al-Ifada wa al-I'tibar), one of the earliest works of Egyptology, in which he measured the Giza pyramids and described the famine of 597 AH (1200 CE) that followed the Nile's failure to flood. During that famine he examined a large number of skeletons and concluded that Galen was wrong about the lower jaw, coccyx and sacrum. The Arabic manuscript, now in the Bodleian Library, was published in Europe in the 1680s and later translated into Latin and French.

full: Diya al-Din Khalid ibn Ahmad al-Baghdadi al-Kurdistani
primaryTitle: Mawlana Khalid — Renewer of the Naqshbandiyya
titles: Mawlana Khalid · Naqshband-i Rumi · Qutb al-Aqtab
bio: Khalid al-Baghdadi (1779-1827), a Kurdish mystic, founder of a branch of the Naqshbandi Sufi order – called Khalidism – had a profound influence not only on his Kurdish homeland, but also on many other regions of the Western Islamic world. His writings are considered among the oldest examples of prose and poetry in the Kurdish language. He acquired the nickname Al-Baghdadi through his stay in Baghdad, because he was in the town of Qara Dagh in the Shahrazur region, about 5 miles from Sulaymaniyah.
bio_full:
Mawlana Khâlid Shahrazuri also known as Khâlid-i Baghdâdî and Mawlana Khalid (Kurdish: مەولانا خالیدی نەقشبەندی, romanized: Mewlana Xalîdî Neqişbendî; 1779–1827) was a Kurdish Sufi, and poet by the name of Shaykh Diya al-Dīn Khalid al-Shahrazuri, the founder of a branch of the Naqshbandi Sufi order - called Khalidi after him - that has had a profound impact not only on his native Kurdish lands but also on many other regions of the western Islamic world. His writings are among the earliest examples of prose and poetry in Central Kurdish.

Shahrazuri acquired the epithet Baghdadi through his frequent stays in Baghdad, for it was in the town of Karadağ (Qaradagh) in the Shahrizur region, about 5 miles from Sulaymaniyah, that he was born in 1779.

He was born in the year 1779 in the village of Karadağ, near the city of Sulaymaniyah, in what is now Iraqi Kurdistan. His family belonged to the Jaff tribe that claimed descent from the 3rd caliph 'Uthman. Hence, the attribution al-'Uthmani is sometimes added to his name. He was raised and trained in Sulaymaniyah, where there were many schools and many mosques and which was considered the primary educational city of his time. Young Khalid studied with the two great scholars of his time, Shaykh `Abdul Karam al-Barzinji and Shaykh `Abdur Rahim al-Barzinji, and he read with Mullah Muhammad `Ali.

One of his disciples, Ismail Sirajuddin Shirvani facilitated the spread of the Khalidiyya Order to Caucasus, triggering the Murid War.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Khalid bin 'Amr bin 'Adi (b. c. 591 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full: Khalid ibn Amr ibn Adi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir give his lineage as Khalid ibn Amr ibn Adi ibn Nabi ibn Amr ibn Sawad, traced back to Ka'b ibn Salama, which places him in the Banu Salama clan of the Khazraj. Both authors, and Ibn Hajar after them, record that he was present at the Second Pledge of al-Aqaba, when men of the Ansar pledged allegiance to the Prophet. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Hajar add that the genealogist Hisham ibn al-Kalbi said he also fought at the Battle of Badr. The classical dictionaries preserve no further details of his life, and no date or place of death is recorded.

bio: Khalid bin al-Bukayr (c. 594–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Khalid ibn al-Bukayr, also called Ibn Abi al-Bukayr, was an early Muslim and Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Layth of Kinana. The classical genealogists give his lineage as Khalid ibn al-Bukayr ibn Abd Yalil ibn Nashib. He and his family were allies of the Banu Adi ibn Ka'b of Quraysh. He accepted Islam early and, with his brothers Aqil, Amir and Iyas, pledged allegiance in the house of al-Arqam. The brothers later emigrated to Medina with their households, and Ibn Abi Hatim counts him among the first Emigrants. According to Ibn Sa'd, the Prophet joined him in brotherhood with Zayd ibn al-Dathinna. Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir report that the Prophet sent him with Abd Allah ibn Jahsh on the raid toward a Quraysh caravan before Badr, the raid in which Amr ibn al-Hadrami was killed. He fought at Badr together with his brothers, and also at Uhud. He was killed at al-Raji' in Safar of 4 AH (625 CE), alongside Asim ibn Thabit and Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, at the age of 34, according to Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Athir and al-Dhahabi. The poet Hassan ibn Thabit mourned the men killed at al-Raji' in verse. Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that he knew of no hadith narrated by him.

bio_full: Khalid ibn al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Hajar, in al-Isaba, gives his lineage as Khalid ibn al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith ibn Abd Rizah ibn Zafar, traced to Malik ibn al-Aws, which places him in the Banu Zafar clan of the Aws. Citing the historian Ibn Asakir, Ibn Hajar records that he took part in the expedition to Mu'ta and was killed there as a martyr. The entry preserves no further details of his life.

primaryTitle: Katib al-Wahy — Scribe of the Revelation
titles: Katib al-Wahy (Scribe of Revelation)
bio: Khalid bin Sa`id ibn al-'As (c. 593–635 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Katib al-Wahy — Scribe of the Revelation.
bio_full: Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-As, known by the kunya Abu Sa'id, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Umayya clan of Quraysh. His father, Sa'id ibn al-As, known as Abu Uhayha, died a polytheist before Badr; his mother was Hind bint al-Mughira of the Banu Makhzum. He was among the earliest converts, and his daughter Umm Khalid reported that he was the fifth person to accept Islam. With his wife Umayma bint Khalaf, whom Ibn Ishaq names Amina, he emigrated to Abyssinia, where his son Sa'id and his daughter Ama, known as Umm Khalid, were born. There he acted as guardian for Umm Habiba in her marriage to the Prophet. Al-Dhahabi cites Umm Khalid as saying he stayed in Abyssinia for ten-odd years before he and his brother Amr returned to the Prophet. He wrote documents for the Prophet: Ibn Manzur calls him a scribe and says he wrote the document for the delegation from Ta'if, and one report names him the first to write 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' The Prophet appointed him to collect alms from the Madhhij, and one report says he was placed over San'a. After the Prophet's death he delayed his pledge to Abu Bakr for about a month, holding that the caliphate belonged to the Banu Abd Manaf. Abu Bakr later gave him command of an army sent to Syria. Accounts of his death differ: Ibn Manda says he was killed at Marj al-Suffar in Syria during Umar's caliphate, while another report, given by Ibn Manda and also mentioned by al-Dhahabi, places his death at Ajnadayn, which Ibn Manda dates to 13 AH.

full: Khalid ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi
primaryTitle: Sayf Allah al-Maslul — The Drawn Sword of God
titles: Sayf Allah al-Maslul · Undefeated General
bio: Khalid ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi was a 7th-century Arab military commander. He initially led campaigns against Muhammad on behalf of the Quraysh. He later became a Muslim and spent the remainder of his career serving Muhammad and the first two Rashidun caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar, as a commander of the Muslim army. Khalid played leading command roles in the Ridda Wars against rebel tribes in Arabia in 632–633, the initial campaigns in Sasanian Iraq in 633–634, and the conquest of Byzantine Syria in 634–638.
bio_full:
Khalid ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi (died 642) was a 7th-century Arab military commander. He initially led campaigns against Muhammad on behalf of the Quraysh. He later became a Muslim and spent the remainder of his career serving Muhammad and the first two Rashidun caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar, as a commander of the Muslim army. Khalid played leading command roles in the Ridda Wars against rebel tribes in Arabia in 632–633, the initial campaigns in Sasanian Iraq in 633–634, and the conquest of Byzantine Syria in 634–638.
As a horseman of the Quraysh's aristocratic Banu Makhzum clan, which ardently opposed Muhammad, Khalid played an instrumental role in defeating Muhammad and his followers during the Battle of Uhud in 625. In 627 or 629, he converted to Islam in the presence of Muhammad, who inducted him as an official military commander among the Muslims and gave him the title of Sayf Allah (lit. 'Sword of God'). During the Battle of Mu'ta, Khalid coordinated the safe withdrawal of Muslim troops against the Byzantines. He also led the Bedouins under the Muslim army during the Muslim conquest of Mecca in 629–630 and the Battle of Hunayn in 630. After Muhammad's death, Khalid was appointed to Najd and al-Yamama to suppress or subjugate the Arab tribes opposed to the nascent Muslim state; this campaign culminated in Khalid's victory over rebel leaders Tulayha and Musaylima at the Battle of Buzakha in 632 and the Battle of Yamama in 633, respectively.
Khalid subsequently launched campaigns against the predominantly Christian Arab tribes and the Sasanian Persian garrisons along the Euphrates valley in Iraq. Abu Bakr later reassigned him to command the Muslim armies in Syria, where he led his forces on an unconventional march across a long, waterless stretch of the Syrian Desert, boosting his reputation as a military strategist. As a result of decisive victories led by Khalid against the Byzantines at Ajnadayn (634), Fahl (634 or 635), Damascus (634–635), and the Yarmouk (636), the Muslim army conquered most of the Levant. Khalid was subsequently demoted and removed from the army's high command by Umar. Khalid continued service as the key lieutenant of his successor Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah in the sieges of Homs and Aleppo and the Battle of Qinnasrin, all in 637–638. These engagements collectively precipitated the retreat of imperial Byzantine troops from Syria under Emperor Heraclius. Around 638, Umar dismissed Khalid from both his military command and his position as governor of Qinnasrin. Khalid died in 642, either in Medina or Homs.
Khalid is generally considered by historians to be one of the most seasoned and accomplished generals in Islamic history, and he is likewise commemorated throughout the Arab world. Islamic tradition credits him with decisive battlefield tactics and effective leadership during the early Muslim conquests. However, historical accounts offer differing perspectives on certain events, including his execution of Malik ibn Nuwayra during the Ridda Wars and his dismissal from command by Umar. Khalid's military fame disturbed some pious early Muslims, most notably Umar, who feared it could develop into a personality cult. In Sunni tradition, Khalid is generally honored as a heroic figure, whereas Shia tradition portrays him more critically.

Ancestry and early life
Khalid's father was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, an arbitrator of local disputes in Mecca in the Hejaz (western Arabia). Al-Walid is identified by the historians Ibn Hisham (d. 833), Ibn Durayd (d. 837) and Ibn Habib (d. 859) as the "derider" of the Islamic prophet Muhammad mentioned in the Meccan suras (chapters) of the Qur'an. He belonged to the Banu Makhzum, a leading clan of the Quraysh tribe and Mecca's pre-Islamic aristocracy. The Makhzum are credited for introducing Meccan commerce to foreign markets, particularly Yemen and Abyssinia (Ethiopia), and developed a reputation among the Quraysh for their intellect, nobility and wealth. Their prominence was owed to the leadership of Khalid's paternal grandfather al-Mughira ibn Abd Allah. Khalid's paternal uncle Hisham was known as the 'lord of Mecca' and the date of his death was used by the Quraysh as the start of their calendar. The historian Muhammad Abdulhayy Shaban describes Khalid as "a man of considerable standing" within his clan and Mecca in general.
Khalid's mother was al-Asma bint al-Harith ibn Hazn, commonly known as Lubaba al-Sughra ('Lubaba the Younger', to distinguish her from her elder half-sister Lubaba al-Kubra) of the nomadic Banu Hilal tribe. Lubaba al-Sughra converted to Islam about c. 622 and her paternal half-sister Maymuna became a wife of Muhammad. She was also half-sister of Asma bint Umais, who successively married to Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, Abu Bakr, and later Ali ibn Abi Talib. Through his maternal relations, Khalid became highly familiarized with the Bedouin (nomadic Arab) lifestyle. Descriptions of Khalid’s appearance are rare, but some accounts claim he so closely resembled Umar in both looks and voice that people with poor eyesight often confused them.

Early military career

Opposition to Muhammad

The Makhzum were strongly opposed to Muhammad, and the clan's preeminent leader Amr ibn Hisham (Abu Jahl), Khalid's first cousin, organized the boycott of Muhammad's clan, the Banu Hashim of Quraysh, in c. 616–618. After Muhammad emigrated from Mecca to Medina in 622, the Makhzum under Abu Jahl commanded the war against him until they were routed at the Battle of Badr in 624. About twenty-five of Khalid's paternal cousins, including Abu Jahl, and numerous other kinsmen were slain in that engagement.

The following year, Khalid commanded the right flank of the cavalry in the Meccan army which confronted Muhammad at the Battle of Uhud north of Medina. According to the historian Donald Routledge Hill, rather than launching a frontal assault against the Muslim lines on the slopes of Mount Uhud, "Khalid adopted the sound tactics" of going around the mountain and bypassing the Muslim flank. He advanced through the Wadi Qanat valley west of Uhud until being checked by Muslim archers south of the valley at Mount Ruma. The Muslims gained the early advantage in the fight, but after most of the Muslim archers abandoned their positions to join the raiding of the Meccans' camp, Khalid charged against the resulting break in the Muslims' rear defensive lines. In the ensuing rout, several dozen Muslims were killed. The narratives of the battle describe Khalid riding through the field, slaying the Muslims with his lance. Shaban credits Khalid's "military genius" for the Quraysh's victory at Uhud, the only engagement in which the tribe defeated Muhammad.

In 628, Muhammad and his followers headed for Mecca to perform the umra (lesser pilgrimage to Mecca) and the Quraysh dispatched 200 cavalry to intercept him upon hearing of his departure. Khalid was at the head of the cavalry and Muhammad avoided confronting him by taking an unconventional and difficult alternate route, ultimately reaching Hudaybiyya at the edge of Mecca. Upon realizing Muhammad's change of course, Khalid withdrew to Mecca. A truce between the Muslims and the Quraysh was reached in the Treaty of Hudaybiyya in March.

Conversion to Islam and service under Muhammad

In the year 6 AH (c. 627) or 8 AH (c. 629) Khalid embraced Islam in Muhammad's presence alongside the Qurayshites Amr ibn al-As and Uthman ibn Talha; the modern historian Michael Lecker comments that the accounts holding that Khalid converted in 8 AH are "perhaps more trustworthy". The historian Akram Diya Umari holds that Khalid embraced Islam and relocated to Medina following the Treaty of Hudaybiyya, apparently after the Quraysh dropped demands for the extradition of newer Muslim converts to Mecca. Following his conversion, Khalid "began to devote all his considerable military talents to the support of the new Muslim state", in the words of the historian Hugh N.

bio: Khalid ibn Ribah (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Freed Slave and Early Muslim.
bio_full: Khalid ibn Rabah, known by the kunya Abu Ruwayha, is listed among the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad as the brother of Bilal ibn Rabah, the Prophet's muezzin. Al-Bukhari and Ibn Abi Hatim name him as Bilal's brother and mention Abu Bakr as patron (mawla); in al-Bukhari's wording the client status belongs to Bilal. Ibn Hibban and Ibn Abd al-Barr state that he was a Companion, and Ibn Abd al-Barr adds that he knew of no hadith narrated by him. The sources disagree about the brotherhood. Several call him Bilal's brother outright, but Ibn al-Athir and Abu Nu'aym record the view that Abu Ruwayha was Bilal's brother only in Islam, paired with him by the Prophet, and not by descent; Ibn Hajar states this view in al-Isaba. According to reports in Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir, Bilal asked Umar to let him remain in Syria, and the two settled at Darayya near Damascus among the Khawlan, where Bilal proposed marriage for both of them and the families accepted. Ibn Sa'd preserves a version in which a woman's family agreed to the match on condition that Bilal attend. Ibn Manda and Ibn Manzur also report that at the Conquest of Mecca he spoke against Suhayl ibn Amr, and the Prophet told him to leave Suhayl, who might one day be better than him. No date of death is recorded. A report in Ibn Manzur's abridgement of the History of Damascus suggests that a tomb in Aleppo may be his, but the author adds 'God knows best'.

The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were distinguished from the Muhajirun (emigrants from Mecca) and held a special place in early Islamic history for their hospitality and dedication to the new faith.

The female companions of the Prophet, known collectively as the sahabiyyat, occupied important positions within the early Muslim community. Living in Medina during this formative period meant that Khalida bint 'Amr would have witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic state, the development of Islamic law and social structures, and the consolidation of the Muslim community under the Prophet's leadership. The Ansari women, in particular, were noted for their active participation in community affairs and their role in supporting both the religious and practical needs of the growing Muslim population.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This timing situates her life entirely within the foundational period of Islam, making her a direct witness to the religion's origins and early development.

While specific details of her individual contributions may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as a companion places her among the first generation of Muslims whose faith, dedication, and presence helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization in Medina.

bio: Khaleda bint Abi Lahab, or Khaleda bint Abd al-Uzza, was a companion and cousin of the Prophet Muhammad. Her mother was Umm Jamil bint Harb bin Umayyah. Othman bin Abi Al-Aas bin Bishr bin Abd bin Dahman Al-Thaqafi married her, and she gave birth to him. Al-Daraqutni said in the book “The Brothers”: There is no narration of it.
bio_full:
Khalida bint Abi Lahab was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, she died in 635 CE, placing her life span during the crucial decades of Islam's emergence and initial expansion.

As her name indicates, Khalida was the daughter of Abu Lahab, making her a cousin of Prophet Muhammad through their shared lineage in the Quraysh tribe of Mecca. Her father Abu Lahab was notably one of the Prophet's most vocal opponents and is specifically mentioned in the Quran for his hostility to the early Muslim community. Her mother was Umm Jamil bint Harb bin Umayyah, connecting her to another prominent Meccan family.

Despite her father's opposition to Islam, Khalida herself is counted among the sahabiyya, the female companions who accepted Islam during the Prophet's lifetime. This conversion would have required considerable personal conviction given her family circumstances and the social pressures she likely faced.

Khalida married Othman bin Abi Al-Aas Al-Thaqafi, a member of the Thaqif tribe, and bore him children. Her husband's tribal affiliation suggests the marriage may have been part of the broader pattern of alliances that developed as Islam spread beyond Mecca to other Arabian communities.

In terms of Islamic scholarship, Khalida is associated with hadith sciences, the field devoted to collecting and authenticating reports about the Prophet's sayings and actions. However, the medieval scholar Al-Daraqutni noted in his work "The Brothers" that no specific narrations are attributed to her, indicating that while she may have been positioned to transmit prophetic traditions given her status as a companion, no verified reports from her have survived in the major hadith collections.

Khalida's significance lies primarily in her status as a sahabiyya during Islam's foundational period and as an example of early converts who embraced the faith despite family opposition. Her life illustrates the complex family dynamics that characterized early Islamic society, where religious conviction sometimes transcended traditional tribal and familial loyalties. While specific details about her religious activities or contributions remain limited in the historical record, her recognition as a companion reflects her acceptance and integration into the early Muslim community.

bio: Khalida bint Anas (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Khalida bint Anas was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn Hajar describe her as Umm Bani Hazm al-Sa'idiyya, that is, the mother of the Banu Hazm, of the Sa'ida clan. She is known for a single report concerning ruqya, spoken formulas recited for healing and protection. According to this report, transmitted through Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Hazm, she came to the Prophet and presented her ruqyas to him, and he directed that they be used. Ibn Hajar notes that Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani and Ibn Manda transmitted it, and Ibn al-Athir records the same account. The sources record no further details of her life, and no date of death survives.

bio: Khallad bin 'Amr bin al-Jamuh (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Khallad ibn Amr ibn al-Jamuh was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Salama clan of the Khazraj. His father was Amr ibn al-Jamuh, and Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Hind bint Amr ibn Haram. Ibn Abd al-Barr lists his brothers as Mu'awwidh, Mu'adh and Abu Ayman. He fought at the Battle of Badr: Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Dhahabi and Ibn al-Athir, citing Ibn Ishaq, all record his presence there, and Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that no one disputed it. He was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Uhud, where his father Amr ibn al-Jamuh and Abu Ayman were also killed. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir mention a view that Abu Ayman was a freed client of Amr ibn al-Jamuh rather than his son. Ibn Sa'd states that Khallad left no descendants.

bio: Khallad bin Rafi' bin Malik (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Khallad bin Rafi' bin Malik was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islamic history in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who resided in Medina during the Prophet's time there.

Khallad is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The Muslims, though significantly outnumbered, achieved a decisive victory that helped establish their position in the Arabian Peninsula and marked a turning point in the early expansion of Islam.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Khallad belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet and witnessed the revelation and early development of Islamic teachings. The companions hold a revered position in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of the Prophet's sayings, actions, and teachings to subsequent generations.

Khallad lived during a period of rapid social, political, and religious transformation in Arabia. The emergence of Islam brought significant changes to tribal structures, social norms, and political alliances throughout the region. As one of the early Muslim converts in Medina, he would have witnessed firsthand the establishment of the first Muslim community and the gradual spread of Islamic teachings beyond the immediate circle of the Prophet's followers.

His death in 634 CE places him among those companions who lived through the Prophet's entire mission and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr, the first Caliph. This was a crucial period when the Muslim community faced the challenge of maintaining unity and continuing the expansion of Islam following the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

While specific details about Khallad's individual contributions beyond his participation in Badr are not extensively documented in the historical sources, his status as a companion places him among the foundational figures of the early Muslim community. The companions collectively played essential roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, participating in the early conquests, and helping to establish the administrative and religious frameworks of the expanding Islamic state.

bio: Khallad ibn Suwayd b Tha'laba (c. 594–627 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Khallad ibn Suwayd ibn Tha'laba was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the establishment of the first Islamic community in Medina.

He is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan tribes who opposed them. The Battle of Badr demonstrated the resilience of the early Muslim community and marked a turning point in establishing Islam's presence in the Arabian Peninsula. Those who fought at Badr were later regarded with particular honor within the Muslim community for their role in this pivotal moment.

Khallad's life spanned the critical period when Islam transitioned from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community in Medina. He lived through the Hijra, the migration of Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, which marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. His presence during these foundational years meant he witnessed firsthand the development of Islamic practices, the formation of the first Muslim political community, and the early conflicts that shaped the religion's trajectory.

His death in 627 CE occurred during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad, placing him among those companions who did not live to see Islam's later expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Like many early companions, Khallad's legacy rests primarily in his participation in the formative events of early Islamic history and his role as a witness to the foundational period of the faith. His inclusion among the Badr companions ensures his remembrance in Islamic historical accounts of this significant battle.

bio: Kharija bin Hudhayfa (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Among the First Judges of Islam.
bio_full: Kharija ibn Hudhafa was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Quraysh of Mecca who later served as a judge and official in Egypt. Ibn Abd al-Barr gives his lineage as Kharija ibn Hudhafa ibn Ghanim ibn Amir, of the Banu Adi ibn Ka'b, though other views place him in the Banu Sahm or Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy. Ibn Sa'd says he accepted Islam early and accompanied the Prophet. He was counted among the horsemen of Quraysh; one account, introduced with 'it is said', rated him equal to a thousand riders, and Umar assigned him a stipend for his bravery. When Amr ibn al-As asked for reinforcements for the conquest of Egypt, Umar sent Kharija with al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and al-Miqdad. He settled in Egypt, acted as Amr's deputy at Fustat while Amr besieged Alexandria, and led campaigns into the Fayyum and Upper Egypt. The sources differ on his office: Ibn Sa'd calls him Amr's judge, Ibn Yunus says he headed the police of Egypt, and Ibn Abd al-Barr records both views. Ibn Abd al-Barr knew only one hadith from him, on the witr prayer, although Ibn Hibban called its chain obscure. In 40 AH (661 CE), Amr, who was unwell, asked Kharija to lead the prayer. A Kharijite who had come to kill Amr struck Kharija instead, believing him to be Amr; Ibn Abd al-Barr names the killer as Zadhawayh. Amr had the assassin executed. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir mention that his tomb in Egypt was known.

full: Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Thabit al-Ansari al-Khazraji
primaryTitle: One of the Seven Jurists of Medina
titles: One of the Seven Jurists · Son of the Quran Compiler
bio: Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Thabit al-Ansari al-Khazraji (c. 660–720) was a historical figure of the Islamic Jurisprudence tradition, based in Medina. Known as One of the Seven Jurists of Medina.
bio_full:
Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Thabit al-Ansari al-Khazraji was a prominent Islamic jurist who lived from approximately 660 to 720 CE in Medina. He belonged to the generation known as the Tabi'un, the "Followers" who came after the Companions of Prophet Muhammad but received religious instruction from them directly.

Kharija was the son of Zayd ibn Thabit, one of the most distinguished Companions of the Prophet Muhammad, who served as the Prophet's primary scribe and was instrumental in the compilation of the Quran. This family connection provided Kharija with direct access to authentic Islamic teachings and legal precedents through his father's knowledge and experience.

As a member of the Tabi'un generation, Kharija played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting Islamic legal knowledge during the formative period of Islamic jurisprudence. He is most notably recognized as one of the Seven Jurists of Medina, a group of scholars who were considered the leading legal authorities in the holy city during the late seventh and early eighth centuries. This group was instrumental in developing the foundations of Islamic law and legal methodology.

The Seven Jurists of Medina were particularly significant because they lived in the city where the Prophet had established the first Islamic community and where many of the Companions continued to reside after his death. Their proximity to these original sources of Islamic knowledge gave their legal opinions particular weight and authority.

Kharija's contributions to Islamic jurisprudence helped establish many of the legal principles that would later be systematized by the major schools of Islamic law. His work, along with that of his fellow jurists in Medina, provided essential groundwork for the development of Islamic legal thought and practice.

Living during a critical period when the Islamic community was expanding rapidly and encountering new legal challenges, Kharija and his contemporaries faced the important task of applying Quranic principles and Prophetic traditions to novel situations. Their scholarly efforts helped ensure the continuity and authenticity of Islamic legal tradition as it passed from the Companion generation to subsequent scholars.

Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Thabit thus represents an important link in the chain of Islamic legal scholarship, bridging the era of direct Prophetic guidance with the later systematic development of Islamic jurisprudence.

bio: Khauliy bin Abi Khauliy (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Khauliy bin Abi Khauliy was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. As one of the early followers of Islam, he lived during the formative period of the Muslim community in the early 7th century CE.

Khauliy is historically recognized as a participant in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces and holds particular significance in Islamic history. Those who participated in this engagement are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as the battle marked a turning point in the early Muslim community's struggle for survival and recognition.

The Battle of Badr involved approximately 300 Muslim fighters against a much larger Meccan force. The Muslim victory at Badr was seen as divine validation of their cause and significantly boosted the morale and standing of the early Muslim community. Participants in this battle, including Khauliy, are remembered for their commitment during this crucial moment in Islamic history.

As a Sahabi, Khauliy would have had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and would have been part of the community that received and preserved the early Islamic teachings. The companions played a vital role in the transmission of Islamic knowledge, practices, and traditions to subsequent generations.

Khauliy's connection to hadith sciences indicates his involvement in the preservation and transmission of the Prophet's sayings and teachings. The companions were the primary source of hadith literature, as they were direct witnesses to the Prophet's words and actions. Their testimonies formed the foundation for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and practice.

He died in 634 CE, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This places his death during the early caliphate period under Abu Bakr, the first Caliph, when the Muslim community was consolidating its teachings and expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about Khauliy's individual contributions beyond his participation in Badr are limited in historical records, his status as both a Badr veteran and a companion places him among the foundational figures of early Islam who helped establish and preserve the religious tradition during its most formative years.

primaryTitle: Khawaja Sahib — Voice of the Cholistan Desert
titles: Khawaja Sahib · Baadshah-e-Tasawwuf · Sultan-e-Auliya of Cholistan
bio: Khawaja Ghulam Farid Chishti Nizami (1845–1901) was a poet of the Sindhi/Punjabi Sufism tradition, based in Chachran Sharif. Known as Khawaja Sahib — Voice of the Cholistan Desert.
bio_full:
Khawaja Ghulam Farid (also romanized as Fareed; c. 1841/1845 – 24 July 1901) was a 19th-century Sufi poet and mystic from Bahawalpur, Punjab, belonging to the Chishti Order. Most of his work is in his mother tongue Multani, which later evolved into the Saraiki language. However, he wrote in many different languages, including Punjabi, Urdu, Pashto, Sindhi, Hindi and Persian, but gained popularity for writing in his mother tongue Multani. His writing style is characterized by the integration of themes such as death, passionate worldly and spiritual love, and the grief associated with love.

He was born into Koreja tribe.

his family was established as saints associated with the Suhrawardī Sufi order. Originally from Thatta, Sindh, the family seat later moved to Mithankot in the early 18th century on the invitation of a disciple and subsequently transferred their allegiance to the Chishtī order. Khawaja Farid was born c. 1841/1845 at Chachran. Farid's father died when he was around eight years of age. He was then brought up by his elder brother, Khawaja Fakhr al-Dīn, and grew up to become a scholar and writer. He received a fine formal education at the royal palace of Ṣādiq Muḥammad IV, the Nawab of Bahawalpur. His brother Fakhr al-Dīn, who had brought him up after their parents' deaths, also died when Farid was 26 years old. Farid performed hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca) in 1875, and then retired to the Cholistan Desert (also known as Rohi) for chilla (retreat) where he spent a total of eighteen years. He died at Chachran on 24 July, 1901, and was buried at Mithankot.

He is mentioned in the Gazetteer of the Multan District (1901-02) prepared and published by Edward Douglas MacLagan in 1902.

His most significant works include:

Masnavi Madan-e-Ishq (1882); Publisher: Gulzar-e-Muhammad Press, Lucknow

Dīwān-i Farīd

Manāqib-i maḥbūbiyya (Persian prose)

Fawāʾid-i Farīdiyya (Persian prose)

A literary award named after Farid  –  the Khwaja Ghulam Farid Award  –  is awarded yearly by the Pakistan Academy of Letters in literature, its recipients including Ismail Ahmedani (in 2013) and Irshad Taunsvi (in 2007) among others.

Fareed Gate is the name of one of the historic gates surrounding the old city of Bahawalpur named in Farid's honour.

The Khawaja Fareed University of Engineering and Information Technology (KFUEIT) in Rahim Yar Khan District was named after Farid.

Shrine of Khawaja Ghulam Farid in Rajanpur, Punjab is among the 10 most visited shrines in Pakistan.

bio: Khawla bint 'Ubayd b. Tha'laba (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Khawla bint 'Ubayd b. Tha'laba was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, Khawla belonged to the community that played a crucial role in the establishment and early development of Islam. The Ansar were the Medinan tribes who provided sanctuary to the Prophet and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca, forming the foundation of the first Islamic state. Her designation as a sahabiyya indicates that she personally knew the Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions, a status that holds particular significance in Islamic tradition.

The historical record preserves limited specific details about Khawla's individual activities or contributions, which reflects the broader challenge of reconstructing the lives of many early Muslim women from the available sources. What can be established is her presence as part of the early Muslim community in Medina during the formative period of Islamic history, spanning roughly from the hijra in 622 CE until her death around 635 CE.

Her life encompassed the critical years of early Islamic expansion, including the period of the Prophet's ministry in Medina and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr. As one of the Ansar, she would have witnessed the transformation of Medina from a collection of competing tribes into the center of a rapidly expanding Islamic state.

Khawla's recognition in Islamic historical sources as a companion of the Prophet reflects the important role that women played in the early Muslim community, even when specific details of their individual contributions may not have been extensively preserved in later historical compilations. Her inclusion among the documented companions serves as a testament to the presence and participation of women in the foundational period of Islamic history.

The relatively short span of her life, ending around 635 CE, coincided with one of the most transformative periods in Arabian and world history, as the Islamic message spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula to establish one of history's major civilizations.

bio: Khawla bint 'Uqba b. Rafi (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Khawla bint 'Uqba b. Rafi was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early 7th century CE. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan inhabitants who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Khawla was part of the indigenous population of Medina who converted to Islam and provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing Islam in Medina, offering protection, resources, and sanctuary to the Prophet and the emigrants (muhajirun) from Mecca who had fled persecution.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime, Khawla would have witnessed the rapid expansion of the Muslim community and the establishment of the first Islamic state in Medina. Her presence among the companions places her within the most revered generation in Islamic history, as the companions are regarded as the direct recipients of the Prophet's teachings and the primary transmitters of Islamic knowledge and practice to subsequent generations.

The status of sahabiyya holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as female companions are recognized for their contributions to the early Muslim community alongside their male counterparts. These women participated in various aspects of community life, from supporting military campaigns to preserving and transmitting religious knowledge.

Khawla's death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This means she lived through the critical transition from the Prophet's direct leadership to the rule of his successors, witnessing the continued expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Her inclusion in historical records as a named companion reflects the importance placed on documenting the lives of those who lived alongside the Prophet Muhammad. While specific details of her individual contributions may not be extensively preserved, her recognition as an Ansari companion of Medina establishes her place within the foundational generation of Muslims whose collective efforts helped establish and spread Islam during its earliest and most crucial period.

bio: Khawla bint al-Yaman (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Khawla bint al-Yaman was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and a sister of the Companion Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman. Ibn Hajar's al-Isaba gives no lineage for her beyond naming her as Hudhayfa's sister, and notes that Ibn Abd al-Barr mentioned her briefly while Ibn Manda recorded her report with its full chain. Her known narration, transmitted from her by Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman, is that she heard the Prophet say there is no good in gatherings of women except at the house of someone who has died, followed by criticism of what is said when they gather. Ibn Manda also reports that the wife of Rib'i ibn Hirash narrated from her. Hudhayfa had more than one sister, among them Fatima bint al-Yaman, and some reports from 'a sister of Hudhayfa' are not assigned to the same woman in every source. The sources record nothing further about her life, and no date of death survives.

bio: Khawla bint As-Samit (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Khawla bint al-Samit ibn Qays ibn Asram was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, whose lineage Ibn Sa'd traces through Ghanm ibn Awf to the Khazraj. He records that she was the full sister of Ubada and Aws, the sons of al-Samit, both of whom fought at Badr. Their mother was Qurrat al-Ayn bint Ubada ibn Nadla, also of the Khazraj. Khawla married Abu Abd al-Rahman Yazid ibn Tha'laba, of the Banu Ghadina of the tribe of Bali and an ally of her clan, and bore him Amir and Umm Uthman. Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet. Some reports, transmitted from al-Sha'bi, name her as the woman who disputed with the Prophet about her husband, the occasion of the verse "God has heard the words of the woman who disputes with you concerning her husband" (Qur'an 58:1). Ibn Sa'd calls this an error and says that woman was Khawla bint Tha'laba, the wife of her brother Aws. No narrations from her and no dates for her birth or death are recorded.

During the formative years of Islam, female companions like Khawla played essential roles in preserving and transmitting religious knowledge. As a hadith narrator, she was part of the chain of transmission that ensured prophetic traditions were accurately passed down to subsequent generations. This function was particularly important for matters related to women's religious practices and daily life, areas where female narrators often had unique access and understanding.

Khawla's life spanned the critical period of early Islamic expansion and community building in Medina. The inclusion of female narrators like Khawla bint Khawli in the hadith transmission process reflects the early Islamic community's recognition of women's important role in preserving religious knowledge. Her contributions, along with those of other female companions, helped ensure that the full spectrum of prophetic guidance was maintained for future Muslim generations.

Khawla bint Khawli died around 635 CE, approximately three years after the death of Prophet Muhammad. Her legacy as a hadith narrator represents the broader participation of women in the intellectual and religious life of the early Muslim community, demonstrating their integral role in the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings during this foundational period of the religion.

bio: Khawlah bint Tha'labah Khawla bint Tha'laba b. Asram b. Fihr b. Qays b. Tha'laba b. Ghanm b. Salm b. 'Auf was a woman in Arabia and one of the disciples (Sahaba) of the Islamic Prophet Muhammad. She is mentioned in the Quran in reference to Zihar. The 58th chapter of the Quran Al-Mujadila, meaning "The pleading woman" derives the name from her reference.
bio_full:
Khawla bint Tha'laba was a prominent female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in the Arabian Peninsula during the early 7th century CE. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Aws tribe of Medina and lived during the formative period of Islamic history.

Khawla is most notably remembered for her pivotal role in addressing a significant social and legal issue within the early Muslim community. She approached the Prophet Muhammad to seek guidance regarding the practice of zihar, a form of divorce declaration used in pre-Islamic Arabian society where a husband would declare his wife forbidden to him by comparing her to his mother or another female relative he could not marry. This declaration left women in a precarious legal limbo—neither divorced nor properly married.

When Khawla's husband, Aws ibn al-Samit, pronounced zihar against her, she refused to accept this unjust treatment and brought her case directly to the Prophet. Her persistence in seeking justice and her eloquent pleading for resolution of this matter led to divine revelation. The 58th chapter of the Quran, Surah al-Mujadila (meaning "The Pleading Woman" or "She Who Disputes"), was revealed in response to her situation and specifically addresses the issue of zihar.

This Quranic revelation established new Islamic guidelines that prohibited the pre-Islamic practice of zihar and provided a clear legal framework for such situations, including prescribed expiation for husbands who made such declarations. The chapter begins with reference to Allah hearing the words of the woman who pleaded concerning her husband.

Khawla's significance extends beyond her individual case. Her actions represent the active participation of women in the early Muslim community's legal and social development. Her willingness to seek justice directly from the Prophet Muhammad, and the subsequent divine response, demonstrates the Islamic principle that individuals, regardless of gender, could approach religious authority to address injustices.

Her case established important precedents in Islamic jurisprudence regarding marriage, divorce, and women's rights. Khawla bint Tha'laba died around 635 CE, but her legacy endures through the Quranic legislation that emerged from her courageous stand for justice, making her an important figure in both Islamic legal history and the broader narrative of women's advocacy in early Islam.

bio: Khawlah bint Hakim (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Khawla bint Hakim ibn Umayya ibn Haritha ibn al-Awqas al-Sulamiyya, also known by the kunya Umm Sharik, was of the tribe of Sulaym and was the wife of the Companion Uthman ibn Maz'un. Both are described as among the earliest people to accept Islam, and Ibn Hibban and Ibn Manjawayh list her among the women who emigrated. One account says that after the death of Khadija she asked the Prophet whether he would marry again, and with his agreement carried proposals on his behalf to Sawda bint Zam'a and to Abu Bakr for his daughter A'isha. Ibn al-Athir describes her as a righteous woman and reports that some say she offered herself in marriage to the Prophet; Abu Nu'aym gives several chains, one going back to A'isha, naming her as that woman. She narrated from the Prophet the supplication to be said on stopping at a place while travelling, which Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas transmitted from her. Ibn al-Athir also records that she asked the Prophet to give her the jewellery of Badiya bint Ghaylan if Ta'if were conquered. Al-Suyuti names Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Urwa and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab among those who narrated from her, and Ibn Manjawayh includes her among the narrators of Sahih Muslim. Al-Tabarani treats a Khawla bint Hakim al-Ansariyya, who asked about ritual bathing after a dream, as a different woman. The sources consulted give no date for her death.
