bio: Lubaba bint Aslam (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Lubaba bint Aslam was a woman of the Ansar of Medina who became a Muslim and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd, in his Tabaqat, gives her lineage as Lubaba bint Aslam ibn Harish ibn Adi ibn Majda'a ibn Haritha, which places her in the Banu Haritha clan. Her mother was Su'ad bint Rafi' ibn Abi Amr of the Banu al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd notes that she was the full sister, by both father and mother, of Salama ibn Aslam ibn Harish, who fought at the Battle of Badr. She married Zayd ibn Sa'd ibn Malik of the Banu Abd al-Ashhal. Ibn Sa'd records no children for her, and the sources consulted give no dates for her birth or death.

bio: Lubna bint al-Khutaym (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Scholar of Quranic Exegesis.
bio_full:
Lubna bint al-Khutaym was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she was among the early Muslim community based in Medina during the Prophet's lifetime.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Lubna bint al-Khutaym belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Islam's founder and witnessed the initial development of the faith. The companions, known collectively as the sahaba, hold a special position in Islamic tradition as the first Muslims who learned Islamic teachings directly from the Prophet and helped establish the early Muslim community.

Lubna bint al-Khutaym is noted for her involvement in Quranic exegesis, the scholarly interpretation and explanation of the Quran's meaning. During the early Islamic period, when the Quranic text was being compiled and Islamic jurisprudence was taking shape, scholars who could interpret and explain the divine revelations played a crucial role in the religious and intellectual life of the Muslim community. Her recognition as a scholar in this field indicates that she possessed significant religious knowledge and contributed to the understanding of Islamic scripture.

Her presence among the early Muslim scholars of Quranic interpretation reflects the broader participation of women in the intellectual and religious life of the early Islamic community. Female companions often served as transmitters of Islamic knowledge, particularly regarding matters they witnessed firsthand or learned directly from the Prophet Muhammad or his family members.

Living in Medina, the political and spiritual center of the early Muslim state, Lubna bint al-Khutaym would have been part of the community that experienced Islam's rapid expansion and the establishment of its fundamental religious and legal frameworks. The companions based in Medina were instrumental in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings, hadith literature, and early interpretations of Islamic law.

Lubna bint al-Khutaym died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, when the first successors to the Prophet Muhammad were consolidating Islamic rule and continuing the religion's expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her contributions to Quranic scholarship represent part of the foundational intellectual work that shaped Islamic religious understanding in its earliest decades.

bio: Lubna bint Qayzi bin Qays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Lubna bint Qayzi bin Qays was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the community of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim emigrants from Mecca following the Hijra in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Madinah, Lubna was part of the indigenous population of Medina who embraced Islam when the Prophet arrived in the city. The Ansar played a crucial role in the establishment and early development of the Muslim community, providing shelter, resources, and support to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca who had left their homes and possessions behind.

The title "Sahabiyya" designates her as a female companion of the Prophet, meaning she lived during his lifetime, met him, believed in his message, and died as a Muslim. The companions hold a special place in Islamic history as the first generation of Muslims who directly received Islamic teachings from the Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the revelation of the Quran.

Lubna's life spanned the critical early period of Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's ministry in Mecca and Medina, until shortly after his death in 632 CE. She died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr, and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate.

The Ansari women, including Lubna, were integral to the social fabric of early Islamic society in Medina. They participated in the religious and social life of the community during this formative period when Islamic practices, laws, and social structures were being established. Their presence and participation helped shape the early Muslim community's development.

While specific details about Lubna's individual contributions are not extensively documented in the historical sources, her recognition as a companion places her among the foundational figures of Islam. The companions, both male and female, are collectively remembered for their role in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings to subsequent generations, making them essential links between the Prophet's time and later Muslim communities.

bio: Lumays bint 'Amr bin Haram (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Lumays bint 'Amr bin Haram was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the Ansar, the community of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Lumays belonged to the indigenous population of Medina who converted to Islam and provided crucial support to the early Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a pivotal role in establishing Islam in Medina and ensuring the survival and growth of the Muslim community during a critical period in Islamic history.

Her designation as a sahabiyya indicates that she lived during the time of Prophet Muhammad and had direct contact with him, placing her among the first generation of Muslims. The female companions of the Prophet hold a special status in Islamic tradition, as they were witnesses to the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices and principles.

Lumays lived during one of the most significant periods in Islamic history, witnessing the transformation of a small religious movement into a major force that would reshape the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime spanned the crucial early decades of Islam, from its emergence in Mecca through its establishment in Medina and the beginning of its expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

She died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following the death of Prophet Muhammad when the first four caliphs led the Muslim community. Her death occurred during the caliphate of either Abu Bakr or the early years of Umar ibn al-Khattab's leadership.

While specific details about her individual contributions or particular roles within the early Muslim community are not extensively documented in available historical sources, her recognition as a companion of the Prophet indicates her participation in the foundational period of Islam. The female companions collectively played important roles in supporting the early Muslim community, participating in religious and social activities, and helping to preserve and transmit Islamic teachings to subsequent generations.

primaryTitle: Prophet of Sodom — Messenger to the Cities of the Plain
titles: Lut · nephew of Ibrahim · prophet to the people of Sodom
dating_source: Genesis 19; Bible Unearthed (Finkelstein); contemporary of Ibrahim
dating_note: Lot/Lut, nephew of Abraham; same era.
bio: Lūṭ ibn Hārān ibn Tārikh (c. 1900–c. 1820 BCE) was a prophet, based in Canaan. Known as Prophet of Sodom — Messenger to the Cities of the Plain.
bio_full:
Lut (Arabic: لُوط), Lot, is a prophet in Islam, the nephew of Ibrahim (Abraham), and the messenger sent to the people of Sodom and the surrounding cities of the plain. His story is recounted across at least fourteen surahs of the Quran, with extended treatment in Surah Hud (11:77-83), Surah al-Hijr (15:57-77), Surah al-Shu'ara (26:160-175), Surah al-Naml (27:54-58), and Surah al-Ankabut (29:28-35).

The Quran describes Lut migrating with Ibrahim from Mesopotamia and being sent as a prophet to a people who had descended into open homosexual aggression, highway robbery, and the public commission of indecency in their assemblies. He is recorded calling them away from these acts: 'Do you approach males among the worlds and leave what your Lord has created for you as mates?' (Surah al-Shu'ara 26:165-166). The community responded with mockery and threats to expel him.

Divine messengers — the same who had brought Ibrahim the news of Ishaq's birth — visited Lut as guests. The townspeople surrounded his house demanding access to them, at which point the angels revealed their identity, blinded the attackers, and ordered Lut to leave the city by night with his believing family. His wife, who had inclined to the wrongdoers, was destroyed with the city; the cities of the plain were overturned and rained upon with stones of baked clay (sijjil).

Classical commentators — al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir — locate the destroyed cities near the Dead Sea, identified with biblical Sodom and Gomorrah, and treat the ruins as a sign for travellers (Surah al-Saffat 37:137-138). The Quran refers repeatedly to the 'overturned cities' (al-mu'tafikat) as a permanent moral lesson.

Lut is counted in Surah al-An'am (6:86) among those whom God preferred over the worlds, alongside Isma'il, al-Yasa, and Yunus.

bio: Ma'ad ibn Adnan (c. 75–c. 10 BCE) was a founding figure, based in Mecca. Known as Ancestor of Prophet Muhammad.
bio_full:
Maʿadd ibn ʿAdnān (Arabic: مَعَدّ ٱبْن عَدْنَان) was a mythic Arab ancestor, traditionally regarded as the son of Adnan and the forefather of several northern Arab tribes, including Quda'a, Mudar, and Rabi'ah. He is considered a key figure in Adnanite genealogy, linking the northern Arabs to Ishmael ibn Ibrahim (Ishmael, son of Abraham) through Adnan.
While Maʿadd eventually became an individual ancestor in Islamic genealogies, the term is first known from pre-Islamic inscriptions where it refers to a group of nomadic and semi-nomadic groups occupying central Arabia, beyond the territorial domain of the major powers of its day: north of the direct territorial control of the Himyarite Kingdom, and south of that of the Lakhmids. Ma'addites retained independence and protected their northern and southern frontiers because they lived in remote areas and had militarized societies. From the fourth to sixth centuries, they were centered at Ma'sal al‐Jumh in the Najd. Ma'add coexisted among other regional identities, including Ghassan, Himyar, and Tayyi'. They are first mentioned in the Namara inscription (328 CE).
The word "Ma'add" was used in related, but different ways, in other sources. Pre-Islamic literature beyond the peninsula composed in Greek and Syriac used it not for a peoples but for militarized camel-herding Bedouin in north Arabia beyond imperial control more generally. In pre-Islamic Arabic poetry, "Ma'add" was a communal identity and ethnonym functioning in the way that the word "Arab" does today. As such, Ma'add encompassed all peoples, including both northern and southern Arab tribes. In Islamic genealogical accounts, which were written at a time when Ma'add began to be thought of as a tribe as opposed to a central Arabian confederation, "Ma'add" could either refer to a figure named Ma'add, the eponymous ancestor of the Ma'add tribe, or to the tribe itself. The tribe was understood in genealogies to be one of several northern Arab tribes that collectively descended from Ma'add's father, Adnan. By contrast, the tribes of South Arabia traced their ancestry to Qahtan. Ma'addite may have been the Arabic dialect that pre-Islamic qasidas were composed in, and it may have a common ancestor with Hijazi Arabic.
The word Ma'add underwent many semantic shifts in the Islamic era. First, the Ma'add geography transitioned from central Arabia to the Fertile Crescent as a result of the movement of peoples during the early Muslim conquests. Then, the word Ma'add went from being used as an ethnonym, to a tribe. To reassert its hegemony in the face of the spread of pan-Arab identity (and as the term 'Arab' came to adopt the communal sense of 'Ma'add' in earlier times) in the eighth century, the Ma'add tribe was traced to a founder figure (named Ma'add) who became the earliest ascertainable ancestor of the Arabs. By the ninth-century, however, Arab genealogical history was extended further back, first to Ma'add's father Adnan, and then his grandfather Udad, and eventually, Ishmael, as the ancestor of all Arabs. Yet another genealogical model then became dominant, which delineated South Arabs as a distinguished line of Arabs descending not from Ishmael or Adnan, but Qahtan. By the end of the ninth century, Ma'addite identity had become largely lost.

Pre-Islamic era

Inscriptions
The first well-dated text that uses the word Ma'add (as MʿDW) is the Namara inscription (c. 328 CE), discovered at Namara in southern Syria. In this Arabic inscription, Ma'add is mentioned in a list of the Arabian groups, including Nizar and Asdayn, subjugated by the Lakhmid king Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Amr, along with other Arab nations from north, west central and South Arabia. In this context, Imru' al-Qays is described as the "King of the Arabs" (malik al-ʿarab) and "King of Maʿadd" (malik maʿadd), indicating his submission of the Ma'add in this time. The inscription is ambiguous regarding the geography of Ma'add. According to Webb, the inscription could imply that they were located in South Arabia, possibly near Najran. Irfan Shahid argues that the inscription offers little specificity as to the locale of Ma'add in Arabia, or whether it was a tribe or a confederation. Shahid speculates the group could have formed out of the chaos among the Arab tribes following either the Roman annexation of the Nabatean Kingdom in 106 CE or the fall of the Palmyrene Empire to Rome in 272, both polities having wielded significant influence or control over Arab tribal life in northern Arabia. After the submission to Imru' al-Qays of the Lakhmids, Ma'add again appears in a successive series of conflicts from 340 to 360 CE, in having to confront Himyarite expeditions against them. A century later, in a source found at Maʾsal Jumḥ, the Himyarite king Abu Karib celebrates a conquest of Ma'add in an expedition that involved an alliance with the tribes of Sabaʾ, Hadhramaut, and Kinda. Another source from 521 CE in the same place describes a Himyarite expedition launched further north from the same region, indicating the maintenance of Himyarite possession over subsequent decades. After another revolt, Abraha finally and permanently defeated Ma'add in 552 CE at Haliban.
The 'Land of Maʿadd' (ʾRḌ MʿDM) is mentioned in an inscription, Jabal Riyām 2006–17. The date of the inscription is unclear, although the editors have placed it in the 3rd century CE. If correct, it would be the earliest source for Ma'add. The inscription ʿAbadan 1 (c. 360 CE) describes campaigns by the Himyarite Kingdom against nomadic groups, among them Ma'add.
Ma'add is mentioned in two Middle Sabaic texts which suggest Ma'add is in central Arabia, slightly at odds with the Namara inscription, potentially signifying fluid borders. Inscriptions during and around the time of Abraha (a Himyarite king) in the 6th century more firmly localize Ma'add to central Arabia. Some corroboration for the idea that the Ma'add belonged to the Himyarite sphere of influence comes from the mid-6th century writings of the Byzantine historian Procopius and Ibn Habib's al-Muhabbar (9th century). From these sources, it may be concluded that the Ma'add were generally north of the territory under Himyarite control, and south of the territory of Lakhmid control. Therefore, they existed beyond the domains of immediate territorial control of the major powers of their time.
A new inscription from the late 3rd century CE allows the territorial extent of Ma'add to be confidently assessed at this point in time. It was centered on Maʾsal Jumḥ. To the southeast, it reached Yabrīn, and to the southwest, it reached Ḥalibān. To the north, it reached ʿĀqil and Wādī al-Ruma, including the valley of al-Kharj.

Poetry
Ma'add is a prominent group described in pre-Islamic Arabic poetry (often used as a signifier for "all people"), with at least a few lines being dedicated to them in virtually every collection of this poetry. They regularly appear as an overarching identity, with whom comparisons are frequently made in order to elevate ones self or their tribe. For example, al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani praises the leader al-Nu'man III ibn al-Mundhir by comparing him with Ma'add:You outstrip the nobles in nobility / Like a stallion outstrips hunting dogs in the chase, / You surpass all of Maʿadd as a patron sought and enemy feared, / From the abundance of praise, you are its first recipient.The Taghlib poet al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq used the term in a similar way, to boast of the supremacy of his own clan:All people of Maʿadd have their tribes / And each have their safe havens. / But we have no mountain strongholds, / Only swords of formidable repute.For some poets, it was a "disgrace" not to descend from either Ma'add or Adnan and Ma'add's glory alone outweighed the rest of that of the history of Arabia. Some poems imply that the Ma'add tribe were the vast majority of pre-Islamic Arabs.

bio: Ma'bad bin 'Abbad b Qushayr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ma'bad bin 'Abbad bin Qushayr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early decades of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam and became one of the Sahaba, the term used to describe those who personally knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad.

Ma'bad is historically recognized as a "Companion of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and involved around 300 Muslim fighters against a larger Meccan army. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment.

Based in Medina, Ma'bad would have been part of the growing Muslim community that formed around the Prophet after the Hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. Medina served as the center of the early Islamic state, where the fundamental principles of Islamic governance and society were established. As a resident companion, Ma'bad would have witnessed the development of Islamic law, community structures, and the expansion of the faith throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

The companions of the Prophet, including Ma'bad, played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings after Muhammad's death in 632 CE. They served as the primary sources for the hadith literature, which records the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet, and were instrumental in the early expansion of Islam beyond Arabia.

Ma'bad bin 'Abbad bin Qushayr died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph. His life spanned the critical period of Islam's emergence and initial establishment, making him a witness to the religion's foundational era. While specific details of his individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in historical sources, his status as a companion places him among the foundational generation of Muslims who helped establish and spread the faith.

bio: Ma'bad bin Qays b Sakhr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ma'bad bin Qays bin Sakhr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Islamic community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Ma'bad is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as it was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the town of Badr, located between Mecca and Medina, and involved approximately 300 Muslim fighters facing a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory at Badr was considered a turning point that helped establish the credibility and strength of the early Islamic state.

As a Sahabi, or Companion of the Prophet, Ma'bad belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct personal contact with Muhammad and accepted Islam during his lifetime. This status holds special reverence in Islamic tradition, as the Companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations. Their accounts and testimonies form a crucial foundation for Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and historical understanding.

Ma'bad lived during a period of rapid expansion and consolidation of Islamic influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Following the Battle of Badr, he would have witnessed the continued conflicts between the Muslim community and various Arabian tribes, the eventual conquest of Mecca, and the unification of much of Arabia under Islamic rule before the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

He died in 634 CE during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following the Prophet's death when the Islamic community was led by the first four caliphs. This was a time of significant territorial expansion as Islamic armies began their conquests beyond the Arabian Peninsula into the Byzantine and Sassanian territories.

While specific details about Ma'bad's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his recognition as a Companion places him among the foundational figures of early Islamic history who helped establish and preserve the religious and social framework of the Muslim community.

bio: Ma'mar bin 'Abdullah (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Ma'mar ibn Abd Allah ibn Nadla was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Adi ibn Ka'b clan of Quraysh. Ali ibn al-Madini, cited by Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir, gave his father's name as Nafi' ibn Nadla, and several authors also call him Ma'mar ibn Abi Ma'mar. Ibn Sa'd reports that he accepted Islam early in Mecca and emigrated to Abyssinia in the second migration. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir say his emigration to Medina came late; Ibn al-Athir and Abu Nu'aym place his arrival with the people of the two ships from Abyssinia. Ibn Sa'd notes that some reports say he met the Prophet at al-Hudaybiyya, and that accounts differ on this point. Ibn al-Athir and Abu Nu'aym report that he shaved the Prophet's head at the Farewell Pilgrimage, after the stoning of Jamrat al-Aqaba and the sacrifice; Ibn Hibban and Ibn Sa'd say instead that he combed the Prophet's hair there, and Ibn Sa'd also has him shaving it at the Umrat al-Qada. Abu Nu'aym records that the Prophet sent him to announce at Mina that the days of Tashriq are days of eating and drinking. His best-known report is the saying "None hoards except a sinner", transmitted from him by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab; when Sa'id was asked about his own hoarding, he answered that Ma'mar had hoarded too. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir say he lived a long life and was counted among the people of Medina. No death date is given in the sources consulted.

bio: Ma'mar bin al-Harith (c. 594–646 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Ma'mar ibn al-Harith ibn Qays ibn Adi ibn Sa'd ibn Sahm was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Sahm clan of Quraysh. Ibn al-Athir, in Usd al-Ghaba, counts him among those who emigrated to Abyssinia, citing Ibn Ishaq's list of the emigrants of Banu Sahm. Ibn Abd al-Barr, in al-Isti'ab, says he made that emigration together with his brother Bishr ibn al-Harith. Both entries are brief and give no battles, dates or place of death for him.

bio: Ma'mar bin Harith bin Ma'mar (c. 594–646 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ma'mar bin Harith bin Ma'mar was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived from approximately 594 to 646 CE. Born in the Arabian Peninsula during the pre-Islamic period, he became one of the early converts to Islam and was based in Mecca during the formative years of the Muslim community.

Ma'mar is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr in 622 CE, which was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. This battle holds significant importance in Islamic history as it established the Muslims as a formidable force and marked a turning point in their struggle for survival and expansion. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are given special recognition in Islamic tradition and are referred to as the "Companions of Badr."

As a companion of the Prophet, Ma'mar would have been among the early Muslims who experienced the initial revelations of the Quran and witnessed the establishment of Islamic practices and community structures. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and traditions of Islam to subsequent generations.

Ma'mar is associated with the early ascetic tradition within Islam, suggesting that he may have been among those companions who emphasized spiritual discipline, simple living, and devotion to worship. The early ascetics were Muslims who focused on spiritual purification and often lived modest lifestyles, dedicating themselves to prayer, remembrance of God, and service to the community.

Living through the foundational period of Islam, Ma'mar witnessed the religion's expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula during the early Islamic conquests that began under the first caliphs following the Prophet's death in 632 CE. His death in 646 CE occurred during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, the third of the rightly-guided caliphs.

The significance of Ma'mar and other companions lies in their role as the first generation of Muslims who directly learned from and supported the Prophet Muhammad. They served as the primary sources for Islamic teachings, legal precedents, and historical accounts that would shape the development of Islamic civilization. Their experiences and testimonies formed the foundation upon which later Islamic scholarship, jurisprudence, and spiritual traditions were built.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Ma'mar bin Hazm ibn Zayd (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Ma'mar ibn Hazm ibn Zayd ibn Lawdhan was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu al-Najjar clan of the Khazraj, among the Ansar of Medina. He was the brother of Amr ibn Hazm; al-Baghawi thought Ma'mar was the younger of the two. Ibn al-Athir, in Usd al-Ghaba, records that he was present at the Pledge of al-Ridwan and at what followed it, and that he was one of the ten men whom Umar ibn al-Khattab sent to Basra with Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. Ibn al-Athir and Abu Nu'aym name him as the grandfather of Abu Tuwala, whom al-Baghawi identifies as Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Ma'mar, a judge in Medina. No date or place of death is given in the sources consulted.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Ma'mar ibn Hazm (Usd al-Ghaba, al-Baghawi Mu'jam al-Sahaba, Abu Nu'aym Ma'rifat al-Sahaba)

full: Abd Allah ibn Harun al-Rashid al-Ma'mun
primaryTitle: Founder of the House of Wisdom
titles: Amir al-Muminin · Al-Ma'mun
bio: Abd Allah ibn Harun al-Rashid al-Ma'mun (786–833) was a ruler of the Islamic Sciences tradition, based in Baghdad. Known as Founder of the House of Wisdom.
bio_full: Abu al-Abbas Abd Allah ibn Harun al-Ma'mun was the seventh Abbasid caliph, reigning from 813 to 833. He was born in Baghdad in September 786, the son of the caliph Harun al-Rashid and Marajil, a concubine from Badghis who died soon after his birth; Harun's wife Zubayda raised him. After Harun's death in 809, rivalry with his half-brother al-Amin turned into civil war. Al-Ma'mun's general Tahir ibn al-Husayn defeated al-Amin's army, besieged Baghdad, and took the city in 813; al-Amin was killed and al-Ma'mun became sole caliph. He governed from Merv in his early years. In 817 he named Ali al-Rida, the eighth Shia Imam, as his heir, and Hashimites in Baghdad responded by proclaiming Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi caliph. Al-Rida died in 818, and Shia sources hold al-Ma'mun responsible. According to al-Tabari, al-Ma'mun entered Baghdad in August 819. The House of Wisdom was established during his reign, and he supported its scholars and the translation of Greek works into Arabic, sending to Byzantium for manuscripts. He favoured Mu'tazili theology, accepted the doctrine that the Qur'an was created, and in 833 began the mihna, a test of officials and scholars in which Ahmad ibn Hanbal was among those persecuted. He campaigned in Anatolia against Byzantium in 830 and again in 832. He died on campaign near Tarsus on 9 August 833, and a tomb in the Tarsus Grand Mosque is reported to be his. His brother succeeded him as al-Mu'tasim.

bio: Ma'mur / 'Amr bin Abu Sarh (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ma'mur, also known as 'Amr ibn Abi Sarh, was a companion (sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early Muslims who accepted Islam during its initial spread in Mecca and the surrounding regions.

Ma'mur is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. The participants in this battle, known as the "Companions of Badr" or "Badriyyun," hold a special status in Islamic tradition due to their early commitment to the faith and their role in this pivotal moment.

As a sahaba, Ma'mur belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam to subsequent generations, making their historical significance extend far beyond their individual contributions.

The designation as being part of the "Early Ascetics" tradition suggests that Ma'mur may have been among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline and devotion, though specific details about his ascetic practices are not well-documented in the historical sources.

Ma'mur's life spanned a critical forty-year period that witnessed the birth of Islam, its initial struggles in Mecca, the migration to Medina, and the establishment of the first Islamic state. His death in 634 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death, placing him among those companions who experienced the transition from the prophetic period to the early caliphal era.

While detailed biographical information about Ma'mur's specific contributions beyond his participation in Badr is limited in the available historical sources, his inclusion among the sahaba marks him as part of the foundational generation that helped establish and spread Islam during its earliest and most crucial phase of development.

bio: Ma'n bin 'Adiy bin al-Jadd (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ma'n bin 'Adiy bin al-Jadd was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of Islamic history during the Prophet's lifetime.

Ma'n is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle, fought between the early Muslim community and the Meccan Quraysh tribe, is considered one of the most significant military encounters in early Islamic history. The Muslims' victory at Badr, despite being outnumbered, was viewed as a pivotal moment that helped establish the credibility and strength of the nascent Muslim community. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr held a special status among the companions and were highly regarded by later generations of Muslims.

As a companion based in Medina, Ma'n would have been part of the community that formed around the Prophet after the Hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. Medina served as the center of the early Muslim state, and the companions who lived there played crucial roles in supporting the Prophet's mission and helping to establish Islamic practices and governance.

The companions of the Prophet, known collectively as the Sahaba, are revered in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and learned Islamic teachings firsthand. Their testimonies and actions became important sources for understanding Islamic law, theology, and practice in later centuries.

Ma'n bin 'Adiy died in 634 CE, just two years after the death of Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. This timing places his death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph. This was a period of rapid expansion of Islamic rule beyond the Arabian Peninsula, though specific details about Ma'n's activities during this time are not well documented in available historical sources.

His recognition as a Companion of Badr ensures his place in Islamic historical memory as one of the early supporters who helped establish the Muslim community during its most vulnerable and formative years.

bio: Ma'qil bin al-Mundhir bin Sarh (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ma'qil bin al-Mundhir bin Sarh was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who resided in Medina, the city that became the center of the nascent Islamic community following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Ma'qil is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement, which took place near the town of Badr in the Hejaz region, involved approximately 300 Muslim fighters facing a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory at Badr was considered pivotal in establishing the credibility and strength of the early Islamic state.

The designation "Companion of Badr" carries special importance in Islamic historical tradition, as those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad in this battle are regarded as having demonstrated exceptional commitment to the faith during a crucial moment. The participants in Badr are often referenced in Islamic sources as examples of early devotion and sacrifice for the cause of Islam.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Ma'qil would have been part of the close circle of followers who directly interacted with Islam's founder during the religion's earliest years. The companions, known as Sahaba in Arabic, played essential roles in the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings, practices, and historical accounts.

Ma'qil's life span, from approximately 594 to 634 CE, encompassed the entire prophetic period of Muhammad's mission and extended into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. His death in 634 CE occurred during a period of rapid Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about Ma'qil's individual contributions or activities beyond his participation in Badr are not extensively documented in available historical sources, his inclusion among the recognized companions and his presence at this foundational battle mark him as one of the early supporters who helped establish the Islamic community during its most vulnerable and formative years in Medina.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Ma'qil bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Ma'qil ibn Maqrn al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE in the Hijaz region, he belonged to the Mazin tribe and became one of the Sahaba, the term used for those who personally knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime.

Ma'qil is historically significant as one of the participants in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, which took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This event occurred when the Prophet Muhammad and approximately 1,400 of his followers were prevented from performing pilgrimage to Mecca and instead pledged their loyalty under a tree. The Quran references this pledge in verse 48:18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those believers who pledged their allegiance. This makes Ma'qil part of a group specifically mentioned in Islamic scripture as having received divine approval for their commitment.

As a companion of the Prophet, Ma'qil would have been present during the formative years of the early Muslim community and witnessed key events in early Islamic history. The companions are collectively regarded as crucial transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices, serving as the primary sources for understanding the Prophet's traditions and sayings that would later be compiled into hadith literature.

Ma'qil died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate period that followed the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This places his death during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, when the rapidly expanding Muslim state was consolidating its control over the Arabian Peninsula and beginning its expansion into neighboring regions.

His inclusion among the participants of the Pledge of Ridwan marks him as one of the companions who demonstrated particular loyalty and commitment during a critical moment in early Islamic history. This event is remembered as a turning point that demonstrated the unity and resolve of the early Muslim community when faced with obstacles to their religious practices. While specific details about Ma'qil's individual contributions beyond his participation in this significant pledge are not extensively documented, his status as a companion places him among the foundational generation of Muslims whose experiences and testimonies helped shape the transmission of Islamic tradition to subsequent generations.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Ma'qil bin Yasar al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Ma'qil bin Yasar al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in the Arabian Peninsula during the early seventh century. Born around 600 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam and became part of the close circle of individuals known as the Sahaba, or Companions of the Prophet.

Ma'qil is historically recognized for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan (Bay'at al-Ridwan), a significant oath of allegiance taken by approximately 1,400 Muslims under a tree at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This event occurred when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers were prevented from performing pilgrimage to Mecca and rumors circulated that the Prophet's envoy had been killed. The pledge represented the companions' commitment to stand by Muhammad even unto death, and it holds special significance in Islamic history as it is referenced in the Quran (48:18), which speaks of God's pleasure with those who pledged their allegiance under the tree.

As a Sahaba, Ma'qil was positioned to witness and transmit the sayings, actions, and teachings of the Prophet Muhammad, making him part of the foundational generation for Islamic scholarship and hadith transmission. The companions served as the primary sources for preserving and passing down the Prophet's traditions to subsequent generations, forming the basis of hadith literature that would become central to Islamic jurisprudence and theology.

Ma'qil lived during the transformative period when Islam emerged and rapidly expanded across the Arabian Peninsula. His presence during key events like the Pledge of Ridwan places him among those who experienced firsthand the crucial moments that shaped early Islamic history. The companions who participated in this pledge were later regarded with particular reverence in Islamic tradition due to the Quranic acknowledgment of their commitment.

He died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, having witnessed both the prophetic period and the beginning of Islam's expansion beyond Arabia. His legacy remains tied to his status as a companion and his participation in one of the most significant pledges in Islamic history, contributing to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings for future generations.

full: Abu Mahfuz Ma'ruf ibn Firuz al-Karkhi al-Baghdadi
primaryTitle: Qutb Baghdad — Teacher of Sari al-Saqati
titles: Qutb Baghdad (Pole of Baghdad) · Spiritual grandfather of Junayd through Sari al-Saqati
bio: Marouf bin Fayrouz Al-Karkhi is one of the great figures in Baghdad. He was nicknamed Abu Mahfouz. He was famous for his asceticism, piety, and piety. He was very generous and tolerant, and people narrated many miracles about him. Ibn al-Jawzi spent a lot of time talking about Karakhi’s Karamat, in his famous book “Sifat al-Safwa.”
bio_full:
Ma'ruf ibn Firuz al-Karkhi (Persian: معروف بن فيروز الكرخي, romanized: Maʿrūf ibn Fīrūz al-Karkhī) was a Sufi Muslim saint.

Maruf was born in the district of Wasit or Karkh in Baghdad. According to some sources, he is of Mandaean origin. His father's name was Firuz, which suggests that he was of Persian origin. Attar narrates in his Memorial of the Saints that Maruf converted to Islam at a young age at the hands of Ali al-Ridha after rejecting all forms of polytheism. Tradition recounts that he immediately went and told his father and mother, who rejoiced at his decision and became Muslims themselves. After accepting Islam, Maruf became a student of Dawud al-Ta'i, and underwent a severe trial of his discipleship. Maruf, however, remained steadfast and proved himself so devout that his righteousness became locally famous.

Maruf is also known to have a close relationship with Ahmad ibn Hanbal, in which ibn Hanbal is reported to have said "True knowledge is only that which Ma‘ruf has achieved.”

In Sufism, those of the order of Marufi are those connected to Maruf Karkhi. Maruf thus forms a penultimate link in what is known as the Golden Chain, the initiation line which forms an unbroken chain to Muhammad. Maruf, being the disciple of Ali al-Ridha, formed part of that lineage, while at the same time maintaining the teachings of his master Dawud Ta'i and thus being his successor as well. Sufis venerate Maruf highly for the multiple spiritual chains which interlock in his teachings.

bio: Mahabba bint ar-Rabi' ibn 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Mahabba bint ar-Rabi' ibn 'Amr was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Mahabba belonged to the community that welcomed Muhammad and his followers to Medina, marking a pivotal moment in Islamic history. The Ansar played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community and providing the foundation for Islam's growth beyond its birthplace in Mecca. Her presence among this group indicates she was witness to the formative years of the Islamic community in Medina.

The companions of the Prophet Muhammad hold special significance in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with him and received Islamic teachings firsthand. Female companions like Mahabba were part of the early Muslim society that developed during the Prophet's lifetime, contributing to the community's social and religious fabric.

Living in Medina during the early decades of Islam, Mahabba would have experienced the establishment of Islamic practices, the development of the Muslim community's social structure, and the challenges faced by the early believers. Her lifetime spanned the crucial period from before the advent of Islam through its establishment as a major religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula.

The recognition of Mahabba as a companion reflects the documented presence and participation of women in the early Islamic community. Female companions are acknowledged in Islamic historical sources for their roles in supporting and participating in the developing Muslim society, though specific details about individual women's contributions often remain limited in the historical record.

Mahabba died around 635 CE, during the early period of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs following the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. Her life encompassed the entire Prophetic period and the beginning of Islam's spread beyond Arabia, making her a witness to one of the most significant religious and historical transformations in world history. As one of the documented female companions, she represents the women who were part of Islam's foundational generation.

bio: Maharab bin Dithar (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Arabia. Known as Among the First Judges of Islam.
bio_full:
Maharab bin Dithar was a companion (sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in 7th-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, he witnessed and participated in the emergence of the Islamic community during its foundational decades.

As one of the companions of Prophet Muhammad, Maharab bin Dithar was among those early Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet and learned Islamic teachings firsthand. This proximity to the source of Islamic revelation and practice positioned him as an important figure in the transmission of religious knowledge to subsequent generations.

Maharab bin Dithar is historically recognized for his role in early Islamic jurisprudence, earning recognition as one of the first judges in the Muslim community. During the rapid expansion of Islam following the Prophet's death in 632 CE, there was an urgent need for qualified individuals who could apply Islamic law and settle disputes according to Islamic principles. His appointment as a judge reflects the trust placed in his understanding of Islamic teachings and his ability to make sound legal decisions.

The role of early Islamic judges was crucial in establishing legal precedents and developing the framework of Islamic jurisprudence that would continue to evolve over centuries. These early jurists had to interpret Quranic principles and the Prophet's teachings (Sunnah) to address practical legal questions facing the growing Muslim community.

Maharab bin Dithar died in 635 CE, just three years after the Prophet Muhammad's death, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr, and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate. His relatively short life span meant that his judicial career occurred during a critical transitional period when the Muslim community was expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula and establishing administrative and legal systems.

His significance to Islamic history lies in his contribution to the early development of Islamic legal institutions. As one of the first judges appointed in the Islamic community, he helped establish the foundations of Islamic jurisprudence that would later be systematized by subsequent generations of Islamic scholars and jurists. His work represented an important bridge between the direct teachings of Prophet Muhammad and the formal legal structures that would govern Islamic societies.

bio: Mahlā'īl ibn Qaynān (legendary–legendary) was a founding figure, based in Mesopotamia. Known as Ancestor of Prophet Muhammad. The sources record 2 teachers.
bio_full:
Mahlā'īl ibn Qaynān is a figure mentioned in Islamic genealogical traditions as part of the ancestral lineage tracing back to the Prophet Muhammad. According to traditional Islamic historical sources, he lived in ancient Mesopotamia during the pre-Islamic period, with dates placing him in the fourth millennium BCE, though these chronological details reflect traditional accounts rather than independently verified historical records.

The name Mahlā'īl appears in various forms across different Arabic sources, reflecting the complex transmission of early genealogical information through oral and written traditions. Islamic historians and genealogists have identified him as a significant link in the chain of descent that ultimately leads to the Prophet Muhammad, making him an important figure in traditional Islamic understanding of prophetic ancestry.

Historical sources indicate that Mahlā'īl had connections to religious or scholarly instruction, with records mentioning two teachers associated with his name, though specific details about these educational relationships are not extensively documented in surviving sources. This suggests he may have been part of early traditions of knowledge transmission in ancient Mesopotamian society.

The geographical association with Mesopotamia places Mahlā'īl within one of the world's earliest centers of civilization, a region that holds particular significance in Islamic historical consciousness as the setting for many prophetic narratives and early human history according to Islamic tradition. This location aligns with broader Islamic historical accounts that trace important ancestral figures to the fertile river valleys of the ancient Near East.

In the context of Islamic genealogical studies, figures like Mahlā'īl represent the scholarly effort to preserve and document ancestral connections across vast spans of time. While the specific biographical details about his life and activities remain limited in historical sources, his inclusion in genealogical records demonstrates the importance placed by Islamic scholars on maintaining comprehensive ancestral documentation.

The significance of Mahlā'īl ibn Qaynān lies primarily in his position within traditional Islamic genealogical frameworks rather than in documented historical achievements or religious teachings. His name serves as one link in the extensive chain of ancestry that Islamic historians have constructed to connect the Prophet Muhammad with earlier generations, reflecting the broader Islamic emphasis on understanding prophetic heritage and maintaining historical continuity across millennia.

bio: Mahmiya bin al-Jaza (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Mahmiya bin al-Jaza was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 593 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca during a time when the nascent Muslim community faced significant persecution from the ruling Quraysh tribe.

Mahmiya is primarily known for his participation in the emigration to Abyssinia, one of the most significant events in early Islamic history. When the persecution of Muslims in Mecca intensified, the Prophet Muhammad advised a group of his followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, present-day Ethiopia, around 615 CE. This migration, known as the Hijra to Abyssinia, represented the first major exodus of Muslims from their homeland and demonstrated the early community's resilience in the face of adversity.

The emigrants to Abyssinia, including Mahmiya, found protection under the rule of the Negus, the Christian king of Abyssinia, who refused demands from Meccan emissaries to return the Muslim refugees. This episode highlighted the early connections between Islam and Christianity and showcased the diplomatic skills of the Muslim community in securing sanctuary abroad.

As one of the early ascetics within Islamic tradition, Mahmiya likely practiced forms of spiritual discipline and devotion that characterized some of the earliest Muslim converts. The early ascetic tradition emphasized simplicity, devotion, and detachment from worldly concerns, values that would later influence various forms of Islamic spirituality.

Mahmiya's life span, ending around 633 CE, coincided with some of the most crucial developments in Islamic history, including the Hijra to Medina in 622 CE and the subsequent expansion of the Muslim community. His status as a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, places him among the revered first generation of Muslims whose experiences and testimonies were considered foundational to Islamic tradition.

The emigration to Abyssinia, in which Mahmiya participated, established important precedents for Muslim communities facing persecution and demonstrated the early Islamic principle of seeking refuge when religious practice was threatened. This event remains significant in Islamic historical memory as an example of the challenges faced by the earliest Muslim community and their strategies for survival and preservation of their faith.

full: Mahmud ibn al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Kashgari
primaryTitle: Father of Turkic Linguistics — Diwan Lughat al-Turk
titles: al-Kashgari — The Kashgarian
bio: Mahmoud bin Al-Hussein bin Muhammad Al-Kashgari is a Turkish scholar and historian from the city of Kashgar, one of the scholars of the eleventh century. He specialized in the genealogies of the Turks and their languages. He wrote his books in Arabic, including “The Diwan of the Languages ​​of the Turks,” printed in Astana in 3 volumes in the year 1333 AH. He was a Muslim from the Qarluq Turks and died in the year 1102 AD.
bio_full:
Mahmud ibn Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Kashgari was an 11th-century Kara-Khanid scholar and lexicographer of the Turkic languages from Kashgar.
His father, Husayn, was the mayor of Barsgan, a town in the southeastern part of the lake of Issyk-Kul (nowadays village of Barskoon in Northern Kyrgyzstan's Issyk-Kul Region) and related to the ruling dynasty of Kara-Khanid Khanate. Around 1057 C.E., Mahmud al-Kashgari became a political refugee, before settling down in Baghdad.

Work

Al-Kashgari studied the Turkic languages of his time and in Baghdad, he compiled the first comprehensive dictionary of Turkic languages, the Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk (English: "Compendium of the languages of the Turks") in 1072–74. It was intended for use by the Abbasid Caliphate, the new Arab allies of the Turks. Mahmud Kashgari's comprehensive dictionary, later edited by the Turkish historian, Ali Amiri, contains specimens of old Turkic poetry in the typical form of quatrains (Persio-Arabic رباعیات, rubā'iyāt; Turkish: dörtlük), representing all the principal genres: epic, pastoral, didactic, lyric and elegiac. His book also included the first known map of the areas inhabited by Turkic peoples. This map is housed at the National Library in Istanbul.
Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk also contains linguistic data about multiple Turkic dialects that may have been gathered from merchants and others involved in trade along routes that travelled through Transoxiana. The origin of the compiled information is not known. Scholars believe it is likely that Kashgari would have gathered most of the content about Oguz-Turkmen from Oguz tribes in Khorasan since he himself was a student in Seljuk Baghdad, but it is possible that some of this material could have come from early Turkmen. Other scholars believe that the compendium was based on the Turkiyya language of the Chigil tribe in the Kara-Khanid confederation. However, scholars have not yet come to a settled conclusion.

Al-Kashgari advocated monolingualism and the linguistic purism of the Turkic languages and held a belief in the superiority of nomadic people (the Turkic tribes had traditionally been nomads) over urban populations. Most of his Turkic-speaking contemporaries were bilingual in New Persian, which was then the urban and literary language of Central Asia.The most elegant of the dialects belongs to those who know only one language, who do not mix with Persians and who do not customarily settle in other lands. Those who have two languages and who mix with the populace of the cities have a certain slurring in their utterances.
Even so, Kashgari praised the dialect spoken by the bilingual Uyghurs as "pure" and "most correct" on par with those of Turkic monolinguals.
Al-Kashgari cautioned against the assimilation of the nomadic way of life into a sedentary culture. He recorded a Turkic proverb that warned, “Just as the effectiveness of a warrior is diminished when his sword begins to rust, so too does the flesh of a Turk begin to rot when he assumes the lifestyle of an Iranian.” 

Death
Some researchers think that Mahmud al-Kashgari died in 1102 at the age of 97 in Upal, a small city southwest of Kashgar and was buried there. There is now a mausoleum erected on his gravesite. But some modern authors reject this assertion, saying that the date of his death is just unknown.

Legacy
He is claimed by Uyghur, Kyrgyz and Uzbek nationalists as part of their respective ethnic groups.
An oriental study university, situated in the capital city of Bishkek in post-Soviet Kyrgyzstan, was named after Makhmud Kashghari, in the 1990s.
UNESCO declared 2008 the Year of Mahmud al-Kashgari.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Mahmoud bin Maslama, a companion of the Ansar from Banu Haritha bin Al-Harith from Aws. He witnessed with the Prophet Muhammad the battles of Uhud, Khandaq, and Khaybar, and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. He was killed at Fort Na’im in the Battle of Khaybar, where a millstone fell from the top of the fort on him, shattering the egg of his head, and the skin of his forehead fell on his face. He died three days later, and was buried in Al-Raja’ with Aamer ibn Al-Akwa’ in one grave. He had two sons, a mother Amr and a mother Saad, and their mother was Umamah bint Bishr. Umm Manzur and Hind, whose mother was Hind bint Qais bin Al-Quraym.
bio_full: Mahmud ibn Maslama was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina and the brother of Muhammad ibn Maslama. Ibn Sa'd, as quoted by al-Baghawi, gives his lineage as Mahmud ibn Maslama ibn Khalid ibn Adi ibn Majda'a ibn Haritha, placing him in the Banu Haritha clan. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir record that he fought at Uhud, the Trench and Khaybar; Ibn Sa'd and Abu Nu'aym add that he was present at al-Hudaybiyya. At Khaybar, according to Ibn Abd al-Barr, Marhab dropped a millstone on him from the fort and it struck his head. He died three days later. Ibn al-Athir dates this to the year 6 AH and records that he was buried at al-Raji' in a single grave with Amir ibn al-Akwa'. Ibn Sa'd notes that on the day Mahmud died his brother Muhammad ibn Maslama killed Marhab. Ibn Abd al-Barr records that Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated from him.

full: Mahmud ibn Sabuktigin Yamin al-Dawla al-Ghaznawi
titles: Sultan al-Ghazi · Yamin al-Dawla
bio: Yamin of the State Abu al-Qasim Mahmoud bin Subuktikin al-Ghaznawi, known as Mahmoud al-Ghaznawi, was the ruler of the Ghaznavid state from 998 AD to 1030 AD during the time of the Abbasid Caliphate. His name in Turkish is Yemin el-Devlet Mahmut, which means the right of the state Mahmoud. In Persian, his name is Abu al-Qasim Mahmoud bin Subuktikin.
bio_full:
Abu al-Qasim Mahmud ibn Sabuktigin (Persian: ابوالقاسم محمود بن سبکتگین, romanized: Abu al-Qāṣim Maḥmūd ibn Sabuktigīn; 2 October 971 – 30 April 1030), usually known as Mahmud of Ghazni or Mahmud Ghaznavi (محمود غزنوی), was Sultan of the Ghaznavid Empire, ruling from 998 to 1030. 
Widely reputed to be undefeated throughout his entire career, Mahmud was known by his honorific title Yamin al-Dawla (یمین‌ الدوله, lit. 'Right Hand of the State'). At the time of his death, his kingdom had been transformed into an extensive military empire, which extended from present-day northwestern Iran proper to the Punjab in the Indian subcontinent, Khwarazm in Transoxiana.
Highly persianized, Mahmud continued the bureaucratic, political, and cultural customs of his predecessors, the Samanids. He established the ground for a future Persianate state in Punjab, particularly centered on Lahore, a city he conquered. His capital of Ghazni evolved into a significant cultural, commercial, and intellectual centre in the Islamic world, almost rivalling the important city of Baghdad. The capital appealed to many prominent figures, such as al-Biruni and Ferdowsi.
Mahmud ascended the throne at the age of 27 upon his father's death, albeit after a brief war of succession with his brother Ismail. He was the first ruler to hold the title Sultan ("authority"), signifying the extent of his power while at the same time preserving an ideological link to the suzerainty of the Abbasid Caliphs. In the thirty-two years of his reign, he made thirty-five major and eleven minor campaigns.

Birth and background
Mahmud was born in the town of Ghazni in the region of Zabulistan (in present-day Afghanistan) on 2 October 971. His father, Sabuktigin, was a Turkic slave commander who laid foundations to the Ghaznavid dynasty in Ghazni in 977, which he ruled as a subordinate of the Samanids, who ruled Khorasan and Transoxiana. Mahmud's mother was a local woman of possible Iranian descent from a landowning aristocrat family in the region of Zabulistan, and he is therefore known in some sources as Mahmud-i Zavuli ("Mahmud from Zabulistan"). Not much about Mahmud's early life is known, other than that he was a school-mate and foster brother of Ahmad Maymandi, a Persian native of Zabulistan.

Creed and religious alignment
Originally Sultan Mahmud was a follower of the Hanafi school of law, but shortly after his accession to the throne he showed inclination towards the Karramite sect and ultimately changed over to the Shafi'i school of law. Although early in his reign Sultan Mahmud showed sympathies with the Karramiyya sect—evidenced by reports that he “would get angry for the Karramiyya” (yaghḍabu lil-Karramiyya). Following Mahmud's death Ghaznavid poet Farrukhi said the heretics can now sleep peacefully:

"Alas and alack, the Qarmatiyan can now rejoice! They will be secure against death by stoning or the gallows."
Mohammad Habib writes, according to contemporary gossip Mahmud had disbelief in the Day of Judgment and in the Hadith "that the scholars (ulama) are the successors of the prophets." He also suspicioned that Subuktigin was not his real father. Mahmud like other Muslim sovereigns paid visits to the renown Muslim saints. Amongst them Abu al-Hassan al-Kharaqani personally influenced him. According to one account, while returning to his palace one night, the Sultan ordered his golden lamp to be given to a poor student whom he saw reading in the light of a shop. That night the prophet Muhammad appeared to him in a dream and said, "Son of Subuktigin, may God honour thee in both the worlds as thou hast honoured my successor!" The Sultan's three doubts were thus removed. 
Afterward, Mahmud came under the influence of the renowned scholar Abu Bakr 'Abdallah ibn Aḥmad al-Qaffal al-Marwazi, Abu Bakr al-Qaffal al-Marwazi a devout follower of the Ash'ari theological school and the Shafi'i madhhab. This shift reflected a broader move within the Ghaznavid court to align with Sunni orthodoxy, distancing itself from anthropomorphic sects like the Karramiyya and from Isma'ili theology. Mahmud's theological stance is described by Al-Dhahabi as that of an Athari in creed and Shafi'i in jurisprudence. He mentioned Mahmud as someone who inclined towards the Athar, quote:

"The Sultan was inclined towards the Athar, except that he was from the Karamiyya."
This quotation reflects his earlier theological position on creed, prior to his later shift towards the Shafi'i Athari view. Following his shift in creed, he was challenged by the Ash'ari theologian Ibn Furak, who contended that describing God as ‘above’ implied also describing Him as ‘below. He answered him by saying, quote:

Abu ʿAlī ibn al-Bannāʾ said: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Akbarī narrated that he heard Abū Masʿūd Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Bajalī say: Ibn Fawrak entered upon Sultan Maḥmūd and said: "It is not permissible to describe God as being above, because that would necessarily entail describing Him as being below. Whoever it is permissible for Him to have an above, it is permissible for Him to have a below." The Sultan replied: "I did not describe Him so that it would be necessary for me to do so. Rather, He described Himself."
It is reported from Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah in his book Bayan Talbis al-Jahmiyyah that Mahmud used to curse the People of Innovation (Ahl al-Bid'ah), and that among them were the Ash'ariyyah. Quote:

“Sultan Mahmud ibn Sabuktigin relied on something similar to this in his kingdom, and he added to it by ordering the people of heresy to be cursed from the pulpits: so the Jahmites were cursed, and the Rafidis and the Haruriyya and the Mu'tazila and the Qadarites, and also the Ash'ariyya were cursed”
He knew Quran by heart and was familiar with Muslim law and tradition. According to Ghaznavid author Abu'l-Fadl Bayhaqi and poet Farrukhi Sistani, the sultan was punctilious in the performance of his religious duties and offered the regular prayers and read the Quran. In the month Ramadan, 2.5% Zakat was collected and spent on the poor. Mahmud did not tolerate any deviation in Muslim subjects. Censorship was applied and an officer was appointed to punish heresy or delinquency. The followers of the Isma'ili Shia Qaramatians and Batini sects were suppressed in the empire. They were captured and imprisoned if they did not recant they were often executed.
Mughal emperor Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) mentioned Mahmud as a sultan who suppressed heresy in his kingdom.

“Sultan Mahmud, may God forgive his crimes did not allow half hearted religious men and heretics to enter his court, nay not even his kingdom, so that other people might not be misled by seeing such persons in the form of the dervish, and they themselves might have no power to mislead others.”

Family
Mahmud married the daughter of Abu'l Haret Ahmad, and they had twin sons, Mohammad and Ma'sud, who succeeded him one after the other; his grandson by Mas'ud, Maw'dud Ghaznavi, also later became ruler of the empire. In 999, Mahmud married Kara-khanid ruler Ilig Khan's daughter. In December 999, Mahmud sent his representatives to Uzgand, capital of Nasr Illig to escort Khan's daughter to Mahmud's palace. The marriage was sealed in 1000 AD. He also had three brothers viz. Isma'il, his initial rival for the throne; Abu'l-Muzaffar Nasr, the long-serving military commander and governor; and Abu Ya'qüb Yusuf, the youngest, who eventually succeeded Nasr in his prestigious roles.
According to Mirat-i-Masudi ("Mirror of Masud"), a Persian-language hagiography written by Abdur Rahman Chishti in the 1620s, Mahmud's sister, Sitr-e-Mu'alla, was purportedly married to Dawood bin Ataullah Alavi, also known as Gazi Saiyyed Salar Sahu, whose son was Ghazi Saiyyad Salar Masud. Mahmud's companion was a Georgian slave, Malik Ayaz, about whom poems and stories have been told.

full: Shaykh Sa'd al-Din Mahmud al-Shabistari al-Tabrizi
titles: Imam of Persian Sufi Poetry · Arif al-Bilad (Gnostic of the Lands)
bio: Shaykh Sa'd al-Din Mahmud al-Shabistari al-Tabrizi (1288–1340) was a poet of the Akbarian tradition, based in Tabriz. Known as Imam of Persian Sufi Poetry.
bio_full:
Mahmoud Shabestari or Mahmūd Shabestarī (Persian: محمود شبستری‎; 1288–1340) is one of the most celebrated Persian Sufi poets of the 14th century.

Shabestari was born in the town of Shabestar near Tabriz in 1288 (687 AH), where he received his education. He became deeply versed in the symbolic terminology of Ibn Arabi. He wrote during a period of Mongol invasions.

His most famous work is a mystic text called The Secret Rose Garden (Gulshan-i Rāz) written about 1311 in rhyming couplets (Mathnawi). This poem was written in response to fifteen queries concerning Sufi metaphysics posed to "the Sufi literati of Tabriz" by Rukh Al Din Amir Husayn Harawi (d. 1318). It was also the main reference used by François Bernier when explaining Sufism to his European friends (in: Lettre sur le Quietisme des Indes; 1688)

Other works include The Book of Felicity (Sa'adat-nāma) and The Truth of Certainty about the Knowledge of the Lord of the Worlds (Ḥaqq al-yaqīn fi ma'rifat rabb al-'alamīn. The former is regarded as a relatively unknown poetic masterpiece written in khafif meter, while the latter is his lone work of prose.
