full: Sayyid Jalal al-Din al-Bukhari 'Makhdum Jahaniyan Jahangasht'
primaryTitle: Jahangasht — World Traveller of Uch Sharif
titles: Makhdum Jahaniyan (Master of the World) · Jahangasht (World Traveller) · Patron of Uch Sharif
bio: Sayyid Jalal al-Din al-Bukhari 'Makhdum Jahaniyan Jahangasht' (1307–1384) was a mystic of the Suhrawardiyya tradition, based in Uch Sharif. Known as Jahangasht — World Traveller of Uch Sharif.
bio_full:
Sayyid Jalal al-Din al-Bukhari, known as Makhdum Jahaniyan Jahangasht, was a prominent Sufi mystic who lived from 1307 to 1384. He belonged to the Suhrawardiyya order, one of the major Sufi traditions that emerged in the medieval Islamic world. His epithet "Jahangasht" means "World Traveller," reflecting his extensive journeys, while he was based primarily in Uch Sharif, located in present-day Pakistan.

The Suhrawardiyya order, to which Makhdum Jahaniyan belonged, was founded by Abu al-Najib al-Suhrawardi in the twelfth century and later developed by his nephew Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi. This Sufi tradition emphasized the importance of spiritual guidance, contemplation, and adherence to Islamic law alongside mystical practice. The order played a significant role in spreading Islamic spirituality across various regions of the Muslim world.

Uch Sharif, where Makhdum Jahaniyan was based, served as an important center of Islamic learning and Sufi activity in the Indian subcontinent during the medieval period. The city attracted scholars, mystics, and students from across the region, contributing to the intellectual and spiritual life of medieval Islamic civilization.

As a mystic of the fourteenth century, Makhdum Jahaniyan lived during a period of significant political and cultural change in the Islamic world. This era saw the consolidation of various Muslim dynasties across different regions, the continued expansion of Islamic influence, and the flourishing of Sufi orders as vehicles for both spiritual development and social organization.

The designation "Makhdum," meaning "master" or "served one," indicates the respect and recognition he received from his contemporaries and followers. This title was commonly used for revered religious figures and scholars in the Indian subcontinent, suggesting his established position within the religious hierarchy of his time.

Makhdum Jahaniyan's significance lies in his role within the broader network of Suhrawardiyya mystics who contributed to the spiritual and cultural landscape of medieval Islamic civilization. His presence in Uch Sharif and his travels, as suggested by his epithet, would have facilitated the transmission of Sufi teachings and practices across different communities and regions during the fourteenth century.

full: Makhul ibn Abi Muslim al-Dimashqi al-Hazali
primaryTitle: Faqih al-Sham — Chief Jurist of Syria
titles: Faqih al-Sham · Chief Mujtahid of Syria
bio: Makhul ibn Abi Muslim al-Dimashqi al-Hazali (c. 660–734) was a historical figure of the Islamic Jurisprudence tradition, based in Damascus. Known as Faqih al-Sham — Chief Jurist of Syria.
bio_full:
Makhul ibn Abi Muslim al-Dimashqi al-Hazali was a prominent Islamic jurist and scholar who lived from approximately 660 to 734 CE. He belonged to the generation known as the Tabi'un, the successors who followed the Companions of Prophet Muhammad, and established himself as one of the most respected legal authorities of his time in the Levantine region.

Based in Damascus during the early Umayyad period, Makhul earned the distinguished title "Faqih al-Sham," meaning the Chief Jurist of Syria. This recognition reflected his exceptional knowledge of Islamic law and his role as the leading legal scholar in the region that encompassed modern-day Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and Palestine. Damascus, as the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate, served as a major center of Islamic learning, and Makhul's presence there positioned him at the heart of legal and scholarly discourse.

As a member of the Tabi'un generation, Makhul played a crucial role in the early development and systematization of Islamic jurisprudence. This generation was particularly significant because they served as a vital link between the direct teachings of the Prophet's Companions and the later, more formalized schools of Islamic law. Their work helped preserve and transmit Islamic legal principles during a formative period of the religion's development.

Makhul's expertise in Islamic jurisprudence made him a sought-after authority for legal opinions and religious guidance. His scholarly work contributed to the broader intellectual tradition that would eventually give rise to the major schools of Islamic legal thought. The fact that he was recognized as the foremost jurist of his region indicates both his deep knowledge of Islamic sources and his ability to apply legal principles to the practical needs of the Muslim community.

Living during the late seventh and early eighth centuries, Makhul witnessed significant political and social changes within the Islamic world. His scholarship helped provide legal continuity and guidance during this dynamic period of Islamic expansion and consolidation. His contributions to Islamic jurisprudence represent an important chapter in the development of Islamic legal tradition, bridging the gap between the earliest generations of Muslims and the more systematic legal scholarship that would follow in subsequent centuries.

full: Malcolm Little, later El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz
primaryTitle: El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz — Voice of Black Muslim America
titles: El-Ḥājj Mālik al-Shabbāz
bio: Malcolm For his fans: Malcolm As for his enemies and those who hate him, they accuse him of being an advocate of racism, black supremacy, and violence. Malcolm X has been described as one of the greatest and most influential African Americans in history.
bio_full:
Malcolm X (born Malcolm Little, later el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz; May 19, 1925 – February 21, 1965) was an African American revolutionary and Black nationalist leader who rose from a background of poverty, family disruption, and criminal activity to a prominent figure during the civil rights movement until his assassination in 1965. He discovered the religious organization the Nation of Islam while in prison and served as its spokesperson from 1952 until 1964. He was also a vocal advocate for Black empowerment and the promotion of Islam within the African American community. A controversial figure accused of preaching violence, Malcolm X is also a celebrated figure with Black people and Muslims worldwide for his pursuit of racial justice.
Malcolm spent his adolescence living in a series of foster homes and with various relatives, after his father's death and his mother's hospitalization. In 1946 he was sentenced to eight to ten years in prison for larceny and burglary. In prison, he joined the Nation of Islam, adopting the name Malcolm X to symbolize his unknown African ancestral surname while discarding "the white slavemaster name of 'Little'", and after his parole in 1952, he quickly became one of the organization's most influential leaders. He was the public face of the organization for 12 years, advocating black empowerment and separation of Black and white Americans, as well as criticizing Martin Luther King Jr. and the mainstream civil rights movement for its emphasis on non-violence and racial integration. Malcolm X also expressed pride in some of the Nation's social welfare achievements, such as its free drug rehabilitation program. From the 1950s onward, Malcolm X was subjected to surveillance by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
In the 1960s, Malcolm X began to grow disillusioned with the Nation of Islam, as well as with its leader, Elijah Muhammad. He subsequently embraced Sunni Islam and the civil rights movement after completing the Hajj to Mecca and became known as "el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz", which roughly translates to "The Pilgrim Malcolm the Patriarch". After a brief period of travel across Africa, he publicly renounced the Nation of Islam and founded the Islamic MMI and the Pan-African Organization of Afro-American Unity (OAAU). Throughout 1964, his conflict with the Nation of Islam intensified, and he was repeatedly sent death threats. On February 21, 1965, he was assassinated in New York City. Three Nation members were charged with the murder and given indeterminate life sentences. In 2021, two of the convictions were vacated. Speculation about the assassination and whether it was conceived or aided by leading or additional members of the Nation, or with law enforcement agencies, has persisted for decades.
He was posthumously honored with Malcolm X Day, on which he is commemorated in various cities across the United States. Hundreds of streets and schools in the US have been renamed in his honor, while the Audubon Ballroom, the site of his assassination, was partly redeveloped in 2005 to accommodate the Malcolm X and Dr. Betty Shabazz Memorial and Educational Center. His autobiography, on which he collaborated with Alex Haley, was published posthumously in 1965.

Early years

Childhood
Malcolm Little was born May 19, 1925, at University Hospital in Omaha, Nebraska. He was the fourth of seven children of Louise Little (née Langdon), born in Grenada and Reverend Earl Little, born in Reynolds, Georgia.Earl was an outspoken Baptist minister and both he and Louise, a seamstress, were admirers of Pan-African activist Marcus Garvey. Malcolm had ten siblings; older siblings were Wilfred, Hilda and Philbert and his younger siblings were Reginald, Wesley, Yvonne (1929-2003), and Robert. Malcolm also had older half-siblings from his father's first marriage, Ella (1914-1996), Mary and Earl Jr. Earl was the local leader of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) and Louise served as secretary and "branch reporter", sending news of local UNIA activities to Negro World; they inculcated self-reliance and black pride in their children.
The family home was located at 3448 Pinkney Street and was designated a historical site by the National Register of Historic Places. Malcolm X later said that white violence killed four of his father's brothers. Due to threats by members of the Ku Klux Klan that Earl's UNIA activities were said to be "spreading trouble" the family were forced to flee to Milwaukee in 1926, and shortly thereafter to Lansing, Michigan. In Lansing, his parents were sued for eviction from their newly purchased home due to a covenant that prevented the sale to non-white buyers. They were frequently harassed by the Black Legion, a white racist group who Earl later accused of burning down their family home in 1929. No fire truck to battle the blaze was dispatched to their home.
In 1931, when Malcolm was six years old, his father Earl died unexpectedly, in what has been officially ruled a streetcar accident. His mother Louise believed Earl had been murdered by the Black Legion. Rumors that local members were responsible for his father's death were widely circulated and were very disturbing to Malcolm X as a child. As an adult, he expressed conflicting beliefs on the question. After a dispute with creditors, Louise received a life insurance benefit (nominally $1,000 ‍—‌about $21,000 in 2025) in payments of $18 per month; the issuer of another, larger policy refused to pay, claiming her husband Earl died by suicide. To make ends meet, Louise rented out part of her garden, and her sons hunted game.
During the 1930s, white Seventh-day Adventists witnessed to the Little family; later on, Louise Little and her son Wilfred were baptized into the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Malcolm said the Adventists were "the friendliest white people I had ever seen."
In 1937, a man Louise had been dating‍—‌marriage had seemed a possibility‍—‌vanished from her life when she became pregnant with his child. In late 1938, she had a nervous breakdown and was committed to Kalamazoo State Hospital. The children were separated and sent to foster homes. Malcolm and his siblings secured her release 24 years later.
Malcolm attended West Junior High School in Lansing and then Mason High School in Mason, Michigan, but left high school in 1941, before graduating. He excelled in junior high school but dropped out of high school after a white teacher told him that practicing law, his aspiration at the time, was "no realistic goal for a nigger." Later, Malcolm X recalled feeling that the white world offered no place for a career-oriented black man, regardless of talent.

Criminal career

From age 14 to 21, Malcolm held a variety of jobs while living with his half-sister Ella Little-Collins in Roxbury, a largely African American neighborhood of Boston.
After a short time in Flint, Michigan, he moved to New York City's Harlem neighborhood in 1943, where he found employment on the New Haven Railroad and engaged in drug dealing, gambling, racketeering, robbery, and pimping. According to biographer Bruce Perry, Malcolm also occasionally had sex with other men, usually for money, though this conjecture has been disputed by those who knew him. He befriended John Elroy Sanford, a fellow dishwasher at Jimmy's Chicken Shack in Harlem who aspired to be a professional comedian. Both men had reddish hair, so Sanford was called "Chicago Red" after his hometown, and Malcolm was known as "Detroit Red". Years later, Sanford became famous as comedian and actor Redd Foxx.
Summoned by the local draft board for military service in World War II in late 1943, he feigned mental disturbance by rambling and declaring: "I want to be sent down South. Organize them nigger soldiers ... steal us some guns, and kill us [some] crackers".

primaryTitle: Social Philosopher of the Islamic Renaissance
titles: Most Significant Muslim Social Philosopher since Ibn Khaldun · Theorist of Colonizability
bio: Malek (Malik) Bennabi ibn al-Hajj Omar (1905–1973) was a philosopher of the Islamic Philosophy tradition, based in Constantine. Known as Social Philosopher of the Islamic Renaissance.
bio_full:
Malik Bennabi (1905–1973) was an Algerian philosopher and social thinker who became one of the most influential Islamic intellectuals of the twentieth century. Born in Constantine during the French colonial period, he witnessed firsthand the challenges facing Muslim societies in the modern era, experiences that would profoundly shape his philosophical work.

Bennabi pursued his education in France, where he studied engineering and later developed his philosophical ideas while observing both Western and Islamic civilizations. His unique perspective as someone educated in European institutions while remaining deeply rooted in Islamic culture allowed him to bridge intellectual traditions and offer fresh insights into the problems facing the Muslim world.

He is best known for his comprehensive analysis of what he termed the "civilizational problem" of contemporary Muslim societies. Bennabi argued that the Islamic world's difficulties stemmed not primarily from external colonialism but from internal civilizational decline. He developed theories about the cyclical nature of civilizations and the conditions necessary for their renewal, emphasizing the importance of ideas, people, and time as the fundamental building blocks of any civilization.

Among his most significant works are "The Quranic Phenomenon," where he examined the Quran from a social and historical perspective, and "The Conditions of Renaissance," in which he outlined his vision for Islamic renewal. He wrote extensively about the psychological and social effects of colonialism, coining terms like "colonizability" to describe the internal weaknesses that made societies susceptible to foreign domination.

Bennabi's approach was distinctly modern, incorporating insights from sociology, psychology, and history while maintaining a firmly Islamic foundation. He emphasized the need for Muslims to develop critical thinking, scientific methodology, and social consciousness rather than simply returning to past models.

His influence extended beyond Algeria to the broader Islamic world, particularly among intellectuals seeking to reconcile Islamic principles with modern realities. His ideas about civilizational renewal, the role of ideas in social transformation, and the psychology of underdevelopment continue to be studied and debated in contemporary Islamic thought.

Though he spent much of his later life in Egypt and France, Bennabi remained connected to his Algerian roots and the broader struggles of decolonizing Muslim nations. His work represents a significant contribution to twentieth-century Islamic philosophy, offering a sophisticated framework for understanding both the challenges and possibilities facing Muslim societies in the modern world.

bio: Malik bin 'Amr (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Malik bin 'Amr was a companion (sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community.

As a Meccan companion, Malik bin 'Amr would have been present during the crucial early years of Muhammad's prophetic mission, when the Muslim community faced significant challenges and persecution from the established tribal authorities in Mecca. His designation as a "Companion of Badr" indicates his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces.

The Battle of Badr holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as it marked a turning point for the early Muslim community. Those who participated in this battle are held in particular reverence within Islamic tradition, as they demonstrated their commitment to the faith during a critical and dangerous period. The Companions of Badr, including Malik bin 'Amr, are remembered for their courage and dedication when the survival of the nascent Islamic community was at stake.

Malik bin 'Amr is associated with the early ascetic tradition within Islam, suggesting he was among those companions who emphasized spiritual discipline, simplicity, and devotion to worship. This ascetic approach represented one of the early expressions of Islamic spirituality, focusing on detachment from worldly concerns and intensive devotion to religious practice.

His death in 634 CE places him among the companions who lived through the entire Prophetic period and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr. This means he witnessed the rapid expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula and the consolidation of the Muslim community after the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

While specific details about his individual contributions and activities remain limited in historical sources, Malik bin 'Amr represents the generation of early Muslims whose commitment and sacrifice during Islam's foundational period helped establish the religion that would eventually spread across vast regions of the world. His status as both a Meccan companion and a participant in Badr places him among the most respected figures in early Islamic history.

bio: Malik bin Abi Khauliy (c. 594–650 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Malik bin Abi Khauliy was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived from approximately 594 to 650 CE. He was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca and became known as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr in 622 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr."

The Battle of Badr holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. Those who participated in this battle, known as the Badriyyun, are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition due to their early support of Islam during a critical period when the Muslim community faced considerable opposition and hardship.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Malik bin Abi Khauliy was part of the generation that directly witnessed and learned from Muhammad during his prophetic mission. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting the teachings of Islam, including the hadith literature that records the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet.

His association with hadith sciences indicates that he was among those who helped preserve and transmit the prophetic traditions that would later form an essential component of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice. The companions' testimonies and narrations became foundational sources for understanding Islamic law, theology, and proper conduct.

Living through the formative period of Islam, from its early days in Mecca through the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina and beyond, Malik bin Abi Khauliy witnessed the transformation of a small religious movement into a significant political and social force in the Arabian Peninsula. His lifespan of approximately 56 years covered the entire prophetic period and extended into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate.

The companions like Malik bin Abi Khauliy served as the vital link between the Prophet's generation and subsequent Muslim generations, ensuring the continuity of Islamic teachings and practices. Their role in the early Muslim community extended beyond mere companionship to include active participation in the religious, social, and political development of the emerging Islamic state. Through their preservation and transmission of prophetic traditions, they contributed to the foundation upon which Islamic scholarship and jurisprudence would be built in later centuries.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Malik bin Iyyas al-Ansari (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Malik ibn Iyas al-Ansari was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj tribe of the Ansar of Medina. Ibn al-Athir, in Usd al-Ghaba, records that he was killed as a martyr on the day of the Battle of Uhud. He adds that Ibn Ishaq does not mention him, and that Ibn Abd al-Barr also recorded him in a brief entry. No further details of his life were found in the sources consulted.

bio: Malik bin Numayla (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Malik bin Numayla was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early years of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community.

Malik bin Numayla is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the outnumbered Muslim army.

The Battle of Badr is considered a turning point in early Islamic history, as it established the military credibility of the Muslim community and demonstrated their ability to defend themselves against more numerous opponents. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition, as they were present during this crucial moment in the religion's development.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Malik bin Numayla belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early revelations and establishment of Islamic practices. The Sahaba played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings, traditions, and example of the Prophet to subsequent generations.

Malik bin Numayla's life was relatively brief, as he died in 625 CE, just one year after the Battle of Badr. His death occurred during the continued conflicts between the Muslim community of Medina and various opposing forces in the region. Like many of the early Muslims, his life was marked by the challenges and struggles faced by the nascent Islamic community as it sought to establish itself in a hostile environment.

While specific details about Malik bin Numayla's personal life, tribal affiliations, or other activities beyond his participation at Badr are not well-documented in widely available historical sources, his inclusion among the Companions of Badr ensures his place in Islamic historical memory. The early Muslim community was relatively small, and those who participated in its foundational moments, particularly the decisive Battle of Badr, are remembered as important figures in the establishment of Islam.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Malik bin Rabi'a, Abu Maryum al-Saluli ( , (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Arabia. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Malik bin Rabi'a, known by his kunya Abu Maryum al-Saluli, was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational period of Islam.

Malik bin Rabi'a is most notably recognized for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan (Bay'at al-Ridwan), a significant oath of allegiance taken by the Prophet Muhammad's companions. This pledge occurred at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE, when approximately 1,400 Muslims swore loyalty to the Prophet under a tree, demonstrating their willingness to fight and die for their faith if necessary. The Quran specifically references this event in verse 48:18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those who pledged their allegiance under the tree, making those who participated in this pledge particularly honored in Islamic tradition.

As a sahabi, Malik bin Rabi'a belonged to the distinguished group of individuals who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad, heard his teachings firsthand, and witnessed the revelation and early implementation of Islamic principles. The companions hold special significance in Islamic history as they served as the primary transmitters of the Prophet's sayings, actions, and approvals, which form the basis of hadith literature - the second most important source of Islamic guidance after the Quran.

His association with hadith sciences indicates that Malik bin Rabi'a played a role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's traditions to subsequent generations. The companions' testimonies and narrations became crucial for establishing Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and practice in the decades and centuries following the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

Malik bin Rabi'a died around 640 CE, during the early period of Islamic expansion under the Rashidun Caliphate. Like many of his fellow companions, he lived through the transformative years of early Islam, from its origins in Mecca through the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina and the subsequent spread of the faith across the Arabian Peninsula. His participation in key events such as the Pledge of Ridwan ensures his place among the notable figures who helped establish the foundation of the Islamic community during its most crucial formative period.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Malik bin Sinan, a companion of the Ansar from the Banu Khudrah of the Khazraj tribe. He witnessed with the Prophet Muhammad the Battle of Uhud, and he was the one who sucked the blood of the Prophet Muhammad that came down from his cheek after removing the two rings of forgiveness that were embedded in his cheek, and he swallowed it that day, and he was told, “Should I drink the blood?” He said, “Yes, I drink the blood of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.” Then the Prophet Muhammad said, “Whoever touches his blood with my blood, the fire will not touch him.” So that day, he fought Malik until he was killed, and the one who killed him was Ghurab bin Sufyan Al-Kanani, and Malik was Abu The companion Abu Saeed Al-Khudri.
bio_full:
Malik bin Sinan was a companion of Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported the early Muslim community. He belonged to the Banu Khudrah clan of the Khazraj tribe, one of the two main Arab tribes of Medina. Born around 597 CE, he lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula.

Malik bin Sinan is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, a significant military engagement between the early Muslim community and the Meccan forces. This battle, fought near Medina, was a crucial moment in early Islamic history where the Muslim army faced challenges after initial success.

During the battle, Prophet Muhammad was injured when metal rings from a helmet became embedded in his face. According to Islamic historical accounts, Malik bin Sinan assisted the Prophet by helping to remove these rings and tending to the resulting wounds. The historical sources describe his devoted care for the Prophet during this difficult moment of the battle.

Malik bin Sinan fought courageously at Uhud and was killed during the engagement, reportedly by Ghurab bin Sufyan Al-Kanani. His death made him one of the martyrs of Uhud, joining approximately seventy other Muslims who lost their lives in this battle. The Battle of Uhud, despite being a tactical setback for the Muslim forces, became an important learning experience that strengthened the community's resolve and military strategy.

His significance in Islamic history extends beyond his individual actions to his role as part of the Ansar community. The Ansar were crucial to the survival and growth of the early Muslim community, providing refuge and support to Prophet Muhammad and the emigrants from Mecca. Their loyalty and sacrifice, exemplified by figures like Malik bin Sinan, were fundamental to Islam's establishment in Medina.

Malik bin Sinan was the father of Abu Said al-Khudri, who became one of the most prominent companions and narrators of prophetic traditions in Islamic history. Through his son's later contributions to Islamic scholarship and his own sacrifice at Uhud, Malik bin Sinan's family became well-regarded in Islamic historical memory as examples of dedication to the early Muslim community.

bio: Malik bin Zama'a b Qays (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Malik ibn Zama'a ibn Qays was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 593 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca during the religion's initial years.

Malik is primarily remembered for his participation in the first migration to Abyssinia, which occurred around 615 CE. This migration, known as the Hijra to Abyssinia, was undertaken by a group of early Muslims who faced increasing persecution from the Meccan authorities. The Prophet Muhammad advised these followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, where they could practice their faith freely under the protection of the Negus, the Christian ruler of the region.

As one of the emigrants to Abyssinia, Malik demonstrated the commitment and sacrifice characteristic of the early Muslim community. The migration required leaving behind family, property, and familiar surroundings to preserve religious freedom and community cohesion. This group of emigrants played a crucial role in Islam's early survival during its most vulnerable period in Mecca.

Malik belonged to the generation of companions known as the Sahaba, those who knew Muhammad personally and accepted Islam during his lifetime. His association with the early ascetic tradition suggests he may have been among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline and devotion, though specific details about his religious practices are not extensively documented.

The migration to Abyssinia represented a significant diplomatic and strategic development in early Islamic history. It demonstrated Islam's capacity to coexist with other monotheistic faiths and established important precedents for religious tolerance and political asylum. The emigrants' successful integration into Abyssinian society helped establish Islam's credibility as an organized religious movement.

Malik died in 633 CE, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE, during the period when the early Muslim community was consolidating under the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. His relatively short life span meant he witnessed the entire prophetic period and the beginning of Islam's expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While detailed accounts of Malik's individual contributions are limited, his participation in the Abyssinian migration places him among the early Muslims whose sacrifices helped ensure Islam's survival during its most challenging initial phase. His story reflects the broader experience of early Muslim converts who prioritized their faith over material security and social standing.

bio:
Malik bin Al-Nadr.
The eleventh grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad bin Abdullah. He is called Abu Al-Harith.
bio_full:
Malik ibn al-Nadr, known by the kunya Abu al-Harith, was a tribal leader and ancestor figure in pre-Islamic Arabian history who lived during the 2nd and 3rd centuries of the Common Era. According to Islamic genealogical traditions, he was an eleventh-generation ancestor of the Prophet Muhammad and a key figure in the lineage of the Quraysh tribe.

Malik ibn al-Nadr is traditionally regarded as the founding patriarch of the Quraysh, the prominent Meccan tribe that would later produce the Prophet Muhammad. His descendants became the dominant clan structure that controlled Mecca and its surrounding territories in the centuries leading up to the rise of Islam. The Quraysh tribe's influence extended throughout the Hejaz region of western Arabia, where they established themselves as successful merchants and guardians of important trade routes.

Living during a period when Arabian society was organized around tribal affiliations and kinship networks, Malik ibn al-Nadr's role as a founding figure placed him at the center of genealogical traditions that would later become significant in Islamic history. The tribal structures and alliances that emerged from his lineage shaped the political and social landscape of pre-Islamic Mecca.

His significance to Islamic history lies primarily in his position within the prophetic genealogy and his role in establishing the tribal framework that would later influence early Islamic society. The Quraysh tribe, tracing their ancestry to Malik ibn al-Nadr, became central to the early Muslim community's leadership structure, with many prominent early Muslims and caliphs claiming descent from various branches of his lineage.

The historical records from this early period of Arabian history are largely based on oral traditions that were later compiled by Islamic historians and genealogists. These sources consistently identify Malik ibn al-Nadr as a pivotal figure in the tribal prehistory of Islam, though detailed contemporary accounts of his specific activities and achievements are limited. His legacy is primarily understood through his role in the genealogical chains that connected later historical figures to the broader tribal networks of pre-Islamic Arabia.

bio: Mandwas bint 'Amr b. Khunays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Mandwas bint 'Amr b. Khunays was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the inhabitants of Medina who supported Muhammad and the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Mandwas was part of the crucial group of Medinan supporters who provided sanctuary and assistance to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a pivotal role in the establishment and survival of the early Islamic state, offering protection and resources when the Muslim community was still vulnerable and establishing itself in Medina.

Living during the foundational period of Islam, Mandwas would have witnessed the rapid transformation of Arabian society as Islamic teachings spread throughout the region. Her lifetime spanned the Prophet's ministry, the establishment of the first Islamic community in Medina, and the beginning of the Islamic conquests under the first caliphs following Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

The fact that Mandwas is remembered and recorded in Islamic historical sources reflects the recognition given to female companions during the early Islamic period. Women among the Ansar, like their male counterparts, were acknowledged for their contributions to the early Muslim community, whether through providing material support, participating in community affairs, or simply being part of the foundational generation that helped establish Islamic society.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph, when the Islamic state was expanding rapidly beyond the Arabian Peninsula. As one of the Ansar, her legacy is tied to the broader historical significance of the Medinan supporters who helped ensure the survival and growth of the early Muslim community during its most critical period.

While specific details about her individual contributions are not extensively documented, her recognition as a companion places her among the generation of Muslims who directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and participated in the foundational moments of Islamic history in Medina.

bio: Mandwas bint 'Ubada b. Dulaim (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Mandus bint Ubada ibn Dulaym was a woman of the Ansar of Medina and the sister of Sa'd ibn Ubada. Ibn Sa'd, in his Tabaqat, traces her lineage through Haritha ibn Abi Hazima ibn Tha'laba ibn Tarif to al-Khazraj ibn Sa'ida, and Ibn al-Athir calls her al-Ansariyya al-Sa'idiyya, of the Banu Sa'ida. Her mother was Amra bint Mas'ud ibn Qays of the Banu al-Najjar. She married Simak ibn Thabit ibn Sufyan of the Khazraj and bore him a son named Thabit. Ibn Sa'd records that she became a Muslim and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad, and Ibn al-Athir reports the same pledge on the authority of Ibn Habib. The sources consulted give no dates for her birth or death.

bio: Mandwas bint Khallad bin Suwayd (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Mandwas bint Khallad bin Suwayd was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the community of Medinan Muslims who provided crucial support to the Prophet and the early Muslim emigrants from Mecca.

As an Ansari companion, Mandwas was part of the indigenous population of Medina (then called Yathrib) who embraced Islam and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE. The Ansar played a fundamental role in establishing the first Muslim community and provided both material and spiritual support during the formative years of Islam.

Living during the pivotal early decades of Islamic history, Mandwas witnessed the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, the development of Islamic law and practices, and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime spanned the entire Meccan persecution period, the Hijra (migration to Medina), and the subsequent consolidation of the Muslim state under the Prophet Muhammad and the first Caliph Abu Bakr.

The female companions of the Prophet held significant positions within early Muslim society, often serving as transmitters of religious knowledge, participants in community affairs, and witnesses to the development of Islamic teachings. While specific details of Mandwas's individual contributions are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as a Sahabiyya indicates her acceptance of Islam during the Prophet's lifetime and her participation in the early Muslim community.

Her death around 635 CE occurred during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, placing her among those companions who lived through both the Prophetic period and the early expansion of the Islamic state under the Rashidun Caliphs. The Ansari companions, including women like Mandwas, are remembered in Islamic tradition for their loyalty and sacrifice in supporting the nascent Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

As with many female companions of this era, the historical record provides limited detail about her specific activities, reflecting the broader patterns of historical documentation from seventh-century Arabia. Her inclusion among the recognized companions represents the important, if often understated, role that women played in the establishment and early development of the Islamic community.

bio: Mandwas bint Qubta bin 'Abdu 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Mandwas bint Qubta bin 'Abdu 'Amr was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who provided crucial support to the Prophet and the early Muslim community.

As an Ansari companion, Mandwas belonged to the group of Medinan Arabs who welcomed Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, an event known as the Hijra. The Ansar played a pivotal role in establishing the first Muslim community, offering shelter, protection, and material support to the Muhajirun (emigrants from Mecca) during Islam's earliest and most vulnerable years.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's residence there, Mandwas would have been witness to the development of Islamic law, practice, and community structure. The female companions of this era participated in various aspects of early Muslim society, including religious gatherings, community affairs, and the transmission of Islamic teachings and traditions.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing means she lived through the entire Medinan period of the Prophet's mission, experiencing firsthand the establishment and early expansion of the Islamic community.

The designation as a sahabiyya holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are regarded as the primary transmitters of Islamic knowledge and practice to subsequent generations. Female companions like Mandwas contributed to the preservation and transmission of religious knowledge, though the specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the surviving historical sources.

Her inclusion among the recognized companions of Medina reflects the important role that women played in the early Muslim community, even when their individual stories may not have been preserved in as much detail as those of some male companions. The Ansari companions collectively represent a crucial foundation of early Islamic society, having provided the necessary support structure that enabled Islam to develop from a small community of believers into a significant religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Marda bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Marda bin Maqrn al-Mazni was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was part of the Mazin tribe and lived in the Hijaz region, which encompassed the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

Al-Mazni is historically significant as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree (Bay'at al-Ridwan). This pivotal event occurred in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah, a location near Mecca, when approximately 1,400 Muslim followers pledged their allegiance to Prophet Muhammad under a tree. The pledge was made in preparation for what the companions believed might be a final confrontation, as they had come to perform pilgrimage but faced potential conflict with the Meccan tribes.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds special significance in Islamic history and is specifically mentioned in the Quran in chapter 48, verse 18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree. This divine approval, as recorded in the Quran, grants particular religious significance to those who participated in this pledge, including al-Mazni.

As a sahabi, al-Mazni was among the generation of Muslims who directly knew, learned from, and supported the Prophet Muhammad during the foundational period of Islam. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, practices, and the Prophet's traditions (hadith) to subsequent generations.

Al-Mazni died around 640 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of the second Caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab. This period marked the rapid expansion of the Islamic state beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about al-Mazni's individual contributions or activities beyond his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his status as a companion who participated in this significant covenant ensures his place in Islamic historical memory. The companions who took part in the Pledge of Ridwan are collectively remembered for their demonstration of loyalty and commitment during a critical moment in early Islamic history.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Mardas bin Malik al-Aslami (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Mardas bin Malik al-Aslami was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he belonged to the Aslam tribe, a group that became allied with the early Muslim community in Medina.

Mardas is historically significant as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree (Bay'at al-Ridwan). This pivotal event took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah, near Mecca, when approximately 1,400 Muslims pledged their allegiance to Prophet Muhammad under a tree. The Quran references this pledge in chapter 48, verse 18, stating that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged their allegiance. This oath was given in a moment of tension when the Muslims believed that their envoy Uthman ibn Affan had been killed by the Meccan forces, though this later proved to be false.

The Pledge of Ridwan is considered one of the most important events in early Islamic history, as it demonstrated the unwavering loyalty of the companions to the Prophet during a critical diplomatic mission. Those who participated in this pledge are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as the Quranic verse explicitly mentions God's pleasure with them.

As a member of the Aslam tribe, Mardas was part of a group that played a supportive role in the early Muslim community. The Aslam tribe was known for their loyalty to the Prophet and their participation in various military expeditions and important events during the formative years of Islam.

Mardas lived during the foundational period of Islamic civilization, witnessing the revelation of the Quran, the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, and the eventual peaceful conquest of Mecca. He died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the rule of Umar ibn al-Khattab.

While detailed accounts of his individual contributions beyond his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan are not extensively documented in historical sources, his status as a companion who witnessed this crucial moment in Islamic history ensures his place in the collective memory of the early Muslim community. His inclusion among those specifically mentioned in the Quranic verse has made him a figure of reverence in Islamic historical consciousness.

bio: Marthad bin Abi Marthad al-Ghanvi (c. 594–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Marthad bin Abi Marthad al-Ghanvi was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was present during the crucial early decades of the Islamic community's development.

Marthad belonged to the Ghanm tribe, as indicated by his designation "al-Ghanvi." Like many early Muslims, he would have experienced the transition from the pre-Islamic tribal society of Arabia to the emerging Islamic community. His life spanned the period of Muhammad's prophetic mission, which began around 610 CE, making him witness to the fundamental changes occurring in Arabian society during this time.

He is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. Those who participated in Badr are traditionally held in high esteem within Islamic historical memory, as the battle marked a turning point in the early Muslim community's struggle for survival and recognition.

Marthad is also associated with the early ascetic tradition within Islam. This suggests he was among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline, simplicity, and devotion to religious practice. The early ascetic movement represented one of the foundational approaches to Islamic spirituality that would later influence the development of various mystical and devotional traditions.

His death in 626 CE places him among the companions who died during the Prophet's lifetime, meaning he witnessed the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina following the migration from Mecca, but did not live to see the rapid expansion of Islam that occurred after Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

As a sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Marthad represents the generation of early Muslims who directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices and community structures. These companions serve as important links in the transmission of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations, though specific details about Marthad's individual contributions to this transmission are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources.

bio: Martin Lings (1909–2005) was a scholar of the Shadhiliyya tradition, based in London. Known as Abu Bakr Siraj al-Din.
bio_full:
Martin Lings (24 January 1909 – 12 May 2005), also known as Abū Bakr Sirāj ad-Dīn, was an English writer, Islamic scholar, and philosopher. A student of the Swiss metaphysician Frithjof Schuon and an authority on the work of William Shakespeare, he is best known as the author of Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources.

Early life and education
Lings was born in Burnage, Manchester, in 1909 to a Protestant family. He began travelling at a young age, spending significant time in the United States because of his father's employment. He attended Clifton College and went on to Magdalen College, Oxford, where he gained a BA in English Language and Literature. At Magdalen, he was a student and then a close friend of C. S. Lewis. After graduating from Oxford Lings went to Vytautas Magnus University, in Lithuania, where he taught Anglo-Saxon and Middle English.
At Oxford he discovered  the writings of René Guénon, a French metaphysician and Muslim convert, and Frithjof Schuon, a German spiritual authority, metaphysician and Perennialist.  In 1938, Lings went to Basel to meet Schuon and embraced the branch of the Alawiyya tariqa led by Schuon. Lings remained Schuon's disciple and expositor for the rest of his life.

Career
In 1939, Lings went to Cairo, Egypt, to visit a friend who was an assistant of René Guénon. Soon after arriving in Cairo, his friend died and Lings began studying Arabic. Cairo became his home for over a decade; he became an English language teacher at the University of Cairo and produced Shakespeare plays annually. Lings married Lesley Smalley in 1944 and lived with her in a village near the pyramids.  Despite having settled comfortably in Egypt, Lings was forced to leave in 1952 after anti-British disturbances.

On returning to the United Kingdom he continued his education, earning a BA in Arabic and a PhD from the School of Oriental and African Studies (University of London). His doctoral thesis became a book on Algerian Sufi Ahmad al-Alawi. After completing his doctorate in 1959, Lings worked at the British Museum and later the British Library, overseeing eastern manuscripts and other textual works, rising to the position of Keeper of Oriental Printed Books and Manuscripts 1970–73.  He was also a frequent contributor to the journal Studies in Comparative Religion.
A writer throughout this period, Lings's output increased in the last quarter of his life.  While his thesis work on Ahmad al-Alawi had been well regarded, his most famous work was a biography of Muhammad, written in 1983, which earned him acclaim in the Muslim world and prizes from the governments of Pakistan and Egypt.  His work was hailed as the "best biography of the prophet in English" at the National Seerat Conference in Islamabad. He also continued travelling extensively, although he made his home in Kent. He died on 12 May 2005.
Lings and a Salafist scholar named Abu Bilal Mustafa al-Kanadi had a public debate about some accounts of Lings's biography of Islamic prophet Muhammad. The exchange was published by Saudi Gazette.
His contribution to Shakespeare scholarship was to point out the deeper esoteric meanings found in Shakespeare's plays, and the spirituality of Shakespeare himself. More recent editions of Lings's books on Shakespeare include a foreword by Charles III. Just before his death he gave an interview on this topic, which was posthumously made into the film Shakespeare's Spirituality: A Perspective. An Interview With Dr. Martin Lings.

bio: Mas'ud bin al-Aswad (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Mas'ud ibn al-Aswad ibn Haritha ibn Nadla was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Adi clan of Quraysh. His mother was al-Ajma', and he was therefore also called Ibn al-Ajma'. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr record that he emigrated together with his brother Muti' ibn al-Aswad, and that he was among the Companions of the Tree who gave the Pledge of al-Ridwan; Ibn Abd al-Barr adds that he was one of the seventy people of Banu Adi who emigrated. Both say he was martyred on the day of Mu'tah; Ibn al-Barqi, cited by Ibn Manzur, places this in the eighth year after the Hijra, and Ibn Manzur locates Mu'tah in al-Balqa'. The accounts are not fully agreed. Ibn Manzur cites Ibn Yunus as saying that Mas'ud took part in the conquest of Egypt, and Ibn Hibban says he lived in Egypt. Ibn Manzur also cites al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar as saying that the man killed at Mu'tah was Mas'ud's cousin, Mas'ud ibn Suwayd, and admits he does not know which account is mistaken. Ibn Qani' records a report from him, through his daughter A'isha, about a woman who had stolen; al-Bukhari also lists reports from him through her.

bio: Mas'ud bin Aws bin Zayd (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Mas'ud ibn Aws ibn Asram ibn Zayd ibn Tha'laba was an Ansari Companion of the Khazraj tribe, from the clan of Malik ibn al-Najjar. His kunya was Abu Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as 'Amra bint Mas'ud, one of the women who gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet. Ibn Sa'd states that he fought at Badr, Uhud, the Trench and all the other battles with the Prophet. Ibn Yunus and Ibn al-Athir add that he took part in the conquest of Egypt, and Ibn Yunus notes that a hadith of his was known in Egypt. Ibn al-Athir reports that he held the witr prayer to be obligatory; when this reached 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, 'Ubada said that Abu Muhammad was mistaken. The classical authors differ over who this Abu Muhammad was: Ibn 'Abd al-Barr says he is said to be Mas'ud ibn Aws, while others give his name as Mas'ud ibn Zayd ibn Subay'. Accounts of his death also differ. Ibn al-Kalbi reported that he lived on and fought alongside 'Ali at Siffin, while Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir say, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr reports, that he died during the caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.

bio: Mas'ud bin Khalada (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Mas'ud bin Khalada was a companion (sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who resided in Medina, the city that became the center of the nascent Islamic community following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Mas'ud bin Khalada is most notably recognized for his participation in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military encounter between the early Muslim community and the Meccan opposition. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the Muslim forces despite being significantly outnumbered. Those who participated in this battle earned the distinguished title "Companion of Badr" and are held in special regard within Islamic tradition.

As one of the companions of the Prophet Muhammad, Mas'ud bin Khalada belonged to the generation of Muslims who directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and observed the Prophet's teachings firsthand. The companions played a crucial role in the early Islamic community, serving not only as followers but as transmitters of Islamic knowledge, practices, and traditions to subsequent generations.

The companions of Badr, including Mas'ud bin Khalada, are considered to have made essential contributions to the survival and establishment of the early Muslim state. Their participation in this pivotal battle helped secure the Muslim community's position in the Arabian Peninsula and contributed to the eventual spread of Islam throughout the region.

Mas'ud bin Khalada died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate period that followed the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. His life spanned the crucial decades that saw the emergence of Islam as a major religious and political force in Arabia. As a companion who witnessed both the struggles of the early Muslim community and participated in its key military victories, Mas'ud bin Khalada represents the generation that helped establish the foundations upon which Islamic civilization would develop in subsequent centuries.

famous: Mas'ud bin Rabi'a b 'Amr of al-Qara
full: Mas'ud bin Rabi'a b 'Amr of al-Qara
bio: Mas'ud bin Rabi'a b 'Amr of al-Qara (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Mas'ud ibn Rabi'a al-Qari, also called Mas'ud ibn al-Rabi', was an early Companion from al-Qara and an ally (halif) of the Banu Zuhra clan of Quraysh. His father's name is given as Rabi'a or al-Rabi'; Ibn 'Abd al-Barr traces him through 'Amr ibn Sa'd ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza, and Ibn al-Kalbi calls him Mas'ud ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'a. Ibn al-Athir records that he accepted Islam early in Mecca, before the Prophet entered the house of al-Arqam. After the emigration to Medina, the Prophet joined him in brotherhood with 'Ubayd ibn al-Tayyihan, and both men fought at Badr. One account adds that he took part in all of the Prophet's campaigns. Abu Nu'aym notes that no narrations from him are known. According to al-Waqidi, Abu Ma'shar and al-Tabari, as cited by Ibn al-Athir, he died in 30 AH at more than sixty years of age.

bio: Mas'ud bin Sa'd (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Mas'ud ibn Sa'd ibn 'Amir ibn 'Adi was an Ansari Companion of the Aws tribe, from the clan of Banu Haritha. Some authorities give his father's name as 'Abd Sa'd. Ibn Ishaq, Abu Ma'shar and Musa ibn 'Uqba, as cited by Ibn Hajar, list him among those who fought at Badr, and he is also reported to have fought at Uhud. Ibn Sa'd states that he left no descendants. Accounts of his death differ: Ibn al-Athir records that he was killed as a martyr on the day of Khaybar, which took place in 7 AH, while another account places his martyrdom at Bi'r Ma'una.

bio: Mas'ud bin Sa'd b Qays (c. 594–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Mas'ud ibn Sa'd ibn Qays ibn Khalid ibn 'Amir ibn Zurayq was an Ansari Companion of the Banu Zurayq, a clan of the Khazraj. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, citing al-Waqidi, records that he fought at Badr and Uhud and was killed as a martyr on the day of Bi'r Ma'una.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Mas'ud bin Zayd bin Subay' (b. c. 591 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full: Mas'ud ibn Zayd ibn Subay' was an Ansari Companion. Ibn al-Athir identifies him as Abu Muhammad al-Ansari and records, with some uncertainty, that Musa ibn 'Uqba listed him among those who fought at Badr. Al-Baghawi likewise names Mas'ud ibn Zayd, Abu Muhammad al-Ansari, as a veteran of Badr. Ibn Manzur's abridgement of Ibn 'Asakir's History of Damascus gives the same name for Abu Muhammad al-Ansari and states that he fought at Badr, Uhud and the Trench, that he died during the caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and that he left no descendants. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr counts Abu Muhammad among the Companions of Syria, and another account says he settled there. He is best known for a report that he held the witr prayer to be obligatory; when this reached 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, 'Ubada said that Abu Muhammad was mistaken. The identity of this Abu Muhammad is not settled in the sources: some authorities, including Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, say he was Mas'ud ibn Aws ibn Zayd ibn Asram of the Banu al-Najjar, another Companion who fought at Badr.

full: Masruq ibn al-Ajda' ibn Malik al-Hamdani al-Kufi
primaryTitle: Great Kufan Scholar and Companion of Aisha
titles: Faqih al-Kufa · Primary Student of Aisha
bio: Masruq ibn al-Ajda' ibn Malik al-Hamdani al-Kufi (c. 620–683) was a historical figure of the Islamic Jurisprudence tradition, based in Kufa. Known as Great Kufan Scholar and Companion of Aisha.
bio_full:
Abu Aisha Masruq bin Al-Ajda’ Al-Wada’i (who died in the year 62 AH) was a follower and mufti of Kufi, and one of the narrators of the Prophet’s hadith.

Al-Ajda' bin Malik bin Umayyah bin Abdullah bin Mur Al-Wadi'i Al-Hamdani, Masruq's father, converted to Islam, and moved his children to Medina, where Masruq grew up and learned from the companions of the Prophet Muhammad. Therefore, he is among the senior followers and among the veterans who converted to Islam during the life of the Prophet Muhammad. Masruq is the nephew of Amr bin Maadi, the knight of Banu Zubaid, and Masruq’s grandfather was one of the knights of Yemen. It is said that he was called stolen because he was stolen when he was young, then he was found and called stolen.

Masruq participated in the Islamic conquest of Persia, and participated in the Battle of Al-Qadisiyah with his brothers Abdullah, Abu Bakr, and Al-Muntashari. His brothers were killed on that day, and Masruq’s hand was paralyzed from an injury he sustained in the battle. When Othman was killed, Masruq chose to withdraw from the strife, and even tried to reconcile the conflict between the combatants, and he walked between the ranks on the day of Siffin, admonishing the combatants to refrain from fighting.

Masruq lived in Kufa, and sat giving fatwas to people and passing judgment among them without taking any reward for that. Masruq worked hard in worship, until his wife, Qumair bint Amr, said: “Masruq used to pray until his feet were swollen, so perhaps I sat behind him crying at what I saw him doing to himself.” Masruq bin Al-Ajda’ died in the year 62 AH, or it was said in the year 63 AH, and he was 63 years old.

It was narrated on the authority of: Omar bin Al-Khattab, Ali bin Abi Talib, Abdullah bin Masoud, Khabbab bin Al-Art, Ubayy bin Ka’b, Abdullah bin Amr bin Al-Aas, Aisha bint Abi Bakr, Ubaid bin Umair Al-Laithi, Umm Ruman bint Amer Al-Kinaniyah, Moaz bin Jabal, Uthman bin Affan, Abdullah bin Omar bin Al-Khattab, Subayah Al-Aslamiyah, Ma’qil bin Sinan, Al-Mughira bin Shu’bah, Zaid bin Thabit and Umm Salamah.

It was narrated on his authority by: Amer al-Sha’bi, Ibrahim bin Yazid al-Nakha’i, Yahya bin Wathhab, Abdullah bin Murra al-Kharfi, Shaqiq bin Salamah, Yahya bin al-Jazzar, Abu al-Duha Muslim bin Subaih, Abdul Rahman bin Abdullah bin Masoud, Ubaid bin Nudhaila, Makhoul al-Shami, Abu Ishaq al-Subaie, his nephew Muhammad bin al-Muntashir bin al-Ajda’, Muhammad bin Nashar al-Hamdani, Ma’bad bin Khalid al-Jadali, Abu al-Ahwas al-Jashmi, and Ayoub bin Hani.

bio: Māttūshalakh ibn Idrīs (legendary–legendary) was a founding figure, based in Mesopotamia. Known as Ancestor of Prophet Muhammad. The sources record 3 family or contemporary relations.
bio_full:
Mattushalakh ibn Idris is a figure mentioned in Islamic genealogical traditions as part of the ancestral lineage leading to the Prophet Muhammad. According to these traditions, he lived in ancient Mesopotamia during the pre-Islamic period, with dates traditionally assigned to approximately 2900-2000 BCE, though these chronological designations should be understood within the context of religious and genealogical literature rather than historical documentation.

The name Mattushalakh appears to correspond to the biblical figure Methuselah, reflecting the shared Abrahamic heritage that connects Islamic, Jewish, and Christian traditions. In Islamic genealogical accounts, he is positioned as the son of Idris, who is identified in Islamic tradition with the biblical Enoch and is recognized as one of the early prophets mentioned in the Quran.

Islamic historical and genealogical sources include Mattushalakh as part of the extended lineage that connects the earliest prophetic figures to later Arabian tribes and ultimately to the family of the Prophet Muhammad. This genealogical framework serves to establish continuity between the primordial religious tradition and the emergence of Islam in seventh-century Arabia.

The historical records concerning figures from this remote period primarily derive from religious and genealogical traditions rather than contemporary documentation. Islamic scholars and historians have preserved these lineages as part of their efforts to trace the prophetic heritage and establish connections between the earliest monotheistic communities and the later development of Islamic civilization.

Mattushalakh's significance in Islamic history lies primarily in his role within these genealogical traditions that seek to demonstrate the continuity of divine guidance through successive generations. The preservation of his name and position in the lineage reflects the importance that Islamic tradition places on maintaining connections to the earliest periods of monotheistic faith.

While specific biographical details about his life and activities are not extensively documented in historical sources, his inclusion in Islamic genealogical literature demonstrates the tradition's commitment to tracing the spiritual and familial connections that link the earliest prophetic period to the emergence of the Islamic community. This genealogical framework has remained an important element in Islamic historical consciousness and religious identity.
