bio: Mu'adha bint 'Abdullah bin 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Mu'adha bint 'Abdullah bin 'Amr was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early decades of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the residents of Medina who supported and welcomed the Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca.

As one of the Ansari companions, Mu'adha would have been among those who witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim community in Medina following the Hijra in 622 CE. The Ansar played a crucial role in providing shelter, resources, and protection to the early Muslim community during this formative period of Islamic history.

Like other female companions of her time, Mu'adha lived during the Prophet's lifetime and the early Rashidun Caliphate period, experiencing the rapid expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. She died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, making her lifespan roughly forty years.

The female companions, including Mu'adha, represent an important but often less documented aspect of early Islamic history. These women were direct witnesses to the Prophet's teachings and the development of Islamic practices and community life. Their presence in the historical record, though sometimes limited in detail, demonstrates the active participation of women in the early Muslim community.

Mu'adha's designation as an Ansari companion places her within a particularly significant group in Islamic history. The Ansar are remembered for their pivotal role in Islam's survival and growth, as their acceptance and support of the Muslim migrants from Mecca was essential to the religion's continuation. Without the assistance of the Ansari families of Medina, the early Muslim community might not have been able to establish the stable base needed for Islam's subsequent expansion.

While specific details about Mu'adha's individual contributions or particular circumstances are not extensively recorded in the surviving historical sources, her status as a Sahabiyya indicates that she was recognized by later Muslim historians and scholars as someone who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was part of the foundational generation of Muslims. Her inclusion in the records of companions serves as a testament to the recognition of women's roles in early Islamic society.

bio: Mu'attib bin 'Auf (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Mu'attib bin 'Auf was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. As one of the early converts to Islam, he lived during the formative period of the Islamic community in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE.

Mu'attib is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as they supported the nascent Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

The Battle of Badr involved approximately 300 Muslim fighters facing a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory was seen as divinely ordained and marked a turning point in the establishment of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. As a Badr veteran, Mu'attib was among this small group of early believers who demonstrated their commitment to the faith through direct participation in this crucial conflict.

Beyond his military participation, Mu'attib is associated with the early ascetic tradition within Islam. This suggests he may have been among those companions who emphasized spiritual discipline, simple living, and devotion to worship, characteristics that were valued in the early Muslim community. However, specific details about his ascetic practices or teachings are not well-documented in the historical sources.

Mu'attib's life spanned the period from before the advent of Islam through the early expansion of the Muslim state. He died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, the first successor to Prophet Muhammad. This means he witnessed not only the prophetic period but also the initial phase of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

His significance lies primarily in his status as a Sahabi and Badr participant, representing the generation of early Muslims who provided the foundation for the Islamic community. Like many companions, his individual contributions may not be extensively recorded, but his presence among the early believers helped establish the religious and social framework that would define Islamic civilization for centuries to come.

bio: Mu'attib bin 'Ubaid (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Mu'attib bin 'Ubaid was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, Mu'attib bin 'Ubaid held a significant position within early Islamic society. The companions were those who met the Prophet Muhammad, believed in his message, and died as Muslims, making them revered figures in Islamic tradition and important sources for understanding the early development of the faith.

Mu'attib bin 'Ubaid is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr." This battle was the first major military victory for the Muslim community and is considered a pivotal moment in Islamic history. The battle occurred when a Muslim force of approximately 300 men, led by the Prophet Muhammad, confronted a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory at Badr was seen as divine validation of their cause and significantly boosted the morale and standing of the early Islamic community.

Those who fought at Badr, known as the Badr veterans or Badriyyun, held special status among the companions. They were considered to have demonstrated exceptional faith and commitment by standing with the Prophet during this crucial and dangerous moment when the survival of the Muslim community was at stake.

Mu'attib bin 'Ubaid's life was relatively brief, as he died in 625 CE at approximately thirty-one years of age. His death occurred during the early years of the Islamic community's establishment in Medina, following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation in Badr are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, his status as both a companion of the Prophet and a Badr veteran places him among the foundational figures of early Islam. The companions collectively played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of the Prophet Muhammad, serving as links between the Prophet's time and subsequent generations of Muslims. Their experiences and testimonies became fundamental sources for Islamic law, theology, and historical understanding.

titles: Amīr al-Muʾminīn · Ḥilm (the Forbearing)
bio: Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān (c. 602–680) was a ruler of the Early Ascetics tradition, based in Damascus. Known as Founder of the Umayyad Caliphate.
bio_full:
Mu'awiya I (c. 597, 603 or 605 – April 680) was the founder and first caliph of the Umayyad Caliphate, ruling from 661 until his death. He became caliph less than thirty years after the death of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and immediately after the four Rashidun ('rightly-guided') caliphs. Unlike his predecessors, who had been close, early companions of Muhammad, Mu'awiya was a relatively late follower of Muhammad.
Mu'awiya and his father Abu Sufyan had opposed Muhammad, their distant Qurayshite kinsman and later Mu'awiya's brother-in-law, until Muhammad captured Mecca in 630. Afterward, Mu'awiya became one of Muhammad's scribes. He was appointed by Caliph Abu Bakr (r. 632–634) as a deputy commander in the conquest of Syria. He moved up the ranks through Umar's caliphate (r. 634–644) until becoming governor of Syria during the reign of his Umayyad kinsman, Caliph Uthman (r. 644–656). He allied with the province's powerful Banu Kalb tribe, developed the defenses of its coastal cities, and directed the war effort against the Byzantine Empire, including the first Muslim naval campaigns. In response to Uthman's assassination in 656, Mu'awiya took up the cause of avenging the murdered caliph and opposed the election of Ali. During the First Fitna, the two led their armies to a stalemate at the Battle of Siffin in 657, prompting an abortive series of arbitration talks to settle the dispute. Afterward, Mu'awiya gained recognition as caliph by his Syrian supporters and his ally Amr ibn al-As, who conquered Egypt from Ali's governor in 658. Following the assassination of Ali in 661, Mu'awiya compelled Ali's son and successor Hasan to abdicate and Mu'awiya's suzerainty was acknowledged throughout the Caliphate.
Domestically, Mu'awiya relied on Syria's loyalist Arab tribes and largely Christian bureaucracy. He is credited with establishing government departments responsible for the postal route, correspondence, and chancellery. He was the first caliph whose name appeared on coins, inscriptions, or documents of the nascent Islamic empire. Externally, he engaged his troops in almost yearly land and sea raids against the Byzantines, including a failed siege of Constantinople. In Iraq and the eastern provinces, he delegated authority to the powerful governors al-Mughira and Ziyad ibn Abihi, the latter of whom he controversially adopted as his brother. Under Mu'awiya's direction, the Muslim conquest of Ifriqiya (central North Africa) was launched by the commander Uqba ibn Nafi in 670, while the conquests in Khurasan and Sijistan on the eastern frontier were resumed.
Although Mu'awiya confined the influence of his Umayyad clan to the governorship of Medina, he nominated his own son, Yazid I, as his successor. It was an unprecedented move in Islamic politics and opposition to it by prominent Muslim leaders, including Ali's son Husayn, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, persisted after Mu'awiya's death, culminating with the outbreak of the Second Fitna. While there is considerable admiration for Mu'awiya in the contemporary sources, he has been criticized for lacking the justice and piety of the Rashidun and transforming the office of the caliphate into a kingship. Besides these criticisms, Sunni Muslim tradition honors him as a companion of Muhammad and a scribe of Qur'anic revelation. In Shia Islam, Mu'awiya is reviled for opposing Ali, accused of poisoning his son Hasan, and held to have accepted Islam without conviction.

Origins and early life

Mu'awiya's year of birth is uncertain, with 597, 603 or 605 cited by early Islamic sources. His father Abu Sufyan ibn Harb was a prominent Meccan merchant who led trade caravans to Syria, then part of the Byzantine Empire. He emerged as the leader of the Banu Abd Shams clan of the polytheistic Quraysh, the dominant tribe of Mecca, during the early stages of the Quraysh's conflict with the Islamic prophet Muhammad. The latter also hailed from the Quraysh and was distantly related to Mu'awiya via their common paternal ancestor, Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy. Mu'awiya's mother, Hind bint Utba, was also a member of the Banu Abd Shams.
In 624, Muhammad and his followers attempted to intercept a Meccan caravan led by Mu'awiya's father on its return from Syria, prompting Abu Sufyan to call for reinforcements. The Qurayshite relief army was routed in the ensuing Battle of Badr, in which Mu'awiya's elder brother Hanzala and their maternal grandfather, Utba ibn Rabi'a, were killed. Abu Sufyan replaced the slain leader of the Meccan army, Abu Jahl, and led the Meccans to victory against the Muslims at the Battle of Uhud in 625. After his abortive siege of Muhammad in Medina at the Battle of the Trench in 627, Abu Sufyan lost his leadership position among the Quraysh.
Mu'awiya's father was not a participant in the truce negotiations at Hudaybiyya between the Quraysh and Muhammad in 628. The following year, Muhammad married Mu'awiya's widowed sister Umm Habiba, who had embraced Islam fifteen years earlier. The marriage may have reduced Abu Sufyan's hostility toward Muhammad and Abu Sufyan negotiated with him in Medina in 630 after confederates of the Quraysh violated the Hudaybiyya truce. When Muhammad captured Mecca in 630, Mu'awiya, his father, and his elder brother Yazid embraced Islam. According to accounts cited by the early Muslim historians al-Baladhuri and Ibn Hajar, Mu'awiya had secretly become a Muslim from the time of the Hudaybiyya negotiations. By 632 Muslim authority extended across Arabia with Medina as the seat of the Muslim government. As part of Muhammad's efforts to reconcile with the Quraysh, Mu'awiya was made one of his kātibs (scribes), being one of seventeen literate members of the Quraysh at that time. Abu Sufyan moved to Medina to maintain his newfound influence in the nascent Muslim community.

Governorship of Syria

Early military career and administrative promotions

After Muhammad died in 632, Abu Bakr became caliph (leader of the Muslim community). He and his successors Umar, Uthman, and Ali are often known as the Rashidun ('rightly-guided') caliphs to distinguish them from Mu'awiya and his Umayyad dynastic successors. Having to contend with challenges to his leadership from the Ansar, the natives of Medina who had provided Muhammad safe haven from his erstwhile Meccan opponents, and the mass defections of several Arab tribes, Abu Bakr reached out to the Quraysh, particularly its two strongest clans, the Banu Makhzum and Banu Abd Shams, to shore up support for the Caliphate. Among those Qurayshites whom he appointed to suppress the rebel Arab tribes during the Ridda wars (632–633) was Mu'awiya's brother Yazid. After that war, Yazid was dispatched as one of four commanders in charge of the Muslim conquest of Byzantine Syria in c. 634. The caliph appointed Mu'awiya commander of Yazid's vanguard. Through these appointments Abu Bakr gave the family of Abu Sufyan a stake in the conquest of Syria, where Abu Sufyan already owned property in the vicinity of Damascus.
Abu Bakr's successor Umar (r. 634–644) appointed a leading companion of Muhammad, Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, as the general commander of the Muslim army in Syria in 636 after the rout of the Byzantines at the Battle of Yarmouk, which paved the way for the conquest of the rest of Syria. Mu'awiya was among the Arab troops who entered Jerusalem with Caliph Umar in 637. Afterward, Mu'awiya and Yazid were dispatched by Abu Ubayda to conquer the coastal towns of Sidon, Beirut and Byblos. Following the death of Abu Ubayda in the plague of Amwas in 639, Umar split the command of Syria, appointing Yazid as governor of the military districts of Damascus, Jordan and Palestine, and the veteran commander Iyad ibn Ghanm governor of Homs and the Jazira (Upper Mesopotamia). When Yazid succumbed to the plague later that year, Umar appointed Mu'awiya the military and fiscal governor of Damascus, and possibly Jordan as well.

bio: Mu'awwidh bin 'Afra' (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Mu'awwidh ibn al-Harith ibn Rifa'a, known after his mother as Mu'awwidh ibn 'Afra', was an Ansari Companion of the Banu al-Najjar. His mother was 'Afra' bint 'Ubayd, and his brothers Mu'adh and 'Awf, also known as sons of 'Afra', fought with him at Badr. Ibn Sa'd and al-Dhahabi report, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq alone, that he was among the seventy at the pledge of al-'Aqaba. At Badr he and his brother 'Awf attacked Abu Jahl. Ibn Sa'd and al-Dhahabi relate that the two struck Abu Jahl until he was disabled, that Abu Jahl turned on them and killed them, and that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud then finished him off. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir say that Mu'awwidh is said to have killed Abu Jahl, and that he fought on until he was killed as a martyr at Badr; Ibn 'Abd al-Barr names his killer as Abu Masafi'. Ibn Sa'd records that he had two daughters, al-Rubayyi' and 'Umayra, whose mother was Umm Yazid.

bio: Mu'awwidh bin 'Amr bin al-Jamuh (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Mu'awwidh ibn 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh ibn Zayd ibn Haram al-Ansari al-Salami was a Companion from the Banu Salima of the Ansar. His father was 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, and Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Hind bint 'Amr ibn Haram; through her, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram was his maternal uncle. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir record that he fought at Badr with his brother Mu'adh, and al-Dhahabi says he was there with both his brothers, Mu'adh and Khallad. Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir add that he also fought at Uhud. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and al-Dhahabi note that Ibn Ishaq did not include him among the Badr veterans in most transmissions of his work. Ibn Sa'd states that he left no descendants.

bio: Mu'ayqayb bin Abi Fatima al-Dausi (c. 593–650 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Mu'ayqayb bin Abi Fatima al-Dausi was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 593 CE, he belonged to the Daus tribe and was among the early converts to Islam in Mecca.

Al-Dausi is primarily remembered for his participation in the first major emigration of Muslims from Mecca to Abyssinia (modern-day Ethiopia), which occurred around 615 CE. This migration, known as the Hijra to Abyssinia, was undertaken by a small group of early Muslims who faced increasing persecution from the Meccan tribes opposed to the new faith. The Prophet Muhammad advised these followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, whose ruler was known for his justice and tolerance.

The emigrants to Abyssinia represented some of the most committed early believers who were willing to leave their homeland, families, and tribal connections for their faith. This group included both men and women from various Meccan clans, and their successful settlement in Abyssinia demonstrated Islam's early encounter with Christian communities and the possibility of peaceful coexistence between the two faiths.

As one of the Sahaba, or companions of the Prophet, al-Dausi held a respected position within the early Muslim community. The Sahaba were those who had direct contact with Muhammad, believed in his message, and supported the establishment of the Islamic community. Their testimonies and experiences formed crucial sources for understanding the early period of Islamic history and the development of Islamic teachings and practices.

Al-Dausi's identification with the early ascetic tradition suggests he may have been among those companions who emphasized spiritual discipline, simple living, and devotion to worship. The early ascetic movement within Islam valued detachment from worldly concerns and focused on spiritual purification and closeness to God.

He died around 650 CE, during the early expansion period of the Islamic community under the Rashidun Caliphate. His life spanned the crucial decades that saw Islam's emergence in Mecca, the community's migration to Medina, and the subsequent establishment of the first Islamic state. As one of the early emigrants and companions, his story reflects the sacrifices and commitment of the first generation of Muslims who helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization.

bio: Mu'ttib bin Qushayr bin Mulayl (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Mu'ttib bin Qushayr bin Mulayl was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who embraced Islam and became part of the community that formed around the Prophet in the Arabian Peninsula.

Mu'ttib is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds immense significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. The engagement marked a turning point for the early Muslim state based in Medina, and those who participated alongside the Prophet in this battle are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition. The Companions of Badr are considered to hold a special status among the Sahaba due to their early commitment to Islam and their presence during this crucial moment.

As a companion of the Prophet, Mu'ttib would have been part of the immediate circle of Muslims who lived during the Prophet's lifetime and had direct contact with him. This status places him among the most important early figures in Islamic history, as the companions collectively served as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings, practices, and the Prophet's sayings and actions to subsequent generations.

His association with hadith sciences indicates his role in the preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge. The companions were the foundational link in the chain of transmission that preserved the prophetic traditions, which became essential sources for Islamic law, theology, and practice. Through their testimonies and teachings, the religious and social framework of Islam was established and passed down to later Muslim generations.

Mu'ttib died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate that followed the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This places his death during a period of rapid expansion and consolidation of the Islamic state under the first caliph, Abu Bakr. His relatively short life span of approximately forty years encompassed the entire prophetic period and the initial phase of Islamic political development, making him a witness to the complete transformation of Arabian society and the emergence of Islam as a major religious and political force.

full: Muadh ibn Jabal ibn Amr al-Ansari al-Khazraji
primaryTitle: Imam al-Halal wa'l-Haram — Master of What is Permitted
titles: Imam al-Halal wa'l-Haram
bio: Abu Abd al-Rahman, Muadh ibn Jabal, al-Ansari, al-Khazraji, al-Madani, a companion, a jurist, a reciter of the Qur’an, a narrator of the Prophet’s hadith, from the Ansar, from the Banu Uday, from Banu Jashm ibn Al-Khazraj. He converted to Islam when he was 18 years old, and he witnessed the Second Pledge of Aqaba, then he witnessed all the scenes with the Prophet Muhammad, and he succeeded Muaz and Abu Musa Al-Ash’ari in Mecca after its conquest. They taught people the Qur’an and jurisprudence in religion, then used it on Yemen after the Battle of Tabuk. Then, after the death of the Prophet Muhammad, he witnessed the Islamic conquest in the Levant. He died in the Levant during the plague of Emmaus.
bio_full:
Muʿādh ibn Jabal (Arabic: مُعاذ بن جبل; 603 – 639) was a sahabi (companion) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Muadh was an Ansar of the Banu Khazraj tribe and compiled the Quran with five companions while Muhammad was still alive. He acquired a reputation for knowledge.
Muhammad called him "the one who will lead the scholars into Paradise".

Biography

Era of Muhammad
Mu'adh accepted Islam before the Second pledge at al-Aqabah in submission before Muhammad. Nevertheless, he was one of those who took the pledge. He was a major companion.
Muhammad sent Mu'adh as the governor of Yemen to collect zakat. When Muhammad sent Mu'adh to Yemen to teach its people about Islam, he personally bade farewell to him, walking for some distance alongside him as he set out to leave the city. It is said that Muhammad informed him that on his return to Medina, he would perhaps see only his masjid and grave. Upon hearing this, Mu'adh began to cry.

After Muhammad
Mu'adh died in 639 due to the Plague of 'Amwas.

Legacy
The college for the study of Shariah law, at Mosul University in Iraq, is named after him.
A mosque in the town of Hamtramck, Michigan, is named Masjid Mu'ath bin Jabal. There is also a mosque named Masjid Mu'adh-ibn-Jabal which is conveniently located on the outskirts of Leicester City Centre, UK in the popular Goodwood area of the city. The Masjid serves the local Muslim community of over 500 Muslim families located in and around Uppingham Road, col Road, Wakerley Road and Spencefield Lane.
There is a Mosque in Crosby, Johannesburg named after him and an accompanying islamic school or Madressah bearing his name. Located on Jamestown avenue it serves as the main Mosque in the Crosby area and surrounds. Masjid Mu’adh Bin Jabal also had a borehole dug which provides free water to all who are in need.

Sayings
Al-Bayhaqi narrated in Shu`ab al-Iman (1:392 #512-513), and so did al-Tabarani, that Mu`adh ibn Jabal narrated that Muhammad said: "The People of Paradise will not regret except one thing alone: the hour that passed them by and in which they made no remembrance of Allah." Ali ibn Abu Bakr al-Haythami in Majma al-Zawa'id (10:74) said that its narrators are all trustworthy (thiqat), while Suyuti declared it hasan in his Jami` al-Saghir (#7701).
Ibn al-Jawzi recorded in Siffatu Safwah that Mu'adh advised his son, "My son! Pray the prayer of he who is just about to leave and imagine that you might not be able to pray ever again.

bio: Mubashshir bin 'Abdul Mundhir (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Mubashshir bin 'Abdul Mundhir was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the crucial early years of the Islamic community.

Mubashshir is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the outnumbered Muslim army.

The Battle of Badr is considered a turning point in early Islamic history, as it demonstrated the military capability of the Muslim community and helped establish their political presence in the Arabian Peninsula. Those who participated in this battle, known as the Badr companions, held a special status within the early Muslim community due to their role in this pivotal event.

Mubashshir's life was cut short in 624 CE, the same year as the Battle of Badr, though the specific circumstances of his death are not clearly documented in available historical sources. His relatively brief lifespan of approximately thirty years encompassed the emergence of Islam and the critical early period of the Prophet Muhammad's mission in Medina.

As a member of the Sahaba, the companions of the Prophet Muhammad, Mubashshir was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community. The companions played essential roles in the transmission of Islamic teachings and the early expansion of the faith beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While detailed accounts of Mubashshir's individual contributions and personal characteristics are limited in the historical record, his participation in the Battle of Badr ensures his place in Islamic historical memory. The Badr companions are remembered collectively for their commitment to the early Muslim community during a period of significant challenge and transformation in seventh-century Arabia.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Mubushir bin al-Bara' bin Ma'rur (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Mubushir bin al-Bara' bin Ma'rur was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 600 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. He was among the early Muslims who became part of the community in Medina during the formative period of Islam in the early 7th century.

Mubushir is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant oath of allegiance taken by Muslim companions to the Prophet Muhammad. This pledge, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, took place at al-Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE when tensions arose during negotiations for the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah with the Meccan tribes. The Quran references this event in chapter 48, verse 18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those believers who pledged their allegiance under the tree.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, Mubushir belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community. The companions held a special status in Islamic tradition as the first recipients and transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices.

The Pledge of Ridwan was considered a pivotal moment in early Islamic history, demonstrating the loyalty and commitment of the Muslim community during a critical period of negotiations with Mecca. Those who participated in this pledge were viewed as having shown exceptional dedication to the faith and to the Prophet's mission.

Mubushir lived during the rapid expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula and into the broader Middle East. His lifetime spanned the Prophetic period in Medina, the establishment of the first Islamic state, and the early conquests under the Rashidun Caliphate following Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

He died around 640 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, when the Islamic empire was expanding into Syria, Iraq, and other regions. Like many companions of his generation, Mubushir witnessed the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to a major political and religious force across much of the known world.

His inclusion among those mentioned in connection with the Pledge of Ridwan ensures his place in Islamic historical memory as one of the early faithful who supported the Prophet during challenging circumstances.

bio: Mudar ibn Nizār (c. 25 BCE–c. 40 CE) was a founding figure, based in Mecca. Known as Ancestor of Prophet Muhammad.
bio_full:
Mudar ibn Nizar (Arabic: مضر بن نزار) is the traditional eponymous ancestor of the Mudar, one of the most powerful northern Arab tribal groupings.

The tradition states that Muhammad was the son of 'Abdullah, b. 'Abdu'I-Muttalib (whose name

was Shayba), b. Hashim (whose name was 'Amr), b. Abd Manaf (whose

name was al-Mughira), b. Qusay (whose name was Zayd), b. Kilab, b.

Murrah, b. Ka'b, b. Lu'ayy, b. Ghalib, b. Fihr, b. Malik, b. al-Nadr, b.

Kinana, b. Khuzayma, b. Mudrika (whose name was 'Amir), b. Ilyas,

b. Mudar, b. Nizar, b. Ma'add, b. Adnan, b. Udd (or Udad),.... b. Qedar, b. Isma'il, b. Ibrahim, the friend of the Compassionate.

According to the Arab genealogists, Mudar was the son of Nizar ibn Ma'ad ibn Adnan by Sawda bint Akk ibn Adnan. He had one full brother, Iyad, and two half-brothers, Rabi'a (who gave his name to the other major tribal grouping) and Anmar. A well-known story is told of how the brothers divided their heritage after their father's death, resulting in Mudar gaining the epithet "the Red" (al-ḥamrāʿ) because he received his father's red tent.

Mudar settled in Mecca, and was buried in al-Rawha, where his tomb became a site of pilgrimage in later centuries. Mudar had two sons: Ilyas (also known as al-Yas), and Aylan al-Nas. Through his sons, Ilyas was the ancestor of the Banu Hudhayl, Banu Asad, Banu Tamim, and Banu Kinana—which includes the Quraysh, the tribe of Muhammad and the early caliphs—while Aylan was the ancestor of the Qays tribes).

The Mudar and Rabi'a are recorded in central Arabia in the Arabic histories of the pre-Islamic period; the kings of the Kindah bore the title of "king of the Ma'add (or Mudar) and Rabi'a", and they played a role in the conflicts with the Yemeni (southern Arab) tribes.

bio: Mudlij bin 'Amr al-Salmi (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Mudlij bin 'Amr al-Salmi was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of the Islamic community.

Al-Salmi is most notably recognized for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle, fought between the early Muslim community and the Meccan Quraysh tribe, holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslims under Prophet Muhammad's leadership. Those who participated in Badr are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition, as they are considered to have demonstrated their commitment to the faith during a critical and uncertain period.

As a sahabi, Mudlij was part of the generation that directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the revelation of the Quran. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, practices, and historical accounts to subsequent generations. Their testimonies and narrations became foundational sources for understanding early Islamic history and religious practice.

Al-Salmi is associated with the tradition of early Islamic asceticism, suggesting he may have been among those companions who emphasized spiritual discipline, simplicity, and devotion in their religious practice. This ascetic tendency was present among some of the early Muslims who sought to emulate the Prophet's example of modest living and spiritual focus.

His death in 634 CE places him during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing means he lived through the entire prophetic period and the beginning of the caliphate under Abu Bakr, witnessing the rapid expansion of the Islamic community from a small group in Mecca to a significant political and religious force in the Arabian Peninsula.

The preservation of his name and designation as a Companion of Badr reflects the importance placed by early Muslim historians on documenting those who participated in the foundational events of Islam, ensuring their contributions to the early community would be remembered by future generations of Muslims.

bio: Mudriqa bin Elias bin Mudar, whose name is Amer, the fifteenth grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad bin Abdullah, the master of the Arabs in the Hijaz, and one of the great nobles of the Mudriqa tribes. His nickname is Abu Hudhail.
bio_full:
Mudrikah ibn Ilyas (Arabic: مُدْرِكَة ٱبْن إِلْيَاس), was a tribal leader in the era of pre-Islamic Arabia. Mudrikah is the father of Hudhayl, who would be the progenitor of the Banu Hudhayl tribe. He is also one of the ancestors of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

According to Ibn Ishaq, the full ancestral lineage of Mudrikah is Mudrikah, son of Ilyas, son of Mudar, son of Nizar, son of Ma'ad, son of Adnan and several generations leading back to Ishmael and Abraham.

Mudrikah, real name Amir, is the son of Ilyas ibn Mudar; with Ilyas being a fourth-generation descendant of the South Arabian patriach Adnan. He had two brothers named Tabikha and Qam'ah, whose real names were 'Amr and 'Umayr respectively. Mudrikah married an Arab woman named Salmah whose origins are disputed; some have claimed her from the tribe of the Quda'a while others claimed she was from Rabi'a ibn Nizar.

From Salmah, he had two sons named Hudhayl and Khuzaymah. Hudhayl was the ancestor of the Banu Hudhayl. Khuzaymah is remembered as the ancestor who connects the lineage of the Islamic prophet Muhammad to Mudrikah and hence to Adnan.

According to a Twelver Shi'ite narration in the book Bihar al-Anwar, Mudrikah and his descendants were monotheists who were saved from falling into polytheism due to being an ancestor of Muhammad.

full: Muḥammad ʿAbduh Ibrāhīm Khudra Abū al-ʿIlm
primaryTitle: Grand Mufti of Egypt — Father of Islamic Modernism
titles: Grand Mufti of Egypt
bio: Muhammad Abduh, an Egyptian Islamic thinker, religious scholar, jurist, judge, and writer, is considered one of the advocates of renaissance and reform in the Arab and Islamic world, and a symbol of renewal in Islamic jurisprudence. After meeting with his teacher, Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, he contributed to the establishment of an Islamic renewal intellectual movement in the late nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth century, aiming to eliminate intellectual and civilizational stagnation and revitalize the Islamic nation to keep pace with the requirements of the times.
bio_full:
Muḥammad ʿAbduh (also spelled Mohammed Abduh; Arabic: محمد عبده; 1849 – 11 July 1905) was an Egyptian Islamic scholar, judge, and Grand Mufti of Egypt. He was a central figure of the Arab Nahḍa and Islamic Modernism in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
He began teaching advanced students esoteric Islamic texts at Al-Azhar University while he was still studying there. From 1877, with the status of ʿālim, he taught logic, theology, ethics, and politics. He was also made a professor of history at Dar al-ʿUlūm the following year, and of Arabic language and literature at Madrasat al-Alsun. ʿAbduh was a champion of the press and wrote prolifically in Al-Manār and Al-Ahram. He was made editor of Al-Waqa'i' al-Misriyya in 1880. He also authored Risālat at-Tawḥīd (Arabic: رسالة التوحيد; "The Theology of Unity") and a commentary on the Quran. He briefly published the pan-Islamist anti-colonial newspaper al-ʿUrwa al-Wuthqā alongside his teacher and mentor Jamāl ad-Dīn al-Afghānī.
ʿAbduh joined Freemasonry and subscribed to various Masonic lodges alongside his mentor al-Afghānī and his other pupils, but eventually left the secret society in his later years. He was appointed as a judge in the Courts of First Instance of the Native Tribunals in 1888, a consultative member of the Court of Appeal in 1899, and he was appointed Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyyah in 1899.

Biography
Muḥammad ʿAbduh was born in 1849 to a father with Turkish ancestry and an Egyptian mother in the Nile Delta. His family was part of the Ottoman Egyptian elite: his father was part of the Umad, or the local ruling elite, while his mother was part of the Ashraf. He was educated in Tanta at a private school. When he turned thirteen, he was sent to the Aḥmadī mosque, which was one of the largest educational institutions in Egypt. A while later, ʿAbduh ran away from school and got married. After a brief period following his marriage, ʿAbduh returned to his school in Tanta. During this period, ʿAbduh studied under the tutelage of his Sufi Muslim uncle Dārwīsh, who was a member of the revivalist and reformist Madaniyya Tarîqâh, a popular branch of the Shadhiliyya order, spread across Egypt, Libya, Algeria, and Tunisia. Apart from spiritual exercises, the order also emphasised proper practice of Islam, shunning taqlid and stressing adherence to foundational teachings. Under the tutelage of his uncle, ʿAbduh began to practice the litany of the Madaniyya. Like many of his fellow students in Tanta, the experience would transform ʿAbduh towards Sufi asceticism with mystical orientations. Abduh would inherit many of his subsequent public views, such as firm opposition to taqlid from his Sufi uncle.

ʿAbduh suffered from acute spiritual crises in his youth, similar to those experienced by the medieval Muslim scholar and Sufi mystic al-Ghazali. He was heavily dissatisfied with the traditional education and representatives of mainstream ulama of his time. Under the influence of Shaykh Dārwīsh al-Khadīr, Tasawwuf provided an alternative form of religiosity which would profoundly shape ʿAbduh's spiritual and intellectual formation. As ʿAbduh would subsequently emerge as a towering scholarly intellectual in Egypt, he concurrently assumed his role as a traditional Sufi Muslim. Tasawwuf as taught to ʿAbduh by Shaykh Dārwīsh transcended the perceived limitations and superficialities of traditional Islamic learning, and was based on an Islamic religiosity led by an intellectual, charismatic authority. For ʿAbduh, Shaykh Dārwīsh and his teachings represented orthodox Sufism, which was different from the Sufi folklore and the charlatans prevalent in rural Egypt during the early modern era. Explaining his conversion to Sufism under the training of Shaykh Dārwīsh, 'Abduh wrote: "On the seventh day, I asked the shaykh: What is your tarîqâh? He replied: Islam is my tarıqa. I asked: But are not all these people Muslims? He said: If they were Muslims, you would not see them contending over trivial matters and would not hear them swearing by God while they are lying with or without a reason. These words were like fire which burned away all that I held dear of the baggage from the past."
In 1866, ʿAbduh enrolled at al-Azhar University in Cairo, where he studied logic, Islamic philosophy, theology, and Sufism. He was a student of Jamāl al-Dīn al-Afghānī, a Muslim philosopher and religious reformer who advocated Pan-Islamism to resist European colonialism. During his studies in al-Azhar, ʿAbduh had continued to express his critiques of the traditional curriculum and traditional modes of repetition. For him, al-Afghānī combined personal charisma with a fresh intellectual approach which the ulama of al-Azhar couldn't provide. As a young 22 year-old Sufi mystic seeking a charismatic guide and alternative modes of learning and religiosity, ʿAbduh chose al-Afghānī as his murshid. Their murid–murshid relationship would last for eight years and al-Afghānī was able to meet the expectations of his young disciple. Under al-Afghani's influence, ʿAbduh combined journalism, politics, and his own fascination with Islamic mystical spirituality. Al-Afghānī enriched ʿAbduh's mysticism with a philosophical underpinning and thereby drew him to a rationalist interpretations of Islam. Al-Afghānī's lessons merged his Sufi mysticism with the esoteric and theosophic tradition of Persian Shīʿīsm. He also taught ʿAbduh about the problems of Egypt and the Islamic world, and about the technological achievements of the Western civilization.
In 1877, ʿAbduh was granted the degree of ʿālim ("teacher") and he started to teach logic, Islamic theology, and ethics at al-Azhar University. In 1878, he was appointed professor of history at Cairo's teachers' training college Dar al-ʿUlūm, later incorporated into Cairo University. He was also appointed to teach Arabic at the Khedivial School of Languages. He is regarded as one of the key founding figures of Islamic Modernism, sometimes called "Neo-Muʿtazilism" after the homonymous medieval school of Islamic theology based on rationalism. ʿAbduh was also appointed editor-in-chief of al-Waqāʾiʿ al-Miṣriyya, the official newspaper of Egypt. He was dedicated to reforming all aspects of Egyptian society and believed that education was the best way to achieve this goal. He was in favor of a good religious education, which would strengthen a child's morals, and a scientific education, which would nurture a child's ability to reason. In his articles he criticized corruption, superstition, and the luxurious lives of the rich.
In 1879, due to his political activism, al-Afghānī was exiled and ʿAbduh was exiled to his home village. The following year he was granted control of the national gazette and used this as a means to spread his anti-colonial ideas, and the need for social and religious reforms. He was exiled from Egypt by the British forces in 1882 for six years, for supporting the Egyptian nationalist ʻUrabi revolt led by Ahmed ʻUrabi in 1879. He had stated that every society should be allowed to choose a suitable form of government based on its history and its present circumstances. ʿAbduh spent several years in Ottoman Lebanon, where he helped establish an Islamic educational system. In 1884 he moved to Paris in France, where he joined al-Afghānī in publishing al-ʿUrwa al-Wuthqā, an Islamic revolutionary journal that promoted anti-British views. ʿAbduh also visited Britain and discussed the state of Egypt and Sudan with high-ranking officials. In 1885, after brief stays in England and Tunisia, he returned to Beirut as a teacher, and was surrounded by scholars from different religious backgrounds. During his stay, he dedicated his efforts toward furthering respect and friendship between Islam, Christianity, and Judaism.

When he returned to Egypt in 1888, ʿAbduh began his legal career.

full: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib al-Hashimi
primaryTitle: Al-Baqir — The Splitter of Knowledge; 5th Imam and Father of Islamic Sciences
titles: Al-Baqir (Splitter/Disseminator of Knowledge) · Abu Jafar · 5th Imam in Shia tradition · Father of Islamic jurisprudence in the Alid tradition
teachers: Jabir ibn Abd Allah al-Ansari (last surviving companion)
quranRef: Q33:33 (verse of purification, revealed for his family)
bio: Abu Jafar Muhammad bin Ali bin Al-Hussein bin Ali bin Abi Talib, Al-Hashimi, Al-Alawi, Al-Madani, Al-Qurashi, Al-Baqir The fifth imam according to the Imami Shiites and (the Ismailis) and one of the infallibles and the Ahl al-Bayt according to the Shiite belief. His father is Ali bin Al-Hussein bin Ali bin Abi Talib and his mother is Fatima bint Al-Hassan bin Ali bin Abi Talib.
bio_full:
Muhammad ibn Ali al-Baqir (Arabic: محمد بن علي الباقر, romanized: Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Bāqir; c. 676 – c. 732) was a descendant of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and the fifth of the twelve Shia imams, succeeding his father, Ali al-Sajjad, and succeeded by his son, Ja'far al-Sadiq. Muhammad's honorific title al-Baqir is short for baqir al-ilm, which means 'the one who splits knowledge open', a reference to his fame as a religious scholar.
Muhammad was born in Medina around 676 CE. In 680, when he was a small child, he witnessed the Battle of Karbala, where his grandfather Husayn ibn Ali and most of his relatives were massacred by the forces of the Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn Mu'awiya (r. 680–683). Upon his father's death around 712, Muhammad was recognised as the next imam by most followers of his father. These were the Imamites, the forerunners of Twelvers and Isma'ilis, which now constitute the majority of Shia Muslims. At the time, however, this quiescent group was a minority compared to other rival Shia groups, who actively worked against the Umayyads. One such rival group were Zaydis. These followed Zayd ibn Ali, a much younger half-brother of al-Baqir, who staged an unsuccessful revolt shortly after al-Baqir's death. In contrast, like his father, al-Baqir was politically quiescent but was nevertheless harassed by the Umayyads, especially by Caliph Hisham (r. 724–743).
Muhammad al-Baqir led a pious and scholarly life in Medina, attracting a growing number of followers, students, and visitors. He is credited with laying the doctrinal and legal foundations of Twelver Shi'ism during some twenty years of his imamate. He may also be regarded as the father of Isma'ili and Zaydi jurisprudence. Finally, he significantly contributed to Twelver exegesis of the Quran. Most of al-Baqir's disciples were based in Kufa, in present-day Iraq, many of whom later became outstanding Shia jurists and traditionists. Some of these, such as Zurara ibn A'yan, may have occasionally disagreed with al-Baqir, who disapproved of such independent views if they went beyond the general theological and legal framework provided by (Shia) imams. In Sunni Islam, al-Baqir is regarded as an authority in law and prophetic tradition, but portrayed as anti-Shia and proto-Sunni.
Muhammad al-Baqir died around 732, poisoned by the Umayyads, according to most Shia reports. He is buried in the Baqi Cemetery in Medina, but the shrine that stood over his grave has been demolished twice by Wahhabis. Al-Baqir was succeeded by his eldest son, Ja'far al-Sadiq, who further developed Shia theology and law.

Ancestry
Muhammad al-Baqir was a descendant of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, through both of his grandsons, namely, Hasan and Husayn, who were the second and third of the twelve Shia imams, respectively. More specifically, al-Baqir's father was Husayn's son, Ali al-Sajjad, the fourth of the twelve imams. Muhammad's mother was Fatima Umm Abd Allah, while his maternal grandfather was Hasan.
Hasan and Husayn were the eldest sons of the first Shia imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib, through his first wife, Fatima, daughter of the Islamic prophet.

Titles
Muhammad's kunya is Abu Ja'far, and his honorific title is al-Baqir, short for baqir al-'ilm, which means either 'the one who splits knowledge open' (brings it to light) or 'the one who possesses great knowledge', both of which are references to Muhammad's fame as a religious scholar.
By some accounts, Muhammad was already known in his lifetime by the title al-Baqir. Shia sources posit that this title was designated by the Islamic prophet, who sent his greetings via his companion Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who lived long enough to meet al-Baqir in his childhood. According to another Shia account, Caliph Hisham, a contemporary of al-Baqir, contemptuously referred to him as al-baqara (lit. 'the cow'), which again suggests that he was known by this title in his lifetime. The occasion was the caliph's meeting with al-Baqir's half brother, Zayd ibn Ali, who reprimanded Hisham and attributed al-Baqir's title to the Islamic prophet.

Biography
Muhammad al-Baqir was born in Medina in about 676 CE (56 AH). Twelver Shias annually celebrate this occasion on the third of Safar. In 680, when Muhammad was a small child, his grandfather Husayn and most of his male relatives were massacred in the Battle of Karbala by forces of the Umayyad caliph Yazid. Muhammad was present in Karbala and witnessed the carnage. Muhammad's youth coincided with power struggles between the Umayyads, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and various Shia groups, while Muhammad's father, al-Sajjad, stayed aloof from politics. When al-Sajjad died around 712, most of his followers accepted the imamate of his son Muhammad, who was about thirty-seven years old. He lived a quiet pious life in Medina, like his father, but was nevertheless harassed by the Umayyads, especially by Caliph Hisham. Muhammad, however, enjoyed certain liberties because the Umayyads were more lenient in this period, or perhaps because they were busy infighting and quelling revolts. During the next twenty years or so, Muhammad al-Baqir thus expounded Shia doctrines and laws, attracting a growing number of followers, students, and visitors.

Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705)
The fifth Umayyad caliph, Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, is credited with issuing an Islamic gold coinage for the first time to replace Byzantine coins. This was likely done at the suggestion of al-Baqir.

Umar II (r. 717–720)
Often praised for his piety, the Umayyad caliph Umar II was favorably disposed to al-Baqir. After meeting with him, the caliph apparently returned the disputed lands of Fadak to Alids, that is, descendants of Ali ibn Abi Talib. In a Sunni tradition, likely circulated by anti-Alids, al-Baqir identifies Umar II as the Mahdi, the promised savior in Islam. In a Shia tradition, however, al-Baqir suggests that Umar's good deeds would not redeem him, for he had usurped the imam's right to rule.

Hisham (r. 724–743)
Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik summoned al-Baqir to the Umayyad capital Damascus several times and imprisoned him at least once. During these visits, the caliph apparently held theological debates in which al-Baqir emerged victorious. On one occasion, the caliph ordered al-Baqir to join an ongoing archery practice, probably hoping to embarrass him, but was astonished by al-Baqir's excellent marksmanship.

Death
Although 732 (114 AH) and 735 (117 AH) are commonly reported, there is considerable disagreement about when al-Baqir died, ranging from 732 to 736. He was about fifty-seven years old at the time, and most likely died before Zayd's revolt in 740. Twelvers annually commemorate his death on the seventh of Dhu al-Hijja.
As with the rest of the twelve imams, Shia sources report that al-Baqir was killed. There is no consensus about the details, and different sources accuse Hisham or his successor, al-Walid II (r. 743–744), of poisoning al-Baqir. According to another account, al-Baqir was poisoned by his cousin, Zayd ibn al-Hasan, once the latter failed to wrest control of the Islamic prophet's inheritance from al-Baqir.

Al-Baqir is buried in the Al-Baqi Cemetery in Medina. A shrine stood over his grave until its demolition in 1806 and then again around 1925, both times carried out by Wahhabis.

Imamate
After al-Sajjad, most of his followers accepted the imamate of his eldest son Muhammad. These were the Imamites, who were the forerunners of Twelver and Isma'ili Shias. Twelver and Isma'ili sources indeed report that al-Sajjad had earlier designated al-Baqir as his successor. Followers of al-Baqir, however, were in minority compared to the rival Kaysanites, which was a (now-extinct) Shia group that traced the imamate through Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, son of Ali ibn Abi Talib and Khawla bint Ja'far, a woman from the Banu Hanifa tribe.

full: Al-Hajj Umar ibn Said Tall al-Futi
primaryTitle: Al-Hajj Umar Tal — Jihad of the Pen and Sword
titles: Al-Hajj Umar · Amir al-Muminin
bio: Al-Hajj Umar ibn Said Tall al-Futi (1794–1864) was a historical figure of the Qadiriyya tradition, based in Futa Toro. Known as Al-Hajj Umar Tal — Jihad of the Pen and Sword.
bio_full:
Al-Hajj Umar ibn Said Tall al-Futi was a prominent 19th-century West African Islamic reformer and military leader who played a significant role in spreading Islam across the region. Born in 1794 in Futa Toro, located in present-day Senegal, he belonged to the Fula ethnic group and became deeply associated with the Qadiriyya Sufi order, one of the major mystical traditions in Islam.

Umar Tall earned the title "Al-Hajj" after completing the pilgrimage to Mecca, a journey that profoundly influenced his religious and political outlook. During his extended travels in the Islamic world, he studied with various scholars and was appointed as a khalifa (representative) of the Tijaniyya Sufi order, which would later become central to his mission. Upon returning to West Africa, he established himself as a religious teacher and began building a following among local communities.

He is historically known for leading what became known as the Umarian jihad, a military and religious campaign that sought to establish Islamic states across the Western Sudan region. His movement combined religious reform with political conquest, aiming to purify Islamic practice and expand Muslim territories. Umar Tall's forces conquered significant portions of present-day Mali, Guinea, and Senegal, establishing the Toucouleur Empire, which became one of the largest states in 19th-century West Africa.

His approach earned him the designation as a practitioner of "Jihad of the Pen and Sword," reflecting his dual emphasis on Islamic scholarship and military action. He was known for his writings on Islamic law and theology, while simultaneously organizing and leading military campaigns against both traditional African kingdoms and French colonial forces.

Umar Tall's significance in Islamic history lies in his role as a major figure in the 19th-century Islamic revival movements in West Africa. His efforts contributed to the further Islamization of the region and demonstrated the complex interactions between religious reform, political power, and resistance to European colonialism. His empire continued to influence the political and religious landscape of West Africa even after his death in 1864, and his legacy remains important in understanding the spread and development of Islam in sub-Saharan Africa during the colonial period.

full: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Ridha al-Jawad al-Taqi al-Hashimi
primaryTitle: Imam al-Jawad — Ninth Imam; Youngest Imam at Age 9
titles: al-Jawad (The Generous) · al-Taqi (The God-Fearing) · Ninth Imam
bio: Abu Jaafar Muhammad bin Ali Al-Jawad is the ninth of the twelve imams of the Twelver Shiites, and he is the eleventh of the fourteen infallibles. He was a contemporary of two of the Abbasid caliphs, Al-Ma’mun and Al-Mu’tasim, and he died during the latter’s caliphate. He was also a contemporary of the Waqifi sect, which believes that the imamate stopped with his grandfather, Musa al-Kadhim, and does not believe in the imamate after him. (1)
bio_full:
Muhammad ibn Ali al-Jawad (Arabic: مُحَمَّدٌ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ ٱلْجَوَادُ, romanized: Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Jawād, c. 8 April 811 – c. 29 November 835) was a descendant of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and the ninth of the Twelve Imams, succeeding his father, Ali al-Rida (d. 818). He is known by the epithets al-Jawād (Arabic: الجواد, lit. 'the generous') and al-Taqī (Arabic: التقي, lit. 'the pious'). Like most of his predecessors, Muhammad kept aloof from politics and engaged in religious teaching, while organizing the affairs of the Imamite Shia community through a network of representatives (wukalāʾ). The extensive correspondence of al-Jawad with his followers on questions of Islamic law has been preserved in Shia sources and numerous pithy religio-ethical sayings are also attributed to him.
Born in Medina in 810–811, Muhammad al-Jawad was the son of Ali al-Rida, the eighth of the Twelve Imams. In 817, the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833) summoned al-Rida to Khorasan and designated him as the heir apparent, possibly to mitigate the frequent Shia revolts. This appointment provoked strong opposition in Iraq, which forced al-Ma'mun to return to the capital Baghdad in 818 and abandon his pro-Shia policies. On the way back to Baghdad, al-Rida suddenly fell ill and died in Tus, likely poisoned by order of al-Ma'mun as he made concessions to the opposition. Upon the death of al-Rida in 818, the succession of his only son Muhammad to the imamate at the age of about seven became controversial. Most Imamite Shias accepted the imamate of al-Jawad because the Imam, in their view, received his perfect religious knowledge through divine inspiration, irrespective of his age. At the time, some instead turned for leadership to al-Jawad's uncle, Ahmad ibn Musa al-Kazim, and some others joined the Waqifites, but the succession of al-Jawad evidently did not create any permanent divisions in the Shia community. Twelver sources often justify the imamate of the young al-Jawad by drawing parallels with Jesus and John the Baptist, both of whom in the Quran received their prophetic missions in childhood.
In 830, al-Jawad was summoned to Baghdad by al-Ma'mun, who married his daughter Umm Fadhl to the former. This marriage, however, was to be without issue and might have been infelicitous. His successor, Ali al-Hadi, was already born in 828 to Samana, a freed slave (umm walad). In 833, al-Ma'mun died and was succeeded by his brother, al-Mu'tasim (r. 833–842), who summoned al-Jawad to Baghdad in 835 and hosted him and his wife, possibly to investigate any links between al-Jawad and new Shia revolts. There al-Jawad died in the same year at the age of about twenty-five. All major Sunni sources are silent about the manner of his death, while Shia authorities are nearly unanimous that he was poisoned by his disaffected wife, Umm al-Fadl, at the instigation of her uncle, al-Mu'tasim. Muhammad al-Jawad was buried next to his grandfather, Musa al-Kazim, the seventh of the Twelve Imams, in the cemetery of the Quraysh, where the Kazimayn shrine was later erected. Kazimayn has since become an important center for pilgrimage.

Titles
Muhammad ibn Ali, the ninth of the Twelve Imams, is occasionally known in Shia sources as al-Taqi (Arabic: التقى, lit. 'the pious'), but more commonly as al-Jawad (Arabic: الجواد, lit. 'the generous') for his munificence. The Imam is cited in the Shia hadith literature as Abu Ja'far al-Thani (Arabic: ابو جعفر الثاني, lit. 'Abu Ja'far, the second'), with the title Abu Ja'far reserved for his predecessor, Muhammad al-Baqir (d. 732), the fifth of the Twelve Imams. His kunya is Abu Ali (Arabic: ابو علي), though he was also known by his contemporaries as Ibn al-Rida (Arabic: ابن الرضا, lit. 'son of al-Rida') because he was the only child of Ali al-Rida.

Life

Birth (c. 810)
Muhammad al-Jawad was born in Medina, or in a village near Medina founded by his grandfather, Musa al-Kazim (d. 799). Sources seem to agree that he was born 195 AH (810–811) but the exact date is disputed. Most Twelver sources record mid-Ramadan 195 AH (mid-June 811) as the birthday of Muhammad but Ibn Ayyas (d. 1522/1524) favors 10 Rajab 195 AH (8 April 811). This latter date agrees with Ziyarat al-Nahiya al-Muqaddasa, a supplication attributed to Muhammad al-Mahdi, the last of the Twelve Imams. It is this date that the Shia celebrate annually. His father Ali al-Rida, the eighth of the Twelve Imams, was a descendant of Ali ibn Abi Talib (d. 661) and Fatima (d. 632), who were the cousin and the daughter of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, respectively. Most records agree that the mother of Muhammad al-Jawad was a freed slave (umm walad) from Nubia, though her name is given differently in sources as Sabika or Durra (sometimes Khayzuran). She might have belonged to the family of Maria al-Qibtiyya, a freed slave of the prophet and the mother of his son Ibrahim, who died in childhood.

Reign of al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833)

Marriage (c. 817)
Muhammad stayed behind in Medina when his father al-Rida traveled to Merv in Khorasan at the request of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833). The caliph designated al-Rida as the heir apparent in 202 AH (817), and also changed the official Abbasid color of black to green, possibly to signify this reconciliation between the Abbasids and the Alids. To form a political alliance, the caliph also married one of his daughters, named Umm Habib, to al-Rida in 202 AH (817) and promised another daughter, named Umm al-Fadl, to Muhammad, who was still a minor at the time, aged about seven. Among Sunni historians, al-Tabari (d. 923), Ibn Abi Tahir Tayfur (d. 893), and Ibn al-Athir al-Jazari (d. 1232–1233) agree on this report. It is likely that Muhammad was absent from the ceremony, even though Abu'l-Hasan Bayhaqi (d. 1169) relates that he visited his father in Merv in 202 AH (817). In contrast, the Sunni historian al-Khatib al-Baghdadi (d. 1071) and the Shia-leaning historians Al-Masudi (d. 956) and Ya'qubi (d. 897–898) place the betrothal of Muhammad after the death of al-Rida in 204 AH (819), following the return of al-Ma'mun to his capital Baghdad. In particular, al-Mas'udi in his Ithbat al-wassiya writes that al-Ma'mun summoned Muhammad to Baghdad, settled him near his palace, and later decided to marry him to his daughter, Umm Fadl, whose given name was Zaynab. According to al-Baghdadi, Muhammad was about nine years old at the time of this betrothal.

Death of his father (c. 818)
Ali al-Rida was a prominent Alid, a descendant of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad. The Alids were viewed as rivals for the caliphate by the Abbasids, who were the descendants of Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, a paternal uncle of Muhammad. The appointment of the Alid al-Rida by the Abbasid caliph thus invoked strong opposition, particularly among the members of the Abbasid dynasty and the Iraqi supporters of Abbasid legitimism. These revolted and installed al-Ma'mun's uncle, Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, as an anti-caliph in Baghdad. The caliph and his entourage thus left Khorasan for Baghdad in 203 AH (818), accompanied by al-Rida. The latter died shortly in Tus after a brief illness, possibly after being poisoned. The death of al-Rida followed the assassination of al-Fadl ibn Sahl (d. 818), the Persian vizier of al-Ma'mun, who had become a divisive figure. Both deaths are linked in Shia sources to al-Ma'mun and viewed as concessions to the Arab party to smooth his return to Iraq. Modern scholars similarly tend to suspect the caliph in the death of al-Rida. After returning to Baghdad in 204 AH (819), al-Ma'mun reversed his pro-Shia policies, and restored the traditional black color of the Abbasids. Muhammad was about seven years old when his father died.

primaryTitle: Imam al-Salat — Reviver of the Shadhili Path
titles: Imam al-Salat · Shaykh al-Tariqa
bio: Abu Abdullah Muhammad bin Suleiman bin Abu Bakr Al-Jazouli Al-Samlali Al-Hasani, often known as Imam Al-Jazouli or Sheikh Al-Jazouli, is known for his compilation of the book Dala’il Al-Khairat wa Shariq Al-Anwar fi Dhikr Al-Salaat upon the Chosen Prophet, which is a book of dhikr for Muslims that is very popular. This book is usually divided into 7 sections for each day of the week. Al-Jazouli is one of the Seven Scholars of Marrakesh.
bio_full:
Abū 'Abdullah Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān ibn Abū Bakr al-Jazūli al-Simlālī (Arabic: أبو عبدالله محمد بن سليمان بن ابوبكر الجزولي السّملالي الحسني) (d. 1465AD = 870AH), often known as Imam al-Jazuli or Sheikh Jazuli, was a Moroccan Sufi Saint. He is best known for compiling the Dala'il al-Khayrat, an extremely popular Muslim prayer book. This book is usually divided into 7 sections for each day of the week. Al-Jazuli is one of the seven saints of Marrakesh and is buried in his mausoleum inside the city.

Muhammad al-Jazuli claimed to be a Sharif (a descent of Muhammad) and  belonged to the Berber Jazulin tribe. He lived in the historic Sous area of Morocco, situated between the Atlantic Ocean and the Atlas Mountains, and studied locally before going to the Madrasat As-Saffarîn in Fez where his room is still pointed out to visitors today. After settling a tribal feud he left the area and spent the next forty years in Makkah, Medina and Jerusalem. After his long journey, he returned to Fez where he completed the prayer book Dala'il al-Khayrat.

He was initiated into the Shadhili Tariqa, a Sufi order, by a descendant of Abu Abdallah Mohammed Amghar, the sheikh of the Banu Amghar. He spent fourteen years in Khalwa (seclusion) and then went to Safi where he gathered around him many followers. The governor of Safi felt obliged to expel him and later poisoned him which led to his death in 1465. He is said to have died during prayer.

It is claimed that in 1541, seventy-seven years after his death, his body was exhumed to be transferred to Marrakesh and found to be uncorrupted.

full: Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Sanūsī al-Khattābī al-Ḥasanī
primaryTitle: Founder of the Sanusiyya — Builder of the Libyan Islamic State
titles: Al-Sayyid al-Mahdi · Imam al-Sanusiyya
bio: Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Sanūsī al-Khattābī al-Ḥasanī (1787–1859) was a mystic of the Sanusiyya tradition, based in Algeria. Known as Founder of the Sanusiyya — Builder of the Libyan Islamic State.
bio_full:
Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi (Arabic: محمد بن علي السنوسي; in full Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Sanūsī al-Mujāhirī al-Ḥasanī al-Idrīsī) (1787–1859) was an Algerian Muslim theologian and leader who founded the Sanusi order in 1837. His militant mystical movement proved very significant and helped Libya to win its freedom from Italy on 10 February 1947. Al-Sanusi's grandson Idris ruled as king of Libya from 1951 to 1969.

Life
Al-Sanusi was born in al-Wasita near Mostaganem, Algeria in 1787, and was named al-Sanusi after Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Sanusi, a venerated Muslim teacher active in Tlemcen in the 13th century. He was an Algerian Walad Sidi Abdallah tribesman who claimed descent from the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

primaryTitle: Shaybani — Systematiser of Hanafi Law and Father of Islamic International Law
titles: Shaykh al-Islam · Imam al-Iraq
bio: Muhammad Shaybani Khan was an Uzbek leader who consolidated various Uzbek tribes and laid the foundations for their ascendance in Transoxiana and the establishment of the Khanate of Bukhara. He was a Shaybanid or descendant of Shiban. He was the son of Shah-Budag, thus a grandson of the Uzbek conqueror Abu'l-Khayr Khan.
bio_full: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Farqad al-Shaybani was an Arab Muslim jurist and legal theorist, and a leading authority of the Hanafi school of law. He was born in Wasit, Iraq, in 749 or 750, the son of a soldier, but chose a life of learning over a military career. He moved as a child to Kufa, the home town of Abu Hanifa, and studied under Abu Hanifa for about two years until the latter's death in 767. He continued his studies with Abu Yusuf, Abu Hanifa's leading disciple, and also learned from Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Awza'i. He spent two to three years in Medina studying with Malik ibn Anas. He later moved to Baghdad, where he had his widest influence. The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid appointed him judge (qadi) of Raqqa; he was removed from the post in 803, later restored to judicial office, and accompanied the caliph to Khorasan as judge. He died at Rayy in 805, on the same day and in the same place as the grammarian al-Kisa'i. His writings include al-Jami' al-Kabir and al-Jami' al-Saghir, a work against the legal views of the people of Medina, and treatises on siyar, the law governing war and relations between Muslim and non-Muslim states. Modern scholars regard him as a founding figure of Islamic international law. His best-known pupil was Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i, who later wrote a refutation of his views while still admiring him.

bio_sources.title: English Wikipedia — Muhammad al-Shaybani

primaryTitle: Imam al-'Ilal — Master of Hadith Analysis
titles: Imam al-'Ilal · One of the Six Masters of Hadith
bio: Abu 'Isa Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Tirmidhi al-Sulami (824–892) was a scholar of the Hadith Sciences tradition, based in Tirmidh (Termez). Known as Imam al-'Ilal — Master of Hadith Analysis.
bio_full:
Abu 'Isa Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Tirmidhi al-Sulami was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from 824 to 892 CE during the Abbasid period. Born in Tirmidh, a city located in present-day Uzbekistan along the Amu Darya river, he became one of the most respected authorities in hadith sciences, earning the title Imam al-'Ilal, meaning "Master of Hadith Analysis."

Al-Tirmidhi dedicated his scholarly career to the systematic collection, evaluation, and classification of hadith—the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. During the 9th century, this field was experiencing significant development as scholars worked to establish rigorous methodologies for authenticating prophetic traditions and distinguishing reliable narrations from weak or fabricated ones.

His most significant contribution to Islamic scholarship is the compilation known as Jami' al-Tirmidhi or Sunan al-Tirmidhi, which became one of the six canonical hadith collections in Sunni Islam. This work contains approximately 3,956 hadith organized by legal and theological topics. What distinguished al-Tirmidhi's approach was his innovative grading system, where he classified each hadith according to its authenticity using terms such as sahih (authentic), hasan (good), da'if (weak), or gharib (rare). This methodological contribution helped establish standards that influenced subsequent hadith scholarship.

Al-Tirmidhi was particularly known for his expertise in identifying defects ('ilal) in hadith transmission chains and texts, which required extensive knowledge of narrator biographies, regional transmission patterns, and textual variants. His analytical approach balanced strict authentication standards with practical considerations for Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

Beyond his hadith work, al-Tirmidhi wrote on various Islamic sciences, though many of these works have not survived. His scholarly reputation extended throughout the Islamic world, and he studied under prominent teachers while also training students who carried forward his methodological approaches.

The enduring significance of al-Tirmidhi's work lies in his contribution to the preservation and authentication of prophetic traditions that form a foundational source for Islamic law, theology, and practice. His collection remains widely studied and referenced by Islamic scholars, and his grading methodology influenced the development of hadith sciences as a distinct academic discipline. Al-Tirmidhi's legacy reflects the broader intellectual flourishing of the Abbasid period, when scholars systematized various branches of Islamic knowledge.

primaryTitle: Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam
dob_s: c. 610 CE (al-Isabah / Usd al-Ghabah / Siyar / Tabaqat (AI-extracted 2026-06, spot-verified))
dod_s: 656 CE (al-Isabah / Usd al-Ghabah / Siyar / Tabaqat (AI-extracted 2026-06, spot-verified))
bio: Muhammad bin Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full:
Muhammad bin Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah was a companion of Prophet Muhammad who holds the distinction of being among the first generation born into Islam. Born around 595 CE, he was the son of Abu Hudhayfah ibn 'Utbah, one of the early converts to Islam who participated in the first migration to Abyssinia (present-day Ethiopia).

Muhammad bin Abu Hudhayfah's significance lies primarily in his unique position as one of the earliest Muslims to be born into the faith rather than converting to it. This made him part of a small but historically important group that represented Islam's transition from a movement of converts to an established religious community with second-generation adherents.

His family's early acceptance of Islam placed them among the pioneering Muslim families. His father, Abu Hudhayfah, was notable for his early conversion and his participation in the migration to Abyssinia, which was the first major emigration undertaken by Muslims fleeing persecution in Mecca. This migration, which occurred around 615 CE, was sanctioned by Prophet Muhammad as a temporary refuge for his followers.

As a companion (sahaba) of Prophet Muhammad, Muhammad bin Abu Hudhayfah would have had direct contact with the Prophet and been witness to the formative period of Islamic history. The companions are revered in Islamic tradition as the most reliable transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices, and their accounts form a crucial foundation for hadith literature and Islamic jurisprudence.

Living during the foundational decades of Islam, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, Muhammad bin Abu Hudhayfah witnessed the religion's emergence in Mecca, the migration to Medina, and the early expansion of the Muslim community. His lifetime spanned the entire prophetic period and extended into the early caliphate period under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's reign.

His status as someone born into Islam rather than converting to it represents an important demographic shift in early Islamic society. While most of the prominent companions were converts who had made conscious decisions to abandon their previous beliefs, Muhammad bin Abu Hudhayfah represented the emergence of a native Muslim generation that would become increasingly important as Islam established itself as a permanent religious and social system.

bio: Muhammad bin Hatib bin al-Harith (c. 593–705 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Muhammad ibn Hatib ibn al-Harith al-Jumahi was a Companion from the Jumah clan of Quraysh. His parents, Hatib ibn al-Harith and Umm Jamil Fatima bint al-Mujallil, emigrated to Abyssinia, and he was born there; Ibn Hibban and others report that he was born on the ship during the emigration. Al-Dhahabi adds that his brother al-Harith was also born in Abyssinia and that their father died there. His kunya is given as Abu Ibrahim or Abu al-Qasim. As a small child his hand was burned, and his mother brought him to the Prophet, who spat on it and recited words of healing; he narrated this account from his mother. He also narrated the hadith on the duff (frame drum) and the voice as what separates the lawful from the unlawful, and he narrated from 'Ali. Simak ibn Harb and Abu Balj are among those who narrated from him. He settled in Kufa, and Hisham ibn al-Kalbi reports that he fought on 'Ali's side at the Camel, Siffin and al-Nahrawan. He died during the caliphate of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. Abu Nu'aym gives his death as 86 AH in Kufa, while Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Khalifa ibn Khayyat and al-Dhahabi give 74 AH, with Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Khalifa placing it in Mecca.

bio_sources.title: Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Siyar, al-Tarikh al-Kabir, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym, Khalifa — Muhammad ibn Hatib (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

primaryTitle: Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam
bio: Muhammad bin Hattab bin al-Harith (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full: Muhammad ibn Hattab ibn al-Harith ibn Ma'mar al-Jumahi was a Companion from the Jumah clan of Quraysh and a paternal cousin of Muhammad ibn Hatib ibn al-Harith. Ibn al-Athir, citing Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, records that he was born in Abyssinia and was brought back from there. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr states that he was older than his cousin Muhammad ibn Hatib, and that if this is so, he was the first to be given the name Muhammad.
