bio: Mulayl bin Wabara bin Khalid (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Mulayl bin Wabara bin Khalid was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the Prophet's time there.

Mulayl is primarily remembered in Islamic historical sources for his participation in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE. This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement occurred near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the Muslim forces despite being significantly outnumbered.

The companions who fought at Badr, known as the Badriyyun, hold a special status in Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment. Their participation in this battle is considered a mark of particular honor and dedication to the early Muslim cause. The Battle of Badr not only secured the survival of the nascent Muslim community but also established its military capability and boosted morale among the believers.

As a sahabi, Mulayl was part of the generation that directly witnessed and supported the Prophet Muhammad's mission during its most crucial years. The companions played essential roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, supporting the community's growth, and participating in the various challenges faced by early Muslims.

Mulayl's death is recorded as occurring around 634 CE, which places it during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph. This was a period of rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While detailed accounts of Mulayl's specific activities beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his inclusion among the companions of Badr ensures his place in the foundational period of Islamic history. The companions of this era are collectively remembered for their sacrifices and contributions to establishing and preserving the early Muslim community during its most vulnerable and formative years.

full: Muhammad ibn Shah Murtada ibn Mahmud al-Kashani
titles: Al-Fayd al-Kashani · Al-Muhaddith
bio: Muhammad ibn Shah Murtada ibn Mahmud al-Kashani (1598–1680) was a scholar of the Islamic Philosophy tradition, based in Kashan. Known as Al-Muhaddith al-Fayd — The Inspired Traditionist.
bio_full:
Muhammad ibn Shah Murtada ibn Mahmud al-Kashani, known as Mulla Muhsin Fayd Kashani or Al-Muhaddith al-Fayd (The Inspired Traditionist), was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from 1598 to 1680. Born and based in Kashan, a city in central Iran, he emerged as one of the most significant intellectual figures of 17th-century Safavid Persia.

Fayd Kashani was a prolific scholar who made substantial contributions across multiple disciplines of Islamic learning. He was particularly renowned for his expertise in hadith (prophetic traditions), Quranic exegesis, Islamic philosophy, and mysticism. His scholarly work bridged different intellectual traditions within Islam, combining rational philosophical inquiry with scriptural scholarship and Sufi mystical insights.

Among his most important works was his comprehensive Quranic commentary, which demonstrated his deep engagement with both the literal and esoteric meanings of the sacred text. He also produced significant collections and analyses of hadith literature, earning him recognition as one of the foremost traditionists of his era. His philosophical writings reflected the rich intellectual environment of Safavid Iran, where Islamic philosophy flourished under state patronage.

Fayd Kashani lived during a period when the Safavid Empire was consolidating Twelver Shia Islam as the official religion of Iran. His scholarship contributed to the development of a distinctly Shia intellectual tradition that integrated various streams of Islamic thought. He was particularly influential in synthesizing philosophical reasoning with religious orthodoxy, helping to establish methodological approaches that would influence subsequent generations of Islamic scholars.

His nickname "Al-Fayd" (The Inspired) reflected the high regard in which his contemporaries held his scholarship and spiritual insight. He represented the kind of comprehensive Islamic learning that characterized the best scholars of his time, combining rigorous textual scholarship with philosophical sophistication.

The significance of Fayd Kashani extends beyond his individual contributions to Islamic learning. He exemplified the intellectual vitality of 17th-century Islamic scholarship and helped preserve and transmit classical Islamic knowledge while adapting it to the needs of his contemporary context. His works continued to be studied and referenced by later scholars, ensuring his lasting influence on Islamic intellectual history, particularly within the Shia tradition but also more broadly across the Islamic world.

full: Sadr al-Din Muhammad ibn Ibrahim Shirazi 'Mulla Sadra'
primaryTitle: Sadr al-Muta'allihin — Founder of Transcendent Wisdom
titles: Sadr al-Muta'allihin (Foremost of Divine Philosophers) · Founder of al-Hikma al-Muta'aliya (Transcendent Theosophy)
bio: Mullah Sadra Muhammad bin Ibrahim Al-Qawami Al-Shirazi. He is Sadr al-Din al-Shirazi, known as Sadr al-Mutalahin, a sage and Twelver Shiite Muslim philosopher who was born in the late tenth century AH in Shiraz. He is the founder of the school of transcendent wisdom with his basic theory of the originality of existence and the essentiality of essence.
bio_full:
Ṣadr ad-Dīn Muḥammad Shīrāzī, more commonly known as Mullā Ṣadrā (Persian: ملا صدرا; Arabic: صدر المتألهین; c. 1571/2 – c. 1635/40 CE / 980 – 1050 AH), was an Iranian Twelver Shi'i Islamic mystic, philosopher, theologian, and ‘Ālim who led the cultural renaissance in the country during the 17th century. According to Oliver Leaman, Mulla Sadra is arguably the single most important and influential philosopher in the Muslim world in the last four hundred years. Though not its founder, he is considered the master of the Illuminationist (or, Ishraghi or Ishraqi) school of Philosophy, a seminal figure who synthesized the many tracts of the Islamic Golden Age philosophies into what he called the Transcendent Theosophy or al-hikmah al-muta’āliyah.
Mulla Sadra brought "a new philosophical insight in dealing with the nature of reality" and created "a major transition from essentialism to existentialism" in Islamic philosophy, although his existentialism should not be too readily compared to Western existentialism. His was a question of existentialist cosmology as it pertained to God, and thus differs considerably from the individual, moral, and/or social, questions at the heart of Russian, French, German, or American Existentialism.
Mulla Sadra's philosophy ambitiously synthesized Avicennism, Shahab al-Din Suhrawardi's Illuminationist philosophy, Ibn Arabi's Sufi metaphysics, and the theology of the Sunni Ash'ari school of Kalam into the framework of Twelver Shi'ism. His main work is The Transcendent Philosophy of the Four Journeys of the Intellect, or simply Four Journeys, In which he attempted to reach Sufism and prove the idea of Unity of Existence by offering a new intake and perspective on Peripatetic philosophy that was offered by al-Farabi and Avicenna in the Islamic world.

Biography
 

Early life
Mulla Sadra was born in Shiraz, Iran, to a notable Persian family of court officials in 1571 or 1572, 
In Mulla Sadra's time, the Safavid dynasty governed over Iran. Safavid kings granted independence to Fars province, which was ruled by Mulla Sadra's father, Khwajah Ibrahim Qavami, who was a knowledgeable and extremely faithful politician. As the ruler of the vast region of Fars province, Khwajah was rich and held a high position. When Mulla Sadra was born, the family named him Muhammad but called him Sadra. Years later, Sadra was nicknamed "Mulla", that is, "great scientist". Sadra was Khwajah's only child. In that time it was customary that the children of aristocrats were educated by private teachers in their own palace. Sadra was a very intelligent, strict, energetic, studious, and curious boy and mastered all the lessons related to Persian and Arabic literature, as well as the art of calligraphy, during a very short time. Following old traditions of his time, and before the age of puberty, he also learned horse riding, hunting and fighting techniques, mathematics, astronomy, some medicine, jurisprudence, and Islamic law. However, he was mainly attracted to philosophy and particularly to mystical philosophy and gnosis.
In 1591, Mulla Sadra moved to Qazvin and then, in 1597, to Isfahan to pursue a traditional and institutional education in philosophy, theology, Hadith, and hermeneutics. At that time, each city was a successive capital of the Safavid dynasty and the center of Twelver Shi'ite seminaries. Sadra's teachers included Mir Damad and Baha' ad-Din al-'Amili.

Teachers
Mulla Sadra became a master of the science of his time. In his own view, the most important of these was philosophy. In Qazvin, Sadra acquired most of his scholarly knowledge from two prominent teachers, namely Baha' ad-Din al-'Amili and Mir Damad, whom he accompanied when the Safavid capital was transferred from Qazvin to Isfahan in 1596 CE / 1006 AH. Shaykh Baha'i was an expert in Islamic sciences but also a master of astronomy, theoretical mathematics, engineering, architecture, medicine, and some fields of secret knowledge. Mir Damad also knew the science of his time but limited his domain to jurisprudence, hadith. and mainly philosophy. Mir Damad was a master of both the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) and Illuminationist schools of Islamic philosophy. Mulla Sadra obtained most of his knowledge of philosophy and gnosis from Damad and always introduced Damad as his true teacher and spiritual guide.
After he had finished his studies, Sadra began to explore unorthodox doctrines and as a result was both condemned and excommunicated by some Shi'i ʿulamāʾ. He then retired for a lengthy period of time to a village named Kahak, near Qom, where he engaged in contemplative exercises. While in Kahak, he wrote a number of minor works, including the Risāla fi 'l-ḥashr and the Risāla fī ḥudūth al-ʿālam .

Return to Shiraz
In 1612, Ali Quli Khan, son of Allāhwirdī Ḵhān and the powerful governor of Fārs, asked Mulla Sadra to abandon his exile and to come back to Shiraz to teach and run a newly built madrasa (Khan School, Persian: مدرسه خان). Mulla Sadra devoted his rest of life to teach the intellectual sciences, particularly his own teachings Transcendent Theosophy.
During his time in Shīrāz, Ṣadrā began writing treatises that synthesized wide-ranging strands of existing Islamic systems of thought at Khan School. The ideas of his school, which may be seen as a continuation of the School of Iṣfahān of Mīr Dāmād and Shaykh Bahāʾī, were promulgated after Sadrā's death by his pupils, several of whom would become sought-after thinkers in their own right, such as, Mullā Muḥsin Fayḍ Kāshānī (Mulla Sadra's son-in-law), and ʿAbd Razzāḳ Lāhidjī.
Although Ṣadrā's influence remained limited in the generations after his death, it increased markedly during the 19th century, when his ideas helped inspire a renewed Akhbārī tendency within Twelver Shīʿism. In recent times, his works have been studied in Iran, Europe, and America. He died in Basra after the Hajj and was buried in the present-day city of Najaf, Iraq.

Philosophical ideas

Existentialism
Although Existentialism as defined nowadays is not identical to Mulla Sadra's definition, he was the first to introduce the concept. According to Mulla Sadra, "existence precedes the essence and is thus principal since something has to exist first and then have an essence." It is notable that for Mulla Sadra this was an issue that applied specifically to God and God's position in the universe, especially in the context of reconciling God's position in the Qur'an with the Greek-influenced cosmological philosophies of Islam's Golden Era.
Mulla Sadra's metaphysics gives priority to existence over essence (i.e., quiddity). That is to say, essences are variable and are determined according to existential "intensity" (to use Henry Corbin's definition). Thus, essences are not immutable. The advantage to this schema is that it is acceptable to the fundamental statements of the Qur'an, even as it does not necessarily undermine any previous Islamic philosopher's Aristotelian or Platonic foundations.
Indeed, Mulla Sadra provides immutability only to God, while intrinsically linking essence and existence to each other, and to God's power over existence. In so doing, he provided for God's authority over all things while also solving the problem of God's knowledge of particulars, including those that are evil, without being inherently responsible for them — even as God's authority over the existence of things that provide the framework for evil to exist. This clever solution provides for freedom of will, God's supremacy, the infiniteness of God's knowledge, the existence of evil, and definitions of existence and essence that leave the two inextricably linked insofar as humans are concerned, but fundamentally separate insofar as God is concerned.
Perhaps most importantly, the primacy of existence provides the capacity for God's judgement without God being directly, or indirectly, affected by the evil being judged.

full: Murad ibn Muhammad ibn Bayezid al-Uthman al-Ghazi
primaryTitle: Ghazi Sultan — Father of Mehmed the Conqueror
titles: Murad Khan · Ghazi · Father of Mehmed the Conqueror
bio: Murad ibn Muhammad ibn Bayezid al-Uthman al-Ghazi (1404–1451) was a ruler, based in Amasya. Known as Ghazi Sultan — Father of Mehmed the Conqueror.
bio_full:
Murad II (Ottoman Turkish: مراد ثانى, romanized: Murād-ı sānī, Turkish: II. Murad; June 1404 – 3 February 1451) was twice the sultan of the Ottoman Empire, from 1421 to 1444 and from 1446 to 1451.

Early life
Murad was born in June 1404 to Mehmed I, while the identity of his mother is disputed according to various accounts. According to 15th century historian Şükrullah, Murad's mother was a concubine. Hüseyin Hüsâmeddin Yasar, an early 20th century historian, wrote in his work Amasya Tarihi that his mother was Şahzade Hatun, daughter of Divitdar Ahmed Pasha. The most widely accepted view is that his mother was Emine Hatun of the Dulkadirid Beylik.
He spent his early childhood in Amasya. In 1410, Murad came along with his father to the Ottoman capital, Edirne. After his father ascended to the Ottoman throne, he made Murad governor of the Amasya Sanjak. Murad remained at Amasya until the death of Mehmed I in 1421. He was solemnly recognized as sultan of the Ottoman Sultanate at sixteen years of age, girded with the Sword of Osman at Bursa, and the troops and officers of the state willingly paid homage to him as their sovereign.

Reign

Accession and first reign

Murad's reign was troubled by insurrection early on. The Byzantine Emperor, Manuel II, released the 'pretender' Mustafa Çelebi (known as Düzmece Mustafa) from confinement and acknowledged him as the legitimate heir to the throne of Bayezid I (1389–1402). The Byzantine Emperor had first secured a stipulation that Mustafa should, if successful, repay him for his liberation by giving up a large number of important cities. The pretender was landed by the Byzantine galleys in the European dominion of the sultan and for a time made rapid progress. Many Ottoman soldiers joined him, and he defeated and killed the veteran general Bayazid Pasha, whom Murad had sent to fight him. Mustafa defeated Murad's army and declared himself Sultan of Adrianople (Edirne). He then crossed the Dardanelles to Asia with a large army but Murad out-manoeuvered Mustafa. After which, Mustafa's force defected in large numbers to Murad II. Mustafa took refuge in the city of Gallipoli, but the sultan, who was greatly aided by a Genoese commander named Adorno, besieged him there and stormed the place. Mustafa was taken and put to death by the sultan, who then turned his arms against the Roman emperor and declared his resolution to punish the Palaiologos for their unprovoked enmity by the capture of Constantinople.
Murad II then formed a new army called Azeb in 1421 and marched through the Byzantine Empire and laid siege to Constantinople. While Murad was besieging the city, the Byzantines, in league with some independent Turkish Anatolian states, sent the sultan's younger brother Küçük Mustafa (who was only 13 years old) to rebel against the sultan and besiege Bursa. Murad had to abandon the siege of Constantinople in order to deal with his rebellious brother. He caught Prince Mustafa and executed him. The Anatolian states that had been constantly plotting against him — Aydinids, Germiyanids, Menteshe and Teke — were annexed and henceforth became part of the Ottoman Sultanate.
Murad II then declared war against Venice, the Karamanid Emirate, Serbia and Hungary. The Karamanids were defeated in 1428 and Venice withdrew in 1432 following the defeat at the second Siege of Thessalonica in 1430. In the 1430s Murad captured vast territories in the Balkans and succeeded in annexing Serbia in 1439. In 1441 the Holy Roman Empire and Poland joined the Serbian-Hungarian coalition. Murad II won the Crusade of Varna in 1444 against John Hunyadi.

Abdication and second reign

Murad II relinquished his throne in 1444 to his son Mehmed II, but a Janissary revolt in the Empire forced him to return.
In 1448 he defeated the Christian coalition at the Second Battle of Kosovo (the first one took place in 1389). When the Balkan front was secured, Murad II turned east to defeat Timur's son, Shah Rukh, and the emirates of Karamanid and Çorum-Amasya. In 1450 Murad II led his army into Albania and unsuccessfully besieged the Castle of Krujë in an effort to defeat the resistance led by Skanderbeg. In the winter of 1450–1451, Murad II fell ill, and died in Edirne. He was succeeded by his son Mehmed II (1451–1481).

As ghazi sultan
When Murad ascended the throne, he sought to regain lost Ottoman territories that had reverted to autonomy following his grandfather Bayezid I's defeat at the Battle of Ankara in 1402 at the hands of Timur. He needed the support of both the public and the nobles "who would enable him to exercise his rule", and utilized the old and potent Islamic trope of the ghazi king.
In order to gain popular international support for his conquests, Murad II modeled himself after the legendary Ghazi kings of old. The Ottomans already presented themselves as ghazis, painting their origins as rising from the ghazas of Osman, the founder of the dynasty. For them, ghaza was the noble championing of Islam and justice against non-Muslims and Muslims alike, if they were cruel; for example, Bayezid I labeled Timur Lang, also a Muslim, an apostate prior to the Battle of Ankara because of the violence his troops had committed upon innocent civilians and because "all you do is to break promises and vows, shed blood, and violate the honor of women."  Murad II only had to capitalize on this dynastic inheritance of doing ghaza, which he did by actively crafting the public image of Ghazi Sultan.
After his accession, there was a flurry of translating and compiling activity where old Persian, Arab, and Anatolian epics were translated into Turkish so Murad II could uncover the ghazi king legends.  He drew from the noble behavior of the nameless Caliphs in the Battalname, an epic about a fictional Arab warrior who fought against the Byzantines, and modelled his actions on theirs.  He was careful to embody the simplicity, piety, and noble sense of justice that was part of the ghazi king persona.

For example, the Caliph in Battalname saw the battle turning in his enemy's favor, and got down from his horse and prayed, after which the battle ended in a victory for him. In the Battle of Varna in 1444, Murad II saw the Hungarians gaining the upper hand, and he got down from his horse and prayed just like the Caliph. The tide soon turned in the Ottoman's favor and Władysław III of Poland, King of Hungary, was killed in a charge.  Similarly, the Caliph in the epic roused his warriors by saying "Those of you who die will be martyrs. Those of you who kill will be ghazis"; before the Battle of Varna, Murad II repeated these words to his army, saying "Those of us who kill will be ghazis; those of us who die will be martyrs."  In another instance, since the ghazi king is meant to be just and fair, when Murad took Thessalonica in the Balkans, he took care to keep the troops in check and prevented widespread looting.  Finally, just as the fictional Caliph's ghazas were immortalized in Battalname, Murad II's battles and victories were also compiled and given the title "The Ghazas of Sultan Murad" (Ottoman Turkish: غزوات سلطان مراد, romanized: Gazavât-ı Sultan Murad).
Murad II successfully painted himself as a simple soldier who did not partake in royal excesses, and as a noble ghazi sultan who sought to consolidate Muslim power against non-Muslims such as the Venetians and Hungarians. Through this self-presentation, he got the support of the Muslim population of not only the Ottoman territories, for both himself and his extensive, expensive campaigns, but also the greater Muslim populations in the Dar-al-Islam – such as the Mamluks and the Muslim Delhi Sultanates of India. Murad II was basically presenting himself not only as "a ghazi king who fights caffres [non-muslims], but also serves as protector and master of lesser ghazis."

Economy
Murad II's reign saw a period of great economic development, with an increase in trade and a considerable expansion of Ottoman cities.

bio: Murrah ibn Ka'b (255–-340) was a founding figure, based in Mecca. Known as Islamic History Founder of Mecca.
bio_full:
Murrah ibn Ka'b (Arabic: مُرَّة ٱبْن كَعْب) ibn Luay ibn Ghalib ibn Fihr ibn Malik was a man from Quraysh tribe, supposed to have lived in the 4th century. He was the sixth-in-line of Muhammad's grandfathers. He is the common ancestor of all four of Muhammad's grandparents. He is also the common ancestor of six of Muhammad's eight great-grandparents. He is also the common ancestor of Muhammad and his friend Abu Bakr.

Abdul Muttalib (Muhammad's paternal grandfather):

Father:Hashim ibn Abd Manaf ibn Qusay ibn Kilab ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b.

Mother:Salma bint Amr An-Najjariya (not a descendant of Murrah).

Fatimah bint Amr (Muhammad's paternal grandmother):

Father:Amr ibn Ae’z ibn Imran ibn Makhzum ibn Yaqza ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b.

Mother:Sakhra bint Abd ibn Imran ibn Makhzum ibn Yaqza ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b.

Wahb ibn 'Abd Manaf (Muhammad's maternal grandfather):

Father:Abd Manaf ibn Zuhra ibn Kilab ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b.

Mother:Atika bint a-Awqas As-Sulamiya (not a descendant of Murrah).

Barrah bint Abdul Uzza (Muhammad's maternal grandmother):

Father:Abdul Uzza ibn Othman ibn Abd Addar ibn Qusay ibn Kilab ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b.

Mother:Um Habib bint Assad ibn Abdul Uzza ibn Qusay ibn Kilab ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b.

His mother was Wahshiya bint Shaiban ibn Muharib ibn Fihr ibn Malik, so his mother was a second cousin of his father.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Murri bin Sinan (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Murri ibn Sinan ibn Tha'laba was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, citing al-'Adawi, records that he took part in the Battle of Uhud and the campaigns that followed it. Ibn Sa'd describes him as the paternal uncle of the Companion Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. He is remembered in connection with the Companion Samura ibn Jundub: Ibn al-Athir reports that after Samura's father died, Murri married Samura's mother, and Samura grew up in his care until he became a young man. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, citing al-'Adawi and al-Waqidi, also notes this step-relationship between the two. His son, Thabit ibn Murri, has his own entry among the Companions in Ibn 'Abd al-Barr's work. No dates of birth or death are recorded for him.

full: Mus'ab ibn Umayr ibn Hashim ibn Abd al-Dar al-Qurashi
primaryTitle: Safeer al-Islam — First Ambassador of Islam
titles: Safeer (Envoy of the Prophet)
quranRef: Q33:23 — 'Among the believers are men true to their pledge'
bio: Abu Abdullah Musab bin Umair Al-Abdari was one of Badr’s first companions to Islam, the envoy of the Prophet Muhammad to call to Islam in Yathrib after the first Pledge of Aqaba, and the standard bearer of the Emigrants in the Battles of Badr and Uhud.
bio_full:
Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr (Arabic: مصعب بن عمير) also known as Muṣʿab al-Khayr ("the Good") was a sahabi (companion) of Muhammad. From the Banū ʿAbd al-Dār branch of the Quraysh, he embraced Islam in 614 CE and was the first ambassador of Islam. He died in the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE.

Early life
Mus‘ab ibn Umair was born to the Banu Abd al-Dar branch of the Quraysh tribe. His exact birth year is not known; it is believed that he was born sometime between 594 and 598 CE since he was very young when he embraced Islam in 614. Mus‘ab was the son of Umayr ibn Hashim and Khunas bint Malik, and his parents were wealthy. Even as a young man, he was permitted to attend meetings of the Quraysh elders.

Conversion to Islam
The first Muslims used to meet with Muhammad at the house of Al-Arqam known as the Islamic Learning Center. Mus'ab became interested and went to this house to find out more about Islam. As a result of hearing the reciting of the Qur'an and the preaching of Muhammad, he converted.
At first Mus'ab kept his faith a secret, for he was afraid of how his mother would react. However, one day, Uthman ibn Talha, saw him entering Al Arqam's house and joining the Muslim prayers. The news spread and eventually reached his mother, who chained him in their house with the intention of making him recant. Mus'ab was confident in his faith and would not renounce it. Muhammad advised him to join the companions who were emigrating to Abyssinia so that he would not be harassed again.

First Ambassador of Islam
Mus‘ab ibn Umayr was appointed the first ambassador of Islam and was sent to Yathrib (Medina) to prepare the city for the forthcoming Hijra after the first pledge with the ansar. A man of Medina named Asad ibn Zurarah assisted him. After they had preached Islam, many residents of Medina were converted, including Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Ubadah. The Medinan converts were known as Ansars ("helpers").

Military campaigns

Battle of Badr
He participated in the Battle of Badr. Muhammad’s forces included Ali, Hamza, Mus`ab ibn `Umair, Az-Zubair bin Al-'Awwam, Ammar ibn Yasir, and Abu Dharr al-Ghifari. The Muslims also brought seventy camels and two horses, meaning that they either had to walk or fit three to four men per camel. However, many early Muslim sources indicate that no serious fighting was expected, and the future Caliph Uthman stayed behind to care for his sick wife Ruqayyah, the daughter of Muhammad. Salman the Persian also could not join the battle, as he was still not a free man.
Many of the Quraishi nobles, including Amr ibn Hishām, Walid ibn Utba, Shaiba, and Umayah ibn Khalaf, joined the Meccan army. Their reasons varied: some were out to protect their financial interests in the caravan; others wanted to avenge Ibn al-Hadrami, the guard killed at Nakhlah; finally, a few must have wanted to take part in what was expected to be an easy victory against the Muslims. Amr ibn Hishām is described as shaming at least one noble, Umayah ibn Khalaf, into joining the expedition.

Death in the Battle of Uhud

In the Battle of Uhud in 624 CE, Muhammad assigned Mus'ab ibn Umayr to carry the Muslim flag. During the battle, some Muslims, who were under the impression that the battle was over, left their positions on the battlefield, giving the opposing forces hope of attacking Muhammad himself. On realizing the danger, Mus'ab, who was of a similar position and colouring to Muhammad, raised his flag and shouted the takbir ("Allah is The Greatest!"), with the intention of diverting the enemies' attention towards himself and allowing Muhammad to remain unhurt. Mus'ab was attacked, and his right hand was severed holding the flag, but he continued to repeat the words of the Quran, and took the flag in his left hand.
When his left hand was severed he took hold of it with his arms but never let the flag fall. "Muhammad is only a Messenger of God. Messengers have passed away before him." (Qur'an, 3:144) Eventually Musab was fatally wounded by Ibn Qami'ah and died.

Burial
Sixty-five Muslims were killed in the battle. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt narrated: We migrated in the company of Allah's Apostle, seeking Allah's Pleasure. So our reward became due and sure with Allah (swt). Some of us have been dead without enjoying anything of their rewards (here), and one of them was Mus'ab bin 'Umair who was martyred on the day of the battle of Uhud, and did not leave anything except a Namira (i.e. a sheet in which he was shrouded). If we covered his head with it, his feet became uncovered, and if we covered his feet with it, his head became visible. So the Prophet (s) said to us, "Cover his head with it and put some Idhkhir (i.e. a kind of grass) over his feet or place Idhkhir over his feet." But some amongst us have got the fruits of their labor ripened, and they are collecting them. Muhammad stood beside Musab's body and recited: "Among the believers are men who have been true to what they have pledged to God. The Messenger of God testifies that you are martyrs in the sight of God." When Mus'ab's wife, Hammanah bint Jahsh, heard about the death of her brother and maternal uncle, she replied, "To Allah we belong and to him we will verily return. I ask Allah's forgiveness for him." But when she heard about the death of her husband Mus'ab, she shouted and cried.

primaryTitle: Kalim Allah — He Who Spoke Directly with God
titles: Musa · Kalim Allah · Khatim al-Anbiya al-Isra'iliyyin · Moses · Kalimu'llah

relations.source: later tradition (Ibn Kathir); not stated in Quran

dating_source: Merneptah Stele; Ramesside Egypt; Kitchen
dating_note: Musa/Moses; Late Bronze Exodus dating (~1250 BCE most common).
bio: Mūsā ibn 'Imrān (c. 1393–c. 1273 BCE) was a prophet, based in Egypt. Known as Kalim Allah — He Who Spoke Directly with God.
bio_full:
Moses (Arabic: موسى ابن عمران Mūsā ibn ʿImrān, lit. 'Moses, son of Amram') is a prominent prophet and messenger of God and is the most frequently mentioned individual in the Quran, with his name being mentioned 136 times and his life being narrated and recounted more than that of any other prophet. Apart from the Quran, Moses is also described and praised in the Hadith literature as well. He is one of the most important prophets and messengers within Islam.
According to the Quran, Moses was born to an Israelite family. In his childhood, he is put in a basket which flows towards the Nile, and is eventually discovered by Pharaoh's (Fir'awn) wife (not named in the Quran but called Asiya in Hadith), who takes Moses as her adopted son. After reaching adulthood, Moses then resides in Midian, before departing for Egypt again to threaten the Pharaoh. During his prophethood, Moses is said to have performed many miracles, and is also reported to have personally talked to God, who bestows the title 'Speaker of God' (Kalīm Allāh) upon Moses. The prophet's most famous miracle is dividing the Red Sea, with a miraculous staff provided by God. After Pharaoh's death, Moses and his followers travel towards the Promised Land and the prophet dies within sight of the land. Moses is reported to have met Muhammad in the seven heavens following his ascension from Jerusalem during the Night Journey (’Isrā’ Miʿrāj). During the journey, Moses is said by Muslims to have repeatedly sent Muhammad back, and request a reduction in the number of required daily prayers, originally believed to be fifty, until only the five obligatory prayers remained.
Moses is viewed as a very important figure in Islam. According to Islamic theology, all Muslims must have faith in every prophet and messenger of God, which includes Moses and his brother Aaron. The life of Moses is generally seen as a spiritual parallel to the life of Muhammad, and Muslims consider many aspects of the two individuals' lives to be shared. Islamic literature also describes a parallel relation between their people and the incidents that occurred in their lifetimes; the exodus of the Israelites from ancient Egypt is considered to be similar in nature to the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina as both events unfolded in the face of persecution—of the Israelites by the ancient Egyptians, and of the early Muslims by the Meccans, respectively. His revelations, such as the Ten Commandments, form part of the contents of the Torah and are central to the Abrahamic religions of Judaism and Christianity. Consequently, Jews and Christians are designated as "People of the Book" for Muslims and are to be recognized with this special status wherever Islamic law is applied. Moses is further revered in Islamic literature, which expands upon the incidents of his life and the miracles attributed to him in the Quran and hadith, such as his direct conversations with God.
Generally, Moses is seen as a legendary figure by biblical scholars, some of whom consider it possible that Moses or a Moses-like figure existed in the 13th century BCE.

Life

Childhood
In Islamic tradition, Musa was born into a family of Israelites living in Egypt. Of his family, Islamic tradition generally names his father Imran, corresponding to the Amram of the Hebrew Bible, traditional genealogies name Levi as his ancestor. Islam states that Moses was born in a time when the ruling Pharaoh had enslaved the Israelites after the time of the prophet Yusuf (Joseph). Islamic literature states that around the time of Moses's birth, the Pharaoh had a dream in which he saw fire coming from the city of Jerusalem, which burned everything in his kingdom except in the land of the Israelites. Another version says that the Pharaoh dreamed of a little boy who caught the Pharaoh's crown and destroyed it, although there is no authentic Islamic reference to whether the dreams actually occurred. When the Pharaoh is informed that one of the male children would grow up to overthrow him, he orders the killing of all newborn Israelite males in order to prevent the prediction from occurring. Experts of economics in Pharaoh's court advise him that killing the male infants of the Israelites would result in loss of manpower. Therefore, they suggest that male infants should be killed in one year but spared the next. Moses's brother, Aaron, was born in the year when infants were spared, while Moses was born in the year when infants were to be killed.

Incident of the Nile

According to Islamic tradition, Jochebed, Moses's mother, suckled him secretly during this period. When they were in danger of being caught, God instructed her to put him in a wicker basket and set him adrift on the Nile. She instructs her daughter to follow the course of the ark and report back to her. As her daughter follows the ark along the riverbank, Moses is discovered by the Pharaoh's wife, Asiya, who convinces the Pharaoh to adopt him. When Asiya ordered wet nurses for Moses, Moses refuses to be breastfed. Islamic tradition states that this is because God forbade Moses from being fed by any wet nurse in order to reunite him with his mother. His sister worries that Moses has not been fed for some time, so she appears to the Pharaoh and informs him that she knows someone who can feed him. After being questioned, she is ordered to bring the woman being discussed. The sister brings their mother, who feeds Moses, and thereafter, she is appointed as the wet nurse of Moses.

Prophethood

Test of prophecy
According to Isra'iliyat hadith, when Moses is on the Pharaoh's lap in his childhood, he grabs the Pharaoh's beard and slaps him in the face. This action prompts the Pharaoh to consider Moses as the Israelite who would overthrow him, and the Pharaoh wanted to kill Moses. The Pharaoh's wife persuades him not to kill him because he is an infant. Instead, he decides to test Moses. Two plates are set before young Moses, one containing rubies and the other glowing coals. Moses reaches out for the rubies, but the angel Gabriel directs his hand to the coals. Moses grabs a glowing coal and puts it in his mouth, burning his tongue. After the incident, Moses suffers a speech defect, but is spared by the Pharaoh.

Escape to Midian and Marriage

After having reached adulthood, according to the Quran, Moses is passing through a city when he comes across an Egyptian fighting with an Israelite. The Israelite man is believed to be Sam'ana, known in the Bible to be a Samaritan, who asks Moses for his assistance against the Egyptian who is mistreating him. Moses attempts to intervene and becomes involved in the dispute. Moses strikes the Egyptian in a state of anger, which results in his death. Moses then repents to God, and the following day, he again comes across the same Israelite fighting with another Egyptian. The Israelite again asks Moses for help, and as Moses approaches the Israelite, he reminds Moses of his manslaughter and asks if Moses intended to kill the Israelite. Moses is reported, and the Pharaoh orders Moses to be killed. However, Moses flees to the desert after being alerted to his punishment. According to Islamic tradition, after Moses arrives in Midian, he witnesses two female shepherds driving back their flocks from a well. Moses approaches them and inquires about their work as shepherds and their retreat from the well. Upon hearing their answers and about the old age of their father, although his identity is contested, generally accepted to be Prophet Shuaib, Moses waters their flocks for them. The two shepherds return to their home and inform their father of Moses. They then invite Moses to a feast. At that feast, their father asks Moses to work for him for eight years in return for marriage to one of his daughters.

primaryTitle: Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam
bio: Musa bin al-Harith bin Khalid (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full: Musa ibn al-Harith ibn Khalid was a child of the early Muslim emigrants to Abyssinia, of the Quraysh clan of Banu Taym ibn Murra. His father, al-Harith ibn Khalid ibn Sakhr ibn 'Amir ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Taym ibn Murra, emigrated to Abyssinia with his wife Rayta bint al-Harith. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Athir and Abu Nu'aym all record that Musa was born to them there, in Abyssinia; Abu Hatim al-Razi also states that he was born in Abyssinia. His sisters 'A'isha, Zaynab and Fatima were born there too, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr's list also names a brother, Ibrahim. Musa died young, and the accounts differ on where. Ibn Sa'd says that in all of his authorities' reports Musa died in Abyssinia, and Mus'ab al-Zubayri likewise says the children died there. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir also report that the father set out with them for Medina and that all died at a watering place on the road except the father. Ibn Sa'd gives a related account from Musa ibn 'Uqba and Abu Ma'shar in which Rayta and her children died at the water except Fatima. No date is recorded for his birth or death.

al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil (Ibn Abi Hatim) — Musa ibn al-Harith ibn Khalid, via hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com

primaryTitle: Sufi commentator and expositor of Ibn Arabi's thought
bio: Abu Abdullah Musab bin Umair Al-Abdari was one of Badr’s first companions to Islam, the envoy of the Prophet Muhammad to call to Islam in Yathrib after the first Pledge of Aqaba, and the standard bearer of the Emigrants in the Battles of Badr and Uhud.
bio_full:
Abd al-Razzaq al-Qashani was a prominent Islamic mystic and scholar who lived from approximately 1201 to 1330 CE. He belonged to the Akbarian school of Islamic mysticism, which followed the teachings and philosophical approach of the renowned Sufi master Ibn Arabi.

Al-Qashani is primarily known for his extensive commentaries on the works of Ibn Arabi, particularly his detailed commentary on Ibn Arabi's "Fusus al-Hikam" (The Bezels of Wisdom), one of the most influential texts in Islamic mystical philosophy. His commentary helped make Ibn Arabi's complex metaphysical concepts more accessible to later generations of scholars and mystics, serving as a bridge between the master's original teachings and subsequent Sufi thought.

As a scholar in the Akbarian tradition, al-Qashani engaged deeply with the doctrine of the Unity of Being, a central concept in Ibn Arabi's mystical philosophy that explores the relationship between the divine and creation. His writings demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of Islamic theology, philosophy, and mystical practice, combining rigorous scholarship with spiritual insight.

Al-Qashani also produced his own original works on Sufism and Islamic spirituality, though he is best remembered for his role as a commentator and interpreter. His scholarly approach was characterized by careful analysis of mystical concepts and their grounding in Quranic and prophetic teachings.

His significance to Islamic history lies primarily in his contribution to the preservation and transmission of Akbarian mystical thought. During a period when Ibn Arabi's teachings faced criticism from some orthodox scholars, al-Qashani's commentaries provided scholarly legitimacy and helped ensure the continuation of this mystical tradition. His works became standard references for later Sufi scholars and contributed to the broader development of Islamic mystical literature.

Through his scholarly efforts, al-Qashani played a crucial role in the intellectual history of Islamic mysticism, helping to establish a systematic approach to understanding and teaching the complex metaphysical concepts that characterized the Akbarian school. His influence extended beyond his lifetime, as his commentaries continued to be studied and referenced by mystics and scholars in subsequent centuries.

famous: Mushin bin Abi Qays bin al-Aslat
full: Mushin bin Abi Qays bin al-Aslat
dob_s: c. 590 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: c. 650 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
bio: Mushin bin Abi Qays bin al-Aslat (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Poet-Companion.
bio_full:
Mushin bin Abi Qays bin al-Aslat was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, he was based in Medina and died in 635 CE, approximately three years after the Prophet's death.

As a member of the Sahaba—the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad—Mushin occupied a significant position in early Islamic society. The Sahaba are collectively revered in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices, having witnessed firsthand the development of the Muslim community during its foundational years.

Mushin is particularly remembered as a poet-companion, indicating his dual role as both a religious follower and a literary figure. Poetry held immense cultural importance in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society, serving not only as entertainment but also as a means of preserving tribal history, expressing social values, and engaging in intellectual discourse. Poet-companions like Mushin played a crucial role in documenting and celebrating the early Islamic experience through verse.

His presence in Medina places him within the context of the Hijra, the migration of Muslims from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, which marked a pivotal moment in Islamic history. Medina became the center of the early Muslim community, where the first Islamic state was established and where many foundational Islamic practices and institutions were developed.

The designation of "Poet-Companion" suggests that Mushin contributed to the rich tradition of Islamic poetry that emerged during this period. Early Islamic poets often composed verses that reflected the spiritual and social transformations occurring within their communities, helping to articulate the new faith's values and experiences.

Living through the Prophet's ministry and dying just a few years after Muhammad's death in 632 CE, Mushin witnessed the entire arc of early Islamic expansion and consolidation. His generation of companions became instrumental in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings to subsequent generations, making their testimonies and contributions fundamental to Islamic historical and religious understanding.

As both a companion and poet, Mushin bin Abi Qays bin al-Aslat represents the intersection of religious devotion and literary expression that characterized many figures in early Islamic society, contributing to the cultural and spiritual foundation of the Muslim community during its most crucial developmental period.

primaryTitle: Director of The Message and Omar Mukhtar — Islamic Cinema Pioneer
bio: Mustafa Akkad is a Syrian-American film director and producer. He was the first Arab to arrive in Hollywood, where he produced the American horror film series Halloween in the 1970s. Then he moved on to produce more serious films about the Arab and Islamic world, such as: the film The Message in 1976, and the film Omar Al-Mukhtar in 1981.
bio_full:
Mustafa Akkad was a Syrian-American filmmaker who played a pioneering role in bringing Islamic and Arab narratives to international cinema during the late twentieth century. Born in Aleppo, Syria in 1930, he later emigrated to the United States where he pursued a career in film production and direction.

Akkad initially established himself in Hollywood through his work on the horror film franchise Halloween, which he produced beginning in the 1970s. This commercial success provided him with the resources and industry connections to pursue more personally meaningful projects focused on Islamic history and Arab culture.

His most significant contribution to Islamic historical cinema came with the 1976 film "The Message," which depicted the early life of Prophet Muhammad and the origins of Islam. The film was notable for its respectful treatment of Islamic religious sensitivities and its attempt to present Islamic history to both Muslim and non-Muslim audiences worldwide. The production faced considerable challenges and controversy, but ultimately succeeded in creating what many consider the first major Hollywood film to seriously engage with Islamic themes.

In 1981, Akkad produced "Lion of the Desert," which told the story of Omar al-Mukhtar, the Libyan resistance leader who fought against Italian colonization in the early twentieth century. This film continued his pattern of highlighting Arab and Islamic historical figures for international audiences.

Akkad's work was significant in the context of Islamic history and culture because he was among the first filmmakers to bring these narratives to mainstream Western cinema at a time when such representations were rare. His films attempted to counter prevailing stereotypes and present Islamic civilization and Arab history with dignity and historical accuracy.

Throughout his career, Akkad maintained his commitment to producing films that would educate audiences about Islamic and Arab heritage while meeting the technical and commercial standards of international cinema. His work represented an early effort at cross-cultural dialogue through film.

Akkad died in 2005 in Jordan. His legacy lies in his pioneering efforts to create respectful, historically-informed cinematic portrayals of Islamic history and Arab culture for global audiences, establishing a foundation for later filmmakers working in similar themes.

primaryTitle: Last Shaykh al-Islam of the Ottoman Empire
titles: Shaykh al-Islam · Mustafa Sabri
bio: Mustafa Sabri was the last Sheikh of Islam in the Ottoman Empire. He is known for his views condemning the Turkish nationalist movement led by Kemal Ataturk. Because of his resistance to Ataturk, he lived half his life in exile in various countries, and died in Egypt.
bio_full:
Mustafa Sabri (Ottoman Turkish: مصطفى صبرى افندی; 1869 – 1954) was an Ottoman theologian and university professor who was the penulitimate Shaykh al-Islām of the Ottoman Empire. He is known for his opinions condemning the Turkish nationalist movement under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. Due to his resistance to Atatürk, he lived half of his life in exile in various countries, and died in Egypt.

Life
His father was Ahmed Efendi. He was born in Tokat in 1869. He began his education in his hometown and quickly memorized the Quran. He pursued his education in Kayseri and Istanbul, where he studied under Ahmed Asim Efendi and received his certificate of proficiency (icazetname). He married the daughter of his master Asım Efendi. He passed the Rüus-ı Tedris examination (teaching qualification exam) and became a teacher (müderris) at Fatih Mosque in Constantinople.
From 1898 until 1914, he attended Huzur lessons (lectures and discussions given by the Ulema in the presence of the Sultan). Between 1900 and 1904, he was the librarian (hafiz-i kutub) of Sultan Abdul Hamid II (r. 1876–1909).
After the re-establishment of the Constitution in July 1908, he entered Parliament as the representative of Tokat. From 1908 to 1912, he was the chief editor of the journal Bayan-ul-Haq (The Exposition of Truth), an intellectual journal published by the Cemiyet-i İlmiye (Religious Scholars’ Association). Although he thanked the CUP (Committee of Union and Progress) and the army in an article in the first issue of Bayan-ul-Haq for ending the Hamidian regime, shortly afterwards he joined the opposition to the party.
He became the founding member of the Ahali Fırkası in 1910 and the Freedom and Accord Party in 1911. In 1912, he participated in the foundation of another political organization, the Cemiyet-i İttihad-ı İslamiye (Islamic Union Association).
In January 1913, after the Bab-i Ali coup, he fled to Egypt and then went to Romania, where he made his living teaching Turkish. After the occupation of Romania by Ottoman troops during the First World War, he was arrested and sent to Turkey, where he was imprisoned in Bilecik. He was exiled for a time to Bursa. After the end of the war, he again entered politics and joined Dar-ul-Hikmet-i İslamiye (Islamic University).
He became the Shaykh al-Islām, but he resigned from this post. In 1919, he was appointed as Shaykh al-Islām in the cabinet of Damad Ferid Pasha. Sabri served as the acting Grand Vizier during the absence of Damad Ferid Pasha while he was attending the Paris Peace Conference, and he was nominated to the senate after the fall of Ferid Pasha's cabinet. He became the first president of the Cemiyet-i Müderrisin (Society of Islamic Scholars), which later became the Teali-i İslam Cemiyeti (Society for the Elevation of Islam).
In 1920, Mustafa Sabri was again appointed as Shaykh al-Islām to the second cabinet of Damad Ferid Pasha.
In 1922, he fled Turkey once more to escape arrest by the Turkish National Movement when his name appeared on a list of 150 political dissidents. He went to Romania for a second time where he published the journal Yarın (Tomorrow).
Sabri first went to Romania and then to Greece, where he published an anti-Kemalist newspaper in which he violently attacked the new Turkish regime and its founder, Kemal Atatürk (1881–1938). He later went to Hejaz, before settling in Egypt, where he continued his intellectual activities.
In the early 1930s he went to Egypt, where he stayed until his death on 12 March 1954.

Works
As a conservative scholar, he produced a number of works. In his writings, he opposed both Western secularism and Islamic modernism, which is affected by Westernization. He proposed a program of Islamization before and after the fall of the Ottoman Empire. He remained within the context of the traditional Ash'arite-Maturidite theology and Ottoman madrasa system. In Egypt, he wrote several books in Arabic in response to such modernist thinkers as Muhammad Farid Wajdi and 'Abbas Mahmud al-'Aqqad as well as Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad 'Abduh, and Muhammad Mustafa al-Maraghi.
He also criticized the views of some Egyptian intellectuals such as: Qasim Amin, Zaki Mubarak, Zaki Naguib Mahmoud, Mohammed Hussein Heikal, Taha Hussein, and 'Ali 'Abdel Raziq, who remained under the influence of Westernization and interpreted the Islamic religion according to Western thought and values.
He responded to the allegations of the Arab historian Muhammad 'Abdullah 'Inan against the Ottoman Turks and refuted his theses. He insisted that Islam was not in conflict with science and it was a religious obligation to cover women according to certain conditions.
One of the persons that he debated on scholarly issues was Mahmud Shaltut, who took office in various levels and rose to prominence with his reformist thoughts. He objected the fatwa of Shaltut who used the thesis that there is no open expression in Quran and in Hadith that support the ascension and descent of Jesus in such as extend to form the basis of faith and the person who rejected this belief would not be in trouble with in terms of faith. He criticized Shaltut and he gave answers to his assertions and the evidences he used.
Mustafa Sabri criticized Musa Bigiev's thought and called him the "Luther of Islam". According to Sabri, Bigiev was an "eminent scholar", but ultimately could not remain "immune to the disease of European material progress". Sabri also criticized some poets like Jamil Sidqi al-Zahawi and Ahmad Shawqi.
After the abolition of the Sultanate and the position of Shaykh al-Islām in 1922, he published his Al-Nakir 'ala Munkiri al-Ni'ma min al-Din wa-al-Khilafa wa-al-Umma (Arabic: النكير على منكري النعمة من الدين والخلافة والأمة). Completed before the abolition decision was made, Sabri's book mentioned the fate of the caliphate very briefly at the conclusion of his work, only as an additional proof for the arguments already advanced in the book. This work is a strong attack on the Kemalists and their evolving vision for post-Ottoman Turkey.
Sabri presents the Kemalists as decadents, Turkish chauvinists who colluded with the British against Islam and the caliphate, and Kemal Atatürk as a concealed Jew. Although the caliphate is not the main focus of the book, Sabri defends the last Sultan/Caliph and describes the separation of the Turkish government from the caliphate as a premeditated step on the part of the Kemalists to establish a non-Islamic government in Turkey.
In the Mas'alat Tarjamat al-Qur'an (Arabic: مسألة ترجمة القرآن, lit. 'The Issue of Translating the Qur'an'), Mustafa Sabri takes up the issue of using the translation of Qur'anic verses in ritual prayers. The book is a direct response to Atatürk's attempt to have all prayers performed in modern Turkish rather than in their original form in Arabic.
His four-volume magnum opus Mawqif al-'Aql wa-al-'Ilm wa-al-'Alim min Rabb al-'Alamin wa-'Ibadihi al-Mursalin (Arabic: موقف العقل والعلم والعالم من رب العالمين وعباده المرسلين, lit. 'The Position of Reason, Knowledge, and the Scholar in Regards to the Lord of the Worlds and His Divinely Sent Servants') is devoted to a detailed analysis and criticism of many issues of twentieth-century Islamic modernism.

bio: Muti'a bint al-Nu'man bin Malik (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Muti'a bint al-Nu'man bin Malik was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the Medinan Muslims who welcomed and supported the Prophet and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca after the Hijra in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions, Muti'a would have been among the residents of Medina who converted to Islam and pledged their allegiance to Prophet Muhammad when he established the first Muslim community there. The Ansar played a crucial role in the early development of Islam, providing both material and moral support to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years in Medina.

The designation "Sahabiyya" indicates that she lived during the time of Prophet Muhammad and had direct contact with him, placing her among the first generation of Muslims whose testimonies and experiences became foundational to Islamic tradition. Female companions like Muti'a were integral to the early Muslim community, participating in religious life and contributing to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This timing suggests she witnessed both the Prophet's lifetime and the initial expansion of the Islamic community under the first caliphs.

While specific details about her individual contributions or particular roles within the community are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, her recognition as a companion reflects her standing within the early Muslim community. The Ansari companions as a group are remembered in Islamic history for their pivotal role in providing sanctuary and support to Islam during its critical early years, helping establish Medina as the center of the growing Muslim community.

Muti'a bint al-Nu'man's place among the companions represents the broader participation of women in the foundational period of Islam and the important role played by the Medinan Muslims in supporting and nurturing the early Islamic community during its transition from a small group of believers to an established religious and political entity.

bio: Na'ila bint 'Ubaid bin al-Hurr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Na'ila bint 'Ubaid bin al-Hurr was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Na'ila would have been among the local inhabitants who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the early Islamic state in Medina, offering their homes, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca.

The designation of sahabiyya indicates that Na'ila had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. This status holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are revered for their firsthand experience of the Prophet's teachings and their role in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge to subsequent generations.

Living during the crucial period of early Islamic expansion, Na'ila witnessed the transformation of the small Muslim community in Medina into a growing religious and political movement. Her lifetime, ending around 635 CE, coincided with the Rashidun Caliphate period under the leadership of the first caliph, Abu Bakr, and the early years of the second caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab.

While specific details about Na'ila's individual contributions or particular roles within the early Muslim community are not extensively documented in available historical sources, her recognition as a companion of the Prophet places her among the foundational figures of Islamic history. The female companions, like their male counterparts, are honored in Islamic tradition for their dedication to the faith and their participation in the early Muslim community.

Her inclusion among the documented companions reflects the presence and participation of women in the early Islamic community in Medina, contributing to our understanding of the diverse composition of the first Muslim society and the role of Medinan supporters in the establishment of Islam.

bio: Na'ila bint Rabi' bin Qays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Na'ila bint al-Rabi' ibn Qays was a woman of the Ansar of Medina who accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad, according to Ibn Sa'd in his Tabaqat. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Na'ila bint al-Rabi' ibn Qays ibn 'Amir ibn 'Abbad ibn al-Abjar, whose line is that of Khudra ibn 'Awf ibn al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj. Her mother was Fatima bint 'Amr ibn 'Atiyya ibn Khansa', whose line Ibn Sa'd traces back to al-Najjar. She was the full sister of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Rabi', and Ibn Sa'd notes that 'Abd Allah was present at al-'Aqaba and at Badr. She married Aws ibn Khalid ibn Qurt, whose lineage also goes back to al-Najjar. Ibn Hajar also includes her among the female Companions in al-Isaba. No children, and no dates of birth or death, are recorded for her.

bio: Na'ila bint Sa'd bin Malik (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Na'ila bint Sa'd bin Malik was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early years of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca following the Hijra in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions, Na'ila bint Sa'd would have witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim community in Medina and lived through the formative period of Islamic history. The Ansar played a crucial role in providing sanctuary and support to the early Muslim community when they faced persecution in Mecca, and their acceptance of Islam was instrumental in the religion's survival and growth.

During her lifetime, Na'ila would have experienced the major events that shaped early Islamic history, including the construction of the first mosque in Medina, the establishment of the Constitution of Medina, and the various military campaigns that secured the Muslim community's position in the Arabian Peninsula. As a female companion living in Medina, she would have been part of the community that directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and received his teachings.

Her designation as a sahabiyya places her among the women who are revered in Islamic tradition for their early acceptance of Islam and their role in supporting the nascent Muslim community. The female companions are recognized for their contributions to preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, supporting the community during times of hardship, and participating in the religious and social life of early Islamic society.

Na'ila bint Sa'd bin Malik died around 635 CE, just a few years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. Her life spanned the crucial transition period from the pre-Islamic era to the establishment of Islam as a major religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula. While specific details about her individual contributions may not be extensively documented in historical sources, her status as an Ansari companion of Medina signifies her importance as one of the early supporters of Islam during its most vulnerable and formative years.

bio: Na'ila bint Salaama bin Waqash (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Na'ila bint Salaama bin Waqash was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who provided support and refuge to the Prophet and the early Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Na'ila would have witnessed and participated in the crucial early years of the Islamic community's establishment in that city. The Ansar played a vital role in Islamic history by offering protection and assistance to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca, helping to ensure the survival and growth of the nascent Muslim community during a particularly vulnerable period.

The designation of sahabiyya indicates that Na'ila had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. This status holds special significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are viewed as the first generation of Muslims who received Islamic teachings directly from the Prophet and helped transmit them to subsequent generations.

Her identification as being "of Medina" suggests she was likely among those who converted to Islam when the Prophet arrived in the city, rather than being one of the earlier converts from Mecca. The early Muslim community in Medina faced numerous challenges, including establishing new social structures, defending against hostile tribes, and integrating immigrants with local residents.

Na'ila lived during a period of rapid expansion and consolidation of Islamic teachings and practices. The Medinan period of Prophet Muhammad's mission, from 622 to 632 CE, saw the development of many fundamental aspects of Islamic law, governance, and community organization. As a female companion, she would have been part of the community of women who learned Islamic teachings and practices directly from the Prophet and his household.

Her death around 635 CE places her among those companions who lived to see the beginning of the Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. The early companions like Na'ila represent an important link in the chain of Islamic historical transmission, serving as direct witnesses to the foundational period of the religion and helping to preserve and pass on the teachings and practices they observed during the Prophet's lifetime.

bio: Na'ila bint al-Furafisa was the wife of the third caliph Uthman. She narrated many hadith including eyewitness accounts of the assassination of Uthman.
bio_full:
Na'ilah bint al-Furafisah was a prominent female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad and the wife of Uthman ibn Affan, who served as the third Caliph of the Islamic community from 644 to 656 CE. Born around 595 CE, she lived during the formative period of Islam and witnessed many of the religion's most significant early developments.

As the wife of Caliph Uthman, Na'ilah occupied a position of considerable social standing within the early Muslim community in Medina. Her proximity to the center of political and religious authority provided her with unique access to important events and conversations that would later prove valuable to Islamic historical and legal scholarship.

Na'ilah's most significant contribution to Islamic tradition lies in her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings and actions of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial foundation of Islamic law and practice. Her narrations were considered reliable by hadith scholars, contributing to the preservation of prophetic traditions for future generations of Muslims.

Her most historically significant testimonies concern the tragic circumstances surrounding her husband's death in 656 CE. Uthman was killed during a siege of his house by rebels who opposed his policies as caliph. As an eyewitness to these events, Na'ilah provided crucial firsthand accounts of the assassination that became important historical sources for understanding this pivotal moment in early Islamic history. Her testimony helped preserve details about the final days of Uthman's life and the circumstances of his death, events that would have lasting consequences for the Muslim community.

The death of Uthman marked the beginning of the first major civil war in Islamic history, making Na'ilah's eyewitness accounts particularly valuable to historians seeking to understand this period. Her narrations provide insight not only into the specific events surrounding the assassination but also into the broader political and social tensions that characterized the early caliphate.

Na'ilah died around 635 CE, though some sources suggest she lived longer. Her legacy endures through her contributions to hadith literature and her role as a witness to one of the most consequential events in early Islamic history. Her accounts remain important sources for scholars studying the period of the Rashidun Caliphate and the early development of the Islamic community.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Na'im bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Na'im bin Maqrn al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early 7th century CE in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE in the Hijaz region, he belonged to the Mazni tribe and became one of the sahaba, the Arabic term for the companions who knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime.

Al-Mazni is historically recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event in early Islamic history that took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge, also known as the Bay'at al-Ridwan or Pledge of the Tree, occurred when approximately 1,400 Muslims who had accompanied the Prophet on what was intended to be a pilgrimage to Mecca were prevented from entering the city by the Meccan authorities. Under a tree at Hudaybiyyah, these companions pledged their loyalty to Muhammad and their willingness to fight if necessary. This event is referenced in the Quran in chapter 48, verse 18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those who pledged allegiance under the tree.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular importance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the unwavering commitment of the early Muslim community to their faith and leader during a moment of potential conflict. Those who participated in this pledge are regarded with special reverence in Islamic tradition, as the Quran explicitly mentions God's satisfaction with their actions.

Al-Mazni lived during the formative period of Islam, witnessing the religion's establishment and early expansion under the Prophet's leadership. He would have experienced the crucial developments of the faith during the Medina period, including various military campaigns and the gradual spread of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Historical records indicate that al-Mazni died around 640 CE, placing his death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the rule of the second caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab. This timing suggests he lived to see the initial expansion of the Islamic state beyond the Arabian Peninsula, though specific details about his role in these later developments are not well documented in available historical sources.

As one of the sahaba and particularly as a participant in the Pledge of Ridwan, Na'im bin Maqrn al-Mazni represents the dedication of the early Muslim community and remains a respected figure in Islamic historical memory.

bio: Nabia bin 'Uthman (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Nubayh ibn 'Uthman ibn Rabi'a ibn Wahb ibn Hudhafa ibn Jumah was a member of the Quraysh clan of Banu Jumah. Ibn Sa'd gives his great-grandfather's name as Wahban rather than Wahb. On the authority of al-Waqidi, both Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir describe him as an early Muslim in Mecca who went to Abyssinia in the second emigration. The sources record a disagreement over this. Muhammad ibn Ishaq held that the emigrant to Abyssinia was not Nubayh but his father, 'Uthman ibn Rabi'a. Ibn Sa'd reports both views and ends with 'God knows best'. Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir also note that Musa ibn 'Uqba and Abu Ma'shar did not name either Nubayh or his father among the emigrants to Abyssinia. No other events in his life, and no dates of birth or death, are recorded for him in these entries.

bio: Nābit ibn Ismā'īl (legendary–legendary) was a founding figure, based in Mecca. Known as Ancestor of Prophet Muhammad.
bio_full:
Nābit ibn Ismā'īl is a figure mentioned in traditional Islamic genealogical accounts as part of the ancestral lineage of the Prophet Muhammad. According to these traditional sources, he lived in the Arabian Peninsula and is considered to be among the ancestors who descended from Ismā'īl (Ishmael), the son of the prophet Ibrāhīm (Abraham).

The historical documentation regarding Nābit ibn Ismā'īl is extremely limited, and much of what is recorded about him comes from later genealogical compilations rather than contemporary historical sources. Islamic tradition places him within the complex tribal genealogies of pre-Islamic Arabia, specifically among the lineages that eventually led to the Quraysh tribe of Mecca.

In Islamic historical methodology, figures from this early period of Arabian history often exist primarily within oral traditions that were later compiled into written genealogies. These genealogical records served important social and political functions in Arabian society, establishing tribal connections and legitimizing leadership claims, but they present challenges for modern historical verification due to the long period of oral transmission before being recorded in writing.

The significance of Nābit ibn Ismā'īl in Islamic history derives primarily from his position within these traditional genealogical accounts rather than from specific historical actions or achievements that can be independently documented. His inclusion in the prophetic lineage connects him to the broader Islamic understanding of Arabian tribal history and the ancestry of Muhammad.

It is important to note that genealogical records from pre-Islamic Arabia, while culturally and religiously significant within Islamic tradition, often cannot be verified through independent historical sources. The historical record for individual figures from this period is generally sparse, and many details about their lives, specific dates, and activities remain within the realm of traditional accounts rather than documented history.

Within the context of Islamic historical studies, figures like Nābit ibn Ismā'īl represent the intersection of genealogical tradition and religious significance, serving as important elements in the traditional understanding of prophetic ancestry while remaining historically elusive in terms of verifiable biographical details.
