bio: Rafi' bin Khadij bin Rafi' (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Rafi' bin Khadij bin Rafi' was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early years of Islam. Born around 595 CE, he belonged to the generation that witnessed the foundational period of the Islamic community in the Arabian Peninsula.

As one of the Sahaba, Rafi' bin Khadij was among those who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and lived during the time of revelation. His presence in Medina placed him at the center of the early Muslim community, which had established itself there following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Rafi' bin Khadij is particularly remembered for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant oath of allegiance taken by the companions under a tree at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge is referenced in the Quran in chapter 48, verse 18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those who pledged their allegiance to the Prophet under the tree. The Pledge of Ridwan occurred during a tense diplomatic mission when the Muslims traveled to Mecca for pilgrimage but were initially prevented from entering the city. The companions' willingness to stand by the Prophet during this critical moment demonstrated their commitment and loyalty to the Islamic cause.

The historical records indicate that Rafi' bin Khadij lived through the crucial early decades of Islam, witnessing the establishment of the Muslim community, various military campaigns, and the consolidation of Islamic teachings. His life spanned the period from the pre-Islamic era through the time of the Prophet and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate.

Like many of the Sahaba, Rafi' bin Khadij's significance lies in his role as a direct witness to the formative period of Islam. The companions served as the primary sources for transmitting the teachings, sayings, and practices of Prophet Muhammad to subsequent generations. Their testimonies and narrations became fundamental to the development of hadith literature and Islamic jurisprudence.

Rafi' bin Khadij died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr or the early years of Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule. His relatively short life coincided with one of the most transformative periods in Arabian and Islamic history, making him part of the generation that established the foundations upon which the Islamic tradition would be built.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Rafi' bin Makayth (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Rafi' bin Makayth was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE, he was among the Muslims who participated in the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant oath of allegiance taken by approximately 1,400 companions under a tree at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge is referenced in the Quran (48:18), which praises those who gave their oath to the Prophet at that momentous occasion.

The Pledge of Ridwan occurred during a tense period when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers had traveled from Medina to Mecca to perform the pilgrimage but were prevented from entering the city by the Meccan tribes. When rumors spread that the Prophet's envoy Uthman ibn Affan had been killed while negotiating with the Meccans, the companions pledged their loyalty and readiness to fight if necessary. This demonstration of unity and commitment became a defining moment in early Islamic history, and those who participated, including Rafi' bin Makayth, earned special recognition for their faithfulness.

As a companion of the Prophet, Rafi' bin Makayth would have been among the first generation of Muslims who directly witnessed and learned from Muhammad's teachings and example. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge, including the Prophet's sayings and actions (hadith), which became fundamental sources for Islamic law and practice after the Quran.

Rafi' bin Makayth lived in the Hijaz region of the Arabian Peninsula, the heartland of early Islam that includes the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He witnessed the rapid expansion of Islam during the Prophet's lifetime and the early caliphate period that followed. His death around 640 CE places him among those companions who lived through the formative decades of Islamic civilization but died before seeing its later territorial expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about his individual contributions may not be extensively documented, his inclusion among the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan marks him as one of the faithful early Muslims whose collective testimony and support helped establish the foundations of the Islamic community during its most critical early years.

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Rafi' bin Malik bin al-'Ajlan (c. 589–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Rafi' ibn Malik ibn al-Ajlan ibn Amr ibn Amir ibn Zurayq was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Zurayq of the Khazraj in Medina. Ibn Sa'd gives his kunya as Abu Malik; Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir add that some call him Abu Rifa'a. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Mawiya bint al-Ajlan.

Ibn Abi Hatim counts him among the first six men of the Ansar to accept Islam. Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn Hibban and Ibn al-Athir state that he attended both the first and the second pledge of al-Aqaba, and he was one of the twelve leaders (nuqaba') appointed there, serving as leader of the Banu Zurayq. Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Manda and Ibn al-Athir (the last two citing Ibn Ishaq) report that he was the first to bring Surat Yusuf to Medina.

Whether he fought at Badr is disputed. Ibn Sa'd and Abu Nu'aym say he did not, though his sons Rifa'a and Khallad did; Musa ibn Uqba and Ibn Hibban count him among those present.

Ibn Sa'd records that he was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Uhud, in Shawwal, thirty-two months after the Hijra (3 AH, 625 CE); Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir agree. Ibn Sa'd names his children as Rifa'a, Khallad and Malik. Ibn Abi Hatim notes that nothing is narrated from him.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Rafi' ibn Malik (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Manda, al-Baghawi, Ibn Abi Hatim)

bio: Rafi' ibn Yazid bin al-Sakan (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Rafi' ibn Yazid ibn al-Sakan was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early decades of Islam. Born around 594 CE, he belonged to the Ansar, the Medinan Muslims who supported Muhammad and the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Rafi' is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are held in special esteem within Islamic tradition, as they were among the earliest supporters who risked their lives for the nascent Muslim state.

As one of the Ansar, Rafi' represented the Medinan tribes who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to Muhammad and the Meccan Muslims who had migrated to their city. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the first Muslim community in Medina, offering protection, resources, and military support during the formative years of Islam.

Rafi' died in 625 CE, likely from wounds sustained in the Battle of Uhud, which took place in that year. This battle, fought between the Muslim community and Meccan forces, resulted in significant casualties among the Muslims, including several prominent companions of the Prophet.

His relatively short life span reflects the dangerous and tumultuous period of early Islamic history, when the Muslim community faced constant military threats from opposing tribes and the established powers of the Arabian Peninsula. Like many of his contemporaries among the early Muslims, Rafi' lived during a time when religious conviction often required military service and personal sacrifice.

Within Islamic historical records, companions like Rafi' ibn Yazid ibn al-Sakan represent the generation that directly witnessed the Prophet's teachings and participated in the foundational events of the Muslim community. Their sacrifices and dedication during these crucial early years helped establish Islam as a major religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula and beyond.

bio: Raibi' bin Rafi' (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Raibi' bin Rafi' was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who resided in Medina, the city that became the center of the nascent Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Raibi' bin Rafi' is historically recognized as one of the "Companions of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the outnumbered Muslim forces.

The designation "Companion of Badr" carries special importance in Islamic tradition, as those who participated in this battle are considered to hold a distinguished position among the Prophet's companions. The Quran makes reference to the participants of Badr, and later Islamic sources often highlight their role in this pivotal encounter that helped establish the military and political strength of the early Muslim state.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Raibi' bin Rafi' would have been part of the close-knit community that formed around the Prophet in Medina. The companions, known as Sahaba in Arabic, were those who met Muhammad, believed in him, and died as Muslims. They played crucial roles in the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Raibi' bin Rafi' died in 634 CE, just two years after the death of Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. This places his death during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph. His relatively early death meant he lived through the foundational period of Islam but did not witness the major territorial expansions that would occur under later caliphs.

While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his recognition as a companion places him among the foundational generation of Muslims who helped establish and preserve the early Islamic community.

bio: Ramla bint 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Ramla bint Abd Allah ibn Ubayy was an Ansari woman of Medina who accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Her father was Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, whom Ibn al-Athir describes as the head of the hypocrites. Ibn Sa'd traces her lineage through Ubayy ibn Malik ibn al-Harith to the Banu Awf of the Khazraj, and Ibn al-Athir places her among the Banu al-Hubla.

Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Lubna bint Ubada ibn Nadla, and records that she was married to Isma ibn Zayd ibn Malil. Both Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir state that she pledged allegiance to the Prophet; Ibn al-Athir cites Ibn Habib for this. The sources consulted say nothing further about her life and give no date of death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Ramla bint Abd Allah ibn Ubayy (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba)

bio: Ramlah bint Abi 'Auf (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Ramla bint Abi Awf ibn Subayra ibn Sa'id ibn Sa'd ibn Sahm was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Sahm of Quraysh in Mecca. Ibn al-Athir describes her as the niece of Abu Wada'a ibn Subayra al-Sahmi, and Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Umm Abd Allah, Sarma' bint al-Harith ibn Awf.

Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam early in Mecca, before the Prophet entered the house of al-Arqam, and pledged allegiance. She was married to al-Muttalib ibn Azhar, and Ibn al-Athir notes that Ibn Ishaq names the two of them together among the early Muslims of Mecca. She emigrated with her husband to Abyssinia in the second migration, and there she gave birth to their son, Abd Allah ibn al-Muttalib. Ibn Abd al-Barr, citing Ibn Ishaq, says this son was said to be the first man in Islam to inherit from his father, and that al-Muttalib died in Abyssinia.

Ibn Hibban states simply that she was a Companion. The sources consulted do not record when or where she died.

bio: Ramlah bint al-Harith (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Ramla bint al-Harith ibn Tha'laba was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu al-Najjar of the Khazraj in Medina. Ibn al-Athir records that Ibn Habib counted her among the women of the Ansar who pledged allegiance to the Prophet. One modern study, drawing on Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Hajar, gives her kunya as Umm Thabit, names her mother as Kabsha bint Thabit ibn al-Nu'man, and names her husband as Mu'adh ibn al-Harith (Ibn Afra'), by whom she had a daughter, Sara.

She is remembered mainly for her house in Medina, which was used for public purposes in the Prophet's time. Ibn al-Athir records that after Sa'd ibn Mu'adh gave his judgement on the Banu Qurayza, the captives were held in the house of Ramla bint al-Harith. According to the same study, citing Ibn Sa'd and others, the house was also used to lodge visiting delegations, among them the Banu Hanifa, the Banu Kilab and the Abd al-Qays, and to hold captives and goods taken in campaigns. The sources consulted do not record the date of her death.

full: Muḥammad Rashīd ibn ʿAlī Riḍā ibn Muḥammad Shams al-Dīn
primaryTitle: al-Manar Editor — Bridge between Salafism and Islamic Modernism
bio: Muhammad Rashid bin Ali Reda, an Islamic thinker, writer and literary figure during the Ottoman era. He was born in the village of Qalamoun in Lebanon, a village located on the Mediterranean coast of Mount Lebanon and about three miles from Tripoli, the Levant. He died in Egypt on Jumada al-Awwal 23, 1354.
bio_full:
Sayyid Muhammad Rashīd Rida Al-Hussaini (Arabic: سيد محمد رشيد رضا الحسيني, romanized: Muḥammad Rashīd Riḍā; 1865 – 22 August 1935) was an Islamic scholar, reformer, theologian and revivalist. An early Salafist, Rida called for the revival of hadith studies and, as a theoretician of an Islamic state, condemned the rising currents of secularism and nationalism across the Islamic world following the abolition of the Ottoman sultanate. He championed a global pan-Islamist program aimed at re-establishing a Caliphate to unite diverse peoples under a single global Islamic authority. 
As a young hadith student who studied al-Ghazali and Ibn Taymiyya, Rida believed reform was necessary to save the Muslim communities, eliminate Sufist practices he considered heretical, and initiate an Islamic renewal. He left Syria to work with Abduh in Cairo, where he was influenced by Abduh's Islamic Modernist movement and began publishing al-Manar in 1898. Through al-Manar's popularity across the Islamic world, Rida became one of the most influential Sunni jurists of his generation, leading the Arab Salafi movement and championing its cause.
He was Abduh's de facto successor and was responsible for a split in Abduh's disciples into one group rooted in Islamic modernism and the other in the revival of Islam. Salafism, also known as Salafiyya, which sought the "Islamization of modernity," emerged from the latter.
During the 1900s Rida abandoned his initial rationalist leanings and began espousing Salafi-oriented methodologies such as that of the Ahl-i Hadith movement. He later supported the Wahhabi movement, revived works by Ibn Taymiyyah, and shifted the Salafism movement into a more conservative and strict Scripturalist approach. He is regarded by a number of historians as "pivotal in leading Salafism's retreat" from the rationalist school of Abduh. He strongly opposed liberalism, Western ideas, freemasonry, Zionism, and European imperialism, and supported armed Jihad to expel European influences from the Islamic World. He also laid the foundations for anti-Western, pan-Islamist struggle during the early 20th century.

Early life and education
Muhammad Rashid Rida was born in al-Qalamoun, Beirut Vilayet, present-day Lebanon, in 1865 into a distinguished Sunni Shafi'i clerical family. His family relied on money earned from their limited olive tree holdings and fees earned by family members who served as ulama (scholars). The Rida ulama had been in charge of the al-Qalamoun mosque for several generations. Rida's father was an imam (prayer leader) in the mosque. The family, who were Sayyids, claimed descent from the Ahl al-Bayt, specifically Husayn ibn Ali.
Rida received a traditional religious education, attending elementary school at the local kuttab in Qalamūn before moving to the Ottoman government school in Tripoli. He then enrolled in Shaykh Ḥusayn al-Jisr's National Islamic School, where he learned hadith and fiqh. He also earned a diploma of ulema in 1897. During his education, he studied the books and treatises of scholars such as Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn Qayyim, Ibn Qudama, al-Ghazali, al-Mawardi, Razi, Taftasani, and Ibn Rajab. Rida began preaching at the communal level and taught tafsir and other religious sciences at the village's central mosque. He also taught separate ibadah classes for women. Around this time, he first read al-Urwa al-Wuthqa, a periodical that was highly influential to him. It was published by Jamal al-Din al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh. According to Lebanese-British historian Albert Hourani, Rida belonged to the last generation of traditionally trained Islamic scholars who could be "fully educated and yet alive in a self-sufficient Islamic world of thought."

Muhammad Abduh

Rida met Muhammad Abduh, one of the editors of Al-Urwah al-Wuthqa, as an exile in Lebanon in the mid-1880s and quickly came to view Abduh as his mentor. In 1897, Rida decided to study under Abduh's co-editor Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, who at that time was in Istanbul. Rida suspected the Hamidian administration was responsible for al-Afghani's death later that year and left Istanbul to rejoin Abduh, one of Afghani's students, now in Egypt. They started the monthly periodical al-Manar, where Rida worked as its chief editor and owner until his death in 1935. At this time, he also studied Ibn Taymiyya and his disciples, which eventually led him to embrace ideas including revulsion against folk Sufism, criticism of taqlid, and the desire to revive hadith studies. All of these became foundational themes of the Salafism.
Following Abduh's death in 1905, Rida was seen as his de facto successor despite privately holding reservations about Abduh's ideas. Rida published several new editions of Abduh's works to make them conform more to the dogmas of the traditionalist creed than to Abduh's modernist beliefs. When interest in Abduh was revived in Egypt around the 1930s, the difference in narrative became more apparent. While Abduh's other disciples, Uthman Amin, Mustafa 'Abd al-Raziq, and Muhammad Naji, painted him as a rationalist, Rida continued to ascribe his own beliefs to Abduh's legacy, either ignoring or outright removing Abduh's more liberal ideas from the new editions of his works. Eventually, Rida's narrative became the dominant perception. Abduh's disciples eventually divided into two camps: one, which included Saad Zaghloul and Ali Abdel Raziq, was founded in modernism and Westernized secularism, and the other, the al-Manar party, was based in the revival of Islam. Salafism, also known as Salafiyya, which sought the "Islamization of modernity," emerged from the latter.

Islamic unity under Ottomanism
In 1897, Rida, along with Rafiq al-'Azm and Saib Bey, formed the Ottoman Consultative Society in Cairo. The group consisted of Turks, Armenians, and Circassians living in Egypt and called for Islamic unity under Ottomanism; at this time, their ideas were consistent with those of the Young Turks. They condemned the autocratic Hamidian rule and European imperialism, and their ideas were distributed in Arabic and Turkish via al-Manar. The society disbanded in 1908 following the Young Turk Revolution, after which Azm joined the Committee of Union and Progress to pursue modernism and Rida became a vocal critic of the Young Turks.
In 1898, Rida began publishing articles encouraging Ottoman authorities to adopt a new religious strategy within the existing caliphal and pan-Islamic policy under Sultan Abd al-Hamid II. He recommended training scholars and sharia judges responsible for issuing fatwas (legal rulings) and discussing religious affairs by standardising the creation of different institutions. In one article, he suggested a World Islamic Congress, which would standardise creed, law, and teachings as its fundamental principle. He envisioned the "greatest branch" of the caliph in Mecca for two reasons: the pilgrimage would bring branch leaders to Mecca, where the caliph would be able to disseminate knowledge; and because it was away "from the intrigues and suspicions of [non-Muslim] foreigners." He envisioned a Congress-published religious journal to counter innovative and heretic ideas and to share translations of religious works. The caliph would oversee affairs but was otherwise just like any other Congress member. Scholars would compile legal works from madhāhib (law schools) and adapt them to contemporary situations, and resulting legislation would be implemented by the caliph in all Muslim societies. The desire for a Muslim Congress would reappear in later works.
This global religious society, according to Rida, would pave the way for a spiritual caliphate. Islamic unity required the abolition of sectarian differences as well as the revival of doctrines practiced by the Salaf, the first three generations of Islam, which pre-dated different sects and madhāhib.

bio: Rayta bint 'Abdullah (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Rayta bint Abd Allah ibn Mu'awiya al-Thaqafiyya, also called Ra'ita, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and the wife of Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Hibban states that she was a Companion, and Ibn Sa'd describes her as Ibn Mas'ud's wife and the mother of his child.

Ibn Sa'd records that she was a craftswoman. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr transmit her hadith: because Ibn Mas'ud had no wealth, she supported him and their children from her work, and she asked the Prophet whether she would be rewarded for this. He told her that she had a reward for what she spent on them. The report reaches later transmitters through Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and his son Hisham; Ibn Hibban gives a chain from Hisham ibn Urwa through her brother, Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah al-Thaqafi.

Her identity is debated. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir report the view that she is the same woman as Zaynab al-Thaqafiyya, Ibn Mas'ud's wife, with Rayta as a by-name, and Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that her hadith is like that of Zaynab al-Thaqafiyya; others held that she was a different wife of Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Abd al-Barr also mentions a view that she was not his wife at all. The sources consulted do not record when she died.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Rayta bint Abd Allah (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Ibn Hibban)

bio: Rayta bint al-Harith bin Jabala (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Rayta bint al-Harith ibn Jabala ibn Amir ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Taym ibn Murra was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Taym of Quraysh in Mecca. Her name is also given as Ra'ita. Ibn Hajar's al-Isaba records that she accepted Islam early in Mecca and pledged allegiance. She was married to al-Harith ibn Khalid ibn Sakhr, also of Banu Taym; Ibn Hibban gives his lineage differently.

She emigrated with her husband to Abyssinia in the second migration. Ibn Abd al-Barr records that she bore him Musa and his sisters there; the children are named as Musa, A'isha, Zaynab and Fatima.

According to Ibn Abd al-Barr, the family later set out from Abyssinia for Medina. On the way they stopped at a watering place and drank from it, and they did not leave it before Rayta and her children died; only her daughter Fatima survived. The sources consulted give no year for her death.

titles: Abd al-Wahid Yahya · Sheikh
bio: René Jean-Marie-Joseph Guénon, also known as Abdalwahid Yahia, was a French-Egyptian intellectual who wrote on topics ranging from esotericism, "sacred science" and "traditional studies" to symbolism and initiation.
bio_full:
René Jean-Marie-Joseph Guénon (15 November 1886 – 7 January 1951), also known as Abdalwahid Yahia (Arabic: عبد الـواحد يحيی; ʿAbd al-Wāḥid Yaḥiā), was a French-Egyptian intellectual who wrote on topics ranging from esotericism, "sacred science" and "traditional studies" to symbolism and initiation.
In his writings, Guénon proposes to hand down eastern metaphysics and traditions, these doctrines being defined by him as of "universal character", and adapt them to western readers "while keeping strictly faithful to their spirit".
Initiated into Islamic esotericism from as early as 1910 when he was 24, Guénon mainly wrote and published in French, and his works have been translated into more than twenty languages; he also wrote in Arabic an article for the journal Al Marifah.

Biography
René Guénon was born in 1886 in Blois in central France 160 km (100 mi) from Paris. Like most Frenchmen of the time, he was born into a Roman Catholic family, originally from the Angevin, Poitou and Touraine provinces in France; his father was an architect. He was very close to his mother and even more to his aunt Mme Duru, a teacher who taught him to read and write, both devout Catholic women. By 1904, Guénon was living as a student in Paris, where his studies focused on mathematics and philosophy. He was known as a brilliant student, notably in mathematics, in spite of his poor health. In Paris in 1905, due to his health problems he abandoned the preparation for the prestigious École Polytechnique and École normale supérieure admission competitions.
Guénon observed and became involved with some students under the supervision of Papus. Guénon soon discovered that the Esoteric Christian Martinist order, also supervised by Papus, was irregular: he wrote later that this occultist milieu had not received any authentic spiritual transmission. He joined the Gnostic Church of France founded by Léonce Fabre des Essarts (Synesius). While he did not take this Gnostic church seriously either, it enabled him to become the founder and main contributor of a periodical review, La Gnose ("Gnosis"), writing under the pen-name "Tau Palingenius" until 1922, and focusing on oriental spiritual traditions (Taoism, Hinduism and Sufism).
From his incursions into the French occultist and pseudo-Masonic orders, he despaired of the possibility of ever gathering these diverse and often ill-assorted doctrines into a "stable edifice". In his book The Reign of Quantity and the Signs of the Times he also pointed out what he saw as the intellectual vacuity of the French occultist movement, which, he wrote, was utterly insignificant, and more importantly, had been compromised by the infiltration of certain individuals of questionable motives and integrity. Following his desire to join a regular Masonic obedience, he became a member of the Thebah Lodge of the Grande Loge de France following the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite.
René Guénon first adopted Islam in 1912, he insisted on recalling that the purely religious concept of an immediate conversion did not apply to his case, indicating he had previous acquaintance with the Islamic faith. According to P. Chacornac, Guénon thought that Islam was one of the only real traditions accessible to Westerners, while retaining authentic possibilities in the initiative domain.
Guénon went on to be discharged from his military service due to his severe health problems; he took this opportunity to study philosophy at the Sorbonne during World War I. In 1917, Guénon began a one-year stay at Sétif, Algeria, teaching philosophy to college students. After World War I, he left teaching to dedicate himself to writing; his first book, Introduction to the Study of the Hindu Doctrines, was published in 1921. From 1925 Guénon became a contributor to a review edited by P. Chacornac, Le Voile d'Isis ("The Veil of Isis"), which after 1935, because of Guénon's influence, became known as Les Études Traditionnelles ("Traditional Studies").
According to indications reproduced by his biographer Paul Chacornac and some of his close friends or collaborators such as Jean Reyor, André Préau and Frans Vreede,  it is possible that René Guénon became acquainted with the initiatic lineage of Shankaracharya, and with Taoism, due to his friendship with Georges-Albert Puyou de Pouvourville, known under the pen-name Matgioi. Pouvourville was initiated into Taoism in Tonkin, Vietnam (circa 1887–1891) by a village chief: the Tong-Song-Luat (the 'Master of Sentences'). Paul Chacornac hypothesized that Guénon would also have received a direct transmission of Taoism via the younger son of the Master of Sentences, Nguyen Van Cang, who came to France with Pouvourville and stayed for a while in Paris. Most biographers recognize that the encounter which marked his life and his work the most is that with Hindus, with at least one of whom having played the role of instructor if not of spiritual teacher. This meeting took place very early during the period of 1904–1909, possibly upon his exact arrival in the occultist world, if not before.
Although the exposition of Hindu doctrines to European audiences had already been attempted in piecemeal fashion at that time by some orientalists, Guénon's Introduction to the Study of the Hindu Doctrines advanced its subject in a uniquely insightful manner, by referring to the concepts of metaphysics and Tradition in their most general sense, which Guénon precisely defined, along with the necessary distinctions and definitions of seemingly unambiguous terms such as religion, tradition, exoterism, esoterism and theology. Guénon explained that his purpose was not to describe all aspects of Hinduism, but to give the necessary intellectual foundation for a proper understanding of its spirit. The book also stands as a harsh condemnation of works presented by certain other European writers about Hinduism and Tradition in general; according to Guénon, such writers had lacked any profound understanding of their subject matter and of its implications. The book also contains a critical analysis of the political intrusions of the British Empire into the subject of Hinduism (and India itself) through Madame Blavatsky's Theosophy. The publication of this book earned him rapid recognition in Parisian circles. René Grousset in his "History of Eastern Philosophy" (1923) already referred to Guénon's work as a "classic". André Malraux would say much later that it was, "At its date, a book capital". On the other hand, Guénon was very disappointed by the reaction of his neo-Thomist friends, his erstwhile supporter Jacques Maritain argued that Guénon's views were "radically irreconcilable with the [Catholic] faith"; he called them a "Hinduist restoration of ancient Gnosis, mother of heresies". After World War II, when Maritain became French Ambassador to the Vatican, he asked for Guénon's work to be listed under the Catholic Index of Prohibited Books, a request which had no effect due to the refusal of Pius XII and the support of Cardinal Eugène Tisserant.
In September 1920, Père Peillaube asked Guénon to write a book against the Theosophical Society. In 1921, Guénon debuted a series of articles in the French Revue de Philosophie, which, along with some supplements, led to the book Theosophy: History of a Pseudo-Religion. His critique of Theosophy was received positively by conservative Catholics. However, his later book Orient et Occident distanced him from his Catholic supporters. During the decade 1920–1930, Guénon began to acquire a broader public reputation, and his work was noted by various major intellectual and artistic figures both within and outside of Paris. Also at this time were published some of his books explaining the "intellectual divide" between the East and West, and the peculiar nature, according to him, of modern civilization: Crisis of the Modern World, and East and West.

titles: Naqqāsh-bāshī (Chief Painter)
bio: Reza Abbasi was a Persian calligrapher of the Isfahan school during the Safavid period, who spent most of his career working for Shah Abbas I. He is considered the last of the craftsmen in this field, and one of his most famous works is marqa or albums, especially drawing young beauties.
bio_full:
Reza Abbasi (Persian: رضا عباسی), also known as Agha Reza (c. 1565 – 1635), was the leading Persian miniaturist of the Isfahan School during the later Safavid period, spending most of his career working for Shah Abbas I. He is considered to be the last great master of the Persian miniature, best known for his single miniatures for muraqqa or albums, especially single figures of beautiful youths.

Life and art
Riza was possibly born in Kashan, as Āghā Reżā Kāshānī is one of the versions of his name; it has also been suggested that he was born in Mashad, where his father, the miniature artist Ali Asghar, is recorded as having worked in the atelier of the governor, Prince Ibrahim Mirza. After Ibrahim's murder, Ali Asghar joined Shah Ismail II's workshop in the capital Qasvin. Riza probably received his training from his father and joined the workshop of Shah Abbas I at a young age. By this date, the number of royal commissions for illustrated books had diminished, and had been replaced by
album miniatures in terms of employment given to the artists of the royal workshop.
Unlike most earlier Persian artists, he typically signed his work, often giving dates and other details as well, though there are many pieces with signatures that scholars now reject. He may have worked on the ambitious, but incomplete Shahnameh, now in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin. A much later copy of the work, from 1628, at the end of Abbas' reign and rendered in a very different style, may also be his. It is now in the British Library (MS Additional 27258). His first dated drawing is from 1601, in the Topkapi Palace.  A book miniature of 1601–2 in the National Library of Russia has been attributed to him; the only other miniature in the book is probably by his father. He is generally attributed with the 19 miniatures in a Khusraw and Shirin of 1631–32, although their quality has been criticised.

His speciality, however, was the single miniature for the albums or muraqqas of private collectors, typically showing one or two figures with a lightly drawn garden background, sometimes in gold, in the style formerly used for border paintings, with individual plants dotted about on a plain background. These vary between pure pen drawings and fully painted subjects with colour throughout, with several intermediate varieties. The most typical have at least some colour in the figures, though not in the background; later works tend to have less colour. His, or his buyers', favourite subjects were idealized figures of stylishly dressed and beautiful young men. According to Barbara Brend:The line of Riza's ink drawings has an absolute mastery conveying texture, form, movement and even personality. His coloured figures, which must often be portraits, are more restrained and lay more emphasis on the fashions of the day, the rich textiles, the carelessly draped turban, the European hat.  Effete figures are often presented standing in a curved posture which accentuates their well-fed waists.  The style he pioneered remained influential on subsequent generations of Persian painters; several pupils were prominent artists, including Mo'en Mosavver, who painted his portrait many decades later (illustrated at top) as well as Riza's son, Muhammed Shafi Abbasi.
His earlier works were signed Aqa Risa (or Riza, Reza etc., depending on the transliteration used), which, confusingly, is also the name of Aqa Riza, a contemporary Persian artist who worked for the Mughal Emperor Jahangir in India.  In 1603, at the age of about 38, the artist in Persia received the honorific title of Abbasi from his patron, the shah, associating him with his name.  In the early 20th century, there was much scholarly debate, mostly in German, as to whether the later Aqa Risa and Reza Abbasi were the same figures. It is now accepted that they were, although his style shows a considerable shift in mid-career. Reza Abbasi, the painter, is also not to be confused with his contemporary Ali Riza Abbasi, Shah Abbas' favourite calligrapher, who in 1598, was appointed to the important position of royal librarian, and therefore in charge of the royal atelier of painters and calligraphers. Both Rizas accompanied the shah on his campaign to Khurasan in 1598 and followed him to the new capital he established in Isfahan from 1597 to 1598. Soon after, Reza Abbasi left the Shah's employ in a "mid-life crisis", apparently seeking greater independence and freedom to associate with Isfahan's "low-life" world, including athletes, wrestlers and other unrespectable types. In 1610, he returned to the court, probably because he was short of money, and continued in the employ of the Shah until his death. A series of drawings copying the miniatures attributed to the great 15th-century artist Behzad, which were in the library of the shrine at Ardabil, strongly suggest that Riza had visited the city, probably as part of the Shah's party and perhaps on his visits in 1618 or 1625.
About the time of his return to court service, there is a considerable change in his style. "The primary colours and virtuoso technique of his early portraits give way in the 1620s to darker, earthier colours and a coarser, heavier line. New subjects only partly compensate for this disappointing stylistic development". He painted many older men, perhaps scholars, Sufi divines, or shepherds, as well as birds and Europeans, and in his last years sometimes satirized his subjects.
Sheila Canby's 1996 monograph accepts 128 miniatures and drawings as by Riza, or probably so, and lists as "Rejected" or "Uncertain Attributions" a further 109 that have been ascribed to him at some point Today, his works can be found in Tehran in the Reza Abbasi Museum and in the library at the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul. They can also be found in several western museums, such as the Smithsonian, where the Freer Gallery of Art has an album of works by him and pupils, the British Museum, Louvre and the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Rifa' bin Waqash (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Rifa' bin Waqash was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early years of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the Muslims who lived in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, Rifa' bin Waqash was part of the close-knit group of early Muslims who directly knew and interacted with Muhammad. The companions held a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of believers who witnessed the revelation of the Quran and participated in establishing the early Muslim community.

Rifa' bin Waqash is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Uhud, which took place in 625 CE near Medina. This battle was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community and the Meccan forces, occurring approximately one year after the Muslim victory at the Battle of Badr. The Battle of Uhud proved to be a challenging engagement for the Muslim forces, resulting in significant casualties among the Prophet's companions.

Rifa' bin Waqash died during this battle at approximately 28 years of age, earning him recognition as one of the martyrs of Uhud. In Islamic tradition, those who die in battle defending the faith are honored as martyrs, a status that carries particular spiritual significance.

The Battle of Uhud itself was a pivotal moment in early Islamic history, testing the resolve of the young Muslim community and providing important lessons about unity, discipline, and trust in divine guidance. The companions who fell in this battle, including Rifa' bin Waqash, are remembered for their sacrifice in defense of the nascent Islamic state.

His life exemplifies the commitment of the early Muslim community members who left behind their previous lives to support the Prophet Muhammad and the establishment of Islam. While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation in the battle are not extensively documented, his status as a companion places him among the revered early figures in Islamic history. The companions collectively played a crucial role in preserving and transmitting the teachings of Islam to subsequent generations, making their individual sacrifices part of the larger foundation upon which the Islamic tradition was built.

bio: Rifa'a bin 'Abdul Mundhir (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Rifa'a ibn Abd al-Mundhir ibn Zanbar was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Amr ibn Awf of the Aws in Medina. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Nusayba bint Zayd ibn Dubay'a.

Ibn Sa'd records that he attended the pledge of al-Aqaba with the seventy men of the Ansar, as reported by Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq, Abu Ma'shar and al-Waqidi, and that he fought at Badr and at Uhud. According to Ibn Sa'd, he was killed as a martyr at Uhud in Shawwal, thirty-two months after the Hijra (3 AH, 625 CE). Ibn Sa'd adds that he left no line of descendants, though he had a daughter, Mulayka, who married Umar ibn Abi Salama.

His identity is disputed. Ibn al-Kalbi and Ibn Hibban treat him as a brother of the Companions Abu Lubaba and Mubashshir ibn Abd al-Mundhir. Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn Manda and Ibn al-Athir, however, treat Rifa'a as the personal name of Abu Lubaba himself, who was sent back from al-Rawha' on the march to Badr to govern Medina and later lived on; Ibn al-Athir sides with the view that they are one man if Abu Lubaba's name is Rifa'a, while praising al-Kalbi's view that they were brothers.

bio: Rifa'a bin 'Amr bin Zayd (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Rifa'a ibn Amr ibn Zayd ibn Amr ibn Tha'laba ibn Malik ibn Salim was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj of Medina. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir trace his line through Salim ibn Ghanm ibn Awf ibn al-Khazraj, and Ibn Sa'd places him in the Banu al-Hubla branch. His kunya was Abu al-Walid, and he was also known as Ibn Abi al-Walid. Abu Nu'aym records a different lineage for him, Rifa'a ibn Amr ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Allah ibn Sinan.

He was among the seventy men of the Ansar at the second pledge of al-Aqaba. He fought at Badr and at Uhud, and was killed as a martyr at Uhud. Ibn Sa'd dates his death to Shawwal, thirty-two months after the Hijra (3 AH, 625 CE), and states that he left no descendants. Ibn Abi Hatim reports from his father, Abu Hatim al-Razi, that no hadith is narrated from him.

famous: Rifa'a bin Rafi' bin Malik bin al-'Ajlan
full: Rifa'a bin Rafi' bin Malik bin al-'Ajlan
bio: Rifa'a bin Rafi' bin Malik bin al-'Ajlan (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Rifa'a bin Rafi' bin Malik bin al-'Ajlan was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. He belonged to the Khazraj tribe, one of the two main Arab tribes of Medina, and lived during the formative period of early Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries.

Rifa'a is primarily known for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle was the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces and holds special significance in Islamic history. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition, as this engagement is considered a pivotal moment that helped establish the Muslim community's survival and growth.

As a resident of Medina, Rifa'a would have witnessed the Prophet's migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE and the subsequent establishment of the first Islamic state. The Medinan companions, known as the Ansar (helpers), played a crucial role in supporting the Prophet and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca during this critical period.

Like many companions of his generation, Rifa'a lived through the foundational years of Islam, experiencing the revelation of much of the Quran and observing the Prophet's teachings and practices firsthand. His presence at Badr places him among the early supporters who risked their lives for the nascent Muslim community when its survival was far from certain.

Rifa'a died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing means he lived through the initial period of Islamic expansion but died before the major conquests that would spread Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

His significance to Islamic history lies primarily in his status as a Badr companion, representing the early generation of Muslims who directly supported the Prophet during Islam's most vulnerable period. While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation in this crucial battle are not extensively documented, his recognition as a Sahabi places him among the revered early followers whose dedication helped establish the foundation of the Islamic community.

bio: Rifa'a bint Thabit (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Rifa'a bint Thabit ibn al-Fakih ibn Tha'laba, known by the kunya Umm al-Qasim, was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn al-Athir places her in the Banu Khatma clan. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Kabsha bint Aws ibn Adi al-Khatmi.

Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet, and Ibn al-Athir likewise lists her among the women who gave him their pledge. According to Ibn Sa'd, she was married to Mahmud ibn Wahwah ibn al-Aslat. The sources consulted give no dates for her birth or death.

full: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad Rūdakī
titles: Ustād-i Shaʿirān
bio: Al-Rudaki Abu Abdullah Jaafar bin Muhammad bin Hakim bin Abdul Rahman bin Adam. A Persian poet, considered the first significant poet in the entire history of Persian literature. He was born in the village of Rudak, one of the villages of Samarkand. One of his most famous works is his poetic translation of the book “Kalila and Dimna,” based on the Arabic translation written by Abdullah bin Al-Muqaffa.
bio_full:
Rudaki (also spelled Rodaki; Persian: رودکی; c. 858 – 940/41) was a poet, singer, and musician who is regarded as the first major poet to write in New Persian. A court poet under the Samanids, he reportedly composed more than 180,000 verses, yet only a small portion of his work has survived, most notably parts of his versification of the Kalila wa-Dimna, a collection of Indian fables.
Born in the village of Banoj (located in the present-day Rudak area), the most important part of Rudaki's career was spent at the court of the Samanids. While biographical information connects him to the Samanid amir (ruler) Nasr II (r. 914–943), he may have already joined the court under the latter's predecessor, Ahmad Samani (r. 907–914).
Rudaki's success was largely due to the support of his primary patron, the vizier Abu'l-Fadl al-Bal'ami (died 940), who played an important role in the blooming of New Persian literature in the 10th-century. Following the downfall of Bal'ami in 937, Rudaki's career deteriorated, eventually being dismissed from the court. He thereafter lived his last years in poverty, dying blind and alone in his hometown.
In Iran, Rudaki is acknowledged as the "founder of New Persian poetry" and in Tajikistan as the "father of Tajik literature".

Name
His full name was Abu Abd Allah Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Adam al-Rudhaki al-Sha'ir al-Samarqandi (Persian: ابوعبدالله جعفر بن محمد بن حکیم بن عبدالرحمن بن آدم الرودکی الشاعر سمرقندی). The proper transliteration of his name is Rōdhakī, while al-Rūdhakī is an arabicised form. Other transliterations include Rudagi, Rawdhagi and Rudhagi.

Background
Little information is available about Rudaki's life, much which has been reconstructed from his poems. He lived during the era of the Samanid Empire (819–999), under which New Persian literature began to develop and flourish. Of Persian stock, Rudaki was born in c. 858, in the village of Banoj (Panjrud), located in the Rudak area between Samarqand and Bukhara. Rudaki's blindness is implied by the writings of early poets such as Daqiqi (died 977), Ferdowsi (died 1020/25), Abu Zura'ah al-Mu'ammari (fl. 10th-century) and Nasir Khusraw (died after 1070). The historian Awfi (died 1242), even says that Rudaki was born blind, but this has been questioned by some modern scholars, due to the expressive picture of nature given by Rudaki in his writings.
Besides being a poet, Rudaki was also a singer and musician. Since the era of Sasanian Iran (224–651), poems were commonly carried out as songs used in music. Under the Sasanians, the official, religious and literary language was Middle Persian. Following the Muslim conquest of Iran, the language entered a new phase, known as New Persian. However, it is not descended from the literary form of Middle Persian (known as pārsīk, commonly called Pahlavi), which was spoken by the people of Fars and used in Zoroastrian religious writings. Instead, it is descended from the dialect spoken by the court of the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon and the northeastern Iranian region of Khurasan. During this period, New Persian was known as darī or parsī-i darī.

Career

By the age of eight, Rudaki had reportedly memorized the Qur'an and was skilled in poetry. He was instructed on how to play the chang by a prominent musician named Abu'l-Abak Bakhtiar. In his early years, Rudaki became a popular figure due to his fine voice, skill with poetry and playing the chang. Surviving biographical information connects Rudaki with the Samanid amir (ruler) Nasr II (r. 914–943) or with his vizier Abu'l-Fadl al-Bal'ami (died 940). However, according to literary scholar Sassan Tabatabai, Rudaki had apparently already joined the Samanid court under Nasr II's father and predecessor Ahmad Samani (r. 907–914). Tabatabai states that this is proven in a poem by Rudaki, where he tries to comfort Ahmad Samani after the death of his father Ismail Samani in 907.
Rudaki's career at the Samanid court is regarded as the most important part of his life. The role of a court poet was more than just entertaining others, and was an essential aspect of the Persian court. According to the first Sasanian king Ardashir I (r. 224–242), a poet was "part of government and the means of strengthening rulership." Besides applauding the suzerain and his domain, a poet was also expected to give advice and moral guidance, which meant that Rudaki was most likely experienced in that field as well. Rudaki's success was largely due to the support of his primary patron, Bal'ami. The latter played an important role in the blooming of Persian literature in the 10th century. Bal'ami regarded Rudaki as the best amongst Persian and Arab poets.
Rudaki was a close friend to his student Shahid Balkhi, a leading poet and scholar of the Samanid realm. Following Shahid Balkhi's death in 936, Rudaki wrote an elegy for him. Rudaki's career started to decline following the downfall of Bal'ami in 937. He soon fell out of favour with the amir and was dismissed from the court. Rudaki thereafter lived his last years in poverty, dying blind and alone in his hometown in 940 or 941.
The French Iranologist Gilbert Lazard considered Rudaki's first successor to have been Abu-Shakur Balkhi, who composed many mathnavis, notably the Afarin-nama.

Works

According to Asadi Tusi, the divan (collection of short poems) of Rudaki consisted of more than 180,000 verses, but most of it has been lost. What little remains of Rudaki's writings, mostly single verses, can be found in Persian dictionaries, particularly the Lughat-i Furs of Asadi Tusi. A few complete poems have also survived, most notably a qasida (eulogy or ode) consisting of almost 100 verses quoted in the anonymous Tarikh-i Sistan. The qasida was dedicated to Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad, who ruled the region of Sistan as a Samanid governor from 923 to 963. In it, Rudaki calls Abu Ja'far an aristocrat of Sasanian ancestry and "pride of Iran", thus indicating a sense of continuity in Iranian identity from the Sasanian to the Samanid period. For this poem, Abu Ja'far rewarded Rudaki with 10,000 dinars.
Rudaki's best known work is his versification of the Kalila wa-Dimna, a collection of Indian fables. Nasr II had ordered Bal'ami to translate the book from Arabic to Persian, and then appointed "interpreters" to read it out loud, so that Rudaki, who was blind, could versify it. Only a few of the verses made by Rudaki have survived. Some of them have been identified in the Lughat-i Furs. Rudaki's surviving poetry is generally easy for literate native Persian readers to understand despite variations in terminology, word forms, and phrase and sentence patterns.
Although Rudaki displayed pro-Isma'ili sympathies in his writings, his poetry is fully secular in nature. Islam was firmly established by the 10th century; however, Persians still remembered their deep-rooted Zoroastrian history. Rudaki was more prone to evoke ancient Iranian and Zoroastrian notions instead of Muslim ones. Some of Rudaki's poems were written in the pre-Islamic andarz style, i.e., ethical teachings, friendly criticism and advice for correct behavior in both private and public. An example of Rudaki's Zoroastrian roots can be seen in an excerpt where he is talking about his patron:

Legacy and assessment
Rudaki is considered to have been the first major poet to write in New Persian. Although he was predated by other poets who wrote in New Persian, such as Abu Hafs Sughdi (died 902), most of their work has not survived. In Iran, Rudaki is acknowledged as the "founder of New Persian poetry" and in Tajikistan as the "father of Tajik literature", both claims which according to the Iranologist Richard Foltz are not contradictory. Rudaki's life is depicted in the 1957 film of A Poet's Fate, written by Satim Ulugzade (died 1997).

bio: Rughayba bint Sahl bin Tha'laba (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Rughayba bint Sahl bin Tha'laba was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet and the Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Rughayba was part of the community that played a crucial role in establishing the early Muslim state in Medina. The Ansar were instrumental in providing sanctuary and assistance to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca, helping to create the foundation upon which the Islamic community would grow and flourish.

Her designation as a Sahabiyya indicates that she had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. The female companions of the Prophet held significant positions within the early Muslim community, often serving as transmitters of religious knowledge, participants in community affairs, and examples of Islamic conduct for future generations of Muslim women.

Rughayba lived during a transformative period in Arabian history, witnessing the emergence and early expansion of Islam. Her lifetime spanned the final years of pre-Islamic Arabian society through the establishment of the first Islamic state in Medina. The Ansari community, of which she was a member, demonstrated the Islamic principles of brotherhood, hospitality, and mutual support that became fundamental to Muslim social organization.

The recognition of Rughayba as a companion reflects the important role that women played in the early Islamic community. Female companions contributed to various aspects of community life, from religious education to social welfare, and their involvement helped establish precedents for women's participation in Islamic society.

While specific details about her individual contributions are not extensively documented in historical sources, her status as an Ansari companion of Medina places her among the foundational generation of Muslims whose collective support enabled the survival and growth of the early Islamic community. She died around 635 CE, having lived through the prophetic period and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate, witnessing the transformation of a small religious movement into a major political and spiritual force in the Arabian Peninsula.

bio: Ruqaya bint Muhammad, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad bin Abdullah from his wife Khadija bint Khuwaylid, and his eldest daughter after Zainab. The Prophet married her to Othman bin Affan after Utbah bin Abi Lahab divorced her when his father, Abu Lahab, forced him to divorce her. Ruqayyah was nicknamed Umm Abdullah and her nickname was the one with two migrations. She was born about seven years before the Prophet’s mission. She converted to Islam and immigrated to Abyssinia and Medina. She died on the day of the Battle of Badr in the year 2 AH with her husband, Othman bin Affan, and she was 21 years old at that time.
bio_full:
Ruqayya bint Muhammad (Arabic: رقية بنت محمد, romanized: Ruqayya bint Muḥammad; c. 601–March 624) was the second eldest daughter of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and Khadija. She married the third caliph Uthman and the couple had a son Abd Allah. In 624, Ruqayya died from an illness.

Early life
Born in Mecca around 601 or 602 CE, Ruqayya was the 3rd child and the second daughter of Muhammad and Khadija, his first wife, who was also a successful merchant.

Marital life

Marriage with Utbah
She was betrothed before August 610 to Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, but the marriage was never consummated. Ruqayya became a Muslim when her mother did. When Muhammad began to preach openly in 613, the Quraysh reminded Muhammad that they had "relieved him of his care for his daughters" and decided to return them so that he would have to support them at his own expense. They told Utbah that they would give him "the daughter of Aban ibn Sa'id ibn Al-As or the daughter of Sa'id ibn Al-As" if he divorced Ruqayya. After Muhammad warned Abū Lahab that he would go to Hell, Abu Lahab said he would never speak to his son again unless he divorced Ruqayya, which Utbah accordingly did.

Marriage with Uthman
By 615, Ruqayya was married to a prominent Muslim, Uthman ibn Affan. She accompanied him on the first Migration to Abyssinia, where she suffered a miscarriage. They returned to Abyssinia in 616, and there Ruqayya gave birth to a son, Abdullah in 619. Abdullah died when he was six years old in Medina. She had no further children.
Uthman and Ruqayya were among those who returned to Mecca in 619. Uthman emigrated to Medina in 622, and Ruqayya followed him later.
When Usama ibn Zayd was sent on an errand to their house, he found himself staring at her and at Uthman in turns. Muhammad asked Usama, "Have you ever seen a more handsome couple than those two?" and he agreed that he had not.

Death
Ruqayya fell ill in March 624. Uthman was excused from his military duties in order to nurse her. She died later in the month, on the day when Zayd ibn Haritha returned to Medina with news of their victory at the Battle of Badr – 17th Ramadan.

full: Ruzbihan ibn Abi Nasr al-Baqli al-Shirazi
primaryTitle: Shaykh-i Shirin — Master of Intoxicated Love
titles: Shaykh-i Shirin (The Sweet Master) · Commentator on ecstatic utterances (shathiyyat)
bio: Rozbahan al-Bakli al-Shirazi, who is Rozbahan bin Abi al-Nasr al-Fasawi al-Shirazi al-Kazrouni, Sadr al-Din, Abu Muhammad al-Bakli. A Sufi was born in Bassa, near Shiraz. He died in 606 AH, or it was said 666 AH.
bio_full:
Abu Muhammad Sheikh Ruzbehan Baqli (1128–1209) was a Persian poet, mystic, teacher and sufi master.  He wrote about his own life as well as published commentaries on Sufi poets and ideas.
Baqli's most renowned work was his autobiography Unveiling of Secrets or Kashf al-asrar.

Life
Ruzbihan Baqli was born in 1128 to a family of Daylamite origin in Fasa in what is today Iran.  As a teenager, Baqli worked as a grocer.  Although Baqli claimed to have had religious visions at ages three, seven, and fifteen, he said that his family was not religious.  He described these visions as dreams and powerful ecstasies in The Unveiling of Secrets.
At age 15, Baqli left Fasa to spend 18 months in desert, during which time he claimed to receive more visions. After leaving the desert, he joined a Sufi sect. In The Unveiling of Secrets, Baqli says he had his first "unveiling" while training with the Sufis. He eventually returned to Fasa to seek a master and spiritual guide; there he met and became a disciple of Shaykh Jamal al-Din Abi al-Wafa’ ibn Khalil al-Fasa’I.
It is speculated that Baqli spent the next years travelling to Syria, Iraq, Kerman in Iran, Arabia, making the hajj twice. He returned to Shiraz in 1165 and set up a hospice where he taught for 50 years.  He married several wives and had two sons and three daughters.
Baqli died in 1209 in Shiraz.

Legacy

Baqli's center for Sufi training and his teachings remained popular several generations after his death.   Ruzbihan Baqli died in 1209 in Shiraz and was placed in a tomb in his ribat. For several generations after his death, Ruzbihan Baqli's legacy as a Sufi master continued and Shiraz became a place of pilgrimage. However, the popularity of his order waned and eventually disappeared and his tomb fell into disrepair.
In 1972, Baqli's tomb was restored by the Iranian Department of Antiquities.
The two most important hagiographies  about him were written by family members almost a century after his death: The Gift to the People of Gnosis, in Memory of the Chief Axis of the World, Ruzbihan (1300); and The Spirit of the Gardens, on the Life of the Master Ruzbihan (1305).  Some groups in the Middle East, Central Asia, India, and Persia still study his texts today.

Literary works
Baqli wrote his spiritual experiences and his poetry in a dense, rhetorical prose style. He composed mostly in Arabic and Persian. His writings are unique because, while they do not include many dates or chronology, he talks about his personal life and his family, while not mentioning other outside events. Baqli was known for his fondness and defense of many early Sufis’ ecstatic sayings (shathiyat) and therefore was dubbed "Doctor Ecstaticus."
Baqli completed his book Commentary on Ecstatic Sayings or Sarh al-shathiyyat in 1174. He also wrote The Spirits’ Font in 1184. The Unveiling of Secrets or Kashf al-asrar was completed in 1189 after  eight years. It is both an autobiography and a diary of visions and Sufi teachings. Many of his works emphasize the Sufi theories of love, and also defend early Sufi saints in their ecstatic utterances. The Sufi saint Hallaj was a primary example in Baqli's text.
While direct literary references to Baqli in later Sufism were not common, perhaps because of the difficulty of the texts, he was known for his love of beauty: fine fragrances, a beautiful face, and sweet voices. His texts were studied, however, by Jāmi of the fifteenth century and a Mughal prince of the seventeenth century.

bio: S'ad bin 'Ubaid al-Qa'ri (c. 594–638 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
S'ad bin 'Ubaid al-Qa'ri was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the early seventh century. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslim community in Medina and died in 638 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab.

As indicated by his epithet "al-Qa'ri," S'ad was associated with the recitation and study of the Quran, reflecting the high regard placed on Quranic literacy in early Islamic society. The title "qari" designated those who had memorized substantial portions of the Quran and were skilled in its proper recitation, making them valuable members of the Muslim community during a period when written texts were less common and oral preservation of religious knowledge was crucial.

S'ad is particularly remembered as a participant in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as a "Companion of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr were later honored with a distinctive status among the companions, as this engagement represented a pivotal moment in the establishment of the early Islamic state.

His involvement in hadith sciences indicates that S'ad played a role in the transmission of prophetic traditions, contributing to the preservation of the Prophet's sayings and practices that would later form one of the fundamental sources of Islamic law and guidance. During the early decades of Islam, companions like S'ad served as living links to the Prophet's teachings, making their testimonies and transmissions essential for later generations of Muslims.

S'ad lived through the Prophet's lifetime in Medina and continued into the early expansion period of Islam under the first caliphs. His death in 638 CE places him among those companions who witnessed the initial rapid growth of the Muslim community but did not see the later extensive conquests that would establish Islam across vast territories. His contributions to Quranic recitation and hadith transmission represent the scholarly and religious dimensions of companionship, complementing the better-known military and political roles of other prominent companions of the Prophet Muhammad.

bio: Sa'd bin 'Uthman bin Khalada (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Sa'd bin 'Uthman bin Khalada was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who experienced the foundational years of the Islamic community.

As a Sahaba, Sa'd was part of the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the establishment of the early Islamic state. He was based in Medina, which served as the political and religious center of the Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Sa'd is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as a "Companion of Badr." This battle was the first major military encounter between the Muslim community and the Meccan tribes, and it holds special significance in Islamic history as a pivotal moment that demonstrated the strength and unity of the early Muslim community. Those who participated in this battle are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition due to their role in this crucial event.

His involvement in hadith sciences reflects the important role that companions played in preserving and transmitting the sayings, actions, and teachings of Prophet Muhammad. The companions served as the primary sources for Islamic teachings and legal principles that would later be codified by Islamic scholars. Their testimonies and reports formed the foundation of hadith literature, which became essential for understanding Islamic law and practice.

Sa'd's life spanned the most transformative period in early Islamic history, from the initial revelation of the Quran through the establishment of the first Islamic state. He witnessed the growth of Islam from a small religious movement to a major political and social force in the Arabian Peninsula.

He died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the death of Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. His relatively short life of approximately forty years encompassed the entire prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs. Like many of the early companions, Sa'd bin 'Uthman bin Khalada represents the generation that directly experienced the origins of Islam and played a crucial role in its early development and preservation.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Sa'd bin Habban bin Munqidh (c. 600 CE–683 CE, Medina, al-Harrah) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Sa'd bin Habban bin Munqidh was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he witnessed and participated in the early development of the Muslim community during the seventh century.

Sa'd is historically recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event in Islamic history that took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, occurred when approximately 1,400 Muslims accompanying the Prophet Muhammad on his journey to Mecca for pilgrimage swore an oath of loyalty under a tree. The Quran references this event in verse 48:18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those believers who pledged their allegiance under the tree.

Based in Medina, Sa'd would have experienced the crucial early years of the Islamic community following the Prophet's migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. As a resident of Medina during this transformative period, he would have witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim political community and the development of Islamic law and practice.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular significance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the solidarity and commitment of the early Muslim community during a tense diplomatic situation. Those who participated in this pledge are regarded with special reverence in Islamic tradition due to the Quranic verse that explicitly mentions God's pleasure with them.

Sa'd lived through the entire prophetic period and well into the early expansion of the Islamic state, dying in 683 CE in the al-Harrah district of Medina at approximately 83 years of age. His longevity meant he witnessed not only the Prophet's lifetime and the period of the first four Caliphs, but also the early Umayyad period, spanning nearly the entire first century of Islamic history.

As one of the Companions of the Prophet, Sa'd bin Habban bin Munqidh represents the generation of early Muslims who directly received Islamic teachings and helped establish the foundations of the Muslim community. His participation in the Pledge of Ridwan marks him as someone who demonstrated loyalty and commitment during a critical moment in early Islamic history.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Sa'd bin Khalifa (c. 597–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Sa'd ibn Khalifa ibn al-Ashraf ibn Abi Huzayma ibn Tha'laba ibn Tarif ibn al-Khazraj ibn Sa'ida was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Sa'ida clan of the Khazraj in Medina. Ibn Hajar, in al-Isaba, records that Ibn Shahin, al-Tabari and al-Adawi state that he fought at the Battle of Uhud. Al-Adawi adds that he was later killed as a martyr at the Battle of al-Qadisiyya in Iraq, fought in 636 CE. Ibn al-Athir also gives him an entry in Usd al-Ghaba. The sources consulted record nothing further about his life.
