bio: Sa'd bin Khaula (c. 594–631 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Yemen. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Sa'd bin Khaula was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early years of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam and became part of the close circle of followers known as the Sahaba.

Sa'd bin Khaula is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. Those who participated in this battle are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition, as they were present during this pivotal moment in early Islamic history.

His association with Yemen suggests he may have had connections to the Arabian Peninsula's southern regions, though the exact nature of his relationship to this area during his lifetime remains unclear from available historical sources. Yemen became an important center for early Islamic expansion and religious development.

Sa'd bin Khaula is also noted within Islamic tradition as being among the early ascetics, indicating that he practiced a form of religious devotion characterized by simplicity and spiritual discipline. This ascetic tradition would later influence various streams of Islamic spirituality and religious practice.

His life spanned the crucial formative period of Islam, from before the Prophet Muhammad's first revelations through the early expansion of the Muslim community. He witnessed the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community in Medina, participating in the military campaigns that secured the survival of the early Muslim state.

Sa'd bin Khaula died in 631 CE, during the final years of the Prophet Muhammad's life or shortly after his death. His relatively short life of approximately 37 years coincided almost entirely with the emergence and establishment of Islam as a major religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula. As one of the Companions of Badr, his name is preserved in Islamic historical records as part of the founding generation of Muslims who played direct roles in the early development of the Islamic community.

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Sa'd bin Khaythama (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Sa'd bin Khaythama was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early converts to Islam from the city of Medina, then known as Yathrib.

Sa'd bin Khaythama is historically significant as one of the participants in the First Pledge of Aqabah, which took place around 621 CE. This pledge was a crucial early agreement between the Prophet Muhammad and representatives from Medina, marking an important step in the establishment of the early Muslim community. The pledge involved a group of men from the Khazraj and Aws tribes of Medina who accepted Islam and promised to support the Prophet's message.

The First Pledge of Aqabah was followed by a Second Pledge of Aqabah the following year, which involved a larger group and included more comprehensive commitments. These agreements were instrumental in paving the way for the Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, an event known as the Hijra that marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

As one of the early Muslim converts from Medina, Sa'd bin Khaythama would have been part of the Ansar, meaning "helpers," which was the term used for the Medinan Muslims who supported the Prophet and the Meccan Muslim emigrants. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the early Muslim community in Medina and providing it with the necessary support and protection.

Sa'd bin Khaythama died in 624 CE, which places his death during the early years of the Muslim community in Medina. This was a period of significant challenges and developments for the nascent Islamic state, as the Muslim community was establishing itself while facing various external pressures and conflicts.

His participation in the First Pledge of Aqabah places him among the early supporters of Islam who helped facilitate the religion's growth beyond Mecca. The companions who participated in these early pledges are remembered in Islamic history for their role in the crucial early development of the Muslim community, though detailed biographical information about many individual participants, including Sa'd bin Khaythama, remains limited in the historical sources.

bio: Sa'd bin Zayd bin Malik (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Sa'd bin Zayd bin Malik was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of the Islamic community.

Sa'd is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The battle took place near the town of Badr, located between Mecca and Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the Muslim forces despite being significantly outnumbered.

Based in Medina, Sa'd was part of the community that formed around the Prophet Muhammad after the Hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. Medina served as the political and spiritual center of the early Muslim state, and companions like Sa'd played important roles in supporting the development of the nascent Islamic community.

The companions who fought at Badr hold a special place in Islamic historical memory, as they are considered to have demonstrated their commitment to the faith during a critical moment when the survival of the Muslim community was at stake. Their participation in this pivotal battle is viewed as having helped secure the future of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula.

Sa'd died in 634 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph after the Prophet Muhammad's death. This places his death during a time of rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Sa'd bin Zayd bin Malik represents the generation of early Muslims who directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices and governance. The companions collectively serve as important transmitters of Islamic tradition and as examples of early Islamic community life. His participation in the Battle of Badr specifically marks him as one of those who helped establish the military foundation upon which the later expansion of the Islamic state would be built.

full: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas ibn Wuhayb al-Zuhri al-Qurashi
primaryTitle: Faris al-Islam — Knight of Islam; Conqueror of Persia
titles: Faris al-Islam · One of the Ten Promised Paradise · First Archer of Islam
bio: Abu Ishaq Saad bin Abi Waqqas Malik Al-Zuhri Al-Qurashi, one of the ten promised Paradise, and one of the first to convert to Islam. It was said that he was the third to convert to Islam, and it was said that he was the seventh, and he was the first to shoot an arrow for the sake of God, and the Prophet said to him: “Throw, may my father and mother be sacrificed for you.” He is one of the uncles of the Prophet, and one of the six companions of the Shura Council whom Omar ibn Al-Khattab chose to choose the caliph after him.
bio_full:
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (584-674 CE) was one of the earliest and most prominent companions of Prophet Muhammad and a key military leader during the early expansion of the Islamic state. Born into the Zuhri clan of the Quraysh tribe in Mecca, he was among the first converts to Islam, accepting the faith while still a young man.

As one of the earliest Muslims, Sa'd faced persecution in Mecca alongside other early converts. He was among those who participated in the migration to Medina and subsequently fought in major battles during the Prophet's lifetime, including the battles of Badr, Uhud, and the Trench. Sa'd gained particular recognition as an archer and is remembered as the first person to shoot an arrow in defense of the Muslim community.

Following the Prophet's death, Sa'd played a crucial role in the Islamic conquests during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab. He served as the commander of Muslim forces during the conquest of the Sassanian Empire, leading the decisive victory at the Battle of Qadisiyyah in 636 CE, which effectively ended Sassanian control over Iraq. He subsequently served as the governor of Kufa, one of the major garrison cities established by the Muslims in Iraq.

Sa'd's political significance extended beyond his military achievements. Caliph Umar included him among the six-member council (shura) tasked with selecting the next caliph after Umar's death. This appointment reflected his standing among the senior companions and his continued influence in early Islamic governance.

Throughout Islamic tradition, Sa'd is remembered as one of the "Ten Promised Paradise," a group of companions who, according to Islamic sources, were assured of paradise during their lifetimes. His long life spanned the entire formative period of Islam, from its earliest days in Mecca through the major conquests that established the Islamic empire.

Sa'd spent his later years in Medina, where he died in 674 CE. His legacy rests primarily on his role as both an early supporter of Islam during its most vulnerable period and as a successful military commander who helped secure the religion's expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. His contributions to early Islamic military strategy and governance made him a significant figure in the establishment of the early Islamic state.

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi' (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' ibn Amr ibn Abi Zuhayr ibn Malik was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj of Medina. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Hazila bint Utba ibn Amr, and notes that Sa'd could write in the pre-Islamic period, when writing was rare among the Arabs.

He attended both pledges of al-Aqaba and was one of the twelve leaders (nuqaba') chosen there, serving as leader of Banu al-Harith together with Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. After the Hijra the Prophet made him a brother of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. Sa'd offered him half of his property and one of his wives; Abd al-Rahman declined, prayed that God bless Sa'd's family and wealth, and asked to be shown the market.

He fought at Badr and at Uhud, where he was killed as a martyr in 3 AH (625 CE). Reports recorded by Malik, Ibn Ishaq and al-Dhahabi describe him being found among the fallen with his last breath. In one report he said he had been stabbed twelve times; in another he sent word to the Ansar that they would have no excuse before God if harm reached the Prophet while any of them still lived. Accounts differ over who found him; Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir name Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

He left two daughters. When their uncle took the estate, their mother brought them to the Prophet, who gave the daughters two-thirds, their mother one-eighth and the uncle the rest; Ibn Abd al-Barr links this to the inheritance verse (Qur'an 4:11). One daughter, Umm Sa'd, was the mother of Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Thabit.

full: Sa'd ibn Muadh ibn al-Numan ibn Imru al-Qays al-Ansari al-Awsi
primaryTitle: Sayyid al-Aws — Chief of the Aws Tribe
dod_s: 627 CE / 5 AH — from wounds at Battle of the Trench
titles: Sayyid al-Aws (Chief of the Aws tribe) · Siddiq al-Ansar (Truthful Man of the Ansar) · Abu Amr
bio: Sa'd ibn Muadh ibn al-Numan ibn Imru al-Qays al-Ansari al-Awsi (c. 590 CE–627 CE / 5 AH) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Sayyid al-Aws — Chief of the Aws Tribe.
bio_full:
Saad ibn Muʿādh al-Ansari (Arabic: سعد بن معاذ الأنصاري) (c. 590-627) was the chief of the Aws tribe in Medina and one of the prominent companions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He died shortly after the Battle of the Trench.

Family
Sa'd was born in Medina 590 CE, the son of Mu'adh ibn al-Numan, of the Abdul-Ashhal clan of the Aws tribe, and of Kabsha bint Rafi, of the Jewish Banu al-Harith clan of the Khazraj tribe. His siblings were Aws (apparently the eldest), Iyas, 'Amr, Iqrab and Umm Hizam.
He married his brother Aws's widow, Hind bint Simak, who was his agnatic second cousin. Her brother had been chief of the Aws tribe until he was killed at the Battle of Bu'ath in 617. They had two sons, Amr and Abdullah.
As'ad ibn Zurarah, chief of the al-Najjar clan of the Khazraj, was Sa'd's maternal first cousin. Usayd ibn Hudayr was his wife's fraternal nephew, and was also said by al-Waqidi to have been Sa'd's first cousin.

Biography

Acceptance of Islam
Sa'd was among the leading figures among the Ansar, as Muhammad had called the people of Aws and Khazraj from Medina who converted to Islam. He converted at the hands of Mus'ab ibn Umair. His conversion led to the immediate conversion of his entire subtribe of the Aus, the Banu Abdul-Ashhal:

"The leader whom his people follow has come to you" As'ad said Mus'ab. So Mus'ab said to him what he had said to Usayd, Sa'd stuck his lance into the ground, and sat down. The same thing happened again [ie. Conversion to Islam] and he went to his people's meeting place accompanied by Usayd [who had converted earlier]. When they saw him coming they said: "We swear by Allah, Sa'd has returned with a different impression."  And when he reached them he asked them how they knew what had happened to him. They replied "You are our Chief, the most active in our interests, the best in your judgement, and the most fortunate in leadership." He then said: "I will not speak to a man or a woman among you until you believe in Allah and his Apostle." As a result every man and woman among the Banu Abdul-Ashhal joined Islam.

Confrontation with Abu Jahl and the start of Badr hostilities
Before the Battle of Badr, Sa'd had visited Mecca once to perform his Umrah with his non-Muslim friend Umayyah ibn Khalaf, when they came across Abu Jahl. They argued, and as it became heated, Sa'd threatened Abu Jahl with preventing his safe passage through Medina if he stopped the Muslims from performing the pilgrimage in Mecca.
Narrated 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud:

From Sa`d bin Mu`adh: Sa`d bin Mu`adh was an intimate friend of Umayya bin Khalaf and whenever Umayya passed through Medina, he used to stay with Sa`d, and whenever Sa`d went to Mecca, he used to stay with Umayya.
When Allah's Messenger arrived at Medina, Sa`d went to perform `Umra and stayed at Umayya's home in Mecca. He said to Umayya, "Tell me of a time when (the Mosque) is empty so that I may be able to perform Tawaf around the Ka`ba." So Umayya went with him at about midday. Abu Jahl met them and said, "O Abu Safwan! Who is this man accompanying you?" He said, "He is Sa`d." Abu Jahl addressed Sa`d saying, "I see you wandering about safely in Mecca even though you have given shelter to the people who have changed their religion (i.e. became Muslims) and have claimed that you will help them and support them. By Allah, if you were not in the company of Abu Safwan, you would not be able to go with your family safely." Sa`d, raising his voice, said to him, "By Allah, if you should stop me from doing this (i.e. performing Tawaf) I would certainly prevent you from something which is more valuable for you, that is, your passage through Medina." On this, Umayya said to him, "O Sa`d do not raise your voice before Abu-l-Hakam, the chief of the people of the Valley (of Mecca)." Sa`d said, "O Umayya, stop that! By Allah, I have heard Allah's Messenger predicting that the Muslim will kill you." Umayya asked, "In Mecca?" Sa`d said, "I do not know." Umayya was greatly scared by that news.
When Umayya returned to his family, he said to his wife, "O Um Safwan! Don't you know what Sa`d told me?" She said, "What has he told you?" He replied, "He claims that Muhammad has informed them (i.e. companions) that they will kill me. I asked him, 'In Mecca?' He replied, 'I do not know." Then Umayya added, "By Allah, I will never go out of Mecca." But when the day of (the Ghazwa of) Badr came, Abu Jahl called the people to war, saying, "Go and protect your caravan." But Umayya disliked going out (of Mecca). Abu Jahl came to him and said, "O Abu Safwan! If the people see you staying behind though you are the chief of the people of the Valley, then they will remain behind with you." Abu Jahl kept on urging him to go until he (i.e. Umayya) said, "As you have forced me to change my mind, by Allah, I will buy the best camel in Mecca. Then Umayya said (to his wife). "O Um Safwan, prepare what I need (for the journey)." She said to him, "O Abu Safwan! Have you forgotten what your Yathribi brother told you?" He said, "No, but I do not want to go with them but for a short distance."

So, when Umayya went out, he used to tie his camel wherever he camped. He kept on doing that till Allah caused him to be killed at Badr.

Battle of Badr
The Muslims originally expected a much smaller Meccan force and were surprised by the large Meccan Army so Muhammad called Shura:

When the Muslim army missed the caravan and the Quraysh army, between nine hundred and one thousand strong, helmeted and drawing closer, Abu Bakr stood up and said something good.
Several more Muhajirun also spoke, all the while the Messenger of Allah repeated: "advise me, O Muslims!", inquiring of what the Ansar, the majority then, had to say.
Then Sa`d bin Mu`adh said, "It looks like you mean us, O Messenger of Allah! By He Who has sent you with the Truth!  If you seek to cross the sea and did go in it, we will follow you, and none among us will remain behind. We will not hate for you to lead us into battle against the enemy tomorrow. We are patient in war, vicious in battle. May Allah allow you to witness from our efforts what comforts your eyes. Therefore, march forward with the blessing of Allah."
The Messenger of Allah was pleased with the words of Sa`d and was encouraged to march on.

Battle of Uhud
Sa'd was one of the few companions who remained on the battlefield, when the Meccans led by Khalid bin Walid counterattacked and he continued to fight on until he was finally forced to retreat away from the Meccans. In fact, Sa'd was the last Muslim Mus'ab ibn 'Umair met (Sa'd by that time had disengaged the Meccans) when he chided other Muslims for retreating and ferociously attacked the Meccans resulting in his brutal martyrdom at the hands of the Meccans. He later met up with Muhammad and was part of the small contingent Muslims defending him.
Sa'd's brother 'Amr and his stepson (nephew) al-Harith ibn Aws were both among those who were killed at Uhud.

Battle of Trench and Qurayza
After the Battle of the Trench in 627 (5 AH), when Medina was unsuccessfully besieged by the Meccan army, the Banu Qurayza had treacherous dealings with the enemy. Later the Muslims laid siege to their stronghold and the Banu Qurayza surrendered.
Several members of the Banu Aws pleaded for their old Jewish allies and agreed to Muhammad's proposal that one of their chiefs should judge the matter. The Banu Qurayza themselves appointed Sa'd, and declared they would agree with whatever was Sa'd's verdict. The verdict for the Banu Qurayza, a Jewish clan in Medina, was consistent with the Old Testament and some scholars claim the verdict was based on Deutoronomy 20:12-14.

Some people (i.e. the Jews of Bani bin Quraiza) agreed to accept the verdict of Sad bin Muadh so the Prophet sent for him (i.e. Sa'd bin Muadh).

full: Sa'd ibn Ubadah ibn Dulaym al-Ansari al-Khazraji
primaryTitle: Sayyid al-Ansar — Chief of the Helpers
titles: Sayyid al-Ansar · Chief of Khazraj
bio: Saad bin Ubadah Al-Saadi Al-Khazraj Al-Ansari, Abu Thabit, and it was said: Abu Qais, one of the most honorable Arab houses, the most ancient in lineage, and he was the leader of the Khazraj before Islam. A companion of mine who converted to Islam early, witnessed the Pledge of Aqaba, lived next to the Messenger Muhammad, and was famous for his generosity and generosity along with his son Qais bin Saad bin Ubadah Al-Saadi. It was said about Saad: “A man from the Ansar would go to his home, with one of the immigrants, or with two, or with three. Saad bin Ubadah used to set off with eighty.
bio_full:
Saʽd ibn ʽUbadah ibn Dulaym al-Ansari al-Khazraji (Arabic: سعدسعد بن عبادة بن دليم الأنصاري الخزرجي) (d. 637) was the chief of the Sa'ida clan of the Khazraj tribe in Medina in the early seventh century. He was later recognised as the chief of the whole Khazraj tribe, and then of all the Ansar. He was a prominent companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and made an abortive attempt to nominate himself as caliph of Islam after Muhammad's death.

Family
He was the son of 'Ubadah ibn Dulaym, chief of the Sa'ida clan, and of Amra al-Thalitha bint Masud, who was from the Najjar clan of the Khazraj. He had two sisters, Mandwas and Layla.
His first wife, Fukayha bint Ubayd ibn Dulaym, was his agnatic cousin. They had three children: Qays, Umama and Sadus. His second wife, Ghaziya bint Sa'd, was also from the Sa'ida clan. Their sons were Sa'id, Muhammad and Abdulrahman.

Early life
Described as physically "very hairy,” Sa'd was reckoned one of the "perfect" Arabs because he was good at archery and swimming and could write in Arabic.
His generosity was widely acknowledged. The Khazraj said of him: "He is our master and the son of our master. They used to provide food during the droughts, to transport the weary, to welcome guests, to give during disasters and to protect the community." His son Qays said that he underwrote the debts of "the most distant relatives" in addition to helping poor people and feeding the community during famines. A Bedouin testified, "You possess the highest and most noble character. You are not censured even by those who have no knowledge of your position." Sa'd used to stand on his fortress, calling, "Whoever likes fat or meat should come to Sa'd ibn Ubadah."
He was also known for his hot temper and for his tribal pride. He used to pray: "O God, give me praise and glory. I can't have glory without action, and I can't act without money. O God, I need more than a little money to put myself right and put right with it." He was annoyed when Muhammad once described the Abdulashhal clan as the best of the Ansar, followed by the Najjar, the Harith, the Sa'ida and then all the rest. He asked, "Are we only fourth?" and had to be dissuaded from confronting Muhammad about it to his face.
Sa'd had commercial relationships with Mecca. He guaranteed the safety of the merchants of Jubayr ibn Mut'im and Harith ibn Harb while they were in the territory of Medina.

Conversion to Islam
Sa'd ibn Ubadah converted to Islam at an early date, in the year before Muhammad's arrival in Medina, and consequently he broke all the idols of the Sa'ida clan.

Second Pledge of Aqaba
Sa'd was among the 75 converts from Medina who took the Second Pledge at Aqaba in July 622. Muhammad selected him as one of the twelve leaders who would "take charge of their people's affairs."
When Quraysh realised that war had been declared on them, they pursued the pledge-takers, who were already on the road home to Medina. They captured Sa'd, tied his hands to his neck and brought him back to Mecca, dragging him by the hair and beating him. Suhayl ibn Amr slapped his face. Finally Abu'l-Bakhtari ibn Hisham took pity on him and asked: "You poor devil, doesn't any Quraysh owe you protection?" Sa'd then remembered to call out the names of Jubayr ibn Mutim and Al-Harith ibn Harb. They came from the Kaaba and told the captors to release him; so Sa'd went home.

The Hijrah
When Muhammad arrived in Medina, Sa'd was among those who invited him to stay in their homes at their expense. But Muhammad said that his camel was under God's orders and she should decide where he would stay.
Sa'd was thought a pious man. Every day he sent a bowl of meat stew or clarified butter or milk to Muhammad, who took it with him as he visited each of his wives in turn. From March 624 until May 627 Sa'd hosted al-Miqdad ibn Amr and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt in his home. At the Battle of the Ditch he supplied the army with a load of dates.

Relationship with Muhammad
Soon after Muhammad's arrival in Medina, Sa'd fell sick. He received a visit from Muhammad, who was red-faced with anger, and his adoptive grandson Usama. Muhammad explained to Sa'd that Abdullah ibn Ubayy had rejected Islam and forbidden him to discuss it in Abdullah's house. Sa'd advised Muhammad: "Don't be hard on him; for God sent you to us as we were making a diadem to crown him, and he thinks that you have robbed him of a kingdom."
On a different condolence-visit, Muhammad was accompanied by Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abdullah ibn Masud. Sa'd was unconscious when his visitors arrived, and Muhammad asked if he had died. Although he had not, Muhammad wept, and his friends wept with him. Muhammad told them that silent tears were permitted but that Allah might punish them for loud wailing. Later Muhammad heard that Sa'd was better, so he asked the assembly who would like to go to visit. More than ten Muslims stood up with him, "and we had neither shoes with us, nor socks, nor caps, nor shirts." They walked "on the barren land" in the scorching heat of Medina until they reached Sa'd's house.
On another occasion, Sa'd was sitting at home when Muhammad knocked at the door, calling, "Peace be with you!" Sa'd kept silent. Muhammad called a second and a third time, then decided that Sa'd must be out. As he was leaving, Sa'd ran up to call him back, explaining: "I did hear you, but I wanted to have a lot of your peace for me and my family."
Muhammad said, on receiving from him a gift of dates and ten camels for slaughter, "What a good man Sa'd ibn Ubadah is! The best of the people in Islam are those who were the best in the Jahiliya when they understand the religion." On the way to the Farewell Pilgrimage, Sa'd heard that Abu Bakr had lost his camel. He and his son Qays came at once to Muhammad to give him a new camel laden with provisions. Muhammad tried to refuse the gift, for the lost camel had been found, but Sa'd told him: "What you take from our wealth is more precious to us than what you do not take."

Questions about Islam
Sa'd's mother, Amra, died while he was away at Dumat al-Jandal in 626. When the army returned to Medina, Muhammad prayed over her grave. Sa'd asked about a vow that Amra had been unable to keep before she died, and Muhammad said, "Fulfil it for her." So Sa'd gave away his garden al-Mikhraf as charity on her behalf. Muhammad said that the best form of charity was "making water flow," and Sa'd donated water for public drinking to the mosque.
Sa'd once asked Muhammad: "Tell me, if a man finds his wife with another man, should he kill him?" Muhammad replied, "No." Sa'd asked if he should wait until he had four witnesses, and Muhammad said, "Yes." "By no means!" exclaimed Sa'd. "I swear, I would hurry to strike him with my sword before then, and not with the flat side!" Muhammad told the assembly: "Listen to what your chief says. Are you surprised at Sa'd's jealousy for his honour? I am more jealous for my honour than he is, and God is more jealous than I am. Because of his jealousy God has prohibited abomination, both open and secret. No person is more jealous than God; and no person is fonder of accepting an excuse than God, on account of which he has sent messengers; and no one is fonder of praise than God, on account of which he has promised Paradise."

Internal politics of Medina

Community relationships
In the early period after Muhammad's arrival, Sa'd urged the Jews of Medina to accept Islam. "Fear God," he said, "for you know right well that [Muhammad] is God's Messenger, of whom you used to speak to us before his mission and describe him to us." The Jews replied: "We never said that to you, and God has sent down no book since Moses nor sent an evangelist or warner after him."
Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the Awf clan and unofficially chief of the Khazraj tribe, lost status in Medina after the Battle of Uhud in 625. Sa'd ibn Ubadah then came to be regarded as the most important Khazraj chief.

famous: Sa'd Mawla Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah
full: Sa'd Mawla Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah
bio: Sa'd Mawla Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Sa'd Mawla Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE, he was present during the crucial early decades of the Islamic community's development.

The designation "mawla" in his name indicates that Sa'd was likely a freed slave or client who became affiliated with Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah, himself a notable companion of the Prophet. This relationship reflects the social mobility that early Islam provided for individuals from diverse backgrounds, allowing them to achieve recognition and respect within the Muslim community regardless of their origins.

Sa'd is historically recognized as one of the "Companions of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces and holds tremendous significance in Islamic history. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in special esteem within Islamic tradition, as this victory was seen as a divine vindication of the Muslim cause and a turning point in the early expansion of Islam.

His association with the early ascetic tradition suggests that Sa'd was among those companions who emphasized spiritual devotion and simple living. The early ascetics in Islam were known for their piety, renunciation of worldly pleasures, and dedication to worship and remembrance of God. This spiritual orientation was particularly valued in the early Muslim community, where material simplicity and focus on the afterlife were emphasized.

Sa'd's life spanned the most critical period of early Islamic history, from the final years of pre-Islamic Arabian society through the Prophet's ministry and into the early expansion under the first caliphs. His death in 634 CE occurred during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just as the Muslim armies were beginning their major conquests beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details of Sa'd's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in historical sources, his recognition as a companion of the Prophet and his inclusion among the early ascetics indicates his respected position within the founding generation of Muslims. His life exemplifies the transformation that early Islam brought to Arabian society and the diverse backgrounds of those who joined the Prophet's community.

bio: Sa'id bin 'Abd Qays bin Laqit (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Sa'id ibn Abd Qays ibn Laqit ibn Amir ibn Umayya ibn al-Harith ibn Fihr was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Fihr clan of Quraysh. Other authorities give his name as Sa'id ibn Ubayd ibn Qays ibn Laqit, and Ibn Hajar records further variants in the lineage. He was the brother of Nafi' ibn Abd Qays.

Ibn Sa'd records that he accepted Islam early in Mecca and emigrated to Abyssinia in the second migration, on the authority of Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq, Abu Ma'shar and al-Waqidi. The sources differ on when he returned. Ibn Abd al-Barr says he stayed in Abyssinia until the time of the Trench and thought he came only with Ja'far; al-Baladhuri, cited by Ibn Hajar, says he came to Medina before Ja'far. The sources consulted do not record when or where he died.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Sa'id ibn Abd Qays (Ibn Sa'd, al-Isti'ab, Usd al-Ghaba)
al-Isaba fi Tamyiz al-Sahaba (Ibn Hajar), vol. 3 p. 94, no. 3282 — Sa'id ibn Abd Qays

bio: Sa'id bin 'Amr al-Tamimi (c. 593–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Sa'id ibn Amr al-Tamimi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and an ally (halif) of the Qurayshi clan of Banu Sahm in Mecca. Ibn Ishaq and Musa ibn Uqba describe him as a maternal brother of the Sahmi sons of al-Harith ibn Qays, and Ibn al-Athir notes a report that Tamim ibn al-Harith ibn Qays was his half-brother through their mother. Al-Waqidi and Abu Ma'shar give his name as Ma'bad ibn Amr.

Ibn Ishaq, Musa ibn Uqba and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar list him among those who emigrated to Abyssinia in the second migration. Ibn Sa'd counts him among the early Muslims who did not fight at Badr. Musa ibn Uqba reports that he was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Ajnadayn in Palestine, fought in 13 AH (634 CE), together with his maternal brother Tamim ibn al-Harith; al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar gives the same account.

bio: Sa'id bin al-Harith (c. 593–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Sa'id ibn al-Harith ibn Qays ibn Adi ibn Sa'd ibn Sahm was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Qurayshi clan of Banu Sahm in Mecca. His mother's name is given differently: Ibn Sa'd names her as a daughter of Urwa ibn Sa'd ibn Hudhaym, while Ibn Abd al-Barr says she was from the Banu Sawa'a ibn Amir.

Ibn Sa'd lists him among the emigrants to Abyssinia in the second migration, and Ibn Abd al-Barr states that he and all his brothers, including Tamim ibn al-Harith, made the journey.

He was killed as a martyr during the conquest of Syria, but the sources name different battles. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr say he died at the Battle of Yarmuk in Rajab 15 AH (636 CE). Musa ibn Uqba, and an account attributed to Urwa and Ibn Shihab, place his death at Ajnadayn, fought in 13 AH (634 CE). Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that reports often confuse who fell at Yarmuk, Ajnadayn and Marj al-Saffar, because these battles were close together in time and place. Abu Nu'aym records that he left no descendants.

primaryTitle: Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam
bio: Sa'id bin Khalid ibn Sa'id (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full:
Sa'id ibn Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-As ibn Umayya was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Umayyad clan of Quraysh. His father, Khalid ibn Sa'id, was one of the early Muslims and emigrated to Abyssinia, and Musa ibn Uqba records that Sa'id was born there during his father's stay. His sister Umm Khalid, whose name was Ama, was born there too. Ibn Sa'd states that the two were full siblings and names their mother as Humayna; another report calls her Umayna bint Khalaf ibn As'ad al-Khuza'i.

Abu Hatim al-Razi counted him among those who travelled 'in the two ships' of the Abyssinian emigrants, and al-Askari listed him among the Companions. Musa ibn Uqba reports that he was killed as a martyr at Marj al-Saffar in Syria, and Sayf ibn Umar gives a long account of his death there.

bio_sources.title: al-Isaba fi Tamyiz al-Sahaba (Ibn Hajar), vol. 3, no. 3263 — Sa'id ibn Khalid

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Sa'id bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Sa'id bin Maqrn al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE in the Hijaz region, he belonged to the Mazn tribe and became one of the notable figures among the Sahaba, the companions who lived during the time of Prophet Muhammad.

Sa'id bin Maqrn is most notably recognized for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, which took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This significant event in early Islamic history is referenced in the Quran in verse 48:18, which speaks of God's pleasure with those believers who pledged their allegiance under the tree. The pledge occurred when the Muslim community, having traveled to perform pilgrimage, was prevented from entering Mecca and rumors spread that the Prophet's envoy had been killed. In response, the companions, including Sa'id bin Maqrn, pledged their loyalty and readiness to fight if necessary.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular importance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the unwavering commitment of the early Muslim community to their faith and their leader. Those who participated in this pledge are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as the Quranic verse explicitly mentions God's satisfaction with their action.

As a member of the Mazn tribe, Sa'id bin Maqrn represented the diverse tribal composition of the early Muslim community. His presence among the companions illustrates how Islam brought together individuals from various Arabian tribes under a unified religious and social framework.

Sa'id bin Maqrn lived through the crucial formative period of Islam, witnessing the establishment and early expansion of the Muslim community. He died around 640 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, having experienced both the prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

His legacy rests primarily on his status as a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, events that place him among the earliest and most committed members of the Islamic community during its foundational years.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Sa'id bin Suwayd bin Qays (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Sa'id ibn Suwayd ibn Qays ibn Amir ibn Abbad ibn al-Abjar was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Khudra clan of Medina; Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir note that al-Abjar is Khudra. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir record that the correct form of one ancestor's name is Ubayd. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Hajar state that he was a maternal half-brother of Samura ibn Jundab.

Ibn Ishaq lists him among those killed as martyrs at the Battle of Uhud in 3 AH (625 CE). Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir name two sons, Uqba and Abd al-Malik. A report on lost property, transmitted by al-Awza'i through Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Suwayd from his father, is attributed to him; Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Hajar both note that the better-known chain for this report runs instead through Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani.

bio_sources.title: al-Isaba fi Tamyiz al-Sahaba (Ibn Hajar), vol. 3 p. 89, no. 3275 — Sa'id ibn Suwayd

full: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib ibn Hazn al-Makhzumi al-Qurashi
primaryTitle: Sayyid al-Tabi'in — Master of the Successor Generation
titles: Sayyid al-Tabi'in · Faqih al-Fuqaha' · One of the Seven Jurists of Medina
bio: Abu Muhammad Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib ibn Hazn al-Makhzumi was one of the foremost authorities of jurisprudence (fiqh) among the taba'een. He was based in Medina. He is the only tabi whose all hadith narration are acceptionally trustworthy despite being mursal. In Shia sources, he is counted among the close companions of Ali al-Sajjad, and was reportedly praised by the latter.
bio_full:
Abu Muhammad Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib ibn Hazn al-Makhzumi (Arabic: سعید بن المسیب, romanized: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib; 637–715) was one of the foremost authorities of jurisprudence (fiqh) among the taba'een (generation succeeding the companions of Muhammad who are referred to as the sahaba). He was based in Medina. He is the only tabi whose all hadith narration are acceptionally trustworthy despite being mursal. In Shia sources, he is counted among the close companions of Ali al-Sajjad, and was reportedly praised by the latter.

Life and contribution to Islamic learning
Sa'id was born in 637, the son of al-Musayyib ibn Hazn of the Banu Makhzum clan of the Quraysh tribe. He was born during the caliphate of Umar (r. 634–644) and met most of the sahaba, including Umar's successors Uthman (r. 644–656) and Ali (r. 656–661). Sa'id was well known for his piety, righteousness and profound devotion to Allah; as for his stature among Sunni Muslims, he is renowned as the most eminent of The Seven Fuqaha of Medina. He began, as did Hasan al-Basri in Basra, to give opinions and deliver verdicts on legal matters when he was around twenty years of age. The Companions admired him greatly. On one occasion, Abdullah ibn Umar remarked, "If [Muhammad] had seen that young man, he would have been very pleased with him."
Sa'id married the daughter of Abu Hurayrah in order to be closer to him and to learn better the hadiths (traditions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and his companions) that he narrated. The two had a daughter. Sa'id had her play not with dolls, but with drums; later she learnt to cook.
During the Battle of al-Harra and the subsequent takeover of Medina by the Syrian troops of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I in 683, Sa'id was the one Medinese who prayed in the Prophet's mosque. After Yazid died, he refused to take the oath of allegiance to the Mecca-based, anti-Umayyad caliph Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. After the Umayyad Abd al-Malik had reconquered the Caliphate, including Medina, he requested Sa'id marry his daughter (born of his marriage to Abu Hurayra's daughter) to Abd al-Malik's son and future caliph Hisham. Sa'id refused and, in the face of increasing pressures and threats, he offered her to Ibn Abi Wada', who stayed in the madrasa. In 705, Abd al-Malik commanded his governors to enforce the oath of allegiance to his son al-Walid I as his successor. Sa'id refused. Hisham ibn Isma'il al-Makhzumi, the governor of Medina, gaoled him and had him beaten daily until the stick was broken, but he did not yield. When his friends, such as Masruq ibn al-Ajda' and Tawus, advised him to consent to al-Walid's caliphate to spare himself further torture, he answered: "People follow us in acting. If we consent, how will we be able to explain this to them?" Hisham's successor Umar II (a maternal grandson of Umar), who governed Medina in 706–712, on the other hand consulted Sa'id in all of his executive decisions.

Hadith
Those who received Islamic rulings and Traditions from Sa'id include Umar II, Qatadah, al-Zuhri and Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari, among others.
Sa'id was from Ahle Hadith School of thought  Qur'an. He did not treat the hadith as a science with isnads (chains of transmission) in the way of those after him (especially al-Zuhri). As a result, many of his rulings have been equipped with spurious isnads and converted into hadiths. It is similar with tafsir (Qur'anic interpretation): Sa'id argued his points from the Qur'an, but refused to expound on verses for their own context or meaning. To the extent a "tafsir of Ibn al-Musayyib" ever existed it was compiled by his students based on his rulings.
The leading jurisprudents Malik ibn Anas and al-Shafi'i took as unquestionably authentic the hadiths that Sa'id narrated from Umar or Muhammad as authentic, without mentioning from whom he received them.

full: Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl al-Adawi al-Qurashi
primaryTitle: One of the Ten Promised Paradise
titles: One of the Ten Promised Paradise · Early Emigrant
bio: Saeed bin Zaid Al-Qurashi Al-Adawi is one of the ten promised Paradise, and one of the first to convert to Islam, as he converted to Islam after thirteen men, and before the Prophet entered Dar Al-Arqam and before he preached in it, his father Zaid was one of the Hanafis in pre-Islamic times. He only worships God and does not prostrate to idols. He is the cousin of Omar bin Al-Khattab, and his sister is Atika bint Zaid, Omar’s wife, and his wife is Omar’s sister Fatima bint Al-Khattab, who was the reason for Omar bin Al-Khattab’s conversion to Islam.
bio_full:
Saʿīd bin Zayd bin ʿAmr bin Nufayl bin ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā al-ʿAdawī al-Qurashī (Arabic: سَعِيد بْن زَيْد بْن عَمْرو بْن نُفَيْل بْن عَبْد ٱلْعُزَّى ٱلْعَدَوِيّ ٱلْقُرَشِيّ; c. 593-671), also known by his kunya Abūʾl-Aʿwar Arabic: أَبُو ٱلۡأَعْوَر (Lit. 'Father of the One-Eyed'), was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and a brother-in-law of Umar.
Sa'id has been described as a tall, hairy, dark-skinned man.

Conversion to Islam
Sa'id became a Muslim not later than 614. His wife Fatima was also an early convert. At first they kept their faith secret because Fatima's brother Umar was a prominent persecutor of Muslims. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt often visited their house and read the Qur'an to Fatima.
One day Umar entered their house while Sa'id was reading and demanded to know what the "balderdash" was. When they denied that anything had been read, Umar seized Sa'id and knocked him to the floor. Fatima stood up to defend her husband, and Umar hit her so hard that she bled. The couple admitted that they were Muslims. At the sight of the blood, Umar was sorry for what he had done, and asked to see what they had been reading. It was Ta-Ha, later to become the twentieth Surah of the Qur'an. Impressed by the beauty of the words, Umar decided to become a Muslim.

Emigration to Medina
Sa'id joined the general emigration to Medina in 622 and at first lodged in the house of Rifa'a ibn Abdul-Mundhir. He was made the brother in Islam of Rafi ibn Malik of the Zurayq clan; but an alternative tradition names his brother in Islam as Talha ibn Ubaydallah.
Sa'id and Talha missed the Battle of Badr because Muhammad sent them ahead as scouts to report on the movements of Abu Sufyan's caravan. When they heard that they had missed the caravan, they returned to Medina, only to find that Muhammad and his army had already reached Badr. They set out for Badr and met the returning victorious army at Turban. However, Muhammad gave them a share of the Maal-e-Ganimat (spoils of war) as if they had participated in the war.
Sa'id participated in all the other battles in which Muhammad personally fought. He served as Muhammad's secretary and recorded the verses of the Quran.

During the time of the Caliphs
In the time of Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan (r. 661–680) he was Governor of Kufa.

Death
He died in 671 CE (51 AH) during the reign of Muawiya at al-Aqiq. His body was carried back to Medina and buried there by Sa`d ibn Abi Waqqas and Abdullah ibn Umar.
Sa'id said that Muhammad once guaranteed Paradise to ten men who were then present and named nine of them. Then he hinted that the tenth man had been himself. This story of the ten to whom Paradise was promised was corroborated by another of the Ten, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf.

Family
He was the son of Zayd bin Amr, from the Adi clan of the Quraysh in Mecca, and of Fatima bint Ba'ja of the Khuza'a tribe.  His father was murdered in 605.

Wives and children
Sa'id had over thirty children by at least eleven different women.

bio: Sa'id/Sa'd bin Suhayl bin Malik (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Sa'd ibn Suhayl was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet from the Banu Dinar ibn al-Najjar, a branch of the Khazraj of Medina. Abu Nu'aym al-Isbahani gives his lineage as Sa'd ibn Suhayl ibn Abd al-Ashhal ibn Haritha ibn Dinar ibn al-Najjar. Ibn al-Athir records a variant in which his father is Suhayl ibn Malik ibn Ka'b ibn Abd al-Ashhal. Some reports call his father Sahl rather than Suhayl, and Ibn al-Athir argues that the separate entries under Sa'd ibn Sahl and Sa'd ibn Suhayl describe the same man. One report places him among the Banu Khansa', which Ibn al-Athir rejects because Khansa' belonged to a different branch of al-Najjar. On the authority of Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri and Ibn Ishaq, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir record that he fought at the Battle of Badr; Ibn al-Athir also cites Ibn al-Kalbi for this. The classical entries give no details of his later life or the date of his death.

bio: Sa'ida bint Bashir bin 'Ubaid (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Sa'ida bint Bashir bin 'Ubaid was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who provided crucial support to the Muslim community during its establishment in that city.

As one of the Ansari companions, Sa'ida belonged to the group of Medinan residents who welcomed and assisted the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim emigrants (muhajirun) when they arrived from Mecca during the Hijra in 622 CE. The Ansar played a pivotal role in the survival and growth of the early Muslim community, offering shelter, protection, and material support during a critical period when the nascent Islamic state was taking root.

Sa'ida lived through the most significant decades of early Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, the various military campaigns and treaties that secured the community's position, and the rapid expansion of Islamic influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime spanned from the pre-Islamic period through the Prophet's ministry and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule.

The designation of Sa'ida as a companion carries particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the sahaba (companions) are regarded as the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad. This status places her among a select group of individuals who experienced firsthand the revelation of the Quran and the development of Islamic practices and community structures.

Like many female companions of her era, specific details about Sa'ida's individual contributions and activities are not extensively recorded in the historical sources that have survived. This reflects the general pattern of early Islamic historiography, which tended to focus primarily on male figures and military or political events, while providing limited documentation of women's roles and experiences.

Sa'ida died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, having lived through the foundational period of Islamic civilization. Her recognition as a companion ensures her place in Islamic historical memory as part of the generation that helped establish and preserve the early Muslim community in Medina.

full: Abu Muhammad Muslih al-Din ibn 'Abd Allah Sa'di al-Shirazi
primaryTitle: Shaykh Sa'di — Master of Persian Moral Poetry
titles: Shaykh Sa'di · Master of Persian prose and verse · 'Bani Adam' poem at the UN entrance
bio: Saadi Al-Shirazi is a Persian poet and mystic. His writings were distinguished by their clear, solemn style and high moral values, which made him the most popular Persian writer. His reputation crossed the borders of Persian-speaking countries to a number of areas and regions of the Islamic world, and reached the West as well, where he was classified as one of the most prominent classical medieval poets.
bio_full:
Saadi Shirazi (1210-1291) was an Iranian Sufi poet. He is recognized for the quality of his writings and for the depth of his social and moral thoughts.
Saadi is widely recognized as one of the greatest poets of the classical literary tradition, earning him the nickname "The Master of Speech" or "The Wordsmith" (استاد سخن ostâd-e soxan) or simply "Master" (استاد ostâd) among Persian scholars. He has been quoted in the Western traditions as well. His book, Bustan has been ranked as one of the 100 greatest books of all time by The Guardian.

Background and name
Abu Mohammad Moshrefoldin Mosleh ebn Abdollah ebn Mosharraf, was of Persian stock and his birth date is uncertain; most scholars consider him to have been born in 1209 or 1210. He was from the city of Shiraz, the provincial capital of the modern day Fars province. Since 1148, the city had been under the rule of the Salghurids, a Persianate dynasty of Turkoman origin.
There is little certainty concerning Saadi's life. Although his own writings, particularly the Bustan and Gulistan, contain many supposedly autobiographical memories, many of these are historically unlikely and are likely made up or cast in the first person for rhetorical effect. Even the earliest references to him in external literature differ in crucial details. Even his real name is uncertain. In sources, his entire name—which consists of his given name, honorific (laqab), agnomen (kunya), and patronymic—is spelled in several differing ways.
The oldest known source to mention his full name is the Talḵiṣ al-majmaʿ al-ādāb fi moʿjam al-alqāb ("Summary of the gathering of refinements concerning the lexicon of honorifics") by Ibn al-Fuwati (died 1323). In a letter dated 1262, he asked Saadi for samples of his Arabic poetry and mentioned his full name as "Muslih al-Din Abu Muhammad Abd-Allah ibn Musharrif." The Iranian scholar Saeed Nafisi favoured this version of his full name. However, the majority of other academics favour the information found in the early manuscripts of Saadi's writings. For instance, the British Iranologist Edward Granville Browne used a text from 1328 to argue that Saadi's full name was "Musharrif al-Din ibn Muslih al-Din Abd-Allah." The majority of subsequent Western academics, including Arthur John Arberry, Jan Rypka, and R. Davis, include "Abd-Allah" in Saadi's patronymic, hence "Abu Abd-Allah Musharrif al-Din Muslih".
The Iranian scholar Zabihollah Safa came to the conclusion that "Muslih" was Saadi's given name and gives his full name as "Abu Muhammad Musharrif al-Din Muslih ibn Abd-Allah ibn Musharrif" based on the preface to one of the oldest surviving compilations of Saadi's collected works, which was created by his fellow townsman Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Abu Bakr Bisotun in 1326. In his book Nafahat al-Uns, the Persian poet Jami (died 1492) provides virtually the same version of the name. This version is also supported by the Iranologist Paul E. Losensky.
His pen name "Saadi" is unambiguous as it appears frequently in his work and acts as his signature in all of his ghazals (amatory poem or ode). However, there are doubts over where it came from. Since two members of the Salghurid dynasty named "Sa'd" ruled for most of Saadi's life, it is likely that the inspiration for the name came from his allegiance to them. The Iranian scholar Abdolhossein Zarrinkoob argues that "Sa'd" or "Banu Sa'd" was also the name of the dynasty itself, hence Saadi's adoption of the name, which demonstrated his loyalty to them.

Biography

Education and travels
Saadi appears to have received his early education from his father, who also instilled in him lifelong tolerance values. During Saadi's adolescence, his father died, thus leaving him an orphan. Probably around 1223/24, when Sa'd I was briefly deposed by Ghiyath al-Din Pirshah, Saadi, still a teenager, left for Baghdad to continue his education there.
The Iranian scholar Badiozzaman Forouzanfar has found notable parallels between Saadi's teachings and those of Sufi master Shihab al-Din Yahya ibn Habash Suhrawardi, suggesting that they were possibly associated. After completing his studies, Saadi spent a considerable amount of time traveling across the Islamic world. According to first-hand reports, he killed a temple priest in India and was captured by the Crusaders in Syria. According to Losensky; "Despite efforts of scholars such as H. Massé and J. A. Boyle, the effort to re-create an exact itinerary of his travels from his works is misguided." The Iranologist Homa Katouzian examined the data and came to the conclusion that while Saadi was probably in Iraq, Syria, Palestine, and the Arabian Peninsula, it was unlikely that he ever made it as far east as Khorasan, India, or Kashgar.

Return to Shiraz

After nearly 30 years of travel, Saadi returned to Shiraz in 1257, and it appears that he was already well-known and well-respected as a poet. This reputation must have come from the widespread publication of his ghazals. He was keen to restore his connections to the Salghurid dynasty, as evidenced by the speed with which the Bustan and Gulistan were published and their dedications. In a short ode, Saadi says he was inspired to go back to Shiraz by the establishment of peace and prosperity established by the Salghurid ruler Abu Bakr ibn Sa'd (r. 1226–1260). However, the Salghurid kingdom did not last long after Saadi came back. In 1256/57, Abu Bakr acknowledged the Mongol Empire as his suzerain. Abu Bakr died in 1260, and was succeeded by his eldest son Sa'd II, who died 12 days later. Their death is the subject of various elegies by Saadi. The ruler after this was Sa'd II's 12-year old son Muhammad I ibn Sa'd, who ruled under the supervision of his mother Tarkhan Khatun. Saadi praises both of them in his poems.
The Salghurid dynasty crumbled apart fast due to progressively escalating pressure by the Mongol Empire. Following Muhammad I's death, two of Abu Bakr's nephews were installed on the Salghurid throne. Saadi composed three poems honoring the second of them, Saljuk Shah ibn Salghur, during his brief five-month reign in 1263. Following an impulsive and alcohol-influenced uprising by Saljuk Shah ibn Salghur, the Mongols killed him, formally handing over power to Abish Khatun, Sa'd II's youngest daughter. However, Shiraz was effectively incorporated under Mongol rule through her forced marriage to Möngke Temür, the son of the ruler of the Mongol Ilkhanate, Hulagu Khan (r. 1256–1265). One of Saadis poems was most likely dedicated to Abish Khatun.
Saadi did not seem to have supported the rise of the Mongol Empire. He composed two qasidas (odes)—one in Arabic and the other in Persian—which grieved over the collapse of the Abbasid caliphate and the death of the last caliph al-Musta'sim (r. 1242–1258) in 1258 during the Mongol attack on Baghdad. In spite of this, Saadi composed a poem in honor of the transition of authority from the Salghurids to the Mongols, and his writings include a number of poems with similar dedications to both the Mongol rulers and their Persian administrators.
Amir Ankyanu, one of the most prominent of these, was the governor of Shiraz from 1268 to 1272. Saadi wrote four qasidas and the prose treatise Dar tarbiat-e yaki az moluk to him. According to Losensky; "None of these works can be considered panegyrics in the usual sense of the word, since they consist mostly of counsel and warnings concerning the proper conduct of rulers." The poems Saadi wrote to Shams al-Din Husayn Alakani, the longtime chief of the chancery in Shiraz, are less cautionary in tone. Shams al-Din Juvayni, the principal finance minister of the Ilkhanate, had assigned him to this position. Along with his brother Ata-Malik Juvayni, the author of Tarikh-i Jahangushay, Shams al-Din Juvayni is honored in some of the most prominent ghazals by Saadi.

bio: Saalam bin 'Umayr (c. 594–670 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Saalam bin 'Umayr was a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the 7th century CE. Born around 594 CE, he lived through the emergence and early expansion of the Islamic community, dying in 670 CE during the early decades of the Islamic empire.

Based in Medina, the second holiest city in Islam and the center of the early Muslim community, Saalam bin 'Umayr witnessed and participated in the crucial developments that shaped the nascent Islamic state. Medina served as the Prophet's base of operations after the migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE, making it the political and spiritual heart of the growing Muslim community.

Saalam bin 'Umayr is particularly remembered as a participant in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE. This engagement holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The battle is considered a turning point that established the Muslims as a formidable force in the Arabian Peninsula. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are honored with the designation "Companions of Badr" and hold a distinguished place in Islamic tradition.

The Sahaba, or companions of the Prophet, represent the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with Muhammad and helped establish the foundations of the Islamic faith and community. Their accounts and testimonies became crucial sources for understanding early Islamic practice and the Prophet's teachings. As one of these companions, Saalam bin 'Umayr belonged to a group whose experiences and perspectives were instrumental in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge to subsequent generations.

His lifetime spanned the entire prophetic period of Muhammad, the era of the Rashidun Caliphate under the first four caliphs, and the beginning of the Umayyad Caliphate. This placed him among the witnesses to Islam's transformation from a small religious movement to a major political and spiritual force that extended across much of the known world. The companions like Saalam bin 'Umayr served as living links between the prophetic era and the rapidly expanding Islamic civilization that followed.

full: Sadr al-Din Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Muhammad al-Qunawi
primaryTitle: Khatm al-Awliya' — Seal of the Friends
titles: Qutb al-Aqtab · Khatm al-Awliya
bio: Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi is a Turkish Sufi, and one of Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi’s students. He wrote many works, most of which are on the authority of Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi, and some manuscripts have survived, including: Insight of the Beginner and Tadhkirat al-Muntahi, Fukuk al-Nasafi fi Documents of Hikam al-Fusus by Sheikh al-Akbar, al-Tajaliyyat, al-Nafhat, and others.
bio_full:
Ṣadr al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Muḥammad ibn Yūnus Qūnawī, (Persian: صدر الدین قونوی; 1207–1274), was a  philosopher, and one of the most influential thinkers in mystical or Sufi philosophy. He played a pivotal role in the study of knowledge—or epistemology, which in his context referred specifically to the theoretical elaboration of mystical/intellectual insight. He combined a highly original mystic-thinker, Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn 'Arabī (1165-1240 CE/560-638 AH), whose arcane teachings Qūnavī codified and helped incorporate into the burgeoning pre-Ottoman intellectual tradition, on the one hand, with the logical/philosophical innovations of Ibn Sīnā (Lat., Avicenna), on the other. Though relatively unfamiliar to Westerners, the spiritual and systematic character of Qūnawī's approach to reasoning, in the broadest sense of the term, has found fertile soil in modern-day Turkey, North Africa and Iran not to mention India, China, the Balkans and elsewhere over the centuries.

Biography
Little is known about Qūnawī's personal life. As a young boy, Ṣadr al-Dīn was adopted by Ibn 'Arabī, whose pupil he was. Of Persian descent, he nevertheless lived and taught in the city of Konya (modern-day Turkey where he is known as Sadreddin Konevî).  There he drew very close to Mawlāna Jalāl-e Dīn Rūmī and participated in his spiritual circle. A master of ḥadīth, people came to Konya from distant lands just to study under him. But while he was reputed for his profound understanding of the Quran and Ḥadīth, he knew the ancient Peripatetic philosophy intimately, no doubt thanks chiefly to Ibn Sīnā, who commented extensively on the works of Aristotle. However, Qūnawī himself may have studied an Arabic translation of Aristotle's "Metaphysics," being one of a handful of truly insightful, post-Avicennan critics of Aristotle, even if he was not a full-fledged commentator in the spirit of Ibn Rushd.

Qūnawī's overall influence appears more strategic than wide. Moreover, some of his students found fame. He instructed Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, who went on to author a commentary, now well-known, on Suhrawardi's Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq. Another student of Qūnawī's, the Sufi poet Fakhr-al-Din Iraqi, was instrumental in introducing Ibn 'Arabī into the Persian language.

Mystical vs. philosophical knowledge
After visiting the grave of Ibn 'Arabī a spell after his teacher and father-in-law had died, Qūnavī described a mystical experience he had about his teacher, Ibn 'Arabī, thus:I walked one summery day through an empty stretch in the Taurus. An easterly wind was stirring the blossoms. I gazed at them and reflected upon God's power, might and majesty (exalted be He). The love of the Merciful [God] filled me with such ardent passion that I labored to part with created things. Then, the spirit of Shaykh Ibn 'Arabī was personified to me in the most splendid form, as if he were a pure light. He called out [to me], “O ye who are perplexed, behold me! If God sublime and transcendent hath shown Himself to me in a flash of manifestation from the noble elevation of the essence, absent hast thou been from me therein by a mere glance of an eye.” I agreed at once and, as if he had been standing there [bodily] before my eyes, the Shaykh al-Akbar [i.e., Ibn Arabī] greeted me with the salutations of reunion after a parting and embraced me affectionately, saying: “Praise be to God who the veil hath lifted and who bringeth those dear unto each other into reunion. No goal, effort or salvation hath been disaffirmed".His recollection of this dream seems to indicate not just continuing deference to his teacher, but also what he saw as the practical end of reason. Though a different intellectual breed than his deceased mentor, Qūnavī too was a practising mystic, not just a thinker and teacher. In other words, he was a mystic who excelled in formal sciences like ḥadīth studies, Qurānic exegesis (tafsīr), dialectical theology (kalām), jurisprudence (fiqh), and philosophical sciences; and he corresponded with contemporaries like Nāsīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī, whose mathematical and astronomical discoveries have become integral to the science we know today.
Qūnavī's significance arises from his firm place in Islam's "post-Avicennan" (or, more precisely, post-Falsafah) period, of which Latin European Scholastics (themselves struggling with the problematics posed by Avicenna) were likely oblivious. And yet, the intellectual current to which he belonged provided the context for, among other developments, the development of systematic reason and the elaborate philosophical tradition that emerged in Iran, including the prodigal Sadr al-Din Shirazi, also called Mulla Sadra.
Although Qūnavī was single-mindedly devoted to the same general philosophical framework as Ibn 'Arabī's, 'Abd al-Raḥmān Jāmī assured us that, despite the pupil's frustrated attempts to follow in his spiritual footsteps,[34] without a proper study of Qūnavī's works the true intention of Ibn 'Arabī regarding the so-called doctrine of Waḥdat al-Wujūd (a doctrine progeny has ascribed to Ibn 'Arabī) could not be discerned in any manner conforming to both reason and religious law (Jāmī 556). His relationship with the aging teacher notwithstanding, Qūnavī had to stake out his own personal connection to higher knowledge. At times, it seems, he distanced himself from Ibn 'Arabī altogether due to the emphasis on personal witness above the interpretation of others’ experience regardless of their social or spiritual station. Al-Munāwī (b. 1265) quoted him as saying that his teacher had striven to lead him to a level where God manifested Himself through flashes of manifestation to all seekers, but that he failed (NJK 222). Mystics describe a manifestation of this kind as a “flash,” because the “direct witnessing of the essence” resembles the light, speed, and evanescence of any ordinary flash or lightning.
Al-Qāshānī likened the “flash” to “the illumination appearing to a person that beckons and summons to the Presence of Proximity to the Lord for a journey within God.” Ibn 'Arabī referred to the deep tranquility felt by the saintly “friends of God,” the awliyā’, who take their repose in it. Because tranquility did not always occur to them, they could only take furtive glances at the manifestation, as if in a flash (Hakim 660–61).
Paradoxically, then, his relationship with Ibn 'Arabī provided Qūnavī with a sound justification for seeking a separate path to spiritual enlightenment, on the one hand, and for developing the proper terms with which to express overarching truths, on the other, which truths paradoxically were accessible only through personal experience, not anyone else's.

Problem of knowledge
Qūnavī considered it his life's task to complete what Ibn Sīnā had begun with his Ishrāqī conception of knowledge. First, he shared with Ibn Sīnā and Ibn 'Arabī the goal of representing the intellectual/spiritual journey in communicable fashion. For any kind of knowledge or noetic discovery to be understood, it must be capable of being passed on to others (pupils, speculatively minded peers, etc.), rather than hoarded in the abstract ether of the mind, as it were. Whatever its technical complexities, it had to be didactically meaningful within a specific time and place, though without losing sight of the root object of knowledge.
He worked out his principles in several treatises. Their most concise and substantial statement consists of a theoretical introduction to his magnum opus, "I'jāz al-bayān," the main body of which consists of a mystical exegesis of the "Sūrat al-Fātiḥah," the opening chapter of the Quran.

bio: Safinah, Client of the Prophet (b. c. 595 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion and Freed Slave.
bio_full:
Safinah was a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. Originally enslaved, he was later freed and became known as a "client" (mawla) of the Prophet, a term used in early Islamic society for freed slaves who maintained a protective relationship with their former owners or patrons.

As one of the Prophet's companions, Safinah lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula, witnessing the early development of the Muslim community. His status as both a freed slave and companion reflects the diverse social composition of the early Islamic community, which included people from various backgrounds and social positions.

Safinah is recognized within the Islamic tradition as a transmitter of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad. This role places him among those early Muslims who helped preserve and transmit the teachings and practices of the Prophet to subsequent generations. The science of hadith transmission became fundamental to Islamic scholarship, as these reports formed a crucial source for Islamic law, theology, and practice alongside the Quran.

His inclusion among the Sahaba is significant because companions of the Prophet hold a special status in Islamic history and religious thought. They are considered the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the revelation of the Quran. Their testimonies and transmissions are regarded as particularly authoritative in Islamic scholarship.

The fact that Safinah, despite his origins as an enslaved person, became a recognized companion and hadith transmitter illustrates important aspects of early Islamic society's approach to social mobility and religious authority. His life span, ending around 635 CE, means he lived through the Prophet's ministry, which began around 610 CE, and into the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate following the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

Safinah's legacy lies primarily in his role as a link in the chain of transmission that preserved prophetic traditions for future generations of Muslims. Through his narrations, he contributed to the body of knowledge that would later be systematically collected and analyzed by hadith scholars, helping to establish one of the foundational sources of Islamic guidance and law.

bio: Safiyah bint 'Amr b. 'Abd Wud (b. c. 606 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Safiyah bint 'Amr b. 'Abd Wud was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the seventh century CE. Born around 606 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, she was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly encountered and learned from the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime.

As a sahabiyya, Safiyah belonged to the distinguished group of early Muslims who had the opportunity to witness the Prophet's teachings, actions, and sayings firsthand. This direct exposure to the Prophet's guidance made the companions invaluable sources of Islamic knowledge and practice for subsequent generations of Muslims.

Safiyah is particularly recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial foundation of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice alongside the Quran. Female companions like Safiyah played an essential role in preserving and transmitting religious knowledge, especially regarding matters that pertained to women's religious obligations, family life, and social interactions.

Her contribution to hadith transmission reflects the broader participation of women in the early Islamic community's intellectual and religious life. Female companions were not merely passive recipients of Islamic teachings but active participants in learning, preserving, and passing down religious knowledge to future generations.

The fact that Safiyah's narrations were preserved and recognized speaks to the early Islamic community's acknowledgment of women's authority in religious matters and their capacity as reliable transmitters of prophetic traditions. Her work in hadith sciences contributed to the systematic collection and verification of prophetic sayings that would later become formal Islamic legal and theological sources.

Living during the crucial decades when Islam was establishing itself as both a religious and social system, Safiyah witnessed the transformation of Arabian society and the emergence of the early Muslim community. Her death around 646 CE placed her among those who lived through both the Prophet's lifetime and the early expansion of Islam under the first caliphs.

Safiyah bint 'Amr b. 'Abd Wud represents the vital role that women played in preserving Islamic teachings during the religion's foundational period, ensuring that prophetic guidance would be accurately transmitted to future generations of Muslims.

bio: Safiyah bint 'Ubiad bin Rabi'a (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Emigrant — Makkah to Madinah.
bio_full:
Safiyah bint 'Ubiad bin Rabi'a was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE in Mecca, she belonged to the first generation of Muslims who witnessed the emergence and establishment of the Islamic community.

As one of the early converts to Islam in Mecca, Safiyah experienced the initial challenges faced by the Muslim community in its birthplace. During the early years of Islam, Muslims in Mecca encountered significant opposition and persecution from the established tribal authorities who viewed the new religion as a threat to their social and economic systems.

Safiyah is historically recognized as one of the Muhajirun, the early Muslims who undertook the significant migration from Mecca to Medina. This migration, known as the Hijra, represents one of the most pivotal events in Islamic history, marking not only the beginning of the Islamic calendar but also the establishment of the first Muslim community-state in Medina. The decision to leave Mecca required considerable personal sacrifice, as migrants left behind their homes, properties, and familiar social networks to join the Prophet Muhammad in building a new society based on Islamic principles.

The migration to Medina was particularly challenging for women of this period, as they faced additional vulnerabilities during travel and resettlement. Female emigrants like Safiyah demonstrated remarkable courage and commitment to their faith by undertaking this journey and contributing to the establishment of the early Muslim community in Medina.

As a Sahabiyya, Safiyah belonged to a generation of women whose experiences and testimonies became part of the foundational Islamic historical record. The female companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, participating in community life, and supporting the development of early Islamic society.

Her death around 635 CE places her within the generation that witnessed both the Prophet's lifetime and the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate. This generation of early Muslims, having lived through Islam's foundational period, held special significance in Islamic historical consciousness as direct witnesses to the religion's origins and early development.

bio: Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib al-Hashimiya al-Qurashi was a companion and poet, the aunt of the Prophet Muhammad, the sister of Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib through his father and mother, and the mother of the companion al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, nicknamed “the disciples of the Messenger of God.”
bio_full:
Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim al-Qurashiyya al-Hashimiyya was a paternal aunt of the Prophet Muhammad and a full sister of Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib; her mother was Hala bint Wuhayb of the Banu Zuhra. Before Islam she married al-Harith ibn Harb ibn Umayya, by whom she had a son, Safi, and later al-Awwam ibn Khuwaylid, the brother of Khadija. With al-Awwam she had al-Zubayr, al-Sa'ib and Abd al-Ka'ba; al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam became a prominent Companion. According to Abu Nu'aym, she was the only one of the Prophet's six paternal aunts to accept Islam. She took the pledge of allegiance and emigrated to Medina.

At Uhud she confronted Muslims who were fleeing, spear in hand, and afterwards came to see the body of her brother Hamza. The Prophet first told al-Zubayr to turn her back, but she insisted and was allowed to see him. During the Battle of the Trench, while the women and children sheltered in the fort of Hassan ibn Thabit, she killed a Jewish man she found spying on it; some accounts place this episode at Uhud. She was present at Khaybar, and the Prophet assigned her forty wasqs of its produce. Elegies for her father, for Hamza and for the Prophet are attributed to her, and she narrated hadith from the Prophet.

She died in Medina during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, in 20 AH (c. 640 CE) by one account, aged 73 according to Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir. She was buried in al-Baqi' near the house of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.
