full: Ṣafiyya bint Abi ʿUbayd ibn Masʿūd al-Thaqafiyya al-Madaniyya
primaryTitle: Wife of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar — Key Narrator of the Umar Household
titles: Zawjat Ibn ʿUmar (Wife of Ibn Umar) · Bint Abi ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr — al-Istīʿāb · al-Mizzī — Tahdhīb al-Kamāl
bio: Safiyya bint Abi Ubaidah bin Masoud Al-Thaqafi, wife of Abdullah bin Omar bin Al-Khattab and sister of Al-Mukhtar bin Abi Ubaidah Al-Thaqafi. She is one of the righteous and worshipful Tabi’i women. Al-Ajli said about her: Safiyya bint Abi Ubaid, a trustworthy follower. Ibn Hibban counted her as one of the trustworthy narrators of hadith. She saw Omar ibn al-Khattab, and narrated on his authority, and she had news with him. She also saw three of the mothers of the believers, Aisha, Hafsa, and Umm Salamah. It was also narrated on the authority of Safiyya by a group of the most prominent and trustworthy followers, and those who were known for knowledge and virtue, including: Salem bin Abdullah bin Omar, Nafi’ the freed slave of her husband, Abdullah bin Dinar and others. Imam Muslim, Abu Dawud and Al-Nasa’i narrated to her.
bio_full:
Safiyya bint Abi Ubayd (632-690 CE) was a prominent female scholar and hadith narrator of the Tabi'un generation, the second generation of Muslims who learned from the Companions of Prophet Muhammad but did not meet the Prophet themselves. Born into the influential Thaqif tribe, she was the daughter of Abu Ubayd and sister of Al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd al-Thaqafi, a notable political figure of the early Islamic period.

Through marriage to Abdullah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, son of the second Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab, Safiyya gained direct access to the inner circles of early Islamic leadership. This connection proved instrumental in her development as a reliable transmitter of Islamic teachings and traditions.

Safiyya's significance in Islamic scholarship stems primarily from her role as a hadith narrator. She had the privilege of learning directly from several key figures of the first generation of Muslims, including Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab himself. She also studied under three of the Mothers of the Believers—Aisha, Hafsa, and Umm Salamah—the wives of Prophet Muhammad who were recognized as important sources of Islamic knowledge, particularly regarding matters of worship, family life, and the Prophet's personal conduct.

Her credibility as a scholar was widely recognized by Islamic authorities. Al-Ajli, a respected hadith critic, described her as "trustworthy," while Ibn Hibban included her in his compilation of reliable narrators. This recognition was significant in a field where scholarly integrity was paramount and women's contributions were carefully evaluated alongside their male counterparts.

Safiyya's teachings reached the next generation through several distinguished students, including Salem ibn Abdullah ibn Umar, Nafi' (the freed slave of her husband), and Abdullah ibn Dinar. These students were themselves recognized as knowledgeable and virtuous scholars, indicating the quality of her instruction.

The major hadith collections compiled by Imam Muslim, Abu Dawud, and Al-Nasa'i include narrations transmitted through Safiyya, demonstrating her lasting impact on Islamic scholarship. Her inclusion in these authoritative collections, which form part of the foundation of Islamic jurisprudence and practice, ensures her contributions continue to influence Muslim understanding of religious teachings. Safiyya represents the important but often understudied role of women in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge during the formative centuries of the Muslim community.

full: Safiyya bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab al-Nadriyya
primaryTitle: Safiyya bint Huyayy — From the Tribe of Aaron and Moses
titles: Umm al-Muminin (Mother of the Believers)
bio: Safiyya bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab al-Nadriyya (c. 610–670 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Safiyya bint Huyayy — From the Tribe of Aaron and Moses.
bio_full:
Safiyya bint Huyayy (c. 610/614 – 664/672) was the tenth wife of Muhammad. Born in Yathrib to the Banu Nadir, one of the Jewish tribes of Arabia, Safiyya's father Huyayy ibn Akhtab and husband Kinana ibn al-Rabi were killed at the Battle of Khaybar in 628, after which she was taken captive by the early Muslims and subsequently married to Muhammad. Like other wives of Muhammad, she is known to Muslims as a "Mother of the Believers" and is buried at the al-Baqi cemetery in Medina.

Early life
Safiyya bint Huyayy was born in Yathrib, Arabia to Huyayy ibn Akhtab, the chieftain of the Arabian Jewish tribe Banu Nadir. Her mother Barra bint Samaw'al belonged to the Banu Qurayza clan. Safiyya's year of birth is uncertain with various sources recording it as around c. 610 and c. 614.
According to a source, she was married off to Sallam ibn Mishkam, who later divorced her. When the Banu Nadir were expelled from Medina in 625, her family settled in Khaybar, an oasis 153 kilometers from Medina. Her father and brother went from Khaybar to join the Meccan and Bedouin forces besieging Muhammad in Medina during the Battle of the Trench. When the Meccans withdrew, Muhammad besieged the Banu Qurayza. After the defeat of the Banu Qurayza in 627, Safiyya's father, a long-time opponent of Muhammad, was captured and executed by the Muslims.
In 627 or early 628, Safiyya was married to Kinana ibn al-Rabi, treasurer of the Banu Nadir; she was about 17 years old at that time. Muslim sources claimed that Safiyya is said to have informed Kinana of a dream she had in which the moon had fallen from the heavens into her lap. Kinana interpreted it as a desire to marry Muhammad and struck her in the face, leaving a mark which was still visible when she first had contact with Muhammad.

Battle of Khaybar

In May 628, Muhammad and the Muslims invaded Khaybar, and several Jewish tribes (including the Banu Nadir) were defeated and surrendered. Some of the Jewish tribes were allowed to remain in the city on the condition that they give half of their annual produce to the Muslims. The land itself became property of the Muslim state. This settlement offer, according to Stillman, did not extend to the Banu Nadir tribe, who were given no mercy. As a result of the battle, Safiyya's then-husband, Kinana ibn al-Rabi, was killed.
Dihya al-Kalbi, one of Muhammad's companions, requested a slave from the captives, and Muhammad granted him the choice. Dihya thus went and took Safiyya. Witnessing this, another companion informed Muhammad, highlighting Safiyya's beauty and her status as the chief mistress of Banu Qurayza and the Nadir. The companion believed she was fit only for Muhammad, leading Muhammad to give the order to call them.
When Safiyya was delivered, she came along with another woman. The latter was distressed by the sight of the slain Jews, which prompted her to cry out and induce self-injury on her face. In response, Muhammad ordered her to be taken away. He directed that Safiyya be placed behind him, with his cloak covering her, indicating to the Muslims that he had chosen her for himself, and told Dihya to take any other slave girl from the captives. It was reported that Dihya got seven slaves in exchange. Muhammad married Safiyya.

Marriage to Muhammad
In the aftermath of the battle, Safiyya's husband was reportedly tortured and executed on Muhammad's orders and Safiyya and her cousins were led past the freshly slain corpses of their kinsmen. According to Martin Lings, Muhammad had given Safiyya the choice of returning to the defeated Banu Nadir or becoming Muslim and marrying him, and Safiyya opted for the latter choice. W. Montgomery Watt and Nomani believe that Muhammad married Safiyya as part of reconciliation with the Jewish tribe and as a gesture of goodwill. John L. Esposito states that the marriage may have been political or to cement alliances. Haykal opines that Muhammad's manumission of and marriage to Safiyaa was partly in order to alleviate her tragedy and partly to preserve their dignity, and compares these actions to previous conquerors who married the daughters and wives of the kings whom they had defeated. According to some, by marrying Safiyya, Muhammad aimed at ending the enmity and hostility between Jews and Islam. Muhammad advised Safiyya to convert to Islam, she accepted and agreed to became Muhammad's wife. Safiyya did not bear any children to Muhammad. According to Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili, Safiyya came to appreciate the love and honor Muhammad gave her, and said, "I have never seen a good-natured person as the Messenger of Allah". Safiyya remained loyal to Muhammad until he died.
Modern historians treat these reports critically because they were recorded generations after the event and emerged from literary and legal traditions invested in portraying Muhammad's actions as just and honorable. In light of the circumstances of conquest, bereavement, and enslavement, scholars note that Safiyya's ability to give free consent in any modern sense cannot be assumed. Academic scholars of Islamic history and gender, such as Kecia Ali, argue that evaluating Safiyya's "choice" to convert to Islam and marry Muhammad requires acknowledging the severe power imbalance of her situation. Because the alternative to conversion and marriage was remaining a captive slave, historians emphasize that modern concepts of consent cannot be applied to women taken as spoils of war. Consequently, secular biographers of Muhammad frequently analyze marriage not as a romantic or honorable gesture, but as a coerced political assimilation of a defeated adversary's nobility. 

Consummation
Regarding the consummation of their marriage and her 'idda (waiting period), several authentic hadith addressed this topic.
Her marriage was nullified after her husband was killed and she was taken as a slave, which is different from the typical case of a divorce or death of a woman's husband. Because of this, consummation was based on istibra' (assurance of being free of pregnancy via menses) rather than 'idda. Numerous authentic hadith reports describe this:

Legacy
Safiyya is honored by Muslims as one of the "Mothers of the Believers". After Muhammad's death, she became involved in the power politics of the early Muslim community, and acquired substantial influence by the time of her death. In 656, Safiyya sided with caliph Uthman ibn Affan, and defended him at his last meeting with Ali, Aisha, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. During the period when the caliph was besieged at his residence, Safiyya made an unsuccessful attempt to reach him, and supplied him with food and water via a plank placed between her dwelling and his.
Safiyya died in 670 or 672, during the reign of Mu'awiya I, and was buried in the Jannat al-Baqi graveyard. She left an estate of 100,000 dirhams in land and goods, one-third of which she bequeathed to her sister's son, who followed Judaism. Her dwelling in Medina was bought by Mu'awiya for 180,000 dirhams.
Her dream was interpreted as a miracle, and her suffering and reputation for crying won her a place in Sufi works.

full: Ṣafiyya bint Shayba ibn ʿUthmān ibn Abi Ṭalḥa al-ʿAbdariyya al-Qurashiyya
primaryTitle: Narrator from the Mothers of the Believers
titles: Ṣafiyya bint Shayba · min Ahl Makkah (Meccan Companion)
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · Ibn Ḥajar — al-Iṣāba · al-Mizzī — Tahdhīb al-Kamāl
bio: Safiya bint Shaybah was considered by some of the female companions to be one of the greatest followers. Her father is Shaybah bin Uthman bin Abi Talha al-Abdari al-Qurashi. He was a partner with his cousin Othman bin Abi Talha in the garden of the Sacred House. Safiyya reached the age of prophethood, and she had companions, and she narrated five hadiths from the Prophet, including what Al-Bukhari narrated, commenting: I heard the Prophet say: God made Mecca sacred, so it was not permissible for anyone before me, nor for anyone after me. It was permissible for me to have an hour of the day during which it would not be alone, nor would it support its trees, nor would its patience be exhausted, and it would not take its shot except for someone who knew it.
bio_full:
Safiyya bint Shayba ibn Uthman ibn Abi Talha al-Abdariyya was a woman of the Banu Abd al-Dar of Quraysh and a narrator of hadith. Her father, Shayba ibn Uthman, was a keeper (hajib) of the Kaaba, and Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Umm Uthman Barra bint Sufyan. Ibn Sa'd also records that she was called Umm Hujayr and that she married Abd Allah ibn Khalid ibn Usayd, to whom she bore children.

Whether she was a Companion is disputed, as Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir note. Ibn Hajar credits her with having seen the Prophet, and argues that she must have, because al-Bukhari cites her report from the Prophet in suspended (mu'allaq) form. Al-Daraqutni held that her seeing the Prophet is not established, al-Dhahabi reports it only as 'it is said', and Ibn Hibban listed her among the trustworthy Successors.

She narrated from A'isha, Umm Salama, Umm Habiba and Asma' bint Abi Bakr. Among those who narrated from her were her son Mansur ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Hajabi, her grandson Muhammad ibn Imran al-Hajabi, Abd al-Hamid ibn Jubayr ibn Shayba, Mus'ab ibn Shayba, al-Hasan ibn Muslim ibn Yannaq, Maymun ibn Mihran and Qatada. Her report on the sacredness of Mecca appears in suspended form in al-Bukhari's Sahih.

No firm death date is recorded. Al-Dhahabi estimated that she lived into the reign of al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik.

bio: Safwan bin Bayda (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Safwan ibn Bayda, born Safwan ibn Wahb ibn Rabi'a, was a Companion of the Prophet from the Banu al-Harith ibn Fihr of Quraysh. He was known by the name of his mother, Bayda, and his brothers included Suhayl ibn Bayda. Ibn Hibban gives his kunya as Abu Amr. He accepted Islam in Mecca and was counted among the early Emigrants (Muhajirun). In Medina he stayed with his brother Suhayl in the house of Kulthum ibn al-Hidm, and the Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Rafi' ibn al-Mu'alla.

He took part in the raiding party of Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, in which booty was taken; Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Manzur, citing Ibn Abbas, connect the Qur'anic verse about fighting in the sacred month with this expedition. Ibn Ishaq lists him among those who fought at Badr.

Accounts of his death differ. One account, given by Ibn Manzur in his abridgement of the History of Damascus, says he was killed at Badr by Tu'ayma ibn Adi. Other reports say he survived Badr: Abu Nu'aym says he died in the plague of Amwas (18 AH); Ibn Hibban gives his death as 30 AH; and another report, also recorded by Ibn Manzur, says he took part in the Prophet's later campaigns and died in Ramadan 38 AH.

full: Abu Muhammad Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tustari
primaryTitle: Qutb al-Tafsir — Pole of Quranic Exegesis
titles: Imam al-Tustari · Qutb al-Tafsir
bio: Abu Muhammad Sahl bin Abdullah bin Yunus al-Tustari, one of the scholars of the Sunnis and the community, and one of the prominent figures of Sunni Sufism in the third century AH. Abu Abdul Rahman al-Sulami described him as “one of the imams of Sufism and their scholars, and theologians on the sciences of sincerity, mathematics, and the defects of actions.” He is originally from “Bustar,” one of the cities of Khuzestan Governorate currently located in Iran.
bio_full:
Sahl al-Tustarī (Arabic: سهل التستري) or Sahl Shushtarī (Persian: سهل شوشتری) according to Persian custom, born Abū Muḥammad Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh (c.818 CE (203 AH) – c.896 CE (283 AH), was a Persian Sunni Muslim Hanbali scholar and early classical Sufi mystic, belonging to the Ahl al-Hadith tradition. He founded the Salimiyah Muslim theological school, which was named after his disciple Muhammad ibn Salim.
Tustari is most famous for his controversial claim that "I am the Proof of God for the created beings and I am a proof for the saints (awliya) of my time" and for his well-known Tafsir, a commentary on and interpretation of the Qur'an.

Biography
Sahl al-Tustari was born in the fortress town of Shushtar (Tustar in Arabic) during the golden age of the Abbasid Caliphate, in Khūzestān Province in what is now southwestern Iran.
From an early age he led an ascetic life with frequent fasting and study of the Qur'an and Hadith, the oral traditions, of the Prophet Muhammad. He practised repentance (tawbah) and, above all, constant remembrance of God (dhikr). This eventually culminated in a direct and intimate rapport with God with whom he considered himself a special friend and one of the spiritual elect.
Tustari was under the direction of the Sufi saint Dhul-Nun al-Misri for a time, and Tustari in his turn was one of the Sufi mystic Mansur Al-Hallaj's early teachers.
Tustari also kept the company of hadith scholars. It is reported that when he met Abu Dawud, he said, "O Abu Dawud, I want something from you." Abu Dawud responded, "What is it?" Sahl said, "On the condition that you will fulfill my request if it is possible." Abu Dawud replied in the affirmative. Sahl said, "Show me that tongue with which you narrate the hadiths of the Prophet (peace be upon him) so that I might kiss it." Abu Dawud assented, and Sahl kissed his tongue. This shows the close proximate of early hadith scholars and early Sufis.
In these early days when the Sufis were becoming established mostly in Baghdad (the capital of modern Iraq), the most notable Sufis of the time elsewhere were: Tustari in southwestern Iran, Al-Tirmidhi in Central Asia and the Malamatiyya or "People of Blame". Also the chief leader of the Hanabila, al-Barbahari, was a disciple of Tustari. 
An Islamic scholar who commented on and interpreted the Qur'an, Tustari maintained that the Qur'an "contained several levels of meaning", which included the outer or zahir and the inner or batin. Another key idea that he unravelled was the meaning of the Prophet Muhammad's saying "I am He and He is I, save that I am I, and He is He", explaining it "as a mystery of union and realization at the center of the Saint's personality, called the sirr ('the secret'), or the heart, where existence joins Being." Tustari also "was the first to put" the Sufi exercise of remembrance of God, Dhikr, "on a firm theoretical basis."

[Tustari] maintained that ultimately [...] it became clear to the recollector that the true agent of recollection was not the believer engaged in recollection but God Himself, who commemorated Himself in the heart of the believer. This realisation of God's control over the heart led the believer to the state of complete trust in the Divine.

Works
al-Tustari, Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah (December 2009). Meri, Yousef (ed.). Tafsir Al-Tustari: Great Commentaries of the Holy Qur'an. Translated by Keeler, Annabel; Keeler, Ali. Fons Vitae. ISBN 978-1-891785-19-1.

Sayings
"I am the Proof of God for the created beings and I am a proof for the saints (awliya) of my time"
Asked "What is food?" Tustari replied: "Food is contemplation of the Living One."
"Whoever wakes up worrying about what he will eat -- shun him!"
"If any one shuts his eye to God for a single moment, he will never be rightly guided all his life long"

bio: Sahl bin 'Atik (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Sahl ibn Atik ibn al-Nu'man ibn Amr ibn Atik ibn Amr ibn Mabdhul was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet from the Khazraj, of the line of Mabdhul (Amir) ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Jamila bint Alqama ibn Amr of the same clan. His brother al-Harith ibn Atik, known as Abu Akhzam, did not fight at Badr and was later killed at the Battle of the Bridge of Abu Ubayd.

According to Ibn Sa'd, citing Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq, Abu Ma'shar and al-Waqidi, Sahl was present at al-Aqaba with the seventy Ansar who pledged allegiance to the Prophet, and he fought at Badr and Uhud. Abu Ma'shar alone called him Sahl ibn Ubayd, which Ibn Sa'd and al-Tabari regarded as a mistake. Ibn Sa'd states that he left no descendants. Ibn Manda reports that he died in the Prophet's lifetime and that the Prophet led the funeral prayer over him.

bio_sources.title: Ibn Sa'd (al-Tabaqat), Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym, Ibn al-Athir (Usd al-Ghaba), Ibn Abi Hatim — Sahl ibn Atik (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Sahl bin Abi Hathma (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Sahl ibn Abi Hathma al-Ansari was a young Companion of the Prophet from the Banu Harith of Medina. His father, known as Abu Hathma, is named variously as Abd Allah, Amir or Ubayd Allah, son of Sa'ida; the Prophet once sent Abu Hathma to assess date harvests. His mother was Umm al-Rabi' bint Salim ibn Adi. Khalifa ibn Khayyat counts his clan among the Khazraj, while Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir, citing Ahmad ibn Zuhayr, place it in the Aws. Sahl's own kunya is given as Abu Yahya, Abu Muhammad or Abu Abd al-Rahman.

Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir state that he was born in 3 AH, and al-Waqidi says he was eight years old when the Prophet died. Abu Hatim al-Razi and others reported that he took the pledge under the tree, guided the Prophet on the night of Uhud and took part in every battle except Badr. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir judge al-Waqidi's account more accurate.

He narrated hadith from the Prophet, including the report on the oath procedure (qasama) after the killing of Abd Allah ibn Sahl, a well-known description of the prayer of fear, and a report on standing close to the prayer barrier (sutra). Those who narrated from him include his son Muhammad, Nafi' ibn Jubayr, Bashir ibn Yasar, Salih ibn Khawwat, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mas'ud and Urwa. He lived in Medina and died there at the beginning of Mu'awiya's reign.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Sahl bin al-Rabi' bin 'Amr (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full: Sahl ibn al-Rabi' ibn Amr ibn Adi ibn Zayd ibn Jusham ibn Haritha al-Ansari al-Harithi was a Companion of the Prophet from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Abd al-Barr, in a brief entry, and Ibn al-Athir, who gives the lineage without Zayd, both record that he took part in the Battle of Uhud. The classical entries give no further details of his life, his narrations or his death.

bio: Sahl bin Hunayf (c. 594–658 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Sahl ibn Hunayf ibn Wahb was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Aws tribe and the clan of Amr ibn Awf. He was the brother of Uthman ibn Hunayf. His kunya is most often given as Abu Thabit, though Abu Sa'id and Abu al-Walid are also recorded. He fought at Badr, and Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir say he took part in all the campaigns with the Prophet; Ibn Sa'd names the Battle of the Trench among them. At Uhud, when many Muslims fled, he stood firm with the Prophet. He is said to have narrated about forty hadiths. After Ali became caliph, Sahl joined him. When Ali left Medina for Basra, he left Sahl in charge of the city. Sahl later fought alongside Ali at Siffin, and Ibn al-Athir reports that Ali appointed him governor of Fars, whose people at first expelled him; another account says Ali placed him over Basra after the Battle of the Camel. He settled in Kufa and died there in 38 AH (658-59 CE), during Ali's caliphate. Ali led his funeral prayer. Ibn al-Athir reports that Ali said six takbirs over him and explained that he was a veteran of Badr; other accounts give four or five. His sons included Abu Umama As'ad and Uthman.

full: Sahl bin Qays bin Abi Ka'b
bio: Sahl bin Qays bin Abi Ka'b (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Sahl ibn Qays ibn Abi Ka'b ibn al-Qayn was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. He belonged to the Banu Salima of the Khazraj, through the clan of Sawad ibn Ghanm; Ibn Manda wrote the clan name as Sawa'a, which Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir treat as an error for Sawad. His mother was Na'ila bint Salama ibn Waqsh, of the Banu Abd al-Ashhal of the Aws, and the poet Ka'b ibn Malik was his paternal cousin. Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir all record that he fought at Badr and was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Uhud. He was buried at Uhud.

bio: Abu Al-Abbas Sahl bin Saad bin Malik Al-Saadi Al-Ansari: A long-lived companion. His father died when he was a boy in the year 2 AH. Concerning this, Al-Waqidi said: “Saad bin Malik prepared to go out to Badr, but he fell ill, and he died, and his grave was at the house of Banu Qariz, so the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, struck him with an arrow and rewarded him.” His brother Tha’labah bin Saad was killed on a Sunday in the year 3 AH.
bio_full: Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Sāʿidī (Arabic: سهل بن سعد الساعدي) was one of the prominent Sahaba, or direct companions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, a member of the Ansar and an early Muslim scholar. He died in 91 AH. He was born as a Muslim; he narrated 188 hadiths.

bio: Sahla bint 'Asim bin 'Ady (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Sahla bint 'Asim bin 'Ady was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Sahla was among the residents of Medina who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the early Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the first Islamic state in Medina, offering protection, resources, and assistance to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca who had left behind their homes and possessions for their faith.

Living during the earliest decades of Islamic history, Sahla witnessed the rapid expansion of the Muslim community and the establishment of Islamic principles and practices. Her lifetime spanned the crucial period of the Prophet Muhammad's ministry in Medina, which lasted from 622 CE until his death in 632 CE. She died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Caliph Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate.

The female companions of the Prophet Muhammad hold significant positions in Islamic history as they represent the women who directly supported the early Muslim community and witnessed the revelation and implementation of Islamic teachings. These women participated in the social, religious, and sometimes political aspects of early Islamic society, contributing to the preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge and traditions.

Sahla's designation as an Ansari companion places her among a distinguished group of early Muslims who demonstrated their commitment to Islam through practical support and sacrifice. The Ansar are remembered in Islamic history for their generosity, loyalty, and pivotal role in ensuring the survival and growth of the Muslim community during its most vulnerable period. While specific details about Sahla's individual contributions may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as a companion reflects her active participation in and commitment to the early Islamic community in Medina.

full: ʿAbd al-Salām ibn Saʿīd al-Tanūkhī, Saḥnūn
primaryTitle: Compiler of Al-Mudawwana — The Constitution of Maliki Law
titles: Qadi al-Qudat · Imam al-Maghrib
bio: Abu Saeed Abdul Salam Sahnoun bin Saeed bin Habib bin Hassan bin Hilal bin Bakkar bin Rabia bin Abdullah Al-Tanukhi Al-Homsi The Moroccan Kairouanian Al-Maliki is a judge and jurist, one of the most famous Maliki jurists in the Maghreb, and (Sahnoun) is the nickname by which he is best known. His lineage goes back to the Tanukh tribe, and his father, Saeed bin Habib, from the people of Homs, was the first to come to Africa. Sahnoun was born in Kairouan in the year 160 AH, and was appointed judge during the era of the majority state between the years of During the reign of King Muhammad I Al-Aghlabi, he died while he was on the throne, and Muhammad I bin Al-Aghlab prayed over him. Abu Al-Arab said about him: “Sahnoun bin Saeed, from the Saliba of the Arabs, and originally from the Levant, from the people of Homs, and his father Saeed came with the soldiers, and he was one of the soldiers of the people of Homs. Sahnoun was a collector of knowledge, a jurist of the body, and in him came together what it met in others: brilliant jurisprudence, sincere piety, strictness in the truth, and asceticism. In this world, and coarseness in clothing and food, and generosity and abandonment, he does not accept anything from the Sultan, and he took over the judiciary in the year two hundred and thirty-four, and he was seventy-four years old at that time. He served as a judge for six years, and did not take any reward for the judiciary.”
bio_full:
Sahnun ibn Said ibn Habib al-Tanukhi (Arabic: سحنون بن سعيد بن حبيب التنوخي) (c. 776/77 – 854/55) (160 AH – 240 AH ) was a jurist in the Maliki school from Qayrawan in modern-day Tunisia.

Biography
His full name was Abu Said Abd al-Salam ibn Said ibn Habib ibn Hassan ibn Hilal ibn Bakkar ibn Rabia al-Tanukhi (أَبُو سَعِيدٍ عَبْدِ السَّلَامِ بْنُ سَعِيدِ بْنِ حَبِيبِ بْنِ حَسَّانَ بْنِ هِلَالِ بْنِ بَكَّارِ بْنِ رَبِيعَةَ التَّنُوخِيُّ). He gained the nickname Saḥnūn (a type of sharp bird) because of his quickness of mind. He was born to an Arab family that originated in Syria, his father was a soldier from Homs in present-day Syria. He was from the tribe of Tanukh.
In his youth Sahnun studied under the scholars of Qayrawan and Tunis. In particular, he learned from the Tripolitanian scholar `Ali bin Ziyad, who had learned from Imam Malik. In 178 AH he traveled to Egypt to study under other pupils of Malik, who died before Sahnun had the financial means to reach them. Later on he continued to Medina and studied under other prominent scholars, returning to North Africa in 191 AH.
Upon accepting the appointment as a jurist, he was said to have told his daughter Khadija, "Today your father has been slain without a knife." He was known to be scrupulous in his judgments and courteous towards litigants and witnesses, but strict towards the men surrounding the emir; he refused to allow them to send representatives on their behalf in litigation, and refused a request from the emir not to interfere in their illegal ventures.
Sahnun's son Muhammad ibn Sahnun (d. 256/870) was also a noted jurist, composing the collection of nawāzil entitled Nawāzil al-ṣalāt min Dīwān Muḥammad ibn Saḥnūn.

Theological Views
Sahnun was known  for his strong orthodoxy, even to the point of refusing to pray behind a Mu'tazilite imam. He excluded heretical sects from the mosque, including the Ibadi, Mu'tazilites and others. The Encyclopedia of Islam states:Hitherto, in the multiple circles of scholarship, representatives of all tendencies were able to express themselves freely in the Great Mosque of Kairouan. In a process amounting to a purging of the community of scholars there, Sahnun put an end to this "scandal". He dispersed the sects of the ahl al-bida; the leaders of heretical sects were paraded ignominiously, and some were compelled to recant in public.

full: Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub al-Kurdi
primaryTitle: Al-Nasir — Defender of the Faith; Liberator of Jerusalem
titles: Al-Nasir Salah al-Din · Sultan al-Islam
bio: Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, commonly known as Saladin, was a Kurdish commander and political leader. He was the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria. An important figure of the Third Crusade, he spearheaded the Muslim military effort against the Crusader states in the Levant. At the height of his power, the Ayyubid realm spanned Egypt, Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, the Hejaz, Yemen, and Nubia.
bio_full:
Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub (c. 1137 – 4 March 1193), commonly known as Saladin, was a Kurdish commander and political leader. He was the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria. An important figure of the Third Crusade, he spearheaded the Muslim military effort against the Crusader states in the Levant. At the height of his power, the Ayyubid realm spanned Egypt, Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, the Hejaz, Yemen, and Nubia.
Alongside his uncle Shirkuh, a Kurdish mercenary commander in service of the Zengid dynasty, Saladin was sent to Fatimid Egypt in 1164, on the orders of the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din. With their original purpose being to help restore Shawar as the vizier to the teenage Fatimid caliph al-Adid, a power struggle ensued between Shirkuh and Shawar after the latter was reinstated. Saladin, meanwhile, climbed the ranks of the Fatimid government by virtue of his military successes against Crusader assaults and his personal closeness to al-Adid. After Shawar was assassinated and Shirkuh died in 1169, al-Adid appointed Saladin as vizier. During his tenure, Saladin, a Sunni Muslim, began to undermine the Fatimid establishment; following al-Adid's death in 1171, he abolished the Cairo-based  Fatimid Caliphate who was an Isma'ili (a branch within Shia Islam), and realigned Egypt with the Baghdad-based Sunni Abbasid Caliphate.
In the following years, Saladin led forays against the Crusaders in Palestine, commissioned the successful conquest of Yemen, and staved off pro-Fatimid rebellions in Egypt. Not long after Nur ad-Din died in 1174, Saladin launched his conquest of Syria, peacefully entering Damascus at the request of its governor. By mid-1175, Saladin had conquered Hama and Homs, inviting the animosity of other Zengid lords, who were the official rulers of Syria's principalities; he subsequently defeated the Zengids at the Battle of the Horns of Hama in 1175 and was thereafter proclaimed the Sultan of Egypt and Syria by the Abbasid caliph al-Mustadi. Saladin launched further conquests in northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia, escaping two attempts on his life by the Order of Assassins before returning to Egypt in 1177 to address local issues there. By 1182, Saladin had completed the conquest of Syria after capturing Aleppo but failed to take over the Zengid stronghold of Mosul.
Under Saladin's command, the Ayyubid army defeated the Crusaders at the decisive Battle of Hattin in 1187, capturing Jerusalem and re-establishing Muslim military dominance in the Levant. Although the Crusaders' Kingdom of Jerusalem persisted until the late 13th century, the defeat in 1187 marked a turning point in the Christian military effort against Muslim powers in the region. Saladin died in Damascus in 1193, having given away much of his personal wealth to his subjects; he is buried in a mausoleum adjacent to the Umayyad Mosque. Alongside his significance to Muslim culture, Saladin is revered prominently in Kurdish, Turkic, and Arab culture. He has frequently been described as the most famous Kurdish figure in history.

Early life

Saladin was born in Tikrit in present-day Iraq. His personal name was "Yusuf"; "Salah ad-Din" is a laqab, an honorific epithet, meaning "Righteousness of the Faith". His parents were of Kurdish ancestry, and had originated from the village of Ajdanakan near the city of Dvin in central Armenia. He was the son of a Kurdish mercenary Najm ad-Din Ayyub.
In Saladin's era, no scholar had more influence than sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani, and Saladin was strongly influenced and aided by him and his pupils. In 1132, the defeated army of Zengi, Atabeg of Mosul, found their retreat blocked by the Tigris River opposite the fortress of Tikrit, where Saladin's father, Najm ad-Din Ayyub served as the warden. Ayyub provided ferries for the army and gave them refuge in Tikrit. Mujahid ad-Din Bihruz, a former Greek slave who had been appointed as the military governor of northern Mesopotamia for his service to the Seljuks, reprimanded Ayyub for giving Zengi refuge, and in 1137 banished Ayyub from Tikrit after his brother Asad ad-Din Shirkuh killed a friend of Bihruz. According to Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad, Saladin was born the same night his family left Tikrit. In 1139, Ayyub and his family moved to Mosul, where Imad ad-Din Zengi acknowledged his debt and appointed Ayyub commander of his fortress in Baalbek. After the death of Zengi in 1146, his son, Nur ad-Din, became the regent of Aleppo and the leader of the Zengids.
Saladin, who now lived in Damascus, was reportedly fond of the city, but information on his early childhood is scarce. About education, Saladin wrote, "Children are brought up in the way in which their elders were brought up". According to his biographers, Anne-Marie Eddé and al-Wahrani, Saladin was able to answer questions on Euclid, the Almagest, arithmetic, and law, but this was an academic ideal. It was his knowledge of the Qur'an and the "sciences of religion" that linked him to his contemporaries; several sources claim that during his studies, he was more interested in religious studies than joining the military. Another factor which may have affected his interest in religion was that, during the First Crusade, Jerusalem was taken by the Christians. In addition to Islam, Saladin knew the genealogies, biographies, and histories of the Arabs, as well as the bloodlines of Arabian horses. More significantly, he knew the Hamasah of Abu Tammam by heart. He spoke Kurdish and Arabic, and knew Turkish and Persian.

Personality and religious leanings

According to Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad (one of Saladin's contemporary biographers), Saladin was a pious Muslim—he loved hearing Qur'an recitals, prayed punctually, and "hated the philosophers, those that denied God's attributes, the materialists and those who stubbornly rejected the Holy Law." He was also a supporter of Sufism and a patron of khanqahs (Sufi hostels) in Egypt and Syria, in addition to madrasas that provided orthodox Sunni teachings. Above all else he was a devotee of jihad:

The sacred works [Koran, hadith, etc.] are full of passages referring to the jihad. Saladin was more assiduous and zealous in this than in anything else.... Jihad and the suffering involved in it weighed heavily on his heart and his whole being in every limb; he spoke of nothing else, thought only about equipment for the fight, was interested only in those who had taken up arms, had little sympathy with anyone who spoke of anything else or encouraged any other activity.
In 1174, Saladin ordered the arrest of a Sufi mystic, Qadid al-Qaffas (Arabic: قديد القفاص), in Alexandria. In 1191, he ordered his son to execute the Sufi philosopher Yahya al-Suhrawardi, the founder of the Illuminationist current in Muslim philosophy, in Aleppo. Ibn Shaddad, who describes this event as part of his chapter on the sultan's piety, states that Al-Suhrawardi was said to have "rejected the Holy Law and declared it invalid." After consulting with some of the ulama (religious scholars), Saladin ordered al-Suhrawardi's execution. Saladin also opposed the Order of Assassins, an extremist Isma'ili Shi'i sect in Iran and Syria, seeing them as heretics and as being too close with the Crusaders.

Saladin welcomed Asiatic Sufis to Egypt, and he and his followers founded and endowed many khanqahs and zawiyas of which al-Maqrizi gives a long list. However, it is not yet clear what Saladin's interests in the khanqah actually were and why he specifically wanted Sufis from outside Egypt. The answers to these questions lie in the kinds of Sufis he wished to attract. In addition to requiring that the Sufis come from outside Egypt, the waqfiyya seems to have specified that they be of a very particular type: The inhabitants of the khanqah were known for religious knowledge and piety and their baraka (blessings) was sought after...

bio: Salama bin Hisham (c. 593–635 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full: Salama ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughira was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Makhzum clan of Quraysh in Mecca. His mother was Duba'a bint Amir ibn Qurt. He was a brother of Abu Jahl (Amr ibn Hisham). Ibn Abd al-Barr records five brothers, of whom only Salama and al-Harith became Muslims; Abu Jahl and al-As were killed at Badr as unbelievers, and Khalid was captured there, ransomed, and died an unbeliever. Ibn Sa'd describes Salama as an early convert in Mecca. He emigrated to Abyssinia, according to Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir, though Ibn Sa'd notes that Musa ibn Uqba and Abu Ma'shar do not list him among those emigrants. Later his family prevented him from emigrating to Medina; Ibn Sa'd, citing Ibn Ishaq, says Abu Jahl held him in Mecca, beat him and kept food and drink from him. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn Abi Hatim state that he was not at Badr. The Prophet prayed for his release in the qunut of the dawn prayer, together with al-Walid ibn al-Walid and Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a. He reached Medina after the Battle of the Trench. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn Hibban and Ibn al-Athir place his death in battle at Marj al-Suffar in Muharram 14 AH, early in Umar's caliphate. Another account places his death at the Battle of Ajnadayn (13 AH).

bio: Salama bin Salaama bin Waqash (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Salama bin Salaama bin Waqash was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the Muslims who resided in Medina during the Prophet's time there.

Salama bin Salaama bin Waqash is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE between the early Muslim community and the Meccan Quraysh tribe. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as it was the first major military victory for the Muslim community and is often seen as a turning point that helped establish Islam's presence in the Arabian Peninsula. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are collectively known as the "Companions of Badr" and hold a special status in Islamic tradition.

As a Sahabi, Salama bin Salaama bin Waqash was part of the generation that directly witnessed and interacted with Prophet Muhammad, making him a primary source for the transmission of Islamic teachings and practices. The companions played a crucial role in preserving and passing down the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet, which form the basis of Hadith literature - the second most important source of Islamic law and guidance after the Quran.

His association with Hadith Sciences indicates that he was among those who contributed to the oral transmission of the Prophet's traditions, though the specific narrations attributed to him would require detailed examination of classical Hadith collections to verify. The companions' testimonies and reports formed the foundation upon which later scholars built the systematic study of Hadith methodology and authentication.

Salama bin Salaama bin Waqash died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph after the Prophet's death. His death occurred during a period when the Muslim community was consolidating its control over the Arabian Peninsula and beginning the early Islamic conquests that would eventually spread Islam across vast territories.

His significance lies primarily in his status as a companion who witnessed the foundational period of Islam and participated in one of its most important early battles, contributing to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings to subsequent generations.

bio: Salama bint al-Hurr al-Fazariyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Salama bint al-Hurr al-Fazariyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Fazara tribe, a branch of the larger Ghatafan tribal confederation that inhabited the Najd region of central Arabia.

As a contemporary of the Prophet Muhammad, Salama lived during the foundational period of Islam in the early seventh century. Her life spanned the pre-Islamic period, the emergence of the Muslim community in Mecca and Medina, and the early expansion of Islam across the Arabian Peninsula. She died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, in the decade following the Prophet's death.

Salama is primarily remembered for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings and actions of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial source of Islamic law and practice alongside the Quran. As a female hadith narrator, she was part of a significant tradition of women who served as transmitters of Islamic knowledge during the religion's earliest period. The female companions who narrated hadith played an essential role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings, particularly regarding matters that involved private or domestic contexts where women had direct access to information that male companions might not have witnessed.

Her tribal affiliation with the Fazara connects her to the broader networks of Arabian society that became integrated into the early Muslim community. The Fazara tribe's eventual acceptance of Islam represents the gradual expansion of the new religion beyond its initial urban centers in Mecca and Medina to encompass the Bedouin tribes of the interior.

The preservation of Salama's name in Islamic historical sources, despite the generally limited documentation of women's lives in early Islamic texts, indicates her recognized contribution to the transmission of religious knowledge. Female hadith narrators like Salama were valued for their reliability and their unique access to certain aspects of the Prophet's life and teachings. Their testimonies were considered authoritative sources for Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

Salama bint al-Hurr al-Fazariyya thus represents the important but often understudied role of women in early Islamic scholarship and the preservation of religious tradition during Islam's formative period.

bio: Salama bint Ma'qil al-Qaysiyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Salama bint Ma'qil al-Qaysiyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE in the Hijaz region, she witnessed and participated in the foundational years of the Islamic community during the late 6th and early 7th centuries.

As one of the sahabiyyat, the female companions of the Prophet, Salama held a distinguished position within the early Muslim community. Her tribal affiliation with the Qays, indicated by her nisba "al-Qaysiyya," connected her to one of the prominent Arab tribal confederations of the pre-Islamic and early Islamic periods. The Qays tribes were significant players in the social and political landscape of the Arabian Peninsula during this transformative era.

Salama's most notable contribution to Islamic scholarship lies in her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. As a female hadith narrator, she formed part of the crucial transmission chain that preserved prophetic traditions for future generations. The early Muslim community relied heavily on such eyewitness accounts from the Prophet's companions to establish religious practices, legal precedents, and moral guidance.

Her position as a hadith narrator reflects the important role that women played in the early preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge. Female companions like Salama were essential links in the isnad, or chain of transmission, that authenticated religious teachings and helped establish the corpus of hadith literature that would become fundamental to Islamic jurisprudence and theology.

The relatively short span of her life, ending around 635 CE, places her death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing suggests she lived through the entire prophetic period and the immediate aftermath that saw the rapid expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about her individual contributions to hadith transmission remain limited in available historical sources, her recognition as a narrator indicates that she was considered a reliable and trustworthy source by the early Muslim community. Her legacy contributes to our understanding of how Islamic knowledge was preserved and transmitted through the testimonies of those who directly witnessed the Prophet's teachings and example.

bio: Saleet bin 'Amr (c. 593–633 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Saleet bin 'Amr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 593 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early converts to Islam during the faith's initial expansion in Mecca.

Saleet is historically significant as one of the Muslims who participated in the migration to Abyssinia, an event that occurred in the early years of Islamic history when the Muslim community in Mecca faced increasing persecution. This migration, which took place around 615 CE, was encouraged by Prophet Muhammad as a means of protecting his followers from the hostilities they encountered from Meccan opponents of the new faith. The migrants sought refuge under the Christian ruler of Abyssinia, known as the Negus, who reportedly provided them protection.

As a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, Saleet bin 'Amr was part of the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and community practices. The companions hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of prophetic teachings and as examples of early Islamic piety and devotion.

Saleet is associated with the early ascetic tradition within Islam, indicating that he was among those early Muslims who emphasized spiritual discipline, simplicity, and devotion to worship. This ascetic tendency was present among some of the earliest Muslim converts who sought to embody the spiritual principles of their new faith through practices of self-restraint and focused religious observance.

His death in 633 CE places him among those companions who died during the period immediately following the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE, during the early years of the first Caliphate under Abu Bakr. This was a critical period in Islamic history when the Muslim community was consolidating its presence in the Arabian Peninsula and beginning its expansion beyond the region.

Saleet bin 'Amr's historical significance lies primarily in his role as an early Muslim convert who experienced both the challenges of persecution in Mecca and the experience of seeking refuge in foreign lands for the sake of religious freedom, representing the dedication of early Muslims to their faith despite considerable hardships.

primaryTitle: Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam
bio: Saleet bin Saleet bin 'Amr (c. 593–635 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full:
Saleet bin Saleet bin 'Amr (c. 593–635 CE) was among the earliest generation of Muslims and holds the distinction of being recognized as one of the first individuals born into the Islamic faith. As a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad, he represents a unique category within early Islamic history as part of the first generation to be raised in Islam from birth, rather than converting from pre-Islamic Arabian traditions.

Saleet's connection to Abyssinia (modern-day Ethiopia) places him within the context of the early Muslim community's migration to this Christian kingdom. The migration to Abyssinia, known as the first Hijra, occurred around 615 CE when a group of early Muslims sought refuge from persecution in Mecca under the protection of the Negus, the Christian ruler of Abyssinia. This migration was significant as it represented the first major movement of Muslims seeking sanctuary outside the Arabian Peninsula.

His designation as "Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam" highlights his historical importance as part of a small cohort who experienced Islam as their native religious tradition rather than as converts. This status would have given him a unique perspective within the early Muslim community, as most of his contemporaries had lived through the transition from pre-Islamic beliefs and practices to Islamic monotheism.

Living during the formative period of Islamic history, Saleet witnessed the religion's early development and expansion. His lifespan, ending in 635 CE, coincided with the rapid growth of the Muslim community following the Prophet's death in 632 CE and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate period.

The presence of early Muslims in Abyssinia established important precedents for Islamic relations with Christian communities and demonstrated the religion's early international character. Saleet's life thus represents both the personal dimension of early Islamic experience and the broader historical patterns of migration, community formation, and interfaith relations that characterized Islam's earliest decades.

While specific details of his individual contributions or activities are not extensively documented, his recognition as a Sahaba indicates his direct association with the Prophet Muhammad and his standing within the early Muslim community.

primaryTitle: Prophet of Thamud — Messenger of the Rock-Hewn City
titles: Salih · Prophet of Thamud · associated with the miraculous she-camel
dating_source: Qur'an 7:73-79; Mada'in Salih (Hegra) site context
dating_note: People of Thamud; Hegra inhabited long before Nabataeans.
bio: Ṣāliḥ ibn 'Ubayd ibn Māshij (legendary–legendary) was a prophet, based in Al-Hijr (Mada'in Salih). Known as Prophet of Thamud — Messenger of the Rock-Hewn City.
bio_full:
Salih or Saleh (Arabic: صَالِحٌ‎, romanized: Ṣāliḥ) is a prophet mentioned in the Qur'an who prophesied to the tribe of Thamud in ancient Arabia, before the lifetime of Muhammad. The story of Salih is linked to that of the she-camel of God, a gift from God to the people of Thamud when they sought a miracle to confirm that Salih was a prophet.

Historical context

The Thamud were a tribal confederation in the northwestern region of the Arabian Peninsula mentioned in Akkadian literature during the reign of Sargon II of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. The tribe's name continues to appear in documents into the fourth century, but by the sixth century, they were regarded as a group that had vanished long ago.
According to the Quran, the city that Saleh was sent to was called al-Ḥijr (Arabic: ٱلْحِجْرْ, lit. 'The Stonetown'), which corresponds to the Nabataean city of Hegra. The city rose to prominence around the 1st century as an important site in the regional caravan trade. Adjacent to the city were large, decorated rock-cut tombs used by members of various religious groups. At an unknown point in ancient times, the site was abandoned and possibly functionally replaced by Al-'Ula. The site has been referred to as Mada'in Salih (Arabic: ﻣﺪﺍﺋﻦ ﺻﺎﻟﺢ, romanized: madāʼin Ṣāliḥ, lit. 'the cities of Saleh') since the era of Muhammad and was named after his predecessor, Salih.
Saleh is not mentioned in any historical texts or in any of the Abrahamic scriptures that precede the Qur'an, but the account of Thamud's destruction may have been well known in ancient Arabia. The tribe's name is used in ancient Arabian poetry as a metaphor for "the transience of all things".

In Islam

Qur'an
According to Muslim tradition, the people of Thamud relied on Salih for support. He was chosen by God as a prophet and sent to preach against the selfishness of the wealthy and to condemn the practice of shirk (polytheism). Although Saleh preached for a sustained period, the people of Thamud refused to heed his warning and instead asked him to perform a miracle for them. They said: “O Ṣāliḥ! We truly had high hopes in you before this. How dare you forbid us to worship what our forefathers had worshipped? We are certainly in alarming doubt about what you are inviting us to.”
Saleh reminded his people of the castles and palaces they built out of stone, and of their technological superiority over neighbouring communities. Furthermore, he told them about their ancestors, the ʿĀd, and how they too were destroyed for their sins. Some of the people of Thamud believed Saleh's words, but the tribal leaders refused to listen to him and continued to demand that he demonstrate a miracle to prove his prophethood.
In response, God gave the Thamud a blessed she-camel (Arabic: نَاقة, romanized: nāqah) as both a means of sustenance and a test. The tribe was told to allow the camel to graze peacefully and avoid harming her. In defiance of Saleh's warning, the people of the tribe hamstrung the camel. Saleh informed them that they had only three more days to live before the wrath of God descended upon them. The people of the city were remorseful, but their crime could not be undone, and all the disbelieving people in the city were killed in an earthquake. Al-Hijr was rendered uninhabitable and remained in ruins thereafter. Saleh himself and the few believers who followed him survived.
The story is expanded upon in the surah an-Naml. Whilst the she-camel is not mentioned explicitly in this chapter, it states that nine men plotted to kill Salih and his whole family, a crime for which they were struck down by God three days later.

Muslim tradition

Muslim writers have elaborated upon the story of Saleh and the she-camel. Early Islamic tradition often involved a motif of the camel miraculously emerging from stone, often accompanied by a calf, and the production of milk from the camel. Al-Tabari states that Saleh summoned his people to a mountain, where they witnessed the rock miraculously split open, revealing the camel. The she-camel had a young calf. Saleh informed the Thamud that the older camel was to drink from their water source on one day, and they were to drink from it the next day. On days when they were not allowed to drink water, the camel provided them with milk. But God informed Saleh that a boy who would hamstring the camel would soon be born to the tribe, and that child was evil and grew unnaturally fast. The camel was indeed killed, and its calf cried out three times, signaling that the Thamud would be destroyed in three days. Their faces turned yellow, then red, then black, and they died on the third day as predicted.
According to some Islamic scholars, the mother of Ismail, Hajar, was a granddaughter of Saleh.
A similar tradition is related in an eighth-century commentary on Islam by John of Damascus and is also mentioned in the works of Ibn Kathir.

In the Baháʼí Faith
The founder of the Baháʼí Faith, Bahá'u'lláh, briefly mentioned the story of the hamstrung she-camel in the Lawh-i-Burhán, and commented also upon Saleh's ministry in the Kitáb-i-Íqán.

bio: Salim bin 'Amr bin Hadida (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Salim bin 'Amr bin Hadida was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he lived during the transition from the pre-Islamic era to the establishment of the early Muslim community.

As one of the Sahaba, the term used for the companions of Prophet Muhammad, Salim bin 'Amr bin Hadida was among those early Muslims who directly interacted with the Prophet and witnessed the foundational events of Islamic history. He was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Salim bin 'Amr bin Hadida is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as a "Companion of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The Battle of Badr is considered a turning point that helped establish the credibility and strength of the early Muslim state. Those who participated in this battle are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition due to their role in this crucial early victory.

His death in 625 CE places him among the early companions who did not live to see the later expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula. He died during the lifetime of Prophet Muhammad, which was common among the early Muslim community given the various military campaigns and harsh conditions of seventh-century Arabian life.

The historical record of Salim bin 'Amr bin Hadida, like many of the early companions, is preserved primarily through Islamic historical sources that document the lives of those who were present during the Prophet's lifetime. His inclusion in the historical records reflects the importance placed on preserving the memory of those who participated in the foundational events of the Muslim community, particularly the significant early battles that helped secure the survival and growth of Islam during its most vulnerable period.

famous: Salim ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar
full: Salim ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab al-Adawi
primaryTitle: One of the Seven Jurists of Medina — Like His Grandfather Umar
titles: One of the Seven Jurists · Like Umar in Conduct · Primary Transmitter of Ibn Umar
bio: Salem bin Abdullah bin Omar Al-Khattab, Tabi’i Madani, one of the narrators of the Prophet’s hadith, and the Mufti of Medina in his time.
bio_full:
Salim ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar was a prominent Islamic scholar and jurist who lived from approximately 660 to 728 CE. He belonged to the generation known as the Tabi'un, the successors who learned directly from the Prophet Muhammad's companions but did not meet the Prophet himself.

Born into a distinguished family lineage, Salim was the grandson of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second Caliph of Islam, through his father Abd Allah ibn Umar, who was himself a renowned companion of the Prophet and a major transmitter of Islamic teachings. This family connection provided Salim with exceptional access to authentic Islamic knowledge and traditions.

Salim spent his life in Medina, the second holiest city in Islam and a major center of Islamic learning during the early centuries. There he established himself as one of the leading religious authorities of his time, eventually serving as the Mufti of Medina, a position that made him the city's primary legal advisor on matters of Islamic law and practice.

His most significant contribution to Islamic scholarship was his role as a transmitter and narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings and actions of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial foundation for Islamic jurisprudence alongside the Quran. Drawing from the extensive knowledge passed down through his family, particularly from his father Abd Allah ibn Umar, Salim helped preserve and transmit numerous prophetic traditions to subsequent generations.

As a jurist, Salim was recognized for his deep understanding of Islamic law and his ability to provide religious guidance on complex legal matters. His position as Mufti of Medina during the early eighth century placed him at the center of Islamic legal development during a formative period when the religion was expanding rapidly and encountering new legal challenges.

Salim's work contributed to the preservation of authentic Islamic teachings during the crucial early centuries following the Prophet's death. His family's direct connection to the Prophet's circle, combined with his own scholarly abilities, made him a vital link in the chain of Islamic knowledge transmission. Through his students and the traditions he preserved, his influence extended well beyond his lifetime, helping to shape the development of Islamic jurisprudence and hadith scholarship for future generations of Muslim scholars.

full: Salim ibn Ma'qil, Mawla Abi Hudhayfah ibn Utba al-Qurashi
primaryTitle: One of the Four Quran Teachers of the Prophet
titles: Salim Mawla Abi Hudhayfah · Abu Abd Allah
bio: Salem Mawla Abu Hudhayfah, a companion who was counted among the Emigrants, witnessed all the scenes, participated in the wars of apostasy, and was among the reciters who were martyred in the Battle of Al-Yamamah.
bio_full:
Salim Mawla Abi Ḥudhayfah (Arabic: سَالِم مَوْلَىٰ أَبِي حُذَيْفَة, Sālim Mawlā ʾAbī Ḥuḏayfah) was a Persian, an early companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and was described to be prominent and knowledgeable. He was named so since he was the freed slave of Abū Ḥudhayfah ibn 'Utba, see Mawla.

Birth
Salim Ibn Ma'qil was born in Istakhr, an ancient city in what is now southwestern Iran. He later became the slave of Abū Ḥudhayfah and was freed by Thubayta bint Ya'ar, the wife of Abū Ḥudhayfah, and was adopted (in the Islamic way).

Re-adoption through breastmilk
When initially brought into Abū Ḥudhayfah's household, Salim was considered to be adopted. However, after he had already aged out of breastfeeding, a Qu'ranic verse established that adopted children are not mahram. This became problematic when Salim reached puberty while remaining in Abū Ḥudhayfah's household as a young man. The Prophet therefore proposed that Salim should drink breastmilk from Abū Ḥudhayfah's wife, in order to establish him as mahram. Umm Salama among others firmly stated that this was not a legal ruling but a special dispensation for Salim. Additionally, modern jurists argue that Salim drank from a cup and did not put his mouth on a woman's breast.

Adulthood
It was recorded that he used to lead the Muhajirun, including Umar, that arrived to Medina before Muhammad arrived as he was the most knowledgeable among them in the Qur'an.
It was also recorded that:

Hanzalah ibn Abi Sufyan narrated from 'Abdul Rahman ibn Sabiṭ that 'Aisha said:
One night, the Messenger of Allah – peace and blessings be upon him – delayed his return, so he asked me: 'What kept you?'
I replied: 'In the mosque, I heard the best recitation of the Qur'an I have ever heard.'
The Prophet then took his cloak and went out to listen. It turned out to be Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah.

The Prophet said: 'Praise be to Allah who has placed someone like you in my Ummah'.
Salim also sold his inheritance to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and it amounted to two hundred dirhams, which he gave to his mother.

Death
It is said, in a hasan hadith, that Salim and his master, Abū Ḥudhayfah, were found after the battle of Al-Yamama with one’s head at the feet of the other, both lying slain. 
It was also said that he dug a trench and stood his ground with the flag of the Muhajirun that day, and fought until he was killed however the commentator of "The Biography of The Nobles" said that the one who reported this is weak.

bio: Salit bin Qays bin 'Amr (c. 594–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Salit ibn Qays ibn Amr ibn Ubayd ibn Malik ibn Adi ibn Amir ibn Ghanm ibn Adi ibn al-Najjar was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj. Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn Hibban, Ibn al-Athir and Abu Nu'aym all count him among those who fought at Badr, and Ibn Abd al-Barr adds that he took part in all the later campaigns. Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abi Hatim mention a son, Abd Allah ibn Salit, who narrated from him, while Abu Nu'aym says he left no descendants. He was killed as a martyr at the Battle of the Bridge of Abu Ubayd in Iraq, fighting under Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi during the caliphate of Umar. Ibn Hibban dates this to 14 AH.

bio: Salma bin Aslam (c. 594–636 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Salama ibn Aslam ibn Harish ibn Adi, known by the kunya Abu Sa'd, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir trace his lineage through Majda'a ibn Haritha, and Ibn Hibban and Ibn al-Athir describe him as an ally of the Banu Abd al-Ashhal of the Aws. One account names his mother as Su'ad bint Rafi'. He fought at Badr, where, according to Ibn Abi Hatim, he took two men captive, al-Sa'ib ibn Ubayd and al-Nu'man ibn Amr. Ibn Abd al-Barr says he went on to take part in all the campaigns with the Prophet. Ibn Manda and Ibn Abi Hatim state that no hadith is known to have been narrated from him. He was killed at the Battle of the Bridge of Abu Ubayd in Iraq in 14 AH, during the caliphate of Umar. Ibn Abd al-Barr gives his age at death as 38 and mentions another report of 63, while Ibn Hibban gives 23. Ibn Manda and Abu Nu'aym, as cited by Ibn al-Athir, call him Salama ibn Salama al-Ashhali.

bio: Salma bin Thabit bin Waqash (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Salma bin Thabit bin Waqash was a companion (Sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of the Islamic community.

Salma is most notably recognized for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as this engagement is considered a pivotal moment that helped establish the early Muslim state.

As a resident of Medina, Salma would have been part of the community during the crucial period following the Hijra, when the Prophet Muhammad migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. This era marked the transition of Islam from a persecuted religious movement in Mecca to an established community with its own political and social structure in Medina.

The companions of the Prophet Muhammad, known collectively as the Sahaba, are revered in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who received direct guidance and instruction from the Prophet. Their accounts and testimonies form an important part of the historical record of early Islam, contributing to the preservation of Islamic teachings and practices.

Salma's relatively short life, ending around 625 CE, means he lived during only the earliest years of the Islamic community in Medina. His death occurred during the period when the Muslim community was still establishing itself and facing ongoing challenges from opposing Arabian tribes and the Meccan confederation.

While specific details about Salma's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in the historical sources, his status as a Companion of Badr places him among the honored early followers who supported the Prophet Muhammad during a critical juncture in Islamic history. The Battle of Badr veterans are traditionally viewed as exemplars of faith and courage, having stood with the Muslim community when its survival was uncertain and its future unclear.

bio: Salma bint 'Amr b. Khunays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Salma bint 'Amr b. Khunays was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community after their migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, Salma witnessed and participated in the formative period of the early Islamic community during the Prophet's lifetime. The Ansar played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim state in Medina, providing sanctuary, support, and resources to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) who had fled persecution in Mecca. Their acceptance of Islam and commitment to the new faith helped create the foundation for the rapid expansion of the Muslim community.

The companions of the Prophet Muhammad, both male and female, hold a special place in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who learned directly from the Prophet and witnessed the revelation of the Quran. Female companions like Salma bint 'Amr b. Khunays contributed to the early Muslim community in various ways, though specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the historical sources that have survived.

Salma lived during a pivotal period in Islamic history, experiencing the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, the early military campaigns, and the consolidation of Islamic practice and law. Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr or the early period of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule.

The recognition of Salma bint 'Amr b. Khunays as a companion reflects the important role that women played in the early Islamic community, even when specific details of their individual lives and contributions have not been extensively preserved in historical records. Her status as an Ansari companion connects her to the broader narrative of Medina's central role in early Islamic history and the collaborative effort required to establish and sustain the first Muslim community.

primaryTitle: Sister of Asma bint Umays; Companion and Narrator
bio: Salma bint Umays is a Khathamiyya companion. She converted to Islam in the past with her sister Asma bint Umays, and she is the wife of Hamza bin Abdul Muttalib, the uncle of the Prophet Muhammad.
bio_full: Salma bint Umays was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the tribe of Khath'am. Her mother was Hind, also called Khawla, bint Awf, and her full sister was Asma bint Umays. Through her mother she was a half-sister of Maymuna bint al-Harith and Lubaba bint al-Harith. Ibn Sa'd reports that she accepted Islam early, together with Asma. She married Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle, and bore him a daughter, named Umara by Ibn Sa'd, Amat Allah by Ibn Abd al-Barr, and Umama in other accounts. Some reports made Asma rather than Salma the wife of Hamza, but Ibn al-Athir rejects this because Asma was in Abyssinia with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn Abd al-Barr also identifies Salma as Hamza's wife. According to one account, Salma and her daughter emigrated to Medina, and after Hamza was killed at Uhud they returned to Mecca. When the Prophet came to Mecca for the make-up pilgrimage (Umrat al-Qada), Ali brought the girl away with the Muslims, and the Prophet gave custody of her to Ja'far because her maternal aunt Asma was his wife. After Hamza's death Salma married Shaddad ibn al-Had of the Banu Layth and bore him Abd Allah ibn Shaddad; Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir also name a son Abd al-Rahman. Ibn al-Athir records a short report on inheritance attributed to her, transmitted through Qatada. The sources consulted do not record when she died.

bio: Salma bint Yi'ar (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Salma bint Yi'ar was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community after their migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions, Salma bint Yi'ar would have been among those who embraced Islam when it was introduced to Medina and who provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a vital role in establishing the first Islamic state, offering not only their allegiance to the new faith but also material and social support to the Muslim emigrants (muhajirun) who had left their homes and possessions in Mecca.

The designation of Salma bint Yi'ar as a companion places her among the most revered figures in Islamic history, as the companions are considered the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad. In Islamic tradition, the companions hold special significance as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings, practices, and the example of the Prophet.

Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period following the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE when the Muslim community was led by the first four caliphs. This places her life span entirely within the foundational period of Islam, making her a witness to both the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina and its early expansion.

While specific details about her individual contributions or particular roles within the early Muslim community are not extensively documented in the historical sources that have survived, her recognition as a companion indicates that she was an active participant in the early Islamic community. The female companions, like their male counterparts, are remembered in Islamic history for their dedication to the faith and their role in supporting and preserving the early Muslim community during its most crucial developmental phase.
