full: Sinan bin Abu Sinan bin Mihsan al-Asadi
bio: Sinan bin Abu Sinan bin Mihsan al-Asadi (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Sinan ibn Abi Sinan ibn Mihsan was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma, allies of the Banu Abd Shams of Quraysh. He was the nephew of the well-known Companion Ukkasha ibn Mihsan; Ibn Abd al-Barr gives his father Abu Sinan's name as Wahb ibn Mihsan. Ibn Ishaq lists him among those who fought at Badr, where, according to Ibn Abd al-Barr, he was present with his father, his brother and his uncle Ukkasha. He went on to take part in all the other campaigns with the Prophet. Al-Waqidi reported that Sinan was the first to give the pledge under the tree at al-Hudaybiyya (Bay'at al-Ridwan); Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir note, however, that most and better-known reports give that distinction to his father Abu Sinan. Ibn Hibban says he was about twenty years younger than his father, who died while the Prophet was besieging the Banu Qurayza. Sinan died in 32 AH (c. 652–653 CE).

bio_sources.title: Ibn Hibban, Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Athir (Usd al-Ghaba), Ibn Abd al-Barr (al-Isti'ab) — Sinan ibn Abi Sinan (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Sinan bin Maqrn al-Mazni (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Sinan bin Maqrn al-Mazni was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he was present during some of the most pivotal moments in early Islamic history.

Al-Mazni is particularly remembered for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, which took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This event occurred when the Prophet Muhammad and approximately 1,400 of his followers were prevented from performing pilgrimage to Mecca. Under a tree, the companions pledged their loyalty to Muhammad, demonstrating their willingness to fight if necessary. This pledge is specifically mentioned in the Quran in verse 48:18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree.

As one of the companions who took this pledge, Sinan bin Maqrn al-Mazni holds a special place among the sahaba, the generation of Muslims who personally knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad. The companions who participated in the Pledge of Ridwan are held in particularly high regard in Islamic tradition, as they demonstrated unwavering loyalty during a tense diplomatic situation that could have resulted in armed conflict.

Living in the Hijaz region of the Arabian Peninsula, al-Mazni would have witnessed the rapid expansion of the Islamic community from its early days in Mecca and Medina. His death around 640 CE places him in the generation that saw not only the establishment of Islam as a major religious movement but also the beginning of its spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Al-Mazni's significance lies primarily in his status as a companion and his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan. In Islamic historical tradition, the companions serve as crucial links in the transmission of Islamic teachings, practices, and accounts of the Prophet's life. Their testimonies and actions help form the foundation of Islamic law, theology, and historical understanding. While specific details about al-Mazni's individual contributions to Islamic scholarship or governance are not extensively documented, his presence at this crucial moment in Islamic history ensures his place in the collective memory of the early Muslim community.

bio: Sinan bin Sayfi b Sakhr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Sinan bin Sayfi bin Sakhr was a companion (Sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE. As one of the early Muslims who accepted Islam during the Prophet's lifetime, he holds a distinguished place among the Sahabah, the generation of believers who directly knew and followed Muhammad.

Sinan is most notably recognized for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle was the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces and is considered one of the most significant events in early Islamic history. The participants in this battle, known as the Badriyyun, are held in special reverence within Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment.

The Battle of Badr took place near the town of Badr, southwest of Medina, and involved approximately 300 Muslims facing a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory at Badr was seen as divine validation of their cause and marked a turning point in the establishment of the early Islamic state. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are remembered for their courage and commitment during this crucial period of Islamic expansion.

Sinan lived during the formative years of Islam, witnessing the religion's emergence from its origins in Mecca through the Hijra (migration) to Medina and the subsequent establishment of the first Muslim community. His life spanned the Prophet's ministry and extended into the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's reign.

He died in 634 CE, during the same year as Abu Bakr, the first Caliph after Prophet Muhammad's death. This places his death at a significant juncture in Islamic history, as the Muslim community was transitioning leadership and beginning the major conquests that would expand Islamic rule beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

As one of the Companions of Badr, Sinan bin Sayfi bin Sakhr represents the generation of early Muslims whose dedication and sacrifice helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization. His participation in this defining battle connects him to a pivotal moment that shaped the trajectory of Islamic history and the development of the early Muslim community.

bio_full:

Su'ad is historically recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant event in early Islamic history that took place in 628 CE at Hudaybiyyah. This pledge, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, occurred when the Prophet Muhammad and approximately 1,400 of his followers were prevented from entering Mecca to perform pilgrimage. The companions pledged their loyalty to the Prophet under a tree, demonstrating their unwavering commitment even in the face of potential conflict with the Meccan forces.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular importance in Islamic tradition as it is referenced in the Quran, specifically in verse 48:18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree. Those who participated in this pledge are considered to hold a special status among the companions of the Prophet Muhammad.

As a female companion, Su'ad was part of the early Muslim community during a crucial period of Islamic development. The companions who lived in Medina witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic state and participated in the community that served as the foundation for the religion's expansion. Her presence among those who took the Pledge of Ridwan indicates her commitment to the early Muslim community during a time of significant challenges and uncertainty.

Su'ad's life spanned the Prophetic period and the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, dying around 640 CE. Like many early female companions, detailed records of her specific activities and contributions are limited in historical sources, reflecting the documentation practices of the time. However, her inclusion among the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan ensures her recognition in Islamic historical tradition as one of those who demonstrated loyalty and faith during a pivotal moment in early Islamic history.

Her status as a companion places her among the first generation of Muslims, those who directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and helped establish the foundations of the Islamic community.

bio_full:
Su'ad bint Salama bin Zuhayr was a female companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet and the Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Sahabiyya, the female companions of the Prophet, Su'ad was part of the foundational generation of Muslims who directly witnessed and participated in the establishment of the early Islamic community. Her designation as an Ansari companion indicates that she was among the Medinan residents who embraced Islam and provided crucial support during the religion's formative years.

The Ansar played a vital role in Islamic history by offering sanctuary to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca and helping establish Medina as the first Islamic state. As an Ansari woman, Su'ad would have been part of this pivotal community that enabled Islam's survival and growth during its most vulnerable period.

Female companions like Su'ad contributed to early Islamic society in various ways, though specific details of individual contributions are often not extensively documented in historical sources. Women of her generation participated in community life, supported the new religious practices, and helped transmit Islamic teachings to subsequent generations.

Su'ad's life spanned the crucial decades of Islamic origins, from the pre-Islamic period of her birth around 595 CE through the Prophet's mission, the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, and the early expansion of Islam following the Prophet's death in 632 CE. She died around 635 CE during the reign of the second Caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab.

Her recognition as a companion reflects the Islamic tradition's acknowledgment of women's roles in the early Muslim community. While detailed accounts of her specific activities may not be extensively preserved, her inclusion among the documented companions indicates her recognized participation in and contribution to the early Islamic community in Medina.

bio: Suada bint 'Auf al-Murriya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Suada bint 'Auf al-Murriya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early decades of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, she was among the early Muslims who personally knew and interacted with the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime.

As a sahabiyya, Suada belonged to the first generation of Muslims whose testimonies and transmitted reports formed a crucial foundation for Islamic religious knowledge. Her primary historical significance lies in her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that serve as a fundamental source of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran.

During the formative period of Islam, female companions like Suada played important roles in preserving and transmitting religious knowledge, particularly regarding matters that concerned women's religious practices and daily life. The early Muslim community relied heavily on the direct testimonies of those who had witnessed the Prophet's teachings and conduct firsthand, making the contributions of companions like Suada essential to the development of Islamic jurisprudence and religious understanding.

Suada lived through the crucial early decades of Islamic expansion, witnessing the religion's growth from a small community in Mecca to a significant force in the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifespan, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompassed the entire prophetic period and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the early years of Umar ibn al-Khattab's leadership.

The preservation of hadith traditions transmitted by female companions like Suada demonstrates the active participation of women in the early Islamic scholarly tradition. These narrations contributed to the comprehensive body of prophetic traditions that would later be systematically compiled by hadith scholars in collections that remain authoritative sources for Islamic law and practice.

While specific details about her individual contributions may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, Suada bint 'Auf al-Murriya represents the broader group of female companions whose direct access to prophetic teachings made them invaluable links in the chain of Islamic religious transmission. Her recognition as a hadith narrator reflects the respect accorded to female religious authorities in early Islamic society.

bio: Subay' bin Qays bin 'Aysha (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Subay' bin Qays bin 'Aysha was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 594 CE. He lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula and was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Subay' is most notably remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as one of the "Companions of Badr." This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The engagement took place near the wells of Badr, southwest of Medina, and involved approximately 300 Muslims facing a much larger Meccan army. The Muslim victory at Badr was viewed as divine validation of their cause and marked a turning point in the early expansion of Islam.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Subay' would have been among those who had direct contact with the Prophet during his lifetime, heard his teachings firsthand, and witnessed the development of Islamic practices and community structures. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's sayings and actions, which later formed the basis of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

The designation as a Companion of Badr carried particular honor within the early Muslim community. Those who fought at Badr were held in high esteem for their early commitment to Islam and their role in securing the religion's survival during its most vulnerable period. Their participation in this pivotal battle demonstrated their dedication to the nascent Muslim community when its future remained uncertain.

Subay' died in 634 CE, during the period of the first Caliph Abu Bakr's rule. This was a time of rapid expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula, though the specific circumstances of his death are not detailed in available historical sources. His life spanned the entire Meccan period of Muhammad's prophethood, the migration to Medina, and the establishment of the first Islamic state, making him a witness to the foundational era of Islamic civilization.

full: Sufyan ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Thawri al-Kufi
primaryTitle: Amir al-Mu'minin fi'l-Hadith — Commander of the Faithful in Hadith
titles: Amir al-Mu'minin fi'l-Hadith · Imam al-Wara' · Founder of Thawri School
bio: Sufyan ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Thawri al-Kufi (716–778) was a scholar of the Islamic Jurisprudence tradition, based in Kufa. Known as Amir al-Mu'minin fi'l-Hadith — Commander of the Faithful in Hadith.
bio_full:
Abū ʿAbd Allāh Sufyān ibn Saʿīd ibn Masrūq ibn Ḥamza al-Thawrī al-Muḍarī al-Kūfī (Arabic: أَبُو عَبْد ٱللَّٰه سُفْيَان بْن سَعِيد بْن مَسْرُوق بْن حَمْزَة ٱلثَّوْرِيّ ٱلْمُضَرِيّ ٱلْكُوفِيّ; 716–778 CE / 97–161 AH), commonly known as Sufyān al-Thawrī (Arabic: سُفْيَان ٱلثَّوْرِيّ), was a Sunni Muslim scholar, jurist, ascetic, traditionist, and eponymous founder of the Thawri school of Islamic jurisprudence, considered one of the Eight Ascetics.
His full name is Abū ʿAbd Allāh Sufyān ibn Saʿīd ibn Masrūq ibn Ḥamza ibn Ḥabīb ibn Mawhiba ibn Naṣr ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Malakān ibn Thawr al-Thawrī al-Rabābī al-Tamīmī al-Muḍarī al-Kūfī (Arabic: أَبُو عَبْد ٱللَّٰه سُفْيَان بْن سَعِيد بْن مَسْرُوق بْن حَمْزَة بْن حَبِيب بْن مَوْهِبَة بْن نَصْر بْن ثَعْلَبَة بْن مَلَكَان بْن ثَوْر ٱلثَّوْرِيّ ٱلرَّبَابِيّ ٱلتَّمِيمِيّ ٱلْمُضَرِيّ ٱلْكُوفِيّ).

Biography
Sufyan al-Thawri was born in Khorosan. His nisba, al-Thawri, is derived from his ancestor Thawr ibn Abd Manah. He moved to Kufa for his education, and in his youth supported the family of Ali ibn Abi Talib against the Umayyad Caliphate. By 748, he had moved to Basra, where he met Abd Allah ibn Awn and Ayyub al-Sikhtiyani. He learned some aspects of Shiasm from them, which he later abandoned. According to Imam al-Dhahabī, he studied with approximately 600 teachers, most of whom narrated from Abū Hurayrah, Jābir, Ibn ʿAbbās and their contemporaries. He also had many students. Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī mentioned that there were more than 20,000, though al-Dhahabī notes this is exaggerated and unrealistic. al-Thawrī formally studied the Qur'an under Ḥamzah al-Zayyāt and recited it to him in full four times. 
It is said the Umayyad authorities offered him high office positions; however, he consistently declined. It is narrated he refused to give to the caliphs moral and religious advice, and when asked why, he responded: "When the sea overflows, who can dam it up?" He was also quoted to have said to a companion of his, "Beware of drawing close and associating with the rulers; do not be deceived by being told that you can drive inequity away. All of this is the deceit of the Devil, which the wicked reciters have taken as a ladder [to self promotion]."
Al-Thawri's jurisprudential thought (usul al-fiqh), after his move to Basra, became more closely aligned to that of the Umayyads and of al-Awza'i. He is reported to have regarded the jihad as an obligation only as a defensive war.
Ath-Thawri was one of the 'Eight Ascetics,' who included (usual list) Amir ibn Abd al-Qays, Abu Muslim al-Khawlani, Uways al-Qarani, al-Rabi ibn Khuthaym, al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Masruq ibn al-Ajda', and Hasan al-Basri.
Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya relates in Madarij al-salikin, and Ibn al-Jawzi in the chapter entitled "Abu Hashim al-Zahid" in his Sifat al-safwa after the early hadith master Abu Nu`aym in his Hilyat al-awliya, that Sufyan al-Thawri said:
If it were not for Abu Hashim al-Sufi (d. 115) I would have never perceived the presence of the subtlest forms of hypocrisy in the self... Among the best of people is the Sufi learned in jurisprudence.
Ibn al-Jawzi also narrates the following:
Abu Hashim al-Zahid said: "Allah has stamped alienation upon the world in order that the friendly company of the murideen (seekers) consist solely in being with Him and not with the world, and in order that those who obey Him come to Him by means of avoiding the world. The People of Knowledge of Allah (ahl al-ma`rifa billah) are strangers in the world and long for the hereafter."
He spent the last year of his life hiding after a dispute between him and the caliph al-Mahdi. On his death the Thawri madhhab was taken up by his students, including Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan. There are sporadic references to his school in the two centuries after his death; however, it never reached the institutional strength as the four major Sunni schools. His school did not survive, but his juridical thought and especially hadith transmission are highly regarded in Islam, and have influenced all the major schools.
Stories of Sufyan ath-Thawri were also collected in Fariduddin Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya, a collection of Sufi hagiographies compiled in the twelfth/thirteenth century.

Works
Of his books, perhaps best known is his Tafsir of the Qur'an, one of the earliest in the genre. An Indian MSS preserves it up to Q. 52:13, as published by Imtiyâz ʿAlî ʿArshî in 1965; also Tabari's tafsir quotes extensively from the whole text. He also preserved the books of his Umayyad predecessors.
He is also known for writing al-Jāmiʿ al-Kabīr, a compilation of the legal opinions of the Companions, the Tābiʿūn, and the Tābiʿal-Tābiʿīn jurists and it likely included al-Thawrī’s own ijtihād and preference. It is widely compared to the Muwaṭṭaʾ of Malik ibn Anas and is considered one of the earliest examples of the sunan and muṣannaf compilations.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Sufyan bin Hatib bin Umayya (c. 597–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Sufyan ibn Hatib was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Abd al-Barr's al-Isti'ab and Ibn al-Athir's Usd al-Ghaba give his lineage as Sufyan ibn Hatib ibn Umayya ibn Rafi' ibn Suwayd ibn Haram ibn al-Haytham ibn Zafar, placing him in the clan of Banu Zafar. Both record that he fought with the Prophet at the Battle of Uhud and that he was later killed as a martyr at Bi'r Ma'una. Ibn al-Athir notes that Ibn Shahin mentioned him. Nothing further about his life is recorded in these sources.

bio_sources.title: Ibn al-Athir, Usd al-Ghaba; Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Isti'ab — Sufyan ibn Hatib (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

bio: The companion Sufyan bin Muammar, nicknamed Abu Jaber. It was said: Abu Junada is the brother of Jamil bin Muammar who migrated two migrations.
bio_full:
Sufyan ibn Ma'mar ibn Habib ibn Wahb ibn Hudhafa al-Jumahi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Jumah of Quraysh, and the brother of Jamil ibn Ma'mar. Ibn al-Athir gives his kunya as Abu Jabir, while Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Nu'aym give it as Abu Junada. Ibn Sa'd records that he accepted Islam early in Mecca and emigrated to Abyssinia in the second migration. According to Ibn Ishaq, he went with his sons Jabir and Junada and his wife Hasana, their mother, together with her son Shurahbil ibn Hasana by another husband; one report says his son al-Harith was also brought back from Abyssinia.

One account, transmitted from Ibn Ishaq, says that Sufyan was originally of the Ansar, from Banu Zurayq of the Khazraj, and that he came to Mecca, where Ma'mar ibn Habib adopted him and married him to Hasana. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar instead says that his mother was an umm walad (a slave mother) and that Hasana was a freedwoman of Ma'mar; he adds that Sufyan and Jamil left no descendants. Ibn Manda reports, citing Ibn Ishaq, that he is said to have been present at Badr. Ibn Abi Hatim notes that no hadith is transmitted from him. According to Ibn Ishaq, Sufyan and his sons Jabir and Junada died during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Sufyan ibn Ma'mar (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, Ibn Manda, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym)

bio: Sufyan bin Nasr bin 'Amr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Sufyan ibn Nasr ibn Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ka'b ibn Zayd was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj, of the clan of Banu Jusham ibn al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj. This form of his name is given by Ibn Hisham, al-Waqidi and Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Umara al-Qaddah. Ibn Abd al-Barr heads his entry Sufyan ibn Bishr ibn Zayd ibn al-Harith, and Yunus ibn Bukayr, transmitting from Ibn Ishaq, gives Sufyan ibn Bashir; the genealogist Muhammad ibn Habib held that the forms Bishr and Bashir are mistakes and that the correct name is Nasr. According to Ibn Ishaq and Abu Ma'shar, as recorded by Ibn Abd al-Barr, he fought alongside the Prophet at Badr and Uhud. The sources consulted give no date or place of his death.

full: Sufyan ibn Uyayna ibn Maysara al-Hilali al-Makki
primaryTitle: Greatest Meccan Hadith Scholar of His Age
titles: Imam al-Mecca · Hafiz · Alim al-Hijaz
bio: Abu Muhammad Sufyan bin Uyaynah bin Abi Imran Maymun Al-Hilali, he is a hadith narrator from the followers of the followers. He was born and raised in Kufa, lived in Mecca, and died there. He sought hadith while he was a boy, and he heard in the year 119 AH and after: Alqamah bin Marthad, Ya’la bin Ata’, Waqdan Abu Ya’four Al-Abdi, Shabib bin Gharqada Al-Barqi, Yahya bin Dinar, Abu Ishaq Al-Subaie, Asim bin Abi Al-Nujoud and others. He has many sheikhs, most of whom are followers, so there is only one person between him and the Companion, and only two people between him and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. My followers and companions.
bio_full:
Sufyan ibn Uyayna (725-814 CE) was a prominent Islamic scholar and hadith narrator who played a crucial role in the early transmission and preservation of prophetic traditions. Born Abu Muhammad Sufyan bin Uyaynah bin Abi Imran Maymun Al-Hilali in Kufa, he later relocated to Mecca, where he spent most of his scholarly career and remained until his death.

As a member of the Tabi' al-Tabi'in (the generation following the Successors), Sufyan ibn Uyayna occupied an important position in the chain of Islamic scholarship that connected later generations to the earliest Muslim community. He began his pursuit of hadith knowledge at a remarkably young age, demonstrating the dedication that would characterize his entire scholarly life.

Starting his formal studies around 119 AH (737 CE), Sufyan ibn Uyayna learned from numerous distinguished teachers, including Alqamah bin Marthad, Ya'la bin Ata', Waqdan Abu Ya'four Al-Abdi, Shabib bin Gharqada Al-Barqi, Yahya bin Dinar, Abu Ishaq Al-Subaie, and Asim bin Abi Al-Nujoud. The breadth of his education is reflected in his extensive network of scholarly mentors, most of whom belonged to the Tabi'in generation, placing him remarkably close to the original sources of Islamic teachings.

His significance in Islamic scholarship lies primarily in his role as a key transmitter of hadith during a critical period in Islamic history when oral traditions were being systematically collected and preserved. The proximity of his scholarly lineage to the Prophet Muhammad—with typically only one intermediary between him and the Companions, and only two between him and the Prophet himself—made his transmissions particularly valuable to later hadith scholars.

Sufyan ibn Uyayna's long residence in Mecca, Islam's holiest city, positioned him at the center of the Islamic scholarly world, where he could interact with pilgrims and scholars from across the Muslim world. This location enhanced his influence and allowed him to contribute to the broader dissemination of Islamic knowledge throughout the expanding Muslim territories.

His nearly nine-decade lifespan, spanning from the Umayyad period into the Abbasid era, made him a living bridge between different generations of Islamic scholarship. Through his meticulous preservation and transmission of hadith, Sufyan ibn Uyayna helped ensure the continuity of prophetic teachings for subsequent generations of Muslims, cementing his place as a foundational figure in the development of Islamic hadith sciences.

primaryTitle: Sahib al-Bayda' — The Byzantine Companion Who Bought His Freedom
titles: Suhaib al-Rumi · He Who Ransomed Himself with His Wealth
bio: Suhaib ibn Sinan al-Rumi al-Nahdi (c. 587–659) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Sahib al-Bayda' — The Byzantine Companion Who Bought His Freedom.
bio_full:
Suhayb ibn Sinan, known as al-Rumi ("the Byzantine"), was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad whose kunya was Abu Yahya. Ibn Abd al-Barr states that all accounts agree he belonged to the Arab tribe of al-Namir ibn Qasit. Al-Dhahabi, citing Ibn Sa'd, names his mother as Salma bint Qu'ayd. His father Sinan, or in some accounts his uncle, governed al-Ubulla for the Persian king. As a young boy he was captured in a Byzantine raid in the region of Mosul and grew up among the Byzantines, which is why he was called al-Rumi. He later came to Mecca and became attached to Abd Allah ibn Jud'an: one account says Ibn Jud'an bought and freed him, another that Suhayb fled the Byzantines and became his ally.

According to a report from Ammar ibn Yasir, he and Suhayb met at the door of the house of al-Arqam, accepted Islam there and left in secret. Like Bilal and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, he was persecuted by the Quraysh. When he set out to emigrate to Medina, the Quraysh demanded his wealth, and he gave it up in return for being let go; the Prophet told him, "The sale has profited, Abu Yahya."

He fought at Badr, and Ibn Manzur adds Uhud, the Trench and the other battles. When Umar ibn al-Khattab was stabbed, he ordered Suhayb to lead the people in prayer until a successor was agreed, and Suhayb led the funeral prayer over Umar. He died in Medina in 38 or 39 AH (c. 659 CE) and was buried in al-Baqi': Ibn Manzur and al-Dhahabi give 38 AH, and Ibn Abd al-Barr also records 39 AH. Reports of his age at death vary; Ibn Manzur gives 70 and Ibn Abd al-Barr 73.

bio: Suhayb bin Sinan ar-Rumi (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Rome. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Ṣuhayb ibn Sinān al-Rumi (English: Suhayb the Roman; Arabic: صُهَيْب ٱبْنِ سِنَان ٱلرُّومِيّ, Ṣuheyb er-Rûmî, born c. 592), also spelled Sohaib, was an originally Arab former citizen in the Byzantine Empire who grew up speaking Greek, and went on to become an early companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and member of the early Muslim community.

Early life
Around the year 591, about twenty years before the commencement of Muhammad's mission, a man named Sinan ibn Malik governed the city of al-Uballah on behalf of the Persian emperor (perhaps Khosrow II). The city, which is now part of Basra, lay on the banks of the Euphrates near Mosul. He had several children and was particularly fond of one of them who was then barely five years old with red hair and named Suhayb (meaning red-head, ginger). His family was from a village called ath-Thani. ath-Thani was attacked by Byzantine soldiers who took a large number of prisoners, including Suhayb.
Ṣuhayb was taken to one of the slave markets of the Byzantine Empire. He passed from one master to another, remaining for about twenty years in Byzantine lands as a slave. He grew up speaking Greek, the language of the Byzantine Empire and practically forgot Arabic. At the first opportunity, Suhayb escaped and headed for Mecca, which was considered a place of asylum. There, people called him ar-Rumi, meaning "the Roman", because of his background, including his Roman accent and his red pinkish skin. He became the representative of an aristocrat in Mecca, Abdullah ibn Judan at-Taymi, engaging in trade and becoming quite wealthy.

Acceptance of Islam and escape to Medina
One day he was told that Muhammad was calling people to a new religion in the house of Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam. After meeting with him, he was convinced of the truth of his message and pledged fealty to Muhammad. The ruling tribe of Quraish soon learned of Suhayb's acceptance of Islam and began torturing and harassing him as also happened with Bilal ibn Rabah and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt. When Muhammad gave permission for his followers to migrate to Medina in 622 to avoid faith-based persecution, Suhayb resolved to accompany Muhammad and Abu Bakr, but the Quraish discovered his intentions and placed guards over him to prevent him from leaving Mecca and taking the wealth he had acquired through trade. After the departure of Muhammad and Abu Bakr, Suhayb continued to bide his time, attempting to escape several times.
One night, Suhayb feigned stomach problems and went out repeatedly as if responding to calls of nature. His captors became relaxed and Suhayb quietly armed himself, readied a mount and headed for Medina. When his captors realized Suhayb was gone, they pursued and eventually caught up with him. Seeing them approach, Suhayb clambered up a hill and holding his bow and arrow, he shouted:
"Men of Quraish! You know, by God, that I am one of the best archers and my aim is unerring. By God, if you come near me, with each arrow I have, I shall kill one of you. Then I shall strike with my sword."
The men responded, "By God, we shall not let you escape from us with your life and money. You came to Mecca weak and poor and you have acquired what you have acquired."
"What would you say if I leave you my wealth?" interrupted Suhayb. "Would you get out of my way?" "Yes," they answered.
Suhayb described the place in his house in Mecca where he had left the money, and they allowed him to go. When Suhayb reached Quba, just outside Medina, Muhammad saw him approaching and said, "Your transaction has been fruitful, O Abu Yahya. Your transaction has been fruitful." He repeated this three times. In this he was referring to the holy verses that had just been revealed, celebrating Suhayb's heroic act and bargain with the Quraysh. Allah says: "And of mankind is he who would sell himself, seeking the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is full of kindness to (His) slaves," (al-Baqarah, 2:207). Suhayb's face beamed with happiness as he said, "By God, no one has come before me to you, Messenger of God, and only Jibril could have told you about this." He took part in many campaigns under the leadership of Muhammad, including the Battle of Badr, Battle of Uhud, and Battle of Hunayn.

Following the death of Umar
Suhayb was chosen by the second caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab to lead the Muslims in prayers for some time.
As Umar lay dying after being stabbed by Abu-Lu'lu'ah in November, 644, he summoned Uthman ibn Affan, Ali, Talhah, Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abdur Rahman bin Awf, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and instructed them to consult among themselves and with the Muslims for three days and choose a successor. 
After Umar's death, Suhayb al-Rumi led his funeral prayer, and until Uthman's appointment as the third caliph, Suhayb was responsible for leading prayers. He died in Medina in March 659 and was buried in Jannat al-Baqi' Cemetery.

bio: Suhayl bin Rafi' (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Suhayl ibn Rafi' ibn Abi Amr was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu al-Najjar of the Khazraj, of the line of A'idh ibn Tha'laba ibn Ghanm ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar. His brother was Sahl ibn Rafi', and one account names their mother as Zughayba bint Sahl. The two brothers were orphans. Musa ibn Uqba reports that they owned the mirbad (a yard for drying dates) on which the Prophet built his mosque in Medina; when the Prophet's camel stopped there on his arrival, he bought the land from them. Accounts differ over who was their guardian: one names As'ad ibn Zurara, another Mu'adh ibn Afra'. Suhayl fought at Badr, Uhud, the Trench and the other battles with the Prophet. According to Ibn Abd al-Barr, he died during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab. Some sources confuse him with Suhayl ibn Amr, an identification Ibn Abd al-Barr rejects as a mistake.

bio: Suhayma bint Aslam (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Suhayma bint Aslam was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Suhayma bint Aslam was part of the community that played a crucial role in establishing the early Islamic state. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were the Medinan tribes who converted to Islam and provided essential support to the Muslim community during its formative years. Their acceptance of Islam and their hospitality toward the Meccan emigrants were fundamental to the survival and growth of the early Muslim community.

Suhayma bint Aslam lived during a pivotal period in Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim community in Medina and the development of Islamic practices and governance. Her lifetime coincided with major events including the Hijra (migration to Medina), the early military campaigns, and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Female companions like Suhayma bint Aslam hold special significance in Islamic history as they represent the women who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and contributed to the early Muslim community. The sahabiyya are revered for their role in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, supporting the community during times of hardship, and participating in the social and religious life of early Islam.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing means she lived through the entire Medinan period of the Prophet's mission and witnessed the beginning of Islamic expansion under the first Caliph, Abu Bakr.

While specific details about Suhayma bint Aslam's individual contributions may not be extensively documented in historical sources, her status as a sahabiyya marks her as an important figure in the foundational period of Islam, representing the women who helped establish and nurture the early Muslim community in Medina.

bio: Suhayma bint Mas'ud bin Aws (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Scholar of Quranic Exegesis.
bio_full:
Suhayma bint Mas'ud bin Aws was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the first generation of Muslims and died around 635 CE, placing her life span during the foundational decades of Islamic civilization.

As a companion of the Prophet, Suhayma was among those who had direct contact with Muhammad and witnessed the revelation and early development of Islamic teachings. Her presence in Medina, the city where the early Muslim community established itself after the migration from Mecca, positioned her at the center of Islamic intellectual and religious life during this crucial period.

Suhayma is recognized for her contributions to Quranic exegesis, the scholarly interpretation and explanation of the Quran's meaning and teachings. This field of Islamic scholarship, known as tafsir, was essential for understanding and transmitting the religious text's complex theological, legal, and spiritual dimensions to the growing Muslim community. Her involvement in this intellectual tradition demonstrates that women played active roles in the early development of Islamic scholarship and religious learning.

Her work in Quranic interpretation would have been particularly valuable during the formative period of Islam when the community needed guidance on understanding and applying the revealed text. The fact that she is remembered specifically for her scholarly contributions suggests she possessed significant knowledge and expertise that was recognized by her contemporaries.

Living through the prophetic period and into the early caliphate, Suhayma witnessed the expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula and the establishment of Islamic governance and law. Her scholarly work contributed to the foundation of Islamic jurisprudence and interpretation that would influence Muslim thought for generations to come.

The preservation of her name and reputation as a scholar of Quranic exegesis reflects the important role that learned women played in early Islamic society, particularly in the transmission and interpretation of religious knowledge. Her legacy represents the participation of female companions in the intellectual life of the early Muslim community and their contributions to Islamic scholarship during its foundational period.

bio: Suhyal bin Bayda' (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Suhyal bin Bayda' was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early Muslims who embraced Islam during its initial spread in Mecca.

As a Sahaba, the Arabic term for companions of Prophet Muhammad, Suhyal bin Bayda' held a significant position within the early Muslim community. The companions were those individuals who met the Prophet during his lifetime, believed in his message, and maintained their faith until their death. This designation placed him among the most revered figures in Islamic history, as the companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Suhyal bin Bayda' is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan tribes and is considered a pivotal moment in early Islamic history. The participants in this battle hold special significance in Islamic tradition, as they are viewed as having played a crucial role in the survival and establishment of the early Muslim state.

His association with the early ascetic tradition suggests that he was among those companions who emphasized spiritual devotion and simple living. The early ascetics in Islam were known for their focus on worship, contemplation, and detachment from worldly pleasures, contributing to the development of Islamic spirituality and mystical practices that would later influence Sufi traditions.

Suhyal bin Bayda' died in 634 CE, shortly after the death of Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE. His life spanned the entire Meccan period of Islam and the beginning of the Medinan period, making him a witness to the religion's foundational developments. Like other companions, his life and conduct served as a model for later generations of Muslims, and his status as both a Companion of Badr and an early ascetic made him a significant figure in the transmission of Islamic values and practices during the religion's crucial formative years.

bio: Sukhta bint Aswad bin 'Ubbad (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Sukhta bint Aswad bin 'Ubbad was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early Islamic period in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Sukhta bint Aswad would have been part of the local population that welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca. The Ansar played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community in Medina, providing both material support and protection to the nascent Islamic movement during its formative years.

The designation "bint Aswad bin 'Ubbad" indicates her lineage, identifying her as the daughter of Aswad, who was himself the son of 'Ubbad. This naming convention was typical of Arabian society during this period and helps establish her tribal and family connections within the community structure of Medina.

Female companions like Sukhta bint Aswad occupy an important place in early Islamic history as witnesses to the foundational period of Islam. The Sahabiyya were women who lived during the time of Prophet Muhammad and had direct or indirect contact with the early Muslim community. Their presence and participation in the community life of early Medina contributed to the development of Islamic society and the preservation of Islamic traditions.

Living through the critical decades of early Islam until her death around 635 CE, Sukhta bint Aswad would have witnessed the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, the various military campaigns, and the expansion of Islamic influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime spanned the Prophet's ministry in Medina and extended into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate.

While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in historical sources, her recognition as a companion places her among those early Muslims whose lives intersected with the foundational period of Islamic civilization in Medina.

bio: Sukhta bint Qays bin Abi Ka'b (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Sukhta bint Qays bin Abi Ka'b was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Sukhta bint Qays lived during the formative period of the early Islamic community. Her presence in Medina during the Prophet's time meant she witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim state and the development of Islamic law and practice. The Ansar played a crucial role in providing refuge and support to the Muslim community during its most vulnerable early years.

Like other female companions of her era, Sukhta bint Qays would have been part of the close-knit community of early Muslims who directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and participated in the daily life of the nascent Islamic society. The female companions, known collectively as the Sahabiyyat, contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings and traditions.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This timing suggests she lived through the critical transition period when the Muslim community faced the challenge of continuing without their founding leader.

The designation as an Ansari companion places Sukhta bint Qays among a historically significant group whose loyalty and support were essential to Islam's survival and growth. The Ansar's willingness to embrace the new faith and provide material and social support to the emigrating Muslims from Mecca was pivotal to the religion's establishment.

While specific details about her individual contributions or particular incidents involving her are not extensively documented in the available historical sources, her recognition as a companion indicates she was among the women who played important roles in the early Muslim community. The female companions collectively contributed to various aspects of early Islamic society, including the transmission of religious knowledge, participation in community affairs, and support during times of conflict and social change.

Her life span covers the most crucial decades in Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic period through the Prophet's mission and into the early expansion of the Muslim state under the first caliphs.

dob_s: c. 611 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: c. 671 CE (Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd vol 8 entry located (OCR 2026-06); no death recorded in sources — generation estimate)
bio: Sulafa bint al-Bara' bin Ma'rur (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Sulafa bint al-Bara' bin Ma'rur was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early years of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the community of Medinan Muslims who welcomed and supported the Prophet and the early Muslim emigrants from Mecca.

As the daughter of al-Bara' bin Ma'rur, Sulafa came from a prominent family among the Khazraj tribe, one of the two main Arab tribes of Medina. Her father was notably one of the early supporters of Islam in Medina and played a role in the community's acceptance of the new faith before the Prophet's arrival in the city.

Sulafa lived during the formative period of the Islamic community in Medina, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim state and the development of Islamic social and religious practices. As an Ansari woman, she would have been part of the community that provided crucial support to the growing Muslim population, including the Muhajirun (emigrants) who had left Mecca to join the Prophet in Medina.

The female companions of the Prophet, known collectively as the sahabiyyat, played important roles in the early Muslim community, though detailed records of their individual contributions are often limited in historical sources. These women participated in the religious, social, and sometimes political life of early Islamic society, contributing to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings and practices.

Sulafa's significance lies in her status as one of the documented female companions who lived through the Prophet's time in Medina and witnessed the crucial developments of the early Islamic period. Her presence in the historical record represents the broader participation of women in the foundational Muslim community, even when specific details of individual contributions may not be extensively preserved in surviving sources.

She died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, having lived through both the Prophetic period and the beginning of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her life spanned the transformation of Medina from a tribal settlement to the center of a rapidly growing religious and political movement that would reshape the region and beyond.

bio: Sulaym bin al-Harith bin Tha'laba (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Sulaym ibn al-Harith ibn Tha'laba ibn Ka'b ibn Abd al-Ashhal ibn Haritha ibn Dinar was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj, of the clan of Banu Dinar ibn al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as al-Sumayra' bint Qays ibn Malik, and through her he was a half-brother of al-Nu'man, al-Dahhak and Qutba, the sons of Abd Amr ibn Mas'ud. Other reports, recorded by Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn Abi Hatim, make him a brother of al-Dahhak ibn al-Harith. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir also mention a report that he had been a slave of Banu Dinar. He fought at Badr. According to Ibn Sa'd, he also fought at Uhud and was killed there as a martyr in Shawwal, thirty-two months after the Hijra (3 AH, 625 CE). Ibn Sa'd records that he left descendants: his sons al-Hakam and Umayra, whose mother was Suhayma bint Hilal of Banu Sulaym ibn Mansur. Ibn al-Athir, following Ibn Abd al-Barr, treats him as a different man from a Sulaym al-Ansari of Banu Salama who appears in other collections.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Sulaym ibn al-Harith (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Ibn Abi Hatim)

bio: Sulaym bin Milhan (c. 594–626 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Sulaym ibn Milhan was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj. Ibn al-Athir gives his father Milhan's proper name as Malik ibn Khalid, and Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Mulayka bint Malik. He was the brother of Haram ibn Milhan and of Umm Sulaym bint Milhan, the mother of Anas ibn Malik and wife of Abu Talha, and, according to Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir, of Umm Haram, the wife of Ubada ibn al-Samit. He was therefore a maternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik. Sulaym and his brother Haram fought at Badr and Uhud, and both were killed as martyrs at Bi'r Ma'una, which Ibn Sa'd dates to Safar, thirty-six months after the Hijra (4 AH). Ibn Sa'd and Ibn al-Athir state that he left no descendants, and Ibn Abd al-Barr reports from Musa ibn Uqba that neither brother left any.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Sulaym ibn Milhan (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Ibn Abi Hatim)

bio: Sulaym bin Qays bin Qahd (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Sulaym bin Qays bin Qahd was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who witnessed and participated in the establishment of the Islamic community in Medina.

Sulaym is historically recognized as one of the Companions of Badr, meaning he participated in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. The battle took place near the town of Badr, located between Mecca and Medina, and is considered a turning point that helped secure the survival and growth of the early Muslim state.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Sulaym would have been part of the close-knit community of believers who directly interacted with the Prophet during his lifetime. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, participating in the community's defense, and later helping to spread Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Like many companions, Sulaym was based in Medina, which served as the center of the early Islamic state after the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina became the hub from which Islamic governance, law, and community life developed under the Prophet's guidance.

The companions who fought at Badr are held in particular esteem within Islamic tradition because of their early commitment to Islam during a period of significant hardship and uncertainty. Their participation in this pivotal battle demonstrated their dedication to the nascent Muslim community when its survival was far from guaranteed.

Sulaym bin Qays bin Qahd died in 634 CE, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This places his death during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under the first caliph, Abu Bakr. His relatively early death meant he was part of the generation that experienced both the Prophet's lifetime and the immediate challenges facing the Muslim community in establishing itself as a major force in Arabian politics and society.

His legacy, like that of other Badr companions, represents the foundation generation of Muslims whose commitment and sacrifices helped ensure the survival and eventual expansion of Islam.

primaryTitle: Malik al-Anbiya — The King of the Prophets
titles: Sulayman · Solomon · builder of Bayt al-Maqdis · master of jinn and wind
dating_source: 1 Kings; Egyptian Shoshenq I campaign (~925 BCE) as fixed point
dating_note: Sulayman/Solomon.
bio: Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd (c. 1000–c. 931 BCE) was a prophet, based in Jerusalem. Known as Malik al-Anbiya — The King of the Prophets.
bio_full:
In the Islamic account, Sulayman (Solomon) was a prophet and king of the Children of Israel, the son of the prophet Dawud (David). When Dawud died, Sulayman inherited his position as prophet-king. The Qur'an (21:78-79) mentions him judging together with his father in a dispute over a field, and this judgment is cited for his wisdom; later commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir told it as the story of sheep that strayed into a vineyard. God subjected the wind to him, made a spring of molten copper flow for him, and placed jinn under his command, who built for him (34:12-13). He was taught the speech of birds (27:16), and in the valley of the ants he understood an ant warning its colony to take shelter lest Sulayman and his armies crush them unknowingly, and he thanked God (27:18-19).

When the hoopoe returned from Sheba with news of a powerful queen whose people worshipped the sun (27:22-23), Sulayman sent her a letter calling her to submit to God (27:28-31). Her throne was brought to him before she arrived (27:38-40), and the queen, whom tradition names Bilqis, submitted to God (27:44). He prayed for a kingdom such as no one after him would have, and God granted it (38:35-40). The Qur'an states that Sulayman never disbelieved and that it was the devils who disbelieved and taught people magic (2:102). He died leaning on his staff, and the jinn working for him did not realise he was dead until a creature ate through the staff, showing that the jinn do not know the unseen (34:14). The Qur'an also praises him in other passages, including 6:84, 21:81-82 and 38:30-31.

bio_sources.title: English Wikipedia — Solomon in Islam

primaryTitle: One of the Seven Jurists of Medina
titles: One of the Seven Jurists of Medina · Freed Slave of Maymuna
bio: Sulayman ibn Yasar al-Hilali al-Madani (c. 634–718) was a historical figure of the Islamic Jurisprudence tradition, based in Medina. Known as One of the Seven Jurists of Medina.
bio_full:
Sulayman ibn Yasar al-Hilali al-Madani was a prominent Islamic jurist who lived in Medina during the late seventh and early eighth centuries. Born around 634 CE and passing away in 718 CE, he belonged to the generation known as the Tabi'un—those who followed the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad but did not meet the Prophet themselves.

As one of the Seven Jurists of Medina, Sulayman ibn Yasar held a distinguished position among the leading legal scholars of his time. This group of seven jurists were recognized as the foremost authorities on Islamic law in Medina during the Umayyad period, when the city remained a crucial center of Islamic learning and legal interpretation. The Seven Jurists were collectively known for their expertise in religious rulings and their role in developing early Islamic jurisprudence.

Sulayman ibn Yasar's legal scholarship was highly regarded by his contemporaries and subsequent generations of Islamic scholars. He was known for his careful approach to legal interpretation and his deep knowledge of the traditions and practices established during the time of the Prophet and the early Muslim community. His opinions and legal rulings were frequently cited by later jurists and contributed to the development of Islamic legal thought.

Living in Medina provided Sulayman ibn Yasar with direct access to the oral traditions and institutional memory of the early Muslim community. Medina, as the city where the Prophet Muhammad had established the first Islamic state, remained a vital center for preserving and interpreting Islamic teachings. The scholars there, including Sulayman ibn Yasar, played crucial roles in transmitting religious knowledge and establishing legal precedents that would influence Islamic jurisprudence for centuries to come.

His contributions to Islamic legal scholarship represent an important link in the chain of transmission from the earliest Muslim community to later systematized schools of Islamic law. Through his teaching and legal opinions, Sulayman ibn Yasar helped preserve and interpret the religious and legal foundations of Islam during a formative period when the Muslim community was expanding rapidly and encountering new legal challenges that required scholarly guidance and interpretation.

full: Suleiman ibn Selim ibn Bayezid al-Uthman
primaryTitle: Kanuni — The Lawgiver; Shadow of God on Earth
titles: Kanuni · Sultan al-Azam · Shah al-Islam
_data_notes: wikidata_qid Q8474 removed on 20260422_193715 (was shared with a different person)
bio: The Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, the glorious and innovative khaqan, the greatest conqueror of the world, the swordsman of the world and the religion, the father of victory and jihad, Suleiman Khan bin Sulaym bin Bayezid al-Uthmani, known for short as Suleiman I, and by his more famous title Suleiman the Magnificent or Suleiman the Great, is the tenth sultan of the House of Othman and the eighth to be held the title of sultan among them after his father Selim I and his grandfathers. From Bayezid II to Murad I, he was the fourth Muslim ruler in general and the Ottoman sultans in particular after his father Selim and his grandfathers Bayezid and the Conqueror, and the second caliph of the Muslims from the line of Othman, and the seventy-fifth in the order of caliphs in general. Some ancient historians counted him as the eleventh sultan of the House of Othman, considering Suleiman Çelebi bin Bayezid, who disputed with his brother Muhammad I for kingship, as a sultan. Then this idea was rejected on the grounds that Suleiman Çelebi did not rule legally and the kingship of all the countries of the state was not granted to him at that time. There was consensus on calling this sultan the first and considering him the tenth king of this state.
bio_full:
Suleiman I (6 November 1494 – 6 September 1566), commonly known as Suleiman the Magnificent,  was the Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566. The longest reign among the Ottoman sultans, his rule brought about a notable peak in the Ottoman Empire's economic, military and political power, and raised the number of the empire's subjects to at least 25 million people. 
After succeeding his father Selim I on 30 September 1520, Suleiman began his reign by launching military campaigns against the Christian powers of Central and Eastern Europe and the Mediterranean; Belgrade fell to him in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, and at Mohács in 1526, Suleiman broke the strength of the Kingdom of Hungary. Hungary was subsequently divided, with much of it incorporated directly into the empire. However, his defeat at the siege of Vienna in 1529 prevented him from advancing further into Europe. Suleiman also fought for years against the Shia Islamic Safavid Empire of Iran and annexed Iraq. In North Africa, Ottoman Tripolitania was established and the Ottoman fleet dominated the seas from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and into the Persian Gulf.
Suleiman personally instituted major judicial changes pertaining to society, education, taxation, and criminal law. His reforms, carried out in conjunction with the Ottoman chief judicial official Ebussuud Efendi, brought together the two forms of Ottoman law: sultanic (Kanun) and Islamic (Sharia). He was also a distinguished poet and goldsmith; and a great patron of fine culture, overseeing the "Golden Age" of the Ottoman Empire which was at the height of its artistic, literary, and architectural development.
In 1534, Suleiman broke with Ottoman tradition by marrying Hürrem, an influential woman from his Imperial Harem who helped usher in the "Sultanate of Women" period in Ottoman history. Upon Suleiman's death in 1566, he was succeeded by his and Hürrem's son Selim II. The death of Suleiman marks a watershed moment in Ottoman history, although scholars typically regard the period after his death to be one of crisis and adaptation rather than of simple decline. In the following decades, the Ottoman Empire began to experience significant political, institutional, and economic changes, a period often referred to as the Era of Transformation.

Alternative names and titles
Suleiman the Magnificent (محتشم سلیمان Muḥteşem Süleymân), as he was known in the West, was also called Suleiman the First (سلطان سلیمان اول Sulṭān Süleymān-ı Evvel), and Suleiman the Lawgiver (قانونی سلطان سلیمان Ḳânûnî Sulṭân Süleymân) for his reform of the Ottoman legal system.
It is unclear when exactly the term Kanunî (the Lawgiver) first came to be used as an epithet for Suleiman. It is entirely absent from sixteenth and seventeenth-century Ottoman sources and may date from the early 18th century.
There is a tradition of Western origin, according to which Suleiman the Magnificent was "Suleiman II", but that tradition has been based on an erroneous assumption that Süleyman Çelebi was to be recognised as a legitimate sultan.

Early life

Suleiman was born in Trabzon on the southern coast of the Black Sea to Şehzade Selim (later Selim I), probably on 6 November 1494, although this date is not known with absolute certainty or evidence. His mother was Hafsa Sultan, a concubine convert to Islam of unknown origins, who died in 1534. At the age of seven, Suleiman began studies of science, history, literature, theology and military tactics in the schools of the imperial Topkapı Palace in Constantinople. As a young man, he befriended Pargalı Ibrahim, a Greek slave who later became one of his most trusted advisers (but who was later executed on Suleiman's orders). At age seventeen, he was appointed as the governor of first Kaffa (Theodosia), then Manisa, with a brief tenure at Edirne.

Accession
Upon the death of his father, Selim I (r. 1512–1520), Suleiman entered Constantinople and ascended to the throne as the tenth Ottoman sultan. An early description of Suleiman, a few weeks following his accession, was provided by the Venetian envoy Bartolomeo Contarini: 

The sultan is only twenty-five years [actually 26] old, tall and slender but tough, with a thin and bony face. Facial hair is evident, but only barely. The sultan appears friendly and in good humor. Rumor has it that Suleiman is aptly named, enjoys reading, is knowledgeable and shows good judgment."

Military campaigns

Conquests in Europe

Upon succeeding his father, Suleiman began a series of military conquests, eventually leading to a revolt led by the Ottoman-appointed governor of Damascus in 1521. Suleiman soon made preparations for the conquest of Belgrade from the Kingdom of Hungary—something his great-grandfather Mehmed II had failed to achieve because of John Hunyadi's strong defense in the region. Its capture was vital in removing the Hungarians and Croats who, following the defeats of the Albanians, Bosniaks, Bulgarians, Byzantines and the Serbs, remained the only formidable force who could block further Ottoman gains in Europe. Suleiman encircled Belgrade on 28 August 1521, with 250,000 Turkish soldiers and over 100 ships. and began a series of heavy bombardments from an island in the Danube. Belgrade was made the seat of the Pashalik of Belgrade (also known as the Sanjak of Smederevo), and quickly became the second largest Ottoman town in Europe at over 100,000 people, surpassed only by Constantinople.
The road to Hungary and Austria lay open, but Suleiman turned his attention instead to the Eastern Mediterranean island of Rhodes, the home base of the Knights Hospitaller. Suleiman built a large fortification, Marmaris Castle, that served as a base for the Ottoman Navy. Following a five-month siege, Rhodes capitulated and Suleiman allowed the Knights of Rhodes to depart. The conquest of the island cost the Ottomans 50,000 to 60,000 dead from battle and sickness (Christian claims went as high as 64,000 Ottoman battle deaths and 50,000 disease deaths).

As relations between Hungary and the Ottoman Empire deteriorated, Suleiman  resumed his campaign in Central Europe, and on 29 August 1526 he defeated Louis II of Hungary (1506–1526) at the Battle of Mohács. The Hungarian army, encouraged by the nobility to engage prematurely, launched a frontal assault that collapsed under coordinated Ottoman counterattacks. King Louis and much of the Hungarian aristocracy were killed, resulting in the destruction of the royal army and the end of the Jagiellonian dynasty in Hungary and Bohemia. The aftermath saw the partition of Hungary between the Ottoman Empire, the Habsburg monarchy, and the Principality of Transylvania. The battle marked the beginning of sustained Ottoman–Habsburg wars and the decline of Hungary as an independent power. Upon encountering the lifeless body of King Louis, Suleiman is said to have lamented: "I came indeed in arms against him; but it was not my wish that he should be thus cut off before he scarcely tasted the sweets of life and royalty." While Suleiman was campaigning in Hungary, Turkmen tribes in central Anatolia (in Cilicia) revolted under the leadership of Kalender Çelebi.
Some Hungarian nobles proposed that Ferdinand, who was the ruler of neighboring Austria and tied to Louis II's family by marriage, be King of Hungary, citing previous agreements that the Habsburgs would take the Hungarian throne if Louis died without heirs. However, other nobles turned to the nobleman John Zápolya, whom Suleiman supported. Under Charles V and his brother Ferdinand I, the Habsburgs reoccupied Buda and took possession of Hungary. Reacting in 1529, Suleiman marched through the valley of the Danube and regained control of Buda; in the following autumn, his forces laid siege to Vienna. This was to be the Ottoman Empire's most ambitious expedition and the apogee of its drive to the West.

full: Hazrat Sultan Bahu ibn Bazid Muhammad al-Qadiri
primaryTitle: Sultan al-Arifin of Punjab — Poet of the Alef
titles: Sultan al-Arifin of Punjab · Author of 140 Persian books · His Punjabi kafis still sung daily
bio: Sultan Al-Arifin Sakhi Sultan Bahu was born in the village of Shorkot in the Punjab province in the year 1039 AH, and he was nicknamed Haq, as he said in one of his classifications, “He is called from Al-Haqq Al-Haqq,” and that Sultan Bahu has special importance in the hearts of Muslims in the region of Pakistan, India, and Afghanistan. He is a Qadiri of conduct and a Hanafi doctrine, and his collections are in Persian and the local language is Punjabi, and we are reminded of the words of the greats such as Imam Al-Ghazali, Abdullah Ansari, and Saadi. Shirazi and others.
bio_full:
Sultan Bahu (also spelled as Sultan Bahoo; Punjabi: [sʊltaːn baːɦuː]; 17 January 1630 – 1 March 1691), was a Punjabi Muslim poet, Sufi, scholar, and historian of the 17th century. Renowned for his mystical poetry, he was active during the reigns of Mughal emperors Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb.
Little is known about Bahu's life, other than what was written in a hagiography called Manaqib-i Sultani seven generations after Bahu's own time. According to these records, he was born in Shorkot into the Awan tribe. He was son of Bayazid Muhammad, an officer in the Mughal Army, and Rasti. He belonged to Qadiri Sufi order, and started the mystic tradition known as Sarwari Qadiri.
More than forty books on Sufism are attributed to him (mostly written in Persian), largely dealing with specialised aspects of Islam and Islamic mysticism. However, it was his Punjabi poetry which had popular appeal and earned him lasting fame. His verses are sung in many genres of Sufi music, including qawwali and kafi, and tradition has established a unique style of singing his couplets.

Education
Sultan Bahu's first teacher was his mother, Mai Rasti. She pushed him to seek spiritual guidance from Shah Habib Gilani.
Around 1668, Sultan Bahu moved to Delhi for further training under the guidance of Syed Abdul Rehman Jilani Dehlvi, a notable Sufi saint of the Qadiriyya order, and thereafter returned to Punjab where he spent the rest of his life.

Literary works
The exact number of books written by Sultan Bahu is not known, but it is assumed to be at least one hundred. Forty of them are on Sufism and Islamic mysticism. Most of his writings are in the Persian language except Abyat-e-Bahu which is in Punjabi verse.
