titles: Faqih al-Yemen · Zahid · Mufti al-Yamani
bio: Abu Abd al-Rahman Tawus bin Kaysan al-Yamani is a jurist, hadith narrator, and Tabi’i, one of the major Tabi’i jurists. He was one of the elite companions of Ibn Abbas, and he was known for his austerity in living and his boldness in admonishing the caliphs and governors.
bio_full:
Tawus Ibn Kaysan (Arabic: طاووس بن كيسان; died 723) was one of the Tabi‘in, one of the narrators of hadith and scholars of fiqh.
He is also known as Tawoos ibn Kaysaan, "Tawoos" or "al-Taus,".

Biography
He was one of the scholars of the Tabi‘in, one of the narrators of hadith, and a companion of, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, Ali Ibn al-Hussein. Ibn Hajar related that Tawus who inhabited an area called al-Jund and that he was the master of Hamadan in Iran. Ibn Hayyan said about him: He was among the worshipers of the people of the Yemen  and the masters of the leading members of the next generation.” He performed the hajj forty times and narrated some of the whispered prayers of Imām Zayn al-‘Ābidin. Ibn Kaysan was also a student of Abdullah ibn Abbas. It was said that he was a great tabi’i who met over 50 companions. Tawus heard all the ahadeeth from the mouth of ibn Abbas. Tawus himself was the main teacher of Umar ibn Abdul Aziz.
Abdullah ibn Abbas loved Tawus so much that he said that "I believe that Tawus is from the people of Jannah".

bio: Tayrah ibn Ya'rub (-1480–-1580) was a founding figure, based in Arabia. Known as Islamic History Founder of Arabia.

Additionally, I cannot find any historical records or scholarly sources that reference a figure by this name in pre-Islamic Arabian history or early Islamic historical accounts. The description as an "Islamic History Founder" during this time period is historically impossible.

bio: Tha'laba bin 'Amr bin Mihsan (c. 594–637 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Tha'laba ibn Amr ibn Mihsan was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj, of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar, in the branch of Banu Amr ibn Mabdhul. Ibn Abd al-Barr gives his lineage as Tha'laba ibn Amr ibn Ubayd ibn Mihsan ibn Amr ibn Atik ibn Amr ibn Mabdhul, whose proper name was Amir ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar. According to Ibn Abd al-Barr (quoted by Ibn al-Athir), he fought at Badr, Uhud, the Trench and all the other battles with the Prophet. His son Abd al-Rahman narrated from him. Ibn Abd al-Barr mentions a claim that he was Abu Amra, but says it is doubtful.

Accounts of his death differ. Musa ibn Uqba, cited by Ibn al-Athir, and Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Ansari, cited by Ibn Abd al-Barr, say that he was killed at the Battle of the Bridge (al-Jisr) alongside Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Abu Nu'aym dates his death at the Bridge to 15 AH. Al-Waqidi instead says he died in Medina during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Tha'laba ibn Amr (Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban)

bio: Tha'laba bin 'Anma ibn 'Adi (c. 594–627 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Tha'laba bin 'Anma ibn 'Adi was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early period of Islamic history. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslim community in Medina and died in 627 CE at approximately thirty-three years of age.

As one of the Sahaba, the term used for the companions of Prophet Muhammad, Tha'laba belonged to the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet. The Sahaba hold a distinguished position in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Tha'laba is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him recognition as a "Companion of Badr." This battle was the first major military encounter between the early Muslim community and the Meccan tribes, occurring near the wells of Badr in present-day Saudi Arabia. The battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as it marked a turning point for the nascent Muslim community, demonstrating their military capability despite being significantly outnumbered.

The designation "Companion of Badr" carries special reverence in Islamic tradition, as those who fought in this battle are considered to have made crucial sacrifices during a pivotal moment in early Islamic history. The participants in Badr are remembered for their role in securing the survival and growth of the early Muslim community during a period of significant challenges and persecution.

Tha'laba's life was relatively brief, spanning the critical early years of Islam when the religion was establishing itself in the Arabian Peninsula. His death in 627 CE occurred during the continued expansion of the Muslim community from Medina, just three years after the Battle of Badr and five years before the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

While specific details about Tha'laba's individual contributions beyond his participation in Badr are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his inclusion among the Sahaba places him within the foundational community that helped establish and spread Islamic teachings. The companions collectively played an essential role in preserving and transmitting the religious, social, and legal practices that would form the basis of Islamic civilization.

bio: Tha'laba bin Hatib bin 'Amr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Tha'laba bin Hatib bin 'Amr was a companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who resided in Medina, the city that became the center of the nascent Islamic community following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Tha'laba is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, which took place in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as it was the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan opposition. The engagement occurred near the wells of Badr, approximately 80 miles southwest of Medina, and resulted in a decisive victory for the outnumbered Muslim forces. Those who participated in this battle, known as the Badriyyun or "Companions of Badr," hold a special status in Islamic historical tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, Tha'laba was part of the generation that directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and observed the establishment of early Islamic practices and governance. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings, sayings, and practices of Prophet Muhammad to subsequent generations, forming the foundation for Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

The companions of Badr are particularly venerated because their participation in this battle demonstrated their commitment to the early Muslim community during a period of significant vulnerability and uncertainty. The victory at Badr provided crucial momentum for the spread of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula and beyond.

Tha'laba lived during the rapid expansion of Islam under Prophet Muhammad's leadership and likely witnessed the subsequent conquests during the early Rashidun Caliphate period. His death around 634 CE places him in the generation that saw Islam transform from a small religious movement in Mecca to a major political and spiritual force across much of the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about Tha'laba's individual contributions beyond his participation in Badr are limited in historical sources, his status as a companion and Badr veteran establishes his place among the foundational figures of early Islamic history. The companions collectively served as the primary sources for Islamic teachings and traditions that would shape the religion's development for centuries to come.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Tha'laba bin Sa'd bin Malik (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Tha'laba ibn Sa'd ibn Malik ibn Khalid ibn Tha'laba was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Khazraj, of the Banu Sa'ida clan. Abu Nu'aym records, through a family report from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, that Sahl said: "My brother Tha'laba ibn Sa'd was present at Badr", and so describes him as Sahl's brother. Ibn Abd al-Barr instead describes him as the paternal uncle of Sahl ibn Sa'd and of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi. All the sources consulted agree that he was killed as a martyr at the Battle of Uhud; Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn Abi Hatim both state this, and Abu Nu'aym adds that he left no descendants.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Tha'laba ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi (al-Isti'ab, Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Abi Hatim)

bio: Thabit bin 'Amr bin Zayd (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Thabit ibn Amr ibn Zayd was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad counted among the Ansar. The sources disagree on his descent. Ibn Manda gives his lineage as Thabit ibn Amr ibn Zayd ibn Adi ibn Sawad ibn Ashja', and Abu Nu'aym calls him al-Ashja'i, an ally of the Ansar. Ibn Abd al-Barr, whose version Ibn al-Athir calls correct, gives Thabit ibn Amr ibn Adi ibn Sawad ibn Malik ibn Ghanm ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar, placing him in the Banu al-Najjar of the Khazraj. Ibn al-Athir explains that allies often came to be counted in the clan they lived among, so both descriptions may refer to the same man.

He fought at Badr, although Ibn al-Athir notes that Ibn Ishaq did not list him among the men of Badr. He was killed at the Battle of Uhud; Ibn Abd al-Barr states that he died there as a martyr according to all accounts.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Thabit ibn Amr (Usd al-Ghaba, citing Ibn Manda, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Abu Nu'aym)

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Thabit bin al-Dahhak bin Khalifa (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Thabit ibn al-Dahhak ibn Khalifa ibn Tha'laba ibn Adi ibn Ka'b ibn Abd al-Ashhal was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Abd al-Ashhal. Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Hibban give his kunya as Abu Zayd, while Ibn Abd al-Barr gives Abu Yazid. Ibn Hibban names his mother as Asma', of the clan of Haritha ibn al-Harith. Ibn Abd al-Barr states that he was born in 3 AH, and Ibn Manda, citing Muhammad ibn Sa'd, says he was eight years old when the Prophet died.

Abu Qilaba reported that Thabit pledged allegiance to the Prophet under the tree, and Ibn al-Athir specifies that this was the Pledge of al-Ridwan at al-Hudaybiyya. His hadith were transmitted mainly by Abu Qilaba, and Abd Allah ibn Ma'qil narrated from him a report prohibiting sharecropping (muzara'a). Ibn Abi Hatim rejects a claim that he was the father of Zayd ibn Thabit. Abu Nu'aym describes as an error a report that he fought at Badr.

Ibn Hibban and Ibn al-Athir give his death as 45 AH, a date al-Baji attributes to Amr ibn Ali; other reports say he died later, during the conflict of Ibn al-Zubayr, without giving a year.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Thabit ibn al-Dahhak (Ibn Manda, Abu Nu'aym, al-Isti'ab, Ibn Hibban, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Baji, Usd al-Ghaba)

bio: Thabit bin Aqram (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Thabit ibn Aqram ibn Tha'laba ibn Adi ibn al-Ajlan al-Balawi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the tribe of Bali of Quda'a and an ally of the Ansar; Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that some say he was an ally of Banu Amr ibn Awf. Ibn al-Athir calls him a cousin of Murra ibn al-Hubab ibn Adi. According to Ibn Sa'd, he fought at Badr, Uhud, the Trench and all the other campaigns with the Prophet, and Ibn Sa'd states that he left no descendants.

At the Battle of Mu'ta, after Abd Allah ibn Rawaha was killed, Thabit took up the banner and rallied the Muslims, then handed it to Khalid ibn al-Walid, saying, "Take the banner, Abu Sulayman." Khalid at first declined and then accepted it. Abu Hurayra reported that at Mu'ta Thabit told him, "You were not with us at Badr; we were not given victory by numbers."

In the caliphate of Abu Bakr he served under Khalid against the tribes who left Islam. At Buzakha, he and Ukkasha ibn Mihsan rode ahead as scouts and were met by Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi and his brother Salama, and both were killed. Accounts differ over who killed Thabit: Ibn Sa'd names Salama, while Ibn Hibban and Ibn Abd al-Barr name Tulayha. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir date his death to 11 AH, and also record 12 AH.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Thabit ibn Aqram (Ibn Sa'd, Mukhtasar Tarikh Dimashq, Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Hibban, al-Isti'ab, Ibn Manda, Usd al-Ghaba, Ibn Abi Hatim)

bio: Thabit bin Hazzal (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Thabit bin Hazzal was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who migrated to or lived in Medina, the city that became the center of the nascent Muslim community after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Thabit bin Hazzal is historically recognized as one of the participants in the Battle of Badr, fought in 624 CE. This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military encounter between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces. The Muslim victory at Badr is considered a pivotal moment that helped establish the political and military foundations of the early Islamic state. Those who participated in this battle, known as the "Badriyyun" or "Companions of Badr," hold a special status in Islamic historical tradition due to their role in this crucial early victory.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Thabit bin Hazzal was part of the generation that directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices and governance. The companions played essential roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and traditions of Islam to subsequent generations, serving as the primary sources for Islamic law, theology, and historical accounts of the Prophet's life and mission.

Living in Medina during Islam's foundational decade, Thabit bin Hazzal would have experienced the rapid transformation of Arabian society as the Muslim community grew from a small group of believers into a significant political and religious force. The period between the migration to Medina in 622 CE and the Prophet's death in 632 CE saw the establishment of the basic institutions of Islamic governance, the compilation of Quranic revelations, and the expansion of Muslim influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Thabit bin Hazzal died in 634 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr, the first Caliph. This period marked the beginning of Islam's expansion beyond Arabia, though the specific circumstances of his death are not detailed in the available historical sources. His legacy remains tied to his participation in the foundational events of early Islamic history, particularly the Battle of Badr, which helped secure the survival and growth of the Muslim community.

bio: Thabit bin Khansa' (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Thabit ibn Khansa' ibn Amr ibn Malik ibn Adi ibn Amir ibn Ghanm ibn Adi ibn al-Najjar was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj. Ibn Abi Hatim, on his father's authority, states that he fought at Badr. Ibn Abd al-Barr, however, notes that his presence at Badr is reported by al-Waqidi alone and not by others. The sources consulted give no further details of his life or his death. He is different from Thabit ibn Khalid ibn al-Nu'man ibn Khansa', a Badr veteran who is reported to have been killed at al-Yamama.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Thabit ibn Khansa' (al-Isti'ab, Ibn Abi Hatim)

bio: Thabit bin Tha'laba bin Zayd (c. 594–629 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Thabit ibn Tha'laba ibn Zayd ibn al-Harith ibn Haram ibn Ka'b was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Khazraj through the clan of Salima (Salama). He is better known as Thabit ibn al-Jidh': al-Jidh' was the nickname of his father Tha'laba ibn Zayd, said by Ibn Sa'd to reflect the firmness and resolve of his heart. Ibn Sa'd names his mother as Umm Unas bint Sa'd, of Banu Udhra of Quda'a.

All the accounts agree that Thabit was among the seventy Ansar who gave the pledge at al-Aqaba. Ibn Ishaq, Musa ibn Uqba and al-Zuhri list him among those who fought at Badr. According to Ibn Sa'd he also took part in Uhud, the Trench, al-Hudaybiyya, Khaybar, the conquest of Mecca and al-Ta'if. He was killed as a martyr at al-Ta'if while with the Prophet, in 8 AH.

Ibn Sa'd lists his children as Abd Allah, al-Harith and Umm Unas, whose mother was Umama bint Uthman ibn Khalda of Banu Zurayq of the Khazraj. He adds that his line continued for a time and then died out.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Thabit bin Waqash (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Thabit bin Waqash was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly knew and followed the Prophet Muhammad.

As one of the Sahaba, the Arabic term for the companions of Prophet Muhammad, Thabit bin Waqash held a significant position in early Islamic society. The Sahaba were those who met the Prophet, believed in his message, and remained Muslim until their death. They are highly revered in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Thabit bin Waqash was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the political and spiritual capital of the emerging Islamic state, making those who resided there particularly important to the development of the Muslim community.

His life came to an end at the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, where he died as a martyr. The Battle of Uhud was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces. This battle took place on March 23, 625 CE, near Mount Uhud, just outside Medina. The conflict arose as the Meccan tribes sought to retaliate against the Muslims following their defeat at the Battle of Badr the previous year.

The battle itself was significant in early Islamic history, representing both challenges and lessons for the young Muslim community. While initially successful, the Muslim forces faced difficulties during the latter part of the battle, resulting in casualties among the companions, including Thabit bin Waqash.

In Islamic tradition, those who die in battle defending their faith and community are considered martyrs, a status that carries special significance. Thabit bin Waqash's death at Uhud thus represents the sacrifice made by early Muslims in establishing and defending their religious community.

His life, though brief, reflects the experiences of many early Muslims who left their mark on Islamic history through their commitment to the faith and their willingness to make ultimate sacrifices for the survival and growth of the Muslim community during its most vulnerable early years.

full: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas al-Ansari al-Khazraji
primaryTitle: Khatib al-Nabi — Orator of the Prophet
titles: Khatib Rasul Allah (Orator of the Prophet) · Martyr of Yamama
bio: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas al-Ansari al-Khazraji (c. 580–633) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Khatib al-Nabi — Orator of the Prophet.
bio_full:
Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās al-Ḥārithī al-Khazrajī (Arabic: ثابت بن قيس بن شماس الحارثي الخزرجي) was a companion of Muhammad, who served as one of his orators and scribes, and a leader of the Ansar, the natives of Medina who gave Muhammad safe haven in their city and were among the earliest converts to Islam.
Following the Muslim victory at Battle of Dhu al-Qassah at the beginning of the Ridda wars in 632, Caliph Abu Bakr appointed Thabit commander of the Ansarite troops. He was placed under the overall command of Khalid ibn al-Walid. He participated in the subsequent battles of Buzakha (632) against the Asad and Ghatafan nomads under Tulayha and Aqraba (633) against the sedentary Hanifa tribe under Musaylima. At Aqraba he recommended to Khalid that the exclusion of nomad contingents in their army as he blamed them for the repeated, failed attempts to overcome the Hanifa warriors. Khalid accepted this counsel and the Muslims afterward routed and killed Musaylima,  and Thabit was killed during fight in the Battle of Yamama.
Alternatively, Chinese Muslims hold that he was involved in the introduction of Islam to China during the Tang dynasty period when he reached China over land and died of in the western Chinese province of Xinjiang.

Divorce
It is said in a narration his wife, Jameelah bint Abdillāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salool asked for divorce and they got divorced after that.
Ibn ‘Abbās said: The wife of Thābit ibn Qays came to Muhammad and said:

“O Messenger of Allah! I find no fault with Thābit ibn Qays in his character or religion, but I would hate to act in disobedience to Islam.” The Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وسلم) said to her: “Will you return to him the garden [that he gave you as a dowry]?” She replied: “Yes.” So Allah's Messenger (صلى الله عليه وسلم) said to Thābit: “Accept the garden and divorce her with one pronouncement.” (Bukhāri, 5273) In another narration, Ibn ‘Abbās said: “He commanded him to divorce her.” (Bukhāri, 5274)
This is the first hadeeth quoted by Al-Hāfidh Ibn Hajr (d. 852H) in his Buloogh Al-Marām, Chapter of Khula’ (باب الخلع).
Amr ibn Shu’ayb reported from his father, from his grandfather that Thābit ibn Qays was unattractive and his wife said: “If it was not for the fear of Allah, when Thābit entered in my presence, I would have spat in his face.” (Ibn Mājah, 2057 and declared weak by Al-Albāni) Also, Ahmad reported in his Musnad (16095) from Sahl ibn Abee Hathmah that: “This was the first Khula’ in Islam.”

Promise of Paradise
It is reported He was promised Paradise.
Sahih al-Bukhari 3613
Narrated Anas bin Malik:
The Prophet (ﷺ) noticed the absence of Thabit bin Qais. A man said, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! I shall bring you his news." So he went to him and saw him sitting in his house drooping his head (sadly). He asked Thabit, "What's the matter?" Thabit replied, "An evil situation: A man used to raise his voice over the voice of the Prophet (ﷺ) and so all his good deeds have been annulled and he is from the people of Hell." The man went back and told the Prophet (ﷺ) that Thabit had said so-and-so. (The sub-narrator, Musa bin Anas said, "The man went to Thabit again with glad tidings)." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "Go and say to Thabit: 'You are not from the people of Fire, but from the people of Paradise."

The title of Khatib of Islam
The title "Khatib-e-Islam" was first used for Thabit bin Qais Ansari  , who used to attend various meetings as a representative of Muhammad. He was also remembered by the titles of Khatib-ul-Ansar and Khatib-e-Rasool-e-Karim.

References

full: Thābit ibn Qurra ibn Marwān al-Ṣābī al-Ḥarrānī
bio: Thabit bin Qurrah bin Marwan, and it was said: Thabit bin Qurrah bin Irfan Al-Harrani, and his nickname: Abu Al-Hassan. His family used to teach the Sabian religion in the past, then they converted to Islam, and from there came the lineage of “Sabian” to his family. He is an Arab scientist, famous for his knowledge of astronomy, mathematics, geometry, and music, and a fixed number are attributed to him. He was born in the Levantine city of Harran, which is on the Balikh River, a tributary of the Euphrates River, and is today in southern Türkiye.
bio_full:
Thābit ibn Qurra (full name: Abū al-Ḥasan Ṯābit ibn Qurra ibn Zahrūn al-Ḥarrānī al-Ṣābiʾ, Arabic: أبو الحسن ثابت بن قرة بن زهرون الحراني الصابئ, Latin: Thebit/Thebith/Tebit; 826 or 836 – February 19, 901), was a scholar known for his work in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and translation. He lived in Baghdad in the second half of the ninth century during the time of the Abbasid Caliphate.
Thābit ibn Qurra made important discoveries in algebra, geometry, and astronomy. In astronomy, Thābit is considered one of the first reformers of the Ptolemaic system, and in mechanics he was a founder of statics. Thābit also wrote extensively on medicine and produced philosophical treatises.

Biography

Thābit was born in Harran in Upper Mesopotamia, which at the time was part of the Diyar Mudar subdivision of the al-Jazira region of the Abbasid Caliphate. Thābit was an Arab who belonged to the Sabians of Harran, a Hellenized Semitic polytheistic astral religion that still existed in ninth-century Harran.
As a youth, Thābit worked as money changer in a marketplace in Harran until meeting Muḥammad ibn Mūsā, the oldest of three mathematicians and astronomers known as the Banū Mūsā. Thābit displayed such exceptional linguistic skills that ibn Mūsā chose him to come to Baghdad to be trained in mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy under the tutelage of the Banū Mūsā. Here, Thābit was introduced to not only a community of scholars but also to those who had significant power and influence in Baghdad.
Thābit and his pupils lived in the midst of the most intellectually vibrant, and probably the largest, city of the time, Baghdad. Thābit came to Baghdad in the first place to work for the Banū Mūsā becoming a part of their circle and helping them translate Greek mathematical texts. What is unknown is how Banū Mūsā and Thābit occupied himself with mathematics, astronomy, astrology, magic, mechanics, medicine, and philosophy. Later in his life, Thābit's patron was the Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tadid (reigned 892–902), whom he became a court astronomer for. Thābit became the Caliph's personal friend and courtier. Thābit died in Baghdad in 901. His son, Sinan ibn Thabit and grandson, Ibrahim ibn Sinan would also make contributions to the medicine and science. By the end of his life, Thābit had managed to write 150 works on mathematics, astronomy, and medicine. With all the work done by Thābit, most of his work has not lasted time. There are less than a dozen works by him that have survived.

Translation

Thābit's native language was Syriac, which was the Middle Aramaic variety from Edessa, and he was fluent in both Medieval Greek and Arabic. He was the author to multiple treaties. Due to him being trilingual, Thābit was able to have a major role during the Graeco-Arabic translation movement. He would also make a school of translation in Baghdad.
Thābit translated from Greek into Arabic works by Apollonius of Perga, Archimedes, Euclid and Ptolemy. He revised the translation of Euclid's Elements of Hunayn ibn Ishaq. He also rewrote Ishaq ibn Hunayn's translation of Ptolemy's Almagest and translated Ptolemy's Geography. Thābit's translation of a work by Archimedes which gave a construction of a regular heptagon was discovered in the 20th century, the original having been lost.

Astronomy
Thābit is believed to have been an astronomer of Caliph al-Mu'tadid. Thābit was able to use his mathematical work on the examination of Ptolemaic astronomy. The medieval astronomical theory of the trepidation of the equinoxes is often attributed to Thābit. But it had already been described by Theon of Alexandria in his comments of the Handy Tables of Ptolemy. According to Copernicus, Thābit determined the length of the sidereal year as 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes and 12 seconds (an error of 2 seconds). Copernicus based his claim on the Latin text attributed to Thābit. Thābit published his observations of the Sun. In regards to Ptolemy's Planetary Hypotheses, Thābit examined the problems of the motion of the Sun and Moon, and the theory of sundials. When looking at Ptolemy's Hypotheses, Thābit ibn Qurra found the Sidereal year which is when looking at the Earth and measuring it against the background of fixed stars, it will have a constant value.
Thābit was also an author and wrote De Anno Solis. This book contained and recorded facts about the evolution in astronomy in the ninth century. Thābit mentioned in the book that Ptolemy and Hipparchus believed that the movement of stars is consistent with the movement commonly found in planets. What Thābit believed is that this idea can be broadened to include the Sun and Moon. With that in mind, he also thought that the solar year should be calculated by looking at the Sun's return to a given star.

Mathematics

In mathematics, Thābit derived an equation for determining amicable numbers. His proof of this rule is presented in the Treatise on the Derivation of the Amicable Numbers in an Easy Way. This was done while writing on the theory of numbers, extending their use to describe the ratios between geometrical quantities, a step which the Greeks did not take. Thābit's work on amicable numbers and number theory helped him to invest more heavily into the Geometrical relations of numbers establishing his Transversal (geometry) theorem.
Thābit described a generalized proof of the Pythagorean theorem. He provided a strengthened extension of Pythagoras' proof which included the knowledge of Euclid's fifth postulate. This postulate states that the intersection between two straight line segments combine to create two interior angles which are less than 180 degrees. The method of reduction and composition used by Thābit resulted in a combination and extension of contemporary and ancient knowledge on this famous proof. Thābit believed that geometry was tied with the equality and differences of magnitudes of lines and angles, as well as that ideas of motion (and ideas taken from physics more widely) should be integrated in geometry.
The continued work done on geometric relations and the resulting exponential series allowed Thābit to calculate multiple solutions to chessboard problems. This problem was less to do with the game itself, and more to do with the number of solutions or the nature of solutions possible. In Thābit's case, he worked with combinatorics to work on the permutations needed to win a game of chess.
In addition to Thābit's work on Euclidean geometry there is evidence that he was familiar with the geometry of Archimedes as well. His work with conic sections and the calculation of a paraboloid shape (cupola) show his proficiency as an Archimedean geometer. This is further embossed by Thābit's use of the Archimedean property in order to produce a rudimentary approximation of the volume of a paraboloid. The use of uneven sections, while relatively simple, does show a critical understanding of both Euclidean and Archimedean geometry. Thābit was also responsible for a commentary on Archimedes' Liber Assumpta.

Physics
In physics, Thābit rejected the Peripatetic and Aristotelian notions of a "natural place" for each element. He instead proposed a theory of motion in which both the upward and downward motions are caused by weight, and that the order of the universe is a result of two competing attractions (jadhb): one of these being "between the sublunar and celestial elements", and the other being "between all parts of each element separately". and in mechanics he was a founder of statics. In addition, Thābit's Liber Karatonis contained proof of the law of the lever. This work was the result of combining Aristotelian and Archimedean ideas of dynamics and mechanics.
One of Qurra's most important pieces of text is his work with the Kitab fi 'l-qarastun. This text consists of Arabic mechanical tradition. Another piece of important text is Kitab fi sifat alwazn, which discussed concepts of equal-armed balance.

bio: Thaqf bin 'Amr (c. 594–628 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Thaqf bin 'Amr was an early companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 594 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early converts to Islam and became part of the close circle of companions known as the Sahaba who supported Muhammad during the establishment of the Muslim community.

Thaqf bin 'Amr is primarily remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, which earned him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the early Muslim community against the Meccan forces. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are held in particular reverence within Islamic tradition, as this victory is viewed as a pivotal moment that helped secure the survival and growth of the nascent Muslim community.

As one of the early ascetics within the Islamic tradition, Thaqf bin 'Amr represented a strand of early Islamic spirituality that emphasized renunciation of worldly pleasures and devotion to religious practice. This ascetic approach would later influence the development of Islamic mystical traditions, though the specific details of his ascetic practices are not extensively documented in historical sources.

His relatively short life, ending around 628 CE at approximately 34 years of age, coincided with the crucial early years of Islamic expansion. He witnessed and participated in the transformation of Islam from a small religious movement in Mecca to an established community that would soon extend across the Arabian Peninsula.

The historical significance of companions like Thaqf bin 'Amr lies not only in their individual contributions but in their collective role as the foundation upon which the early Islamic community was built. Their direct relationship with the Prophet Muhammad and their participation in key events such as the Battle of Badr established them as important figures in the Islamic historical narrative and sources of religious authority for subsequent generations of Muslims.

While detailed accounts of his specific contributions beyond his participation at Badr are limited in historical sources, his inclusion among the recognized Sahaba indicates his accepted status as a reliable transmitter of early Islamic teachings and practices.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Thaqf bin Farwa bin al-Badi (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Thaqf bin Farwa bin al-Badi was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he lived during the transitional era when Islamic teachings were first being established and the Muslim community was taking shape in the Hijaz region.

As one of the Sahaba, the companions who knew and followed Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime, Thaqf bin Farwa was part of the early Muslim community that formed around the Prophet's teachings. The Sahaba played crucial roles in the preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge, practices, and traditions during Islam's foundational years.

Thaqf bin Farwa's life came to an end at the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, where he died as a martyr. The Battle of Uhud was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces, taking place on the slopes of Mount Uhud near Medina. This battle occurred during a critical period when the early Muslim state was establishing itself and defending against opposition from Meccan tribes who sought to suppress the growing Islamic movement.

The Battle of Uhud holds significant importance in Islamic history as it tested the resolve and faith of the early Muslim community. Despite initial success, the Muslim forces faced challenges during the battle, and many companions, including Thaqf bin Farwa, gave their lives in defense of their faith and community. Those who died at Uhud are remembered in Islamic tradition as martyrs who sacrificed themselves for the cause of Islam.

His death at such a young age, around twenty-eight years old, reflects the dangerous circumstances faced by early Muslims as they worked to establish and protect their religious community. The companions who died at Uhud, including Thaqf bin Farwa, are remembered for their dedication to the early Islamic cause during a pivotal moment when the survival of the Muslim community was uncertain.

As with many of the early companions, Thaqf bin Farwa represents the commitment and sacrifice of those who supported the Prophet Muhammad during Islam's earliest and most vulnerable period, contributing to the foundation upon which the later Islamic civilization would be built.

famous: The Aunt of HUsayn bin Mihsan
full: The Aunt of HUsayn bin Mihsan
dob_s: c. 590 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: c. 650 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
bio: The Aunt of HUsayn bin Mihsan (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
The Aunt of Husayn bin Mihsan was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early decades of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly encountered and learned from the Prophet during his lifetime.

As indicated by her name, she was known primarily through her familial relationship to Husayn bin Mihsan, though the specific details of their family connection and her given name have not been preserved in the historical record. This naming convention was common in early Islamic society, where individuals were sometimes identified through their relationships to more prominent family members, particularly in the case of women whose individual names may not have been as widely recorded by later historians.

She resided in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. As a Medinan resident during this crucial period, she would have witnessed the establishment and development of the first Islamic state and community.

Her primary contribution to Islamic tradition lies in her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. As a female narrator, she was part of an important tradition of women who served as transmitters of prophetic traditions, helping to preserve and pass down essential religious knowledge to subsequent generations. The hadith literature forms one of the fundamental sources of Islamic law and practice, making the role of early narrators like her significant for the development of Islamic scholarship and jurisprudence.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph, meaning she lived through the Prophet's lifetime and into the early expansion period of Islam. While specific details about her individual contributions or the particular hadith she transmitted may not be extensively documented, her inclusion among the recognized female companions and hadith narrators indicates her accepted place within the early Muslim community and her role in preserving prophetic tradition for future generations of Muslims.

bio: Thubayta bint al-Dahhak (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Thubayta bint al-Dahhak was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she was among the early Muslim community in Medina and died in approximately 635 CE, during the early years of the Islamic expansion under the Rashidun Caliphate.

As a sahabiyya, Thubayta belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the foundational period of Islam. The companions hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the primary transmitters of the Prophet's teachings and the earliest practitioners of the faith. Their accounts and testimonies form the basis of much Islamic jurisprudence and religious understanding.

Thubayta is specifically recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad. In the early Islamic community, both men and women served as transmitters of these crucial religious accounts, helping preserve the Prophet's teachings for future generations. Female companions like Thubayta played an essential role in this transmission process, particularly in matters relating to domestic life, family relations, and situations where women had closer access to certain aspects of the Prophet's daily conduct.

The preservation and transmission of hadith represents one of the most significant scholarly endeavors in early Islam. Narrators were expected to maintain accuracy and reliability in their accounts, as these reports would later be scrutinized by hadith scholars who developed sophisticated methodologies to verify their authenticity. The inclusion of female narrators in this system demonstrates the recognition of women's contributions to Islamic scholarship from its earliest period.

Thubayta's significance lies in her participation in this foundational process of Islamic knowledge transmission. While specific details about her individual contributions may not be extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as a hadith narrator places her among the women who helped shape the preservation of Islamic teachings. Her life span, covering the prophetic period and extending into the early caliphate, positioned her as a witness to the rapid transformation of Arabian society and the establishment of the early Muslim community that would eventually spread across much of the known world.

bio: Thubayta bint al-Rabi' bin 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Thubayta bint al-Rabi' bin 'Amr was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She lived during the foundational period of Islam in the early 7th century and died around 635 CE, placing her life span during the crucial decades when Islam was first established and began to spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

As an Ansari companion, Thubayta belonged to the community of Medinan supporters who welcomed and assisted the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were the local tribes of Medina who converted to Islam and provided crucial support to the early Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

Her designation as a companion of the Prophet indicates that she lived during Muhammad's lifetime, likely interacted with him, and was recognized as part of the early Muslim community in Medina. The companions hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices and principles.

Thubayta's presence in the historical record, though limited in detail, represents the significant role that women played in the early Islamic community. Female companions like her were part of the social and religious fabric of early Muslim society in Medina, contributing to the growth and development of the community during its formative years.

Her life spanned the most critical period of early Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's mission, the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate following Muhammad's death in 632 CE. As one of the Ansar, she was part of the group that helped transform Medina into the first Islamic city-state and the center from which Islam would eventually spread throughout the known world.

While specific details about her individual contributions are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as a companion places her among the founding members of the Muslim community whose support was essential to Islam's early survival and growth.

bio: Thubayta bint Salit bin Qays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Thubayta bint Salit bin Qays was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who welcomed and supported the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Thubayta witnessed and participated in the foundational period of the Islamic community. The Ansar played a crucial role in establishing Islam in Medina, providing shelter, resources, and protection to the early Muslim community during a critical phase of its development. Her presence among this group indicates that she was part of the local Medinan society that embraced Islam and actively supported the Prophet's mission.

Living during the lifetime of Prophet Muhammad, Thubayta would have experienced the rapid transformation of Medina from a collection of feuding tribes into a unified Islamic community. She lived through the period when fundamental Islamic practices, laws, and social structures were being established, and when the early Muslim community faced various challenges including conflicts with Meccan forces and internal community building.

The designation "Sahabiyya" places her among the female companions who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad, a status that holds particular significance in Islamic tradition. The companions, both male and female, are regarded as important figures who helped preserve and transmit Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Thubayta's death around 635 CE means she lived to see the early expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the first Caliph Abu Bakr. Her forty-year lifespan encompassed the pre-Islamic period of her youth, the emergence and establishment of Islam in Medina, and the beginning of the Islamic conquests that would transform the religious and political landscape of the Middle East and beyond.

While specific details about her individual contributions are not extensively documented in historical sources, her recognition as a Sahabiyya indicates her place among the women who were part of the first Muslim community and who contributed to the early development of Islamic society in Medina.
