bio: Umar bin Abi Salamah (c. 646 CE–701 CE, Medinah) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia or Medina. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full: 'Umar ibn Abi Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi, known by the kunya Abu Hafs, was the son of the Companion Abu Salama and of Umm Salama, who later married the Prophet Muhammad. He was therefore the Prophet's stepson and grew up with his mother in the Prophet's household; the Prophet and Abu Salama were also foster-brothers. He was born in Abyssinia. Sources differ on the year: one account places his birth two years before the Hijra, while Ibn Hibban gives the first year after the Hijra and Ibn al-Athir the second. Several dictionaries say he was nine years old when the Prophet died. He is known for the hadith, recorded by Muslim, in which the Prophet taught him to say God's name, eat with his right hand and eat from what is nearest to him. Abu Nu'aym says he transmitted fewer than ten hadith from the Prophet. When 'Ali ibn Abi Talib set out for Basra, Umm Salama, who declined to go herself, sent her son with him. Ibn al-Athir says he fought on 'Ali's side at the Battle of the Camel; al-Khatib al-Baghdadi instead says he joined 'Ali on the march to Siffin. 'Ali appointed him governor of Bahrain and later replaced him with al-Nu'man ibn 'Ajlan al-Zuraqi; Ibn al-Athir adds that he was also appointed over Fars. He married Mulayka bint Rifa'a ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir, who bore him Salama, Muhammad and Zaynab. He died in Medina in 83 AH (702 CE), during the caliphate of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan.

full: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān
primaryTitle: Umar II — The Just Caliph, the Fifth Rightly-Guided
titles: ʿUmar al-Thānī · Khāmis al-Khulafāʾ al-Rāshidīn
bio: Commander of the Faithful and Caliph of the Muslims, the devout and pious ascetic Imam Abu Hafs Omar bin Abdul Aziz bin Marwan bin Al-Hakam bin Abi Al-Aas Al-Umayyad Al-Qurashi, known for short as Omar bin Abdul-Aziz or Omar II due to his resemblance to the biography of his maternal grandfather, the Rashidun Caliph. Omar bin Al-Khattab. He is the eighth caliph of the Umayyads, and the thirteenth caliph in the order of caliphs after the Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
bio_full:
Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan (Arabic: عُمَر بْن عَبْد الْعَزِيز بْن مَرْوَان, romanized: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Marwān; c. 680 – February 720) was the eighth Umayyad caliph, ruling from 717 until his death in 720. He is credited with instituting significant reforms to the Umayyad central government, by making it much more efficient and egalitarian. His rulership is marked by the first official collection of hadiths and the mandated universal education to the populace.
He dispatched emissaries to China and Tibet, inviting their rulers to accept Islam. It was during his three-year reign that Islam was accepted by huge segments of the populations of Persia and Egypt. He also ordered the withdrawal of the Muslim forces in various fronts such as in Constantinople, Central Asia and Septimania. Despite this, his reign witnessed the Umayyads gaining many new territories in the Iberian Peninsula. 
Umar is regarded by many Sunni scholars as the first mujaddid and is sometimes referred to as the "fifth rightly guided caliph" due to his reputation for just governance. Some Sunni scholars consider Hasan ibn Ali’s brief caliphate (661) as part of his father Ali ibn Abi Talib’s rule, citing a hadith that describes the rightly guided caliphate as lasting thirty years. Umar was also honorifically called Umar al-Thani (Umar II) in reference to his great-grandfather, Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (r. 634–644).

Early life
Umar was likely born in Medina around 680. His father, Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, belonged to the wealthy Umayyad clan resident in the city, while his mother, Layla bint Asim, was a granddaughter of the second Rashidun caliph Umar (r. 634–644). His lineage from the much-respected Caliph Umar would later be emphasized by historians to differentiate him from the other Umayyad rulers.
At the time of his birth, another branch of the Umayyads, the Sufyanids, ruled from their capital Damascus. After Caliph Yazid I (r. 680–683) and his son and successor, Mu'awiya II (r. 683–684), died in quick succession in 683 and 684, Umayyad authority collapsed across the Caliphate. The Umayyads of the Hejaz, including Medina, were expelled by supporters of the rival caliph, the Mecca-based Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr (r. 683–692). The Umayyad exiles took refuge in Syria, where loyalist Arab tribes supported the dynasty. Umar's grandfather, Marwan I (r. 684–685), was ultimately recognized by these tribes as caliph and, with their support, reasserted Umayyad rule in Syria.
In 685, Marwan ousted Ibn al-Zubayr's governor from Egypt and appointed Umar's father to the province. Umar spent part of his childhood in Egypt, particularly in Hulwan, which had become the seat of his father's governorship between 686 and his death in 705. He received his education in Medina, however, which was retaken by the Umayyads under Umar's paternal uncle, Caliph Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705), in 692. Having spent much of his youth in Medina, Umar developed ties with the city's pious men and transmitters of hadiths. Following the death of Umar's father, Abd al-Malik recalled Umar to Damascus, where he arranged Umar's marriage to his daughter, Fatima. Umar had two other wives: his maternal cousin Umm Shu'ayb or Umm Uthman, the daughter of Shu'ayb or Sa'id ibn Zabban of the Banu Kalb tribe, and Lamis bint Ali of the Balharith. From his wives he had seven known children, as well as seven other children from concubines.

Governor of Medina
Shortly after his accession, Abd al-Malik's son and successor, al-Walid I (r. 705–715), appointed Umar governor of Medina. According to Julius Wellhausen, al-Walid's intention was to use Umar to reconcile the townspeople of Medina to Umayyad rule and "obliterate [sic] the evil memory" of the preceding Umayyad governors, namely Hisham ibn Isma'il al-Makhzumi, whose rule over Medina had been harsh for its inhabitants. Umar took up the post in February/March 706 and his jurisdiction later extended to Mecca and Ta'if.
Information about his governorship is scant, but most traditional accounts note that he was a "just governor", according to historian Paul Cobb. He often led the annual Hajj pilgrimage in Mecca and showed favor toward the Islamic legal scholars of Medina, notably Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. Umar tolerated many of these scholars' open criticism of the Umayyad government's conduct. However, other accounts hold that he showed himself to be materialistic during his early career. On al-Walid's orders, Umar undertook the reconstruction and expansion of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina beginning in 707. Under Umar's generally lenient rule, the Hejaz became a refuge for Iraqi political and religious exiles fleeing the persecutions of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, al-Walid's powerful viceroy over the eastern half of the Caliphate. According to Cobb, this served as Umar's "undoing" as al-Hajjaj pressured the caliph to dismiss Umar in May/June 712.

Courtier of al-Walid and Sulayman
Despite his dismissal, Umar remained in al-Walid's favor, being the brother of the caliph's first wife, Umm al-Banin bint Abd al-Aziz. He remained in al-Walid's court in Damascus until the caliph's death in 715, and according to the 9th-century historian al-Ya'qubi, he performed the funeral prayers for al-Walid. The latter's brother and successor, Sulayman (r. 715–717), held Umar in high regard. Alongside Raja ibn Haywa, an influential religious figure in the Umayyads' court, Umar served as a principal adviser of Sulayman. He accompanied the latter when he led the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca in 716 and on his return to Jerusalem. Likewise, he was at the caliph's side at the Muslims' marshaling camp at Dabiq in northern Syria, where Sulayman directed the massive war effort to conquer the Byzantine capital of Constantinople in 717.

Caliphate

Accession
According to the traditional Muslim sources, when Sulayman was on his deathbed in Dabiq, he was persuaded by Raja to designate Umar as his successor. Sulayman's son Ayyub had been his initial nominee, but predeceased him, while his other sons were either too young or away fighting on the Byzantine front. The nomination of Umar voided the wishes of Abd al-Malik, who sought to restrict the office to his direct descendants. The elevation of Umar, a member of a cadet branch of the dynasty, in preference to the numerous descendants of Abd al-Malik surprised these princes. According to Wellhausen, "nobody dreamed of this, himself [Umar] least of all". Raja managed the affair, calling the Umayyad princes into Dabiq's mosque and demanding that they recognize Sulayman's will, which Raja had kept secret. Only after the Umayyads accepted did Raja reveal that Umar was the caliph's nominee. Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik voiced his opposition, but relented after being threatened with violence. A potential intra-dynastic conflict was averted with the designation of a son of Abd al-Malik, Yazid II, as Umar's successor.
According to the historian Reinhard Eisener, Raja's role in the affair was likely "exaggerated"; "more reasonable" was that Umar's succession was the result of "traditional patterns, like seniority and well-founded claims" stemming from Caliph Marwan I's original designation of Umar's father, Abd al-Aziz, as Abd al-Malik's successor, which had not materialized due to Abd al-Aziz predeceasing Abd al-Malik. Umar acceded without significant opposition on 22 September 717.

Reforms

The most significant reform of Umar was effecting the equality of Arabs and mawali (non-Arab Muslims). This was mainly relevant to the non-Arab troops in the Muslim army, who had not been entitled to the same shares in spoils, lands and salaries given to Arab soldiers. The policy also applied to Muslim society at large. Under previous Umayyad rulers, Arab Muslims had financial privileges over non-Arab Muslims. Non-Arab converts to Islam were still expected to pay the jizya (poll tax) that they paid before becoming Muslims.

full: Sharaf al-Din 'Umar ibn 'Ali ibn al-Farid al-Hamawi al-Misri
titles: Sultan al-'Ashiqin (Sultan of Lovers) · Mawla al-'Arifin
bio: Sharaf al-Din 'Umar ibn 'Ali ibn al-Farid al-Hamawi al-Misri (1181–1235) was a poet of the Persian Poetry tradition, based in Cairo. Known as Sultan al-'Ashiqin — Sultan of Lovers.
bio_full:
Umar Ibn al-Farid (1181-1235) was an influential Sufi poet who lived and worked primarily in Cairo during the Ayyubid period. Born Sharaf al-Din 'Umar ibn 'Ali ibn al-Farid al-Hamawi al-Misri, he came to be known by the honorific title "Sultan al-'Ashiqin" (Sultan of Lovers), reflecting his mastery of mystical love poetry.

Ibn al-Farid spent most of his life in Cairo, which served as a major center of Islamic learning and culture during his lifetime. The city provided him with access to scholarly circles and Sufi communities that influenced his spiritual and poetic development. He was part of the broader tradition of Islamic mystical poetry that flourished during the medieval period, contributing to the rich literary heritage of Sufism.

His poetry focused primarily on themes of divine love, spiritual longing, and the mystic's journey toward union with God. Writing in Arabic rather than Persian, Ibn al-Farid distinguished himself within the mystical poetry tradition through his sophisticated use of classical Arabic literary forms and his ability to express complex spiritual concepts through accessible imagery. His verses often employed the conventional language of earthly love to describe the soul's relationship with the divine, a common technique in Sufi literature.

Ibn al-Farid's work gained recognition among both religious scholars and literary critics for its technical excellence and spiritual depth. His poems were studied and memorized by subsequent generations of Sufis and continue to be regarded as masterworks of Arabic mystical literature. His most famous compositions include lengthy poems that trace the spiritual journey from separation to unity, using intricate metaphors drawn from wine, love, and pilgrimage.

The poet's significance to Islamic history lies in his contribution to the development of Arabic Sufi poetry and his role in articulating mystical experiences through literary expression. His work represents an important bridge between formal Islamic scholarship and popular spiritual practice, making complex theological concepts accessible through poetic beauty. Ibn al-Farid's influence extended beyond his lifetime, with his poetry continuing to inspire later generations of Islamic mystics and poets throughout the Arabic-speaking world.

full: Umar ibn al-Khattab ibn Nufayl al-Qurashi
titles: Al-Faruq · Amir al-Muminin · Umar al-Akbar
bio: Abu Hafs Omar bin Al-Khattab Al-Adawi Al-Qurashi, nicknamed Al-Farouq, is the second of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and one of the major companions of the Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and one of the most famous leaders in Islamic history and one of the most influential and powerful. He is one of the ten promised Paradise, and one of the scholars and ascetics of the Companions. He assumed the Islamic Caliphate after the death of Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq on August 23, 634 AD, corresponding to the twenty-second of Jumada al-Akhira, 13 AH. Ibn al-Khattab was an expert judge and was famous for his justice and redress of injustices to people, whether they were Muslims or non-Muslims, and that was one of the reasons for him being called Al-Farouq, for his distinction between truth and falsehood.
bio_full:
Umar ibn al-Khattab (Arabic: عُمَر بْن ٱلْخَطَّاب, romanized: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb; c. 584 – 644), also spelled Omar, was the second Rashidun caliph, ruling from August 634 until his assassination in 644. He succeeded Abu Bakr (r. 632–634) and is regarded as a senior companion and father-in-law of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
Initially, Umar opposed Muhammad, who was his distant Qurayshite kinsman. However, after converting to Islam in 616, he became the first Muslim to openly pray at the Kaaba. He participated in nearly all of Muhammad's battles and expeditions, and Muhammad conferred upon him the title al-Fārūq ("the Distinguisher") for his sound judgement. After Muhammad's death in June 632, Umar pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr as the first caliph and served as his chief adviser. In 634, shortly before his death, Abu Bakr nominated Umar as his successor.
During Umar's reign, the caliphate expanded at an unprecedented rate, conquering the Sasanian Empire and more than two-thirds of the Byzantine Empire. His campaigns against the Sasanians resulted in the conquest of Persia within two years (642–644). According to Jewish tradition, Umar lifted the Christian ban on Jews entering Jerusalem and permitted them to worship there. Umar was assassinated by the Persian slave Abu Lu'lu'a Firuz in 644.
Umar is widely credited with expanding the Islamic world beyond Arabia and introducing the Hijri Calendar. Historians generally regard him as one of the most powerful and influential Muslim caliphs in history. In Sunni Islamic tradition, he is revered as a just ruler and a paragon of Islamic virtues, with some hadiths identifying him as the second greatest of the Sahabah after Abu Bakr. In Twelver Shia tradition, however, he is viewed negatively.

Early life
Umar was born in Mecca to the Banu Adi clan, which was responsible for arbitration among the tribes. His father was Khattab ibn Nufayl, and his mother was Hantamah bint Hisham of the Banu Makhzum tribe. In his youth, Umar tended his father's camels in the plains near Mecca. His father, a merchant, was renowned for his intelligence among his tribe. Umar later recalled: "My father, al-Khattab, was a ruthless man. He used to make me work hard; if I didn't work, he used to beat me and he used to work me to exhaustion".
Although literacy was uncommon in pre-Islamic Arabia, Umar learned to read and write during his youth. While not a poet himself, he developed a love for poetry and literature. In accordance with the traditions of the Quraysh, he was trained in martial arts, horse riding, and wrestling during his adolescence. He was tall, physically powerful and a renowned wrestler. He was also recognized as a gifted orator and succeeded his father as an arbitrator among the tribes.
Umar became a merchant and made several journeys to Byzantine and Sasanian territories, where he is said to have met various scholars and analyzed Byzantine and Sasanian societies. As a merchant, he was unsuccessful. Like others around him, Umar was fond of drinking in his pre-Islamic days.

Early military career

Opposition to Islam
In 610, Muhammad started preaching the message of Islam. However, like many others in Mecca, Umar opposed Islam and even threatened to kill Muhammad. He resolved to defend the traditional polytheistic religion of Arabia. He was adamant and cruel in opposing Muhammad and very prominent in persecuting Muslims. He recommended Muhammad's death. He firmly believed in the unity of the Quraysh and saw the new faith of Islam as a cause of division and discord.
Due to persecution, Muhammad ordered some of his followers to migrate to Abyssinia. When a small group of Muslims migrated, Umar became worried about the future unity of the Quraysh and decided to have Muhammad assassinated.

Conversion to Islam and service under Muhammad
Umar converted to Islam in 616, one year after the Migration to Abyssinia. The story was recounted in Ibn Ishaq's Sīrah. On his way to murder Muhammad, Umar met his best friend Nu'aym ibn Abd Allah, who had secretly converted to Islam but had not told Umar. When Umar informed him that he had set out to kill Muhammad, Nu'aym said, "By God, you have deceived yourself, O Umar? Do you think that Banu Abd al-Manaf would let you run around alive once you had killed their son Muhammad? Why don't you return to your own house and at least set it straight?"
Nu'aym then told him to inquire about his own household, where his sister, Fatima bint al-Khattab, and his brother-in-law had converted to Islam and were taking lessons from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt. Upon arriving at her house, Umar found Fatima and her husband, Sa'id ibn Zayd, who was also Umar's cousin, reciting verses of the Quran from Surat Ta-Ha. He began quarreling with Sa'id and physically attacked him. When his sister attempted to rescue her husband, Umar also began arguing with her. Sources differ on what happened next, as some state that upon hearing these words, Umar slapped his sister so hard that she fell to the ground, while others claim Fatima was hit by accident and lost her balance while trying to pull Umar away from Sa'id. In both accounts, his sister began to bleed from her mouth. After seeing what he had done, Umar calmed down due to a sense of guilt and asked Fatima to give him the text she had been reciting. She refused and told him that he was unclean and that no person in an unclean state could touch the Scripture. He insisted on seeing it, but his sister was not prepared to allow him to touch the pages until he had washed his body. Umar eventually gave in to her request. He washed his body and then began to read the verses which stated that it is truly He, that He is Allah, that there is no god worthy of worship except Him, and that one should worship Him alone and establish prayer for His remembrance (Quran 20:14). He wept and declared, "Surely this is the word of Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah". Upon hearing this, Khabbab came out from his hiding place and told Umar that there were glad tidings for him, as Muhammad had prayed to Allah the previous day to strengthen Islam with either Umar or Abu Jahl, and it appeared that the prayer had been answered in his favor."
Umar then went to Muhammad with the same sword he intended to kill him with and accepted Islam in front of him and his companions. Umar was 39 years old when he accepted Islam.
According to one account, after his conversion to Islam, Umar openly prayed at the Kaaba as the Quraysh chiefs, Abu Jahl and Abu Sufyan, reportedly watched in anger. This further helped the Muslims to gain confidence in practicing Islam openly. At this stage, Umar even challenged anyone who dared to stop the Muslims from praying, although no one dared to interfere with Umar when he was openly praying.
Umar's conversion to Islam granted power to the Muslims and to the Islamic faith in Mecca. It was after this event that Muslims offered prayers openly in Masjid al-Haram for the first time. Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said,

Umar's embracing Islam was our victory, his migration to Medina was our success, and his reign a blessing from Allah. We didn't offer prayers in al-Haram Mosque until Umar had accepted Islam. When he accepted Islam, the Quraysh were compelled to let us pray in the Mosque.

Migration to Medina
In 622, due to the safety offered by Yathrib (later renamed Medīnat an-Nabī, or simply Medina), Muhammad ordered his followers to migrate to Medina. Most Muslims migrated at night fearing Quraysh resistance, but Umar is reported to have left openly during the day saying:

Any one who wants to make his wife a widow and his children orphans should come and meet me there behind that cliff
Umar migrated to Medina accompanied by his cousin and brother-in-law Saeed ibn Zaid.

Life in Medina

Muslims remained in peace in Medina for approximately a year before the Quraysh raised an army to attack them.

bio: Umara bin Hazm ibn Zayd (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: 'Umara ibn Hazm ibn Zayd ibn Ludhan ibn 'Amr, of the clan of Malik ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj, was an Ansari Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and the brother of 'Amr ibn Hazm; Ibn 'Abd al-Barr names a third brother, Ma'mar. His mother was Khalida bint Anas, of Banu Sa'ida. According to all accounts he was one of the seventy who pledged allegiance at al-'Aqaba, and the Prophet paired him in brotherhood with Muhriz ibn Nadla. The History of Damascus, as abridged by Ibn Manzur, says that after accepting Islam he and two others broke the idols of Banu Malik. He fought at Badr, Uhud, the Trench and all the other campaigns, and carried the banner of Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar on the day of the conquest of Mecca. Ibn Qani' and Ibn al-Athir each record a hadith through him; Ibn Qani's is that the Prophet decided cases by an oath together with one witness. In the caliphate of Abu Bakr he fought the apostates under Khalid ibn al-Walid and was killed as a martyr at al-Yamama. The History of Damascus dates this to 12 AH, while Abu Nu'aym gives 11 AH. Ibn Hibban and others state that he left no descendants. One report in the History of Damascus has him living into Mu'awiya's time, but the same source adds that this is not sound.

bio: Umara bint Hubbasha bin Jwaybit (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umara bint Hubbasha bin Jwaybit was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She lived during the formative period of Islam in the early 7th century, witnessing the establishment and early expansion of the Muslim community.

As an Ansari companion based in Medina, Umara belonged to the group of Medinan Muslims who welcomed and supported Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca following the Hijra in 622 CE. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" or "supporters," played a crucial role in providing refuge and assistance to the early Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

Umara's designation as a sahabiyya places her among the women who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and were part of the first generation of Muslims. The female companions held significant status in Islamic tradition, as they were considered witnesses to the Prophet's teachings and examples of early Islamic practice. They often served as sources of religious knowledge and guidance for subsequent generations of Muslim women.

Living in Medina during the Prophet's time, Umara would have experienced the major events of early Islamic history, including the establishment of the first Muslim state, various military campaigns, and the development of Islamic law and social practices. The period from 622 to 632 CE marked the consolidation of the Muslim community and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

The female companions like Umara contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings, particularly regarding matters that concerned women's religious and social roles. Their experiences and participation in the early Muslim community provided important precedents for women's involvement in Islamic society.

Umara's death around 635 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, the period immediately following Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This was a time of rapid territorial expansion and the spread of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the leadership of the first four caliphs.

Her recognition as an Ansari companion reflects the important role that the people of Medina played in Islamic history. The Ansar's support was instrumental in the survival and growth of the early Muslim community, and their contributions are acknowledged as foundational to the establishment of Islam as a major world religion.

bio: Umayma bint 'Abd al-Muttalib (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca.
bio_full: Umayma bint 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim was a paternal aunt of the Prophet Muhammad, born in Mecca into the clan of Hashim. Her mother, according to Ibn Sa'd, was Fatima bint 'Amr of the Makhzum clan. She married Jahsh ibn Ri'ab, of the tribe of Asad ibn Khuzayma, and bore him six children: three sons, 'Abd Allah, 'Ubayd Allah and 'Abd, known as Abu Ahmad, and three daughters, Zaynab, who later became a wife of the Prophet, Habiba, known as Umm Habib, and Hamna. Her children became Muslims and emigrated to Medina in 622, but according to Ibn Ishaq's biography she did not go with them. Whether she herself became a Muslim is disputed. Ibn Hajar notes that Ibn Ishaq denied that she accepted Islam and that only Ibn Sa'd records her. Ibn Sa'd reports that the Prophet assigned her an annual allowance of forty wasqs of dates from Khaybar, so she was still alive in 628. No date of death is recorded.

bio: Umayma bint 'Amr bin Sahl (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umayma bint 'Amr bin Sahl was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the community of Medinan supporters who welcomed and assisted the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca when they arrived in Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions, Umayma was part of the indigenous population of Medina who converted to Islam and played a crucial role in establishing the early Muslim community. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were distinguished from the Muhajirun (emigrants from Mecca) and held a special position in early Islamic society for their support of the nascent Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

Living during the formative years of Islam, Umayma would have witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic state in Medina and the development of key Islamic institutions and practices. Her presence in Medina during this period places her among those who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and participated in the early Muslim community's social and religious life.

The designation of Sahabiyya indicates that she was recognized as having met the Prophet Muhammad while believing in his message, making her part of the first generation of Muslims whose accounts and experiences became foundational to Islamic tradition. Female companions like Umayma played important roles in the early Muslim community, participating in religious life, social affairs, and the transmission of Islamic knowledge and practices.

Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, following the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing suggests she lived through the critical transition period when the Muslim community faced the challenge of continuing without their Prophet's direct guidance.

While specific details about Umayma's individual contributions or particular activities are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as a Sahabiyya indicates her significance within the early Muslim community. The female companions collectively contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings and played vital roles in the social fabric of early Islamic society in Medina.

bio: Umayma bint Abi Hathma (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umayma bint Abi Hathma was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the foundational period of Islam in the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE, she was among the early Muslim community that established itself in Medina following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As a sahabiyya, Umayma belonged to the generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. This proximity to the Prophet's daily life and teachings positioned her as an important source of religious knowledge for subsequent generations of Muslims.

Umayma is particularly recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial component of Islamic religious guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions who served as hadith narrators played an essential role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings, especially regarding matters that pertained to women's religious practices, family life, and social conduct.

The preservation of hadith through oral transmission was a meticulous process that required reliable witnesses who could accurately recount the Prophet's words and deeds. As someone who lived in Medina during the Prophet's lifetime, Umayma would have had opportunities to observe his conduct and hear his teachings directly, making her testimony valuable for later Islamic scholarship.

Her contributions to hadith sciences represent part of the broader participation of women in the early Islamic community's intellectual and religious life. Female companions like Umayma helped ensure that Islamic teachings were comprehensively documented and transmitted across generations, particularly in areas where women's perspectives and experiences were most relevant.

Umayma's life span, ending around 635 CE, places her death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This timing means she lived through the entire Medina period of the Prophet's mission and witnessed the initial expansion of the Islamic community beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Her legacy lies in her contribution to the hadith tradition, which became fundamental to Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and daily practice. Through her role as a narrator, she helped preserve essential elements of early Islamic history and religious guidance for future Muslim generations.

bio: Umayma bint Abul-Haytham (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umayma bint Abul-Haytham was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported and assisted the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari women of Medina, Umayma lived during the foundational period of Islam in the early seventh century. The Ansar played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community, providing shelter, resources, and protection to the Prophet and the migrants (Muhajirun) who had left Mecca due to persecution.

The designation "bint Abul-Haytham" indicates she was the daughter of a man known as Abul-Haytham, following the Arabic naming convention of the time. Her presence in the historical record as a named companion reflects her recognition within the early Muslim community, though specific details about her individual contributions or activities are not well-documented in the surviving historical sources.

Umayma's significance lies primarily in her status as one of the female companions who witnessed and participated in the early development of the Islamic community in Medina. The women of the Ansar, like their male counterparts, were instrumental in the survival and growth of the nascent Muslim community during its most vulnerable period. They provided practical support, participated in community life, and helped establish the social foundations of the first Islamic society.

Her life span, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompasses the entire prophetic period and extends into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's reign. This places her among those who experienced the complete transformation from pre-Islamic Arabian society to the establishment of the Islamic state.

While specific biographical details about Umayma's personal life, family relationships, or particular contributions remain limited in the historical record, her inclusion among the recognized companions (Sahaba) indicates her acceptance of Islam and her role within the early Muslim community of Medina. The preservation of her name in Islamic historical tradition reflects the importance placed on documenting those who supported the Prophet and the early Muslim community during this formative period.

bio: Umayma bint al-Nu'man bin al-Harith (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umayma bint al-Nu'man bin al-Harith was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who provided crucial support to the Prophet and the early Muslim community following the migration (Hijra) from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Umayma belonged to the indigenous population of the city who embraced Islam and offered protection and assistance to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca. The Ansar played a foundational role in establishing the first Islamic community in Medina, providing both material support and political backing that proved essential for the survival and growth of the early Muslim state.

The female companions like Umayma held important positions within the early Islamic community, participating in religious life and contributing to the social fabric of Medinan society. Women among the Sahabiyya were recognized for their roles in supporting the community during its formative years, though specific details about individual contributions often remain limited in historical records.

Umayma lived during one of the most transformative periods in Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the first Muslim community in Medina, the gradual expansion of Islamic influence throughout the Arabian Peninsula, and the consolidation of Islamic teachings and practices. Her lifetime spanned the crucial decades when Islam evolved from a small religious movement to a major political and spiritual force in Arabia.

She died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the leadership of Abu Bakr and the early period of Umar ibn al-Khattab's caliphate. This placed her death during the initial phase of Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Like many female companions of her era, Umayma represents the important but often under-documented role of women in early Islamic history. The Ansari women of Medina were integral to the success of the early Muslim community, providing the social foundation upon which the Islamic state was built. Her inclusion among the recognized companions reflects the acknowledgment of women's contributions to the establishment and early development of the Islamic community.

bio: Umayma bint Ruqayqa (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Umayma bint Ruqayqa was a female Companion who narrated from the Prophet Muhammad. She is known by her mother's name, Ruqayqa. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir give her father as 'Abd ibn Bijad, of the clan of Taym ibn Murra of Quraysh, while Ibn Hibban names him 'Abd Allah ibn Najjad. According to Ibn Sa'd and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, her mother Ruqayqa was a daughter of Khuwaylid ibn Asad and a sister of Khadija, which made Umayma Khadija's niece; Mus'ab al-Zubayri instead made Ruqayqa a daughter of Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza. Ibn Manda and Abu Nu'aym called Umayma herself Khadija's sister, which Ibn al-Athir rejects. Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir also list an Umayma bint Ruqayqa bint Abi Sayfi of Hashim as a separate woman. She was among the women who gave the pledge of allegiance. Her best-known hadith, recorded by al-Tirmidhi, Malik and others, describes how she came with a group of women to pledge that they would not associate anything with God, steal, commit adultery, kill their children, bring slander or disobey him in what is right. The Prophet answered, 'In what you are able and can bear,' and said, 'I do not shake hands with women; my word to a hundred women is like my word to one woman.' Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir and her daughter Hukayma narrated from her. Ibn Sa'd names her husband as Habib ibn Ka'b ibn 'Utayr al-Thaqafi, by whom she had children. Mus'ab al-Zubayri and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar report that Mu'awiya moved her to Syria and built her a house there.

bio: Umayma bint Ruqayqa bint Abi Sayfi (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca.
bio_full:
Umayya bint Ruqayqa bint Abi Sayfi was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. As one of the early followers of Islam, she lived during the foundational period of the Islamic community in the early seventh century.

Like other female companions of her era, Umayma would have experienced the dramatic social and religious transformations that accompanied the emergence of Islam in Arabian society. The period of her lifetime, spanning approximately four decades until her death around 635 CE, encompassed the entire Meccan period of Muhammad's prophetic mission, the pivotal migration (hijra) to Medina, the establishment of the first Islamic state, and the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate.

Her significance to Islamic tradition lies primarily in her role within the early Muslim community and her connection to the preservation of Islamic teachings. As indicated by her association with hadith sciences, she likely served as one of the many companions who helped transmit the sayings, actions, and teachings of Prophet Muhammad to subsequent generations. This function was particularly important among the female companions, who often had access to aspects of the Prophet's life and teachings that were not always witnessed by male companions, particularly those relating to family life and interactions with women.

The early female companions like Umayma played crucial roles in the development and transmission of Islamic knowledge, though the specific details of their individual contributions are often less extensively documented than those of their male contemporaries. Their participation in the early Islamic community helped establish precedents for women's roles in religious scholarship and community life.

Umayma's relatively short lifespan of about forty years meant that she lived through the most formative period of Islamic history, witnessing the religion's growth from a small group of followers in Mecca to a established religious and political force across much of the Arabian Peninsula. Her death around 635 CE occurred during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, just a few years after the Prophet's passing, placing her among those companions who experienced the transition from the prophetic period to the early institutional development of the Islamic state.

bio: Umayna bint Khalaf (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Umayna bint Khalaf was among the early female companions of the Prophet Muhammad, known in Islamic tradition as a Sahabiyya. Born around 593 CE in Mecca, she lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula and witnessed the initial spread of the faith during the early seventh century.

Umayna is historically recognized as one of the Muslims who participated in the emigration to Abyssinia, a significant event in early Islamic history that occurred around 615 CE. This migration, known as the first Hijra, took place when a group of early Muslims sought refuge in the Christian kingdom of Aksum to escape persecution in Mecca. The emigration to Abyssinia preceded the more famous migration to Medina and represented one of the earliest instances of Muslims seeking sanctuary outside the Arabian Peninsula.

As an emigrant to Abyssinia, Umayna would have been among the small community of Muslims who lived under the protection of the Aksumite ruler, traditionally identified as the Negus. This experience would have exposed her to a different cultural and religious environment while maintaining her Islamic faith during a period of significant hardship for the early Muslim community.

The historical record places Umayna within the tradition of early Islamic ascetics, suggesting she may have been known for practices of spiritual discipline and devotion. However, specific details about her ascetic practices or teachings are not well-documented in surviving historical sources.

Umayna's life spanned the crucial early decades of Islam, from before the Prophet Muhammad's mission began until shortly after his death in 632 CE. She died around 633 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr's leadership.

Her significance in Islamic history lies primarily in her status as one of the early female companions who demonstrated commitment to the new faith during its most challenging period. As part of the Abyssinian emigrant community, she represents the experience of early Muslims who maintained their religious identity while living as minorities in foreign lands. Her inclusion among the recognized Sahabiyya reflects the important role that women played in the early Islamic community, particularly during times of persecution and migration.

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Umayr bin Habib bin Hubbasha (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Umayr bin Habib bin Hubbasha was a companion (sahaba) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 600 CE, he was among the Muslims who migrated to Medina and became part of the early Islamic community there.

Umayr is historically recognized as one of the Companions of the Pledge of Ridwan, a significant oath of allegiance taken by Muslim followers under a tree at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This pledge, referenced in the Quran (48:18), occurred during a tense diplomatic mission when Muslims traveled from Medina to Mecca to perform pilgrimage but were initially prevented from entering the city. The approximately 1,400 companions who took this pledge committed to stand by Prophet Muhammad regardless of the consequences, demonstrating their loyalty during a critical moment in early Islamic history.

The Pledge of Ridwan marked a turning point in Muslim-Meccan relations, ultimately leading to the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which established a temporary peace between the two communities. Those who participated in this pledge, including Umayr, are held in special regard within Islamic tradition due to the Quranic verse that expresses divine approval of their commitment.

As a resident of Medina, Umayr would have witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim community and the development of Islamic law and practice. The companions who lived in Medina during this period played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings and sayings of Prophet Muhammad, contributing to what would later become the science of hadith literature.

Umayr's death around 640 CE placed him among the early companions who did not live to see the major territorial expansions of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula. His generation of companions served as the foundational link between Prophet Muhammad's teachings and the subsequent generations of Muslims, making their testimonies and preserved accounts essential sources for Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

While specific details about Umayr's individual contributions beyond his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan are not extensively documented in major historical sources, his status as a companion who witnessed key events in early Islamic history places him among the important figures of the first Muslim generation.

bio: Umayr bin Ma'bad bin al-'Az'ar (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Umayr bin Ma'bad bin al-'Az'ar was a companion (sahaba) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslim community based in Medina following the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

Umayr is historically recognized as one of the "Companions of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds particular significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces, and those who participated alongside the Prophet are held in special esteem within Islamic tradition. The battle marked a turning point in the early Muslim community's struggle for survival and establishment.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Umayr would have been part of the close-knit community that formed around the Prophet during the Medina period. The companions played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the teachings, sayings, and practices of the Prophet, which later became fundamental sources for Islamic law and practice through the hadith literature.

The companions who lived in Medina during this period witnessed the development of the first Islamic society and the establishment of many religious and social practices that would become central to Islamic civilization. They served not only as the Prophet's followers but also as the primary sources for later generations seeking to understand and implement Islamic teachings.

Umayr's death in 634 CE places him among those companions who lived through the Prophet's entire Medina period, which lasted until the Prophet's death in 632 CE, and into the early years of the first Caliph Abu Bakr's rule. This timing meant he experienced both the foundational period of Islamic community building and the beginning of the rapid expansion that would follow.

While specific details about Umayr's individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in the historical record, his status as a companion and participant in this pivotal battle secured his place in early Islamic history. The companions collectively represent the human link between the Prophet Muhammad and subsequent generations of Muslims, serving as the primary witnesses to the formative events and teachings of early Islam.

bio: Umayr bin Ri'ab bin Hudhayfa (c. 593–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Umayr bin Ri'ab bin Hudhayfa was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the foundational period of Islam in the late sixth and early seventh centuries CE. Born around 593 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, he was among the early converts to Islam during its initial spread in Mecca.

Umayr is most notably remembered as one of the Muslims who participated in the migration to Abyssinia, a pivotal event in early Islamic history. This migration, which occurred around 615 CE, took place when the early Muslim community in Mecca faced increasing persecution from the ruling Quraysh tribe. The Prophet Muhammad advised a group of his followers to seek refuge in the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, where they could practice their faith freely under the protection of the Negus, the Abyssinian king.

As one of these early emigrants, Umayr demonstrated the commitment and sacrifice characteristic of the first generation of Muslims. The migration to Abyssinia required leaving behind family, property, and familiar surroundings to preserve religious freedom and community survival. This group of emigrants included some of the most devoted early Muslims, and their willingness to undertake this journey reflected the serious challenges facing the nascent Muslim community in Mecca.

Umayr's inclusion among the early ascetics suggests he was known for his pious lifestyle and spiritual devotion. The early ascetic tradition in Islam emphasized simplicity, devotion to worship, and detachment from worldly concerns, values that were particularly important during the formative years of the Muslim community.

He lived through the crucial early decades of Islamic history, witnessing the religion's establishment and initial expansion. His death in 634 CE occurred during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just two years after the Prophet Muhammad's death, placing him among those companions who experienced both the prophetic period and the beginning of the post-prophetic era.

While specific details about Umayr's individual contributions are limited in historical sources, his status as a companion and early emigrant places him among the foundational figures of Islam. The companions who made the migration to Abyssinia hold particular significance in Islamic history as examples of faithfulness under persecution and willingness to sacrifice for religious principles during Islam's most vulnerable early period.

bio: Umair bin Abi Waqqas, a companion of Badr, migrated to Yathrib, participated with the Prophet Muhammad in the Battle of Badr, and was killed in the battle.
bio_full: 'Umayr ibn Abi Waqqas was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Zuhra of Quraysh and a brother of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; Ibn 'Abd al-Barr gives their father's name as Malik ibn Wuhayb. His mother was Hamna bint Sufyan ibn Umayya ibn 'Abd Shams. Ibn al-Athir describes him as an early convert and an emigrant, and Abu Nu'aym calls him one of the early emigrants. According to Ibn Sa'd, the Prophet paired him in brotherhood with 'Amr ibn Mu'adh, brother of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. Sa'd reported that before Badr, when the army was being reviewed, 'Umayr hid for fear that he would be sent back. The Prophet judged him too young, and 'Umayr wept, after which the Prophet allowed him to go. Sa'd recalled that he used to tie the straps of 'Umayr's sword for him because he was so young; Abu Nu'aym's report says the Prophet tied them. 'Umayr was killed at Badr aged sixteen, and the sources name 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd as the man who killed him. Ibn al-Athir reports Sa'd's statement that God granted 'Umayr the martyrdom he had sought.

bio_sources.title: Umayr ibn Abi Waqqas — Ibn Sa'd, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr (al-Isti'ab), Ibn al-Athir (Usd al-Ghaba), Ibn Hibban, Abu Nu'aym (hadithtransmitters.hawramani.com)

bio: Umayr/'Amr bin 'Auf (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Ansari, also called 'Umayr, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad who fought at Badr. Most sources describe him as an ally (halif) of Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy of Quraysh; Ibn Ishaq instead calls him a client (mawla) of Suhayl ibn 'Amr. Ibn Sa'd, citing al-Waqidi, says he was of Yemeni origin, that he accepted Islam early and that he accompanied the Prophet. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir say he lived in Medina and left no descendants. The Companion al-Miswar ibn Makhrama narrated a single report from him. It relates that the Prophet took the jizya from the Magians of Bahrain and sent Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah there; when Abu 'Ubayda returned with wealth, the Ansar came to the dawn prayer, and the Prophet told them, 'By God, it is not poverty that I fear for you,' warning instead that worldly wealth would be spread out before them. He is distinct from 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Muzani, another Companion, who died late in the reign of Mu'awiya.

Her mother was Umama bint Bukayr ibn Tha'laba, whose line Ibn Sa'd traces back to Jushm ibn al-Khazraj. She married Bajjad ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Amir ibn Mujamma' ibn al-'Attaf ibn Dubay'a. Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and pledged allegiance (bay'a) to the Prophet Muhammad. His short entry gives no further details of her life and no date of birth or death.

bio: Umayra bint Jubayr bin Sakhr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umayra bint Jubayr bin Sakhr was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. As an Ansari companion, she belonged to the indigenous inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, played a crucial role in the establishment of the early Islamic community in Medina. They provided refuge, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) from Mecca, demonstrating their commitment to the new faith despite facing significant social and economic challenges. As one of the Ansari women, Umayra would have been part of this foundational support network that enabled Islam to take root and flourish in Medina.

Female companions like Umayra occupied important positions in early Islamic society, often serving as transmitters of religious knowledge, caregivers during conflicts, and active participants in community life. The women of Medina, particularly those from the Ansar, were known for their strength, independence, and direct involvement in religious and social matters. They frequently sought religious guidance directly from the Prophet Muhammad and played vital roles in preserving and passing down Islamic teachings to subsequent generations.

Umayra's designation as a companion indicates that she lived during the prophetic period and had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad, placing her among the first generation of Muslims whose testimonies and experiences became fundamental sources for understanding early Islamic history and practice. The companions, both male and female, are revered in Islamic tradition as the primary witnesses to the Prophet's teachings and conduct.

Her death around 635 CE places her within the generation that witnessed both the establishment of Islam in Medina and the beginning of the rapid expansion of the Islamic state under the first caliph, Abu Bakr. The Ansari companions like Umayra represent the local Medinan contribution to Islamic civilization, demonstrating how the indigenous population embraced and helped shape the emerging Muslim community. Their support was instrumental in transforming Islam from a persecuted movement in Mecca to a thriving religious and political entity in Medina.

Umayra bint Qurat bin Khansa' was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she was among the Ansar, the residents of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions based in Medina, Umayra belonged to the community that played a crucial role in establishing the first Islamic state. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were the Medinan tribes who converted to Islam and provided essential support to the early Muslim community during its most vulnerable period. Their acceptance of Islam and protection of the Prophet Muhammad was fundamental to the religion's survival and growth.

Umayra lived during a pivotal time in Islamic history, witnessing the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, the development of Islamic law and social structures, and the early expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime spanned the Prophet's ministry in Medina from 622 CE until his death in 632 CE, as well as the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr.

The female companions of the Prophet Muhammad, known collectively as the Sahabiyyat, hold a significant place in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslim women. They are regarded as exemplars of faith and are remembered for their contributions to the early Islamic community, though specific details about many individual companions' lives have not been extensively preserved in historical records.

Umayra's designation as an Ansari companion places her among the Medinan supporters who were instrumental in Islam's early development. The Ansar's role in Islamic history is commemorated in the Quran and prophetic traditions, where they are praised for their generosity, faith, and sacrifice in supporting the nascent Muslim community.

She died around 635 CE during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second Rashidun caliph, at a time when Islamic expansion was beginning to extend beyond the Arabian Peninsula into the Byzantine and Sassanian territories.

Umayya bint Khulayfa bin 'Adi was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the indigenous inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Umayya was part of the community that played a crucial role in the establishment of the early Muslim state in Medina. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, were primarily from the tribes of Aws and Khazraj who had converted to Islam before the Prophet's arrival and provided essential support during the formative years of the Muslim community.

Living during the foundational period of Islam, Umayya would have witnessed the major developments of the early Muslim community, including the establishment of the first Islamic constitution, the construction of the Prophet's Mosque, and the various military campaigns that secured the nascent Muslim state. The female companions like Umayya contributed to the early Muslim society in various ways, supporting the community's religious, social, and economic activities.

Her designation as a Sahabiyya places her among the distinguished group of women who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and embraced Islam during his lifetime. These women companions are revered in Islamic tradition for their early acceptance of Islam and their role in transmitting Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

The Ansari women, in particular, were known for their active participation in community life. They supported the muhajirin (emigrants from Mecca) through various means and contributed to the social fabric of Medina's diverse Muslim community.

Umayya's death around 635 CE occurred during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, just a few years after the Prophet's passing in 632 CE. This places her among the early companions who lived through both the Meccan and Medinan periods of Islamic history and witnessed the transition from the Prophet's leadership to the era of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs.

Her inclusion in historical records as a named Sahabiyya reflects the recognition given to women companions in early Islamic sources, acknowledging their contributions to the establishment and development of the Muslim community in its earliest and most critical phase.

bio: Umm 'Abdullah bin 'Aidy b. Khuwaylid (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm 'Abdullah bin 'Aidy b. Khuwaylid was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Mecca during the early formative period of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she witnessed the emergence and early development of the Islamic community during the late 6th and early 7th centuries.

As a contemporary of the Prophet, Umm 'Abdullah belonged to the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and experienced the initial decades of Islamic teaching and practice. Her presence in Mecca placed her at the geographical heart of early Islam, where the religion first emerged and where many of its foundational experiences occurred.

Umm 'Abdullah is primarily recognized in Islamic historical sources for her role as a narrator of hadith—the recorded sayings, actions, and teachings of Prophet Muhammad. As a female hadith narrator, she contributed to the preservation and transmission of prophetic traditions that would later become essential sources for Islamic law, theology, and practice. The hadith literature represents one of the most important foundations of Islamic scholarship, second only to the Quran itself, making the work of early narrators like Umm 'Abdullah crucial to the religion's development.

Her inclusion among the recognized female companions who transmitted hadith reflects the active participation of women in the early Islamic community's scholarly and religious activities. Female companions played significant roles in preserving and passing down Islamic teachings, particularly in areas where they had direct access to the Prophet's household and daily life.

Living during the crucial period between approximately 595 and 635 CE, Umm 'Abdullah's life spanned the pre-Islamic era, the initial revelation of the Quran, the establishment of the first Muslim community, and the early expansion of Islam following the Prophet's death in 632 CE. Her forty-year lifespan encompassed the entire prophetic period and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate.

The historical record of Umm 'Abdullah represents the broader contribution of first-generation Muslim women to the preservation of Islamic tradition. Through their roles as hadith narrators, these women ensured that prophetic teachings reached subsequent generations, contributing to the scholarly foundation upon which Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice would be built.

bio: Umm 'Abdullah bint 'Azib (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Abd Allah bint Azib was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Abd Allah bint Azib ibn al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Jusham ibn Majda'a ibn Haritha, and lists her among the women of Banu Haritha, a clan of the Aws. She was the full sister, through both father and mother, of the Companion al-Bara' ibn Azib.

Ibn Sa'd names their mother as Umm Habiba bint Abi Habiba ibn al-Hubab, of Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar. He also records another account, which says their mother was Umm Khalid bint Thabit ibn Sinan ibn Ubayd ibn al-Abjar. He states that Umm Abd Allah accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Messenger of God. Ibn Sa'd records no marriage, children or date of death for her.

bio: Umm 'Abdullah bint Milhan (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Abd Allah bint Milhan was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Abd Allah bint Milhan ibn Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Haram ibn Jundub ibn Amir ibn Ghanm ibn Adi ibn al-Najjar, and lists her among the women of Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj. He gives exactly the same paternal lineage for Umm Sulaym bint Milhan and Umm Haram bint Milhan, and places her entry directly after theirs.

On the authority of Muhammad ibn Umar al-Waqidi, Ibn Sa'd reports that she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Messenger of God. He records nothing further about her: no mother, marriage, children or date of death is given.

bio: Umm 'Abdullah bint Sawad bin Razn (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm 'Abdullah bint Sawad bin Razn was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early 7th century. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the residents of Medina who supported and assisted the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Umm 'Abdullah was among the indigenous population of Medina who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community. The Ansar played a vital role in the establishment and growth of the early Islamic state, offering shelter, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca known as the Muhajirun.

Her designation as a Sahabiyya places her within the revered category of the Prophet's companions, individuals who met, believed in, and died as Muslims during the Prophet Muhammad's lifetime. The companions hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly received the teachings of Islam and witnessed the Prophet's example firsthand.

Living in Medina during this transformative period, Umm 'Abdullah would have experienced the foundational years of the Islamic community, including the establishment of the first Muslim society, the compilation of the Constitution of Medina, and the various challenges faced by the early Muslim community. Her presence in Medina during the Prophet's time suggests she was part of the social and religious fabric of the community that supported the development of Islamic practices and governance.

The Ansari women, including Umm 'Abdullah, contributed to the early Muslim community in various capacities, though specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the historical sources. Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

Her recognition as a companion of the Prophet reflects the important role that women played in the early Islamic community and their acknowledgment within the historical tradition. As part of the Ansar, she represents the crucial support system that enabled the survival and growth of Islam during its most vulnerable early years in Medina.

bio_full:
Umm 'Amir bint 'Amr bin Hadida was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Umm 'Amir witnessed and participated in the formative period of Islamic history. The Ansar played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community, providing both material support and protection to the nascent Islamic movement during its most vulnerable early years. Her presence in Medina during this period means she would have experienced firsthand the development of Islamic teachings, practices, and community structures as they took shape in the first Muslim city-state.

The designation of sahabiyya, or female companion, indicates that Umm 'Amir had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as part of the generation that personally knew and followed him. This status holds particular significance in Islamic tradition, as the companions are regarded as the primary transmitters of Islamic knowledge, practices, and authentic accounts of the Prophet's life and teachings.

Living in Medina during the 620s and 630s CE, Umm 'Amir would have been present during many of the key events that shaped early Islamic history, including the establishment of the Constitution of Medina, the development of Islamic law and social practices, and the consolidation of the Muslim community. Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

While specific details about her individual contributions or particular roles within the early Muslim community are not extensively documented in surviving historical sources, her recognition as an Ansari companion underscores the important role that the women of Medina played in supporting and sustaining the early Islamic community. The Ansari women, in particular, were instrumental in providing the social foundation that allowed Islam to flourish in its new home, contributing to both the practical and spiritual development of the community during its crucial formative years.

bio: Umm 'Ammarah Nasaybah ( , (b. c. 591 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Umm 'Ammarah Nasaybah bint Ka'b al-Maziniyyah was a female companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century. Born around 591 CE, she belonged to the Khazraj tribe and played a notable role during the formative period of the Islamic community.

She is most recognized for her participation in the Second Pledge of Aqabah, also known as the Pledge of War, which took place around 622 CE. This gathering was significant as it involved representatives from Medina who pledged to protect Muhammad and invited him to migrate to their city. Umm 'Ammarah was among the small number of women who participated in this crucial political and religious agreement that facilitated the Prophet's migration from Mecca to Medina, marking the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

According to historical accounts, Umm 'Ammarah demonstrated remarkable courage during the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, where she reportedly defended the Prophet when Muslim forces faced difficulties. Islamic historical sources describe her active participation in protecting Muhammad during critical moments of the battle, though the specific details vary across different accounts.

She is also mentioned in various hadith collections, where her actions and statements are recorded as part of the oral tradition that preserved the sayings and practices of early Islamic figures. Her inclusion in these sources reflects her recognized status within the early Muslim community and her proximity to significant events during the Prophet's lifetime.

As one of the female companions, Umm 'Ammarah represents the active role that women played in the early Islamic community, particularly in Medina. Her participation in key political agreements and military events illustrates that women were involved in the foundational moments of Islamic history beyond domestic spheres.

Her legacy is preserved in Islamic historical literature as an example of the Sahaba, the generation of Muslims who lived during the time of Prophet Muhammad. The accounts of her life contribute to the broader understanding of how the early Muslim community was established and the diverse individuals who participated in its formation. She died around 631 CE, shortly before the Prophet's own death, having witnessed the transformation of the Arabian Peninsula and the establishment of the early Islamic state.

According to Ibn Sa'd, she was first married to Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib of the tribe of Thaqif, and bore him a son, Abd Allah. She later married her cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and bore him a daughter, Atika.

Ibn Sa'd's short entry on her gives only her lineage and marriages. It does not state that she accepted Islam or gave the pledge to the Prophet, and no date or place of death is recorded.

bio: Umm 'Amr bint Mahmud bin Maslama (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.

Umm Amr bint Mahmud was a woman of the Ansar of Medina who accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Amr bint Mahmud ibn Maslama ibn Salama ibn Khalid ibn Adi ibn Majda'a ibn Haritha, and names her mother as Umama bint Bishr ibn Waqsh, of the clan of Abd al-Ashhal. Ibn al-Athir notes that she was the niece of the Companion Muhammad ibn Maslama, and that her father Mahmud ibn Maslama was killed at Khaybar.

According to Ibn Sa'd, she married her cousin Abd Allah, son of Muhammad ibn Maslama, and bore him two sons, Amr and Humayd. After him she married Zayd ibn Sa'd ibn Zayd of the clan of Abd al-Ashhal.

Ibn al-Athir records her pledge on the authority of Ibn Habib. Ibn Sa'd also has an entry on her sister Umm Manzur bint Mahmud, mother of the jurist Mahmud ibn Labid, who likewise accepted Islam and gave the pledge. No date of death is recorded for Umm Amr.

bio_full:
Umm 'Amr bint Salaama bin Waqash was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the initial decades of Islamic history and died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate following Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Umm 'Amr belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE. This migration, known as the Hijra, marked a crucial turning point in Islamic history, and the Ansar played a vital role in establishing the early Muslim community in Medina. The city, originally called Yathrib, became the center of the growing Islamic state under Muhammad's leadership.

Her designation as a sahabiyya indicates that she personally knew Muhammad and accepted Islam during his lifetime. The companions of the Prophet hold a special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly received Islamic teachings and witnessed the establishment of the faith. Female companions like Umm 'Amr were part of the early Muslim community that helped shape Islamic society during its foundational period.

Living in Medina during this transformative era, Umm 'Amr would have experienced the major events that defined early Islamic history, including the establishment of the Muslim community, various military campaigns, and the consolidation of Islamic teachings and practices. The Ansar, as the local supporters of the Muslim cause, were instrumental in providing the social and material foundation necessary for Islam's growth beyond its origins in Mecca.

Her lifespan, covering approximately four decades from the late sixth to early seventh century, places her among those who witnessed Islam's emergence from a small religious movement to a significant political and social force in the Arabian Peninsula. As one of the female companions, she represents the important role that women played in the early Islamic community, though specific details about her individual contributions and activities are not extensively documented in the historical sources that have survived to the present day.

bio: Umm 'Ubayd bint Suraqa (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Ubayd bint Suraqa was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the clan of Adi ibn al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Ubayd bint Suraqa ibn al-Harith ibn Adi ibn Malik ibn Adi ibn Amir ibn Ghanm ibn Adi ibn al-Najjar. She was the full sister of Haritha ibn Suraqa, who fought at Badr and was killed there as a martyr. Their mother was al-Rubayyi' bint al-Nadr ibn Damdam, known as Umm Haritha.

According to Ibn Sa'd, her first husband was Rafi' ibn Zayd ibn Adi of the clan of al-Najjar. After him she married Tamim ibn Ghaziyya ibn Amr of the clan of Mazin ibn al-Najjar.

Ibn Sa'd states that Umm Ubayd and her mother both accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn al-Athir also lists her among the women who pledged, on the authority of Ibn Habib. No date of death is recorded.

bio: Umm 'Ubays (b. c. 594 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Early Muslim — Tortured for Faith.
bio_full:
Umm ʿUbays (Arabic: أُمُّ عُبَيْسٍ) or Umm ʿUmays was a woman in Arabia who was an early convert to Islam and one of the disciples (Sahaba) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

Biography
She was a slave in Mecca who became an early convert to Islam. After 614 she was tortured in an attempt to force her to renounce her faith. Abu Bakr bought and  manumitted her. It was in response to the purchase of these slaves that Abu Bakr's father protested: "I see that you are freeing weak slaves. Why don't you free powerful men who could defend you and protect you?" Abu Bakr replied, "I am only trying to do what I am attempting for God's sake."
Umm Ubays had a sister, Harithah bint al-Muammil.
It is sometimes asserted that Umm Ubays was the daughter of Al-Nahdiah. This is apparently due to the ambiguous wording of Ibn Saad.

bio: Umm 'Uthman or Umm Walad Shayba (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Uthman bint Sufyan was a woman of Quraysh from the clan of Abd al-Dar. Ibn Abd al-Barr describes her as the mother of the elder sons of Shayba, and lists her among the women who gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir also state that she pledged.

Safiyya bint Shayba narrated from her, and Abd Allah ibn Musafi' narrated from his mother, who narrated from her. Abu Nu'aym records a hadith from her that the Prophet called Shayba, who opened the House (the Ka'ba) for him. When the Prophet came out, he said he had seen a horn inside and told Shayba to cover it, because nothing should be in the House that distracts a person praying.

In their entries on her, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir also give a report through Budayl ibn Maysara and Safiyya bint Shayba from a woman called 'Umm walad Shayba' (the mother of Shayba's child). She said she saw the Prophet running between al-Safa and al-Marwa, saying that the valley bed is crossed only by running. Neither author states outright that Umm walad Shayba and Umm Uthman are the same woman. No date of death is recorded.
