bio: Umm Aban bint 'Utba b. Rabi'a (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Aban bint Utba ibn Rabi'a ibn Abd Shams ibn Abd Manaf was a woman of Quraysh from the clan of Abd Shams. Ibn al-Athir notes that she was the maternal aunt of Mu'awiya.

According to Ibn al-Athir, she was in Syria with her husband Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-As, who was killed at the battle of Ajnadayn, after which she returned to Medina. Both Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir report that when she came back from Syria, Umar, Ali, al-Zubayr and Talha each asked to marry her. She refused all of them except Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, whom she married.

Ibn Abd al-Barr states that he knew of no narration from her, and Ibn al-Athir says the same. No date of death is recorded.

bio: Umm al-'Ala' al-Ansariyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm al-Ala al-Ansariyya was a woman of the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam, gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad, and narrated from him. He adds that she took part in the Khaybar campaign with the Prophet. The sources do not give her father's name.

She is best known for the account of Uthman ibn Maz'un. When the Emigrants arrived in Medina, the Ansar competed to host them and drew lots, and Uthman ibn Maz'un fell to her household. Abu Nu'aym records, through Kharija ibn Zayd and al-Zuhri, that when Uthman died she declared that God had honoured him. The Prophet objected that no one, not even he, could know this. She said she would never again vouch for anyone. She later saw in a dream a spring flowing for Uthman, and the Prophet told her it was his good deeds.

Ibn Abd al-Barr says her hadith was known in Medina, and that Kharija ibn Zayd ibn Thabit and Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr narrated from her. Abd al-Malik's report is that the Prophet visited her when she was ill and told her that illness expiates a Muslim's sins. Ibn al-Sakan held that the Umm al-Ala narrated by Kharija and the one narrated by Abd al-Malik were two different women. Ibn al-Athir also gives a separate entry for an Umm al-Ala who was the paternal aunt of Hizam ibn Hakim. No date of death is recorded.

bio_full:
Umm al-Dahhak bint Mas'ud was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the term used for the inhabitants of Medina who supported and assisted the Prophet and the early Muslim community following the migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari women of Medina, Umm al-Dahhak would have been among those who witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim community and the development of early Islamic society. The Ansar played a crucial role in providing sanctuary and support to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca, helping to establish the foundation of the Islamic state in Medina.

The title "Umm al-Dahhak" indicates she was the mother of someone named al-Dahhak, following the Arabic naming convention of referring to individuals by their relationship to their children. Her father's name, Mas'ud, suggests she came from a notable family within the Medinan community, as family lineages were important markers of identity and social standing in Arabian society of that period.

Living during the formative years of Islam, Umm al-Dahhak would have experienced the rapid expansion of the Muslim community and the social transformations that accompanied the new faith. The women companions of this era, particularly those from Medina, contributed to the early Muslim society in various ways, including supporting the community's needs, participating in religious life, and helping to transmit Islamic teachings and practices.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, approximately three years after the Prophet's death and during a period of significant expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula. As a sahabiyya, she holds a revered position in Islamic tradition, representing the generation of women who directly encountered the Prophet and participated in the foundational period of the Muslim community.

While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the historical record, her recognition as a companion of the Prophet reflects her significance within the early Muslim community and her role in the establishment of Islam in Medina.

full: Umm al-Fadl Lubaba al-Kubra bint al-Harith ibn Hazn al-Hilaliyya
primaryTitle: Second Woman to Accept Islam; Aunt of Khalid ibn al-Walid
bio: Umm al-Fadl Lubaba al-Kubra bint al-Harith ibn Hazn al-Hilaliyya (c. 594 CE–655 CE, Medinah) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Second Woman to Accept Islam; Aunt of Khalid ibn al-Walid.
bio_full:
Umm al-Fadl Lubaba bint al-Harith ibn Hazn was a woman of the Banu Hilal, a branch of Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, and the wife of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle. Her mother was Hind bint Awf. Her full sister was Maymuna, wife of the Prophet, and her half-sister Lubaba the Younger was the mother of Khalid ibn al-Walid. Through her mother she was also half-sister of Asma and Salma, daughters of Umays.

Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr report it is said she was the first woman to become Muslim after Khadija. The Prophet used to visit her and take his midday rest at her house. A report from Ibn Abbas quotes the Prophet calling Maymuna, Umm al-Fadl, Salma and Asma believing sisters. One account relates that after Badr, when Abu Lahab beat Abu Rafi of al-Abbas's household in Mecca, she struck Abu Lahab with a tent pole and split his head.

She bore al-Abbas six sons, al-Fadl, Abd Allah, Ubayd Allah, Ma'bad, Qutham and Abd al-Rahman, and Ibn Abd al-Barr adds a daughter, Umm Habiba. Ibn Abd al-Barr says she narrated many hadiths. Among those who narrated from her were her son Abd Allah ibn Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, her freedman Umayr and Kurayb. She reported that the Prophet recited Surat al-Mursalat in the sunset prayer, and that it was the last time she heard him recite it.

Ibn Abd al-Barr states that she died before al-Abbas, during the caliphate of Uthman, who led her funeral prayer.

He did not grant it, and instead taught them to glorify, praise and magnify God after every prayer. Ibn al-Athir also cites a report from her, transmitted by Qatada, that the Prophet ate meat from a shoulder and then prayed without renewing his ablution. The sources give no date of birth or death for her.

bio: Umm al-Husayn al-Ahmasiyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm al-Husayn al-Ahmasiyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community.

As a companion of the Prophet, Umm al-Husayn held the distinguished status of sahabiyya, a title reserved for those who met Muhammad, believed in his message, and died as Muslims. This designation places her among the most revered figures in Islamic history, as the companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

Umm al-Husayn was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the early Muslim community after the Prophet's migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the political and spiritual capital of the nascent Islamic state, making her residence there significant for her role in the community's development.

Her primary contribution to Islamic scholarship lies in the field of hadith sciences, where she served as a narrator of prophetic traditions. Female companions like Umm al-Husayn played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. These hadith form an essential component of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice, second only to the Quran in their importance to Muslim scholarship.

The participation of women like Umm al-Husayn in hadith transmission demonstrates the active role that female companions played in preserving Islamic knowledge during the religion's earliest period. Their contributions were recognized and valued by the early Muslim community, and their narrations were included in the formal collections of hadith that would later become authoritative sources for Islamic law and theology.

Umm al-Husayn died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of the second Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab, placing her death within the Rashidun period when the Islamic empire was rapidly expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Her relatively short life of approximately forty years encompassed the crucial decades of Islam's establishment and early growth, making her witness to one of the most transformative periods in religious and world history.

bio: Umm al-Mundhir bint Qays bin 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Umm al-Mundhir bint Qays ibn 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd was a woman of the Ansar of Medina from the Banu al-Najjar. Ibn Sa'd traces her line to 'Adi ibn al-Najjar, while al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym place her family in the Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar. Her personal name is given as Salma bint Qays by al-Tabarani and others; Ibn al-Athir reports it with 'it is said'. She was a full sister of Sulayt ibn Qays, who fought at Badr and was killed as a martyr at the Battle of the Bridge (Jisr Abi 'Ubayd); their mother was Rughayba bint Zurara. She married Qays ibn Sa'sa'a ibn Wahb and bore him a son, al-Mundhir. Ibn Sa'd records that she accepted Islam, pledged allegiance (bay'a) to the Prophet Muhammad and narrated from him. Abu Nu'aym, quoted by Ibn al-Athir, calls her one of the Prophet's maternal aunts and says she prayed towards both qiblas with him. Her best-known report, recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Sa'd, tells how the Prophet visited her with 'Ali, who was recovering from illness. The Prophet ate from hanging bunches of dates but stopped 'Ali, saying he was still convalescent; when she then served barley and chard, the Prophet told 'Ali to eat from that, as it suited him better. It was transmitted from her by Ya'qub ibn Abi Ya'qub. The sources give no date of birth or death.

bio: Umm al-Rubayyi' bint Aslam (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm al-Rubayyi' bint Aslam was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community after their migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions, Umm al-Rubayyi' was part of the indigenous population of Medina who converted to Islam and played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community. The Ansar were instrumental in providing shelter, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) who had left Mecca due to persecution, making the successful establishment of the early Islamic state possible.

The designation "Umm al-Rubayyi'" indicates she was known by her relationship to her child, following the common Arabic naming convention of using "Umm" (mother of) followed by the name of one's child. Her father's name was Aslam, indicating her lineage within the tribal structure of pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society.

Living during the foundational period of Islam, Umm al-Rubayyi' would have witnessed the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, the development of Islamic law and practice, and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. As a female companion, she represents the important but often less documented role of women in early Islamic history.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This timing suggests she lived through the entire Medinan period of the Prophet's life and the beginning of Islamic expansion under the first caliphs.

While specific details about her individual contributions are not extensively recorded in surviving historical sources, her status as a recognized companion places her among the first generation of Muslims whose acceptance of Islam and support for the early community were considered foundational to the religion's establishment. The companions, both male and female, are regarded in Islamic tradition as exemplary figures whose proximity to the Prophet Muhammad and early participation in the Muslim community gave them special religious and historical significance.

According to Ibn Sa'd, she was the mother of Ubayy's sons al-Tufayl and Muhammad, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr says she took her kunya from her son al-Tufayl. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr counts her as a Companion who narrated hadith. Ahmad, al-Tabarani and al-Hasan ibn Sufyan record, through Busr ibn Sa'id, that Ubayy and 'Umar disagreed about a pregnant widow, Ubayy holding that she may remarry once she gives birth. Umm al-Tufayl then said that the Prophet had ordered Subay'a al-Aslamiyya to marry once she had given birth. Ibn Hajar notes that Ibn Lahi'a is in its chain. A second report, about a dream the Prophet described, comes through Marwan ibn 'Uthman, whom Ibn Hajar calls abandoned (matruk). Those who transmitted from her include her son Muhammad ibn Ubayy and 'Umara ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm. The sources give no date of birth or death for her.

bio: Umm Atiyya Nusayba bint al-Harith al-Ansariyya al-Khazrajiyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Umm Atiyya — Most Authoritative Female Voice on Funeral Rites.
bio_full:
Umm Atiyya Nusayba bint al-Harith al-Ansariyya al-Khazrajiyya was a prominent female companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Khazraj tribe, one of the two main Arab tribes that welcomed the Prophet and early Muslim community to Medina in 622 CE.

As a Sahabiyya, or female companion, Umm Atiyya was among the women who directly interacted with Prophet Muhammad and learned Islamic teachings firsthand. Her proximity to the Prophet's household and her active participation in the early Muslim community positioned her as an important transmitter of religious knowledge, particularly in areas concerning women's religious practices and Islamic law.

Umm Atiyya is most renowned for her authoritative knowledge of Islamic funeral rites and burial practices. Her detailed understanding of proper procedures for washing, shrouding, and preparing the deceased made her the most trusted female voice on these matters in the early Islamic community. This expertise was particularly crucial for establishing correct practices for preparing deceased women, as Islamic law requires that women handle the funeral preparations for female deceased when possible.

Her contributions to Islamic scholarship extend beyond funeral rites to various aspects of women's religious observances and daily practices. As a hadith transmitter, she preserved and passed down authentic sayings and practices of Prophet Muhammad, contributing to the development of Islamic jurisprudence and religious tradition. Her narrations were considered reliable and were recorded by later hadith scholars who compiled the major collections of prophetic traditions.

Umm Atiyya's role exemplifies the significant contributions of early Muslim women to the preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge. During a formative period when Islamic practices and laws were being established and codified, her firsthand knowledge and careful attention to religious detail helped ensure accurate transmission of important ritual practices to subsequent generations.

She died around 635 CE in Medina, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab. Her legacy endures through the hadith literature, where her narrations continue to inform Islamic legal rulings and religious practices, particularly those relating to funeral rites and women's religious obligations. Her life demonstrates the active role that women played in the early Islamic community as scholars, teachers, and preservers of religious tradition.

bio: Umm Ayman, Barakah (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia. Known as Female Jurist and Scholar.
bio_full:
Baraka bint Thaʿlaba (Arabic: بَـرَكَـة بنت ثَعلَبَة), commonly known by her kunya Umm Ayman (Arabic: أمّ أيمن), was an early Muslim and one of the disciples (Sahaba) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
She was an Abyssinian slave of Muhammad's parents, Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and  Aminah bint Wahb. Following the death of Aminah, Baraka helped to raise Muhammad in the household of his grandfather, Abd Al-Muttalib ibn Hashim. He saw her as a motherly figure. Muhammad later freed her from slavery, but she continued to serve Muhammad and his family. She was an early convert to Islam, and was present at the important battles of Uhud and Khaybar.
Following her freedom, Muhammad also arranged her marriage, first to Ubayd ibn Zayd of the Banu Khazraj, with whom she had a son, Ayman ibn Ubayd, giving her the kunya Umm Ayman (meaning mother of Ayman). She was later married to the adopted son of Muhammad, Zayd ibn Harithah. Her son with Zayd, Usama ibn Zayd, served as a commander in the early Muslim army and led the Expedition of Usama bin Zayd into the Byzantine Empire.

Background
Baraka was the daughter of Tha'laba bin Amr, an Abyssinian. She served as a slave in the household of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Aminah bint Wahb. She cared for Muhammad during infancy and childhood, after the death of Aminah.

Muhammad's childhood
Following Aminah's death in Al-Abwa, Baraka looked after Muhammad, and moved with him to the household of his grandfather in Mecca, where she served him during his childhood  and afterwards, in his adulthood.
According to Ibn Kathir, Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad's paternal grandfather, had told Baraka not to neglect his grandson, especially as many of the Ahl al-Kiṫâb (Arabic: أَهـل الـكِـتـاب, People of the Book) predicted that he would be a prophet of the nation.

Marriages and children
When Muhammad married Khadija, he arranged for Baraka's freedom and marriage to a Khazrajite companion named Ubayd ibn Zayd. Through this marriage, Baraka bore a son named Ayman, and thus she was known as "Umm Ayman" ("Mother of Ayman"). Ayman ibn Ubayd was later killed fighting in the Battle of Hunayn.
Muhammad's adopted son Zayd ibn Harithah later married Baraka. They had a son named Usama who appointed as an army leader by Muhammad and led the successful Expedition of Usama bin Zayd into the Byzantine Empire.

Migration
After Muhammad announced his Prophethood, Umm Ayman became one of his first followers. Later, she migrated to Medina.

Participation in battles

Umm Ayman was present at the Battle of Uhud. She fetched water for the soldiers and helped treat the injured. She also accompanied Muhammad in the Battle of Khaybar.
In the battle of Uhud, many men ran away toward Medina after rumor of the death of Muhammad. Umm Ayman sprinkled dust on the face of some fugitives, gave them a spindle and told them: "give me your sword and [you] spin spindle." Then she went toward the battlefield along with several women. Subsequently, she was injured by an arrow which Hebban bin Araqa, an enemy soldier, shot at her.

Relationships with other early Muslims
Muhammad was fond of Umm Ayman, even thinking of her as like a mother. Several hadiths describe Muhammad's esteem for her. He visited Umm Ayman at her house, and after him, Caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar did the same. In some hadith sources there is a heaven about the virtues of Umm Ayman. She is also praised in Shi'ite sources.
A few hadith have been narrated from her. Those such as Anas ibn Malik, Abu Yazid Madani and Hanash bin Abdullah San'any have narrated from her.

Death
The exact date of Umm Ayman's death is not clear. Some have suggested that she died approximately five months after Muhammad's death. But according to ibn Sa'd, she was alive in the early days of the caliphate of Uthman.

bio: Umm Ayoub bint Qays bin Sa'd (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Ayyub bint Qays ibn Sa'd was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the tribe of al-Khazraj. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Ayyub bint Qays ibn Sa'd ibn Qays ibn Amr ibn Imru' al-Qays ibn Malik al-Agharr, and records from al-Waqidi that she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad.

Ibn Abd al-Barr, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir identify her as the wife of the Companion Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. The Prophet stayed with their household, and she narrated that they once prepared food for him containing some vegetables he disliked. He told his Companions to eat, saying that he was not like one of them, and that he feared to cause discomfort to his companion. This report reached later scholars through Sufyan ibn Uyayna, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Yazid, from his father, from her.

Abu Nu'aym also records from her that the Qur'an was revealed in seven modes (ahruf), and that whichever of them one recites is correct. He opens his entry with a saying of the Prophet that divorcing Umm Ayyub would be a sin.

The sources record no date of death for her.

bio: Umm Ayyash, Client of Ruqayya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Arabia. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Ayyash was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she lived during the formative period of Islam and died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate.

Her name indicates that she was a client (mawla) of Ruqayya, meaning she was likely a freed slave or someone under the protection of a woman named Ruqayya. The institution of clientage was common in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society, where freed slaves often maintained relationships with their former owners' families, gaining social status and protection while providing loyalty and service.

As a sahabiyya, Umm Ayyash was among the women who personally knew the Prophet Muhammad and accepted Islam during his lifetime. The female companions played crucial roles in early Islamic society, often serving as sources of religious knowledge and legal guidance, particularly on matters concerning women's practices and private aspects of the Prophet's life that male companions might not have witnessed.

Umm Ayyash is specifically noted as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. Hadith literature forms one of the fundamental sources of Islamic law and guidance, second only to the Quran. Female companions like Umm Ayyash were essential links in the chain of transmission that preserved the Prophet's teachings for future generations.

The fact that she is remembered as a hadith narrator indicates that later scholars recognized her reliability and that her transmitted accounts were considered authentic enough to be preserved in the hadith collections. Women narrators were particularly important for transmitting knowledge about religious practices, family life, and social customs, areas where they had direct access and observation.

Her inclusion in biographical dictionaries of the companions demonstrates that early Islamic scholarship recognized and valued women's contributions to preserving religious knowledge. Though specific details about her individual narrations or particular contributions may not be extensively documented in surviving sources, her identification as a hadith narrator places her among the important early transmitters who helped establish the foundation of Islamic religious scholarship and legal methodology.

bio: Umm Bujayd al-Ansariyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Bujayd al-Ansariyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she was part of the Ansar, the Medinan supporters who welcomed and aided the Prophet and the Muslim community following the Hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the female companions who had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad, Umm Bujayd contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings through the narration of hadith. The hadith literature, which records the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet, became a fundamental source of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions like Umm Bujayd played a crucial role in this process, particularly in transmitting knowledge about matters that were observed in domestic and social settings where women were present.

Her designation as "al-Ansariyya" indicates her belonging to the Ansar community, distinguishing her from the Muhajirun (emigrants) who had migrated from Mecca. The Ansar held a special position in early Islamic history as the local Medinan tribes who converted to Islam and provided essential support to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years.

The involvement of women like Umm Bujayd in hadith transmission reflects the active participation of female companions in the early Islamic community's religious and social life. These women served as important links in the chain of transmission that helped preserve prophetic traditions for future generations of Muslims.

Umm Bujayd's death around 635 CE places her among the early generation of companions who witnessed the foundational period of Islam and the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina. While detailed biographical information about her specific contributions remains limited in historical sources, her recognition as a narrator of hadith underscores the role that female companions played in the preservation of Islamic knowledge and the continuity of religious instruction during the crucial early decades following the Prophet's death in 632 CE.

Her legacy, like that of other female companions, represents the broader participation of women in the transmission of Islamic teachings and their contributions to the development of hadith sciences as a formal discipline within Islamic scholarship.

bio: Umm Burda, Khawla bint al-Mundhir ( , (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Khawla bint al-Mundhir, known by her kunya Umm Burda, was born around 595 CE and died in 635 CE. She was among the Sahabiyya, the female companions of Prophet Muhammad, and lived in Medina during the early Islamic period.

As an Ansari companion, Khawla belonged to the Ansar, the Muslim inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported Prophet Muhammad and his followers when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE. The Ansar played a crucial role in establishing the early Muslim community in Medina, providing shelter, resources, and protection to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca.

Khawla's designation as a companion of the Prophet indicates that she lived during his lifetime, witnessed his teachings, and was part of the early Muslim community that formed around him in Medina. The companions, both male and female, hold special significance in Islamic tradition as they were direct witnesses to the Prophet's words and actions, and their accounts and experiences became important sources for understanding early Islamic teachings and practices.

Her life spanned a critical period in Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's mission and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate. She would have witnessed the transformation of Arabian society through the spread of Islam, the establishment of the first Muslim state in Medina, and the early expansion of the Muslim community.

The female companions like Umm Burda represent an important but often less documented aspect of early Islamic history. These women were active participants in the early Muslim community, contributing to its social, religious, and sometimes political life. Their presence in historical records, even when limited, demonstrates the role women played in the foundational period of Islam.

Khawla bint al-Mundhir's identification as an Ansari companion places her among a group that Islamic tradition particularly honors for their support of the Prophet and the early Muslim community. Her forty-year lifespan encompassed the most transformative period in early Islamic history, making her part of the generation that witnessed and participated in the establishment of Islam as both a religious and social system in the Arabian Peninsula.

bio: Umm Farwa bint Abi Quhafa bin Amer bin Amr Al-Taymiyyah Al-Qurashi was a companion from the people of Mecca, and she was the sister of the Rashidun Caliph Abu Bakr Al-Siddiq, one of the ten promised Paradise. Her brother Abu Bakr married her to Al-Ash'ath ibn Qais, and she bore him: Muhammad, Ismail, Ishaq, Hubaba, and Qariba.
bio_full:
Umm Farwa bint Abi Quhafa was a woman of Quraysh from the clan of Taym, and the sister of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ibn Sa'd gives her father's name as Uthman ibn Amir ibn Amr ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Taym ibn Murra, known as Abu Quhafa, and her mother as Hind bint Nuqayd ibn Bujayr ibn Abd ibn Qusayy; another source gives the mother's father's name as Nufayl.

According to Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr, her brother Abu Bakr married her to al-Ash'ath ibn Qays al-Kindi. Ibn Sa'd names their children as Muhammad, Ishaq, Isma'il, Hababa and Qurayba.

Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir list her among the women who gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad, and Ibn Hibban states that she was a Companion. Abu Nu'aym calls her 'the owner of the necklace' who is mentioned in the account of the conquest of Mecca.

Scholars differed over whether she is the Umm Farwa who narrated, through al-Qasim ibn Ghannam, that the deed most beloved to God is prayer at the start of its time. Ibn Abd al-Barr placed this hadith under her name and called the view that the narrator was an Ansari woman a mistake. Ibn al-Athir, noting that al-Qasim ibn Ghannam was of the Ansar, held that Abu Bakr's sister had no connection to that narration. The sources consulted give no date of death.

bio: Umm Habib bint Jahsh (c. 594 CE–667 CE, Medinah) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Habib bint Jahsh, also called Umm Habiba or Habiba, was a female Companion of the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn al-Athir gives her as the daughter of Jahsh ibn Ri'ab al-Asadi, and the sister of Zaynab bint Jahsh, Mother of the Believers. Her mother was Umayma bint Abd al-Muttalib, an aunt of the Prophet, which made her his first cousin. Her brother was Abd Allah ibn Jahsh.

She was an early convert to Islam and emigrated to Medina with her brother Abd Allah. She married Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. In 628 the Prophet granted her 30 wasqs of produce from Khaybar.

She is known for her question about prolonged bleeding (istihada). In the version recorded by Muslim from A'isha, Umm Habib, the wife of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, had this bleeding for seven years. The Prophet told her it was from a vein and not menstruation; she was to stop praying for the length of her usual period, then bathe and pray. In a version transmitted by Ibn Ishaq through al-Zuhri and Urwa, he ordered her to bathe for every prayer; in another account she bathed before every prayer of her own accord.

Many biographers attributed this case to her sister Hamna bint Jahsh, whom Abu l-Fath al-Azdi describes as the wife of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, known as Umm Habiba. Ibn Abd al-Barr, as cited by Ibn al-Athir, said both sisters had this bleeding, and Ibn Sa'd held that they were two different women. She died in Medina; the sources consulted give no year.

bio: Umm Habiba bint Nabbata al-Asadiyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Emigrant — Makkah to Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Habiba bint Nabbata al-Asadiyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Banu Asad tribe, as indicated by her name al-Asadiyya.

Like many early Muslims, Umm Habiba was originally based in Mecca, the birthplace of Islam and the Prophet Muhammad's home city. During this period, the small Muslim community faced increasing persecution and hostility from the established Meccan society, which viewed the new monotheistic faith as a threat to their traditional religious and economic systems.

Umm Habiba is particularly remembered in Islamic history as one of the emigrants who participated in the hijra, the pivotal migration from Mecca to Medina that took place in 622 CE. This migration marked a crucial turning point for the early Muslim community, as it allowed them to escape persecution and establish the first Islamic state in Medina under the Prophet's leadership. The hijra was so significant that it later became the starting point of the Islamic calendar.

Her participation in this historic migration demonstrates her commitment to the early Muslim community and her willingness to sacrifice the familiar surroundings of her birthplace for the sake of her faith. The emigrants, known as muhajirun, held a special status in early Islamic society and were praised in the Quran for their sacrifice and dedication.

As a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Umm Habiba was part of the first generation of Muslims who directly witnessed the revelation of Islam and the establishment of the early Muslim community. The companions, both male and female, are revered in Islamic tradition for their role in preserving and transmitting the teachings and practices of Islam to subsequent generations.

Umm Habiba died around 635 CE, during the reign of the first Caliph Abu Bakr, in the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate period. Her life spanned the entire Meccan period of Islam and the early years of the Islamic state in Medina, making her a witness to the foundational decades of Islamic civilization. Her story represents the experiences of the early Muslim women who played important roles in the establishment and spread of Islam.

full: Ramla bint Abi Sufyan ibn Harb al-Umawiyya (Umm Habibah)
primaryTitle: Umm Habibah — Daughter of Abu Sufyan; Married by the Negus
titles: Umm al-Muminin (Mother of the Believers)
bio: Ramla bint Abi Sufyan ibn Harb al-Umawiyya (Umm Habibah) (c. 589–666 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Umm Habibah — Daughter of Abu Sufyan; Married by the Negus.
bio_full:
Ramla bint Abi Sufyan ibn Harb (Arabic: رَمْلَة بِنْت أَبِي سُفْيَان ٱبْن حَرْب, romanized: Ramla bint Abī Sufyān ibn Ḥarb; c. 589 or 594–665), commonly known by her kunya Umm Habiba (Arabic: أُمُّ حَبِيبَة, romanized: Umm Ḥabība), was a wife of Muhammad.

Early life
She was born in circa 589 or 594. She was the daughter of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and Safiyyah bint Abi al-'As. Abu Sufyan was the chief of the Umayya clan, and she was the daughter of the leader of the whole Quraysh tribe and the most powerful opponent of Muhammad in the period 624–630. However, he later accepted Islam and became a Muslim warrior. The first Umayyad caliph, Muawiyah I, was Ramla's half-brother, and Uthman ibn Affan was her maternal first cousin and paternal second cousin.

Marriage to Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh
Her first husband was Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh, a brother of Zaynab bint Jahsh, whom Muhammad also married.
Ubayd-Allah and Ramla were among the first people to accept Islam. In 616, in order to avoid hostilities from Quraish, they both emigrated to Abyssinia (Ethiopia), where she gave birth to Habibah bint Ubayd-Allah.
In Abyssinia, Ubayd-Allah converted to Christianity. He tried to persuade Ramla to do the same, but she held on to Islam. His conversion led to their separation (Ibn Hajar, Al-Isabah, vol. 4, p. 305).

Marriage to Muhammad
Muhammad sent Ramla a proposal of marriage, which arrived on the day she completed her Iddah (widow's waiting period).
The marriage ceremony took place in Abyssinia even though Muhammad was not present. Ramla chose Khalid ibn Said as her legal guardian. The Negus (King) of Abyssinia gave Khalid a dower of 400 dinars and hosted a huge wedding feast after the ceremony. Muhammad did not give a dower larger than this to any of his other wives.
The Negus then arranged to send all thirty of the remaining immigrant Muslims back to Arabia. They travelled to Medina in two boats. Shurahbil ibn Hasana accompanied Ramla on this journey. According to some sources, she married Muhammad one year after the Hijra, though she did not live with him until six years later, when Muhammad was sixty years old and she was thirty-five. Tabari writes that her marriage took place in 7 A.H. (628) when "she was thirty-odd years old."

Life in Medina
On one occasion, Abu Sufyan visited his daughter Ramla in her house in Medina. "As he went to sit on the apostle’s carpet she folded it up so that he could not sit on it. 'My dear daughter,' he said, 'I hardly know if you think that the carpet is too good for me or that I am too good for the carpet!' She replied: 'It is the apostle’s carpet and you are an unclean polytheist. I do not want you to sit on the apostle’s carpet.' 'By God,' he said, 'since you left me you have gone to the bad.'"
Ramla died in the year 45 A.H. (664 or 665 C.E.) during the rule of her half-brother, Muawiyah I. She was buried in the Jannat al-Baqi cemetery next to other wives of Muhammad.

Legacy
The Hadith literature includes about sixty-five hadiths narrated by Ramla.

bio: Umm Hakim bint 'Abd al-Muttalib (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in .est.
bio_full:
Umm Hakim al-Bayda' bint Abd al-Muttalib was a paternal aunt of the Prophet Muhammad and the grandmother of the caliph Uthman ibn Affan through her daughter Arwa. Ibn Sa'd names her mother as Fatima bint Amr ibn A'idh of the clan of Makhzum. She was born in Mecca around 546, and one account describes her as the twin sister of Abd Allah, the Prophet's father. She was called al-Bayda', 'the fair one'.

According to Ibn Sa'd, she married Kurayz ibn Rabi'a of the clan of Abd Shams in the pre-Islamic period, and bore him Amir, Arwa, Talha and Umm Talha. Arwa bint Kurayz became the mother of Uthman ibn Affan, and later married Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt.

Ibn Sa'd's entry does not say that she accepted Islam or gave the pledge to the Prophet. One account states that she died before 610, which is before the start of the Prophet's mission.

bio: Umm Hakim bint al-Nadr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Hakim bint al-Nadr was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the clan of Adi ibn al-Najjar of al-Khazraj. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Hakim bint al-Nadr ibn Damdam ibn Zayd ibn Haram ibn Jundub ibn Amir ibn Ghanm ibn Adi ibn al-Najjar. Her mother was Hind bint Zayd ibn Sawad ibn Malik ibn Ghanm ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar.

According to Ibn Sa'd, she married Amr ibn Tha'laba ibn Wahb ibn Adi ibn Malik ibn Adi ibn Amir ibn Ghanm ibn Adi ibn al-Najjar, a man of her own clan. Their children were a son, Abu Hakim, a son, Abd al-Rahman, and a daughter also called Umm Hakim, whose name was Sahla.

Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. No date or place of death is recorded.

bio_full:
Umm Hakim bint Qariz bin Khalid was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the crucial decades when Islam emerged and established itself as a major religious and social force in the region.

As one of the Ansar (Helpers) of Medina, Umm Hakim belonged to the community that welcomed and supported Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. The Ansar played a vital role in the survival and growth of the early Muslim community, providing shelter, resources, and protection during Islam's most vulnerable period.

The designation "Ansari Companion of Madinah" indicates her significant role within the early Muslim community in Medina, which served as Islam's first political and spiritual center. During her lifetime, she would have witnessed major events in Islamic history, including the establishment of the first Muslim state, various military campaigns, and the codification of Islamic law and practice.

Like other female companions of the Prophet, Umm Hakim would have been part of the generation that directly learned Islamic teachings and practices from Prophet Muhammad himself. The female companions played important roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge, particularly regarding matters of worship, family life, and social conduct that they observed firsthand.

Her death around 635 CE places her among those early companions who died during the period of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet's death in 632 CE. This timing means she lived through the initial expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the first caliphs.

The historical record of Umm Hakim, like many female companions, is limited compared to more prominent male figures of the era. However, her recognition as a Sahabiyya acknowledges her contribution to the early Muslim community and her role in the foundational period of Islamic civilization. Her life represents the experiences of the women who were part of the first generation of Muslims and who helped establish the religious and social frameworks that would guide Islamic society for centuries to come.

Umm Hakim bint Wida' was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE in the Hijaz region, she witnessed and participated in the foundational years of the Islamic community during the late 6th and early 7th centuries.

As one of the female companions of the Prophet, Umm Hakim belonged to the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with Muhammad and experienced the early development of Islamic teachings and practices. Her proximity to the Prophet and the early Muslim community positioned her as an important witness to the events, sayings, and customs that would later become central to Islamic tradition.

Umm Hakim is primarily recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial source of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions like Umm Hakim played a vital role in preserving and transmitting these prophetic traditions, particularly those related to matters that men might not have witnessed or that concerned women's religious and social practices.

Her contributions to hadith sciences represent part of the broader participation of women in early Islamic scholarship and religious transmission. The female companions served as essential links in the chain of narration that allowed prophetic traditions to be preserved and passed down to subsequent generations of Muslims. Their testimonies and narrations helped establish the authenticity and reliability of various hadith collections that would later be compiled by Islamic scholars.

Living until approximately 635 CE, Umm Hakim witnessed not only the prophetic period but also the early expansion of Islam under the first caliph, Abu Bakr. Her forty-year lifespan encompassed the crucial decades during which Islam transformed from a local Arabian religious movement into a rapidly expanding civilization.

The inclusion of Umm Hakim among the recognized narrators of hadith underscores the important role that women played in early Islamic society as preservers and transmitters of religious knowledge. Her legacy lies in her contribution to the vast corpus of prophetic traditions that continue to guide Muslim religious practice and understanding, representing the vital participation of female companions in establishing the foundations of Islamic scholarship and jurisprudence.

bio:
Umm Hani, Fakhta bint Abi Talib bin Abdul Muttalib Al-Hashimiya Al-Qurashi, is known by her nickname, which is Umm Hani. She is the cousin of the Messenger of God, and her name is Fakhta or Hind bint Abi Talib bin Abdul Muttalib bin Hashim bin Abd Manaf bin Qusay.
Her mother, Fatima bint Asad bin Hashim bin Abd Manaf bin Qusayy, was married to Hubayra bin Abi Wahb Al-Makhzoumi, and she bore him Ja`dah bin Hubayra, and the Messenger of God fed her forty wasqs in Khaybar.
bio_full:
Fākhitah bint Abī Ṭālib (Arabic: فاختة بنت أبي طالب), also known as Hind and better known by her kunya Umm Hānī,  was a cousin and companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

Early life
She was the eldest daughter of Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Fatima bint Asad, hence a sister of Ali and cousin of Muhammad.

Marriage
Before 595, the young Muhammad asked Abu Talib's permission to marry Fakhitah, but Abu Talib accepted an alternative proposal from Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb, a member of the wealthy Makhzum clan. Muhammad asked: "Uncle, why have you married her off to Hubayra and ignored me?" Abu Talib replied: "Nephew, they are our in-laws, and the noble is an equal for the noble." This cryptic reply might have meant that Abu Talib owed a favour to the Makhzum clan; but the more likely meaning was that Muhammad had no money.
Hubayra, who was a poet, is described as "wise and influential". He and Fakhitah had at least seven children, three daughters and four sons: Hani (from whom she took her kunya Umm Hani), Ja'da, Yusuf, Umar, Fulan, Aqla and Amr.
Muhammad was a guest in Fakhitah's house one night in 621. The next morning, he told her that he had miraculously travelled to Jerusalem and then to Heaven during the night. She urged him not to tell anyone, as the Quraysh would only laugh at him, and she tried to restrain him physically. Muhammad ignored this advice.

Conversion to Islam
Fakhitah became a Muslim when Muhammad conquered Mecca in January 630. Hubayra did not want to convert, so he fled from Mecca and took refuge in the Christian city of Najran. This caused an automatic divorce. Muhammad proposed to Fakhita again, but she refused him, saying that she would not be able to do justice to both young children and a new husband. Muhammad responded: "The Quraysh are the best women on camel-back! They are so kind to their children and so careful of their husbands' property!"
Later Fakhitah told Muhammad that her children had grown up and she was now ready to marry him.

bio: Umm Hani' al-Ansaria (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Hani' al-Ansaria was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the crucial decades that witnessed the emergence and establishment of the Islamic community in Medina.

As indicated by her name "al-Ansaria," she belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca when they arrived in 622 CE. The Ansar played a vital role in providing the early Muslim community with a secure base from which Islam could develop and spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula.

Umm Hani' is primarily remembered for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. During the early Islamic period, many companions, both male and female, served as repositories of the Prophet's teachings and transmitted them to subsequent generations. Female companions like Umm Hani' were particularly important in preserving accounts of the Prophet's private life and his interactions within domestic settings, providing perspectives that might not have been accessible to male companions.

The preservation and transmission of hadith became one of the fundamental Islamic sciences, as these narrations served alongside the Quran as sources for Islamic law, theology, and practice. Companions who had direct contact with the Prophet were considered the most reliable sources for such narrations, making their contributions essential to the development of Islamic scholarship.

Umm Hani' lived during a period of rapid change and expansion for the Muslim community. Her lifetime spanned from the pre-Islamic period through the Prophet's ministry, the establishment of the first Muslim state in Medina, and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate following the Prophet's death in 632 CE. She died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr or the early years of Umar ibn al-Khattab's rule.

Her significance lies in her contribution to the preservation of Islamic teachings through hadith narration, representing the important role that female companions played in maintaining and transmitting the foundational knowledge of Islam to future generations of Muslims.

bio: Umm Haram bint Milhan (c. 593–648 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Umm Haram bint Milhan was a woman Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu al-Najjar clan of the Khazraj. Ibn al-Athir gives her lineage as daughter of Milhan ibn Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Haram, of the Banu 'Adi ibn al-Najjar, and names her mother as Mulayka bint Malik. Her own given name is not firmly established; names suggested for her include al-Rumaysa' and al-Ghumaysa'. She was the sister of Umm Sulaym and of Haram and Sulaym, the sons of Milhan, and the maternal aunt of Anas ibn Malik. The Prophet often visited the house of the two sisters. She was married to 'Ubada ibn al-Samit. According to one modern account, she tended wounded fighters at Uhud and Hunayn. Her narrations appear in the major hadith collections except that of al-Tirmidhi; those who transmitted from her include Anas ibn Malik, 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, 'Amr ibn al-Aswad and Ya'la ibn Shaddad. During the caliphate of 'Uthman she sailed with her husband on the naval campaign to Cyprus commanded by Mu'awiya. There she was thrown from her mount and died. Modern accounts date her death to 648 CE, the year of the campaign; Ibn al-Athir dates the campaign to 27 AH. Her tomb is at Larnaca in Cyprus, and the mosque built beside it is known as Hala Sultan Tekke; Turkish tradition calls her Hala Sultan.

Her mother was Fukayha bint Sakan ibn Zayd, also of the Banu Salama. She was the full sister, through both parents, of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir ibn Nabi', who fought at Badr. bio: Umm Hisham bint Haritha bin Al-Numan Al-Ansariyya. It was said that Umm Hashim was a famous companion, and her father and mother were companions.
bio_full: Umm Hisham bint Haritha ibn al-Nu'man was a woman Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina, of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar; some sources give her kunya as Umm Hashim. Ibn Hajar reports that Ibn Sa'd named her mother as Umm Khalid, and that she married 'Umara ibn al-Hubhab ibn Sa'd ibn Qays. Ahmad ibn Zuhayr reported hearing from his father that she took part in the Pledge of Ridwan. She said that her family's oven and the Prophet's oven were one and the same for two years, or a year and part of a year; this report is recorded in Sahih Muslim. She also said that she learned Surat Qaf only from the Prophet's own recitation, as he recited it every Friday in his sermon; this report is found in Abu Dawud and in al-Hakim's al-Mustadrak. Those who transmitted from her include Khubayb ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yasaf, Yahya ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurara, 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Ma'n and 'Amra bint 'Abd al-Rahman. Her date of death is not recorded.

Born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, she was part of the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime.

As a sahabiyya, Umm Jundab held a distinguished position in early Islamic society. The companions of the Prophet were considered the most authoritative sources for Islamic teachings and practices, having witnessed firsthand the words and actions of Muhammad. This direct exposure to the Prophet's teachings made their testimonies invaluable for later generations of Muslims seeking to understand and follow Islamic principles.

Umm Jundab is particularly recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and tacit approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. During an era when literacy was limited and oral transmission was the primary means of preserving knowledge, hadith narrators played a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of Islamic teachings. Female companions like Umm Jundab were especially important in transmitting knowledge about aspects of Islamic life that pertained to women's religious practices and social conduct.

Her contributions to hadith sciences represent part of the broader participation of women in the early Islamic scholarly tradition. Female companions served as essential links in the chain of transmission (isnad) that authenticated Islamic teachings for subsequent generations. Their participation ensured that comprehensive knowledge of the Prophet's teachings, including those related to family life and women's concerns, was preserved and transmitted accurately.

Living in the Hijaz region, the heartland of early Islam, Umm Jundab would have been present during the critical early decades of Islamic expansion and consolidation. Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, a period of significant territorial expansion and administrative development for the nascent Islamic state.

The preservation of Umm Jundab's name and recognition as a hadith narrator reflects the respect accorded to female religious authorities in early Islam. Her inclusion among the recognized companions and hadith transmitters demonstrates the active role women played in preserving and transmitting Islamic knowledge during the religion's foundational period, contributing to the scholarly framework that would support Islamic civilization for centuries to come.

As a resident of Medina, Umm Jundub was part of the Muslim community during a crucial era when Islamic teachings and practices were being developed and codified. Her proximity to the Prophet and the early Muslim community positioned her to observe and participate in significant religious and social developments of the time.

Umm Jundub is recognized primarily for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a fundamental source of Islamic guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions who served as hadith narrators played an essential role in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings, particularly regarding matters that involved women's religious practices, family life, and social conduct.

The companions of the Prophet, both male and female, are highly regarded in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly learned from and interacted with Muhammad. Their testimonies and narrations provide crucial links to understanding early Islamic practices and the Prophet's teachings. Female narrators like Umm Jundub were particularly important in preserving knowledge about aspects of Islamic life that male companions might not have witnessed or understood as fully.

Her contributions to hadith literature represent part of the broader participation of women in the early Islamic community's religious scholarship and knowledge transmission. During this period, women actively participated in learning, teaching, and preserving religious knowledge, establishing precedents for female scholarship in Islamic history.

Umm Jundub's life spanned the pre-Islamic period, the Prophet's ministry, and the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, making her a witness to the transformation of Arabian society through Islamic teachings. Her role as a hadith narrator ensures her place among the companions who helped preserve the foundational texts and oral traditions that would guide Muslim communities for generations to come.

bio: Umm Khalid bin Khalid ibn Sa'id (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Abyssinia. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full: Umm Khalid, whose name was Amah, was the daughter of Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As ibn Umayya. Her mother was Humayna bint Khalaf al-Khuza'iyya; some sources give the name as Amina or Umayma. She was born in Abyssinia, where her parents had emigrated, as was her brother Sa'id ibn Khalid. In a report transmitted by al-Waqidi, she recalls that when the emigrants left Abyssinia on two ships, the Negus asked them all to convey his greetings to the Prophet. The Prophet once had a small black garment with a green or yellow pattern brought, called for Umm Khalid and dressed her in it himself, saying 'Wear it out, and wear it out again', and calling the pattern 'sana', an Abyssinian word meaning good or beautiful. She married al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam and bore him 'Amr and Khalid. Al-Bukhari included her narrations in his Sahih, among them in the chapters on clothing. Those who transmitted from her include Musa and Ibrahim, the sons of 'Uqba, Kurayb ibn Sulaym al-Kindi and Sa'id ibn 'Amr ibn Sa'id. One classical account places her death between 71 and 80 AH and suggests she may have been the last of the women Companions to die.

bio: Umm Khultum bint Suhayl (b. c. 593 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Umm Khultum bint Suhayl was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 593 CE in Mecca, she was part of the early Muslim community that formed around Muhammad's prophetic mission.

She is historically recognized as one of the Muslims who participated in the emigration to Abyssinia (modern-day Ethiopia), a significant event in early Islamic history that occurred around 615 CE. This migration represented the first major exodus of Muslims from Mecca, undertaken to escape persecution from the ruling Quraysh tribe who opposed the growing Islamic movement. The emigration to Abyssinia demonstrated the early Muslim community's commitment to preserving their faith despite facing hostile conditions in their homeland.

As a sahabiyya, Umm Khultum bint Suhayl held the distinguished status of having lived during the Prophet's lifetime and being part of his community. The companions of the Prophet are revered in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly received and transmitted the teachings of Islam. Her inclusion among the early ascetics indicates that she was associated with a lifestyle of spiritual devotion and self-discipline that characterized some of the earliest Muslim practitioners.

Her participation in the Abyssinian emigration places her within a select group of early Muslims who made significant sacrifices for their religious convictions. This migration was crucial in Islamic history as it established the precedent of hijra (emigration for religious reasons) and demonstrated the international dimension of the early Muslim community's struggles and survival strategies.

The historical record of Umm Khultum bint Suhayl's life reflects the important role that women played in the early Islamic community, both as believers who faced persecution and as individuals who made difficult decisions to preserve and practice their faith. Her story represents the broader experience of early Muslim women who contributed to the establishment and spread of Islam during its foundational period.

She died in 633 CE, during the early years of the rapidly expanding Islamic state under the first Caliph Abu Bakr, having witnessed the transformation of Islam from a persecuted religious movement in Mecca to the dominant force in the Arabian Peninsula.

bio: Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqba (Arabic: أُمُّ كُلثُوم بِنْتِ عُقبَة) (c. 610–654) was a follower or companion (Sahabiyyah) of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. A verse of the Qur'an, 60:10, was revealed in response to her situation.

Emigration
Born in Mecca, she was the daughter of Uqba ibn Abu Mu'ayt and Arwa bint Kurayz; hence Caliph Uthman was her uterine half-brother. Their mother Arwa was a first cousin of Muhammad.
Umm Kulthum's father Uqba was an outspoken opponent of Muhammad, but she became a Muslim before 622. She remained in Mecca after the Hijra. Uqba was killed at the Battle of Badr in 624.
After the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah in 628, Umm Kulthum left Mecca for Medina in the company of a man from the Khuza'a tribe. Her brothers, Walid and Ammara, pursued her, and she arrived in Medina only one day ahead of them. Her brothers asked Muhammad to return her to them, in accordance with the treaty, which stated that Muslims who escaped from Mecca to Medina should be returned to their families. Umm Kulthum pleaded that "women are weak" and that she might not have the strength to remain firm in her faith if she had to live among polytheists. Muhammad then announced the new revelation:

O you who believe! When believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them; Allah knows best as to their faith, then if you ascertain that they are true believers, send them not back to the disbelievers. They are not lawful for the disbelievers nor are the disbelievers lawful for them. But give them (disbelievers) that which they have spent (on their dower).
After this prophecy, he pointed out that the word in the treaty for "escaped people" was masculine, so it did not apply to women. However, escaped women must be tested for the genuineness of their faith. Umm Kulthum was asked whether she had come to Medina "for love of Allah and his Apostle and Islam" or whether she was seeking or escaping a husband or hoping to make money. After she had passed the test, Muhammad told her brothers: "Allah has broken the treaty regarding women by what you know, so leave."
Other women then followed Umm Kulthum's example and also left Mecca for Medina.

Marriage
Four men asked for her hand in marriage, and in fact she was to marry all four of them in rotation. She asked her brother Uthman which suitor she should accept, and he advised her to consult Muhammed. He instructed her to marry Zayd ibn Harithah. The couple had two children, of whom Zayd died in infancy, but Ruqayya lived to come under the protection of Uthman. Zayd divorced Umm Kulthum, but was killed soon afterwards at the battle of Mu'tah.
She then married Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, whom she "disliked" because he had "some harshness towards women." She asked him for a divorce, but he refused. So "she pestered him while he was doing wudu for the prayer, and he divorced her with a single divorce." She then left the room and gave birth to their daughter Zaynab, which immediately ended her 'iddah. When Zubayr heard, he complained, "She tricked me, may Allah trick her!" Muhammad advised him to "propose to her again," but Zubayr replied: "She will never come back to me."
Her third husband was Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. They had six children: Muhammad, Ibrahim, Hamid (or Humayd), Ismail, Hamida and Amat ar-Rahman.

bio: Umm Kulthum bint Ali bin Abi Talib, and her mother is Fatima Al-Zahra, and she is the youngest granddaughter of the Prophet Muhammad. There was a difference in her name between: Ruqayya and Zainab, and whoever said the latter called her Zainab the Younger to distinguish her from her sister Zainab the Elder. Omar ibn al-Khattab married her, and she gave birth to him: Zaid and Ruqayyah. After his murder, her cousin Aoun ibn Jaafar al-Tayyar succeeded her, then his brother Abdullah ibn Jaafar. She witnessed the Battle of Karbala and the killing of her brother Hussein and the rest of her family. The year of her death and her burial are disputed.
bio_full:
Umm Kulthūm bint ʿAlī (Arabic: أُمّ كُلْثُوم بِنْت عَلِيّ), also known as Zaynab al-Ṣughrā (Arabic: زَيْنَب ٱلصُّغْرَىٰ, lit. 'the junior Zaynab'), was the youngest daughter of Fatima and  Ali ibn Abi Talib. The former was the daughter of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and the latter was his cousin. Ali is also recognized as the fourth Rashidun caliph (r. 656–661) and the first Shia imam. A young Umm Kulthum lost her grandfather and mother in 632 CE. While she was still a child, the second Rashidun caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (r. 634–644) asked for her hand in marriage, which was resisted by Umm Kulthum and her father Ali, possibly due to Umar's reputation for harsh treatment of women. By one Sunni account, Ali finally agreed to the marriage when Umar enlisted the support of prominent Muslims for his proposal.
Umm Kulthum survived the Battle of Karbala in 680, where her brother Husayn and most of her male relatives were massacred by the forces of the Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn Mua'awiya (r. 680–683). Women and children in Husayn's camp were taken captive after the battle and marched to Kufa and then the Umayyad capital Damascus. A public speech ascribed to Umm Kulthum in Kufa condemns Yazid, defends Husayn, and chastises the Kufans for their role in his death. She was later freed and returned to her hometown Medina.

Early life

Umm Kulthum was the fourth child of Fatima and Ali ibn Abi Talib, and their youngest daughter. The former was the daughter of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and the latter was his cousin. Ali is also recognized as the fourth Rashidun caliph (r. 656–661) and the first Shia Islamic imam. Umm Kulthum is also known as Zaynab al-Sughra (lit. 'the junior Zaynab') to distinguish her from her older sister Zaynab al-Kubra (lit. 'the senior Zaynab'). The Arabic word zaynab literally means 'adornment of father'. Umm Kulthum was still a young child in 632 CE when her grandfather Muhammad and her mother Fatima both died.

Alleged marriage to Umar
The second Rashidun caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab is said to have asked Umm Kulthum for her hand in marriage during his reign (r. 634–644), according to the Sunni historian Ibn Sa'd (d. 845) in his biographical Tabaqat. Still a child at the time, Umm Kulthum resisted this proposal, the report by Ibn Sa'd continues. This refusal is attributed by the Islamicist W. Madelung (d. 2023) to Umar's reputation for harsh treatment of women. Ali too was reluctant but eventually gave in, according to Ibn Sa'd, when Umar enlisted the support of prominent Muslims for his proposal. This proposal was likely an overture by Umar, who may have considered Ali's cooperation necessary in his collaborative scheme of government. While Ali reputedly advised Umar and his predecessor Abu Bakr (r. 632–634) in certain matters, their conflicts with Ali are also well-documented, but largely downplayed or ignored in Sunni sources, where there is often a tendency to neutralize the conflicts among the companions after Muhammad. In contrast, these conflicts might have been magnified in Shia sources.

Battle of Karbala

Ali was himself elected caliph in 656, and later assassinated in his de-facto capital Kufa in January 661. Soon after Ali's death, his eldest son Hasan was elected caliph in Kufa, but later abdicated in favor of Mu'awiya (r. 661–680) in August 661. The peace treaty between Hasan and Mu'awiya stipulated that the latter should not appoint a successor. Hasan kept aloof from politics after his abdication in compliance with the peace treaty, but was poisoned and killed in 669, most likely at the instigation of Mu'awiya, who thus paved the way for the succession of his son Yazid (r. 680–683). Hasan was then succeeded as the head of Muhammad's family by his brother Husayn, who nevertheless upheld the treaty with Mu'awiya.
Mu'awiya designated his son Yazid as his successor in 676, in violation of his earlier agreement with Hasan. Yazid is often remembered by Muslim historians as a debaucher who openly violated the Islamic norms, and his nomination was met with resistance from the sons of Muhammad's prominent companions, including Husayn ibn Ali. On Mu'awiya's death and Yazid's succession in 680, the latter instructed the governor of Medina to secure Husayn's pledge of allegiance by force. Husayn immediately left his hometown Medina for Mecca at night to avoid recognizing Yazid as the caliph. After receiving letters of support from some Kufans, whose intentions were confirmed by his envoy, Husayn later left Mecca for Kufa, accompanied by some relatives and supporters, including Zaynab and Umm Kulthum. On their way to Kufa, Husayn's small caravan was intercepted by Yazid's army and forced to camp in the desert land of Karbala on 2 October 680 away from water and fortifications. The promised Kufan support did not materialize as the new governor of Kufa killed the envoy of Husayn and intimidated Kufan tribal chiefs. Having been surrounded for some days and deprived of the drinking water of the nearby Euphrates river, Husayn was later killed on 10 October 680, alongside most of his male relatives and his small retinue, in the Battle of Karbala against the army of the Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn Mu'awiya (r. 680–683).
After the battle, the women and children in Husayn's camp were taken prisoner and marched first to Kufa and later to the capital Damascus in Syria. Yazid eventually freed the captives, and they returned to Medina. The Muslim historian Ibn Abi Tahir Tayfur (d. 893) records two speeches about Karbala in his Balaghat al-nisa', which is an anthology of eloquent speeches by women. He attributes one of the two speeches to Umm Kulthum in the market of Kufa, and the other to her sister Zaynab in the court of Yazid in Damascus. Most Shia authors, however, have later attributed both sermons to Zaynab, which the Islamicist T. Qutbuddin considers highly likely. Concerning the first sermon, Ibn Tayfur writes that the Kufans wailed and wept when they saw Muhammad's family in captivity.

bio: Umm Kulthum bint Muhammad bin Abdullah is the third daughter of the Prophet Muhammad from his wife Khadija bint Khuwaylid after Zainab and Ruqayya. Her father, the Prophet Muhammad, married her to Othman bin Affan after Otaiba bin Abi Lahab divorced her out of hatred for her father and after his father ordered him to do so. She was born six years before the Prophet’s mission, embraced Islam and immigrated to Medina. She died in the year 9 AH with her husband, Othman bin Affan, and she was 27 years old at that time.
bio_full:
Umm Kulthūm bint Muḥammad (Arabic: أم كلثوم بنت محمد) (c. 603–630) was the third daughter of the Islamic prophet Muhammad by his first wife Khadija bint Khuwaylid.

Conversion to Islam
She was born in Mecca, the fifth of their six children. She was legally married before August 610 to Utaybah ibn Abi Lahab, but the marriage was never consummated. She was still living with her parents when Muhammad was declared a prophet by God, and Umm Kulthum became a Muslim soon after her mother did.
After Muhammad warned Abu Lahab of hellfire in 613, Abu Lahab told Utaybah that he would never speak to him again unless he divorced Umm Kulthum, so he did. Her maternal brother, Hind ibn Abi Hala, asked Muhammad, "Why did you separate Umm Kulthum from Utaybah?" Muhammad replied, "Allah did not allow me to marry her to a person who is not going to Paradise."
Muhammad left Mecca in September 622. Before long Zayd ibn Haritha brought instructions to Umm Kulthum and her sister Fatima to join their father in Medina. Their uncle Al-Abbas put them on a camel; but as they were setting off, Huwayrith ibn Nuqaydh goaded the animal so that it threw them to the ground. However, Umm Kulthum and Fatima arrived safely in Medina. When Muhammad conquered Mecca in 630, he sentenced Huwayrith to death for his involvement in the conspiracy to assassinate him.

Second marriage
After the death of her sister Ruqayya left Uthman a widower, he married Umm Kulthum. The marriage was legally contracted in August/September 624, but they did not live together until December. The marriage was childless.

Death
Umm Kulthum died in November/December 630.

bio_full:
Umm Kurz al-Khuza'iyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE in the Hijaz region, she belonged to the Khuza'a tribe, one of the prominent Arab tribes of the time.

As a companion of the Prophet, Umm Kurz had direct contact with Muhammad during his prophetic mission, which began around 610 CE and continued until his death in 632 CE. This proximity to the Prophet's teachings and daily life positioned her among the earliest generation of Muslims who witnessed the development of Islamic practices and received religious instruction firsthand.

Umm Kurz is recognized in Islamic tradition as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial source of Islamic law and guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions who transmitted hadith played an essential role in preserving and passing down the prophetic traditions, particularly regarding matters that pertained to women's religious practices, family life, and social conduct within the early Muslim community.

The inclusion of women like Umm Kurz among the recognized hadith narrators reflects the active participation of female companions in the religious and social life of the early Islamic community. These women served as bridges between the Prophet's household and the broader community of believers, ensuring that prophetic teachings reached both men and women of subsequent generations.

Her tribal affiliation with the Khuza'a is historically significant, as this tribe maintained important relationships with the emerging Muslim community. The Khuza'a had connections to Mecca and played roles in various political and military developments during the early Islamic period.

Umm Kurz died around 635 CE, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph of Islam. Her death occurred during a period when the Muslim community was rapidly expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula and establishing itself as a major political and religious force in the region.

While specific details about the content and number of hadiths attributed to her may vary in different sources, her recognition as a hadith narrator establishes her place within the chain of transmission that preserved Islamic teachings for future generations. Her contribution represents the broader role of female companions in maintaining the continuity of Islamic knowledge and practice during the crucial early decades of the religion's development.

bio_full:
ʿĀtika bint Khālid al-Khuzāʿīyya (Arabic: عاتكة بنت خالد الخزاعية) nicknamed Umm Maʿbad (Arabic: أم معبد) was a woman from the Khuza'ah tribe who lived during the time of the Islamic prophet, Muhammad and provided a physical description of him.
According to a book written by Ghulam Shabbir she is also known for a story narrated in some Islamic sources. In 622 CE Muhammad set out for his migration to Medina (an oasis 300 miles north of Mecca). When she was very old, during Muhammad's migration to Medina he stopped near her tent. Muhammad's companion Abu Bakr wanted milk from a goat which did not give even give a drop of milk. According to the legend Muhammad stroked one of the goat's udders, whereupon the goat gave a large amount of milk.
She and her husband then went to Medina with her brother, Khunays (or Hubaysh) ibn Khalid, and converted to Islam.

bio_full:
Umm Ma'qil al-Asadiyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the late 6th and early 7th centuries CE. Born around 595 CE, she was among the first generation of Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet and witnessed the early development of the Islamic community.

As indicated by her name, Umm Ma'qil belonged to the Banu Asad tribe, one of the Arab tribal groups in the Arabian Peninsula. The designation "Umm Ma'qil" follows the Arabic naming convention where women were often known by their relationship to a male relative, in this case likely meaning "mother of Ma'qil."

Her primary significance to Islamic history lies in her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and teachings of Prophet Muhammad. During the early Islamic period, both men and women served as transmitters of these crucial religious texts that would later form one of the fundamental sources of Islamic law and theology alongside the Quran. Female companions like Umm Ma'qil played an essential role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings to subsequent generations.

The participation of women in hadith transmission was particularly important because they had access to aspects of the Prophet's private life and teachings that male companions might not have witnessed. Female narrators were especially valued for their accounts of religious practices, family life, and guidance specifically directed toward women in the community.

Umm Ma'qil's death around 635 CE places her among the companions who lived through the Prophet's lifetime and into the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's reign. This timing meant she witnessed not only the establishment of Islam but also its initial expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Her inclusion among the recognized female hadith narrators demonstrates the active role that women played in the early Islamic community's religious and intellectual life. While specific details about the content of her transmitted hadith or the exact circumstances of her life remain limited in available historical sources, her recognition as a sahabiyya and hadith narrator establishes her place among the foundational figures who helped preserve and transmit Islamic teachings during the religion's crucial early decades.
