bio: Umm Malik bint Ubayy bin Malik (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Malik bint Ubayy was a woman of the Ansar of Medina. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Malik bint Ubayy ibn Malik ibn al-Harith ibn Ubayd ibn Malik ibn Salim ibn Ghanm ibn Awf, and places her among the women of the Banu Salim ibn Ghanm ibn Awf. She was the sister of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul; Ibn Sa'd notes that Salul was a woman of Khuza'a. Her mother was Salma bint Matruf. He adds that her ancestor Ubayd ibn Malik ibn Salim was the poet known as al-Murmiq.

She accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. She was married to Rafi' ibn Malik ibn al-Ajlan, of the Banu Zurayq, and bore him two sons, Rifa'a and Khallad, both of whom fought at Badr.

Ibn Sa'd records no date or place of death for her.

bio: Umm Mani' bint 'Amr ibn 'Adi (b. c. 591 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Second Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Umm Mani' bint Amr was a woman of the Ansar of Medina, from the Banu Salama, and was also known as Umm Shubath. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Mani' bint Amr ibn Adi ibn Sinan ibn Nabi ibn Amr ibn Sawad ibn Ghanm ibn Ka'b ibn Salama. Her mother was Arwa bint Malik ibn Khansa' ibn Sinan ibn Ubayd, also of the Banu Salama. Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Abd al-Barr give her own name as Asma bint Amr; Ibn al-Athir reports this name with "it is said".

She was married to Abu Shubath Khadij ibn Salama ibn Aws, an ally of the Banu Haram. According to Ibn Sa'd, she gave birth to their son Shubath on the night of al-Aqaba, and Khadij attended the pledge of al-Aqaba with his wife Umm Mani'. She accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir also record that she witnessed the pledge of al-Aqaba; Ibn al-Athir says that she and Nusayba, Umm Umara, were the only women present there.

Ibn Sa'd adds that she was also present with the Prophet at Khaybar. No date or place of death is recorded for her.

bio: Umm Mubashir al-Ansariyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Mubashir al-Ansariyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early seventh century. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the Medinan Muslims who welcomed and supported the Prophet and his followers after their migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the sahabiyyat, Umm Mubashir held a distinguished position in early Islamic society as someone who had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the formative period of the Muslim community. Her designation as "al-Ansariyya" indicates her connection to the Ansar, the native inhabitants of Medina who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community during its establishment in the city.

Umm Mubashir is recognized primarily for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and tacit approvals of Prophet Muhammad that form a fundamental source of Islamic guidance alongside the Quran. Female companions like Umm Mubashir played vital roles in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings, particularly regarding matters that pertained to women's religious practices, family life, and social conduct.

Her contribution to hadith sciences represents the broader participation of women in the early transmission of Islamic knowledge. The female companions were essential links in the chain of narration that preserved the Prophet's teachings for subsequent generations. Their testimonies and recollections helped establish important precedents for Islamic law and practice.

Living through the critical decades of Islam's emergence, Umm Mubashir witnessed the transformation of Arabian society and the establishment of the first Muslim community in Medina. Her death around 635 CE places her among the early generation of Muslims who experienced both the prophetic period and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the early years of Umar ibn al-Khattab's leadership.

The historical record of Umm Mubashir, while limited, reflects the important but often understated role of women in early Islamic history. Female companions like her served not only as witnesses to pivotal religious and social developments but also as active participants in preserving the foundational teachings of Islam through their careful transmission of prophetic traditions to later generations of Muslims.

bio: Umm Qays bint Mihsan al-Asadi (c. 594 CE–634 CE, Medina) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Qays bint Mihsan was a woman Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the tribe of Asad ibn Khuzayma, and the sister of the Companion Ukkasha ibn Mihsan. Al-Baji and Ibn Hibban give her lineage as Umm Qays bint Mihsan ibn Hurthan ibn Qays ibn Murra ibn Kabir ibn Ghanm, al-Baji continuing it to Dudan ibn Asad ibn Khuzayma. Her own name is uncertain: Ibn Hajar reports that al-Suhayli gave it as Amina, while Abu al-Qasim al-Jawhari said it was Umayya.

Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir state that she accepted Islam early in Mecca, pledged allegiance to the Prophet, and emigrated to Medina; Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Manjuwayh likewise count her among the women emigrants.

She narrated hadith that al-Bukhari and Muslim included in their collections. In one, she brought her infant son, who had not yet eaten food, to the Prophet; the child urinated on him, and he called for water and sprinkled it over the place. In another, she brought a son suffering from a throat ailment, and the Prophet told the family to use Indian aloeswood instead of harsh treatment, saying it holds seven cures, including one for pleurisy.

Those who narrated from her include Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utba, Wabisa ibn Ma'bad and her freedman Adi ibn Dinar. Al-Uqayli, quoted by Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir, notes that a separate hadith about whether the dead visit one another came from a different, Ansari woman called Umm Qays, not from her.

No date of death is recorded for her in these sources.

bio: Umm Razn bint Sawad bin Razn (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Razn bint Sawad bin Razn was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE and died in 635 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the helpers of Medina who supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community after the Hijra in 622 CE.

As an Ansari companion, Umm Razn was among the indigenous population of Medina who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the Prophet and the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) who had migrated from Mecca. The Ansar played a pivotal role in establishing the first Muslim community in Medina, offering their homes, resources, and protection to the early Muslims during a critical period in Islamic history.

Living during the foundational years of Islam, Umm Razn would have witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic state in Medina, the development of Islamic law and social practices, and the expansion of the Muslim community. Her lifetime spanned the crucial period from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's ministry and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's reign.

The female companions hold particular significance in Islamic history as they represent the women who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and contributed to the early Muslim community. These women participated in various aspects of community life, from supporting the household economy to caring for the wounded during conflicts, and some served as transmitters of Islamic teachings and traditions.

As a Sahabiyya from Medina, Umm Razn represents the broader category of Ansari women who played essential but often understated roles in nurturing and sustaining the early Muslim community. While specific details of her individual contributions may not be extensively documented in historical sources, her status as a companion indicates her acceptance of Islam and her integration into the community that formed around the Prophet Muhammad.

Her death in 635 CE places her passing during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, meaning she lived to see the initial expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula. The companions of this generation are revered in Islamic tradition as the first Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet and helped establish the foundations of Islamic civilization.

bio: Umm Rimtha/Rumaytha (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Rimtha, also known as Umm Rumaytha, was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in the early seventh century CE. Born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula, she was among the women who personally knew and interacted with the Prophet during the formative years of the Islamic community.

As a companion of the Prophet, Umm Rimtha belonged to the distinguished group of individuals who witnessed the revelation of the Quran and observed the Prophet's teachings firsthand. Her proximity to the Prophet Muhammad positioned her as a direct source of knowledge about his sayings, actions, and guidance, making her an important figure in the preservation of Islamic teachings.

Umm Rimtha is particularly recognized for her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings and traditions of the Prophet Muhammad. In the early Islamic community, women companions like Umm Rimtha served as crucial links in the chain of transmission that preserved the Prophet's teachings for future generations. Her contributions to hadith literature represent the significant role that women played in maintaining and transmitting Islamic knowledge during the religion's earliest period.

The hadith sciences, in which Umm Rimtha participated, became one of the foundational disciplines of Islamic scholarship. The careful preservation and transmission of the Prophet's sayings and practices were essential for establishing Islamic law, theology, and practice. Female companions who served as hadith narrators were particularly important for transmitting knowledge about matters that occurred in domestic settings or concerned women's religious obligations and practices.

Living during the crucial decades when Islam was first established, Umm Rimtha witnessed the transformation of Arabian society and the emergence of the early Muslim community. Her death around 635 CE placed her among the earliest generation of Muslims, those who experienced both the challenges and triumphs of the new faith's initial spread.

The preservation of Umm Rimtha's name in Islamic historical records, despite the limited documentation of many early figures, particularly women, indicates her recognized importance as a transmitter of religious knowledge. Her legacy lies in her contribution to the hadith tradition that became central to Islamic scholarship and jurisprudence, demonstrating the vital role of female companions in preserving and transmitting the foundational teachings of Islam.

full: Umm Ruman bint Amir ibn Uwaimir al-Kinaniyya
primaryTitle: Mother of Aisha; Companion of the Prophet
bio: Umm Ruman bint Amir ibn Uwaimir al-Kinaniyya (c. 594 CE–628 CE, Medina) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in est.. Known as Mother of Aisha; Companion of the Prophet.
bio_full:
Umm Ruman was the wife of Abu Bakr and the mother of A'isha and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr. One account gives her name as Zaynab bint Amir. Ibn al-Athir, following al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar, gives her lineage as Umm Ruman bint Amir ibn Uwaymir ibn Abd Shams ibn Attab ibn Udhayna ibn Subay' ibn Duhman ibn al-Harith ibn Ghanm ibn Malik ibn Kinana. He notes that genealogists disagreed widely over her line, but all agreed that she was of the Banu Ghanm ibn Malik ibn Kinana.

Her first husband was Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Sakhbara of the Azd, by whom she had a son, al-Tufayl; al-Waqidi names him Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith and says he came to Mecca and became an ally of Abu Bakr before Islam. After his death she married Abu Bakr and bore him A'isha and Abd al-Rahman.

After the Prophet emigrated, Abu Bakr wrote to his son Abd Allah to bring the family, including Umm Ruman, to Medina; A'isha's report, transmitted by Hisham ibn Urwa, says they arrived while the Prophet was building the mosque. She was alive at the time of the slander against A'isha (al-ifk).

Al-Waqidi and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar date her death to Dhu al-Hijja 6 AH (628 CE). Some said 4 or 5 AH, which Ibn al-Athir rejects because she was alive at the ifk in Sha'ban 6 AH. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr report that the Prophet went down into her grave and asked forgiveness for her. Al-Bukhari includes reports transmitted by Masruq from her; al-Kalabadhi argues that if al-Waqidi's date is right Masruq cannot have heard from her, and Ibn Abd al-Barr calls the report mursal.

bio: Umm Sahl bint Mas'ud b. Sa'd (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Sahl bint Mas'ud was a woman of the clan of Zurayq. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Sahl bint Mas'ud ibn Sa'd ibn Qays ibn Khalida ibn Amir ibn Zurayq. Her mother was Kabsha bint al-Fakih ibn Qays ibn Mukhallad ibn Amir ibn Zurayq, of the same clan.

Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. His short entry names no husband or children, and records no narrations or date of death.

bio_full:
Umm Sahl bint Rumi was a woman of the clan of Abd al-Ashhal. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Sahl bint Rumi ibn Waqsh ibn Zughba ibn Za'ura' ibn Abd al-Ashhal. Her mother was Suhayma bint Abd Allah ibn Rifa'a ibn Najda ibn Numayr, of the Banu Waqif of al-Aws.

According to Ibn Sa'd, she married Salkan ibn Salama ibn Waqsh ibn Zughba ibn Za'ura' ibn Abd al-Ashhal, a man of her own clan, and bore him children, who are not named.

In the report of Muhammad ibn Umar al-Waqidi, cited by Ibn Sa'd, she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. No narrations or date of death are recorded.

bio: Umm Sahl bint Sahl bin 'Atik (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Sahl bint Sahl, also said to be called Umm Thabit, was a woman of the Banu al-Najjar, from the line of Mabdhul. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Sahl bint Sahl ibn Atik ibn al-Nu'man ibn Amr ibn Atik ibn Amr ibn Mabdhul, adding that Mabdhul was Amir ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar. Her mother was Umayma bint Uqba ibn Amr ibn Adi ibn Zayd ibn Jushm ibn Haritha ibn al-Harith.

Ibn Sa'd records that she married Sinan ibn al-Harith ibn Alqama ibn Amr ibn Thaqf and bore him children. After him she married Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn Asim ibn Amr ibn Awf ibn Mabdhul ibn Amr ibn Ghanm ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar.

Ibn Sa'd states that she accepted Islam and gave the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. No narrations or date of death are recorded.

bio: Umm Sakhar bint Sharik ibn Anas (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Sakhar bint Sharik ibn Anas was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the foundational period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the crucial decades that witnessed the emergence and early expansion of the Islamic community.

As an Ansari companion, Umm Sakhar belonged to the local inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca following the Hijra in 622 CE. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" in Arabic, played a vital role in establishing the early Muslim community in Medina by providing shelter, resources, and protection to the nascent Islamic movement.

Her designation as a Sahabiyya indicates that she personally encountered the Prophet Muhammad and lived as a Muslim during his lifetime. The female companions of the Prophet held important positions within the early Muslim community, often serving as transmitters of religious knowledge, participants in community affairs, and examples of Islamic practice for later generations of Muslim women.

Umm Sakhar lived during a period of significant historical transformation in Arabia. Her lifetime spanned the pre-Islamic era, the Prophet's mission in Mecca and Medina, and the early expansion of Islam under the first caliphs. This generation of Muslims experienced firsthand the transition from tribal Arabian society to the establishment of a unified Islamic state.

The Ansari companions like Umm Sakhar were instrumental in the survival and growth of the early Muslim community. Their willingness to embrace Islam and support the Muslim emigrants demonstrated the cross-tribal appeal of the new faith and helped establish Medina as the political and spiritual center of the emerging Islamic state.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, a period marked by rapid Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula. The first generation of Muslims, including companions like Umm Sakhar, are remembered in Islamic tradition as the Salaf al-Salih, the "righteous predecessors," whose proximity to the Prophet and direct experience of early Islamic society gave them special significance in Islamic history and religious scholarship.

While specific details of her individual contributions may not be extensively documented, Umm Sakhar represents the broader group of female companions whose presence and participation were integral to the formation of the early Muslim community in Medina.

bio_full:
Umm Salama bint Mas'ud was a woman of the clan of Zafar. Ibn Sa'd gives her lineage as Umm Salama bint Mas'ud ibn Aws ibn Malik ibn Sawad ibn Zafar. Her mother was al-Shumus bint Amr ibn Haram ibn Tha'laba ibn Haram, of the Banu Salama.

primaryTitle: Umm al-Muʾminīn — Mother of the Believers
titles: Umm al-Muʾminīn · Zād al-Rākib (for her father's epithet: Provider of the Traveller) · Akhbar al-Umahāt (Most Knowledgeable of the Mothers)
source: Ibn Saʿd — Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā · al-Dhahabī — Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ · Ibn Ḥajar — al-Iṣāba
bio: Umm Salamah Hind bint Abi Umayyah Al-Makhzoumiyya Al-Qurashi was one of the wives of the Messenger Muhammad, one of the mothers of the believers, and one of the first to convert to Islam. She was the wife of Abu Salamah bin Abdul-Assad, and she migrated with him in the first migration to the land of Abyssinia, and upon the migration to Medina, her people prevented her from immigrating with her husband, then they released her, so she took her son and traveled, until she met Uthman bin Talha at Tan’im, who brought her to Yathrib, and it was said: She was the first woman to emigrate. To Abyssinia, and the first woman to enter Medina. When Abu Salamah died, the Prophet married her.
bio_full:
Hind bint Abi Umayya (Arabic: هِنْد ابِنْت أَبِي أُمَيَّة, Hind ʾibnat ʾAbī ʾUmayya, c. 580 or 596 –  680 or 683), better known as Umm Salama (Arabic: أُمّ سَلَمَة) or Hind al-Makhzūmiyya (Arabic: هِنْد ٱلْمَخْزُومِيَّة) was the sixth wife of Muhammad.
"Umm Salama" was her kunya meaning, "mother of Salama". She was one of the most influential female companions of Muhammad. She is recognized largely for recalling numerous Hadiths, or sayings and narrations attributed to Muhammad. Twelver Shia Muslims believe that Umm Salama was Muhammad's most important wife after Khadija.

Before marriage with Muhammad
Umm Salama's birth name was Hind. Her father was Abu Umayya ibn Al-Mughira ibn Abdullah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum ibn Yaqazah also known as Suhayl or Zad ar-Rakib. He was an elite member of the Quraysh tribe, known for his great generosity, especially to travelers. Her mother was 'Ātikah bint 'Āmir ibn Rabī'ah, of the Firas ibn Ghanam branch of the Kinana.

Marriage to Abu Salama
Before her marriage to Muhammad, Umm Salama was married to Abu Salama Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Asad, whose mother was Barrah bint Abdul Muttalib. Abu Salama was Muhammad's foster brother and one of his close companions. Umm Salama bore with Abu Salama four children: Salama, Umar, Zaynab and Ruqayyah.

Conversion to Islam
Umm Salama and her husband Abu Salama were among the first who converted to Islam. Only Ali and a few others were Muslims before them. Despite intense anger and persecution from the powerful Quraysh in response to their conversion to Islam, Umm Salama and Abu Salama continued their devotion to Islam.
As the persecution grew in severity, the new Muslims began to look for life away from Mecca. Muhammad instructed his newly converted followers, including Umm Salama and Abu Salama, to make a migration to Abyssinia. Umm Salama abandoned her honorable life in her clan in Mecca to migrate. While in Abyssinia, these Muslims were told that there had been a decrease in persecution along with an increase in numbers of Muslims in Mecca. This information caused Umm Salama, her husband, and the rest of the Muslim emigrants to travel back to Mecca. Upon their return to Mecca, the Quraysh again began viciously persecuting the Muslims. In response, Muhammad gave his followers instructions to make a migration to Medina, also known as the hijrah. Umm Salama, along with her husband and son planned to make the hijra together, however this was stopped when Umm Salama's clan forced her to stay in Mecca, while Abu Salama's clan took the child.
Umm Salama recounted this story: 

Before we were out of Makkah, however, some men from my clan stopped us and said to my husband: 'Though you are free to do what you like with yourself, you have no power over your wife. She is our daughter. Do you expect us to allow you to take her away from us?' Then they pounced on him and snatched me away from him. My husband's clan, Banu 'Abd al-Asad,  saw them taking me and became hot with rage. 'No! By Allah' they shouted, 'we shall not abandon the boy. He is our son and we have a first claim over him.' They took him by the hand and pulled him away from me.
Abu Salama made the trip to Medina alone, leaving his wife and child in Mecca. After some time, Umm Salama was permitted by the Quraysh to leave Mecca, and was given her son back by her husband's tribe. With her son, she completed the hijra and was reconnected with her husband.

Death of Abu Salama
During her marriage to Abu Salamah, Umm Salamah (in a story related by Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam) is said to have asked her husband to make agreement that when either of them died, the other would not remarry. However, in this tradition, Abu Salamah responded by instructing Umm Salamah to remarry after his death. He then prayed, "O God, provide Umm Salamah after me with a better man than me who will not grieve her or injure her!"
During the Battle of Uhud (March 625), Abu Salamah was severely injured. While Abu Salamah was dying due to these wounds, he recalled a story to Umm Salamah involving a message he had heard from Muhammad: "I heard the Messenger of God saying, 'Whenever a calamity afflicts anyone he should say, "Surely from God we are and to Him we shall certainly return."' And he would pray, 'O Lord, give me in return something better from it which only You, Exalted and Mighty can give'". This traditional story has been transmitted with various differences, but the fundamental principles of the hadith remain intact.
Her husband eventually died from the wounds he received in the Battle of Uhud. Umm Salamah remembered the hadith recalled by her husband prior to his death, and began reciting the given prayer.
Following Abdullah ibn Abdulasad's death in the battle of Uhud she became known as Ayyin al-Arab - "the one who had lost her husband". She had no family in Medina except her small children, but she was given support by both the Muhajirun and Ansar. After finishing the iddah of four months and ten days, the prescribed period that a woman must wait after the death of her husband before she can remarry, Umm Salama got offers of marriage. Abu Bakr and then Umar asked to marry her, but she declined. Muhammad himself then proposed to Umm Salama. She initially hesitated, stating, "O Messenger of Allah, I have three characteristics. I am a woman who is extremely jealous and I am afraid that you will see in me something that will anger you and cause Allah to punish me. I am a woman who is already advanced in age and I am a woman who has a young family."
However, Muhammad appeased each of her concerns, "Regarding the jealousy you mentioned, I pray to Allah the Almighty to let it go away from you. Regarding the question of age you have mentioned, I am afflicted with the same problem as you. Regarding the dependent family you have mentioned, your family is my family."

Muhammad era
Umm Salama was married to Muhammad at the age of 29 Umm Salamah was a widow with 3 children and a fourth born almost immediately after their marriage.
When Fatimah bint Asad (mother of the 4th Caliph Ali) died, Muhammad is said to have chosen Umm Salama as the guardian of Fatimah bint Muhammad. However, the latter Fatimah is thought to have married Ali in 1 AH or 2 AH, Fatimah bint Asad died in 4 AH, and Umm Salama married Muhammad in year 5, so any guardianship must have been purely nominal.
The verse of purification (33:33) in the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad in her house.

Umm Salama and the wives of Muhammad
In the fourth year following the migration to Medina (4 AH), Umm Salama accepted a marriage proposal from Muhammad . After sharing her three reservations about the marriage, and hearing the response from Muhammad, Umm Salama was so pleased that she accepted the proposal. Umm Salama became the eldest of all of Muhammad's wives. She became the second highest-ranking wife of Muhammad along Ayesha, only behind Khadija. Her elevated status among the rest of the wives was a result of her presence in many wars and her defense of the household of Muhammad. Attributes that distinguish Umm Salama from the rest of the wives of Muhammad include the following: Her role in Fatimah's upbringing (who Umm Salama proclaimed displayed more knowledge than ever herself in all affairs), her political activism, her accounts of Muhammad's narrations, and her unwavering defense of Ali's personality and leadership following Muhammad's death.
The greatest attribute of the wives of Muhammad is demonstrated as being known as the "Mothers of the believers". They were also prohibited from marrying another man ever again. (33:53) The Qur'an indicates that the wives of Muhammad had to be role models in society (33:30-32). She was often looked up to by the rest of the wives of Muhammad due to her intelligence and political knowledge. Umm Salama herself narrated 378 Hadith, among them being some of the most important.

bio: Umm Salit al-Najjariyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Umm Salit al-Najjariyya was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE in the Arabian Peninsula. She belonged to the Banu al-Najjar tribe, one of the prominent Arab tribes of Medina, as indicated by her nisba "al-Najjariyya."

As an Ansari companion, Umm Salit was among the inhabitants of Medina who supported the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community following the Hijra in 622 CE. The Ansar, meaning "helpers" or "supporters," were the Medinan Muslims who welcomed and assisted the Prophet and the Muhajirun (emigrants from Mecca) when they arrived in their city. This group played a crucial role in establishing the first Muslim community and providing the foundation for the early Islamic state.

The Banu al-Najjar tribe held particular significance in early Islamic history, as they were among the first tribes in Medina to accept Islam and pledge allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. The tribe was also notable for being the maternal relatives of the Prophet's grandfather, Abdul-Muttalib, creating ancestral connections between the Prophet and this Medinan tribe.

Living during the formative period of Islam, Umm Salit would have witnessed the establishment of the Muslim community in Medina, the development of early Islamic practices, and the expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Her lifetime, spanning approximately four decades from 595 to 635 CE, encompassed the entire prophetic mission of Muhammad and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr.

Female companions like Umm Salit represent an important dimension of early Islamic history, demonstrating women's participation in the foundational Muslim community. While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in the primary historical sources, her recognition as a Sahabiyya indicates that she was among the women who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad and participated in the early Muslim society of Medina.

Her death around 635 CE places her among the early generation of Muslims who lived through both the prophetic period and the initial years of Islamic expansion under the first caliph, making her part of the generation that witnessed Islam's transformation from a local Arabian movement to a rapidly expanding religious and political force.

Umm Sharahbil lived through the critical early decades of Islamic history, from the religion's emergence in Mecca through its establishment in Medina. Like many female companions, her specific contributions and activities are not extensively documented in historical sources, reflecting the limited preservation of women's individual stories from this period. However, her recognition as a companion acknowledges her participation in the foundational Muslim community and her role in the early Islamic society of Medina.

The female companions collectively played important roles in the early Muslim community, participating in religious life, supporting the community's needs, and helping to establish Islamic social practices. As part of the Ansar, Umm Sharahbil represented the local Medinan population that made the growth and stability of the early Islamic community possible through their acceptance and support of the new religion and its adherents.

Her lineage is traced through her father Fadala bin 'Adi, connecting her to the tribal structure that was central to Arabian society of that era.

Living during the formative decades of Islam, Umm Simak would have witnessed the transformation of Medina from a collection of feuding tribes into the first Islamic state. She lived through the period of the Prophet's ministry in Medina, which lasted from 622 CE until his death in 632 CE, and died shortly thereafter in 635 CE during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate.

Her recognition as a companion of the Prophet places her among a distinguished group of early Muslims whose direct association with Muhammad gave them special status in Islamic tradition. The companions, both male and female, are revered in Islamic history for their role in preserving and transmitting the teachings of Islam to subsequent generations. bio: Umm Subayya al-Juhayniyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Hijaz. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Umm Subayya al-Juhayniyya was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she lived through the crucial decades when Islam emerged and established itself as a major religious and social force in the region.

As indicated by her name, Umm Subayya belonged to the Juhaynayn, an Arabian tribe. The designation "al-Juhayniyya" identifies her tribal affiliation, which was a common way of distinguishing individuals in Arabian society. Her given name, Umm Subayya, follows the Arabic naming convention using "Umm" (mother of), suggesting she was the mother of someone named Subayya.

Her most significant contribution to Islamic history lies in her role as a narrator of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad. During the early Islamic period, both men and women who had direct contact with the Prophet served as crucial links in preserving and transmitting his teachings to later generations. As a sahabiyya, Umm Subayya had the unique distinction of having personally witnessed or heard the Prophet's words and actions, making her testimony invaluable for establishing authentic Islamic teachings and practices.

The preservation of hadith was essential for the development of Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and daily practice. Female companions like Umm Subayya played an important role in this transmission process, particularly in matters that might have been observed in domestic or women-only contexts. Their contributions helped ensure that a comprehensive record of the Prophet's guidance was maintained across different social spheres.

Umm Subayya lived during the pivotal years when the early Muslim community was establishing its identity and practices in the Hijaz region of western Arabia. Her death around 635 CE places her among the earliest generation of Muslims who experienced both the initial revelation period and the rapid expansion of Islam during the early caliphate.

bio: Umm Sulaym bint Milhan Al-Khazrajiya was a companion who was one of the Ansar’s first converts to Islam in Yathrib, and she was the mother of the companion Anas bin Malik, servant of the Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.
bio_full:
Al-Rumayṣāʾ bint Milḥān (Arabic: الرميصاء بنت ملحان; died c. 650 CE; 28 AH), popularly known by her kunya as Umm Sulaym, was a follower or companion (Sahabiyyah) of Islamic prophet Muhammad and was one of the earliest women converts to Islam in Yathrib (now Medina).

Biography
Umm Sulaym was the daughter of Milhan bin Khalid al-Ansari who belonged to Najjar clan of Banu Khazraj. She was the sister of Umm Haram bint Milhan and Haram bin Milhan.
She was first married to Malik ibn al-Nadr and her son by this marriage was Anas ibn Malik, a notable companion of Muhammad. Ibn an-Nadr was polytheist and was angry for her conversion to Islam. He left her and went to Syria and died there.
Following the death of her first husband, Abu Talha al-Ansari resolved to become engaged to her before anyone else did. He was confident that Umm Sulaym would not pass him over for another. He was quite rich, an accomplished horseman, and a skilful archer and he belonged to the same clan as Umm Sulaym, the Banu Najjar. But she refused. Abu Talha did not take no for an answer. He asked her if there was someone more worthy for her than him, and she explained that she was a Muslim and could not marry a polytheist. He accepted Islam and they were married, and she started educating him in Islam. Abu Talhah became a devout Muslim who loved to be in the company of Muhammad.

bio: Umm Waraqa bint Abdullah ibn al-Harith al-Ansariyya (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as First Woman Appointed to Lead Prayer; Martyr.
bio_full:
Umm Waraqah bint 'Abdullah b. Al-Harith Ansariah (commonly known as Umm Waraqah; Arabic: أم ورقة بنت عبد الله بن الحارث) was one of the female companions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. She was appointed by Islamic prophet Muhammad to lead prayers at her household.

Life
Umm Waraqah was one of very few people to have memorized the entire Qur'an, she was one of its few oral transmitters before it was recorded in writing. She was killed by "two servants, a male and a female who were under her charge."

Interpretations
The example of Umm Waraqah is based on a Hadith which has been graded Hasan (Acceptable) by Al Albani. The hadith also refutes the argument made by Imam Nawawi as it states that the Muezzin was an old man who prayed behind her so she did lead men in prayer.
The example of Umm Waraqah serves as the basis for the opinion among some Islamic jurists that women are permitted to not only lead other women in prayer, but that they may also lead mixed-sex congregations under the circumstance that she leads from behind the male congregation, does not beautify her voice, that there is no man available with any knowledge of the Quran, and that she leads them in a nafl prayer and not a fardh prayer. This is a minority opinion in the Hanbali tradition.

bio: Umm Zayd bint Qays bin al-Nu'man (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Umm Zayd bint Qays ibn al-Nu'man was a woman of the Ansar of Medina who accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd, in the women's volume of al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, gives her lineage as Umm Zayd bint Qays ibn al-Nu'man ibn Sinan ibn Ubayd ibn Adi ibn Ghanm ibn Ka'b ibn Salama, which places her in the Banu Salama clan. Her mother was Adam bint al-Qayn ibn Ka'b ibn Sawad. She married Khalid ibn Adi ibn Amr ibn Adi ibn Sinan ibn Nabi' ibn Amr ibn Sawad. Ibn Sa'd records that she became a Muslim and gave the pledge to the Prophet. His short entry names no children and gives no dates for her birth or death, and it records no further events of her life.

bio_sources.title: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (entry 634) — Umm Zayd bint Qays, via Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia

bio: Unays bin Qatada (c. 594–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Unays bin Qatada was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who joined the nascent Muslim community in Medina during the seventh century.

Unays is historically recognized as one of the Sahaba, the Arabic term for the companions of Prophet Muhammad who lived during his lifetime and embraced Islam. This designation places him among a select group of individuals who witnessed and participated in the foundational events of Islamic history during the Prophet's mission from 610 to 632 CE.

He is particularly remembered for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, which earned him recognition as a "Companion of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The participants in this battle are held in high regard within Islamic tradition, as they were part of what many consider a pivotal moment that helped establish the early Muslim state in Medina.

Unays lived during the crucial Medinan period of early Islam, when the Muslim community was establishing its social, political, and religious institutions under the Prophet's leadership. Based in Medina, he would have witnessed the development of the first Islamic society and the implementation of Islamic law and governance.

His life span, from approximately 594 to 625 CE, places him entirely within the pre-Islamic period and the early years of Islamic expansion. He died relatively young, around the age of thirty-one, during the continued consolidation of Muslim power in the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about his individual contributions beyond his participation at Badr are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his status as a Sahaba indicates he was part of the close-knit community that surrounded the Prophet during the religion's foundational years. The companions as a group played crucial roles in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings and practices to subsequent generations, making them collectively significant to the development and spread of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

bio: Unaysa bint 'Abdullah bin 'Amr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full: Unaysa (also read Anisa) bint Abd Allah ibn Amr was a woman of the Ansar of Medina who accepted Islam and pledged allegiance to the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd, in the women's volume of al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, gives her lineage as Unaysa bint Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Malik ibn al-Ajlan ibn Amir ibn Bayada, which places her in the Banu Bayada clan. Her first husband was Abbas ibn Ubada ibn Nadla, whose lineage Ibn Sa'd traces through Salim ibn Awf to al-Khazraj. After him she married Amr ibn Aws ibn Amir ibn Tha'laba, whose line Ibn Sa'd traces to al-Khazraj ibn Sa'ida. Ibn Sa'd records that she became a Muslim and gave the pledge to the Prophet. His entry does not name her mother or any children and gives no dates for her birth or death.

bio: Unaysa bint 'Amr bin Qays (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Unaysa bint 'Amr bin Qays was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the residents of Medina who embraced Islam and provided support to the Prophet and the Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Unaysa would have been among those who witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim community and the development of early Islamic society. The Ansar played a crucial role in Islamic history by welcoming the Muslim emigrants from Mecca and helping to establish Medina as the center of the growing Muslim community.

Like other female companions of her era, Unaysa lived during the foundational period of Islam, experiencing the major events that shaped the early Muslim community. This included the Prophet's migration to Medina, the establishment of the Constitution of Medina, and the various challenges faced by the nascent Islamic state during its formative years.

The female companions, including Unaysa, contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic teachings and practices. Women of this generation often served as sources of religious knowledge, particularly regarding matters of worship, family life, and social conduct within the Islamic framework.

Her death around 635 CE places her passing during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate, shortly after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This means she lived through the critical transition period when the Muslim community was establishing its governance structure under the first caliph, Abu Bakr.

While specific details of Unaysa's individual contributions are not extensively documented in the historical sources that have survived, her status as a companion places her among the first generation of Muslims who directly interacted with the Prophet Muhammad. This generation is held in special regard within Islamic tradition as the witnesses to the original Islamic community and the direct recipients of the Prophet's teachings.

Her identification as an Ansari companion connects her to the broader narrative of Medina's role as the city that provided sanctuary to the early Muslim community and served as the base from which Islam spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula and beyond.

Unaysa bint 'Anma ibn 'Adi was a female companion (sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the inhabitants of Medina who welcomed and supported the Prophet and the Muslim community when they migrated from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Unaysa would have been among the local population who embraced Islam and provided crucial support to the nascent Muslim community during its formative years. The Ansar played a vital role in the establishment of the first Islamic state in Medina, offering protection, resources, and solidarity to the Muslim emigrants (Muhajirun) who had left their homes and possessions in Mecca.

The female companions of the Prophet hold a significant place in Islamic history as they were direct witnesses to the revelation of the Quran and the development of Islamic teachings and practices. These women participated in the religious, social, and sometimes political life of the early Muslim community, contributing to the preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge and traditions.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime, Unaysa would have experienced the critical period of Islamic expansion and consolidation in the Arabian Peninsula. This era, spanning roughly from 610 to 632 CE, saw the revelation of the Quran, the establishment of Islamic law and social practices, and the unification of various Arabian tribes under the banner of Islam.

The companions, both male and female, are revered in Islamic tradition for their proximity to the Prophet and their role in preserving and transmitting his teachings to subsequent generations. Their accounts and testimonies form an essential part of the Islamic historical record and religious scholarship.

Unaysa's life would have encompassed the major events of early Islamic history, including the migration to Medina, the various military campaigns, and the final pilgrimage of the Prophet. She died around 635 CE, during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, when the Muslim community was expanding beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the leadership of the first caliphs.

While specific details about her individual contributions may not be extensively documented in the surviving historical sources, her recognition as a companion places her among the foundational figures of Islamic history whose collective witness helped establish the religious and social framework of Islam.

bio: Unaysa bint 'Urwa bin Mas'ud (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Unaysa bint 'Urwa bin Mas'ud was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE and died around 635 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the early Muslim community of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the Muslim emigrants from Mecca.

As the daughter of 'Urwa bin Mas'ud, Unaysa came from a notable Arabian family. Her father was a prominent figure from the Thaqif tribe of Ta'if who initially opposed Islam but later converted and became an influential supporter of the Muslim community. This family background placed her within the social and political networks that were significant during the early expansion of Islam.

Living in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community, Unaysa would have witnessed the establishment of the first Muslim state and the development of Islamic law and society. As one of the Ansari companions, she was part of the Medinan Muslim community that provided crucial support to the early Islamic movement, offering hospitality and protection to Muslim emigrants and participating in the growth of the new faith.

The designation of Sahabiyya indicates that she had direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and was recognized as one of his companions. Female companions played important roles in early Islamic society, contributing to religious, social, and sometimes political aspects of the developing Muslim community. They participated in religious gatherings, supported community welfare, and helped establish many of the social practices that became integral to Islamic culture.

Unaysa's life span encompasses the critical decades of early Islamic history, including the Hijra (migration to Medina), the establishment of the Islamic state, and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate period. Her presence as an Ansari companion represents the vital role that the Medinan community played in providing the foundation for Islam's growth and development during its most crucial formative years.

While specific details of her individual contributions are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, her recognition as a Sahabiyya confirms her place among the early Muslim women who contributed to the establishment and early development of the Islamic community in Medina.

Unaysa bint Hilal bin al-Mu'alla was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early Islamic period. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the designation given to the inhabitants of Medina who supported and assisted Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community after the migration (Hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari women of Medina, Unaysa would have been among those who witnessed the transformation of her city into the first Islamic state and the center of the growing Muslim community. The Ansar played a crucial role in Islamic history by providing refuge, support, and allegiance to Prophet Muhammad and the Meccan Muslims who had migrated to escape persecution.

The designation "Ansari Companion of Madinah" indicates that Unaysa was recognized as having direct contact with Prophet Muhammad and being part of the community that surrounded him during his time in Medina. Female companions held important positions in early Islamic society, often serving as transmitters of religious knowledge, participants in community affairs, and witnesses to significant events in Islamic history.

During Unaysa's lifetime, Medina served as the political and spiritual center of the Islamic community. The city was where many foundational Islamic practices were established, where the Prophet's Mosque was built, and where the early Muslim community developed its social and religious structures. As an Ansari woman, she would have been part of this formative period in Islamic civilization.

Unaysa died around 635 CE, during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate that followed Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This places her death during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, a period marked by rapid Islamic expansion beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

The preservation of her name in Islamic historical records reflects the important role that female companions played in the early Muslim community, even when specific details of their individual contributions may not have been extensively documented. Like other Sahabiyya, her status as a companion represents her direct connection to the prophetic era and her place among those who helped establish and support the early Islamic community in Medina.

bio: Unaysa bint Khubayb bin Isaf (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Female Narrator of Hadith.
bio_full:
Unaysa bint Khubayb bin Isaf was a female companion (Sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived in Medina during the early years of Islam. Born around 595 CE, she witnessed the formative period of the Islamic community and died in 635 CE, just three years after the Prophet's death.

As one of the Sahabiyyat, Unaysa belonged to the distinguished group of women who personally knew and interacted with Prophet Muhammad. Her status as a companion placed her among the most revered figures in Islamic history, as the companions are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings and the living link between the Prophet's era and subsequent generations of Muslims.

Unaysa is particularly recognized for her role in the preservation and transmission of hadith, the recorded sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad. As a female narrator of hadith, she contributed to the vast oral tradition that would later be compiled into written collections that form a cornerstone of Islamic jurisprudence and practice. The participation of women like Unaysa in hadith transmission was crucial for preserving teachings related to matters of particular concern to Muslim women, including religious practices, social conduct, and family life.

Her residence in Medina placed her at the center of the early Islamic community. Medina served as the Prophet's base after the Hijra (migration from Mecca) in 622 CE and was where much of Islamic law and practice was developed and implemented. Living in this environment, Unaysa would have had direct access to the Prophet's teachings and witnessed the establishment of the first Islamic state.

The role of female hadith narrators like Unaysa demonstrates the active participation of women in the early Islamic scholarly tradition. These women served as important sources of religious knowledge and helped ensure the accurate transmission of the Prophet's teachings across generations. Their contributions highlight the significant, though sometimes overlooked, role that women played in the development and preservation of Islamic religious sciences.

Unaysa's legacy lies in her contribution to the hadith corpus, which remains fundamental to Islamic scholarship and practice. Her position as both a companion of the Prophet and a transmitter of his teachings makes her an important figure in understanding the early development of Islamic tradition and the role of women in its preservation.

Unaysa bint Qays, also known as Nufaysa bint Qays, was a female companion of Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the helpers of Medina who supported the Prophet and the early Muslim community following the hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Sahabiyya, the female companions of the Prophet, Unaysa bint Qays lived through the crucial decades when Islam was establishing itself as both a religious and social movement. Her presence in Medina placed her at the center of the nascent Muslim community during its most critical developmental phase, when the foundations of Islamic society, law, and practice were being laid.

The Ansar held a distinctive and honored position in early Islamic history, as they were the Medinan tribes who welcomed and protected the Muslim emigrants from Mecca when they faced persecution. Women of the Ansar like Unaysa bint Qays played important roles in supporting the community through their participation in religious, social, and sometimes military activities of the early ummah.

Her life span, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompassed the entire prophetic period of Muhammad's mission as well as the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr. This means she witnessed the revelation of the Quran, the establishment of Islamic practices and institutions, and the initial expansion of the Muslim community beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

Like many female companions, Unaysa bint Qays represents the significant but often under-documented contributions of women to early Islamic society. The female companions served as transmitters of Islamic teachings, particularly regarding matters that concerned women's religious and social obligations. They participated in the religious life of the community and helped establish precedents for Muslim women's roles in worship, family life, and community participation.

Her recognition as a Sahabiyya places her among the first generation of Muslims whose direct contact with Prophet Muhammad gave them special status in Islamic tradition. The companions are revered for their role in preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings to subsequent generations, making figures like Unaysa bint Qays important links in the chain of Islamic historical and religious knowledge.

bio: Uqba bin 'Amir al-Juhayni (c. 622 CE–677 CE, Cario) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in HIjaz. Known as Poet-Companion.
bio_full:
Uqba ibn Amir al-Juhani was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived from approximately 622 to 677 CE. Born into the Juhayna tribe, he became one of the Sahaba, the direct companions of Prophet Muhammad, and played notable roles in the early Islamic community.

Uqba is particularly remembered for his literary abilities, earning recognition as the "Poet-Companion" due to his skill in Arabic poetry. His poetic talents made him a valued figure in early Islamic society, where oral tradition and eloquent expression held significant cultural importance. Poetry served not only as artistic expression but also as a means of preserving historical events, tribal genealogies, and Islamic teachings during the formative period of the Muslim community.

As a companion of the Prophet, Uqba would have witnessed and participated in the crucial early years of Islam in the Hijaz region of the Arabian Peninsula. The Sahaba held special status in Islamic tradition as the first generation of Muslims who directly learned from and interacted with Prophet Muhammad, making their testimonies and teachings foundational to Islamic knowledge and practice.

Uqba's contributions extended beyond poetry into the field of hadith sciences. As someone who had direct contact with the Prophet, his narrations and accounts became part of the broader corpus of hadith literature that would later be compiled by Islamic scholars. These narrations served as sources for understanding prophetic teachings, practices, and sayings that helped shape Islamic law and theology.

Later in his life, Uqba moved to Egypt, where he spent his final years until his death in 677 CE in Cairo. This relocation reflects the broader pattern of early Muslim expansion and settlement beyond the Arabian Peninsula following the initial conquests.

Uqba ibn Amir al-Juhani represents the intersection of pre-Islamic Arabian literary tradition with the emerging Islamic intellectual framework. His role as both poet and hadith transmitter illustrates how early Islamic society incorporated and transformed existing cultural forms while establishing new religious and scholarly traditions. His legacy lies in his dual contribution to Arabic literature and Islamic religious sciences, embodying the cultural continuity and religious transformation that characterized the early Islamic period.

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Uqba bin 'Amir bin Nabi (c. 594–634 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full: Uqba ibn Amir ibn Nabi was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr give his lineage as Uqba ibn Amir ibn Nabi ibn Zayd ibn Haram ibn Ka'b ibn Ghanm ibn Ka'b ibn Salama, and Ibn Abd al-Barr calls him al-Ansari al-Khazraji al-Sulami, of the Banu Salama clan. He was among the earliest Ansar to give allegiance: Ibn Ishaq lists him among those present at the First Pledge of al-Aqaba, and Ibn Kathir is cited as saying he also attended the Second Pledge. He fought at Badr, Uhud and the Battle of the Trench, and took part in all the Prophet's other campaigns. At Uhud he was recognised by a green band on his helmet. A report transmitted by Zayd ibn Aslam says he brought his young son to the Prophet and asked him to teach the boy prayers of supplication; Ibn al-Athir notes that this report is mursal, since Zayd did not meet Uqba. He was killed as a martyr at the Battle of al-Yamama, which al-Isaba of Ibn Hajar, as cited, dates to 12 AH (633–634 CE). Ibn al-Athir stresses that he is a different man from the better-known Companion Uqba ibn Amir al-Juhani, who belonged to the Juhayna tribe.

bio: Uqba bin 'Uthman bin Khalada (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Uqba bin 'Uthman bin Khalada was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative years of the Islamic community in seventh-century Arabia. Born around 594 CE, he lived through the crucial period of Islam's establishment and early expansion, dying in 634 CE during the caliphate of Abu Bakr.

As one of the Sahaba, the companions who knew and followed Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime, Uqba held a position of respect within the early Muslim community. He was based in Medina, the city that became the center of the nascent Islamic state after the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

Uqba is particularly remembered as a "Companion of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against their Meccan opponents. The encounter, though involving relatively small numbers of fighters, proved to be a turning point that helped establish the credibility and strength of the early Islamic state. Those who participated in this battle alongside the Prophet are held in particularly high regard in Islamic tradition.

The designation as a Companion of Badr places Uqba among a select group of early Muslims who demonstrated their commitment to the faith during one of its most challenging periods. His presence at this pivotal moment indicates he was among those who made the significant decision to support the Prophet Muhammad when the outcome of the new religious movement remained uncertain.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime and the early caliphate period, Uqba witnessed the rapid transformation of Arabian society and the establishment of Islamic governance. His death in 634 CE came during the early expansion of Islamic influence beyond the Arabian Peninsula, marking the end of a life that spanned the entire foundational period of Islam.

While specific details about his individual contributions or role within the community are limited in historical sources, his recognition as a companion and participant in the Battle of Badr establishes his place among the early supporters who helped establish the Islamic community during its formative decades.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Uqba bin Qayzi bin Qays (c. 597–635 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full:
Uqba bin Qayzi bin Qays was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 597 CE, he was among the Muslims who formed the core community in Medina following the Prophet's migration from Mecca in 622 CE.

As a Sahabi, or companion of the Prophet, Uqba belonged to the generation that directly witnessed and participated in the establishment of the early Muslim community. The companions held a special position in Islamic tradition as the first followers who lived alongside Muhammad and helped establish the practices and teachings that would define the religion.

Uqba's most notable historical significance stems from his participation in the Battle of Uhud in 625 CE, where he lost his life and earned recognition as a martyr. The Battle of Uhud was the second major military encounter between the Muslim community of Medina and the Meccan forces, taking place approximately three years after the Prophet's migration to Medina. This battle was a crucial event in early Islamic history, as it tested the resolve and unity of the nascent Muslim community during a period when their survival was far from certain.

The battle itself was a complex engagement that demonstrated both the vulnerabilities and strengths of the early Muslim forces. Those who died fighting in defense of the community, like Uqba, were remembered as martyrs who had made the ultimate sacrifice for their faith and community.

Uqba's death at Uhud in 635 CE places him among the early companions who did not live to see the rapid expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula that would occur in the decades following the Prophet's death. His brief life span of approximately 38 years was entirely contained within the transformative period when Islam emerged from a small religious movement to become the dominant force in the Arabian Peninsula.

While specific details about Uqba's individual contributions or personal characteristics are not extensively documented in historical sources, his status as a companion and martyr of Uhud ensures his place in Islamic historical memory as one of the early believers who helped establish and defend the Muslim community during its most vulnerable period.

bio: Uqba bin Wahb al-Asadi (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Uqba ibn Wahb ibn Rabi'a al-Asadi, also called Uqba ibn Abi Wahb, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad who fought at Badr. Abu Nu'aym's Ma'rifat al-Sahaba gives his lineage as Uqba ibn Wahb ibn Rabi'a ibn Asad ibn Suhayb ibn Malik ibn Kathir ibn Ghanm ibn Dudan ibn Asad ibn Khuzayma, of the Arab tribe of Asad. He was the brother of the Companion Shuja' ibn Wahb. The brothers were allies of the Quraysh clan of Abd Shams; Ibn Ishaq, as quoted by Abu Nu'aym, counts them among the allies of the Banu Umayya. Abu Nu'aym records that Uqba emigrated to Medina with the Prophet, and Ibn Hibban lists him as having companionship with the Prophet. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir both state that he and his brother Shuja' were present at Badr, and Ibn Abd al-Barr adds that they took part in all the later battles; he says he knows of no hadith narrated by either brother. Ibn Ishaq, in a report transmitted by Abu Nu'aym, says that Uqba, with Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Sa'd ibn Ubada, urged the Jews of Medina to fear God, since they knew Muhammad was God's Messenger. The sources consulted do not record when or where he died. Ibn al-Athir distinguishes him from another Badr Companion of similar name, Uqba ibn Wahb ibn Kalada al-Ghatafani, an ally of the Khazraj.
