primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Uqba bin Wahb bin Kalda (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full:
Uqba bin Wahb bin Kalda was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he died in 634 CE, meaning his life spanned the crucial decades when Islam emerged and began its rapid expansion beyond Arabia.

Uqba is historically recognized as one of the participants in the First Pledge of Aqabah, a pivotal event in early Islamic history that took place around 621 CE. This pledge marked the initial formal agreement between the Prophet Muhammad and representatives from the city of Yathrib, later known as Medina. The meeting occurred during the annual pilgrimage season when various Arab tribes gathered in Mecca, providing an opportunity for discreet negotiations between Muhammad and potential supporters from outside his home city.

The First Pledge of Aqabah was significant because it represented the first organized acceptance of Muhammad's message by people from outside Mecca, offering him and his followers a potential sanctuary from the increasing persecution they faced from the Meccan establishment. Those who participated in this pledge committed to basic principles of the Islamic faith and provided the groundwork for what would become the larger Second Pledge of Aqabah the following year.

As one of these early supporters, Uqba bin Wahb bin Kalda played a role in facilitating what would eventually become the Hijra, the historic migration of the Muslim community from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. This migration marked the beginning of the Islamic calendar and established the first Muslim political community.

Being based in Medina, Uqba would have witnessed and participated in the establishment of the early Muslim state and the various challenges it faced during its formative years. His status as a Sahaba, or companion of the Prophet, indicates that he had direct contact with Muhammad and was part of the close-knit community that surrounded the Prophet during this crucial period.

Uqba's participation in the First Pledge of Aqabah places him among a small group of individuals whose early support proved instrumental in the survival and eventual success of the Islamic movement, making him a notable figure in the foundational period of Islamic history.

bio: Urwa bin Abi Athatha bin 'Abdul-'Uzza (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Urwa bin Abi Athatha bin 'Abdul-'Uzza was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 593 CE in Mecca, he was among the early converts to Islam during a time when the nascent Muslim community faced significant persecution from the established Meccan tribes.

Urwa is primarily known for his participation in the first migration to Abyssinia (modern-day Ethiopia), which occurred around 615 CE. This migration, known as the Hijra to Abyssinia, represented a pivotal moment in early Islamic history when a group of Muslim converts sought refuge from religious persecution in Mecca. The migration was undertaken with the Prophet Muhammad's guidance, as the early Muslim community faced increasing hostility from the Quraysh tribe and other opponents of the new faith.

The decision to migrate to Abyssinia was strategic, as the Christian kingdom was ruled by the Negus (King) Najashi, who was known for his just treatment of religious minorities. The Muslim emigrants, including Urwa, found protection under this Christian ruler, demonstrating the early Islamic principle of seeking sanctuary where justice could be found, regardless of the host community's religious affiliation.

Urwa's status as a companion (Sahaba) places him among the revered early Muslims who had direct contact with the Prophet Muhammad and witnessed the revelation and development of Islamic teachings firsthand. The companions are considered crucial figures in Islamic history for their role in preserving and transmitting the Prophet's teachings and practices to subsequent generations.

His death in 633 CE occurred during the period immediately following the Prophet Muhammad's passing in 632 CE, a time when the early Muslim community was consolidating under the leadership of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. This was a critical period in Islamic history when the foundations of the Muslim state were being established and the compilation of Islamic law and tradition was beginning.

While specific details about Urwa's individual contributions to Islamic jurisprudence or his particular activities during his lifetime are not extensively documented in widely available historical sources, his significance lies in his representation of the early Muslim community's commitment to their faith despite persecution and his participation in one of Islam's most important early migrations.

full: Urwa ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam al-Asadi al-Qurashi
primaryTitle: First Islamic Historian — Transmitter of Sira
titles: Muarrikh al-Sira · One of the Seven Jurists of Medina
bio: Abu Abdullah Urwa bin Al-Zubayr bin Al-Awwam Al-Asadi, a follower, hadith scholar, and Muslim historian, one of the seven jurists of Medina, one of the many narrations about his aunt Aisha bint Abi Bakr, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, and one of the first to seek to codify the hadith. He also had pioneering contributions in codifying excerpts from the beginnings of Islamic history, upon which the Muslim historians who came after him relied. He was also known to be one of the people who recited poetry.
bio_full:
Urwa ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam al-Asadi (Arabic: عُرْوَة بْن الزُّبَيْر بْن الْعَوَّام الأَسَدِيّ, romanized: ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām al-ʾAsadī; c. 644–713) was an early Muslim traditionist, widely regarded as a founding figure in the field of historical study among the Muslims. He was a son of Muhammad's close aide al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, and a nephew of his wife A'isha. He spent much of his life in Medina, witnessed the First Fitna (656–661) as a youth, and supported his elder brother Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr in his failed attempt to establish his caliphate in the Second Fitna (680–692). After Abd Allah's elimination by his Syria-based Umayyad rivals, Urwa reconciled with the Umayyads, whom he paid occasional visits and maintained a literary correspondence with.
Urwa's relations with important early Islamic figures gave him access to first-hand accounts on the early Islamic period, which he collected from his father, his aunt, and a number of companions of Muhammad, passing these on to his students, above all his son Hisham and Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, as well as Abu al-Aswad Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman (d. 132/750). A large number of these traditions are reported in the hadith and historical literature. Some of his literary correspondences with the Umayyad caliphs Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (r. 685–705) and al-Walid I (r. 705–715) have also been reported in historical works. Combined, they cover almost all important events of Muhammad's prophetic career as well as early caliphate, and are central to the historical study of Muhammad. Modern Western historians have debated the authenticity of the Urwa corpus of traditions. Some hold that most of the traditions reported on his authority did indeed originate with him and the core of the information contained therein is genuine, although they have been modified and colored by later transmitters to some extent. On the other hand, some hold that much of the corpus is later, retrospective attribution to Urwa.

Biography
Sources differ on Urwa's birth year, placing it in 22, 23, 26, or 29 AH. 23 AH, corresponding to 643/644 CE, is most likely. His father was al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, a senior companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, and his mother was Asma, a daughter of the first caliph Abu Bakr (r. 632–634) and sister of Muhammad's wife A'isha. Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, the counter-caliph of the Second Fitna, was his full brother.
Urwa spent his early life in Medina, during the caliphate of the third caliph Uthman (r. 644–656). After Uthman's assassination, he accompanied his father, brother, and his aunt A'isha to the southern Iraqi town of Basra, where the three elders fought against the fourth caliph Ali (r. 656–661). Urwa was not allowed to participate in the fight due to his young age. His father was killed in the battle and Urwa returned to Medina with his aunt. His father's considerable fortune enabled Urwa to concentrate on studies, and he began collecting and studying reports on the earlier period of Islam. His main informant was A'isha. It is unclear exactly when he started the activity, but he is reported to have held regular sessions of study with his friends in the Prophet's Mosque of Medina during the later years of the reign of Mu'awiya I (r. 661–680), the first caliph of the Umayyad Caliphate, which succeeded the earlier Medina-based Rashidun Caliphate after the First Fitna (656–661). The group included among others, his half-brother Mus'ab and the future caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. Arab historian al-Baladhuri (d. 892) narrates a report from Urwa that he spent seven years in Egypt, which according to the historian Joseph Horovitz would fall between 678 and 685, and married there. The historian Gregor Schoeler considers it unlikely that he spent seven continuous years in Egypt.

In the Second Fitna (680–692), his elder brother Abd Allah established his counter-caliphate in opposition to the Umayyads, and Urwa supported him. When the Umayyad general al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf besieged Mecca in 692 to overthrow Abd Allah, Urwa is reported to have negotiated Abd Allah's surrender with al-Hajjaj, who agreed to grant him safety. Abd Allah ultimately decided to die fighting; al-Hajjaj struck his body on a cross. Urwa escaped al-Hajjaj to Medina, where he deposited the wealth of the Zubayrid family, and then rode to Caliph Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705) in Damascus, the capital of the Umayyads, informing him of Abd Allah's death even before al-Hajjaj's messenger could reach him. The Caliph treated him with respect and granted his request to retrieve Abd Allah's body. Urwa returned to Mecca to bury Abd Allah and offered funeral prayers over him. The sources do not mention any further Damascus visits by Urwa in Abd al-Malik's time, but the two maintained correspondence, as Abd Al-Malik would consult him on the events of early Islamic period.
After the end of the civil war, Urwa settled in Medina and continued his scholarly activity. After Abd al-Malik's death in 705, Urwa traveled to Damascus to give his allegiance to the new caliph al-Walid I (r. 705–715). During this stay, Urwa's son Muhammad died in an accident, while Urwa himself suffered from gangrene in one of his feet, which had to be amputated. In 706, he was appointed to the newly established ten-member council of fuqaha (jurists) by the then governor of Medina, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. The council was tasked to advise the governor on legal matters. Urwa died on his estate near Rabadha, which lay 200 km east of Medina, and was buried there. The year of his death is given variously between 93 AH and 101 AH, the most likely being 94 AH, which corresponds to 712/713 CE.
The sources describe Urwa as a person with upright character who avoided discord and lived a pious life. He is regarded as one of the 'Seven Fuqaha of Medina'. They were, according to the sources, the most prominent of a number of Medinan jurists who played a significant part in the development of the Medinan school of fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence). In the view of Joseph Schacht, a scholar of Islamic Law, none of them actually held to the legal doctrines of the Medinan school, since the doctrines developed only later and were ascribed to them in retrospect. Urwa is reported to have written books on law, but these have not survived. According to a report by his son Hisham (d. 763/764), Urwa destroyed them on the day of the Battle of al-Harra (August 683), when the army of the second Umayyad caliph Yazid I (r. 680–683) stormed Medina to quell the rebellion there. The scholars of the early period of Islam would write books for private use, destroying them before their deaths out of fear that they might fall into others' hands and compete with the Qur'an. Urwa destroyed the books anticipating his death in the battle. He later used to express deep regret for this loss.

Transmission of historical material
Urwa serves as a source for two types of materials on the early Islamic period: hadith and letters. His situation in an important early Islamic family enabled him to obtain first hand information on the period. He would gather accounts from his father, mother, as well as his aunt, but also reported from other authorities such as Abd Allah ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, Usama ibn Zayd, and Abu Dharr al-Ghifari.

Hadith
Urwa narrated a number of hadiths (traditions about the sayings and deeds attributed to Muhammad as well as early Muslims) which are transmitted through his son Hisham and his student Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri (d. 742). These have been reported in hadith collections—Musnad of Ibn Hanbal (d. 855), and the canonical compilations of al-Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim (d. 875) among others—legal works like Muwatta of Malik ibn Anas (d. 795), historical works (Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri), and the exegetical works (e.g. Tafsir al-Tabari).

primaryTitle: From the First Pledge of Aqabah
bio: Usaid bin Hudair bin Sammak (b. c. 589 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as From the First Pledge of Aqabah.
bio_full: Usayd ibn Hudayr ibn Simak al-Ashhali was a leading Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Aws tribe of Medina, of the clan of Banu Abd al-Ashhal. Al-Bukhari and Ahmad ibn Hanbal give his kunya as Abu Yahya, and other kunyas are also recorded. His mother was Umm Usayd bint al-Sakan. He accepted Islam through Mus'ab ibn Umayr, whom the Prophet had sent to Medina, before his friend Sa'd ibn Mu'adh did: he came to drive Mus'ab away, but after hearing him recite the Qur'an he declared his Islam. He was present at the Second Pledge of al-Aqaba, and Ibn Hibban, Ibn Manjuwayh and Ibn Abd al-Barr name him as one of the delegates (nuqaba') chosen by the Ansar there. Whether he fought at Badr is disputed: Ibn Ishaq and Ibn al-Kalbi say he did not, while Khalifa ibn Khayyat and others say he did. At Uhud he is reported to have received seven wounds and to have stood firm with the Prophet when others fled, and he took part in the later campaigns. He was known for his fine recitation of the Qur'an; in a well-known report the Prophet told him that angels had drawn near to listen as he recited Surat al-Baqara. Abu Bakr is reported to have given no one of the Ansar precedence over him. He died in Medina in Sha'ban 20 AH (641 CE); some say 21 AH. Umar ibn al-Khattab carried his bier, led the funeral prayer, and he was buried at al-Baqi'.

primaryTitle: Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam

relations.source: Sirat Ibn Hisham (half-brothers; Ayman son of Ubaid al-Habashi, Usamah son of Zayd ibn Harithah; shared mother Umm Ayman)

bio: Usamah ibn Zayd (c. 608 CE–663 CE, Medinah) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Born Muslim — First Generation Born into Islam.
bio_full:
Usama ibn Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi (Arabic: أسامة بن زيد بن حارثة الكلبي, romanized: ʾUsāma ibn Zayd ibn Ḥāritha al-Kalbī) was an early Muslim and companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
He was the son of Zayd ibn Haritha, Muhammad's adopted son, and Umm Ayman, a servant of Muhammad.
Muhammad appointed Usama ibn Zayd as the commander of an expeditionary force which was to invade the region of Balqa in the Byzantine Empire to avenge the Battle of Mu'tah, in which Usama's father and Muhammad's adopted son, Zayd ibn Harithah, had been killed. This campaign was known as the Expedition of Usama bin Zayd. 
Usama's campaign was successful and his army was the first Muslim force to successfully invade  Byzantine territory, thus paving the way for the subsequent Muslim conquest of the Levant and Muslim conquest of Egypt.

Background and early life
Usama was the son of Barakah (Umm Ayman), an Abyssinian, and her second husband, Zayd ibn Haritha. His parents were married "after Islam" and Usama was born before Hijrah.
Usama's mother, Umm Ayman served as a slave in the household of Muhammad's parents, Abdullah ibn Abdul-Muttalib and  Aminah bint Wahb. She became Muhammad's slave after the death of Aminah. Following Aminah's death in Al-Abwa, Barakah looked after Muhammad, and moved with him to the household of his grandfather Abdul-Muttalib ibn Hashim in Mecca, where she served him during his childhood and afterwards, in his adulthood. When Muhammad married Khadija, he arranged for Barakah's freedom and marriage to a Khazrajite companion named Ubayd ibn Zayd, who was her first husband. Through this marriage, Usama's half brother, Ayman ibn Ubayd was born, and thus she was known as "Umm Ayman" ("Mother of Ayman").
Usama's father, Zayd ibn Haritha, was a companion and adopted son of Muhammad. He is commonly regarded as the third person to have accepted Islam, after Muhammad's wife Khadija bint Khuwaylid, and Muhammad's cousin Ali ibn Abi Talib. He was an Arab of the Udhra branch of the Kalb tribe of Najd, central Arabia Zayd's mother, Suda bint Thaalaba, was from the Maan branch of the Tayy tribe.
As such, Usama was born into a family with strong connections to Muhammad and both his parents were prominent in the early Muslim community. His family migrated to Medina with Muhammad to escape the religious persecution of the Quraysh in Mecca.
Usama had a close relationship with Muhammad and he fought with Muhammad in the Battle of Hunayn. Ibn Kathir writes that according to Ibn Ishaq, Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who witnessed the battle, reported that the Muslim army were panicked by a surprise attack from the enemy and many men fled the battlefield. However, a group of Muhajirun stood firmly and defended Muhammad the battlefield. These men were Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, Fadl ibn Abbas, Rabi'ah ibn al-Harith, Usama ibn Zayd and Ayman ibn Ubayd. Usama's half-brother Ayman ibn Ubayd was killed that day whilst defending Muhammad.

Expedition of Usama ibn Zayd

The Expedition of Usama bin Zayd was a military expedition of the early Muslim Caliphate led by Usama ibn Zayd that took place in June 632, in which Muslim forces raided Byzantine Syria.
After the Farewell Pilgrimage, Muhammad appointed Usama ibn Zayd as the commander of an expeditionary force which was to invade the region of Balqa in the Byzantine Empire. Muhammad commanded all the sahaba, except for his family, to go with Usama to Syria to avenge the Muslims’ defeat at the Battle of Mu'tah, in which Usama's father and Muhammad's adopted son, Zayd ibn Harithah, had been killed. Usama's leadership was initially rejected by some because of his young age at the time, however Muhammad dismissed these concerns.
In reference to this event, the Sahih al-Bukhari states that:

The Prophet appointed Usama as the commander of the troops (to be sent to Syria). The Muslims spoke about Usama (unfavorably). The Prophet said, "I have been informed that you spoke about Usama. (Let it be known that) he is the most beloved of all people to me" Sahih al-Bukhari, 5:59:744
However, soon after the expedition was dispatched, people stayed in Medina refusing to go under Usama's army and disobeyed the prophet  The campaign was not reengaged until leadership of the community passed to Abu Bakr, who chose to honour Muhammad's wishes and reaffirmed Usama's command. Usama's campaign was successful and his army was the first Muslim force to invade and raid Byzantine territory successfully, thus paving the way for the subsequent Muslim conquest of the Levant and Muslim conquest of Egypt, both of which took place during Usama's lifetime.

Later life
After the death of Muhammad, Usama settled in Wadi al-Qura, then later in Medina.

primaryTitle: Chief of Banu Abd al-Ashhal — Noble Ansari
titles: Chief of Banu Abd al-Ashhal · Among the Best of Ansar
bio: Usayd bin Hudayr al-Awsi is a companion, and he was the leader of the Aws in Medina before his conversion to Islam. He inherited his position from his father, as he was one of the most prominent Arab nobles in pre-Islamic times and one of their staunch fighters. He inherited the honorable Kabir from Kabir. He was the owner of a pure thought, an upright, strong and clear personality, and an insightful opinion. Some commentators have mentioned that he was the reason for the revelation of the verse on tayammum. He died in a year.
bio_full:
Usayd ibn Hudayr al-Awsi (Arabic: أسيد بن حضير الأوسي, romanized: Usayd ibn Huḍayr al-Awsī, also Usaid ibn Hudair or Osayd ibn Hudayr) was a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and a leader of the Banū Aws tribe in the city of Medina before his conversion to Islam. He inherited his leadership position from his father who was a fierce fighter, and one of the senior Arab noblemen in Jahiliyyah.

Descent
Usayd son of Hudayr, son of Simak, son of Atik, son of Umru' al-Qays, son of Zayd, son of Abd al-Ashhal, son of Jashm, son of Harith, son of al-Khazraj, son Amr, son of Malik, son of Aws, son of Haritha, son of Tha'laba, son of Amr, son of Amir, son of Haritha, son of Tha'laba, son of Ghassan, son of al-Azd, son of al-Ghawth, son of Nabt, son of Malik, Son of Zayd, son of Kahlan, son of Saba, son of Yashjab, son of Ya'rob, son of Qahtan, al-Ashhali al-Awsi.
According to Tabari, Usayd ibn Hudayr were known from his pre-Islamic life as noble who excels at swimming and archery, while he also known as al-Kamil (The perfect one)

Conversion to Islam
Muhammad had sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr to Medina to teach and educate Muslims of the Ansar (those Medina residents who supported Mohammad) and to invite others to the religion of Allah. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh who was a friend of Usayd learned of this plan and wanted to incite him against Mus'ab. Sa'd asked Usayd to go to Mus'ab and drive him away. Usayd went to Mus'ab, who was hosted by of As'ad ibn Zurara, of the city leaders predating the calling of Islam. At As'ad's place Usayd ran into a crowd of people listening with attention to Mus'ab's call to Islam. Mus'ab invited Usayd to sit and listen before acting, then Mus'ab recited to Quran. Usayd was moved by what he heard and inquired how to join the new religion, he followed Mus'ab's instructions and declared his Islam.
Usayd died in the month of Sha'ban in the 20th year of the Hijra. His casket was carried by Umar ibn al-Khattab and he was buried in Al-Baqi Cemetery.

Qualities and virtues

Descent of angels
Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "He was among the best people in reciting the Qur'an." Asyad said: "I recited Surah Al-Baqarah one night, and I had a horse tied up, and my son Yahya was lying close to me, and he was a young boy. The horse stirred, so I got up, and I had no concern except for my son. Then I recited again, and the horse stirred, so I got up, and I had no concern except for my son. Then I recited again, and the horse stirred, so I lifted my head, and there was something like a shadow with lamps coming from the sky facing me, which startled me, so I stopped reciting. When morning came, I went to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and informed him. He said: 'Recite, O Abu Yahya.' I said: 'I have already recited.' The horse stirred, so I got up, with no concern except for my son.' He said to me: 'Recite, O Abu Yahya.' I said: 'I have already recited.' The horse stirred again, so he said: 'Recite, Abu Hudhayfah.' I said: 'I have already recited.' So I lifted my head, and there was something like a shadow with lamps in it coming from the sky facing me, which startled me. He said: 'Those were angels who drew near to your voice.

bio: Usayma (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Usayma was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative period of early Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he was among the early Muslims who joined the nascent Islamic community in Medina during the 7th century.

Usayma is historically recognized as one of the Sahaba, the Arabic term for the companions of Prophet Muhammad who met him, believed in his message, and died as Muslims. This designation places him among the first generation of Muslims who directly witnessed the development of Islamic teachings and practices under the Prophet's guidance.

He is particularly known for his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, earning him the designation "Companion of Badr." This battle holds special significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory for the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The Battle of Badr is considered a pivotal moment that helped establish the early Muslim state in Medina and demonstrated the viability of the new religious and political order. Those who fought alongside the Prophet at Badr are especially honored in Islamic tradition for their early commitment and sacrifice.

As a resident of Medina, Usayma would have been part of the community that welcomed the Prophet Muhammad during the Hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE. This migration marked the beginning of the Islamic calendar and the establishment of the first Muslim political entity. The companions who lived in Medina during this period played crucial roles in supporting the development of Islamic law, governance, and community practices.

Usayma died in 634 CE, placing his death during the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under the first Caliph, Abu Bakr. This timing means he lived through the entire prophetic period and witnessed the initial expansion of Islam beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

His historical significance lies primarily in his status as an early companion and participant in one of Islam's most important early battles. Like other companions of his generation, Usayma represents the foundational community that helped establish and preserve the early Islamic tradition, serving as a direct link between the Prophet's teachings and subsequent generations of Muslims.

dob_s: c. 617 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: c. 677 CE (Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd vol 8 entry located (OCR 2026-06); no death recorded in sources — generation estimate)
bio: Usayma bint Jabbar bin Sakhr (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Usayma bint Jabbar bin Sakhr was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad, born around 595 CE. She belonged to the Ansar, the group of Medinan Muslims who supported and welcomed the Prophet and his followers when they migrated from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Usayma was part of the foundational Muslim community that helped establish Islam in its early years. The Ansar played a crucial role in providing refuge and assistance to the Muslim emigrants (muhajirun) from Mecca, demonstrating the spirit of brotherhood and solidarity that became central to Islamic teachings.

Like other female companions of her era, Usayma would have witnessed the rapid expansion of the Muslim community and the development of Islamic practices and governance in Medina. The female companions, known collectively as the sahabiyyat, were integral members of the early Muslim society, participating in community life and supporting the growth of the new faith.

Her lifespan, from approximately 595 to 635 CE, encompassed the most transformative period in early Islamic history. She lived through the Prophet's ministry, the establishment of the first Muslim state in Medina, and the beginning of the Rashidun Caliphate following Muhammad's death in 632 CE. Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early years of the caliphate, as Islam was beginning to expand beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

The female companions like Usayma represent an important dimension of early Islamic history, demonstrating that women were active participants in the founding Muslim community. While detailed records of individual female companions are often limited compared to their male counterparts, their collective presence and contributions were significant to the establishment and early development of Islam.

As an Ansari companion, Usayma's legacy is tied to the broader story of Medina's role as the first Islamic city-state and the model for subsequent Muslim communities. Her generation of companions, both male and female, are revered in Islamic tradition as the exemplary first generation of Muslims who directly witnessed and supported the Prophet's mission.

full: Uthman ibn Muhammad ibn Uthman ibn Salih al-Fodio
titles: Shehu (Fulani Scholar-Saint) · Amir al-Mu'minin · Mujaddid of West Africa
bio: Othman bin Fodi is a Nigerian innovator and religious scholar. He was a Maliki sect and an Ash’ari sect, a Sufi in the Qadiriyya order, before he traveled for Hajj. He was influenced by the call of Muhammad bin Abdul Wahhab and became a follower of his call.
bio_full:
Shehu Usman dan Fodio  (Arabic: عثمان بن فودي, romanized: ʿUthmān ibn Fūdī; 15 December 1754 – 20 April 1817) was a Fulani scholar, Islamic religious teacher, poet, revolutionary and a philosopher who founded the Sokoto Caliphate and ruled as its first caliph. 
Born in Gobir, Usman was a descendant of the Oudah clans Fulani people living in the Hausa Kingdoms since the early 1400s. In early life, Usman became well educated in Islamic studies and soon, he began to preach Sunni Islam throughout territories that would later become parts of independent Nigeria and Cameroon. He wrote more than a hundred books concerning religion, government, culture and society. He developed a critique of existing African Muslim elites for what he saw as their greed, paganism, violation of the standards of the Sharia.
Usman formed and began an Islamic religious and social revolution which spread from Gobir throughout modern Nigeria and Cameroon. This revolution influenced other rebellions across West Africa and beyond. In 1803, he founded the Sokoto Caliphate and his followers pledged allegiance to him as the Commander of the Faithful (Amīr al-Muʾminīn). Usman declared jihad against the Hausa land and defeated them. Under Usman's leadership, the caliphate expanded into present-day Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Southern Niger and most of Northern Nigeria. Ɗan Fodio declined much of the pomp of rulership, and while developing contacts with religious reformists and jihad leaders across Africa, he soon passed actual leadership of the Sokoto state to his son, Muhammed Bello.
He encouraged literacy and scholarship, for women as well as men, and several of his daughters emerged as scholars and writers. His writings and sayings continue to be much quoted today, and are often affectionately referred to as Shehu in Nigeria. Some followers consider ɗan Fodio to have been a mujaddid, a divinely sent "reformer of Islam".
Shehu dan Fodio's uprising was a major episode of a movement described as the jihad in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries. It followed the jihads successfully waged in Futa Bundu, Futa Tooro and Fouta Djallon between 1650 and 1750, which led to the creation of those three Islamic states. In his turn, the Shehu inspired a number of later West African jihads, including those of Seku Amadu, founder of the Massina Empire and Omar Saidou Tall, founder of the Toucouleur Empire, who married one of ɗan Fodio's granddaughters.

Early life

Lineage and childhood
Usman Danfodio belongs to the generation of wandering scholars who started settling in Hausaland since the 1300–1400s, some 400–500 years before the Jihad. The Sheikh's ancestors were Toronkawa who migrated from Futa Tooro in the 1300s under the leadership of Musa Jokollo. Musa Jokollo is the 11th grandfather of the Shehu. There were 11 generations between Musa Jokollo and Shehu Danfodio. 
Abdullahi dan Fodio stated that the Torankawa (Turubbi/Torobe) have Arab ancestry through one Uqba who married a Fulani woman called Bajjumangbu. Muhammed Bello was not sure if it was Uqba ibn Nafi, Uqba ibn Yasir or Uqba ibn Amir. Usman dan Fodio's mother Hauwa is believed to be a direct descendant of Muhammad as she was descended from Maulay Idris I, the first Emir of Morocco, who was the great-grandchild of Hasan, grandson of Muhammad. Ahmadu Bello, the first Premier of Northern Nigeria and great-grandson of Muhammed Bello, also said this in his autobiography, tracing his family's connection to Muhammad through Hauwa and Muhammad Fodio.
The Toronkawa first settled in a village called Konni on the borders of Bornu Empire and Songhai Empire, till persecution drove them to Maratta under the leadership of Muhammad Sa'ad, the Sheikh's great-grandfather. A faction of them split and moved to Qoloba. It was in Maratta that Usman Danfodio was born on 15 December 1754. He was born as bi Fodiye, dan Fodio or Ibn Fudiyi, 'the son of Fodiye', his father has earned the Fulani title of Fodiye 'the learned'. A further move by the sheikh's father, Muhammad Bn Fodio after 1754 brought them from Maratta to Degel, but several of their relatives still stayed in the town of Konni. Other Toronkawa, such as Gidado's family moved to Kebbi.
His father Muhammad Fodio was an Islamic scholar who the Young Danfodio will later mention in his books as having great influence on him. Muhammad Fodio died in Degel and is buried there. Usman's mother is Hauwa Bn Muhammad. She is believed to be a direct descendant of the Islamic prophet Muhammad as she was descended from Maulay Idris I, the first Emir of Morocco. Usman and Abdullahi's first teacher was their mother Hauwa who came from a long line of famous literary scholars. Her mother, Usman's grandmother, was Ruqayyah bin Alim, who was a well respected ascetic and teacher. According to Murray Last, Ruqayya is linked to the branch of the family noted for its learning. Ruqayyah's work Alkarim Yaqbal was popular among Islamic scholars of the 18th and 19th century. Hauwa's father and Ruqayyah's husband, Muhammad bin Uthman bin Hamm, was even more famous and respected than Ruqayya. He was regarded as the most learned Fulani cleric of the time.

Education
While Usman was young, he and his family shifted to Degel where he studied the Quran. After studying the Qur'an with his father, Danfodio moved to other teachers. They included his relations, Uthman Bn Duri, and Muhammad Sambo. After being taught by Uthman Binduri, Danfodio joined Jibril bin Umar. Ibn Umar was a powerful intellectual and religious leader at the time, who was a staunch proponent of Jihad. Jibrin Ibn Umar was a controversial figure who later fall out with Danfodio; his preaching on defining who a Muslim is became a subject of disagreement between him and Shehu later in life. The Son of Ibn Umar later joined Shehu at the beginning of the Jihad. Other students of Ibn Umar include Danfodio's brother Abdullahi dan Fodio, and cousins Muhammad Firabri and Mustapha Bin Uthman  At age 20, Usman set up his school in Degel, where he preached and studied at the same time. In time, he became well educated in classical Islamic science, philosophy, and theology, and also became a revered religious thinker. 
In 1786, Danfodio attended the assembly of his cousin Muhammad bn Raji where he received further academic certifications (p.7). 
By 1787, Danfodio was writing a number of books in Arabic  and composing long poems in Fulfulde. He finished one of his most famous books, "Ihyā’ al-sunna wa ikhmād al-bid’a (The Revival of the Prophetic Practice and Obliteration of False Innovation)" by 1773, which established Danfodio's reputation among contemporary scholars. In his dispute with local scholars over scholasticism, he wrote over 50 works against the quibbles of local scholars.

Call to Islam
In 1774, Usman began his itinerant preaching as an  Mallam and continued preaching for twelve years in Gobir and Kebbi, followed by further five years in Zamfara. Among Usman's well-known students include his younger brother Abdullah, the Hausa King Yunfa, and many others.
His preaching tours took him from to Faru. After his return from Faru, he continued to tour going beyond Kebbi as far as Illo across the Niger River, and in the South travelling to Zugu beyond the Zamfara River valley.
Usman criticized the ruling elite with his writings, condemning them for enslavement, worshiping idols, sacrificial rituals, overtaxation, arbitrary rule and greed. He also insisted on the observance of the Maliki fiqh in personal observances as well as in commercial and criminal law. Usman also denounced the mixing of men and women, pagan customs, dancing at bridal feasts, and inheritance practices against women contrary to Sharia. Soon, the young Danfodio got massive followership among the peasants and other lower class.
Usman broke from the royal court and used his influence to secure approval for creating a religious community in his hometown of Degel that would, he hoped, be a model town.

bio: Utba bin 'Abdullah b Sakhr (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full: Utba ibn Abd Allah ibn Sakhr was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr give his lineage as Utba ibn Abd Allah ibn Sakhr ibn Khansa ibn Sinan ibn Ubayd ibn Adi ibn Ghanm ibn Ka'b ibn Salima, of the Khazraj, and call him al-Salami al-Ansari. According to Ibn Sa'd his mother was Bisra bint Zayd, also of the Salima line. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr both state that he was present at the Pledge of al-Aqaba and fought at Badr, and Ibn Ishaq lists him among the fighters at Badr. Ibn Sa'd records that he took part in Badr and Uhud. Ibn al-Athir notes that Abu Musa gave a shorter lineage leaving out Sakhr, Khansa and Sinan, and argues from Ibn Ishaq's list of the Badr fighters that the fuller lineage is correct. Ibn Sa'd says he died leaving no descendants. The sources consulted give no date or place for his death.

bio_sources.title: Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab and Ibn Sa'd's Tabaqat — Utba ibn Abd Allah ibn Sakhr, via Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia

primaryTitle: Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18
bio: Utba bin 'Uwyam bin Sa'ida (b. c. 600 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of the Pledge of Ridwan — Quran 48:18.
bio_full:
Utba bin 'Uwyam bin Sa'ida was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early seventh century CE. Born around 600 CE, he was among the Muslims who migrated to or resided in Medina during the formative period of the Islamic community.

Utba is most notably remembered for his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan, also known as the Pledge of the Tree, which took place at Hudaybiyyah in 628 CE. This significant event occurred when the Prophet Muhammad and approximately 1,400 of his followers were traveling to Mecca for pilgrimage but were prevented from entering the city by the Meccan tribes. Under a tree at Hudaybiyyah, the companions pledged their allegiance to the Prophet, vowing to stand by him even unto death if necessary. This pledge is referenced in the Quran in verse 48:18, which states that God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree.

The Pledge of Ridwan holds particular significance in Islamic history as it demonstrated the unwavering loyalty of the early Muslim community to their Prophet during a moment of potential conflict. Those who participated in this pledge are held in special regard within Islamic tradition, as the Quranic verse explicitly mentions divine approval of their actions.

As a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, Utba would have been part of the generation that directly witnessed the revelation of the Quran and the establishment of Islamic practices. The companions, known as Sahaba in Arabic, are considered the primary transmitters of Islamic teachings, including hadith literature that forms a crucial foundation for Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

Utba's death is recorded as occurring around 640 CE, placing him among those companions who lived through the Prophet's lifetime and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Bakr and the beginning of Umar ibn al-Khattab's reign. His life span thus encompassed the crucial decades during which Islam was established as a religious and political force in the Arabian Peninsula and began its expansion beyond Arabia's borders.

While specific details of his individual contributions beyond his participation in the Pledge of Ridwan are not extensively documented, his status as a companion places him among the foundational figures of early Islamic history.

bio: Utba bin Abi Lahab (b. c. 606 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca.
bio_full: Utba ibn Abi Lahab was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad from the clan of Hashim of Quraysh who accepted Islam at the conquest of Mecca. He was a son of Abu Lahab, whose name was Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and of Umm Jamil bint Harb ibn Umayya, sister of Abu Sufyan, whom Ibn al-Athir identifies with the 'carrier of firewood' of the Qur'an. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Sa'd report that he was engaged to the Prophet's daughter Ruqayya. After Sura 111 ('Perish the hands of Abu Lahab') was revealed, his father said he would cut ties with him unless he broke the engagement, and he broke it. When the Muslims conquered Mecca in 8 AH (630 CE), Utba and his brother Mu'attib kept away from the Prophet. The Prophet sent their uncle al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib to bring them, and both accepted Islam and pledged allegiance. Utba then fought with the Prophet at Hunayn; al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar reports that he and Mu'attib were among those who stood firm and did not flee, though Abu Musa doubted this. The brothers also took part in the siege of al-Ta'if. They stayed in Mecca and did not move to Medina, and Ibn al-Athir records that both left descendants. The sources consulted give no firm date for his death.

bio_sources.title: English Wikipedia — Utbah ibn Abi Lahab
Usd al-Ghaba (Ibn al-Athir) — Utba ibn Abi Lahab, via Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia

bio: Utba bin Rabai'a bin Khalid (b. c. 594 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Utba bin Rabai'a bin Khalid was a companion (sahabi) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the early formative period of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 594 CE, he lived through the pre-Islamic period and witnessed the emergence and establishment of the Muslim community.

As one of the sahaba, Utba was among those who personally knew, interacted with, and followed the Prophet Muhammad during his lifetime. This designation places him within the most revered circle of early Muslims, whose testimonies and actions helped shape the foundational practices and understanding of Islam.

Utba is particularly remembered as a "Companion of Badr," referring to his participation in the Battle of Badr in 624 CE. This battle holds exceptional significance in Islamic history as the first major military victory of the Muslim community against the Meccan forces. The battle marked a turning point for the early Muslim community in Medina, demonstrating their military capability and strengthening their position in the Arabian Peninsula. Those who fought alongside the Prophet Muhammad at Badr are held in special esteem within Islamic tradition due to their role in this pivotal moment.

Based in Medina, Utba would have been part of the community that developed around the Prophet Muhammad after the Hijra (migration) from Mecca in 622 CE. Medina served as the political and spiritual center of the growing Muslim community, where many of the fundamental Islamic practices and social structures were established.

Utba's life spanned the crucial period of Islamic origins, from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's mission and into the early years of the Rashidun Caliphate following Muhammad's death in 632 CE. He died in 634 CE, during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, having witnessed approximately four decades of transformative change in Arabian society.

The companions of the Prophet Muhammad, including Utba bin Rabai'a bin Khalid, are considered vital links in the transmission of Islamic teachings and practices. Their direct experience with the Prophet Muhammad and their participation in the foundational events of Islam made them crucial figures in preserving and passing down the religious and social frameworks that would guide the rapidly expanding Muslim community in subsequent generations.

primaryTitle: Martyr of the Battle of Uhud
bio: Utba bin Rabi' bin Rafi' (c. 597–625 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Martyr of the Battle of Uhud.
bio_full: Utba ibn Rabi' ibn Rafi' was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Ansar of Medina who was killed at the Battle of Uhud. Ibn Ishaq, as transmitted by Abu Nu'aym in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba, gives his lineage as Utba ibn Rabi' ibn Rafi' ibn Mu'awiya ibn Ubayd ibn Tha'laba ibn al-Abjar, and counts him among the Ansar of the Banu al-Abjar, who are the Banu Khudra. Ibn Abd al-Barr's al-Isti'ab gives the last name in the chain as Abd al-Abjar and calls him al-Khudri al-Ansari. Both Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Abd al-Barr record that he was killed as a martyr at Uhud; in Abu Nu'aym's words, he was martyred at Uhud with the Prophet. Ibn Ishaq includes him in his list of the Ansar who fell there. The sources consulted give no further details of his life.

bio_sources.title: Ma'rifat al-Sahaba (Abu Nu'aym) and al-Isti'ab (Ibn Abd al-Barr) — Utba ibn Rabi' ibn Rafi', via Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia

bio: Abu Abdullah Utbah bin Masoud bin Ghafil Al-Hudhali is a companion and jurist who was an ally of Banu Zahra, and he is the brother of Abdullah bin Masoud. He immigrated to Abyssinia the second migration with his brother Abdullah, and came to Medina, and witnessed Uhud and all the sights that came after it, and he died during the caliphate of Omar bin Al-Khattab, and he prayed for him. His brother Abdullah cried for him, so he was told: “Are you crying?” He said: “My brother, and my companion is with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.”
bio_full:
Utba ibn Mas'ud al-Hudhali was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad and the brother of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. The family belonged to the tribe of Hudhayl and were allies of the Meccan clan of Banu Zuhra. Ibn Abd al-Barr notes that most authorities count Utba and Abdullah as full brothers, though some say Utba's mother was a different Hudhali woman.

According to Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr, Utba emigrated to Abyssinia with his brother Abdullah in the second migration, and later came to Medina. Both authors state that he was present at Uhud and at the later campaigns with the Prophet.

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abd al-Barr and al-Bukhari report that he died in Medina during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who led the funeral prayer over him; al-Dhahabi adds that Umar waited for their mother, Umm Abd, before the prayer. Ibn Hibban and Ibn Abi Hatim say he died before his brother Abdullah. A different report, transmitted by Abu Nu'aym through al-Layth ibn Sa'd and cited by Ibn al-Athir from al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman, places his death in 44 AH, which would be after Abdullah's death.

When Utba died, Abdullah wept for him. Asked why he was crying, he answered that Utba was his brother and his companion with the Messenger of God, and the person dearest to him after Umar; al-Dhahabi, Ibn al-Athir, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Abu Nu'aym all relate this.

Al-Dhahabi records that Utba's son Abdullah ibn Utba lived in the Prophet's time and narrated hadith; he was the father of Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah ibn Utba, one of the Seven Jurists of Medina.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Utba ibn Mas'ud (Ibn Sa'd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban)
Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Utba ibn Mas'ud al-Hudhali (Siyar, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab, Abu Nu'aym)
Arabic Wikipedia — عتبة بن مسعود

full: Utbah ibn Ghazwan ibn Jabir ibn Wahb al-Mazini, Confederate of Banu Nawfal
primaryTitle: Founder of the City of Basra
dod_s: 639 CE / 17 AH — died from injuries near Madinah
titles: Seventh Muslim · Founder of Basra · First Governor of Basra · Abu Ghuzayyah
bio: Utbah bin Ghazwan, a companion of Badri, was an ally of Banu Nawfal bin Abd Manaf in pre-Islamic times. He converted to Islam and migrated to Yathrib. He participated with the Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings of God be upon him, in all of his conquests. Then he participated in the conquest of Iraq. He was the one who captured Basra and was its first governor.
bio_full:
Utba ibn Ghazwan al-Mazini (Arabic: عُتبة بن غَزْوان المازني, romanized: ʿUtba ibn Ghazwān al-Māzinī) (c. 581–638) was a well-known companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. He was the seventh person to convert to Islam and participated in the hijra to Abyssinia, but returned to stay with Muhammad in Mecca before making the second hijrah to Medina. He fought at the battle of Badr (624), the battle of Uhud (625), the Battle of the Trench (627) and many others, including the battles of Yamamah.
During the caliphate of Umar (r. 634–644), Utba commanded a force of 2,000 men in a campaign against Ubullah which lasted from June through September 635. Once Uballah was occupied, Utba sent a force across the Tigris River which occupied the district of Furat, followed by Meisan and Abarqubaz. He was soon appointed governor of Basra (Iraq) by the caliph. In 639 Utba left for the Hijaz to perform hajj and to request Umar to relieve him of his office as governor. Umar refused, but while returning to Basra, Utba fell from his camel and died. He was succeeded by al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah as governor.

Origins and companion of Muhammad
Utba born c. 581, the son of Ghazwan ibn al-Harith ibn Jabir. He belonged to the Banu Mazin, a minor clan from the Mansur ibn Ikrima branch of the Qays tribe in the Hejaz (western Arabia). Utba was a confederate of the Banu Nawfal clan of the Quraysh tribe of Mecca. He became an early convert to Islam and companion of Muhammad. He was known to be the seventh person to embrace Islam and he participated in the two Muslim emigrations from Mecca to Abyssinia, as well as playing combat roles in the Battle of Badr and several of the raids led or ordered by Muhammad. Utba was married to a daughter of al-Harith ibn Kalada of the Banu Thaqif; according to al-Baladhuri her name was Azda, while according to al-Mada'ini her name was Safiyya.

Conquest of Iraq
During the caliphate of Abu Bakr (r. 632–634), the Muslims led by Khalid ibn al-Walid may have launched their first campaigns against the Sasanian Persians in lower Mesopotamia (Iraq), but these their gains were short-lived or limited. Abu Bakr's successor Umar (r. 634–644) dispatched Utba to this front from the capital at Medina, which marked the commencement of the definitive conquest of Iraq. His force was relatively small, ranging from 300 to 2,000 men, according to the medieval Arabic sources. Its ranks were dominated by members of the Banu Thaqif, with whom Utba had marital links,  and partly consisted of nomadic Arab tribesmen who joined Utba's army while it was on the move.
Utba launched an assault against the town of Ubulla and its 500-strong garrison of Persian cavalry. He set up camp at a nearby village called Khurayba, then bested Ubulla's defenders and occupied and plundered the town. He installed one of his lieutenants, his brother-in-law Nafi ibn al-Harith ibn Kalada, to guard the town, which he used as a base of operations against other Sasanian positions in the area. He and/or his lieutenant commanders al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba and Mujashi ibn Mas'ud al-Sulami thereafter captured the towns of al-Furat and Maysan and the districts of Abazqubadh and Dast Maysan, all located along the lower Tigris river banks.

Bibliography

dob_s: c. 590 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: c. 650 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
bio: Uthayla bint al-Harith (b. c. 595 CE) was a female companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Medina. Known as Ansari Companion of Madinah.
bio_full:
Uthayla bint al-Harith was a female companion (sahabiyya) of the Prophet Muhammad who lived during the formative years of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula. Born around 595 CE, she belonged to the Ansar, the term used to describe the inhabitants of Medina who supported and welcomed the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community after their migration (hijra) from Mecca in 622 CE.

As one of the Ansari companions of Medina, Uthayla would have witnessed and participated in the crucial early development of the Muslim community during its establishment in the city then known as Yathrib. The Ansar played a vital role in providing shelter, protection, and support to the Muslim emigrants from Mecca, helping to ensure the survival and growth of the nascent Islamic community during a critical period.

Living during the Prophet's lifetime, Uthayla was part of the first generation of Muslims who received religious instruction directly from Muhammad and observed the practical implementation of Islamic teachings in daily life. The female companions of this era contributed to the preservation and transmission of Islamic knowledge, customs, and practices to subsequent generations, though the specific details of individual contributions are often not extensively documented in historical sources.

Uthayla's life span of approximately forty years covered the most transformative period in early Islamic history, from the pre-Islamic era through the Prophet's mission and the initial expansion of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. She lived through the establishment of the first Muslim state in Medina, the gradual conversion of Arabian tribes to Islam, and the consolidation of Islamic religious and social practices.

Her death around 635 CE occurred during the early period of the Rashidun Caliphate, just a few years after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. This places her among those companions who witnessed the immediate aftermath of the Prophet's passing and the beginning of Islamic expansion beyond Arabia under the first caliphs.

While specific details about Uthayla's individual activities and contributions are not extensively preserved in available historical sources, her status as a sahabiyya indicates her recognized position within the early Muslim community and her role as part of the foundational generation that helped establish Islamic civilization.

bio: Uthman bin 'Abd Ghanm bin Zuhayr (b. c. 593 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Emigrant to Abyssinia.
bio_full:
Uthman ibn Abd Ghanm ibn Zuhayr ibn Abi Shaddad was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from Quraysh, of the clan of al-Harith ibn Fihr; Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr call him al-Qurashi al-Fihri. Ibn Sa'd traces his lineage through Rabi'a, Hilal, Malik, Dabba and al-Harith to Fihr, and says his mother was from the clan of Zuhra. The genealogist Hisham ibn al-Kalbi gives his name instead as Amir ibn Abd Ghanm, with the kunya Abu Nafi'.

Ibn Sa'd states that he accepted Islam early in Mecca and emigrated to Abyssinia in the second migration, citing Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq, Abu Ma'shar and al-Waqidi. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr say all authorities count him among the emigrants to Abyssinia.

Ibn Sa'd names two sons, Nafi' and Sa'id, whose mother was Barza bint Malik. He reports that Uthman died after this and left no surviving line of descendants. None of the sources consulted gives a date or place of death.

bio_sources.title: Hadith Transmitters Encyclopedia — Uthman ibn Abd Ghanm (Ibn Sa'd, Usd al-Ghaba, al-Isti'ab)

relations.person: Abdur Rahman ibn Uthman bin Maz'un

bio: Uthman bin Maz'un (c. 594–624 CE) was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, based in Mecca. Known as Companion of Badr.
bio_full:
Uthman ibn Maz'un ibn Habib ibn Wahb, known by the kunya Abu al-Sa'ib, was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad from the Jumah clan of Quraysh. Ibn al-Athir names his mother as Sukhayla bint al-Anbas, and Ibn Hibban notes that he was the brother of Qudama ibn Maz'un. He was among the earliest converts, as was his wife Khawla bint Hakim.

He emigrated to Abyssinia in the first migration together with his son al-Sa'ib, and Abu Nu'aym describes him as the leader of that group of emigrants. Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abd al-Barr, citing Ibn Ishaq, state that he took part in both migrations to Abyssinia. Abu Nu'aym relates that on returning to Mecca he entered the protection of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, later gave that protection up, and was then struck in the eye. Abu Nu'aym also describes him as an ascetic.

After the emigration to Medina he fought at Badr, as Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr record. Ibn al-Athir calls him the first of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) to die in Medina, and Ibn Sa'd says he was the first Muslim buried in the cemetery of al-Baqi'. Ibn Abd al-Barr adds that the Prophet placed a stone at the head of his grave, and Ibn Hibban and Abu Nu'aym report that the Prophet kissed him after his death.

The sources differ on the date. Ibn Sa'd places his death in Sha'ban, about thirty months after the Hijra. Ibn al-Athir, Ibn Abd al-Barr and Abu Nu'aym give 2 AH, and Ibn Abd al-Barr also mentions a report of twenty-two months after the Hijra.
