primaryTitle: Founder of the Zahediyya Sufi order and spiritual grandfather of the Safavids
bio: Zahed Gilani (1216–1301 CE) was a mystic of the Zahediyya tradition, based in Lahijan. Known as Founder of the Zahediyya Sufi order and spiritual grandfather of the Safavids.
bio_full:
Zahed Gilani (1218 – 1301) He was an Iranian Sufi grandmaster of Talysh origin and the founder of the Zahediye Sufi order in Gilan; this order became known as the Safavid order after his son-in-law Safi al-Din succeeded him.
Through his daughter's marriage to his disciple Safi al-Din, Zahed Gilani is a biological ancestor of the Safavid dynasty.
According to Minorsky and Elwell-Sutton at the Encyclopaedia of Islam, the tomb of Sheikh Zahed is situated a few miles to the south of the town of Lankaran. However, another tomb dedicated to him can be found in Lahijan.

Life
Zahed Gilani was probably a Talysh. Since the mid-13th century, Sheikh Zahed has been revered as a spiritual authority and his tomb near Lahijan in Iran's Gilan Province, on the shores of the Caspian Sea, draws numerous pilgrims to the village of Sheikhanvar. His ancestors came from the ancient Iranian city of Sanjan in Khorasan (located in present-day Turkmenistan). Fleeing the Seljuk invasion that would eventually conquer large parts of Iran, his ancestors settled in Gilan in the late 11th century. Taj Al-Din Zahed Gilani was able to attain cultural and religious influence on the Ilkhanid rulers (1256–1353), descendants of Genghis Khan, who followed Seljuq rule.
His most notable disciple was Safi-ad-Din Ardabili (1252–1334), the Eponym of the Safavid dynasty (1501–1736). He wed Zahed's daughter Bibi Fatima and, overgoing the interest of Zahed's firstborn son, Gamal Al-Din Ali, was entrusted with the Grand Master's Zahediyeh Sufi Order, which he transformed into his own, the Safaviyya (Sufi order) Order. Zahed Gilani's second-born son, Sadr al-Dīn, wed Safi Al-Din's daughter from a previous marriage. 170 years after Safi Al-Din's death (and 200 years after the death of Sheikh Zahed Gilani) Safaviyya had gained sufficient political and military power to claim the Throne of (Northern) Iran for the Safavid Heir, Shah Ismail I Safavi. The two families were to be intertwined for many centuries to come, by blood as well as mutual spiritual causes.
The Sil-silat-al-nasab-e Safaviyeh or Genealogy of the Safavids, was written by Pir Hossein Abdul Zahedi, a 17th-century descendant of Zahed Gilani.

bio: Zaki Naguib Mahmoud (1905–1993 CE) was a philosopher of the Philosophy tradition, based in Cairo. Known as Egyptian logical positivist philosopher.
bio_full:
Zaki Naguib Mahmoud (Arabic: زكي نجيب محمود‎) (February 2, 1905 – September 8, 1993) was an Egyptian intellectual and thinker, and is considered a pioneer in modern Arabic philosophical thought. He was described by Abbas Mahmoud al-Akkad as "the philosopher of authors and author of philosophers". Mahmoud adhered to logical positivism and adopted science interpretation with social motivations to reconcile the Arab tradition with modernism. Mahmoud defines the "Arab tradition" as the configuration of techniques by which our ancestors lived, and he viewed logical positivism as the spirit of "Modernism".

Life
Zaki Naguib Mahmoud was born in the Damietta governorate in northern Egypt. There he attended the traditional Islamic school (kuttāb) where he memorized part of the Qur'an in his early years. He went to elementary school in Cairo and then in Sudan, where his father worked as a civil servant. He studied at the Gordon Memorial College in Khartoum and attended two years of his secondary school there before returning to Egypt where he continued his secondary education. Afterwards he entered the high school of teachers and graduated in 1930. He then worked as a teacher until 1944.
He was married to Dr Munira Helmy, a professor of psychology at Ain Shams University.

Academic life
Zaki Naguib Mahmoud finished his education at Ain Shams University, and then travelled to the United Kingdom to do his PhD at King's College London in Philosophy. He defended his dissertation titled "self-determination" successfully and obtained his PhD in 1947, later on the dissertation was translated by his student Dr. Abdul-Fattah Emam.
When he came back, he was appointed as a lecturer, then, assistant professor and finally professor of philosophy at the Faculty of Arts, Cairo University. Among the distinguished positions Zaki Naguib Mahmoud held are: professor of philosophy in the University of Kuwait (1968), member of the Supreme Council of Culture, and of the National Council of Education and Scientific Research. In addition, he worked in 1953 as a visiting professor of philosophy in The University of South Carolina in Columbia, USA for one semester, and in Washington State University in Pullman, Washington in the second, and then he worked as a cultural attaché in the Embassy of Egypt in Washington, D.C. (1954–1955).
Zaki Naguib Mahmoud was given the State Incentive Award in 1960, Order of Merit Award in 1970, Arab Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization Award in 1984, The American University in Cairo Honorary Doctorate in 1985, and the necklace of Sultan Al-Owais of the U.A.E. in 1991, an award which is exclusive to the most distinguished figures in the Arab world.

His thought
Zaki Naguib Mahmoud's thought can be divided into two or three phases, according to the measure we use to approach and evaluate it. In the general meaning of the term "thought" it is evident according to his own writings as well as other scholars that he passed through three phases of thinking.

Evolution of his thought
Zaki Naguib started his intellectual life, in its first phase, with a religious if not a Sufi position in which he defended religious miracles, human freedom as well as metaphysical contemplation of human life. It is believed that this phase extended until his studies for PhD and peaked in his dissertation "self-determination". In this work he attacked Hume's empiricism as well as behaviorism in their rejection of the concept of the psych. Following this attack he purported to support the view of objective free will of human psych or mind, albeit with the acknowledgement of the deterministic nature of its environment as well as its own constitution determined through history.
His second phase of thought began in the late 1940s and early 1950s. Dr. Mahmoud was exposed during his studies in England to analytic philosophy and was greatly influenced by the thought of Bertrand Russell and attended a lecture by Alfred Ayer on "Logical Positivism". This constituted a form of preparation for his second phase, in which he strictly adopted the principles of the new philosophical school of Logical positivism. Logical positivism rejected philosophy in its metaphysical sense and rendered it to the status of the analysis of scientific knowledge and analysis of meanings of the regular language. This period extended to somewhere between 1960 after writing The Artist East and 1968, when he left to teach in Kuwait. Landmarks of this period are his books: On Positivist Logic (1951), The Philosophy of Science (1952), The Myth of Metaphysics (1953) and The Theory of Knowledge (1956).
In particular, in The Myth of Metaphysics, he empathized on the well-known idea of the Logical Positivists that non-scientific phrases that cannot be verified scientifically are void of objective meaning. This was understood by the wider community as an indirect rejection of religion in general and Islam in particular. The book has invoked a storm of attack and criticism to its topic and to the author. In a late response, 1984, Zaki Naguib has reprinted the book with a slightly more moderate title A Stance from Metaphysics.
The third and last period has clarified itself during the period he stayed in Kuwait University between 1968 and 1973. This period can be viewed as a synthesis of the two previous stages. For it is marked by his deep interest in the intellectual Islamic heritage as well as the Islamic view as possessing specific characteristics. This new synthesis has revealed itself in domination of the problematic known as "Authenticity and Modernity" on his thought. This period is best marked, among many other writings by his books: The Rational and the Irrational in our Intellectual Heritage (1975), Our Culture in Front of Contemporary Time, (1976), and An Islamic Vision (1987).
However, if we adopt a strict philosophical measure in assessing his works we would be speaking about two phases of philosophical thought. Moreover, these two phases should be understood within one philosophical theme that comprises the essence of his philosophy.

Philosophy
Mahmoud's philosophy can be found in one recurrent theme that constitutes the driving motive behind his successive views and phases. According to his own interpretation in his intellectual autobiography, A Story of a Mind, we may present such a central theme in one phrase: "Scientific thinking as a basic social value". His central problem was, as much as every thinker in the Arabic modernist era, how to transform a backward society like our present Arabic and Islamic societies into an advanced one. The answer was, in his view, to get rid of superstitious and irrational ways of thinking, and replace them by scientific thinking.
Hence, his enthusiasm for Logical Positivism was essentially a pragmatic move, his vision was that he can make use of this philosophical/scientific construct to uplift and boost his central idea. However, we should say that his writings during the first phase do not show any provisions, deviations or partial criticism of this philosophy. Hence, we can conclude correctly that such a pragmatic explanation of his position at that period applies only on the subconscious level, in which contradictions of this view with his traditional convictions has been running on the subconscious level.
In any case, "Scientific thinking", as an absent value in our societies, has taken for him the form of a philosophical project. The basic aim of such a project is to push toward implementing such thinking in the society, and the means with which this goal will be achieved is the position of logical positivism, or "scientific empiricism", the term he prefers.

full: Aminah bint Wahb ibn Abd Manaf al-Zuhriyyah
titles: Umm al-Nabi (Mother of the Prophet)
bio: Mother of Prophet Muhammad; married Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib. Widowed while pregnant. Died at al-Abwa aged ~28 while returning from Yathrib with 6-year-old Muhammad.
bio_full:
Amina bint Wahb ibn Abd Manaf al-Zuhriyya (Arabic: آمنة بنت وهب, romanized: Āmina bint Wahb, c. 549–577) was the mother of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. She belonged to the Banu Zuhra tribe.

Early life and marriage
Aminah was born to Wahb ibn Abd Manaf and Barrah bint 'Abd al-'Uzzā ibn 'Uthmān ibn 'Abd al-Dār in Mecca. Her tribe, Quraysh, were said to be descendants of Ibrahim (Abraham) through his son Isma'il (Ishmael). Her ancestor Zuhrah was the elder brother of Qusayy ibn Kilab, an ancestor of Abdullah ibn Abdul-Muttalib, and the first Qurayshi custodian of the Kaaba. Abd al-Muttalib proposed the marriage of Abdullah, his youngest son, to Aminah. Some sources state that Aminah's father accepted the match; others say that it was Aminah's uncle, Wuhaib, who was serving as her guardian. The two were married soon after. Abdullah spent much of Aminah's pregnancy away from home as part of a merchant caravan and died of disease before the birth of his son in Medina.

Birth of Muhammad and later years

Three months after Abdullah's death, in 570–571 CE, Muhammad was born. As was tradition among all the great families at the time, Aminah sent Muhammad to live with a milk mother in the desert as a baby. The belief was that in the desert, one would learn self-discipline, nobility, and freedom. During this time, Muhammad was nursed by Halimah bint Abi Dhuayb, a poor Bedouin woman from the tribe of Banu Sa'ad, a branch of the Hawāzin.
When Muhammad was six years old, he was reunited with Aminah, who took him to visit her relatives in Yathrib (later Medina). Upon their return to Mecca a month later, accompanied by her slave, Umm Ayman, Aminah fell ill. She died around the year 577 or 578, and was buried in the village of Al-Abwa'. Her grave was destroyed in 1998. The young Muhammad was taken in first by his paternal grandfather, Abd al-Muttalib, in 577, and later by his paternal uncle Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib.

Religious belief

Islam rebukes the idea that lineage plays a part in one's final destination, as each person is responsible for themselves and their deeds. Muslims are split between whether or not Aminah was granted Heaven. One Hadith mentions Muhammad’s father: "Verily, a person said: Messenger of Allah, where is my father? He said: (He) is in the Fire. When he turned away, he (the Holy Prophet) called him and said: Verily my father and your father are in the Fire."

However, Sahih Muslim 976b states: The Apostle of Allah (ﷺ) visited the grave of his mother and he wept, and moved others around him to tears, and said: I sought permission from my Lord to beg forgiveness for her but it was not granted to me, and I sought permission to visit her grave and it was granted to me so visit the graves, for that makes you mindful of death." 
Here, it is clearly mentioned that the permission to visit the grave is given by Allah, and Muslims have not the permission to visit the graves of kafirs, but that permission has cleared that she was a momin.
Islamic scholars have long been divided over the religious beliefs of Muhammad's parents and their fate in the afterlife. One transmission by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah states that God refused to forgive Aminah for her kufr (disbelief). Another transmission in Musnad al-Bazzar states that Muhammad's parents were brought back to life and accepted Islam before returning to the Barzakh. 
Some Ash'ari and Shafi'i scholars argued that neither would be punished in the afterlife as they were Ahl al-fatrah, or "people of the interval" between the prophetic messages of 'Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad. The concept of Ahl al-fatrah is not universally accepted among Islamic scholars, and there is debate concerning the extent of salvation available for active practitioners of Shirk (Polytheism). The majority of scholars have come to agree with it and disregard the ahadith stating that Muhammad's parents were condemned to Hell.
While a work attributed to Abu Hanifa, an early Sunni scholar, stated that both Aminah and Abdullah died condemned to Hell (Mata 'ala al-fitrah), some later authors of mawlid texts related a tradition in which Aminah and Abdullah were temporarily revived and embraced Islam. Scholars such as Ibn Taymiyya stated that this was a lie (though Al-Qurtubi stated that the concept did not disagree with Islamic theology). According to Ali al-Qari, the preferred view is that both the parents of Muhammad were Muslims. According to Al-Suyuti, Ismail Hakki Bursevi, and other Islamic scholars, all of the ahadith indicating that the parents of Muhammad were not forgiven were later abrogated when they were brought to life and accepted Islam. 
Shia Muslims believe that all of Muhammad's ancestors—Aminah included—were monotheists and therefore entitled to Paradise.

bio: Uncle of Prophet Muhammad; raised him after the deaths of Aminah and Abd al-Muttalib. Chief of Banu Hashim. Died 619 CE (Year of Sorrow).
bio_full:
Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib (Arabic: أَبُو طَالِب بن عَبْد ٱلْمُطَّلِب, romanized: ʾAbū Ṭālib bin ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; c. 535 – 619) was the leader of Banu Hashim, a clan of the Qurayshi tribe of Mecca in the Hejazi region of the Arabian Peninsula. As he was the brother of Abdullah, the father of the Islamic Prophet Muhammad, he was the Islamic Prophet Muhammad's uncle and father of Ali. After the death of his father Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, he inherited this position as tribal chieftain, and the offices of Siqaya and Rifada. He was well-respected in Mecca.
According to the majority of Sunni scholars, Abu Talib did not accept Islam before his death.
However, Shia scholars maintain that Abu Talib was a devout believer who concealed his faith to protect Prophet Muhammad.

Early life
Abu Talib was born in the city of Mecca in the Hijaz region in 535 CE. He was the son of the Hashimite chief, Abd al-Muttalib, and a brother of Muhammad's father, Abdullah, who had died before Muhammad's birth. After the death of Muhammad's mother Aminah bint Wahab, Muhammad, a child still, was taken into the care of his grandfather, Abd al-Muttalib. When Muhammad reached eight years of age, Abd al-Muttalib died. One of Muhammad's uncles was to take him in. The oldest, Al-Harith was not wealthy enough to accept guardianship for his nephew. Abu Talib, despite his poverty, took in Muhammad in an act of selfless generosity.
Although Abu Talib was responsible for providing Siqaya and Rifada (Food and Beverages) for Hajj pilgrims, he lived in poverty. In order to fulfill his obligations towards the pilgrims, he had to borrow money from his brother Abbas, which he failed to return, thus being forced to let Abbas take over the duty. Nevertheless, his social position did not take any harm from this failure.
Muhammad loved his uncle, and Abu Talib loved him in return. Abu Talib is remembered as a gifted poet, and many poetic verses in support of Muhammad are attributed to him. Once, as Abu Talib was about to leave for a trading expedition, Muhammad wept and could not bear being separated from him. To this Abu Talib responded, "By God I will take him with me, and we shall never part from each other."
Later in life, as an adult, Muhammad saw that Abu Talib was struggling financially after a severe drought. Muhammad decided to take charge of one of Abu Talib's children and he convinced Al-'Abbas to do the same. They discussed this matter with Abū Ṭālib, who asked that his favorite child 'Aqīl be left with him. Al-'Abbās chose Ja'far, and Muhammad chose 'Alī.

Protecting Muhammad
In tribal society, a tribal affiliation is important, otherwise a man can be killed with impunity. As the leader of the Banu Hashim, Abu Talib acted as a protector to Muhammad. After Muhammad began preaching the message of Islam, members of the other Qurayshite clans increasingly came to feel threatened by Muḥammad. In attempts to quiet him, they pressured Abū Ṭālib to silence his nephew or control him. Despite these pressures, Abu Talib maintained his support of Muḥammad, defending him from the other leaders of the Quraysh. Leaders of the Quraysh directly confronted Abu Talib several times. Abu Talib brushed them off and continued to support Muhammad even when it put a rift between him and the Quraysh. In one account, the Quraysh even threatened to fight the Banu Hashim over this conflict. In a particular narration of one such confrontation, Abu Talib summoned Muhammad to speak with the Quraysh. Muhammad asked the Quraysh leaders to say the shahada and they were astounded.
The Quraysh even tried to bribe Abu Talib. They told Abu Talib that if he let them get hold of Muhammad, then he could adopt 'Umarah ibn al Walid ibn al Mughirah, the most handsome youth in Quraysh. When this also failed, the Quraysh elicited the support of other tribes to boycott trading with or marrying members of the Banu Hashim lineage. This boycott started seven years after Muhammad first received revelation and lasted for three years. The goal was to put pressure on the Hashimites and even starve them into submission. For the sake of security, many members of the Banu Hashim moved near to Abu Talib, and the place became like a slum. This didn't cause undue hardship because many had family members in other tribes that would smuggle goods to them. Abu Talib's brother, Abu Lahab, sided with the Quraysh on this issue; he moved to a house in the district of Abd Shams to demonstrate support for the Quraysh. He thought Muhammad was either mad or an impostor.
Protecting Muhammad put considerable pressure on Abu Talib and the Banu Hashim. In one instance Abu Talib exclaimed to Muhammad, "Save me and yourself, and do not put a greater burden on me than I cannot bear." Muhammad responded, "Oh uncle! By God Almighty I swear, even if they should put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left that I abjure this cause, I shall not do so until God has vindicated it or caused me to perish in the process." Seeing his nephew's emotion, Abu Talib responded, "Go, nephew, and say what you like. By God, I will never hand you over for any reason."

Death

Abū Ṭālib died around 619 CE, at more than 80 years of age, about 10 years after the start of Muhammad's mission. This year is known as the Year of Sorrow for Muhammad, because not only did his uncle Abu Talib die, but also his wife Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, within a month of Abu Talib.
After Abu Talib's death, Muhammad was left unprotected. Abu Talib's brother and successor as the chief of the family, that is Abu Lahab, did not protect him, as he was an enemy of Muhammad, so Muhammad and his followers faced incredible persecution. Muhammad is quoted as exclaiming, "By God, Quraysh never harmed me so much as after the death of Abu Talib." The early Muslims relocated to Abyssinia and then to Medina in order to escape persecution by the Quraysh.

Views of different sects
The memory of Abu Talib is influenced by political aims of the Sunni and Shia Muslims.

Sunni
It is reported in Sunni Islam that the Quranic verse 28:56 ("O Prophet! Verily, you guide not whom you like, but Allah guides whom He will") was revealed concerning Abu Talib's embrace of Islam at the hands of his nephew.
During the time of Prophethood, the Prophet Muhammad took all possible measures to protect himself from the tribe. He was called a person of Hell for not accepting Islam in Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum, where it is said that Muhammad said that he would be placed in the depths of Hellfire because of his association with him and his support for him, or he would have been plunged into the abyss of Hell.

Family

Abu Talib was married to Fatima bint Asad. They had four sons:

Talib, He was his father's firstborn child, and Abu Talib received his kunya from him. Little is known about him; he had no children and his body was never discovered after around c. 624.
'Aqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib (Abu Muslim), married Fatima bint Uqba and had many children: Abu Sa'id, Muslim, Musa, Abd Allah, Ramla, Ja'far, Muhammad and Abd al-Rahman.
Ja'far ibn Abī Ṭālib (Abu Awn), married Asma bint Umays and had 3 sons: Abd Allah, Muhammad and Awn also had a daughter: Na'mi.
'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib (Abu Hasan), married a number of women, including Fatima bint Muhammad.

classif: Bedouin wet nurse of the Prophet
titles: Halimah al-Sa'diyyah
bio: Bedouin wet nurse from Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr who nursed Prophet Muhammad in infancy. Later embraced Islam.
bio_full:
Halima bint Abi Dhu'ayb al-Sa'diyya (Arabic: حليمة بنت أبي ذؤيب السعدية) was the foster-mother of the Islamic prophet  Muhammad. Halimah and her husband were from the tribe of Sa'd b. Bakr, a subdivision of Hawazin (a large North Arabian tribe or group of tribes).

Relationship with Muhammad
Aminah bint Wahb, the mother of Muhammad, was waiting for the arrival of the Banu Sa'd; the women within the tribe of the Banu Sa'd were foster mothers. They would take the children of Mecca to the desert and teach them classical Arabic and other skills; in return, they would receive a salary from the family of the child in Mecca. Halimah's husband was al-Harith bin Abdul Uzza and his nickname was Abu Kabsheh. Halima's father was Abu Dhu'ayb Abd Allah bin Harith bin Shejna Saadi, from the tribe of Saad bin Bakr bin Hawazin.
Her son was named Abdullah, while the daughters were named Unaysa and Hudhafa. While traveling to Mecca, she was unable to feed her child because her she-camel stopped lactating. In Mecca, all those looking for foster children rejected taking care of the half-orphan Muhammad because they feared not getting paid since his father was dead. Halimah felt sad that every woman in her tribe had received a child except her. So she told her husband al-Harith: "By God, I do not like the idea of returning with my friends without a child; I will go and take that orphan." Her husband agreed. Immediately after accepting him, blessing came to her and her family. Her husband's flock during a time of great famine was healthy and producing milk while the rest of the people's flocks were dying.
A few months later Muhammad's foster brother shouted: that two men in white cut Muhammad's chest. When Halimah and Al-Harith asked Muhammad what happened, he said: "Two men came and opened my chest and took a portion of it". After this she gave up fostering him and told his mother what had happened. Muhammad spent five years in the Bani Saad bin Bakr tribe. Then Halima brought him back to his mother and grandfather Abdul Mutalib when he was five years old.

Years later, after Muhammad married Khadijah, Halimah went to him in Mecca and complained about the hardships of the times. Muhammad talked about her with Khadija and Khadija gave her some sheep and camels. After the advent of Islam, Halima joined Muhammad and along with her husband converted to Islam
Halima bint Abi Dhu'ayb later accepted Islam after the Battle of Hunayn.

Death
She died in 9 A.H. and her grave is in Jannatul Baqi, Medina. The remains of the place she used to live in and where Muhammad grew up still stand today.

primaryTitle: First Wet Nurse of the Prophet
classif: Freedwoman of Abu Lahab; first nurse of Prophet
bio: Freedwoman of Abu Lahab; nursed Prophet Muhammad briefly before Halimah. Also nursed Hamza, making them milk-brothers.
bio_full:
Thuwaibah Al-Aslamiyah was the wet nurse of the Prophet Muhammad and the slave-girl of his uncle Abu Lahab.

She is Thuwaybah, Abu Lahab’s servant, and it was narrated that she was the first wet nurse to the Prophet. Ibn Saad narrated on the authority of Barrah bint Abi that the first person to breastfeed Thuwaybah with the milk of a son of hers, called Masrooh, days before Halima came forward. She breastfed Hamza before him, and after him Abu Salamah bin Abdul Asad.

Ibn Mandah said: There was disagreement about her conversion to Islam, and Abu Nu`aym said: I do not know of anyone who has proven her conversion to Islam, and in the chapter on who breastfed the Prophet from the ranks of Ibn Saad there is evidence that she did not convert to Islam. Ibn As'ad narrated on the authority of more than one scholar: They said: Thuwaiba was the wet nurse of the Messenger of God, who prayed for her while he was in Mecca, and Khadija used to honor her, while she was in the possession of Abu Lahab, and she asked him to sell it to her, but he refused. When the Messenger of God emigrated, Abu Lahab freed her, and the Messenger of God was sending her ties and clothing until the news came that she died in the year seven of his return from Khaybar, and her son Masroh died before her. Ibn Hajar Al-Asqalani said: I did not find any evidence that her son Masrooh converted to Islam, and it is possible.

While some Shiite scholars deny and question Thuwaibah’s breastfeeding of the Prophet Muhammad, Mr. Jaafar Murtada Al-Amili says: “In any case, all of the above, and more, makes us very doubtful that Thuwaybah breastfed the Messenger of God, Hamzah, and Abu Salamah with the milk of her son Masroh, so that they would all be brothers through breastfeeding.”

full: Wahb ibn Abd Manaf ibn Zuhra al-Zuhri
classif: Chief of Banu Zuhra; father of Aminah
titles: Sayyid Banu Zuhra
bio: Chief of Banu Zuhra clan of Quraysh; father of Aminah, maternal grandfather of Prophet Muhammad.
bio_full:
Wahb ibn 'Abd Manaf (Arabic: وهب بن عبد مناف) ibn Zuhrah ibn Kilab ibn Murrah, was the chief of Banu Zuhrah, and the father of Aminah bint Wahb. He was the maternal grandfather of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

Wahb's great-grandfather was Zuhrah ibn Kilab, the progenitor of the Banu Zuhrah clan of the Quraysh tribe in Mecca. His mother Qaylah (Hind) bint Wajz Ibn Ghalib of Banu Khuza'a. His brother was Wuhayb ibn 'Abd Manaf.

Wahb was married to Barrah bint Abdul Uzza of the Banu Abd ad-Dar clan of the Quraysh tribe. Wahb's chief wife, Barrah bint Abdul Uzza, was a great-granddaughter of Qusayy, and his other wife was Rughaybah bint Zurarah ibn Addas, one of the eminent women of Yathrib (Medina). His son, Abdu Yaghuth, was himself a notable chief.

When Wahb died, and possibly also his wife Barrah (for there is no other mention of her) Ayyilah took Barra's daughters Halah and Aminah into her care. The widow Rughaybah chose not to accept the proposal of her husband's brother, but instead married Qays ibn Amr of the Banu Adiy ibn Najjar, returned to Yathrib, and in due course gave birth to Salmah (Umm Mundhir), and Salit. Ayyilah also had a daughter of her own of marriageable age, also called Halah.

When Abdullah ibn Abdul-Muttalib reached the right age his father, Abdul-Muttalib began searching for a wife for him. One of Abdul Muttalib's cousins, Muttalib's daughter Ayyilah, was already married into the Banu Zuhrah; her husband was Zuhrah's grandson and Wahb's brother, Wuhayb. Abdul-Muttalib requested Halah for himself, despite being over 70 years old. Halah's age is not known, but Aminah was about 15 when she married Abdullah. Both girls gave consent and the two marriages were organised to take place at the same time.

full_name_ar: قتيبة بن سعيد البلخي
bio_full:
Qutayba ibn Sa'id al-Balkhi (767-854 CE) was one of the most prolific and influential hadith transmitters of the early Islamic period. Born in the region of Baghlan in present-day Afghanistan, he lived during a crucial era when Islamic scholars were systematically collecting and preserving the sayings and traditions of the Prophet Muhammad.

Al-Balkhi distinguished himself through his extensive travels across the Islamic world in pursuit of hadith knowledge, a practice known as "rihlah fi talab al-hadith." This dedication to gathering authentic prophetic traditions from multiple sources made him a bridge between different generations of scholars, as he learned from and transmitted to three successive generations of hadith experts.

His reputation for reliability and the breadth of his knowledge earned him recognition from the most respected hadith collectors of his time. The two most authoritative hadith collections in Sunni Islam, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, drew heavily from his transmissions. Imam al-Bukhari included 308 of his narrations, while Imam Muslim incorporated 668 hadiths from al-Balkhi's collection. His contributions extended beyond these two collections, as five of the six canonical hadith collections (known as the Kutub al-Sittah) included his transmissions, with only Ibn Majah's collection not drawing from his work.

Al-Balkhi's significance lies not merely in the quantity of hadiths he transmitted, but in his role as a critical link in the chain of Islamic scholarly transmission. During his 87-year lifespan, he witnessed and participated in the formative period of hadith compilation, when oral traditions were being carefully verified and recorded for future generations. His extensive travels and connections with scholars across different regions helped ensure that hadith knowledge was preserved and disseminated widely throughout the Islamic world.

The trust placed in al-Balkhi by the major hadith collectors reflects the rigorous standards applied to hadith transmission during this period. His work contributed to the preservation of prophetic traditions that would become fundamental sources of Islamic law, theology, and practice. Through his dedication to learning and teaching, Qutayba ibn Sa'id al-Balkhi played an essential role in maintaining the continuity of Islamic scholarship and the authentic transmission of prophetic knowledge across generations.

full_name_ar: حماد بن زيد بن درهم
bio_full:
Hammad ibn Zayd ibn Dirham (716-795 CE) was a prominent Islamic scholar and hadith transmitter who lived his entire life in Basra, in what is now southern Iraq. Born into a Persian mawla family—indicating non-Arab Muslim converts or their descendants who were affiliated with Arab tribes—he became one of the most respected authorities in hadith sciences during the formative period of Islamic scholarship.

Hammad specialized in the collection, preservation, and transmission of hadith, the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad that form a crucial foundation of Islamic law and practice alongside the Quran. During his lifetime, the systematic compilation and verification of hadith was still developing, making the work of scholars like Hammad essential for establishing reliable chains of transmission and authentic texts.

Known for his exceptional memory and meticulous attention to detail, Hammad earned recognition among his contemporaries for his reliability and precision in transmitting hadith. His reputation for accuracy was such that later hadith scholars consistently regarded his transmissions as authoritative. This trust was crucial in an era when the authenticity of religious texts depended heavily on the credibility of individual transmitters.

Contemporary sources describe Hammad as one of the four great imams of his time and refer to him as "the Imam of Basra in Sunnah," highlighting his preeminent position in his city's scholarly community. Basra was then a major center of Islamic learning, home to numerous scholars and an important hub for the development of Islamic jurisprudence and hadith studies.

Hammad's contributions came during a critical period when Islamic scholarship was becoming more systematized. His work helped establish the rigorous standards of hadith criticism that would later be formalized by subsequent generations of scholars. Through his students and the traditions he preserved, his influence extended well beyond his lifetime, contributing to the broader corpus of authenticated prophetic traditions that would guide Muslim communities.

His legacy lies not in revolutionary innovations but in the careful, methodical work of preservation and transmission that characterized the best hadith scholars of his era. This foundational work proved essential for the development of Islamic law and religious practice in subsequent centuries.

full_name_ar: هشام بن عروة بن الزبير بن العوام القرشي الأسدي
bio_full:
Hisham ibn Urwah ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam al-Qurashi al-Asadi was a prominent scholar of hadith and Islamic jurisprudence who lived from 680 to 763 CE. Born into one of the most distinguished families of the Quraysh tribe in Medina, he belonged to the generation known as the Tabi'un—those who learned directly from the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad but did not meet the Prophet themselves.

His father, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, was one of the seven foremost jurists of Medina and a key figure in early Islamic scholarship. Through this paternal lineage, Hisham was connected to al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, one of the ten Companions promised paradise according to Islamic tradition. This noble ancestry placed him at the center of Medina's scholarly and religious elite.

Hisham received his early education in Medina, where he studied extensively under his father, absorbing vast knowledge of Islamic law, history, and prophetic traditions. He also learned from his wife, Fatima bint al-Mundhir, who was herself a scholar and transmitter of hadith. This dual source of learning—from both his father and wife—gave him access to a rich repository of early Islamic knowledge.

As a hadith scholar, Hisham became known for his reliability and precision in transmitting prophetic sayings and legal opinions. The renowned Islamic historian al-Dhahabi praised him as trustworthy and steadfast in his scholarship. His meticulous approach to preserving and transmitting Islamic teachings made him a sought-after source for later generations of scholars.

Later in life, Hisham migrated from his native Medina to Baghdad, the new capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. This move reflected the shifting center of Islamic learning eastward during the eighth century. In Baghdad, he continued his scholarly work and taught numerous students who would themselves become important transmitters of Islamic knowledge.

Hisham's significance lies primarily in his role as a crucial link in the chain of Islamic scholarly transmission. Through his careful preservation and teaching of his father's knowledge, combined with his own scholarly contributions, he helped ensure that the legal and religious traditions of early Islam were accurately passed down to subsequent generations. His work contributed to the systematic development of hadith sciences and Islamic jurisprudence during a formative period of Islamic civilization.

full_name_ar: معمر بن راشد الأزدي الصنعاني
bio_full:
Ma'mar ibn Rashid al-Azdi al-San'ani (714-770 CE) was a pioneering Islamic scholar whose work laid crucial foundations for the preservation of early Islamic historical and religious knowledge. Born in Basra during the Umayyad period, he emerged as one of the most important figures in the early development of hadith sciences and prophetic biography.

Ma'mar's scholarly formation took place under some of the most respected teachers of his generation. He studied extensively with Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, the renowned hadith scholar, at Resafa in Syria. He also learned from prominent Basran scholars including Qatada ibn Di'ama and al-Hasan al-Basri, both influential figures in early Islamic jurisprudence and Quranic interpretation. This diverse educational background provided him with a comprehensive grounding in the religious sciences of his time.

During the political upheavals and civil conflicts that marked the transition from Umayyad to Abbasid rule, Ma'mar relocated to Yemen, where he would spend the final two decades of his life. Settling in Sanaa, he established himself as a major center of learning, attracting students from across the Islamic world who came to study hadith and early Islamic history under his guidance.

Ma'mar's most significant contribution to Islamic scholarship was his role as one of the earliest systematic compilers of prophetic traditions and biographical material about Muhammad. His "Kitab al-Maghazi" represents one of the oldest surviving works of sira literature, documenting the military campaigns and key events from the Prophet's life. This work became an essential source for later historians and biographers, including Ibn Hisham, whose famous biography of Muhammad drew heavily on Ma'mar's compilations.

Beyond his work in prophetic biography, Ma'mar was instrumental in the early development of hadith methodology. His careful collection and transmission of prophetic traditions helped establish standards for authenticating and preserving religious knowledge that would influence Islamic scholarship for centuries to come.

Ma'mar's significance lies not only in his individual contributions but also in his position as a bridge between the earliest generation of Islamic scholars and later systematic compilation efforts. His work represents a crucial stage in the transition from oral to written preservation of Islamic religious and historical knowledge, making him an indispensable figure in understanding the development of classical Islamic scholarship.

bio_full:
Abd al-Malik ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Jurayj was a prominent Islamic scholar of the early eighth century who played a crucial role in the development of hadith literature. Born in Mecca in 699 CE to a family of Byzantine origin, he became one of the most respected religious authorities of his time, serving as the Mufti of Mecca during the Umayyad period.

As a member of the Tabi'un generation—those who learned directly from the Companions of Prophet Muhammad—Ibn Jurayj occupied a vital position in the transmission of Islamic knowledge. He dedicated nearly two decades to studying under Ata ibn Abi Rabah, one of Mecca's leading scholars, and spent seven years learning from Amr ibn Dinar, another distinguished authority. This extensive period of study under renowned teachers established his credentials as a reliable transmitter of religious knowledge.

Ibn Jurayj's most significant contribution to Islamic scholarship was his pioneering work in hadith compilation. He is credited with developing the musannaf genre, a systematic method of organizing hadith collections by subject matter rather than by chain of transmission. This innovative approach made religious texts more accessible to scholars and students, as materials could be easily referenced according to specific topics of Islamic law and practice.

Beyond hadith sciences, Ibn Jurayj authored works on Quranic interpretation (tafsir) and detailed treatises on pilgrimage rites, reflecting his deep connection to Mecca as both a resident and religious authority. His scholarship encompassed the practical aspects of Islamic worship, making him particularly valuable to pilgrims who sought guidance on proper ritual observance.

His position as Mufti of Mecca during the Umayyad era placed him at the center of Islamic legal and religious life. Mecca's status as the holiest city in Islam meant that his legal opinions and religious guidance influenced Muslims from across the expanding Islamic world who came for pilgrimage.

Ibn Jurayj died in 768 CE, leaving behind a substantial scholarly legacy. His methodological innovations in hadith compilation influenced subsequent generations of Islamic scholars, while his role in preserving and transmitting early Islamic teachings helped ensure the continuity of religious knowledge from the Prophet's era to later generations. His work represents a crucial bridge between the earliest Islamic community and the systematic scholarly traditions that would define later Islamic civilization.

full_name_ar: يحيى بن يحيى بن كثير الليثي
bio_full:
Abu Muhammad Yahya ibn Yahya ibn Kathir ibn Wislasen al-Laythi was an influential Andalusian scholar who lived from 769 to 848 CE and played a pivotal role in establishing the Maliki school of Islamic jurisprudence in al-Andalus. Born into the Layth tribe, he became one of the most significant religious authorities in medieval Iberian Islamic society.

Yahya ibn Yahya's most notable achievement was his journey eastward to study directly under Malik ibn Anas, the founder of the Maliki school, in Medina. This direct connection to the school's founder gave him exceptional authority in transmitting Maliki teachings. He is particularly renowned for producing the most widely accepted recension of the Muwatta, Malik's foundational legal text. His version of this work became the standard transmission throughout the western Islamic world, cementing his reputation as a master of hadith sciences and Islamic jurisprudence.

Upon returning to al-Andalus, Yahya ibn Yahya established himself as the preeminent religious scholar in Cordoba, the capital of the Umayyad Emirate. His influence extended far beyond academic circles, as he served on the shura, the advisory council to the Umayyad rulers. In this capacity, he wielded considerable power over judicial appointments throughout al-Andalus, effectively shaping the legal and religious landscape of the region for generations.

His significance to Islamic history lies primarily in his role as the architect of Maliki dominance in the western Mediterranean. Through his teaching, his authoritative transmission of the Muwatta, and his institutional influence in Cordoba, he ensured that the Maliki school became the predominant legal tradition in al-Andalus and eventually in North and West Africa. His students and their successors continued his work, making Malikism the defining characteristic of Islamic jurisprudence in these regions for centuries to come.

Yahya ibn Yahya's legacy demonstrates the crucial role individual scholars played in the geographic spread of Islamic legal schools. His combination of direct scholarly authority, institutional power, and strategic position in al-Andalus allowed him to fundamentally shape the religious character of Iberian Islamic civilization during a formative period of its development.

bio_full:
Zuhayr ibn Harb ibn Shaddad al-Nasa'i was a distinguished scholar of hadith who lived in Baghdad during the early Abbasid period, from 780 to 849 CE. As a muhaddith, he dedicated his life to the collection, preservation, and transmission of prophetic traditions that form a cornerstone of Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice.

Born in the late eighth century, Zuhayr lived during a pivotal era in Islamic scholarship when the systematic compilation of hadith was reaching its zenith. Baghdad, the Abbasid capital where he resided, served as the intellectual heart of the Islamic world, attracting scholars from across the empire and fostering unprecedented scholarly activity in religious sciences.

Zuhayr's expertise and reliability as a transmitter of hadith earned him recognition among his contemporaries and subsequent generations of scholars. His narrations were deemed sufficiently authentic and precise to be included in all six canonical hadith collections, known as the Kutub al-Sittah. These collections, compiled by scholars such as al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah, represent the most authoritative sources of prophetic traditions in Sunni Islam.

The scope of Zuhayr's influence is perhaps best illustrated by his relationship with Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, the compiler of Sahih Muslim, one of the two most revered hadith collections in Islamic tradition. Muslim transmitted over 1,200 hadiths from Zuhayr and chose to open his entire collection with a narration from this trusted scholar, demonstrating the exceptional regard in which Zuhayr was held.

Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, the renowned eleventh-century historian and hadith scholar, praised Zuhayr's scholarly qualities, describing him as reliable, trustworthy, and precise. Such endorsements from later authorities reflect the lasting impact of Zuhayr's work on the preservation of Islamic religious tradition.

Through his meticulous approach to hadith transmission, Zuhayr ibn Harb contributed significantly to the preservation of prophetic traditions that continue to guide Muslim religious practice and legal interpretation today. His work represents part of the broader scholarly effort during the early Abbasid period that established the methodological foundations for Islamic religious sciences, ensuring the authentic transmission of religious knowledge across generations.

full_name_ar: عمرو بن دينار الجمحي المكي
bio_full:
Amr ibn Dinar al-Jumahi al-Makki was a prominent Islamic scholar of the second generation of Muslims, known as the Tabi'un, who lived from 666 to 744 CE. Born and based in Mecca, he belonged to the Jumahi tribe and became one of the most respected religious authorities of his time in the holy city.

As a member of the Tabi'un, Amr ibn Dinar had the significant advantage of learning directly from several Companions of the Prophet Muhammad, including the renowned scholars Ibn Abbas and Jabir ibn Abdullah. This direct connection to the Prophetic generation gave his teachings and legal opinions particular weight and authenticity in the early Islamic community. Through these relationships, he gained access to firsthand accounts of the Prophet's sayings and practices, which he would later transmit to subsequent generations.

Amr ibn Dinar's expertise encompassed both hadith transmission and Islamic jurisprudence. His role as a hadith transmitter was crucial during a formative period when the systematic collection and verification of Prophetic traditions was still developing. His careful preservation and transmission of these traditions contributed to the foundation of Islamic legal and religious thought.

His reputation as a jurist led to his appointment as Mufti of Mecca, succeeding the distinguished scholar Ata ibn Abi Rabah in this position. As mufti, he was responsible for issuing religious legal opinions and guidance to Muslims, particularly those undertaking pilgrimage to the holy city. This role placed him at the center of Islamic religious life, as Mecca's status as the direction of prayer and pilgrimage destination meant that his rulings had influence throughout the Muslim world.

The reliability of Amr ibn Dinar's scholarship earned recognition from later prominent figures in Islamic learning. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who would become the founder of one of the four major schools of Sunni jurisprudence, praised his trustworthiness. Similarly, Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj, a respected hadith scholar, considered him exceptionally reliable compared to his contemporaries.

Amr ibn Dinar's significance lies in his role as a bridge between the Companions of the Prophet and later generations of Islamic scholars. His work in preserving and transmitting religious knowledge, combined with his practical application of Islamic law as Mecca's mufti, helped establish foundations for Islamic jurisprudence and hadith sciences that would influence Islamic thought for centuries to come.

bio_full:
Hammad ibn Usama ibn Zayd ibn Sulayman al-Qurashi al-Kufi was a prominent eighth and ninth century Islamic scholar who dedicated his life to the preservation and transmission of hadith literature. Born in 738 CE in Kufa, Iraq, he lived during a crucial period in Islamic scholarship when the systematic collection and verification of prophetic traditions was being formalized.

As a mawla, or client, of the prestigious Banu Hashim clan, Hammad occupied an important position within Kufan scholarly circles. He spent his entire career in Kufa, one of the major centers of Islamic learning in the early Abbasid period, where he developed a reputation for exceptional precision and reliability in hadith transmission.

Hammad's scholarly contributions were recognized by leading authorities of his time. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the founder of one of the four major Sunni legal schools, praised him for his meticulous approach to hadith scholarship. The renowned Islamic historian and critic al-Dhahabi honored him with the titles "al-Hafiz al-Thabit," meaning "the Reliable Memorizer," indicating both his exceptional memory for hadith texts and his trustworthiness as a transmitter.

The scope of Hammad's scholarly work was remarkable for his era. He reportedly transcribed 100,000 hadiths by hand, demonstrating both his dedication to preserving Islamic tradition and his role in the transition from oral to written transmission of religious knowledge. This massive corpus of handwritten material represented a significant contribution to the standardization of hadith literature.

Hammad's scholarly reputation is perhaps best measured by the widespread acceptance of his narrations. His transmitted hadiths appear in all six canonical Sunni hadith collections, known as the Kutub al-Sitta, including the most authoritative works of Bukhari and Muslim. This universal inclusion indicates that later hadith critics consistently regarded his transmissions as authentic and reliable.

He died in 817 CE, leaving behind a legacy that helped establish the methodological foundations of hadith sciences. His work contributed to the preservation of prophetic traditions that would become central to Islamic law, theology, and practice. Through his meticulous scholarship and reliable transmission methods, Hammad ibn Usama played a vital role in maintaining the continuity of Islamic religious knowledge during a formative period of the faith's intellectual development.

full_name_ar: إبراهيم بن يزيد النخعي
bio_full:
Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i was a prominent Islamic jurist and scholar who lived from 666 to 714 CE in Kufa, Iraq. As a member of the Tabi'un—the generation that followed the Prophet Muhammad's companions—he played a crucial role in the early development of Islamic jurisprudence and legal methodology.

Al-Nakha'i received his Islamic education primarily through his maternal uncle, Alqama ibn Qays, who was a direct student of the renowned companion Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. This scholarly lineage connected al-Nakha'i to one of the most respected transmitters of Islamic knowledge from the Prophet's era, particularly the tradition of Quranic interpretation and legal reasoning that flourished in Kufa.

His most significant contribution to Islamic scholarship was his pioneering work in qiyas, or analogical reasoning, which became one of the fundamental sources of Islamic law. This methodology allowed jurists to derive legal rulings for new situations by drawing analogies to established principles from the Quran and Sunnah. His systematic approach to legal reasoning helped establish frameworks that would influence Islamic jurisprudence for centuries.

Al-Nakha'i's scholarly legacy was preserved and expanded through his student Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, who continued developing the legal school that al-Nakha'i had established. This intellectual tradition later provided the foundation for what would become the Hanafi madhhab, one of the four major schools of Sunni Islamic jurisprudence. The Hanafi school would eventually become the most widely followed legal school in the Islamic world.

Beyond his scholarly achievements, al-Nakha'i demonstrated moral courage in his opposition to the political oppression of his time. He openly criticized al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the notorious Umayyad governor known for his harsh rule and persecution of religious scholars. This stance reflected his commitment to Islamic principles even when facing potential persecution.

Al-Nakha'i's work in hadith sciences and legal methodology established him as one of the most influential figures in early Islamic scholarship. His contributions to the development of systematic legal reasoning and his role in preserving and transmitting authentic Islamic knowledge made him a bridge between the companion generation and later Islamic jurisprudence. His influence extended far beyond his lifetime through the legal school he established and the methodological innovations he pioneered.

famous: Hisham ibn Abi Abdullah Sinbar al-Ruba'i al-Basri al-Dastawa'i
full: Hisham ibn Abi Abdullah Sinbar al-Ruba'i al-Basri al-Dastawa'i
bio: Prominent Basran hadith transmitter named after the Dustawa textile trade. A key link in chains from Qatadah and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir. Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj and many major scholars transmitted from him. Hadith critics unanimously graded him trustworthy and firm.
tribe_or_lineage: al-Ruba'i (Rabi'ah)
key_events: Studied under Qatadah ibn Di'amah in Basra
Became a leading hadith authority in the Basran school
full_name_ar: هشام بن أبي عبد الله سنبر الربعي البصري الدستوائي
bio_full:
Hisham ibn Abi Abdullah Sinbar al-Ruba'i al-Basri al-Dastawa'i was a prominent eighth-century Islamic scholar who played a crucial role in the early transmission of hadith literature. Born in 706 CE and living until 771 CE, he spent his scholarly career in Basra, one of the major intellectual centers of the early Islamic world.

His name reveals important biographical details about his background and profession. The epithet "al-Dastawa'i" indicates his connection to the dustawa, a type of textile trade that was economically significant in Basra during this period. This occupational designation suggests he may have been involved in the textile business alongside his scholarly pursuits, reflecting the common practice of early Islamic scholars who often maintained trades to support themselves while dedicating time to religious learning.

As a hadith transmitter, Hisham occupied a vital position in the chains of transmission that preserved the sayings and actions of Prophet Muhammad. He served as a key intermediary, receiving traditions from earlier authorities and passing them to the next generation of scholars. Two of his most important teachers were Qatadah ibn Di'amah, a renowned Quranic exegete and hadith scholar from Basra, and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, another respected traditionalist. Through these connections, Hisham helped preserve numerous prophetic traditions that might otherwise have been lost.

The scholarly community of his time held Hisham in high regard. Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj, one of the most respected hadith critics and transmitters of the era, was among those who transmitted traditions from him. This endorsement was particularly significant, as Shu'bah was known for his stringent standards in evaluating hadith transmitters. Many other major scholars of the period also relied on Hisham's transmissions, indicating his widespread acceptance in scholarly circles.

The unanimous assessment of hadith critics regarding Hisham's reliability speaks to his exceptional reputation. In a field where scholars were often subject to intense scrutiny regarding their memory, character, and accuracy, being universally considered "trustworthy and firm" represented the highest possible endorsement. This classification meant that traditions transmitted through Hisham were considered authentic and could be relied upon for legal and religious guidance.

His sixty-five-year lifespan allowed him to bridge different generations of hadith scholarship, making him an essential link in preserving Islamic textual heritage during the crucial formative period when oral traditions were being systematically collected and verified.

bio: Prominent Tabi'i jurist, hadith transmitter, and Quranic exegete from Kufa. Studied under Ibn Abbas and was considered one of the leading jurists of his time. Participated in Ibn al-Ash'ath's rebellion against al-Hajjaj. Executed by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf in Wasit after a famous dramatic dialogue.
tribe_or_lineage: Freedman of Banu Walibah (of Banu Asad); possibly of Abyssinian ancestry
key_events: Studied under Ibn Abbas
Participated in Ibn al-Ash'ath's rebellion (82 AH)
Executed by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf in 95 AH/714 CE
First person associated with blindfold chess

full_name_ar: سعيد بن جبير الأسدي الكوفي
bio_full:
Sa'id ibn Jubayr al-Asadi al-Kufi was a prominent Islamic scholar of the Tabi'un generation, born around 665 CE in Kufa, Iraq. As a member of the Tabi'un, he belonged to the generation that followed the Companions of Prophet Muhammad, representing a crucial link in the transmission of Islamic knowledge and tradition.

Sa'id studied under Abdullah ibn Abbas, one of the most renowned Companions known for his expertise in Quranic interpretation and Islamic jurisprudence. Under Ibn Abbas's tutelage, Sa'id developed into one of the leading jurists and scholars of his era. He became particularly distinguished in three areas of Islamic scholarship: jurisprudence (fiqh), hadith transmission, and Quranic exegesis (tafsir).

His reputation as a scholar spread throughout the Islamic world, and he was recognized as one of the foremost authorities on Islamic law and Quranic interpretation of his time. Students and scholars sought his knowledge, and his legal opinions carried significant weight in judicial matters. His expertise in hadith sciences made him an important transmitter of the Prophet's traditions, contributing to the preservation and authentication of Islamic teachings.

Sa'id's life took a dramatic political turn when he joined the rebellion led by Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Ash'ath against the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf around 701 CE. This uprising reflected broader tensions between religious scholars and the Umayyad administration's increasingly secular approach to governance. After the rebellion's failure, Sa'id fled but was eventually captured.

His final confrontation with al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf in Wasit became legendary in Islamic historical literature. The dialogue between the scholar and the governor, recorded by various historians, highlighted the tension between religious authority and political power in early Islamic society. Despite his scholarly stature, Sa'id was executed by al-Hajjaj in 714 CE.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr's significance extends beyond his individual contributions to Islamic scholarship. He represents the critical early generation that preserved and transmitted Islamic knowledge from the Companions to subsequent generations. His expertise in multiple Islamic sciences and his role as a teacher helped establish the foundations of Islamic jurisprudence and exegetical tradition. His tragic end also symbolized the broader struggle between the scholarly class and political authorities during the Umayyad period, making him a significant figure in both Islamic intellectual history and the political dynamics of early Islamic society.

famous: Yazid ibn Harun ibn Zadhi al-Sulami al-Wasiti
full: Yazid ibn Harun ibn Zadhi al-Sulami al-Wasiti
bio: A leading hadith memorizer and transmitter from Wasit, Iraq. Known as Sheikh al-Islam, he was famed for his extraordinary memory and piety. His teaching gatherings reportedly attracted up to 70,000 attendees. He opposed theological innovations and was a key link in transmitting prophetic traditions to the next generation.
tribe_or_lineage: Sulami by wala (clientage); originally from Bukhara
key_events: Taught massive hadith gatherings in Wasit attracting tens of thousands
Opposed Jahmite theological innovations
full_name_ar: يزيد بن هارون بن زاذي السلمي الواسطي
bio_full:
Yazid ibn Harun ibn Zadhi al-Sulami al-Wasiti was a prominent Islamic scholar of hadith sciences who lived from 736 to 821 CE. Born and based in Wasit, a major city in Iraq during the early Abbasid period, he became one of the most influential hadith transmitters of his generation.

Al-Wasiti dedicated his life to the collection, memorization, and transmission of prophetic traditions (hadith). During an era when Islamic scholarship was flourishing and hadith sciences were becoming more systematized, he played a crucial role in preserving and passing down the sayings and practices attributed to the Prophet Muhammad. His reputation for having an exceptional memory made him a sought-after authority among students and fellow scholars.

The scale of al-Wasiti's influence as a teacher was remarkable for his time. His educational gatherings in Wasit drew enormous crowds, with reports indicating that tens of thousands of students would attend his sessions. This reflected both his scholarly reputation and the central importance of hadith studies in Islamic education during the 8th and 9th centuries.

Al-Wasiti earned the honorary title "Sheikh al-Islam," which recognized his standing as a leading religious authority. Beyond his scholarly accomplishments, he was noted for his personal piety and religious devotion. He took a conservative theological stance, opposing what he viewed as innovations in Islamic doctrine and practice.

His significance lies primarily in his role as a vital link in the chain of hadith transmission. During a formative period in Islamic history, when scholars were working to authenticate and preserve prophetic traditions, al-Wasiti served as a bridge between earlier generations of hadith collectors and later scholars who would further develop the science of hadith criticism. His students carried forward the traditions he had preserved, ensuring their continuation for future generations.

Al-Wasiti's work contributed to the broader intellectual movement of his era that sought to establish reliable foundations for Islamic law and theology based on Quranic teachings and authenticated prophetic traditions. His emphasis on careful transmission and his opposition to theological innovations reflected the scholarly priorities of his time and helped shape the development of orthodox Sunni Islamic thought.

famous: Yahya ibn Sa'id ibn Qays al-Ansari
full: Yahya ibn Sa'id ibn Qays al-Ansari
bio: Senior Tabi'i scholar, hadith transmitter, jurist, and judge from Medina. He served as mufti of Medina and was one of the most prominent hadith narrators of his generation. He met several companions of the Prophet and transmitted their knowledge to major scholars including Malik, Shu'bah, and both Sufyans.

Transmitted hadith from multiple Sahaba
full_name_ar: يحيى بن سعيد بن قيس الأنصاري
bio_full:
Yahya ibn Sa'id ibn Qays al-Ansari was a prominent Islamic scholar who lived from 688 to 761 CE and belonged to the generation known as the Tabi'un—those who followed the Companions of Prophet Muhammad but did not meet the Prophet himself. Born in Medina, he emerged as one of the most significant hadith transmitters and legal authorities of his time.

As a senior Tabi'i scholar, Yahya ibn Sa'id occupied a crucial position in the transmission of Islamic knowledge during the early formative period of Islamic scholarship. He had the distinguished opportunity to meet and learn directly from several Companions of the Prophet, making him a vital link in preserving and transmitting the prophetic traditions and early Islamic teachings to subsequent generations.

Yahya ibn Sa'id served as the mufti of Medina, a position that required extensive knowledge of Islamic law and the ability to issue legal opinions on matters affecting the Muslim community. His role as a judge further demonstrated his expertise in Islamic jurisprudence and his standing within the scholarly community of his era.

His significance in Islamic intellectual history lies particularly in his role as a hadith narrator and transmitter. He became one of the most prominent hadith scholars of his generation, known for his reliability and extensive knowledge of prophetic traditions. His students included several major figures who would themselves become pillars of Islamic scholarship, including Imam Malik ibn Anas, the founder of the Maliki school of Islamic law, as well as Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj and the two scholars known as "the Sufyans"—likely referring to Sufyan al-Thawri and Sufyan ibn Uyaynah.

Through his teaching and transmission of hadith and legal knowledge, Yahya ibn Sa'id contributed significantly to the preservation and systematization of Islamic learning during a critical period when oral traditions were being carefully documented and verified. His influence extended through his distinguished students, who carried forward his scholarly methodology and transmitted the knowledge they received from him to future generations of Islamic scholars.

Yahya ibn Sa'id's legacy represents the essential role played by the Tabi'un generation in maintaining the continuity of Islamic scholarship and ensuring the accurate transmission of religious knowledge from the earliest Muslim community to later periods of Islamic civilization.

famous: Ibrahim ibn Sa'd ibn Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf al-Zuhri
full: Ibrahim ibn Sa'd ibn Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf al-Zuhri
bio: Prominent hadith scholar and judge from Medina who later settled in Baghdad. Great-grandson of the Companion Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. Served as qadi in Baghdad. Known for transmitting hadith via chains from al-Zuhri. Also noted as a musician and oud player, unusual among hadith scholars.
tribe_or_lineage: Qurayshi; great-grandson of the Companion Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf
key_events: Appointed judge (qadi) in Baghdad
Transmitted key hadith chains from Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri
full_name_ar: إبراهيم بن سعد بن إبراهيم بن عبد الرحمن بن عوف الزهري
bio_full:
Ibrahim ibn Sa'd ibn Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf al-Zuhri was an influential hadith scholar and judge who lived during the formative period of Islamic jurisprudence in the eighth century CE. Born in 727 and dying in 800, he bridged the early Islamic period with the emerging scholarly traditions of the Abbasid era.

A member of the distinguished Zuhri family, Ibrahim was the great-grandson of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, one of the ten Companions of the Prophet Muhammad promised paradise according to Islamic tradition. This prestigious lineage connected him directly to the earliest Muslim community and likely facilitated his access to authentic hadith transmission chains.

Ibrahim began his scholarly career in Medina, the second holiest city in Islam and a major center of hadith learning. He later relocated to Baghdad, the newly established Abbasid capital, where he served as qadi (judge). This judicial appointment reflected both his legal expertise and the trust placed in him by the Abbasid administration during a period when Islamic law was being systematized and codified.

As a hadith scholar, Ibrahim was particularly known for transmitting prophetic traditions through chains that included al-Zuhri, the renowned early hadith scholar Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri. These transmission chains were crucial for establishing the authenticity of hadith literature, which formed the foundation of Islamic law and practice alongside the Quran.

What distinguished Ibrahim from many of his scholarly contemporaries was his musical talent. He was noted as an accomplished oud player, which was relatively uncommon among hadith scholars of his era. This combination of religious scholarship and artistic ability suggests a more diverse intellectual culture among early Islamic scholars than is sometimes assumed.

Ibrahim's career spanned a crucial period in Islamic history when scholarly institutions were being established and religious knowledge was being systematically preserved and transmitted. His work as both a hadith transmitter and a judge contributed to the development of Islamic jurisprudence during the early Abbasid period. His family background, scholarly activities, and judicial service positioned him as an important figure in the intellectual networks that shaped classical Islamic learning, particularly in the field of hadith sciences that would become central to Islamic legal methodology.

famous: Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Hudhali al-Basri al-Karabisi
full: Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Hudhali al-Basri al-Karabisi
bio: Leading Basran hadith transmitter, the foremost student of Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj. His written records of Shu'bah's hadith were considered the definitive reference when scholars disagreed. Ibn al-Mubarak said Ghandar's book was the judge between disputants on Shu'bah's narrations. Graded trustworthy by consensus.
tribe_or_lineage: al-Hudhali (mawla of Hudhayl); also called al-Karabisi (cloth-seller)
key_events: Traveled to Hijaz where he studied under Ibn Jurayj and earned the nickname Ghandar
Became the primary written authority on Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj's hadith
full_name_ar: محمد بن جعفر الهذلي مولاهم البصري الكرابيسي
bio_full:
Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Hudhali al-Basri, known by his nickname Ghandar, was one of the most prominent hadith scholars of the second Islamic century. Born in 744 CE in Basra, he lived during a crucial period in the development of Islamic scholarship when the systematic collection and transmission of prophetic traditions was being established.

Ghandar's most significant contribution to Islamic scholarship was his role as the foremost student of Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj, one of the great hadith masters of his era. Under Shu'bah's tutelage, Ghandar became not merely a transmitter of oral traditions but a meticulous recorder who committed his teacher's narrations to writing. This practice, while becoming more common in his time, was still relatively new in the field of hadith transmission.

The reliability and accuracy of Ghandar's written records became legendary among scholars. When disputes arose regarding what Shu'bah had actually narrated, scholars would turn to Ghandar's books as the definitive reference. The renowned scholar Ibn al-Mubarak, himself a leading authority of the period, declared that Ghandar's written collection served as the final arbiter in disagreements about Shu'bah's transmissions.

Ghandar's reputation for trustworthiness was unanimously recognized by his contemporaries and later hadith critics. This consensus regarding his reliability was particularly significant given the rigorous standards that hadith scholars applied when evaluating transmitters. His credibility was essential not only for preserving Shu'bah's narrations but also for establishing precedents in the careful documentation of prophetic traditions.

Working from Basra, one of the major centers of Islamic learning in Iraq, Ghandar was part of a scholarly network that included many of the most influential hadith transmitters of his generation. His methodical approach to recording and preserving hadith represented an important step in the transition from purely oral transmission to systematic written documentation.

Ghandar died in 809 CE, having spent his career establishing standards of accuracy and documentation that would influence hadith scholarship for centuries. His work exemplified the dedication to precision and reliability that characterized the best hadith scholars of the early Islamic period, contributing to the preservation of prophetic traditions that would become foundational sources for Islamic law and theology.

famous: Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub ibn Abdullah al-Ansari al-Misri
full: Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub ibn Abdullah al-Ansari al-Misri
bio: The foremost hadith scholar and mufti of Egypt in his era. Originally from Medina, he settled in Egypt where he became the leading authority in hadith preservation. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said no one in Egypt was sounder in hadith than al-Layth, with Amr coming close behind.
tribe_or_lineage: Ansari by wala (mawla of Qays ibn Sa'd ibn Ubadah)
key_events: Served as mufti and leading hadith authority of Egypt
Tutored sons of Salih ibn Ali al-Hashimi
full_name_ar: عمرو بن الحارث بن يعقوب بن عبد الله الأنصاري المصري
bio_full:
Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub ibn Abdullah al-Ansari al-Misri was a prominent Islamic scholar of the 8th century CE, recognized as one of the leading authorities in hadith sciences during the early Abbasid period. Born in 713 CE and passing away in 765 CE, he lived during a crucial time in Islamic intellectual development when the systematic collection and preservation of prophetic traditions was taking shape.

Originally from Medina, the city of the Prophet Muhammad, Amr ibn al-Harith later relocated to Egypt where he established himself as the preeminent hadith scholar of his region. His epithet "al-Misri" reflects his strong association with Egypt, where he spent much of his scholarly career and built his reputation as a religious authority.

As a hadith scholar, Amr ibn al-Harith specialized in the collection, verification, and transmission of prophetic traditions - the sayings, actions, and approvals attributed to Prophet Muhammad. During this period, hadith scholarship was essential for developing Islamic jurisprudence and religious practice, as these traditions served as the second primary source of Islamic law after the Quran.

His expertise earned him recognition not only as a hadith scholar but also as a mufti, meaning he was qualified to issue religious legal opinions (fatwas) based on his deep knowledge of Islamic sources. This dual role highlights his comprehensive understanding of Islamic religious sciences and his ability to apply traditional knowledge to contemporary religious questions.

The esteem in which Amr ibn al-Harith was held by his contemporaries is evidenced by the praise of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the founder of one of the four major Sunni schools of Islamic jurisprudence. Ahmad ibn Hanbal reportedly stated that no one in Egypt was more reliable in hadith transmission than al-Layth ibn Sa'd, with Amr ibn al-Harith being the closest to that standard. This comparison places him among the most trusted hadith transmitters of his time.

Amr ibn al-Harith's work contributed to the broader effort of early Islamic scholars to preserve and authenticate the prophetic traditions that would become fundamental to Islamic religious and legal thought. His position as Egypt's leading hadith authority during the mid-8th century represents an important link in the chain of Islamic scholarly transmission that helped establish the foundations of classical Islamic learning.

famous: Hammad ibn Salama ibn Dinar al-Basri
full: Hammad ibn Salama ibn Dinar al-Basri
bio: A leading hadith scholar, Arabic grammarian, and mufti of Basra. He was the most accurate transmitter of hadith from Thabit al-Bunani and was renowned for his piety and devotion. His student Sibawayh became the father of Arabic grammar.

key_events: Served as Mufti of Basra
Taught Sibawayh, who became the founder of Arabic grammar
Recognized as the foremost narrator from Thabit al-Bunani
full_name_ar: حماد بن سلمة بن دينار البصري
bio_full:
Hammad ibn Salama ibn Dinar al-Basri (701-784 CE) was a prominent Islamic scholar of the eighth century who made significant contributions to hadith transmission and Arabic linguistic studies. Born and based in Basra, one of the major intellectual centers of early Islamic civilization, he lived during the formative period of Islamic scholarship when systematic approaches to preserving and transmitting religious knowledge were being established.

As a hadith scholar, Hammad ibn Salama gained recognition for his careful and accurate transmission of prophetic traditions. He was particularly noted for his expertise in transmitting hadiths from Thabit al-Bunani, a respected early transmitter, and his precision in this work earned him considerable respect among his contemporaries and later scholars. His role as a hadith transmitter was crucial during an era when oral transmission remained the primary method of preserving Islamic traditions, requiring exceptional memory and scrupulous attention to accuracy.

Beyond hadith sciences, Hammad ibn Salama was accomplished in Arabic grammar and linguistics. His expertise in this field contributed to the early development of Arabic grammatical studies, which were essential for understanding and interpreting Islamic texts. This linguistic knowledge complemented his hadith work, as proper understanding of Arabic was fundamental to accurate transmission and interpretation of prophetic traditions.

Hammad ibn Salama served as a mufti in Basra, issuing religious legal opinions and guidance to the community. This position reflected his broader scholarly authority and the trust placed in his knowledge by his contemporaries. His reputation for piety and devotion enhanced his credibility as both a scholar and religious authority.

One of his most significant contributions to Islamic intellectual history was his role as a teacher. Among his students was Sibawayh, who would later become known as the father of Arabic grammar and author of the foundational work "Al-Kitab," which systematized Arabic grammatical rules. This teacher-student relationship demonstrates Hammad ibn Salama's influence on the development of Arabic linguistic sciences that would prove essential for Islamic scholarship.

Hammad ibn Salama's work represents the scholarly dedication of early Islamic intellectuals who preserved and transmitted religious knowledge while developing the methodological foundations that would guide Islamic learning for centuries. His contributions to both hadith sciences and Arabic grammar illustrate the interconnected nature of early Islamic scholarship, where linguistic expertise and religious knowledge reinforced each other in the service of understanding and preserving Islamic tradition.

bio: Basran Tabi'i hadith scholar and judge. Served as judge of al-Mada'in under Caliph al-Mansur and supervised weights and measures in Kufa. Considered one of Basra's three greatest hadith preservers alongside Sulayman al-Taymi and Dawud ibn Abi Hind.
