primaryTitle: Kurdish Mufassir, Author of Tafsir Rebar
dob_s: c. 590 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
dod_s: c. 650 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
bio: Muhammad Mulla Rebar Kurdi was a historical figure of the Quranic Sciences tradition, based in Kurdistan. Known as Kurdish Mufassir, Author of Tafsir Rebar.
bio_full:
Muhammad Mulla Rebar Kurdi was a Kurdish Islamic scholar who dedicated his life to the study and interpretation of the Quran. He belonged to the tradition of Quranic Sciences, a field that encompasses the systematic study of the holy book's text, interpretation, and related disciplines within Islamic scholarship.

Mulla Rebar Kurdi is primarily remembered for his contribution to Quranic exegesis through his work known as Tafsir Rebar. This commentary represents his scholarly effort to explain and interpret the meanings of Quranic verses, following the established tradition of tafsir literature that has been central to Islamic learning throughout history. His work was conducted in the Kurdish language, making Quranic interpretation more accessible to Kurdish-speaking Muslims in his region.

The title "Mulla" indicates his status as a learned religious scholar, a designation commonly used in Kurdish and Persian-speaking regions for individuals who have achieved recognition for their Islamic knowledge. As a mufassir, he joined the ranks of Quranic commentators who have contributed to the vast body of interpretive literature that helps Muslims understand their sacred text.

His work took place within the broader context of Islamic scholarship in Kurdistan, a region that has produced numerous notable Islamic scholars throughout history. The creation of Quranic commentary in local languages has been an important tradition in Islamic scholarship, as it serves to make the sacred text more comprehensible to diverse Muslim communities who may not be fluent in Arabic.

Tafsir Rebar stands as Mulla Rebar Kurdi's primary scholarly legacy, representing his contribution to the ongoing tradition of Quranic interpretation. Through this work, he participated in the centuries-old practice of Islamic scholars who have sought to illuminate the meanings and teachings of the Quran for their contemporaries and future generations.

The preservation of his name and association with his tafsir work indicates that his scholarship was valued within Kurdish Islamic scholarly circles. His contribution reflects the broader pattern of regional Islamic scholarship, where local scholars have played important roles in making Islamic knowledge accessible to their communities while contributing to the wider body of Islamic learning.

primaryTitle: Sufi Mufassir, Author of Kashf al-Asrar
bio: Abu'l-Fadl Rashid al-Din al-Maybudi (c. 1080 CE–c. 1135 CE / after 520 AH) was a historical figure of the Sufism tradition, based in Maybud. Known as Sufi Mufassir, Author of Kashf al-Asrar.
bio_full:
Abu'l-Fadl Rashid al-Din al-Maybudi was a prominent Sufi mystic and Quranic commentator who lived during the late 11th and early 12th centuries CE, roughly from 1080 to 1135. He was associated with the town of Maybud, located in present-day Iran, which gave him his nisba or place-name identifier.

Al-Maybudi is best known for his monumental work "Kashf al-Asrar wa 'Uddat al-Abrar" (The Unveiling of Secrets and the Provision of the Righteous), a comprehensive mystical commentary on the Quran. This extensive tafsir represents one of the most significant examples of Sufi Quranic interpretation from the medieval period. The work demonstrates al-Maybudi's deep engagement with both traditional Islamic scholarship and Sufi mystical insights, combining rigorous textual analysis with spiritual interpretation.

His commentary is structured in multiple layers, providing literal, allegorical, and mystical readings of Quranic verses. This multi-dimensional approach reflects the sophisticated hermeneutical methods that characterized mature Sufi scholarship of his era. Al-Maybudi's work draws upon earlier Sufi masters and incorporates their teachings into his interpretive framework, making it both a commentary on the Quran and a compendium of Sufi wisdom.

The title "Sufi Mufassir" (Sufi commentator) by which he became known indicates his particular contribution to Islamic scholarship—bridging the gap between mainstream Quranic exegesis and mystical interpretation. His work demonstrates how Sufi thinkers integrated their spiritual insights with traditional Islamic sciences, particularly Quranic studies.

Al-Maybudi lived during a period of significant intellectual and spiritual development in the Islamic world, when Sufism was becoming increasingly systematized and influential. His commentary reflects the mature state of Sufi thought in the 12th century, incorporating established mystical concepts while maintaining connection to orthodox Islamic tradition.

The "Kashf al-Asrar" has remained influential in Persian-speaking regions and continues to be studied by scholars interested in Sufi approaches to Quranic interpretation. Al-Maybudi's work represents an important contribution to the rich tradition of Islamic mystical literature and demonstrates the sophisticated theological and exegetical methods employed by medieval Sufi scholars in their approach to sacred texts.

full: Kamal al-Din Abd al-Razzaq ibn Ahmad al-Kashani
primaryTitle: Sufi Mufassir, Author of Ta'wilat al-Qur'an
bio: Kamal al-Din Abd al-Razzaq ibn Ahmad al-Kashani (c. 1260 CE–1329 CE / 730 AH) was a historical figure of the Sufism tradition, based in Kashan. Known as Sufi Mufassir, Author of Ta'wilat al-Qur'an.
bio_full:
Abd al-Razzaq al-Kashani was a prominent Sufi mystic and Quranic commentator who lived during the late 13th and early 14th centuries. Born around 1260 CE in or near Kashan, a city in central Persia, he became one of the most significant interpreters of Islamic mystical thought during the Ilkhanate period.

Al-Kashani is best known for his monumental work "Ta'wilat al-Qur'an" (Mystical Interpretations of the Quran), a comprehensive commentary that applies Sufi hermeneutics to the entire Quran. This work represents one of the most systematic attempts to provide mystical interpretations of Islamic scripture, drawing heavily on the theoretical framework established by the renowned Sufi master Ibn Arabi. The commentary demonstrates al-Kashani's deep engagement with esoteric spirituality and his ability to synthesize complex metaphysical concepts with scriptural exegesis.

Beyond his Quranic commentary, al-Kashani authored several other works on Sufi doctrine and practice. His writings reflect the intellectual sophistication of Persian Sufism during this period and show influence from the school of Ibn Arabi, particularly in their emphasis on the unity of being and the symbolic interpretation of religious texts. Al-Kashani's approach to mystical interpretation became influential among later Sufi scholars and contributed to the development of theoretical Sufism in the Persian-speaking world.

Al-Kashani lived during a time of significant political transition in Persia, as the Mongol Ilkhanate rulers gradually converted to Islam and Persian culture experienced both disruption and renewal. Despite these turbulent circumstances, centers of learning like Kashan continued to foster Islamic scholarship, allowing figures like al-Kashani to pursue their intellectual and spiritual work.

His significance in Islamic history lies primarily in his contributions to Sufi exegesis and mystical theology. By providing systematic mystical interpretations of the Quran, he helped establish a scholarly tradition that would influence subsequent generations of Sufi thinkers. His work represents an important bridge between the foundational period of theoretical Sufism in the 12th and 13th centuries and later developments in Islamic mysticism. Al-Kashani died in 1329 CE, leaving behind a body of work that continues to be studied by scholars of Islamic mysticism and Quranic interpretation.

dob_s: c. 745 CE (7 Safar 128 AH) - Abwa', between Mecca and Medina
dod_s: c. 799 CE (25 Rajab 183 AH) - Baghdad; poisoned in prison under Harun al-Rashid
titles: al-Kazim (the Forbearing); al-'Abd al-Salih; Bab al-Hawa'ij; kunya Abu Ibrahim / Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal
bio: Seventh of the Twelve Imams in Twelver Shia Islam. Son and successor of Ja'far al-Sadiq. Period of Imamate: 35 years (765-799 CE). Lived under intense Abbasid pressure during the reigns of al-Mansur, al-Mahdi, al-Hadi and Harun al-Rashid. Spent much of his life under surveillance or imprisonment in Basra and Baghdad. Died in al-Sindi ibn Shahiq's prison in Baghdad, traditionally believed to have been poisoned on orders of Harun al-Rashid. Buried in the Quraysh cemetery, which grew into the modern shrine city of al-Kazimiyya. Known for exceptional patience (the source of his title al-Kazim) and his teaching network of representatives across the Abbasid empire.
bio_full: Musa ibn Ja'far, known as al-Kazim, is the seventh Imam of Twelver Shia Islam. He was born, probably on 7 Safar 128 AH (745), in Medina or at nearby al-Abwa' between Medina and Mecca; other dates are also reported. His father was the sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, and his mother was Hamida, a Berber slave-woman. When his father died in 765, most of al-Sadiq's followers accepted Musa as Imam, while others held to the line of his elder brother Isma'il, who had died before their father; the Isma'ili line descends from him. The title al-Kazim is usually understood as 'the one who restrains his anger'; he was also called al-Abd al-Salih, 'the righteous servant'. His imamate (765-799) fell under the Abbasid caliphs al-Mansur, al-Mahdi, al-Hadi and Harun al-Rashid. He was kept under watch, briefly imprisoned in Baghdad under al-Mahdi, and accused under al-Hadi of backing the Alid revolt of 786. Harun had him arrested in 793 or 795 (sources differ) and held first in Basra under Isa ibn Ja'far, then in Baghdad, finally in the custody of the police chief al-Sindi ibn Shahik. He is believed to have organised a network of agents who collected religious dues, especially khums, from his followers across the empire. He died in al-Sindi's prison in Baghdad in Rajab 183 AH (799); Twelvers mark the date as 25 Rajab. Twelver sources, such as al-Shaykh al-Mufid, hold that he was poisoned on Harun's orders, while al-Tabari gives no cause and most Sunni authors regard the death as natural. He was buried in the Quraysh cemetery of Baghdad, now the shrine town of Kazimayn, where his grandson Muhammad al-Jawad also lies. Most of his followers then recognised his son Ali al-Rida as Imam.

dob_s: c. 828 CE (16 Dhu al-Hijja 212 AH) - Surayya, near Medina
dod_s: c. 868 CE (26 Jumada al-Thani / 3 Rajab 254 AH) - Samarra; poisoned during the caliphate of al-Mu'tazz
titles: al-Hadi (the Guide); al-Naqi; kunya Abu al-Hasan al-Thalith
bio: Tenth of the Twelve Imams in Twelver Shia Islam. Son of Muhammad al-Jawad. Became Imam at age six after his father's death in 835 CE. Summoned around 848 CE from Medina to the Abbasid garrison city of Samarra by caliph al-Mutawakkil. Held under close surveillance for the rest of his life. Managed a network of representatives who collected religious dues and disseminated his teachings across the empire. Died in 868 CE, traditionally believed to have been poisoned. Buried in his residence in Samarra, the site of the al-Askari shrine.
bio_full: Ali ibn Muhammad al-Hadi is the tenth Imam of Twelver Shia Islam. The best-attested report places his birth in mid-Dhu al-Hijja 212 AH (March 828) at Surayya, a village near Medina; other dates up to 214 AH are also given. His father was the ninth Imam, Muhammad al-Jawad, and his mother a slave-woman named Samana or Susan, probably of North African origin. He was still a child when his father died in Baghdad in 835, and most of his father's followers recognised him as Imam. Around 848 the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil, alerted by the governor of Medina, summoned him to the garrison city of Samarra and sent an armed escort; he arrived on 1 May 848. He lived there for the rest of his life, about twenty years, under constant watch, though one historian notes that he could move about the town. From Samarra he kept in secret contact with a network of agents who handled religious dues and other affairs in regions stretching from Iraq and western Iran to the Hijaz, Yemen and Egypt. He died in Samarra, according to al-Tabari and al-Kulayni on 26 Jumada al-Akhira 254 AH (21 June 868), aged about forty, during the caliphate of al-Mu'tazz; other dates up to Rajab 254 AH are reported, and Shia communities commemorate 3 Rajab. Most Shia sources say he was poisoned by the Abbasids, but early writers differ: al-Mufid gives no cause, and Ibn Babawayh names as poisoner caliphs who were not then in power. The caliph's brother al-Muwaffaq led his funeral prayer, and he was buried in his own house, the site of the present al-Askari shrine. Most of his followers recognised his son Hasan al-Askari as the next Imam; an elder son, Muhammad, had died before him.

dob_s: c. 844 CE (8 Rabi' al-Thani 232 AH) - Medina
dod_s: c. 1 January 874 CE (8 Rabi' al-Awwal 260 AH) - Samarra; poisoned, age c. 28
titles: al-Askari (of the garrison city, i.e. Samarra); kunya Abu Muhammad
bio: Eleventh of the Twelve Imams in Twelver Shia Islam. Son of Ali al-Hadi. Brought to the garrison city of Samarra in 848 CE as a child and remained there under Abbasid surveillance until his death in 874 CE. Contact with the Shia population was restricted; he communicated with his followers through a network of representatives. Period of Imamate: about six years (868-874 CE). Traditionally believed to have been poisoned. Buried beside his father in Samarra at the al-Askari shrine. Succeeded by his son Muhammad al-Mahdi.
bio_full: Al-Hasan ibn Ali, known as al-Askari, is the eleventh Imam of Twelver Shia Islam. He was born in Medina; the date is uncertain, with reports ranging from 230 to 232 AH (844-847), and Shia communities celebrate 8 Rabi' al-Thani. His father was the tenth Imam, Ali al-Hadi, and his mother a freed slave-woman named Hudayth or Susan in different reports. As a small child he was taken with his father to Samarra in 233 or 234 AH (847-849) on the order of the caliph al-Mutawakkil, and he lived there for the rest of his life. According to Imami tradition his father designated him a few months before his own death in 868; his elder brother Muhammad had already died, and his brother Ja'far disputed his claim. During his imamate of about six years he lived under close Abbasid surveillance and, by some accounts, had little contact with ordinary followers; he communicated through agents, chief among them Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Asadi. He was imprisoned for periods, including an arrest by the caliph al-Mu'tamid in 260 AH. He died in Samarra after an illness of about a week, on 8 Rabi' al-Awwal 260 AH (1 January 874), aged about 28; 1 Rabi' al-Awwal is also reported, and Ibn Khallikan gives 8 Jumada al-Ula. Shia sources commonly attribute his death to poisoning at the instigation of al-Mu'tamid; this is disputed, and other accounts mention only the illness. He was buried beside his father in their house in Samarra, the site of the al-Askari shrine. Twelvers hold that his son Muhammad, born a few years earlier and kept hidden, succeeded him as the twelfth Imam. His death without a publicly known heir divided the Shia into as many as twenty groups.

dod_s: c. 929 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
titles: al-Mahdi (the rightly guided); al-Qa'im; Sahib al-Zaman; Baqiyyat Allah; al-Muntazar; Sahib al-Amr; Hujjat Allah; kunya Abu al-Qasim / Abu Salih
bio: Twelfth and final Imam in Twelver Shia Islam, the awaited Mahdi. Son of Hasan al-Askari. Born in Samarra in 869 CE; according to Twelver tradition, his birth was kept hidden from the Abbasid authorities. Became Imam at age five after his father's martyrdom in 874 CE. Entered the Minor Occultation immediately, during which he communicated with the Shia community through Four Deputies in succession. The Major Occultation began in 941 CE and continues to the present. Twelvers believe he will reappear at the end of time to fill the earth with peace and justice.
bio_full: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, known as al-Mahdi, is in Twelver Shia belief the twelfth and final Imam, now in occultation and awaited to return. According to Twelver tradition he was born in Samarra around 255 AH (c. 868), most accounts giving the day as 15 Sha'ban, to Hasan al-Askari and a slave-woman usually named Narjis; her origin is reported variously, and the stories of her as a captured Byzantine princess have been described as hagiographic. Twelver accounts say his birth was kept secret from all but a few trusted associates for fear of the Abbasids; one early author, al-Nawbakhti, says he was born after his father's death. When his father died in 260 AH (874) without a publicly known heir, Twelver sources say the boy appeared once, to lead the funeral prayer, and then went into concealment; one modern reference work dates his disappearance to 878. During the Minor Occultation, of about seventy years, Twelvers held that he guided the community through four successive deputies: Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Asadi, his son Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Uthman, Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn ibn Ruh al-Nawbakhti and Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Samarri. When al-Samarri died in 329 AH (940-941) without naming a successor, Twelvers hold that the Major Occultation began, and that it continues today. Twelvers believe he will reappear at God's command before the Last Judgment to establish peace and justice, assisted by Jesus, and that the time of his return is unknown. His father's death without an evident heir split the Shia into many groups, most of which disappeared within a century, leaving the Twelvers.

dob_s: c. 497 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)

bio: Mother of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib (the Prophet's father); from the Banu Makhzum clan of Quraysh. Wife of Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim.
bio_full: Fatimah bint Amr ibn A'idh ibn Imran ibn Makhzum was the paternal grandmother of the Prophet Muhammad. She belonged to the Makhzum clan of Quraysh in Mecca. Her mother, Sakhrah bint Abd ibn Imran, was also of Makhzum, and her maternal grandmother was Takhmur bint Abd ibn Qusayy. She married Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim; unlike most of his other wives, who came from outside tribes, she was from Quraysh. Ibn Kathir names her as the mother of Abdullah, Abu Talib (whose name was Abd Manaf) and al-Zubayr, and of all Abd al-Muttalib's daughters except Safiyya. These daughters are named as Atika, Arwa, Barrah, Umm Hakim al-Bayda and Umayma. Through Abdullah she was the grandmother of the Prophet, and through Abu Talib the grandmother of Ali, Ja'far and Aqil ibn Abi Talib.

bio: Mother of Aminah bint Wahb (the Prophet's mother); from the Banu Abd al-Dar clan of Quraysh. Wife of Wahb ibn Abd Manaf al-Zuhri.
bio_full: Barrah bint Abd al-Uzza ibn Uthman ibn Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy was the maternal grandmother of the Prophet Muhammad. She belonged to the Abd al-Dar clan of Quraysh in Mecca. Her mother was Umm Habib bint Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza, a sister of Khuwaylid ibn Asad, the father of Khadija; Barrah was therefore a first cousin of Khadija, the Prophet's first wife. Her mother's mother was Barrah bint Awf, and her parents were second cousins. With Wahb ibn Abd Manaf she was the mother of Aminah bint Wahb, the Prophet's mother, who belonged to the Zuhra clan of Quraysh. Her lineage is recorded by al-Tabari and Ibn Sa'd.

classif: Wife of Hashim ibn Abd Manaf; mother of Abd al-Muttalib
bio: Wife of Hashim ibn Abd Manaf and mother of Abd al-Muttalib (Shayba). From the Banu Najjar of Yathrib (later Medina).
bio_full: Salma bint Amr ibn Zayd ibn Labid, of the clan of Adi ibn al-Najjar of the Khazraj in Yathrib (later Medina), was the wife of Hashim ibn Abd Manaf and the mother of Abd al-Muttalib, making her the Prophet Muhammad's great-grandmother. Ibn Hisham gives her lineage this way; the Companion dictionaries of Ibn Abd al-Barr, Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Hajar, in their entries on her son Amr ibn Uhayha, call her Salma bint Zayd of the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar. Later accounts describe her as a woman of standing in her clan who traded on her own account, and who agreed to marry Hashim, a Meccan merchant who came to Yathrib's market, on condition that she remain in Yathrib in charge of her own affairs. Their son, named Shayba, was raised among her people in Yathrib, and she also bore Hashim a daughter, Ruqayya. Hashim died at Gaza on a trading journey to Syria. While the boy was still young, Hashim's brother al-Muttalib came to take him to Mecca, and Salma agreed to let him go. According to the Companion dictionaries, after Hashim's death she married Uhayha ibn al-Julah and bore him Amr ibn Uhayha, a maternal half-brother of Abd al-Muttalib; other accounts place her marriage to Uhayha before Hashim.

bio: Egyptian Coptic Christian woman gifted by the Muqawqis of Egypt to the Prophet in 7 AH. Mother of the Prophet's son Ibrahim. Her status as wife or concubine is historically debated among scholars.
bio_full: Maria bint Sham'un, known as Maria the Copt, was an Egyptian Coptic woman and the mother of the Prophet Muhammad's son Ibrahim. Ibn Abd al-Barr gives her father's name as Sham'un, and al-Maqrizi places her origin in Hebenu, a village near Antinoöpolis in Egypt. Al-Muqawqis, the Christian ruler of Alexandria, sent her to the Prophet as a gift together with her sister Sirin; al-Tabari places this in 6 AH (627–628 CE), when Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a returned from his mission to al-Muqawqis. According to al-Tabari, Hatib invited both sisters to Islam on the journey and they accepted. The Prophet gave Sirin to Hassan ibn Thabit, to whom she bore Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan. Maria was first lodged with Umm Sulaym bint Milhan, and one account places her later home at al-Aliya, outside the centre of Medina, on a property afterwards called after her as Umm Ibrahim's. She bore Ibrahim in Dhu al-Hijja 8 AH; according to al-Waqidi, as cited by Ibn Kathir, he died at about eighteen months in Rabi al-Awwal 10 AH. Scholars differ on her status. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa'd and al-Tabari are cited as describing her as a wife, and Ibn Kathir reports that she is said to have married him, while Abu Ubayda and Ibn Qayyim call her a concubine, and Ibn al-Athir describes her as the Prophet's concubine and freedwoman. Ibn Abd al-Barr reports a narration that her son's birth freed her, but judges its chain weak. She died in Muharram 16 AH (637 CE), during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who gathered the people for her funeral and prayed over her. Ibn Abd al-Barr records that she was buried in al-Baqi.

bio: Eldest son of the Prophet Muhammad and Khadija bint Khuwaylid. Died in infancy in Mecca before the Hijra. The Prophet's kunya 'Abu al-Qasim' derives from him.
bio_full: Al-Qasim was the son of the Prophet Muhammad and Khadija bint Khuwaylid, born in Mecca before his father's prophethood began. Ibn Sa'd and Hisham al-Kalbi, reporting from Ibn Abbas, name him as the Prophet's eldest child, and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar states that the Prophet's kunya, Abu al-Qasim ('father of al-Qasim'), was taken from him. He died young in Mecca; al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar reports that he was the first of the Prophet's children to die there. Reports differ on how old he was. Mujahid is reported to have said he lived seven nights, which al-Mufaddal called an error, giving seventeen months instead; al-Zuhri said two years; and Qatada said he lived until he had begun to walk. Ibn Majah reports that he died before completing the age of nursing. One modern account dates his life to 598–601 CE and places his grave in the Jannat al-Mu'alla cemetery in Mecca.

dod_s: c. 681 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
classif: Granddaughter of the Prophet; daughter of Zaynab bint Muhammad and Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi
source: Ibn Hisham; al-Tabari; Ibn Sa'd; Sahih al-Bukhari (carried by the Prophet during prayer)
bio: Daughter of Zaynab bint Muhammad and Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi; granddaughter of the Prophet Muhammad. Famously carried by the Prophet during prayer (recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari). After the death of Fatimah al-Zahra, she married Ali ibn Abi Talib at Fatimah's request.
bio_full: Umamah bint Abi al-As was a granddaughter of the Prophet Muhammad through his eldest daughter, Zaynab. Her father was Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi, of the Abd Shams clan of Quraysh. Ibn Abd al-Barr says she was born during the Prophet's lifetime; one modern account gives her birth as 618 CE. The Prophet loved her, and Abu Qatada reported that he carried her on his shoulder while praying, setting her down when he bowed or prostrated and lifting her again when he stood. A report from A'isha, cited by Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir, tells that when a necklace was brought to the Prophet he said he would give it to the dearest of his family; the women expected it to go to A'isha, but he called Umamah and fastened it around her neck. After the death of her aunt Fatima, Ali ibn Abi Talib married her. Abu Nu'aym and Ibn al-Athir say Fatima had asked him to do so, while Ibn Abd al-Barr says al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam gave her in marriage, acting on her father's bequest. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Athir report that when Ali was fatally wounded he feared Mu'awiya would seek her hand, and told al-Mughira ibn Nawfal to marry her. After her waiting period she married al-Mughira and, by these accounts, bore him a son, Yahya, though another report says she had no children by either husband. She died while married to al-Mughira. Al-Tabari places her death at al-Safri around 680 CE; another account gives 670 CE (50 AH).

bio: Son of Uthman ibn Affan and Ruqayya bint Muhammad. Born in Mecca; died in Medina around 4 AH (624 CE) at approximately six years of age, reportedly from a wound to the eye. Uthman's kunya 'Abu Abdullah' derives from him.
bio_full: Abd Allah ibn Uthman was the son of Uthman ibn Affan, later the third caliph, and Ruqayya, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr state that Ruqayya bore him in Abyssinia, where she and Uthman had migrated, and Ibn Hajar also gives Abyssinia as his birthplace. Uthman, previously known by the kunya Abu Amr, took the kunya Abu Abd Allah after him. The boy died at the age of six. According to Ibn al-Athir and Ibn Abd al-Barr, a rooster pecked him in the eye (in Ibn Sa'd's version, the face); his face swelled, he fell ill and died. They date his death to Jumada al-Ula 4 AH (625 CE) and state that the Prophet prayed over him. Ibn Hajar cites a different report that he died a year before his mother, which would place his death in 1 AH.

bio: Third son of Ali ibn Abi Talib and Fatimah al-Zahra. Died in infancy or was stillborn; circumstances are historically disputed across Sunni and Shia traditions.
bio_full: Muhsin ibn Ali was a son of Ali ibn Abi Talib and Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, and a younger brother of al-Hasan and al-Husayn. Like his brothers' names, his comes from the Arabic root h-s-n and can mean 'beneficent'; some narrations say the Prophet chose the name. Ibn Hanbal and Ibn Abd al-Barr list him among Fatima's children. Sunni and Shia sources disagree about how and when he died. Most Sunni sources give no birth date and say only that he died young: Ibn Qutayba, al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri and Ibn Kathir describe him as dying in childhood, and Ibn Hazm adds 'very soon after his birth', while Salihi al-Shami and Ibn Sabbagh say he died through miscarriage. Shia accounts hold that Fatima miscarried him in 11 AH (632 CE), in the weeks after the Prophet's death, as a result of a raid on her house during the dispute over the succession; one version of Kitab Sulaym ibn Qays, Ibn Qulawayh's Kamil al-ziyarat and al-Mufid's al-Irshad are among the works cited for this view. Al-Shahristani records that the Mu'tazili al-Nazzam claimed a blow on the day of the pledge caused a miscarriage. Sunni scholars reject the account of an attack. No first-hand early source names his burial place.

full: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Sa'd ibn Mani' al-Basri al-Hashimi
primaryTitle: Author of Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kubra - Biographer of the Companions
titles: Katib al-Waqidi
bio: Muhammad ibn Sa'd was a 9th-century historian and biographer, known as the scribe of al-Waqidi. His Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kubra is one of the earliest surviving biographical dictionaries of the Prophet's companions and their successors.
bio_full:
Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Sa'd ibn Mani' al-Basri al-Hashimi, known simply as Ibn Sa'd, was born in Basra around 168 AH (784 CE) and settled in Baghdad, where he spent most of his scholarly life. He became the close student and secretary of the historian al-Waqidi, earning the lifelong nickname Katib al-Waqidi, the Scribe of al-Waqidi. He travelled to Kufa and Medina in pursuit of knowledge and studied with leading scholars of his generation.

His great work, Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (The Great Book of Generations), is one of the earliest and most important surviving biographical collections in Islam. Arranged by generation, it records the lives of the Prophet Muhammad, his Companions and Helpers, and the Successors who carried their knowledge forward, with a dedicated volume on the women of early Islam. Later biographical dictionaries across the Islamic tradition drew heavily on it.

Ibn Sa'd died in Baghdad in 230 AH (845 CE) at the age of 62 and was buried at the cemetery of the Syrian gate.

full: Fatima bint Musa b. Ja'far al-Ma'suma
primaryTitle: Daughter of Imam Musa al-Kazim — Lady of Qom
titles: al-Ma'suma (the Immaculate); Masuma-e-Qum
bio: Daughter of Musa al-Kazim, the seventh Twelver Imam. Born in Medina c. 790 CE; in 816 she travelled toward Merv to join her brother Ali al-Rida, fell ill on the way and died in Qom, where her shrine became one of the major pilgrimage centres of Shia Islam.
bio_full: Fatima bint Musa, known by the title al-Ma'suma ('the immaculate'), was a daughter of Musa al-Kazim, the seventh Twelver Shia Imam, and a sister of the eighth Imam, Ali al-Rida. She was born in Medina around 790 CE; her mother is named as Najma, also called Tuktam. After her father died in an Abbasid prison in 799, she was raised in the household of her brother al-Rida. When the caliph al-Ma'mun summoned al-Rida to Khurasan, Fatima set out from Medina to join him at Merv. On the way she fell ill at Saveh and asked to be taken to the nearby Shia town of Qom. One account says a local Shia notable, Musa ibn Khazraj al-Ash'ari, brought her to Qom and hosted her in her last days. She died there a few days after arriving, possibly after seventeen days, in 816 or 817; her age at death is not known with certainty. Reports that she was poisoned appear only in later accounts, not in early sources such as the Tarikh-i Qom of Hasan ibn Muhammad Qumi (written 988). She was buried outside the town on land owned by Musa al-Ash'ari, and the house where she stayed became a mosque. Traditions attributed to al-Rida and to his son Muhammad al-Jawad encourage pilgrimage to her grave. Successive dynasties enlarged the shrine, and the present complex dates largely from the Safavid and Qajar periods. It is uncertain when she was first called al-Ma'suma; the earliest known use is in an order of the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Jahan Shah in the fifteenth century.

dob_s: c. 850 CE (estimated from husband and son)
dod_s: c. 874 CE (260 AH per al-Saduq; disputed)
titles: Umm Muhammad; also recorded as Malika, Rayhana, Susan, Sayqal
bio: Wife of Hasan al-Askari, the eleventh Twelver Imam, and mother of Muhammad al-Mahdi, the twelfth. Sources differ on her origin (Byzantine or Nubian) and her exact death date; her tomb is in the al-Askari shrine in Samarra.
bio_full: Narjis was the wife of Hasan al-Askari, the eleventh Twelver Shia Imam, and, according to Twelver sources, the mother of the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi. Sources also call her Sawsan, Rayhana, Sayqal or Maryam; the flower names were probably given to her by her owner, Hakima Khatun, while Sayqal may have been her original name. Accounts of her origin differ. Some sources describe her as a Nubian slave. Ibn Babawayh (d. 991), the earliest source on her origin, and later writers such as al-Tusi and al-Majlisi describe her as a captured granddaughter of the Byzantine emperor who learned of her future marriage in a dream; modern scholars regard these accounts as hagiographic. Al-Mufid (d. 1022) says she was born and raised in the household of Hakima Khatun, daughter of the ninth Imam al-Jawad and aunt of al-Askari, and that the tenth Imam, Ali al-Hadi, gave her in marriage to his son. Twelver sources report that she bore Muhammad al-Mahdi around 255 AH (868 CE), most giving the date as 15 Sha'ban. After al-Askari's death in 260 AH, one account says she claimed to be pregnant to divert officials searching for his child; she was held in the palace of the caliph al-Mu'tamid, later escaped, and was protected by the Nawbakhti family. Her tomb is in the al-Askari shrine in Samarra, Iraq, alongside those of Hasan al-Askari, Ali al-Hadi and Hakima Khatun.

dod_s: c. 780 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
titles: Hamida al-Musaffa; Hamida al-Andalusiyya; Hamida Khatun
bio: A woman of Berber origin, wife of Ja'far al-Sadiq, the sixth Twelver Imam, and mother of Musa al-Kazim, the seventh. Shia sources describe her as learned in religious law; al-Sadiq sent women to her to learn religious rulings, and two hadiths are narrated from her.
bio_full:
Hamida, also written Humayda, was the wife of Ja'far al-Sadiq, whom Twelver Shia regard as their sixth Imam, and the mother of Musa al-Kazim, the seventh. Her titles include al-Musaffa, al-Barbariyya and al-Andalusiyya. Accounts of her origin differ: she is described as Berber, Andalusian, Roman or non-Arab ('Ajam), and later Shia scholars name her father as Sa'id and her brother as Salih. According to al-Kulayni, Muhammad al-Baqir bought her as a slave and advised his son Ja'far to marry her. Al-Majlisi lists four children born to her: Musa al-Kazim, Ishaq, Muhammad and Fatima. Abu Basir reports that Musa was born while al-Sadiq was travelling in the region of al-Abwa'.

In Shia sources al-Baqir praised her and al-Sadiq praised her purity. Al-Sadiq sent women to her to learn religious rulings, and placed her and Umm Farwa in charge of some financial matters in Medina. She narrated two hadiths from al-Sadiq: one on the rules of hajj for children, recorded by al-Kulayni, and one on al-Sadiq's death, recorded by al-Majlisi. Shia sources also report that she bought a slave woman named Najma and, after a dream, gave her to her son Musa al-Kazim in marriage, advising him to treat her well. Her date of death is not recorded in the sources consulted; her grave is placed at Mashrabat Umm Ibrahim in Medina.

primaryTitle: Wife of Imam Muhammad al-Jawad; Mother of Imam Ali al-Hadi
dob_s: c. 805 CE (estimated from son Ali al-Hadi b. 828)
dod_s: c. 865 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
titles: Samana al-Maghribiyya; Umm al-Fadl is a different wife
bio: Wife of Muhammad al-Jawad, the ninth Twelver Imam, and mother of Ali al-Hadi, the tenth, and of Musa al-Mubarqa. Of Maghribi origin per Shia sources.
bio_full:
Samana al-Maghribiyya, known as Sayyida and by the kunya Umm al-Fadl, was the wife of Muhammad al-Jawad, whom Twelver Shia regard as their ninth Imam, and the mother of Ali al-Hadi, the tenth. Shia sources describe her as a slave woman bought for seventy dinars on al-Jawad's order. Ibn Abi al-Thalj, however, names al-Hadi's mother as Asma'. Al-Jawad's other wife, the daughter of the caliph al-Ma'mun, also bore the kunya Umm al-Fadl.

According to Shia sources, all of al-Jawad's children were born to Samana: the sons Ali al-Hadi, Musa al-Mubarqa', Husayn and 'Imran, and the daughters Fatima, Khadija, Umm Kulthum and Hakima. These sources describe her as fasting and praying often, and report that Ali al-Hadi called her one who truly knew his rights and a dweller of paradise. She is listed among women who transmitted hadith. She lived in Samarra in the Abbasid period. Her date of death is not recorded in the sources consulted; her grave is in the shrine of the two Askari Imams in Samarra, beside those of Ali al-Hadi, Narjis, Hakima and Hudayth.

primaryTitle: Wife of Imam Ali al-Hadi; Mother of Imam Hasan al-Askari
dob_s: c. 825 CE (estimated from son Hasan al-Askari b. 846)
dod_s: c. 885 CE (survived al-Askari, honoured as Jadda — estimated)
titles: also recorded as Susan or Salil; honoured as Jadda (the Grandmother)
bio: Wife of Ali al-Hadi, the tenth Twelver Imam, and mother of Hasan al-Askari, the eleventh. Her name is recorded variously as Hudayth, Susan, or Salil. After al-Askari's death she was honoured among the Shia as Jadda, the grandmother of the Hidden Imam.
bio_full:
Hudayth was the wife of Ali al-Hadi, whom Twelver Shia regard as their tenth Imam, and the mother of Hasan al-Askari, the eleventh. Her name is also recorded as Salil, Susan, Hurayba and 'Asfan, and her kunya was Umm al-Hasan. Like the mothers of some other Imams, she had been a bondwoman. She lived in Medina and Samarra. Besides Hasan al-Askari, Shia sources name her children as Muhammad, Husayn, Ja'far and 'A'isha.

Shia sources report that Hasan al-Askari sent her on the hajj before his death and made her executor of his will, with charge of his endowments and charities. On learning of his death she went from Medina to Samarra. When her son Ja'far claimed the imamate and seized the inheritance, she complained to the ruler and the judge ruled in her favour; later, when Ja'far lost his wealth, she paid the living costs of him and his children. Shia sources describe her as a link between al-Mahdi, whom Twelver Shia regard as their Twelfth Imam, and the people, and she was called Jadda, "grandmother", because Twelver Shia hold that she was the grandmother of al-Mahdi. They describe her as honourable, pious and ascetic. Her date of death is not recorded in the sources consulted. She asked to be buried in her own house, and her grave now lies inside the shrine of Ali al-Hadi and Hasan al-Askari in Samarra.

full: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali al-Hadi (Sayyid Muhammad)
primaryTitle: Son of Imam Ali al-Hadi — Sayyid Muhammad of Balad
dob_s: c. 844 CE (estimated; elder brother of al-Askari b. 846)
titles: Sayyid Muhammad; Sab' al-Dujayl
bio: Eldest son of Ali al-Hadi, the tenth Twelver Imam, and elder brother of Hasan al-Askari. Known for piety; some Shia expected him to be the next Imam, but he died in 866 CE at Balad near Samarra during his father's lifetime. His shrine at Balad is a major visitation site.
bio_full:
Abu Ja'far Muhammad, known as al-Sayyid Muhammad, was the eldest son of Ali al-Hadi, whom Twelver Shia regard as their tenth Imam, and the elder brother of Hasan al-Askari and Ja'far. His mother was Hudayth. One account places his birth in 228 AH (842–43 CE) at Sarya, a village near Medina. Local people call him Sab' al-Dujayl, "the lion of Dujayl".

Many Shia expected him to succeed his father as Imam, but he died during his father's lifetime. In Twelver belief al-Hadi then indicated that Hasan al-Askari would be the next Imam. A group known as the Muhammadiyya held that Muhammad had not died and was the rightful successor; after al-Askari's death in 874, some argued he had been the true eleventh Imam and turned to his descendants or regarded him as the Mahdi. Another group, the Nafisiyya, believed he had named his brother Ja'far as successor through a servant named Nafis.

According to Shia sources, he set out for the hajj in 252 AH, fell ill at Balad near Samarra, and died there on 29 Jumada II 252 (17 July 866). Some suspected that the Abbasids had poisoned him. One modern account says only that he died in Samarra. Al-Majlisi records that his father held a mourning ceremony for him. He was buried at Balad, about 85 km north of Baghdad, in a shrine regarded as sacred by Twelver Shia; its first building is thought to date from the 4th/10th century, and it was attacked on 7 July 2016. His line continued through his sons Ahmad and Ali.

Wikipedia — Muhammad ibn Ali al-Hadi

primaryTitle: Alid leader; Governor of Yemen and Mecca
titles: al-Murtada
bio: Son of Musa al-Kazim, the seventh Twelver Imam, and brother of Ali al-Rida. He led an Alid rising in Yemen after the Fourth Fitna, seized Mecca around 817, and was then recognised by Caliph al-Ma'mun as governor of Mecca (817-820) and led the hajj in 818.
bio_full:
Ibrahim ibn Musa, called al-Murtada, was a son of Musa al-Kazim, whom Twelver Shia regard as their seventh Imam, and a brother of Ali al-Rida. He was born in Medina in 763. After the civil war of 811–813 weakened Abbasid rule, the Alid rebel Abu al-Saraya appointed him in 815 to take Yemen. The governor withdrew, and Ibrahim entered Sana'a in September 815. He ruled for about a year and minted coins in his own name; his harsh rule, with killings, enslavement and confiscations, earned him the name al-Jazzar, "the Butcher".

In 816 his forces failed to enter Mecca during the pilgrimage season, and the Abbasid commander Hamdawayh ibn Ali then defeated him and took Sana'a. By about 817 he had taken Mecca. Accounts differ on his movements: al-Ya'qubi has him go straight from Yemen to Mecca, while Yemeni writers keep him in Yemen until 818. Caliph al-Ma'mun reconciled with him, recognised him as governor of Mecca and also granted him Yemen, which Hamdawayh still held. Ibrahim enforced the oath of allegiance to Ali al-Rida as heir. He led the hajj in 818 and named his brother as heir in the prayers; al-Mas'udi calls him the first descendant of Abu Talib to lead the pilgrimage in Islam. A second attempt on Yemen in 818 failed. In 820 he was sent to Baghdad and replaced as governor of Mecca. He died in Baghdad, reportedly by poison; his death is dated after 837, or in 825. He was buried beside his father in the Quraysh cemetery at al-Kazimiyya.

bio_sources.title: Wikipedia — Ibrahim ibn Musa al-Kazim

full: Zayd ibn Musa ibn Ja'far, Zayd al-Nar
primaryTitle: Son of Imam Musa al-Kazim — Zayd al-Nar
dob_s: c. 770 CE (estimated from father Musa al-Kazim b. 745)
dod_s: c. 835 CE (lived under al-Ma'mun after 815 revolt — estimated)
titles: Zayd al-Nar (Zayd of the Fire)
bio: A younger son of Musa al-Kazim, the seventh Twelver Imam. He joined the Alid uprising of Abu al-Saraya in 815, captured and governed Basra, and earned the name Zayd al-Nar for burning the houses of Abbasid supporters. He surrendered under a letter of safe passage after the revolt failed.
bio_full:
Zayd ibn Musa was a younger son of Musa al-Kazim, whom Twelver Shia regard as their seventh Imam, and a brother of Ali al-Rida and of Ibrahim ibn Musa. In 815 he joined the unsuccessful Alid uprising led by Abu al-Saraya against the Abbasid caliphate. During the revolt he captured and governed Basra. According to al-Tabari, his rule there was marked by attacks on supporters of the Abbasids, and he became known as Zayd al-Nar, "Zayd of the Fire", because he had many houses belonging to Abbasids and their followers burned.

After Abu al-Saraya was defeated at Kufa, the Abbasid commander Ibn Abi Sa'id took Basra. Zayd received a letter of safe passage from him and surrendered. He later escaped from imprisonment and in June 816 rose again at Anbar together with Abu al-Saraya's brother, but they were soon defeated and recaptured. He died in Iraq; the sources consulted give no date of death or place of burial.

full: Abd Manaf ibn Zuhrah ibn Kilab
dob_s: c. 495 CE (estimated from son Wahb b. 520)
dod_s: c. 555 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
titles: of Banu Zuhra
bio: Pre-Islamic Quraysh figure of the Banu Zuhra clan in Mecca; son of Zuhrah ibn Kilab and father of Wahb ibn Abd Manaf, making him the great-grandfather of Aminah bint Wahb, the Prophet Muhammad's mother.
bio_full:
Abd Manaf ibn Zuhra was a man of Quraysh in pre-Islamic Mecca, a son of Zuhra ibn Kilab, from whom the clan of Banu Zuhra takes its name. The genealogist Mu'arrij al-Sadusi lists him and his brother al-Harith as the sons of Zuhra. His son Wahb was the father of Amina, the mother of the Prophet Muhammad; Abd Manaf was therefore Amina's grandfather and the Prophet's great-grandfather on his mother's side. Ibn Sa'd records Wahb's mother as Qayla (also called Hind) bint Wajz of the Khuza'a tribe.

Through another son, Uhayb, Abd Manaf was the ancestor of the Companion Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his brother 'Amir, who emigrated to Abyssinia, and of Makhrama ibn Nawfal, whom al-Sadusi calls the most knowledgeable of men about Quraysh. Nothing more about his own life is recorded in the sources consulted.

bio_sources.title: Mu'arrij al-Sadusi, Hadhf min Nasab Quraysh — sons of Zuhra b. Kilab (shamela)
Wikipedia — Wahb ibn Abd Manaf (citing Ibn Hisham and Ibn Sa'd)

full: Yusuf ibn al-Hakam ibn Abi Aqil al-Thaqafi
primaryTitle: Chief of Thaqif — Father of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf
dob_s: c. 635 CE (estimated from son al-Hajjaj b. 661)
dod_s: c. 695 CE (estimated — generation method; no recorded date survives)
titles: of Banu Thaqif
bio: A nobleman and head of the Thaqif tribe of Ta'if, closely allied to the household of Marwan ibn al-Hakam. He fought in Marwan's campaigns, including the Umayyad recovery of Egypt in 684, and was the father of the Umayyad viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf and of the governor Muhammad ibn Yusuf.
bio_full:
Yusuf ibn al-Hakam ibn Abi 'Aqil al-Thaqafi, known as Abu al-Hajjaj, was a man of the Banu 'Awf branch of Thaqif from Ta'if, and the father of the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf and of Muhammad ibn Yusuf. Modern historians, drawing on early accounts, describe him as a teacher in Ta'if before he and al-Hajjaj took up military service under the Umayyads. Ibn Manzur's abridgement of Ibn Asakir's History of Damascus states that he left Ta'if with the army of Muslim ibn 'Uqba sent against Medina, and al-Hajjaj is reported to have fought beside him at al-Harra. He later joined Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and the Egyptian historian Ibn Yunus records that he came to Egypt with Marwan in 65 AH (684–85) together with al-Hajjaj. Marwan sent him with the force of Hubaysh ibn Dulja; at al-Rabadha he and al-Hajjaj were captured, but both escaped unharmed.

As a hadith transmitter, al-'Ijli called him trustworthy (thiqa) and noted that he narrated only one hadith, on the honour of Quraysh, which he related from Muhammad ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. Ibn Hibban says people of the Hijaz narrated from him. The sources in Ibn Asakir's history describe him as virtuous, and al-Hajjaj is quoted calling him a man who fasted and prayed much. One report has him rebuking his son for wanting to kill a man and warning him that he would die a tyrant. His date of death is not recorded in the sources consulted.

bio: Known through the patronymic of his daughters Dubayya and Ruqayya bint Thabit bin Khalid, companions of Medina. A Badr-era Ansari companion of this name is recorded, but the identification is not certain enough to merge here.
bio_full: Thabit ibn Khalid ibn al-Nu'man ibn Khansa' was a Companion of the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Sa'd traces his lineage through 'Usayra ibn 'Abd ibn 'Awf ibn Ghanm, and Ibn Hibban counts him among the Banu al-Najjar. Ibn Manda notes that Musa ibn 'Uqba, citing al-Zuhri, gives his clan as Banu Taym Allah, while Ibn Ishaq places him among the Banu Ghanm. He fought at Badr, and Ibn Sa'd adds that he was also present at Uhud. Ibn Sa'd records that he had a daughter named Dubayya, whose mother was Idam bint 'Umar ibn Mu'awiya of the Banu Murra. Dubayya married Yazid ibn Thabit ibn al-Dahhak, the brother of Zayd ibn Thabit, and bore him a son, 'Umara. According to Ibn Sa'd, Thabit's line later died out and he left no descendants. Abu Nu'aym al-Asbahani and Ibn Manda report that he was killed as a martyr at the Battle of al-Yamama. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr gives the same account and also mentions another report that he was killed at Bi'r Ma'una.

bio: A sage named in the Quran to whom God granted wisdom; his counsel to his son is recorded in Surah Luqman (31:12-19). Mostly regarded as a wise man rather than a prophet. Dates legendary and undated; placed in the pre-Islamic Near Eastern era.
bio_full: Luqman, known as al-Hakim ("the Wise"), gives his name to the thirty-first chapter of the Qur'an, Surat Luqman, the only place where he appears in the Qur'an. There God says that He gave Luqman wisdom and told him to be grateful to God (31:12). The chapter then records his advice to his son: not to associate anything with God, for that is a great wrong (31:13); that God will bring forth any deed, even one the weight of a mustard seed hidden in a rock, in the heavens or in the earth (31:16); to establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong and bear patiently what befalls him (31:17); not to turn away from people in contempt or walk proudly on the earth (31:18); and to be moderate in his walk and lower his voice (31:19). Verses 14 and 15, set within this advice, are God's own command to be grateful to one's parents. Traditional Muslim scholars did not count Luqman among the prophets; Ikrima is named as an exception. According to most versions of his story, God offered him the choice between prophethood and wisdom, and he chose wisdom. Qur'an commentators record differing traditions about his origin: some describe him as a Black slave of Ethiopian or Nubian origin, others as an Egyptian, a carpenter or a shepherd. Most accounts of the Islamic period make him a counsellor (vizier) of the Prophet Dawud. Al-Tha'labi and al-Nisaburi gave chapters to his wisdom in their Stories of the Prophets.

bio_sources.title: Qur'an 31:12–19 (Sahih International, legacy.quran.com)
Wikipedia — Luqman

bio: Named once in the Quran (9:30), where the claim that he was 'son of God' is rejected. Widely identified with the biblical Ezra. Dates follow Jewish tradition (c. 5th century BCE), an estimate, not from the Quran.
bio_full: 'Uzayr is named once in the Qur'an, at 9:30, which states that the Jews said "'Uzayr is the son of God" just as the Christians said the Messiah is the son of God; the verse rejects both as sayings of their mouths that imitate earlier unbelievers. Ibn Kathir and Maududi are among the Muslim scholars who identify him with Ezra. Classical scholars often explained the verse as referring to a small group of Jews, or to extreme reverence for religious teachers. Some commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, identify 'Uzayr with the unnamed man of Qur'an 2:259, who passed by a ruined town and wondered how God would bring it back to life; God caused him to die for a hundred years and then raised him, showing him his food unspoiled and the bones of his donkey brought back together. Ibn Kathir relates that after the Torah had been destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, 'Uzayr restored it for the Israelites by having it written out from his memory, and that some Jews began to call him "son of God" because of this. Some Muslim scholars, Ibn Kathir among them, held that 'Uzayr was a prophet. A report that God removed his name from the list of prophets is graded weak and is rejected by most Islamic scholars.

bio_sources.title: Qur'an 9:30 (Sahih International, legacy.quran.com)
Wikipedia — Uzair

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — the wealthy rebel of Musa's people

relations.source: later tradition (Ibn Kathir); not stated in Quran

bio: A wealthy man of Musa's people who grew arrogant and was swallowed by the earth with his dwelling (Quran 28:76-82). Later tradition (Tafheem, Ibn Kathir) calls him a cousin of Musa — a tradition, not stated in the Quran. Era of Musa; dates legendary.
bio_full: Qarun is named in the Qur'an as one of the people of Musa who behaved arrogantly toward them (28:76). God had given him treasures whose keys alone would weigh down a band of strong men. Some of his people told him not to exult, to seek the Hereafter with what God had given him without forgetting his share of this world, to do good as God had done good to him, and not to spread corruption in the land (28:76–77). He replied that he had been given it only because of knowledge he possessed (28:78). When he went out before his people in his finery, those who desired worldly life wished for what he had, while those given knowledge said God's reward is better for those who believe and do good (28:79–80). God then caused the earth to swallow him and his home, and no one could help him; those who had envied him the day before recognised that God gives provision abundantly or sparingly as He wills (28:81–82). The Qur'an also names him with Pharaoh and Haman as those to whom Musa was sent and who called him a sorcerer and a liar (40:23–24), and among those who were arrogant in the land and could not escape God's punishment (29:39–40). Islamic tradition gives his lineage as Qarun ibn Yashar ibn Qahat ibn Lawi, making him a cousin of Musa; the Qur'an does not state this. Al-Baydawi relates that Qarun falsely accused Musa, and that God told Musa to command the earth, which swallowed Qarun with his riches and his palace. Ibn Kathir drew from the story the lesson that wealth is no sign that God is pleased with its owner.

bio_sources.title: Qur'an 28:76–82 (Sahih International, legacy.quran.com)

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — high minister of Pharaoh
bio: A high minister and aide of Pharaoh, named in the Quran among those who oppressed Musa's people (e.g. 28:6, 40:24). Era of Musa; dates legendary and undated.
bio_full: Haman is named six times in the Qur'an (28:6, 28:8, 28:38, 29:39, 40:24, 40:36) as an official of Pharaoh in the time of Musa. God says that He would show Pharaoh, Haman and their soldiers, through the oppressed Israelites, the very thing they feared (28:5–6), and that Pharaoh, Haman and their soldiers were sinners (28:8). Musa was sent to Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun, who called him a sorcerer and a liar (40:23–24). Pharaoh, declaring that he knew of no god for his chiefs other than himself, ordered Haman to fire clay into bricks and build him a lofty tower so that he might look upon the God of Musa, whom he thought a liar (28:38; 40:36–37). The Qur'an counts Haman, with Pharaoh and Qarun, among those to whom Musa brought clear proofs but who were arrogant in the land and could not escape God's punishment (29:39–40). God seized Pharaoh and his soldiers and cast them into the sea (28:40); of Haman and those named with him, the Qur'an says each was seized for his sin and some were drowned (29:40).

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — first king of the Israelites
bio: The king God appointed over the Israelites, who led them against Jalut (Goliath); Dawud served in his army (Quran 2:247-251). Identified with the biblical Saul. Dates legendary, era of the early Israelite monarchy.
bio_full: Talut is the king whom God appointed over the Children of Israel, according to the Qur'an (2:246–251). After the time of Musa, the leaders of the Israelites asked a prophet of theirs to appoint a king so that they could fight in God's cause. The prophet told them that God had appointed Talut as their king. They objected that they had more right to kingship and that he had not been given abundant wealth; the prophet answered that God had chosen him over them and increased him in knowledge and stature (2:247). The sign of his kingship was that the Ark would come to them, carried by the angels, bringing reassurance from their Lord and relics left by the families of Musa and Harun (2:248). Leading out his army, Talut told them God would test them with a river: whoever drank from it was not with him, except one who took a single handful. Most drank. After he crossed with the believers, some said they had no strength that day against Jalut and his soldiers, but those certain of meeting God said that many a small company had overcome a large one by God's permission (2:249). By God's permission they defeated the enemy, and Dawud killed Jalut (2:251). In a narration from al-Bara', the Companions at Badr were as many as those who crossed the river with Talut, more than three hundred and ten, and only believers crossed with him. Muslim exegetes explain the name Talut as meaning "tall". He is regarded as a divinely appointed king rather than a prophet.

bio_sources.title: Qur'an 2:246–251 (Sahih International, legacy.quran.com)
Wikipedia — Talut

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — the champion slain by Dawud
bio: The enemy champion killed by Dawud in the army of Talut (Quran 2:249-251). Identified with the biblical Goliath. Era of Dawud; dates legendary.
bio_full: Jalut is the leader of the army that Talut and the Israelites fought, named in the Qur'an at 2:249–251. After Talut's men had crossed the river with him, some of them said they had no strength that day against Jalut and his soldiers, but those who were certain they would meet God replied that many a small company had overcome a large one by God's permission, for God is with the patient (2:249). As they advanced against Jalut and his forces, they prayed for patience, firm footing and victory over the disbelieving people (2:250). By God's permission they defeated them, and Dawud killed Jalut; God then gave Dawud kingship and prophethood and taught him what He willed (2:251). The Qur'anic account of him is brief. Muslim scholars most commonly traced his origins to the Amalekites, and in early scholarly tradition his name became a byword for the oppressors of the Israelites before Dawud. Muslim tradition also saw the battle against him as a foreshadowing of the Prophet Muhammad's Battle of Badr.

bio_sources.title: Qur'an 2:246–251 (Sahih International, legacy.quran.com)
Wikipedia — Goliath (section: Islam)

bio: A righteous traveller-king named by title in the Quran (18:83-98), who built a barrier against Gog and Magog. His historical identity is debated in tradition. Dates legendary and undated.
bio_full: Dhul-Qarnayn ("the one of the two horns") is a ruler whose story the Qur'an tells at 18:83–98, in answer to those who asked the Prophet about him. God says He established him in the land and gave him the means to everything. He travelled until he reached the setting place of the sun, which he found setting in a murky spring, and near it a people; given the choice to punish them or treat them well, he said he would punish the wrongdoer, while whoever believed and did good would have the best reward. He then reached the rising place of the sun, where it rose on a people given no shelter from it. Next he came between two mountains, where a people who could hardly understand speech complained that Gog and Magog (Ya'juj and Ma'juj) were spreading corruption, and offered him tribute to build a barrier. He refused payment, saying what his Lord had given him was better, and asked only for their labour. He filled the gap with blocks of iron, had them heated, and poured molten copper over them, so that Gog and Magog could neither climb nor pierce it. He called it a mercy from his Lord, which his Lord will level when His promise comes (18:98). Islamic tradition relates that the Quraysh, advised by Jewish rabbis, put this question to the Prophet to test him. His identity is disputed. Alexander the Great was the most widespread identification among traditional Muslim scholars, but Ibn Kathir and Ibn Taymiyya rejected it because Alexander was not a monotheist. Al-Tabari distinguished an earlier Dhul-Qarnayn of Abraham's time from a later one; Ibn Hisham, drawing on Wahb ibn Munabbih, made him a Himyarite king; and the modern Muslim writers Sayyid Ahmad Khan and Abul Kalam Azad identified him with Cyrus.

bio_sources.title: Qur'an 18:83–98 (Sahih International, legacy.quran.com)
Wikipedia — Dhu al-Qarnayn

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — the tyrant king of Egypt
bio: The tyrant king of Egypt who opposed Musa and drowned pursuing the Israelites. The Quran uses the title 'Fir'awn' (Pharaoh), not a personal name. His minister was Haman. Era of Musa; dates legendary and undated.
bio_full:
Fir'awn (Pharaoh) is the ruler of Egypt who opposed the prophet Musa in the Qur'an. The Qur'an uses the title Fir'awn and gives him no personal name; in the earlier story of Yusuf the Egyptian ruler is instead called a king (malik).

The Qur'an describes Fir'awn's people oppressing the Children of Israel, killing their sons and sparing their women (2:49). When Musa came to him, Fir'awn questioned him about his Lord, claimed divinity for himself, called Musa mad and threatened him with prison. Musa's staff became a serpent and his hand shone white; Fir'awn's counsellors called this sorcery, and he summoned his magicians to a contest on a festival day. The Qur'an names Haman with him (28:4-8, 40:36). His wife, whom tradition names Asiya, believed (66:11), and a believing man of his own household spoke up for Musa (40:28-45).

Fir'awn drowned pursuing the Israelites. As he drowned he declared belief in the God of the Children of Israel, but the Qur'an says this came too late (10:90-91). Ibn Kathir cites a hadith of the Prophet through Ibn Abbas, graded hasan gharib sahih by al-Tirmidhi, that Jibril pushed mud from the sea into his mouth. The Qur'an says his body would be kept as a sign for those after him (10:92); Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas and others that the sea cast his body ashore because some Israelites doubted his death. Citing al-Bukhari through Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir states that Fir'awn and his people were destroyed on the day of Ashura.

bio_sources.title: Wikipedia — Pharaoh in Islam
Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur'an 10:90-92 (quran.com)

full: al-Aziz, minister of Egypt and master of Yusuf
primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — the Egyptian official who bought Yusuf
bio: Title meaning 'the Mighty One' used in the Quran for the Egyptian official who bought Yusuf and in whose house the seduction episode occurs (12:30, 12:51). Later tradition (Ibn Kathir) names him Qitfir/Potiphar. NOT to be confused with the same title 'al-Aziz' applied to Yusuf himself once he held office (12:78, 12:88). Era of Yusuf; dates legendary.
bio_full:
Al-Aziz is the title the Qur'an gives to the Egyptian official who bought the young Yusuf (12:21-35); the Qur'an does not give his personal name. Ibn Kathir explains that the man who bought Yusuf was the Aziz of Egypt, its vizier. Later reports name him: Ibn Abbas, through al-Awfi, called him Qitfir, while Ibn Ishaq called him Itfir ibn Ruhayb, in charge of the treasuries of Egypt under the king al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, an Amalekite. Ibn Ishaq named his wife Ra'il bint Ra'a'il; others called her Zulaykha.

When he bought Yusuf, al-Aziz told his wife to make his stay honourable, hoping he would be useful to them or that they might adopt him as a son (12:21). Ibn Kathir cites a report from Ibn Mas'ud that the three most perceptive people were the Aziz of Egypt when he said this, the woman who told her father to hire Musa, and Abu Bakr when he appointed Umar.

When Yusuf grew up, al-Aziz's wife tried to seduce him; Yusuf refused, calling her husband his lord (12:23). Her husband found them at the door and she blamed Yusuf. A member of her household advised checking Yusuf's shirt: torn at the front meant Yusuf was guilty, torn at the back meant she was. It was torn at the back, and al-Aziz believed Yusuf and told his wife to ask forgiveness. Even so, Yusuf was later imprisoned; the Qur'an says it seemed good to them to imprison him for a time (12:35). Years later, when the king inquired into the matter, al-Aziz's wife admitted Yusuf's innocence.

Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur'an 12:21 (English, quran.com)

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — the servant who taught Musa
bio: Unnamed in the Quran, which describes him as 'a servant from among Our servants whom We had granted mercy and knowledge' (18:65); the teacher Musa travels with. Named al-Khidr in later tradition. Regarded by some scholars as a prophet, by others as a righteous servant/wali. Dates legendary and undated.
bio_full:
Al-Khidr is the name Muslim tradition gives to the unnamed servant of God whom the prophet Musa meets in Surat al-Kahf (18:65-82). In a hadith from Ubayy ibn Ka'b cited by Ibn Kathir, Musa, asked who was the most learned of people, said that he was. God rebuked him for not leaving knowledge to Him and told him of a servant more learned than he at the junction of the two seas; Musa was to carry a fish, and where he lost it he would find the servant. Ibn Kathir states that this servant was al-Khidr, as the authentic hadiths indicate.

Musa asked to accompany him and learn from his knowledge. On the journey the servant damaged a boat, killed a boy, and rebuilt a falling wall in a town that had refused them hospitality, and each time Musa objected. The servant then explained: the boat was damaged so that a king who seized every boat by force would not take it from its owners; the boy's parents were believers and he would have burdened them with disobedience and ingratitude, and God would give them a better child; and the wall hid a treasure belonging to two orphans, which they could claim once grown.

Abu Hurayra reported that the Prophet said he was named al-Khadir ('the green one') because he sat on barren white land and it turned green with plants after him (al-Bukhari).

Muslim traditions differ on his status, describing him as a prophet or as a wali (saint). Whether he is still alive is also disputed: Ibn Ata Allah wrote that the Sufis agree he is alive, while other scholars doubt this. In Sufism he is seen as receiving knowledge directly from God, and several Sufi orders include him in their spiritual chains.

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — the Queen of Sheba
bio: Unnamed in the Quran, which calls her a woman ruling the people of Sheba; named Bilqis in later tradition. She submits to God alongside Sulayman (Quran 27:22-44). Era of Sulayman; dates legendary.
bio_full:
The Queen of Sheba appears in Surat al-Naml (27:22-44), where she is unnamed; the Qur'an calls her a woman ruling the people of Sheba. Later Muslim commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, name her Bilqis.

In the Qur'anic account, the hoopoe returns to the prophet Sulayman with news of Sheba, ruled by a queen whose people worship the sun instead of God. Sulayman sends her a letter inviting her and her people to submit to God. She calls the letter noble and consults her chiefs, who say they are strong and ready for war but leave the decision to her. She chooses instead to send envoys with a gift. Sulayman rejects the gift, saying God has given him better, and warns that he will come with forces they cannot resist. Before she arrives, a man with knowledge of the Scripture brings her throne in the blink of an eye; Sulayman has it disguised and asks whether it is hers, and she recognises it. She is then invited into a palace hall; thinking its glass floor is water, she lifts her skirt, and Sulayman tells her it is smooth glass. She says she has wronged herself and submits with Sulayman to God, Lord of the worlds.

Later tradition adds details that are not in the Qur'an. Al-Hamdani made her the daughter of the Sabaean king Ilsharah Yahdib, and al-Tabari is cited as giving her name as Yalamqa bint Alisharah.

bio: Unnamed in the Quran, which calls him one of the two sons of Adam (5:27-31); named Habil (Abel) in later tradition. The brother who was murdered. First human generation; dates legendary and undated.
bio_full:
Habil (Abel) is the name Muslim tradition gives to one of the two sons of Adam whose story the Qur'an tells without naming them (5:27-31). Each brother offered a sacrifice to God; Habil's was accepted and his brother's was not. When his brother threatened to kill him, Habil replied that God accepts only from the righteous, and that he would not raise his hand to kill his brother, because he feared God, Lord of the worlds. His brother killed him, and God then sent a crow scratching at the ground to show the killer how to hide his brother's body.

Ibn Kathir cites a report from Ibn Abbas, whose chain he calls better than good, explaining the dispute. Each pregnancy produced a boy and a girl, and Adam married each son to the other son's twin. Qabil's twin was beautiful and he refused to give her up, so both brothers offered a sacrifice. Habil offered a sheep and it was accepted; Qabil's offering of produce was rejected. Ibn Kathir also reports from Abdullah ibn Amr that Habil was the stronger of the two, but his fear of God held him back from fighting.

The Qur'an follows the story with the ruling that killing one soul unjustly is like killing all people, and saving one is like saving all people (5:32).

bio: Unnamed in the Quran, which calls him one of the two sons of Adam (5:27-31); named Qabil (Cain) in later tradition. The brother who committed the first murder. First human generation; dates legendary and undated.
bio_full:
Qabil (Cain) is the name Muslim tradition gives to the son of Adam who killed his brother, in a story the Qur'an tells without naming either brother (5:27-31). Each brother offered a sacrifice to God; his brother's was accepted and his was not. He threatened to kill his brother, who answered that God accepts only from the righteous and that he would not raise his hand against him. Qabil killed him. God then sent a crow scratching at the ground to show him how to hide his brother's body, and he lamented that he could not even be like the crow, and became one of the regretful.

Ibn Kathir cites a report from Ibn Abbas, whose chain he calls better than good: each pregnancy produced a boy and a girl, and Adam married each son to the other son's twin. Qabil's own twin was beautiful and he wanted her for himself, so both brothers offered a sacrifice. Habil's sheep was accepted; Qabil's offering of produce was rejected. Al-Suddi, attributing it to the Companions, said two crows fought, one killed the other and the survivor buried it.

Ibn Mas'ud reported that the Prophet said that whenever a soul is killed unjustly, the first son of Adam bears a share of it, because he was the first to commit murder; Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad and the major collections except Abu Dawud record it. The Qur'an follows the story with the ruling that killing one soul unjustly is like killing all people, and saving one is like saving all people (5:32).

primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — maker of the golden calf
bio: Named (with the article) in the Quran as the man who made the golden calf while Musa was on the mountain, leading the Israelites into idolatry (20:85, 87, 95). Era of Musa; dates legendary and undated.
bio_full:
As-Samiri is the man who, according to the Qur'an (20:85-97), made the calf for the Children of Israel while the prophet Musa was away on the mountain. He moulded it from the people's ornaments, and it gave out a lowing sound. Harun had warned the people that they were being tested. When Musa returned he questioned Harun and then as-Samiri, who said he had seen what the others did not see and had taken a handful from the trace of the messenger and thrown it in (20:96). Musa sentenced him to go away and to say all his life, 'No touching' (la misas), told him he could not escape his appointed fate, and had the calf burned and its remains scattered in the sea (20:97).

Most classical commentators understood the 'messenger' to be the angel Jibril and the 'trace' to be dust from the hoofprint of his horse, which gave the calf its sound. A minority view, reported by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi from Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, took the messenger to be Musa and the trace to be his teaching.

The word al-Samiri is a nisba. Classical commentators mostly took it as a name or as descent from a group called al-Samira; al-Baydawi records several views on his origin, including Kerman and Bajarma in Iraq, and the name Musa ibn Zafar. Commentators understood the sentence of 'no touching' as a life of exclusion as an outcast.

full: Numrud, the king who disputed with Ibrahim
primaryTitle: Quranic Figure — the king who disputed with Ibrahim
bio: Unnamed in the Quran, which describes the king who disputed with Ibrahim about his Lord (2:258) and, in tradition, threw him into the fire (21:68-69); named Nimrod in later tradition. Era of Ibrahim; dates legendary and undated.
bio_full:
Numrud (Nimrod) is the name Muslim commentators give to the king who disputed with the prophet Ibrahim about his Lord in the Qur'an (2:258), where the king is not named. Ibn Kathir, following Mujahid and others, gives his lineage as Numrud ibn Kan'an ibn Kush ibn Sam ibn Nuh, noting another lineage introduced with 'it was also said'. Mujahid said four kings ruled the whole earth, east and west: two believers, Sulayman and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and two unbelievers, Numrud and Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar).

In the Qur'an, Ibrahim tells the king that his Lord gives life and causes death; the king answers, 'I give life and cause death.' Ibrahim then says God brings the sun from the east, so let him bring it from the west, and the king is left confounded. Qatada, Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi explained his claim as pardoning one condemned man and executing another; Ibn Kathir saw it rather as stubborn pretence. Al-Suddi placed the debate after Ibrahim had been thrown into the fire.

Ibn Kathir relates from Zayd ibn Aslam that God sent an angel to call the king to belief and he refused. He gathered his army at sunrise, and God sent a swarm of gnats so thick they hid the sun, which ate his soldiers' flesh. One gnat entered the king's nostril and stayed there four hundred years, and he struck his head with mallets until God destroyed him by it. Ibn Kathir adds, with 'it is said', that he ruled for four hundred years. Al-Tabari reports that Numrud built a tower in Babil which God destroyed.
